The *Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha*,
accompanied by the commentary *Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā*, [edited] by Vāsudeva Śarman, son of the eminent scholar Lakṣmaṇa Śarman surnamed Paṇaśikara.
Revised (p. 1): Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Rāma.
The Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha,
accompanied by the commentary Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā.
The Section on Dispassion (Vairāgyaprakaraṇa).
The splendor known as Narasimha is the non-dual reality imagined through one's own ignorance.
I bow to Him who is to be known through the Vedānta, the embodiment of supreme bliss. (1)
The Veda proclaimed that the entire multitude of living beings breathes through the grace of the Supreme Bliss;
how then can the greatness of that Teacher, the Soul of all, who is thus declared by the Vedas, ever be fully described? || 2 ||

I worship from afar the Lord of the Universe, who is the sole adversary of the mountain of worldly existence, whose playful sport is solely the bestowing of knowledge, whose lotus feet are worshipped by multitudes of the best of sages,
who has shaken off all defects, and who is the embodiment of truth and wisdom, praised by hundreds of Vedas.

May he whose lotus feet are worshipped by all the gods protect us— he who, dwelling at the threshold of the royal capital of Śiva, wards off hundreds of obstacles with a mere glance, as if desiring to receive the external and internal honors rendered to him.

May that Śāradā— who, like the triple-pathed Gaṅgā, is to be served by all the gods, and whose plunging into the ocean of great majesty instantly purifies every person from the outcaste down to the dog-cooker— swiftly grant me all supreme boons. May the Gaṅgā of the sage Vālmīki’s speech flow forth in a thousand streams.
May my words, which have reached the ocean of Brahman, purify you thoroughly.
In the ritual of worshiping the lotus feet of Vasiṣṭha and Rāma, may my words become flowers and my mental fluctuations become lamps. (7)
Having bowed with devotion and my head to the words of the illustrious Guru Gaṇeśāna, which grant all desired objects, I compose this *Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā*.
Desiring to cross the ocean of Vasiṣṭha’s teachings as easily as Hanumān did [the ocean], I do so through devotion to the lotus feet of Rāma; may the wise ones grant me their forgiveness. 9.
Salutation to that All-Self, the pervasive Lord who shines as the nature of illumination within me— in heaven, on earth, in space, and both externally and internally. (1)

Then, at the beginning of the kalpa, the Supreme Self, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa— who is truth, knowledge, bliss, and non-dual— created the fields (kṣetras), which are dominated by darkness (tamas), and the individual souls (jīvas), which are dominated by consciousness (cit), in accordance with their respective dispositions, knowledge, and past actions. Thus it has been said by the Teachers:

"Through cultivation, knowledge, and action, that which is dominated by *tamas* among the fields (*kṣetra*) and that which is dominated by consciousness among the conscious selves (*cidātman*) attain the status of the supreme cause. Now, for the sake of the prosperity and liberation of the living beings created by Himself, [He] exists as the means and the goal.
He taught the meaning of the Vedas, characterized by ritual action and knowledge, to Marīci and others, as well as to Sanaka and others.

Observing that the practice of that Vedic meaning— which had been taught by them and was being performed by living beings— was being obstructed by thieves such as Rāvaṇa, he [acted] out of a desire to protect it.

The Blessed One, who has mastered all illusions and whose resolve is truth, having assumed the status of a servant through his own will, descended from Daśaratha into Kausalyā. Having descended, and assuming the role of a disciple of Vasiṣṭha,
he [Vālmīki] composed a dialogue adorned with a series of various narratives.

He manifested the essence of the nectar of knowledge (*jñānāmṛtarasa*) and set forth ritual action (*karma*); by the slaying of the hosts of Rākṣasas, he accomplished the protection of both. In this context, Rāma’s status as a disciple is intended to demonstrate that only Brahman is qualified for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Thus says the Śruti: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman..."

"Then he knew only himself through the thought, 'I am Brahman. Therefore, he became all that. And so says the Vārttika: "That very same formless Supreme, mounted upon the mirror of its own reflection, attains the status of being qualified for the knowledge of Brahman due to its twofold nature. And that...
The blessed Vālmīki, endowed with divine knowledge, composed the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma in thirty-two thousand verses;
this very work is the ocean of the Vasiṣṭha.

Observing that this ocean of the world—which establishes dispassion, the seeker of liberation, worldly conduct, the origin and maintenance of the universe, and its cessation and nirvāṇa; which is the abode of jewels such as discernment, dispassion, renunciation, and higher knowledge; and which is difficult for those of dull intellect to cross—the supremely compassionate Kashmiri scholar named Abhinanda composed six thousand verses.
Therefore, he extracted it.
We shall now explain this Vāsiṣṭha [text] according to our own understanding for the benefit of those of dull intellect.

In order to ensure the completion of the work he intends to compose without obstacles and for its widespread propagation, the venerable Teacher performs at the outset an auspicious invocation consisting of a salutation to his chosen deity; by doing so, he also indicates, through implication, the subject matter to be expounded in the treatise: "In heaven... and so forth.

Because the word "which" (*yat*) denotes a well-known referent, and because the Self (*ātman*) is well known, the Self is connected as the subject—namely, "the Self which [is this]. The connection is: "Salutation to that Self which shines forth to me. He shows its essential nature with the words "manifestation" (*avabhāsa*): manifestation is consciousness, the Self.
He whose nature is such is "tathā"; the word "vibhu" (all-pervading) excludes limitation by space.

The meaning is that it pervades all regions. He establishes its omnipresence with the words beginning "In heaven," etc. Thinking that an object taught through both summary and detail causes the intellect of the listener to ascend [to understanding] without effort, he [now] sets forth the meaning already explained in detail.
He states it concisely: "both outside and inside. Alternatively, [it refers to] Him who shines both within and without the three worlds, according to the Śruti:
"Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without"; and according to the Smṛti: "Both moving and non-moving beings, both outside and inside. In such a nature of the Self—
The venerable Vālmīki indicates that the experience of the wise is the authoritative means of knowledge with the words: "He who shines forth..."

If it is argued that because of the existence of entities distinct from the Self, there would be a real limitation (*pariccheda*) [of the Self], he says "no": "To Him, whose nature is the ultimate reality. By the negation of the limitation of the Self by entities, its limitation by time should also be understood as negated; for time, too, is in reality merely imagined within the Self.

Because it bestows the manifestation of existence, it is impossible for the Self to be delimited by that [body]. Alternatively, salutations to Him who shines as the witness within the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra) which is illuminated by ignorance, within the gross body (sthūla-śarīra) which is the ground of worldly activity, and within the causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra) called the unmanifest (avyākṛta), which is like space; the rest is as before. Now, he who is other than...

"He who worships a deity [thinking], 'That one is another, I am another,' does not know; he is, as it were, a beast of the gods"— thus the Śruti [condemns] the perception of a deity as distinct from the Self.

Because of the censure [of external deities] and because of the *Manusmṛti* stating that "the Self alone is all the deities," it should be understood that the Self itself is saluted as one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Alternatively, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is connected as the subject [of the sentence];
since that which is the Supreme Self is well-known as the Lord (*īśvara*), [the author] precludes its difference from the individual souls (*jīva*s).
"Of the self of all" (*sarvātmane*): salutation to the Self of all living beings, whose nature is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-svarūpa*). The rest is the same.

Alternatively, by mentioning "earth" at the beginning and "space" at the end, the three intermediate elements are also included by the logic of the "tongs" (*saṃdaṃśa-nyāya*), since they are grasped through the mention of the causal elements.

And this is the meaning: salutation to Him who shines within the elements and elemental products, such as space and the rest, as the inner Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), and who shines externally in heaven, in His own majesty, beyond the cycle of worldly existence—according to the Vedic revelation:
"All beings constitute one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven. Thus it is.

It has thus been shown that the reality to be propounded by the scripture is the conscious self (cidātman), which is devoid of the threefold distinctions and is eternally non-dual and perfect. || 1 ||
He who possesses the conviction, "I am bound; may I become liberated," is neither entirely ignorant nor fully wise; such a person alone has the qualification for this scripture.

Having shown the subject matter at the beginning of the treatise as a necessary factor for the listener’s engagement, [the author] now shows the qualified candidate and indicates the purpose and the relationship [between them] with the words: "I am bound. The construction is as follows: he who possesses the conviction, "I am bound; may I be liberated," is the one qualified to hear this treatise.

He shows the initial knowledge (*āpātajñāna*) which prompts the hearing and other [stages] of that [Brahman] with the words "not absolutely" (*nātyantam*). The word division is *no* (not). The word *tat* refers to Brahman, according to the traditional teaching: "Oṃ, Tat, Sat—this is declared to be the threefold designation of Brahman.
The phrase *tajjñaḥ* means "one who knows that," i.e., a knower of Brahman; or alternatively, the word division is *na uta jñaḥ* (nor even a knower).

The word *uta* has the sense of "also" (*api*). According to Amarasimha, *uta* is used for the meanings "also" (*api*) and "option" (*vikalpa*). Thus, *jña uta* means "even one who knows. Since it is impossible to engage in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth when Brahman is either perfectly known or entirely unknown, the meaning is that the qualified seeker is one who knows [Brahman] only superficially (*āpātataḥ*). This is indicated by the phrase "may I be liberated."

It has been indicated that the cessation of bondage is the purpose of hearing this scripture. Furthermore, by the statement "not entirely ignorant" and so forth, it is made known that the relationship between the scripture and Brahman is characterized as that of the means of communication and the object to be communicated. || 2 ||
Having prostrated himself before his teacher Vālmīki, the all-seeing one, who was seated in a secluded place, Bharadvāja questioned him in a gentle voice. (3)

Thus, having first performed the ritual invocation of auspiciousness (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) and indicated the subject matter (*viṣaya*) with the first verse, and having then made known the qualified student (*adhikārin*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the relationship (*saṃbandha*) with the second [verse], the author, commencing the treatise, introduces the sequence of teacher and disciple in order to illuminate its initial form as a narrative of dialogue, beginning with the words "the Guru."

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: Bharadvāja, the disciple, having bowed down before his teacher Vālmīki—who was seated in a secluded place for the sake of savoring the bliss of Brahman and whose nature was characterized by equanimity—questioned him in a soft tone, in such a way that it was a gentle sound. || 3 ||
"O Blessed One, I wish to know how Rāma conducted himself within this perilous cycle of existence; out of compassion, tell me, O Teacher. (4)
"Bhagavan" means "O Lord. *Saṃkaṭam* means "distress" (*saṃbādhaḥ*). According to Amara, *saṃkaṭa* is masculine, while *saṃbādha* is neuter.

*Vyavahṛtaḥ* means "he conducted himself" or "he acted. Here, the construction requires supplying an ellipsis: "Having attained the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), how did Rāma conduct himself within the distress of worldly existence?"

How is it known that Bharadvāja asked about this very same matter? It is stated in the *Bṛhadvāsiṣṭha*: in response to the earlier question, "How did Rāma conduct himself amidst the perils of saṃsāra? [it is said]: "O Brahmin, having first established the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) for the descendant of Raghu..."

From the statement, "Tell me in due order so that I may always be happy," and from the commencement of the reply, "Listen as I tell you how the high-minded Rāma attained the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta)," it is clear. Furthermore: "Those followers of Rāma, or those sons of his ministers, who were of great intellect..."

"Freedom from suffering. This is understood from the question following those concerning Rāma, Bharata, and others—asking how they attained it—and from the subsequent question regarding the manner of attaining liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), characterized by the state of being free from suffering for the sons of the ministers. Thus, [the text] says: "Tell me clearly how these very states were attained."
This very same point was asked by Bharadvāja. || 4 ||
Vālmīki said:
Well done, dear Bharadvāja; you are worthy, so I shall tell it to you.
By means of which sacred learning you shall cast the impurity of delusion far away. || 5 ||
"Excellent, my child!"—this should be connected by supplying the thought: "What you have asked is excellent.

You are fit to hear it. To you (*te*): by which means of attaining liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*) as Rāma, you will cast far away delusion (*saṃmoha*), that is, ignorance (*ajñāna*). [Thus,] with ignorance destroyed...
The meaning is "you shall become [so]. Alternatively, delusion itself is the impurity because it is to be abandoned; for this very reason, its casting far away is appropriate. || 5 ||
O virtuous one, regarding this worldly delusion that has arisen like the color of the sky,
I consider its non-recollection to be better than mere forgetting.

In response to the question, "O Rāma, how did he conduct himself amidst the perils of saṃsāra?", the author will first state the means for attaining the direct realization of the Self— which serves as the instrument for the aforementioned liberation while living— by means of the following passage beginning with, "How the high-minded Rāma attained the state of one liberated while living. This is intended to describe the means for the purification of the mind.

Meditation, characterized by the state where only pure consciousness remains and well-known as *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*, is intended to be explained in detail through the narrative of Rāma’s life; however, for the sake of ease of understanding, he states it briefly along with its means in the verse beginning with "bhramasya. Alternatively, [it refers to] the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).

Intending to provide the answer to the question with the words beginning "attained" (*prāpta*), [the author] first states the meaning of the scripture— namely liberation and its means— in brief for the sake of facilitating understanding, using the verse beginning with "of delusion" (*bhramasya*).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: I consider the forgetting of the world—that is, of the delusion pertaining to the world—to be the best and most excellent means, just like the color of space or the dark-blue of space. Furthermore, "non-recollection" (*apunaḥ-smaraṇam*) refers to that forgetting in which there exists no recollection of the object of the world-delusion as being real.

Alternatively, when the root ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) has been severed by knowledge, the very absence of delusion is intended by the word "forgetting"; for this reason, it is called "non-recollection again" (*apunaḥsmaraṇa*). || 6 ||
If, through the realization that "the visible does not exist," the cleansing of the mind's objects of perception is accomplished,
then the supreme bliss of nirvāṇa has arisen.

Regarding the phrase "the visible": if the cleansing of the visible— from the mind (*manas*), which consists of volition and is part of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— has been accomplished through the knowledge produced by scripture and other means, namely that "the visible does not exist as something imagined apart from the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the seer," then...
The cessation of nirvāṇa, which is the bliss of liberation, becomes manifested upon its arising.
He precludes the possibility that it possesses any degree of gradation, as is the case with sensory pleasures, by stating "supreme" (para).

When the firm conviction regarding the falsity of the visible world is established, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that world cease; because attachment does not arise therein, the mind turns away from it and plunges into the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*). Consequently, through direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) free from all obstructions, liberation (*nirvāṇa*) occurs—this is the intended meaning. || 7 ||
Otherwise, for you who roam amidst the pits of the scriptures and possess unrefined ignorance, there will be no peace even in aeons. (8)
He states the fault for those who do not achieve the mind's turning away from sense objects through the power of knowledge with the words "otherwise."

Without attaining inwardness in the manner described, those who, through outwardness, wallow in the pits of the scriptures— wherein the scriptures themselves are the pits or wells— and who perform mere physical exertions;
for such non-knowers of Brahman as yourselves, Bharadvāja and others, there exists only unauthentic knowledge (*akṛtrimājñā*).

Even in an exceedingly vast duration of time, measured in *kalpas*, there is no *nirvṛti*—that is, the bliss of liberation. Alternatively, the two words "akṛtrimā" (unartificial) and "ajñānām" (of the ignorant) may be connected as follows: for the ignorant, there is no unartificial *nirvṛti*.
This is just as for those wallowing in a pit, their wallowing results only in suffering produced by contact with mud and the breaking of limbs.
In the same way, for those whose minds are directed outwardly, listening to the scriptures leads only to suffering and not to happiness; this is the intended meaning.
The complete renunciation of all latent impressions (vāsanās), which is supreme, is called liberation by the wise; that alone is the stainless path.
Since the cleansing of the visible world occurs only through the cessation of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the visible, the abandonment of these impressions must be practiced;
for it is the supreme means to liberation by way of cleansing the visible and so forth. Thus he says:
"Without remainder. How [is this] abandonment of impressions [achieved]?

Anticipating the objection that this might imply the state of liberation itself [is the means], he says "that very [thing]" with the intention that it is so by way of metaphorical designation. The meaning is that the abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone is the stainless sequence, the pure method for liberation. || 9 ||
Impression (vāsanā) is said to be of two kinds: pure and likewise impure. The impure is the cause of birth; the pure is the destroyer of birth. (10)

Since it is stated in general that "the abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā) is the means to liberation," and this might lead to the conclusion that all latent impressions must be abandoned without distinction, the author states the twofold nature of latent impressions in order to show that pure latent impressions are not to be abandoned: "Vāsanā... [and so forth].

He demonstrates that these two produce contrary effects for the purpose of making known what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted: "Stained," "dense with the form of ignorance," "possessing thick egoism," and "producing rebirth"—thus is the stained latent impression (*vāsanā*) described by the wise. (11)

In this regard, he states the definition of impure latent impressions (*malinavāsanā*): "By ignorance... and so forth. That [impression] whose form is very dense, very compact, or very firm due to ignorance is described as such. For it is only when ignorance exists that the density of the latent impression occurs, and not otherwise. It shines—that is, it manifests—through a dense, compact, or firm ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
Thus she was possessed of dense egoism. || 11 ||
Having abandoned the sprouts of rebirth like a fallen seed, she remains;
though she sustains a body for its sake, she is called "pure" because she has known that which is to be known.
He states the definition of pure latent impression (*śuddhavāsanā*) as follows: "Rebirth... and so forth.
Like a seed that has been scorched—that is, like a seed properly roasted so that it is incapable of sprouting again—it remains [in this state] for the sake of the body;

it is maintained for the purpose of sustaining the present body. It is described as such because the object of knowledge (jñeya), namely Brahman, has been known by it, with that [knowledge] serving as the instrumental cause. || 12 ||

Those of great intellect whose latent impressions are purified so that they are no longer vessels for the miseries of rebirth, and who have known that which is to be known, are called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 13 ||

He elaborates on the very point already stated: "Those whose... and so forth. Birth itself is the misfortune; those persons who are vessels—that is, receptacles—of that misfortune of birth are "vessels of the misfortune of birth. Those individuals who possess pure latent impressions (*vāsanā*), who have known what is to be known, and who are of great intelligence, do not again become vessels for the misfortune of birth; and they are called "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*).

The interpretation (*yojanā*): Since pure and impure latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have such characteristics, therefore, by one desiring liberation, the pure impression is not to be abandoned, but rather the defiled one; however, the pure one is to be cultivated with effort—this is the collective meaning.
(9) Listen as I shall tell you how the high-minded Rāma attained the state of liberation while living, for the sake of pacifying old age and death. 14.

Thus, having briefly described samādhi— which serves as the means for the knowledge that is the instrument for liberation while living (jīvanmukti)— as well as liberation with its means and the meaning of the scriptures which characterizes those means, [the author now asks]: by what sequence did Rāma, having attained the state of one liberated while living, conduct himself amidst the perils of worldly existence?

He provides the answer to the question, preceded by a formal proposition, through the composition of the subsequent text beginning with "jīvanmukta" and so forth: "The state (*pada*)—meaning the station (*sthāna*) or sovereignty (*svārājya*) characterized by the supreme bliss of liberation (*nirvāṇa*)—of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), in what way (*yathā*) and by what method (*yena prakāreṇa*); that is to say, by what sequence (*krama*). (14)
Having departed from the house of learning, the lotus-eyed Rāma spent his days at home, free from all fear, in playful diversions.
From the house of knowledge—that is, from the place of acquiring learning or from the teacher's house. *Rājīvam* means a lotus. || 15 ||
Then, as time passed, the mind of the virtuous Rāma became eager to behold the series of sacred fords and holy hermitages.
"Sacred fords and holy hermitages" refers to *tīrthapuṇyāśramas*; "their rows" means their lines.
"Longing" (*utkaṇṭhitam*) means that a yearning (*utkalikā*) has arisen in him; the meaning is that his passion has been awakened. || 16 ||
Having reflected thus, Rāghava approached his father’s feet and grasped them by their claws and hair— those two fresh lotuses— as a swan might seize two new lotuses.
The two feet are so described because their very nails are fresh and new filaments, like the pollen-tufts of a flower. || 17 ||
Rāma said:
"O Lord, O Father, my mind is eager to behold sacred fords, temples of the gods, forests, and shrines. (18)
*Devasadyāni* refers to temples; *āyatanāni* and *caityāni* are also [temples]. Amara states: "A *caitya* and an *āyatana* are synonymous."
Therefore, O Lord, you ought to make this former request of mine fruitful;
for there is no petitioner in the world who has not been honored by you. (19)
Therefore; "arthī" means a beggar. || 19 ||
Thus entreated by Vasiṣṭha,
the king then deliberated and released Rāma first, even though he was the primary petitioner.
The indeclinable *samam* is used in the sense of "together with"; as stated in the Amarakośa: "sākam, sārdham, samam, and saha [are synonyms]."
While putting it on, he effected its release. || 20 ||
On an auspicious day under a favorable constellation, Rāghava, intent on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, departed from his home together with his two brothers.
A day accompanied by a lunar mansion is a *nakṣatradivasa*; on such a day he went forth, having departed. || 21 || 22 ||
Then, beginning from his own territory, he gradually beheld the Kosala region,
preceded by ritual bathing, charity, recitation, and meditation.
Rivers, sacred fords, holy forests, and sanctuaries;
wildernesses at the edges of the woods, and the shores of oceans and mountains. (23)

"Jāṅgalas" refers to regions abounding in wind, according to the statement that "jāṅgala is characterized by a preponderance of wind. Alternatively, *jaṅgala* is a forest situated in a desert region; the lands associated with that are *jāṅgalas*. || 23 ||
Honored by gods, kinnaras, and humans, the joy of the Raghus, having surveyed this entire earth, returned to his own home like the Lord Śiva after wandering through the quarters of the world.
He by whom the quarters have been traversed and played with is thus described. || 24 ||
Scattered with handfuls of parched grain and flowers by the city-dwellers,
the glorious Jayanta entered the city like [Indra] entering heaven.
Jayanta is the son of Indra; viṣṭapa means heaven. || 25 ||
From that time forward, Rāghava lived happily in his home,
describing the various customs and manners of the different regions here and there.
He dwelt; he has resided. || 26 ||
Having risen in the morning and performed the twilight devotions according to the rules, Rāma then beheld his father, who was seated in the assembly hall like Indra himself. (27)
"Sabhāsaṃstham" means one whose establishment and abiding are in the assembly (sabhā). || 27 ||
Having spent a fourth part of the day with Vasiṣṭha and the others, he remained surrounded by most varied discourses filled with wisdom.
By those narratives in which knowledge is contained within their womb. || 28 ||
Permitted by his father and surrounded by a vast army, he went to the forest—thick with boars and buffaloes—with the desire to hunt. (29)
With a great desire for the hunt, that is, with a longing for the chase. || 29 ||
Then, having returned to his home and performed his ablutions and other rites in due order,
he ate together with his friends and kinsmen and passed the night with his companions.
The dwelling is the house. || 30 ||
Thus, having returned from his pilgrimage, Rāghava, following his daily routine, dwelt together with his two brothers in his father’s house.
"Thus, 'the daily conduct' constitutes one section. || 31 ||

The sinless king passed his days with this moonlight-like conduct, which was pleasing to the royal administration, delightful to the hearts of the virtuous, and as tender as the flowing essence of nectar.
With that which was pleasing to the king’s conduct, delightful through its royal propriety,
a moonlight to the minds of the virtuous— bringing joy like the light of the moon—
and tender as if dripping with the essence of nectar; for the root *sru* means "to flow."
Like the essence of nectar, the essence of immortality, so too [it was] tender and charming. || 32 ||
Then, while in his sixteenth year, that scion of Raghu’s lineage grew thinner day by day, like a pure lake in autumn.

Herein lies the sequence of means for the attainment of the supreme good as declared in the Śruti: from the performance of the duties of one’s own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) without desire for rewards, merit arises; from that, the destruction of sin occurs, according to the Śruti text, "By merit one drives away evil. From that, the mind acquires the capacity for discrimination (*viveka*). From that—

The thorough knowledge of the reality of saṃsāra; from that, dispassion and so forth; from that, the desire for liberation (mumukṣutva); from that, the search for the means to liberation; from that, the renunciation of all actions (sarvakarmasaṃnyāsa); from that, approaching the feet of a guru; from that, the practice of hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth; from that, the direct realization of Brahman as the Self (brahmātmasākṣātkāra); and from that, the destruction of ignorance.

Consequently, there is an abiding in *svārājya* (sovereignty) itself; for the scripture states: "This serene being (*saṃprasāda*), having risen up from this body and having attained the highest light, manifests in its own true form. This sequence [of stages] is intended for the benefit of only a few preeminent men who are devoted to the worship of the lotus feet of Rāma, the Teacher of the World.

Now, wishing to demonstrate the performance of desireless action by the son of Daśaratha— who, though being the Supreme Person, bore the burden of eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman out of a desire to favor the worlds— the author has described that performance through the preceding textual composition; he shall now describe its fruit.

He shows the characteristics of discernment (*viveka*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*) with the word "atha" (now). "Ūna" means deficient; "ṣoḍaśa" is that which completes the sixteen. Thus, "ūna-ṣoḍaśa" means when that sixteenth year is nearly completed—this is the meaning. || 33 ||
Gradually, O large-eyed one, his face took on a pallid hue,
like a white lotus with blossoming petals that has turned pale at its stalk.

"Viśālākṣam" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound [meaning "having large eyes"]. "With its petals (*dala*) fully blossomed (*utphulla*) through ripening (*pāka*), that is to say, by the ripening of time"—this refers to the lotus. "Accompanied by a row of bees (*ali*)" means it exists together with a line of bees; thus, it is "sālimālam. || 34 ||
With his palms resting upon the surface of his cheeks, seated in the lotus posture, he became silent and inactive, entirely overcome by anxiety. || 35 ||
The connection is that he became silent. || 35 ||
Possessed by thoughts of his emaciated body, distressed and deeply dejected,
he said nothing to anyone, like one fixed in a painting.

"Extremely dejected" means one whose mind is utterly devoid of joy; he is so described because he resembles a painting depicted or fixed upon a wall or similar surface by the act of painting. || 36 ||
Being entreated again and again by his attendants out of weariness,
he performed his daily ritual with his lotus-like face faded.
By the retinue, that is, by the servants. || 37 ||
(13) "O son, what is this heavy anxiety of yours?"— thus King Daśaratha asked with affectionate words, repeatedly taking him onto his lap. (38)
"Dense" (ghanā) means thick or firm. "Lap" (utsaṅga) means the fold [of a garment] or the bosom. || 38 || 39 ||
Having said, "Father, I have no suffering at all," Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, remained seated on his father's lap in total silence.
At that very time, however, the great seer known as Viśvāmitra arrived to see that lord of men in Ayodhyā.

Having thus briefly established that dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the fruit of action performed without desire, and wishing now to explain this very point in detail through a series of questions and answers, [the author] introduces the context for the question with the words beginning "In this...
[etasmimn ityādi]. "Renowned" (*viśruta*) means famous or well-known. (40)
Seeing him adorned with splendor, the king, his face beaming with joy, offered a golden seat and personally presented the guest-offering (arghya).
By *lakṣmī*, which consists of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Spiritual luster is indeed the radiance residing in the skin produced by vows and Vedic study.
"Mālita" means that a garland has been produced; the sense is that he was surrounded by the splendor of a garland-maker. "Svarṇaviṣṭara" means a golden seat. || 41 || 42 || 43 ||
To that wise Viśvāmitra who was seated,
he repeatedly offered water for his feet, the guest-offering, and a cow.
Having honored Viśvāmitra according to the prescribed rites, the king, with palms joined in reverence and a composed mind, spoke these words with a joyful heart. (43)
O holy one, we have been graced by your radiant vision, which has appeared unexpectedly; we are like beds of lotuses favored by the sun.

"Aśaṅkitopanītam" means brought near unexpectedly and without prior intention; that is to say, brought into one's presence without my own volition. It is "bhāsvatā" (shining), because its object is luminous, or alternatively, because it is clearly manifest. That the sun is "unexpectedly brought near" and is "shining" is indeed well known. || 44 ||
(Repeat page 13)
(Repeat page p.
14) That which is beginningless, that which is unimpaired, and that which is free from states of woe.
O Sage, that blissful joy has been attained today through the sight of you.

He demonstrates that it is favored [by the scriptures] with the words: "That which is beginningless" (*yadanādi*). He says "imperishable" (*apāya*) so that it may not be non-eternal like a prior negation (*prāgabhāva*), even though it is beginningless; "perishing" (*apāya*) means destruction. He says "beginningless" (*anādi*) so that it may not be something with a beginning, like a posterior negation (*pradhvaṃsa*), even though it is imperishable. Furthermore, even for that which is devoid of beginning and end, there is no immutability (*kūṭasthanityatva*).
To the objection that it is like the earth and other elements for those who maintain the eternity of the world, he says: "unimpaired."

The term *akṣuṇṇa* means that, unlike earth and other elements, it is not in any place "crushed" or broken into parts; thus it is *kūṭastha*, meaning eternal. *Ānanda-sukha* is the bliss of Brahman. "He understood that bliss is Brahman"; "Brahman is consciousness and bliss"; "If this bliss did not exist in the ether... [so it is said].
Because Brahman is well-known in such scriptural passages as "Bliss, verily, is Brahman" as being the referent of the word "bliss. || 45 ||
Just as the attainment of nectar, just as rain in a time of drought, and just as the recovery of sight for the blind—such is your arrival. (46)
In the phrase "yathāmṛtasya," the word division is "amṛtasya. || 46 ||
Just as there is joy when a dead man returns from traveling through the sky, so too, O Brahmin, is there joy at your arrival; welcome to you, O great sage! 47.
And what is your supreme desire? What may I do for you?
O Brahmin, you have arrived as a holy place of pilgrimage for me, being most righteous. (48)
It is called *kāma* because it is desired (*kāmyate*). || 48 ||
Just as joy would arise in me from being sprinkled by the waters of the Gaṅgā,
so does the joy from seeing you cool my inner self, as it were.
It cools, that is, it removes heat; the word "iva" is used for emphasis. || 49 ||
Free from desire, fear, and anger, devoid of passion and free from affliction—
O Brahmin, it is truly marvelous that you have come to me.

"Free from" (*vigatā*): *icchā* (desire) has as its object merely a thing in general; *rāga* (passion) has as its object specific things such as women. Some say that *icchā* is the mere longing for an object not yet attained, while *rāga* is the longing for what has already been attained. The connection [of the verse] is: "that this [you] have come to me is most wonderful. (50)
"O bull among sages, whatever task you have come for and for whatever purpose, know that it is already accomplished; for you are indeed highly honored by me. (51)

The grammatical connection is as follows: "Know that whatever task was to be done by me for the sake of that purpose and motive for which you have arrived has already been accomplished. The reason for this is: "Because you are worthy of honor. || 51 ||
Having heard those words of the tiger among kings, which were of wonderful extent,
the highly effulgent Viśvāmitra, his hair standing on end with joy, spoke.
He whose body hairs stood on end due to joy was thus [described]. || 52 ||
O tiger among kings, this is indeed worthy of you alone upon this earth—
you who are born of a great lineage and abide in the tradition of Vasiṣṭha.
"O tiger among kings, O best of kings! [This is according to Amara-kośa: "The words *siṃha*, *śārdūla*, *nāga*, and so forth, when used in the masculine gender, denote excellence. (53)
"O bull among men, I have undertaken a religious observance for the sake of attaining perfection;
however, terrible Rākṣasas stand in my way, intent on creating obstacles. (54)

"I take my stand" means I rely upon it. Although Viśvāmitra has already achieved his purpose, he nevertheless speaks thus—"for the sake of perfection"—by taking recourse to the perspective of worldly convention. "Perfection" (*siddhi*) here refers to the attainment of fitness for steadfastness in knowledge by the aggregate of causes and effects (the body). This is because liberation, characterized as final release, cannot be directly attained through ritual action. [This applies] to me, regarding that discipline...
The connection is with the phrase "those who create obstacles. || 54 ||
You ought to protect me, who am distressed and have come seeking refuge;
you possess a glorious son whose prowess is like that of a proud tiger. (55)

The word *śaraṇa* denotes a protector, according to the statement: "A *śaraṇa* is a house or a protector. One whose prowess—that is, supreme power—is like that of a proud *śārdūla*, a tiger full of arrogance, is called *dṛptaśārdūlavikrama*. According to Amara, "prowess (*vikrama*) is supreme power (*atiśaktitā*). || 55 ||
(16) Rāma, the destroyer of demons, is equal to Mahendra in valor.
O tiger among kings, [entrust] that son Rāma, whose prowess is truth, [with this task]. || 56 ||
"Satyaparākramaḥ" means one whose prowess (parākrama) is true (satya), that is, unfailing and culminating in its fruit; he is thus described. || 56 ||
"You ought to give me your eldest son, the hero who wears the side-locks of youth;
for he, protected by me, is capable [of this] through his own divine splendor."
The "crows' wings" (kākapakṣa) are his crest. He dispels the suspicion that he might be unfit for the slaying of the Rākṣasa due to being devoid of power by saying "power" (śakti). || 57 ||
O King, you ought not to feel such affection for your son regarding the suppression of those Rākṣasas who do you harm.

The grammatical connection is as follows: he is capable of suppressing the heads of those who do harm, that is, those who commit injuries. Now, one might object that being endowed with divine splendor and being protected by a sage are contradictory; but this is not so, because even in his descent through ignorance, it is possible for him to manifest divine splendor by means of the sage’s bestowing of weapons and the like. || 58 ||
"There is nothing in this world that cannot be given by the high-souled;
indeed, I promise you this: consider those Rākṣasas already slain.
For wise men such as we do not engage in actions when the outcome is uncertain. (59)

Accepting the possibility of incapacity, he says: "Not that" (*na tat*). The connection is as follows: there is nothing that cannot be given by great souls (*mahātman*). For it is recorded in the Smṛti: "Karṇa gave his skin, Śibi his flesh, Jīmūtavāhana his life, and Dadhīci his bones; what is there that cannot be given by great souls? Indeed!
According to Amara, [the word *harṣa*] means joy or compassion. The term *saṃdigdhakāryasaṃpravṛtti* is a bahuvrīhi compound;
the "correctness" (*samyaktva*) of the engagement (*pravṛtti*) refers to its firmness. || 59 ||
I know the high-souled Rāma, whose eyes are like lotuses;
and so does Vasiṣṭha of great splendor, as well as those others who are far-sighted.
[Objection: But how can a mere child possess such power that he has made this vow of yours? To this, he says:
"I am... (verse 60). I know—that is, I am aware of—the Great Soul, the Supreme Self, who is capable of constructing and dismantling the hut of the universe by mere volition.
(17) "If righteousness, greatness, and fame reside within your mind, then you ought to grant me your own desired son. (61)

"If it is dharma... [If] dharma and so forth remain in your mind as something not to be abandoned, then you ought to give your own son—your own child—who is "abhipreta," meaning desired or beloved. 61.
Having thus spoken these words consistent with dharma and artha, the righteous and highly effulgent Viśvāmitra, lord of sages, became silent.
"He ceased" means he became silent. || 62 || 63 ||
Having heard those words spoken by Viśvāmitra, that tiger among kings remained motionless for a moment and then spoke thus with dejection: || 63 ||
This lotus-eyed Rāma is less than sixteen years of age;
I do not see in him the fitness for battle with the rākṣasas.
The sixteenth [year] is that which completes the sixteen; and that year was "ūna," meaning slightly less than sixteen years for him—one who was thus [described]. || 64 ||
Surrounded by this complete akṣauhiṇī army of which I stand as the lord,
I shall give battle to the flesh-eaters.
"Of the flesh-eaters, the meat-eaters, the rākṣasas. Regarding "piśita," Amara states: "tarasa, māṃsa, palala, kravya, and āmiṣa [are synonyms for] flesh. (65)
Rāma is a mere child among armies; he does not know strength from weakness.
He has seen no ground of battle other than the inner apartments.
The battlefield is the field of combat. || 66 ||
"O Kauśika, nine thousand years have passed since my birth;
these four sons were produced by me with great hardship. (67)
In some places it is said to be nine thousand years; in another, sixty thousand years. (67)
Among them, the lotus-eyed Rāma is the foremost;
without him, even the other three cannot sustain their lives here.
16) repeat (p.
17) repeat (p. 18)
That very Rāma is being led by you toward the Rākṣasas;
if that be so, know me to be as good as dead this very moment, deprived of my son. (69)
The connection is: "If [he] is being led away to the Rākṣasas. In that case, then... || 69 ||
Furthermore, if that Rāvaṇa creates obstacles for you, then we shall not be able to withstand that evil-minded one in battle. (70)
He says "and another" (anyacca) to indicate that there is yet another reason suspected for not giving [the kingdom] to Rāma. || 70 ||
At various times, the diverse and abundant manifestations of power arise among living beings, and they dissolve again through the power of time.

Now, one might ask: from where does Rāvaṇa possess such prowess, and why is there a reversal of that very power in those born of the lineage of Kakutstha and others, who possess even greater strength than Rāvaṇa and his ilk?
To this, he says: "Time," and so forth. [They were] distinct, separate, mutually different, and possessed of immense valor.

Manifestations—the perfections of great heroism—attain prosperity and become manifest among living beings when favorable conditions appear from time to time; this is because, in due course, conditions become conducive to dissolution. || 71 ||
But now, at this time, we are not capable of standing before our enemies, Rāvaṇa and the others; such is the certainty of destiny. (72)
At this time, which is adverse to us; therein, regarding the enemies such as Rāvaṇa and others who are objects of perception; destiny is fate.
This is one such time that makes even the virtuous appear frail;
for even Rāghava has fallen into a state of wretchedness, worn out by old age.

He demonstrates the very adversity of time with the words, "this [time] is another": *pelavīkṛtasajjanaḥ* means one who has made virtuous people sparse—that is, one who has thinned out the company of the good. According to Amara, *ghana* means continuous or dense, while *pelava* means sparse, thin, or meager.
This time (*kāla*) is "another" (*anyatama*), meaning extremely different; the sense is that it is utterly contrary to what came before.

"Vārddhaka" means old age; "vārddhakajarjaraḥ" means one who is worn out like an old man. Even though Rāghava was less than sixteen years of age, he became worn out as if in a state of old age, and at that time, he fell into a state of wretchedness, a miserable condition, and sorrow. Some say that the word "Rāghava" here refers to Daśaratha. || 73 ||
Having heard those words of his, whose syllables were choked with affection,
Kauśika, filled with indignation, replied to the lord of the earth.
Kauśika, of the Kuśika lineage, is Viśvāmitra. || 7 ||
Having promised "I shall do it," you now wish to abandon your vow;
having become a lion, you desire the state of a deer. (75)
Kesarī means a lion. || 75 ||
If you are unable [to grant my request], O King, I shall depart as I came; having failed in my vow, O descendant of Kakutstha, may you remain happy along with your kinsmen.
"Incapable" means powerless. The address "O Kākutstha" is intended with a specific purpose. || 76 ||
When that great-souled Viśvāmitra was thus overcome with anger, the entire earth trembled and fear entered the gods. || 77 ||
Perceiving that the Great Sage, the friend of the world, was overcome by anger, the wise Vasiṣṭha— steadfast, firm in his vows, and intelligent— spoke these words.
"Even though you are born of the Ikṣvāku lineage and are yourself Daśaratha, if you do not uphold my word, who else will? (79)
Sentient beings do not abandon the boundaries established by the conventional usage set forth by you and others; therefore, you ought not to forsake them. (80)
Guarded by that lion among men as the nectar was guarded by Garuḍa,
the Rākṣasas will not be able to overcome him, whether he has mastered the divine weapons or not.
He by whom weapons have been mastered, practiced, or perfected—that "master of weapons" (kṛtāstra)—they shall not be able [to overcome him];
they will not be capable [of doing so]. The word "to harass" (gharṣayitum) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 81 ||
Vālmīki said:
While Vasiṣṭha was speaking thus, the wise king questioned Rāma’s servants: "How is Rāma? Of what nature is he? From where does he come? (82)
The meaning is: "Where is Rāma? Where is Rāma? || 82 || 83 || 84 || 85 ||
The servants of Rāma said:
Ever since Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals,
arrived here from his pilgrimage along with the brahmin, he has been dejected in spirit.
Through our diligent entreaties, this very person—his face unfaded—performs or does not perform his own daily duties. (84)
"What is prosperity? What is adversity? What is home? What is striving?
Having said, "All this is indeed non-existent," he remains alone in silence. (85)
O King, by turning his back on the giving of clothing, drink, and food, he thus follows the ascetic who observes the dharma of a wandering mendicant.

"One whose dharma is that of a wandering mendicant" means one whose religious duties consist of detachment and so forth, which are the characteristics of wandering mendicants—that is, renunciants (saṃnyāsins). || 86 ||
He does not assume pride, nor does he desire sovereignty;
he neither rises nor sets amidst the fluctuations of pleasure, pain, and the like. (87)
"It rises and rejoices; it sets and desponds"—this is what is meant. || 87 ||
"Life has been spent in activities devoid of attaining the state free from weariness"—thus she sings again and again in a plaintive tone. (88)
Nirvāṇa is the state free from exertion. [He spoke] with a *kākalī*, a very subtle sound; for Amara states: "The word *kākalī* refers to that which is broken (*kala*) and subtle (*sūkṣma*). || 88 ||
"Do you desire wealth as the sole refuge in times of distress? Having thus instructed him, he bestowed his entire possession upon those who sought it.

Having instructed—having given this teaching—"O seeker, what, what wealth do you desire? What do you long for? as the foremost refuge and abode for those in distress, he bestows—gives away—all his possessions to the petitioner, the beggar. || 89 ||
(21) "O lotus-petal-eyed one, we do not know what we should do for that mighty-armed one of such a disposition; for you alone are our refuge in this matter. (90)
The connection [of the verse] is: "What can we do for him whose mind is such? We do not know. || 90 ||
"Who on this earth could be such a Great Being that he would be capable of employing him in ordinary worldly affairs? (91)
Who indeed on this earth could be such a great being capable of establishing Rāma in ordinary worldly affairs? What person might there be? Such is the connection [of the words]. || 91 || 92 ||
Viśvāmitra said:
If this be so, O sirs, let you quickly bring that highly wise delight of the Raghus here, as lions bring a deer.
This delusion of the Lord of the Raghus arose neither from calamities nor from passion;
this awakening, born of discernment and dispassion, is of great exaltation.

It is called "great arising" (*mahānudaya*) because it is the manifestation of supreme bliss; this [state] is metaphorically designated as "delusion" (*moha*) because such a delusion serves as the cause for awakening (*bodha*). || 93 || 94 || 95 || 96 || 97 ||
When this delusion has been skillfully wiped away, that descendant of Raghu will find rest in that supreme state, just as we have.
And the honorable one, with a perfectly fulfilled mind, will maintain his own natural and worldly tradition of practice in its entirety and without interruption. (95)
While the Lord of Sages was speaking thus, the lotus-eyed Rāma then approached to perform the salutation at his father’s feet.
First he bowed to his father, then to the sages who were honored by all; thereafter he prostrated before the Brahmins, then his kinsmen, and finally his teachers.
Then,
with his gaze, then with his head slightly bowed, and finally with his voice,
he accepted that succession of prostrations performed by the circle of kings. (98)
"Manāṅmūrdhnā" means with a slight shaking of the head. || 98 ||
While the king was saying, "O son, stay on my lap," he sat down upon a seat spread out on the ground by his attendants.

"nyaviśata" means he sat down. It is the first person singular in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense from the verbal root *viś* (to enter). The *ātmanepada* (middle voice) ending is applied according to the rule "neviśaḥ. [99] [100] [101]
Daśaratha said:
"My son, you have attained discernment and are a vessel for all that is auspicious;
let not your soul be surrendered to weariness through an intellect as worn-out as that of a fool. (100)
By one like you who practices what has been proclaimed by aged Brahmins and gurus, a meritorious state is attained; it is not reached by one who pursues delusion.
Calamities remain far away and fragile only so long,
my son, as no expansion of delusion is permitted.
*Paripelavāḥ* means sparse; *prasaraḥ* means movement or range. || 102 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed prince, you are a hero; by you these enemies of the senses have been conquered—those which are difficult to sever and difficult to assail. (103)

Those whose destruction is with difficulty are "hard to destroy" (*durucchedāḥ*). Those whose initial undertaking or activity is wicked are "difficult to begin" (*durārambhāḥ*); or rather, *durārambhāḥ* means difficult to undertake, which is to say, difficult to accomplish. || 103 ||
Why do you sink, like one ignorant of this, into this ocean of delusion—filled with turbulent waves and characterized by dullness—which is fit only for the ignorant? (104)

"Like one ignorant of that" means like one who does not know Brahman. "Waves" refers to great surges; in the ocean of delusion, these are the waves of fierce calamities. In the context of the ocean, the quality of being *jāḍya* (dullness) signifies the state of being *śiśira* (cold); according to Amara, *śiśira* means dull (*jaḍa*). || 104 ||
Viśvāmitra said:
What is their basis, who are they, by what means, how many are they, and for what reason do these anxieties utterly destroy the mind, just as rats devour a house? (105)

He introduces the questions of Viśvāmitra, which serve as the cause for the composition of the subsequent section of the text that explains in detail the dispassion (*vairāgya*) previously set forth in brief:
"They plunder your mind; they cut it apart specifically. In what do they culminate? Upon what objects are they firmly based?"
Regarding the statement "they remain": upon what are they based? What are they in their essential nature? By what cause were they born? How many are they, and what is their magnitude? || 105 ||
Speak quickly whatever you desire, O sinless one, and you shall obtain it all; furthermore, by this means, mental afflictions shall never again overcome you.

He dispels the doubt that providing answers to questions might be purposeless with the words "yathā" (just as): "O sinless one, tell me that desired thing by obtaining which all mental anxieties shall not afflict you again, and which you shall obtain quickly exactly as intended"—this is the syntactical connection. 106.

Having heard these words of his, which were pregnant with the grace of appropriate meaning, the wise banner of Raghu’s lineage abandoned his grief, just as a peacock does when it perceives that its desired goal will be accomplished by the thundering of a rain-cloud.

*Keturdhvajaḥ*: Just as a banner (*ketu*) is an ornament for a chariot, so too is he an ornament for the lineage of Raghu—this is the meaning. *Ucitānām arthānām vilāsaḥ*: that in whose womb there is the play or expansion of appropriate matters; such is the compound. *Vārivāhaḥ* means a cloud. *Barhī* means a peacock. *Anumitābhimatārthasiddhiḥ*: he by whom the accomplishment of the desired object or purpose is inferred.
Thus it has been said: || 107 ||
Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Exposition of the Arising of Dispassion," in the section on Dispassion within the *Mokṣopāya* of the venerable Vālmīki.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Origin of Dispassion," in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā, composed by Śrīmad Ātmasukha, the disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Uttamasukha Pūjyapāda. || 1 ||
(24) Second Canto.
Vālmīki said:
Thus questioned by the Lord of Sages, Rāghava, having been comforted,
spoke these words— charming, full of meaning, and delivered with measured gravity.

We have already stated that the purpose of the subsequent composition of the text is to explain in detail the dispassion (*vairāgya*) which was previously set forth in brief. In that regard, at the conclusion of the past creation, the questions "In what do they culminate? were introduced; to provide a resolution for those, the text says that Rāma spoke these words—thus [the author] says "iti" (thus). Slowly...
"Mandagāmin" means "deep. According to Amarasimha, "mandagāmin" means "slow-moving" or "sluggish. || 1 || 2 || 3 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, now that you have questioned me, I shall relate everything exactly as it is, even though I am ignorant; for who can disregard the words of the virtuous? (2)
I was indeed born in this, my father’s own house; in due course I attained growth, acquired knowledge, and have remained here. (3)
Thereupon, O leader of sages, becoming devoted to the conduct of the virtuous,
I wandered over the earth girt by the oceans for the purpose of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
She whose girdle or waistband is the ocean—that is how she is described; [he approached] her. || 4 ||
And during this time, while removing my attachment to this saṃsāra, there has arisen in my mind this very reflection. (5)
"Of such a kind" means of the manner that is about to be described. || 5 ||
Tell me, what indeed is this so-called happiness that constitutes the state of cyclic existence? The world is born for the sake of death, and it dies for the sake of birth. (6)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Tell me, what kind of happiness is this state of existence in *saṃsāra*? He demonstrates that it produces nothing but unhappiness with the verse beginning "He is born" (*jāyate*). He is born for the sake of death; the meaning is that birth is inseparable from death.
And he dies for the sake of birth; the meaning is that for the ignorant person, death is necessarily a cause of rebirth. || 6 ||
All these states of being, which are the grounds for worldly prosperity and the movements of all that is mobile and immobile, are entirely unstable; they are the abode of all calamities and are evil.
"Characterized by the movements of the moving and the unmoving" means they are produced by the moving and the unmoving. "Sins" refers to evil states that are the causes of sin.

"Bases of power" are the grounds for sovereignty. The syntactical connection is that these states, which are bases of power, become the "abode of all calamities. In some versions, the reading is "lords of calamities" (āpadāṃ patayaḥ). || 7 ||
Like iron rods, phenomena are mutually unattached;
they cling together solely through their own mental construction.

He states that saṃsāra is indeed created by the mind alone, just like a dream or a forest: "This [world]," etc. By nature, they are mutually unattached, meaning they lack any reciprocal connection. As an illustration for this natural lack of connection, he says:
"Like iron rods," etc. They are similar to spikes made of iron; for iron rods do not stick together like lacquer and wood.

They are connected. Entities—meaning things characterized as son, wife, and so forth—are merely embraced and bound by one's own mental construction, such as "this is my son," "this is my wife," "this is my husband," and so on. (8)
What use have I for sovereignty, what use for enjoyments; who am I, and what is this that has come?
Let that which is false remain false; indeed, to whom does it belong, and what is it that has come?
"Who am I?"—among the body, senses, mind, intellect, ego, thought, ignorance, the reflection of consciousness, the original object, and the absolute (kevala), who am I?
Which one am I? Is this manifested world that has arrived real or unreal?
Upon thorough investigation, let that world be merely false; for the false can never become real. Therefore, of what [is it true]?

What indeed has come [into being]? For no harm or benefit whatsoever accrues to anyone by means of a false object. Just as the mirage-water neither serves as an ornament nor a disfigurement for the earth, the sense is that nothing at all occurs to the Self, which is the underlying substratum, by means of the imagined phenomenal world. || 9 ||
O Brahmin, as I reflected in this way, a distaste for all worldly existences then arose within me, just as a traveler feels toward desert wastes. (10)
He states what the fruit of such an investigation into the true nature of saṃsāra is: "Thus," etc.
Then, from that reflection, there arose a lack of interest and a failure to find delight. "Pāntha" means a traveler; "maruṣu" means in desert lands. || 10 ||
"How can this suffering be stilled?"— thus am I tormented by anxiety,
like an old tree by a fierce fire situated within its hollow.
Having thus provided this introduction for the purpose of answering questions such as "Upon what is it based?", he now states those answers:

"It is stilled," and so forth. I am tormented and distressed by the thought, "How, by what means, is this suffering of saṃsāra stilled—that is, destroyed? An old tree is a decayed tree; a hollow is a cavity, a hole in a tree.

It should be understood that the answer to the question, "For what reason do anxieties (ādhi) destroy?"—namely, "because of the failure to understand the means for the pacification of saṃsāra"—is effectively stated right here [in the preceding verses]. || 11 || 12 ||
For my heart is as solid as a stone from the suffering of saṃsāra;
indeed, out of fear for my own world, I do not weep, though tears fall.
To me, wealth is not for the sake of joy, but rather wheels for the accumulation of anxiety;
and houses with wives and children are like dwellings for those facing fierce calamities.

Anticipating the objection, "How can you describe only suffering when you are surrounded by all objects of enjoyment, like a pauper?", [the author], showing that everything is harmful and indeed wicked, first censures wealth as the cause of manifold misfortunes: "Cintā...
The phrase *cintānāṃ nicayāḥ* means collections or multitudes; those whose wheels are these very multitudes of anxieties are so described. These are specific types of weapons. Thus it is said.

For the accumulation of anxiety produced by wealth tears a man apart like a wheel. "Houses where wives have given birth" refers to those dwellings in which wives (*kalatra*)—meaning spouses—have properly and fully brought forth offspring. "Of those with fierce calamities" refers to those men for whom the calamities (*āpada*) are fierce; they are thus called *ugrāpada*. Just as...

For householders overwhelmed by mounting calamities, houses filled with many children and surrounded by wives—which generate a multitude of anxieties comparable to a wheel—do not lead to happiness but rather to suffering alone; the meaning is that the same applies to wealth as well. || 13 ||
(27) O Sage, this noble prosperity, though it stands firm in this world which is so fragile, surely leads only to delusion and does not grant happiness. 14.

Following the censure of wealth, he censures fortune (*śrī*), the cause of wealth, with these seven verses beginning with "This [fortune] resides in this... In this world, that fortune which resides here—vast and great (the *Amara* lexicon states: "the word *udāra* refers to a generous person or something great")—yet fragile and unstable on all sides—that very fortune does not bestow happiness or comfort.
The construction is as follows: "Surely" (*nūnam*) expresses certainty; on the contrary, it leads to total delusion. || 14 ||
Indeed, like the common folk of a king, fools—without any investigation into merits and defects—cling to one who has mounted them, even if he is by their side. 15.
Since there is no fixed rule that Fortune (Lakṣmī) resorts only to the virtuous, the author describes the wickedness of her resort by the verse beginning with "guṇa...

[The commentary explains: "durārūḍhā" means ascended with difficulty; that is to say, she is accompanied by suffering. Alternatively, by the word "ārūḍha," the act of ascending (āroha) is indicated; thus, "durārohā" means difficult to achieve. This is because she depends upon the investigation of virtues and vices.
"Without deliberation as to whether this one possesses merit or that one lacks it, he relies upon whoever is at his side. The word *kila* is used here in the sense of report (*vārtā*);
Amara states that *kila* is used for both report and possibility. "Like the nature of a king" means like the character of a monarch.
Just as the nature of a king relies upon whoever is near him—whether wicked or virtuous—without discrimination, and becomes difficult to ascend [or control] in that manner, so too does he act.
Alternatively, the king's nature depends upon his ministers and others. || 15 ||
By various such actions, this [suffering] undergoes expansion, just as the milk of the venomous serpent's poison spreads out. (16)

Having spoken thus regarding the increase of prosperity (*lakṣmī*), he says to him: "By action" (*karmaṇā*). It follows its expansion and increase through various good or bad actions. He says that even when increased, it leads to misfortune:
"It behaves like the spreading of the force of poison from serpents; just as [the milk] of a serpent..."

The meaning is that just as [the milk] increases the force of poison, so too does the milk in the form of Lakṣmī increase the power and the poisonous force of the serpents that are the *doṣas*. The connection with the preceding verse is: "that milk which spreads out is this very one. 16.
As long as a person remains in their own station, they possess a cold and gentle touch; but once they are made harsh by prosperity, they are like frost driven by a whirlwind. (17)

When it is said that "the milk spreads forth," he clarifies this with the four verses beginning with *tāvat*. A person whose touch—meaning his contact—is cool, pleasant, soft, and possesses qualities such as gentle and sweet speech, is described as such.
A *vātyā* is a whirlwind. *Paruṣīkṛtaḥ* means made harsh or rough, like snow stirred up by a whirlwind.
The meaning is that contact with suffering occurs when the mind is made unsteady by prosperity, which is like a touch that gives pain. || 17 ||
Those who are wise, heroic, grateful, skillful, and gentle—
by Fortune they have been rendered harsh, like gems covered by a handful of dust.

The wise are the learned. The grateful are those who do not forget favors received. The skillful are the clever; for Amara states: "In the sense of 'clever,' [the words] *dakṣa*, *catura*, *peśala*, and *paṭu* [are synonymous]. Jewels are gems and the like. || 18 ||
One who is illustrious yet beyond reproach, one who is heroic yet free from boastfulness, and one who is a lord yet possesses an even gaze—these three kinds of men are rare to find. (19)
"One who is not censured by people" means one who is not subject to public reproach. "Not boastful" means free from such idle chatter as, "I am a hero;

who indeed is my equal? It should be understood that since a person who is both illustrious and beyond reproach is difficult to find, those such as the "hero" are mentioned here as examples [of qualities] while remaining devoid of self-praise. || 19 ||
The mind’s activity is drawn toward that which is enchanting, yet it is achieved through hardship and is momentary;
fortune is like a flowering creeper rising from a chasm, its body coiled upon the limbs of a serpent. 20.

"Arising from a hollow" means produced from a hole such as that of an anthill; for Amara states: "chidra, nirvyathana, roka, randhra, śvabhra, vapā, and śuṣira [are synonyms for a hole]. Like a flowering creeper—that is, like a creeper adorned with blossoms—Lakṣmī, being charming due to her superficial beauty, draws the mind's activity toward herself; the meaning is that she turns it toward her own presence.

To be accomplished through hardship means to be achieved by means of a miserable object born of servitude to the base and the like. "A row of *vyālas*" refers to bodies rolled about; *vyālas* are rogues. According to Amara, the word *vyāla*—which takes both masculine and neuter genders—is used for a rogue, while in the masculine it denotes a beast of prey or a serpent. Their "row" (*āvalī*) is a line, and by it their bodies were rolled (*vivṛtta*) or tossed about upon the limbs.
She who possesses [that] is so described. In the case of the creeper, however, "vyālāvalīgātravivṛttadehā" means one whose body is coiled around the bodies of a row of serpents. || 20 ||
(29) Life, as fragile as a drop of water on the tip of a young leaf,
suddenly abandons the body like a madman and departs prematurely. (21)

Following the censure of Lakṣmī, he censures the lifespan that serves as the basis for the enjoyment of Lakṣmī: "Lifespan," etc. Lifespan is as fragile as a drop of water hanging from the tip of the corner—the final part—of a sprout; it perishes prematurely, at an untimely moment. According to the *Nāmānuśāsana* (Amara-kośa), "kāṇḍa" is used in the sense of a staff, an arrow, a section, an opportunity, and water. [Thus, it perishes] having abandoned the body.

The grammatical connection is "he goes. Here is the illustration: "like a madman. Just as one who is not mad abandons a madman, so it is here. Alternatively, the connection is: "the body, which remains like a madman. || 21 ||
For those whose minds are worn out by attachment to the venomous snakes of sense-objects,
and who lack mature self-discrimination, life is merely a cause of exhaustion.
"But is it not seen that in some cases even a long life-span exists? True;

yet even that is useless for the knowledge of the Self and leads only to misfortune, as he says: "By objects... Objects themselves are venomous serpents; by attachment to, or association with, them, minds become worn out—that is, loosened and weakened.
For those who are so described; for those whose discrimination regarding the self (*ātma-viveka*) is immature and undeveloped, they are so described.
O Sage, we have reached a certainty established through limited forms; we find no peace in this lifespan, which is like a mass of lightning amidst the clouds of saṃsāra. (23)

Furthermore, he demonstrates the instability of life with these three verses beginning with "We": "We," meaning those whose intellects are firm and who have established their certainty upon that which is not the Self— namely, that which has a limited and circumscribed form—
are not at peace, nor are they happy, within this life, which is like a mass of lightning amidst the clouds of saṃsāra, a collection of flashes from the clouds of worldly existence.
It is as logical to attempt to wrap the wind or to break open space, as it is to tie knots in waves; likewise, placing one's trust in life is not logical. (24)
*Granthana* means binding. || 24 ||
Like an autumn cloud, like a lamp without oil, or like a wave, it is perceived as already gone, flickering and unstable. (25)
"Pelava" means thin. According to Amara, "pelava," "virala," and "tanu" are synonyms for thin. || 25 ||

With an unresting mind, the deluded person strives for a life that is empty and extended only for the sake of suffering, just as a female mule carries a fetus within her womb only to her own destruction.

[Objection: But surely, one is seen in the world who, by means of a particular method, even achieves a stable lifespan. [Reply: True. However, even that leads to misfortune for one who does not know Brahman; thus he says: "aviśrānta... etc. "Vimūḍhaḥ" means especially deluded, and therefore one whose mind does not rest in Brahman. "Śūnyam" means empty or useless. "Ātatam" means extended.

The meaning is that he strives and exerts himself for the sake of suffering alone, even though his life-span is extensive. It is well known that the fetus of a mule—born from a female donkey by a male horse—destroys that very mother. || 26 ||
That by which the attainable is fully attained, by which one no longer grieves, and which is the abode of supreme bliss—that is called true life. (27)

Having censured a life that is useless for the attainment of knowledge, he praises a life that is useful for it in order to establish its worthiness of acceptance through three verses beginning with "That which is to be attained" (*prāpyam*). By means of that life, Brahman—which is the goal to be attained—is fully realized. For this very reason, by means of that life, one does not grieve again because there is no further acquisition of another birth. That life which lasts until the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma is the supreme...

That which is the locus of the bliss of *nirvṛti*—which is distinct from the pleasure derived from sense objects—is called "life" (*jīvita*). The meaning is that it is called "true life. For when there is praise of an effect, praise of its cause necessarily follows; thus, in this context, praise is offered for "life," which is the effect of longevity (*āyus*) and is characterized by the maintenance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). || 27 ||
Even trees live, and beasts and birds live;
but he alone truly lives whose mind lives by means of contemplation alone. (28)

That person whose mind, though under the sway of evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*), lives only through reflection—that is, by the investigation into the true nature of reality—lives only when that [mind] is sublated by the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) produced by such reflection and other means; this is the meaning of "he truly lives."
Only those beings born in this world have lived a truly virtuous life who shall not be born here again; all others are but aged donkeys.
"Jaraṭhagardabhāḥ" means donkeys afflicted with old age. || 29 ||
The scripture is a burden to the undiscerning, and knowledge is a burden to the passionate;
the mind is a burden to the unpeaceful, and the body is a burden to one who has not realized the Self.

By demonstrating that the life of an ignorant person is as miserable as the life of a tree or similar entities, it is implicitly shown that even their body and so forth are defective; this he clarifies with the two verses beginning with "bhāraḥ" (a burden).

Just as a burden that is difficult to bear does not come under one's own control, likewise, for one who lacks discernment and so forth, the scriptures and other such things do not come under their own control.

This is the meaning: here, "one who lacks discrimination" (avivekin) refers to one of dull intellect who is incapable of discernment. It should be understood that everything else has been presented as an illustration for the statement, "the body of one who does not know the Self is a burden. || 30 ||
Form, life-span, mind, intellect, ego, stability, and effort—all these lead only to suffering for the one of dull intellect, just as a burden leads to suffering for the bearer of that burden. (31)

But surely, even for the knower of the Self, the body is merely a burden; why then is it said that "the body is a burden only for the non-knower of the Self"? This is not so, because for the knower of the Self, the body itself does not exist. Since there is no attachment to that which is merely illusory, as in the previous case, he remains indifferent toward its acquisition or destruction. This is what is intended by the term *sthirehita*.

"Steady in its activity": it is steady because its object is a steady task; thus, the effort (*īhita*) remains stable. In some versions, the reading is *asthitehitam*, but even there the meaning is the same. || 31 ||
In just a few days, having been recognized [as such],
the wicked man is deprived of his youth with disdain, just as a virtuous person is parted from it.

Anticipating the objection that form and other qualities serve for pleasure during the stage of youth, he says "dinaiḥ" (by days), etc., to show that this is not so because of its instability. Having recognized [it as] "durjanaḥ" (a wicked person)—meaning having known it—and "gatādaram" (without regard)—this is an adverbial modifier. || 32 ||
p. 30) repeat p. 31) repeat p. 32)

In this world, there is nothing so devoid of quality as this life, which, though appearing stable and pleasant, is constantly abandoned like a piece of worthless, inferior wood, and is destined for death.

He concludes the censure of life with the words "by its stability": [life] is constantly abandoned and forsaken by that well-known stability—[a stability] which is pleasant to speak of, pleasant to illuminate, and pleasant to behold; yet it is possessed of that which is most fragile and lacks true essence. According to Amara, *asāra* means "without essence," *phalgu* means "trifling," and *śūnya* means "void. This life is thus a vessel for death.
The meaning is that there is no other thing in the world devoid of qualities as much as that [Self] is devoid of qualities. || 33 ||
Rising up in vain through delusion, we revolve in vain;
we are terrified by the enemy of false egoism, which consists of nothing but illusion.
Since egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is the cause of misfortune by way of being the door to the conceit of "life," immediately after the censure of that [life],
he censures egoism— the primary door through which it bestows misfortune— with these seven verses beginning with "In vain" (*mudhaiva*).

"Evil egoism" (durahaṃkāra) means a wicked sense of self; this very evil egoism is the enemy, the "enemy that is evil egoism. It has arisen in vain—that is, fruitlessly and pointlessly—due to delusion, which is ignorance, having risen up directly against [the Self]. Having stated the futility of the arising of egoism, he now speaks of its growth: "in vain," etc.
"Consisting of falsehood" means having a false nature. For the Teachers have said: "The notion 'I' is indeed the first superimposition. (34)
Through the power of ego comes calamity; through ego come heavy anxieties;
through the power of ego comes worldly striving—there is no enemy greater than ego.

He establishes the enmity of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) with the words "by the power of egoism. "Evil anxieties" (*durādhayaḥ*) are wicked mental torments. "Striving" (*īhā*) is desire. "Supreme" (*para*) means excellent. || 35 ||
Relying upon that supreme and long-standing enemy, egoism (ahaṅkāra), O Sage, I neither eat nor do I drink water; how much less could I enjoy worldly pleasures? (36)
He states the fruit of thoroughly knowing the enmity of egoism with the words "that" (tam) || 36 ||
(33) Whatever I have enjoyed, taken, or done under the influence of egoism—all that is indeed insubstantial; the substance is the state of being empty of egoism. (37)

[Objection: "Is it not observed in the world that even one who has taken refuge with an enemy engages in activities such as eating? Why should it not be the same for you? To this he says: "By the power of the *ahaṃkāra*. [The activity] is indeed non-existent, being merely unreal. The meaning is: just as in a dream, eating and so forth are performed under the influence of the *ahaṃkāra* and are utterly false, so too is it in the waking state. [This is] the state of being devoid of *ahaṃkāra*.
The absence of ego-grasping; the thing-in-itself is the ultimate reality. || 37 ||
O Brahmin, as long as the cloud of egoism expands,
so long does the cluster of *kuṭaja* flowers of craving blossom.
Having stated "by the power of egoism," he elaborates upon this with the verse beginning "O Brahman.

The "cloud of egoism" (*ahaṃkāravārida*) refers to the cloud of egoism. *Kuṭaja* is the tree known as *vatsaka*. As Amara states: "Then *kuṭaja*, *śakra*, and *vatsaka* are synonyms for *jaya*. Thirst itself is the cluster of blossoms (*mañjarī*) of that *kuṭaja* tree; for the *kuṭaja* tree indeed [blooms] at the arrival of the rainy season.
It becomes covered with blossoming clusters of flowers. || 38 ||
