"O Brahmin, for me, whose mental state is devoid of ego yet who is sinking in grief due to my own folly, you ought to tell me whatever is appropriate in this situation. (39)

Having thus demonstrated his own fitness for the teacher’s instruction, he now requests that instruction with the verse beginning "nirahaṃkāra": "Of one whose mode of being—that is, whose conduct—is free from egoism (nirahaṃkāra), [the instruction is given] to him who is sinking, that is, despairing, due to folly (maurkhyāt). Regarding 'folly' (maurkhya), Amara states: 'ajña, mūḍha, yathājāta, mūrkhā, vaidheya, and bāliśa' all mean a fool."

O Great-Souled One, instruct me with what remains: I shall not, even with effort, resort to that abode of egoism which is the dwelling place of all calamities, unstable, situated within, and abandoned by the Supreme Being; it is exceedingly painful on all sides. (40)

"All calamities"—this is an elaboration of what preceded. "The abode of egoism" (*ahaṃkṛtipada*) means the object of egoism or the locus of egoism. Amara states: "The word *pada* [is used] in the senses of resolve, protection, place, characteristic mark, foot, and object.
The connection is: "I do not, with effort, resort to that which is the abode of egoism. "Abode" (*nilaya*) means a refuge. It stands within.

"Abiding within the body"—by the remainder, namely by that "non-this" portion which remains after the abandonment of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) as its witness, "instruct thoroughly," meaning perform complete instruction. Here we state the implied meaning: the word "I" is made by the *ahaṃkṛt* (the agent of ego); the "foot" is the state existing therein. Alternatively, it is the activity (*kṛti*), that is, the effort, which has the word "I" as its object.

The "foot" (*pada*) refers to the hoof of that cow which possesses the ego-sense (*sāhaṃkṛti*). Thus, the meaning is as follows: it is unstable and flickering; situated within, located in the region of the belly; released—that is, abandoned—by the highest quality, namely the best rope; and [subjected to] extreme suffering on all sides through blows and other such means.
Since that state of egoism is like the footprint of an untamed cow, which a person of discernment does not resort to, I shall not resort to that state of egoism. || 40 ||
(34) Having fallen into a state of decay due to its defects, the mind wavers restlessly from noble deeds practiced by the wise, like a drop of slime within the wind. (41)

Following the censure of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), he censures the mind (*manas*), which is the product of the ego, with these eleven verses beginning with "By defects" (*doṣaiḥ*). The flickering mind, having reached a state of decay and laxity through defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like, deviates from the task practiced by the noble ones, characterized by the performance of the means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Now...

The single phrase "because the effect exists [in the cause]" (*satkāryāt*) serves as an illustration for the mere agency of motion; it is like a drop of viscous fluid within the wind, or like a fragment of a peacock feather situated in the midst of the air. (41)
It runs aimlessly and restlessly here and there, further and further away, like a village dog that barks long and loud from afar. (42)

Now, one might object that movement is not a fault when there is a purpose; therefore, he says, "And for this reason. The word "long" (*dīrgham*) is used to prevent the sense of "far" (*tara*), which implies extreme distance, from being limited to [mere] hundreds of *yojanas* and so forth. A "kauleyaka" is a dog. Amarasimha states: "Kauleyaka, sārameya, kukkura, mṛgadaṃśaka, śunaka, bhaṣaka, and śvā are synonyms for a dog. (42)
It does not attain anything anywhere, even through the acquisition of great forests;
it reaches no internal fullness, like a small casket filled with water.
"It runs after [the object] in vain" is untenable, because one is sometimes seen to actually obtain the object; to this he replies:
"Even though obtained," etc. Here, *karaṇḍaka* refers to a basket made of bamboo. || 43 ||
"O Brahmin, my mind has been devoured by a cruel and dull-witted beast of a dog— namely, craving— which follows after its wife, thirst. (44)
He states that not only is the movement of the mind useless, but it also brings about harm, by saying: "By the cruel... etc.
Stupidity is the lack of discrimination, and craving alone follows that [stupidity] as its wife; thus, he is "one followed by the wife of craving.

Just as a corpse is devoured by a dog—another name for which is *kauleyaka*—which follows its wife the female dog, so too have I been devoured, meaning I have been afflicted, by the mind characterized by those aforementioned attributes. || 44 ||
Driven by my mind, I have been carried far away—as if by a fierce wind carrying a blade of grass—to either fall into an intermediate state or to wander in the void. (45)

He states with two verses beginning with "In the interval" that it is not only my mind that is a cause of suffering while I am alive, but also the seeds of karma that lead to rebirth in the realms of hell, animals, and so forth once I have died.

The intermediate insertion refers to being cast down after having ascended. Wandering in the void means wandering in a womb such as that of an animal, which is devoid of the means for achieving the goals of human life. Regarding the alternative reading "in the void of grass," it means wandering about in the formless sky. || 45 || 46 ||
As I was traveling from Pātāla to the earth, and from the earth back to Pātāla,
I have been ensnared by that evil-minded one, like a wooden wedge driven into a well.
"Like a child seized by a bard, I have been captured by this evil-minded one, who, though false, assumes a grand form and dissolves upon investigation. (47)

One might object: "Since the scripture establishing the reality of the Self states, 'For He is without breath, without mind, pure, higher than the high Imperishable,' you yourself do not even possess a mind; how then can there be such a thing as its being impelled? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It is indeed false... [and so on]. "With a vast form" means with manifold forms. "Tending to disperse" means having the nature of spreading out. Just as a child...
The meaning is that it is seized by a vetāla (vampire) superimposed upon one's own shadow and so forth;
in the same way, both the expansion and the subsequent dissolution [of that expansion] through inquiry are identical for the mind and the vetāla. || 47 ||
p. 34) repeat p. 35) repeat p. 36)
O Brahman, his mind and its grasp are more intensely hot than fire, more difficult to traverse than even a mountain, and firmer than even a thunderbolt; thus, they are hard to restrain.

[Objection: "In that case, let the mind that performs evil deeds be restrained. To this he says: "Of fire," and so forth. That which has a foot-step and an ascent of a most difficult course is described as such. *Manograha* means consisting of the mind. (48)
O virtuous one, even more difficult than drinking up the great ocean, or uprooting Mount Sumeru, or even consuming fire, is the restraint of the mind. (49)
From uprooting Mount Sumeru, from tearing out Meru, and from consuming fire like a thunderbolt. || 49 ||
The mind is the cause of all objects; when it exists, the three worlds exist. When it is extinguished, the world is extinguished; therefore, it must be treated with diligent effort. (50)
If the restraint of the mind is thus exceedingly difficult, then one might think that it should be disregarded and something else should be done for the sake of human purpose;
to this, he says "the mind," and so forth. The mind is the cause—the material cause—of all objects, such as space and other categories.
As it has been stated in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*: "The liberated and the unliberated are the wise and the ignorant..."

The entire universe, from space down to the earth, other than you, is known to arise from your own ignorance and to be a vibration of your own mind; do not grasp it otherwise. While that mind exists, the three worlds exist as its effect. When that cause is exhausted and destroyed, its effect, the world, becomes exhausted as well.
Therefore, that very mind must be diligently treated—that is, it must be healed—by means of the medical treatment to be described for the sake of the goal of the Puruṣa;
the meaning is that it must be grasped [and transformed]. || 50 ||
O Sage, these hundreds of mental joys and sorrows have surely come to you like wild elephants from the forest;
I believe they are now skillfully dissolving away as they grow thin through the power of your solitude.
From the mountain-king Agava—according to Amara, *naga* and *avaga* both mean "mountain" or "tree"—in that mind, they attain thinness; that is, they dissolve skillfully.
The meaning is that they utterly perish. The connection is: "I think they are dissolving. || 51 ||
(37) By that very same insatiable craving, which is a night of darkness within the heart,
rows of owls in the form of moral defects flutter about in the sky of consciousness. (52)

Because craving is the cause of misfortune through the gateway of the mind, craving is censured immediately after the mind for the purpose of its abandonment: "By that night of the darkness of the heart"—that is, by a night (*śarvarī*) devoid of moonlight (*candrikā*), which is both a night and a night of the darkness within the heart (*hārdāndhakāraśarvarī*)—craving is characterized; it is "ending in misery" (*durantā*), meaning its conclusion is suffering.

In the space of consciousness, consciousness itself is the sky; therein are the rows of *kauśikas*—the *doṣas*, which are faults such as anger, are themselves the *kauśikas*, or owls—and their rows. According to Amara, the word *kauśika* is used for Mahendra, guggulu, an owl, and a snake-catcher. [This is] the well-known night of darkness, [characterized by] the rows of owls in the well-known sky.
It is well known that this is the cause of vibration. || 52 ||
Whichever excellence of virtue I take refuge in, that very thing my craving cuts away, like a rat gnawing at a string. (53)
He says—“Whichever [object]... —to show that craving not only produces defects but also destroys virtues.
In such a way that it remains free from obstruction and devoid of attachment; [he beheld] the splendor of qualities, the beauty of virtues. || 53 ||
We, whose intellects are powerless, are unable to reach our own true abode;
we are utterly deluded by the snare of craving, just like birds caught in a net. (54)

He censures craving in detail—“to go,” etc. One’s own abode is one’s true nature (*svarūpa*), which has all afflictions (*kleśa*) cast out and is characterized by supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). “Net” refers to a snare. In the case of a bird, however, one’s own abode is its own nest. || 54 ||
O dear one, I am thus scorched by the flame called craving that I do not hope for the cessation of this burning even through nectars.

He censures craving because it is the cause of unsurpassed suffering, saying: "By that which is called craving... (p. 38). The connection is as follows: "Just as I do not expect the subsiding of a burning fever even by means of ambrosias—that is, by means of nectars—so too am I consumed."
In this world, craving—like a dark night—is like the goddess Kālī: it terrifies even the steadfast, blinds even the wise eye, and afflicts even the peaceful heart. (56)

[Objection: But how can this [suffering] cause a burning of thirst for you, who are steadfast, discerning, and devoid of activities that accord with thirst? To this, he says: "It terrifies even... One who possesses *dhīra* (steadfastness) is *dhīra-yukta*; one whose *īhā* (endeavor) is such is *dhīreha*. He exists together with *īkṣaṇa*, which is called discernment (*vicāra*), thus he is *sa-īkṣaṇa*. One whose *īhā* (endeavor) is *śāntā* (quiescent) is... [he is *śānteha*].
Likewise, the meaning is that even though it is devoid of activity that produces weariness, it nonetheless causes weariness. || 56 ||
Even when her mind is not won over, craving pursues everything; yet it obtains no fruit at all, like an aged woman in love. (57)
There is yet another wickedness of craving; he states it by means of the example of an elderly woman who desires respect: "anāvarjitā" (unconvinced), etc.

That by which the mind is not won over and not brought under control is so described. It pursues and follows everything, whether it be a wicked person or a virtuous one. Since a person’s pursuit is driven by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is said that "craving pursues. Thus, in the subsequent cases as well, the agency of craving is merely figurative.
It should be observed. || 57 ||
Even when she is unable to do so, she adopts the gait of a frantic dancer; like an aged actress, craving dances even without joy. 58.
He censures craving in another way with the words, "that which one is unable to [attain]. She assumes a *tāṇḍavinī* gait, meaning a dancing gait;
that is to say, she goes as if she were dancing. She dances in such a way as to be devoid of joy upon reaching her destination.
She proceeds with agitation even toward an impossible goal. Without craving, there is no happiness.
The meaning is that he exerts himself with difficulty. || 58 ||
Though she has already stepped upon the unassailable, she still seeks further fruit; though satisfied, she desires more;
she does not remain in one place for long—thirst is a restless female monkey. (59)
He states other defects— namely, that [this desire] arises even with regard to an unattainable object, that it is difficult to satisfy, and that it is unstable—
in the verse beginning with "pada" (59).
In one moment it descends into the underworld, in another it ascends to the vault of heaven;
in a moment it wanders through the bowers of the quarters—such is craving, a bee within the lotus of the heart. (60)
He demonstrates precisely the lack of stability in one place with the word "moment" (kṣaṇam). A six-legged female bee (alinī). || 60 ||
Craving alone is the giver of long-lasting suffering among all the defects of saṃsāra; it casts even one dwelling in the inner apartments into extreme distress. (61)
What is the use of much? Listen to a summary; with the intention of explaining the wickedness of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), he says: "All," etc.
In the midst of all the defects of saṃsāra. || 61 ||
This entire world abandons all suffering when freed from anxiety;
indeed, the abandonment of anxiety is said to be the mantra for the cholera of craving. (62)

What, then, is the means for abandoning craving? To this he says: "This world... This world, meaning people, abandons—that is, relinquishes—all suffering by means of having abandoned—that is, having cast off—sinful thought; of this there is no dispute. In that regard, the abandonment of thought is the cause for the relinquishment of all suffering only through the accomplishment of the abandonment of craving, which is the cause of suffering.

This being appropriate, he says: "the mantra for the cholera of craving" (*tṛṣṇāviṣūcikā*). The word *hi* indicates well-known fact. The construction is as follows: the abandonment of thought—that is, the abandonment of thought regarding sense objects—is called the mantra for the cholera of craving. Craving itself is the disease known as cholera; the mantra that removes it is the "mantra for the cholera of craving. Regarding sense objects...

For it is through the thought of attractiveness that craving arises; by abandoning such thought, craving—which is synonymous with passion—does not arise. Therefore, it is rightly said that the abandonment of thought is the mantra for the cholera of craving. 62.
Disease, suffering, and thirst for women quickly bring even a man of profound depth to the surface, just as the rays of the sun cause a lotus to rise.

To further reinforce the statement that among all defects, craving is the long-lasting bringer of suffering, he censures craving again with three verses beginning with "disease and affliction" (rogārti). [He describes] the upright posture of the body, which contradicts the prone position familiar to infants at the breast. (63)

40) Neither the edge of a sword, nor the fire of a thunderbolt, nor the glowing sparks of heated iron are so sharp, O Brahmin, as this craving that dwells within the heart. (64)
The vajra-fire is a thunderbolt that burns; it is the flame of glowing iron sparks, the radiance of heated drops of molten metal. (64–65)
This craving, in the blink of an eye, treats even the best of men as mere straw—be he wise as Mount Meru, heroic, or steadfast. (65)
Dense with the strings of moist intestines, subject to transformation, and filled with burning heat, this body throbs within saṃsāra; even it leads only to suffering. (66)

Thus, having censured the *liṅga-śarīra* along with its characteristics by means of verses beginning with "Risen thus in vain through delusion" and ending with "the wise one who is like Mount Meru," he censures the *sthūla-śarīra* with nine verses beginning with "moist.

[The verse reads: "The intestines and the veins; moist intestines themselves are the strings, and by them it is dense... [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be the beginning of a commentary on a verse describing the physical body.]
Difficult to enter, it is dense with the strings of moist intestines; "paritāpavān" means possessing heat on all sides, which is suffering.
In some versions, it reads "paripātavān. With one end fastened to the gourd-like head, the body quivers and shines like the staff of a lute. 66.
With a slight [cause] one attains joy, and with a slight [cause] one falls into weariness;
there is no object of grief equal to the body, which is base and devoid of virtue.
By "stokena" is meant by a small amount. || 67 ||
O Sage, this body is the great house for the dweller who is the ego; let it be plundered or let it attain stability—what does that matter to me? (68)

Regarding the phrase "the body" (kalevaram): the body is the physical frame. It is egoism itself that is the householder; let it plunder, traverse, or perish—this is the meaning. What does this body avail me, who am free from attachment? Nothing at all. || 68 ||
This house of the body is not desired by me; its senses are like cattle bound in rows, its courtyard is the flickering thirst, and its joy is produced by the servant that is the mind. (69)
In which the ten animal-like sense-faculties are bound in the form of a row— that is, bound as a line—

and in which the courtyard of the house of flickering craving exists— that is, where the fickle woman of the house is craving itself— and in which joy is produced by the mind as a servant— that is, the mind itself acting as a servant therein.

"Ānanda" refers to that which has been described as such. Just as in the world a house—where the courtyard is crowded with many untamed animals lined up in rows, where there is no room for others to enter, and where the womenfolk are constantly agitated—is given only to a servant and is not desired by a person of discernment; so too [is this].
The meaning is: "my body" as well. || 69 ||
(41) This house of the body is not desired by me; it is terrifying with the gateway of the mouth overrun by the monkey of the tongue, and its fragments of teeth and bones are visible. (70)

*Jihveti* (he licks). It is terrifying because the mouth-cavity is occupied by the "monkey" that is the tongue; the tongue itself is the monkey, and it is fearsome due to the mouth-cavity—another term for which is *vaktra*—being occupied by it. It is so described because fragments of bone, namely the teeth themselves, are seen as fragments of bone within it. (70)
What is the use of prosperity, what use is sovereignty, what use is the body, and what use is worldly endeavor?
In just a few days, Time cuts away everything.
"What is prosperity? Prosperity (*śrī*) is the attainment of wealth, grain, and so forth; effort (*īhā*) is exertion. 71, 72, 73.
O Sage, tell me: what loveliness can there be in this body, composed of blood and flesh, including both its exterior and interior, whose sole nature is destruction? (72)
At the time of old age, it undergoes decay; at the time of death, it likewise meets its end.
To one who lacks discernment, the body is exactly the same for both the wealthy man and the pauper. (73)
He who has determined stability in lightning, in autumnal clouds, and in the cities of the Gandharvas— let him place his trust in physical combat.
In the compound *vigraha*, it means "body. || 74 ||
Even having obtained birth in this ocean of worldly existence, which is fickle in form and surging with the waves of karmic duties, childhood leads only to suffering. (75)

Having thus censured the body, he proceeds to censure its various states, beginning with youth, by means of eight verses starting with "Even having obtained... (*labdhvāpi*). The word *api* is used here in the sense of censure (*garhā*).
According to Amara, *api* is used in the senses of censure, conjunction, inquiry, doubt, and possibility. [The body] has a flickering form, that is, a restless form.

In that ocean of worldly existence (saṃsāra-sāgara), which is characterized by waves that are the burdens of duties—both those pertaining to this world and the next—to one who has obtained birth and is currently existing therein... [the verse continues]. (75)
Incapacity, calamity, craving, muteness, dull-wittedness,
greed, fickleness, and wretchedness— all these are established in childhood. (76)
"Incapacity" (aśakti): *tṛṣṇā* is the longing for objects in general;
*gardha* is the greedy desire for specific objects. || 76 ||
The mind is restless by its very nature, and childhood is the height of fickleness; O dear one, when these two are joined together, what end can there be to their wickedness?

"Mind" (manaḥ) || While the two breasts are in close contact, that is, joined together, what end is there to their "wicked fickleness" (kucāpale)? None at all. The meaning is that there is no end to the wicked fickleness of the breasts. In the phrase "like what" (ka iva), the word *iva* is used for emphasis (avadhāraṇe). || 77 ||
O Brahmin, those whose minds are overcome by childhood have learned fickleness from the eyes of women, from masses of lightning, from garlands of flames, and from the waves. (78)

"Of one whose mind is overcome by childhood": he is so described because his mind (cetas) is overcome (ākānta) by that childhood (śaiśavam), which is the state of being a child (śiśutvam). Or else, it refers to that mind which is itself overcome by childhood; from that [state], namely, from infancy (bālyāt). || 78 ||
With the slightest [inducement] he comes under control, and with the slightest [provocation] he undergoes transformation;
like a dog, the fool delights only in impurity. (79)
Regarding the word *stokena*: *stoka* means "little"; *kauleyaka* means "dog. || 79 ||
How could that delusion by which one, being overjoyed, desires to devour the world and seize the moon from the sky, ever lead to happiness? (80)

How could that folly— which, for the sake of enjoyment, desires to devour whatever is seen in the world, and by which one, out of ignorance, wishes to seize the moon from the sky under the suspicion that it is a piece of salted fruit, rice, curd, or a morsel of food— how could such folly, which is synonymous with delusion and the like, lead to happiness? It cannot.
In some way. || 80 ||
In childhood, there is fear of the teacher, as well as of the mother and the father; there is fear of people and of elder children—childhood is a temple of fear. (81)
"In childhood" means in the state of being a child; "from an elder child" means from a child who is superior in age. || 81 ||

O great sage, for no one here indeed does this childhood—whose heart is struck by all the states of defect and which is the playground of non-discrimination—even though it be a home, bring about complete satisfaction. 82.

Having proposed the thesis that "childhood leads only to suffering," he concludes the demonstration with the word "sakala-": "Childhood here is the abode of the playful lack of discrimination, wherein the internal organ (āśaya)—assailed and afflicted by all conditions of the defects such as passion and the like—is likewise situated. It is also the dwelling place of the libertine of non-discrimination. Thus ends the section on childhood.
The intention is that in saṃsāra, nothing whatsoever is sufficient for the complete satisfaction or contentment of any person; on the contrary, it leads only to extreme suffering. || 82 ||
Then, having abandoned the state of childhood, the man—his inner disposition already struck down—ascends to youth with agitation only to fall. (83)

One might suspect that while childhood may indeed be a source of many defects and lead to suffering, youth—possessing qualities such as physical strength and eloquence—leads to happiness; anticipating this, he censures it with seven verses, beginning with "bālya-". [The word] *abhihata* means one whose *āśaya*, or internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is afflicted and oppressed by desire and other passions.
It is so; for the sake of falling, that is, for the sake of falling away from youth. || 83 ||
Helpless, one is overwhelmed by the demon of desire, which dwells within the cavity of one's own mind and bestows various delusions through its force. (84)

One's own mind is the "cave" or the hollow; he whose abiding is perfectly established within that is so described. By him—by that very demon of desire for women, which bestows various delusions. || 84 ||
For even a mind that is expansive, serene, and pure may become turbid in youth, just as a river becomes so during the rainy season.
Extensive and revealing many meanings; [it removes] turbidity, that is, cloudiness. || 85 ||
The deer of the mind, rushing toward the mirage of youth that arises from the heat of the winds of the body, fall into the pit of sense objects. (86)
The body is a desert land; "arisen from the heat of the body's wind" means produced there by the heat of the fire (vaiśvānara) favored by time. "The mirage of youth" (*yuvatāmṛgatṛṣṇikām*);
or alternatively, the reading is *yuvatā-mṛgatṛṣṇikām*. Youth is adolescence, and that itself is the mirage.
The state of being water in a mirage; "avaṭa" means a pit. || 86 ||
Whenever youth ascends to its highest peak, desires surge forth with feverish intensity; at that time, they lead only to destruction. (87)

Having described the fault at the onset of youth, he speaks of it as it increases: "When... This means that whenever youth reaches its highest point, the uppermost stage; the fever here is born of desire (*kāma*), and "desires" refers to those who possess them. || 87 ||
They are worthy of veneration, they are great souls, and they alone are true men on this earth,
O virtuous one, who have safely crossed over the perils of youth.

Having thus described the defects of youth and established that desire and its like are the seeds of suffering for those intent on this world, [the author] shows that one who seeks liberation must exert great effort to escape from them and cross over them, by saying: "They are to be revered.
[The Buddha is] adorned with discipline, the abode of noble beings, radiant with compassion, and encircled by virtues.
For here in this world, auspicious youth is indeed as difficult to find as a forest situated in the sky. || 89 ||
Having stated that youth is a locus of defects, he speaks of its lack of virtues: "vinaya... etc. "Āvalita" means encircled.
The connection here is with the word "jagati" (in this world). || 89 ||
In this woman’s cage-like body, which is a puppet made of flesh, restless with its mechanical joints and adorned with sinews, bones, and knots—what indeed is beautiful about it? (90)

Since youth generally causes harm through women, after censuring youth, he now censures the woman who serves as the instrument for that harm, beginning with the verse "māṃsa... (flesh). A *pāñcālikā* is a doll made of cloth or other materials; as Amara states: "A *pāñcālikā* is a doll made of cloth, ivory, and so forth. [He speaks] of this doll made of flesh (*māṃsapāñcālikā*).
Of a doll fashioned from flesh, abounding in sinews, bones, and knots: *snāyu* (sinew) and *vasnasā* (tendon) are the bonds of the body. According to Amara:

"The intestine (*antra*), the small intestine (*purītat*), the spleen (*gulma*), and the liver (*plīhā*)—the last two being masculine; furthermore, *vasnasā*, *snāyu*, and *striyām* [are feminine]; while *kālakhaṇḍa* and *yakṛt* are both neuter. Thus, [it is] by means of the knots of the sinews and the bones. Or else:

It is so described because it "shines" (śālate) or is adorned with sinews, bones, and knots of flesh; [it resides] in the cage of limbs, the nest of the body of that woman. Of what kind? "Moving like a machine," meaning as flickering as a water-wheel or similar device. || 90 ||
Having separated the eye into its components—skin, flesh, blood, and the water of tears—look closely at it;
if it is beautiful, why do you delude yourself in vain? (91)

One might object: "How can it be questioned what is beautiful about the cage-like body of that woman, whose eyes are as lovely as trembling blue lotuses, and whose breasts are encircled by shimmering white necklaces and possess the splendor of golden jars?
He dispels this doubt with three verses, beginning with *tvak* (the skin). *Bāṣpāmbu* means tears.

The compound *tvan-māṃsa* and so forth is a dvandva treated as a singular. If the eye—which is essentially a collection of skin, flesh, and other elements—is beautiful from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), then having separated the skin and other parts, examine the eye;
look at it properly. [Otherwise, you are viewing it] in vain (*mudhā*). || 91 ||
In which breast the splendor of a pearl necklace was seen, resembling the rush of the Ganges water gleaming upon the slopes of Mount Meru’s peak. 92.

The connection with the second verse is as follows: that very breast of a woman, upon which the splendor of a pearl necklace was seen to resemble the rush of the Gaṅgā’s waters shimmering on the slopes of Mount Meru’s peaks, is now being devoured by dogs in the cremation grounds at the ends of the quarters, like a small lump of food for a blind dog in the course of time. [The phrase] "shimmering on the slopes of Mount Meru’s peaks" means shining or gleaming there.

[The phrase] *meruśṛṅgataṭollāsi* means: either that which shines upon the slopes of the peak of Meru; or, that whose splendor (*ullāsa*) is comparable to the force (*raya*)—that is, the velocity—of the Ganges water surging forth on the slopes of Meru’s peak.

"Splendorous" (*ullāsaśālī*) refers to that which shines (*śālate*) or is beautiful due to its splendor or its overflowing abundance; the state of being such is *tattā*. *Andhasaḥ* means food. [Synonyms for boiled rice are: *bhissā* (feminine), *bhakta*, *adhaḥ-anna*, and *odana* (masculine/neuter).
Thus says Amara [in verses 92 and 93].
In cremation grounds at the ends of the quarters, that very same breast of a woman is devoured by dogs in due time, like a small morsel of food. (93)
(46) Bearing hair like soot, difficult to touch yet pleasing to the eye,
women— flames of the fire of evil deeds— burn men like straw. (94)

"Keśa... [means]: bearing hair-ink; that is, they bear their very hair as if it were ink or collyrium (maṣī), because they cause suffering. They are difficult to touch. They are the flames of the fire of evil deeds; that is, sins themselves are the fires, and these are their crests or tongues of flame. || 94 ||
Even when blazing at a great distance, women—though full of passion—are devoid of essence; indeed, they are the beautiful yet dreadful fuel for the fires of hell.
Regarding the phrase "jvalatām" (of those blazing): the connection is that women become the beautiful yet dreadful fuel for the intensely blazing fires of hell.

Here, by the word "cāru" (beautiful), what is intended is its wondrous nature; "dāruṇam" means terrifying. The epithet is used to establish how women serve as beautiful fuel. "Though full of essence, they are devoid of essence": here, "rasa" means essential sap.

The meaning is that, through deluded vision, they appear full of essence (*sarasa*), yet through the other [vision], they are sapless (*nīrasa*) and devoid of substance; for by the word "essence" (*rasa*), even a liquid is expressed. In the world, fuel is either moist or dry, but never both at once. Since women, however, are both full of essence and yet sapless, they constitute excellent fuel. For this reason, even when situated at a distance...
They kindle the fires characterized by hell; therefore, even this [fire] becomes both beautiful fuel and terrible fuel. || 95 ||
Women, scattered by the hunter named Desire, are the snares for binding the limbs of those bird-like men whose minds are deluded. (96)

"By the name of desire": for men who are like birds—those of deluded minds and confused hearts—the nets that bind their limbs, which are the snares for binding the body-parts, are scattered and cast about by the hunter named "desire. Or, "aṅga" may be used as a vocative particle. Here, the word *vāgurā*, which denotes a snare for catching deer, refers to nets.
They are perceived. || 96 ||
For men who are like fish in the pond of birth, wandering in the mud of the mind, a woman is a baited hook on the line of evil latent tendencies. (97)

For those who are like fish in the pond of birth—where "birth" itself is the "pond," meaning a small lake (according to Amara: *veśanta*, *palvala*, and *alpasara* are synonyms for a small lake, while *vāpī* is a long pond)—the mud of that pond is the mind. For men who move within that mud, it is their own evil tendencies (*durvāsanā*) that become the fishing line held in the hand of the fisherman named "non-discrimination. Woman, however, is the baited hook.

It becomes so; that is to say, at the tip of the line of the fish-catcher *baḍiśa*—a hook made of iron or similar metal attached to the end of a rope—is placed a baited lump of meat intended to catch the fish. || 97 ||
By means of this well-fashioned casket of all the jewels of faults, this woman—who is a constant chain of suffering—may she be sufficient for me forever. (98)

Having thus demonstrated the faults of women, he states the fruit of their thorough knowledge: "Of all these," and so forth. Faults themselves are the jewels; by means of a *samudgikā*—a beautiful casket (the *Amara-kośa* defines *samudgaka* as a casket)—in the form of a woman who is a chain that bestows suffering, let there be enough (*alam*). The word *alam* is used here in the sense of prohibition.
According to Amara, the word *alam* signifies ornament, sufficiency, ability, and prohibition. || 98 ||
O Brahmin, in just a few days, a woman goes from having flesh here, blood there, and bones here, to a state of putrefaction.
And because of her instability, he says "woman" is unsteady; [he explains] "here" as having the nature of dispersal (*visarārutā*), that is, the tendency to scatter. 99.
He who has a wife has a desire for enjoyment; for one devoid of a wife, where is the ground for enjoyment?
Having abandoned the woman, the world is abandoned; having abandoned the world, one becomes happy. (100)
Now, one might object: "If there is a desire for enjoyment, why say, 'Enough of a wife for me'? To this, he says: "He who has a wife... and so forth.

For that man who possesses a woman, there is a desire for enjoyment. Since it is impossible for a skillful person to maintain possession of something when the desire for enjoyment is absent, where could there be a ground for enjoyment for one devoid of women—one who avoids the possession of women? Desire for enjoyment exists nowhere at all; for as long as desire for enjoyment exists, it is impossible to avoid possessing its object. Let this be so, yet even then—
He states what would result from the mere abandonment of women: "A woman... (verse 100).

O Brahmin, I do not delight in enjoyments that are difficult to transcend and charming only at first sight, flickering like the wings of a bee; out of fear of death, disease, old age, and the like, I seek peace and attain the supreme state.
Through effort. || 101 ||
He concludes the meaning of the section with the verse beginning "āpāta-": "Āpāta" refers to the falling toward one another of objects and the senses;

that is, the contact between objects and the senses. "In those [objects] which delight at the mere onset"—that is, at the very moment of onset—or alternatively, "in those from which delight arises merely by the mere onset. [They are] difficult to cross, flickering like the wings of bees.
In the flickering [motions] of the edges of the bees' wings—as they say: "the base of the wing (pakṣati) is the root of the wing, and it is also called the edge of the wing (pakṣāṃśa). || 101 ||
For childishness, being insatiable, forcibly drinks up youth;
and thereafter, old age drinks up youth—behold their mutual harshness! 102.

Having generally censured women as the gateway through which youth brings about misfortune, the author now introduces the censure of old age—which follows immediately after youth—by means of the subsequent textual composition, demonstrating the relationship of mutual suppression between childhood and the other stages of life, beginning with the verse: "It is insufficient. This means it is incapable of satisfying the demon of youth.
It drinks up childhood, the state of being a child; and youth forcibly drinks up old age and harshness—the meaning is cruelty. || 102 ||
When people have been seized by old age with its effortless torment,
wisdom flees away like a woman who has fled from a rival wife who has struck her.
The verses beginning with "anāyāsakadarthinyā" have clear meanings. Among them, some verses are now explained. She who torments or causes suffering without effort is "anāyāsakadarthinī. (103, 104)
Servants, sons, wives, kinsmen, and friends likewise laugh at a man trembling with old age, as if he were a madman. (104)
Difficult to behold, withered, wretched, and devoid of virtues and prowess—just as a vulture approaches a tree, so does greed approach old age, which is not long-lasting. (105)
*Jaraṭha* means old or aged; *gardha* is greed, which is a desire for a specific object. (105)
(49) In old age, a longing that consists of the fault of wretchedness, which causes a long-lasting burning in the heart and is the sole companion of all calamities, increases. (106)
Longing has as its object only material wealth. || 106 ||
"What must I do? What is the terrible suffering in the next world that is so extremely dreadful?
Indeed, in old age, grows a fear that is impossible to remedy. (107)
"In the next world there will be extremely terrible suffering; what should I do?"—this is a fear that is beyond remedy.
In old age, greed arises with a longing to enjoy, yet one is unable to do so; indeed, the heart is consumed by the wretchedness of one's lack of power.
"With joy" means with agitation; "due to the impairment of power" means, that is to say, due to a deficiency of power. || 108 ||
Beholding it as if fully ripened, grey with the ash of age, Time—the Lord, so they say—consumes the gourd-like head of men. (109)

Old age itself is like ash mixed with grey hair; by that [ash], it becomes slightly pale and greyish-white (*vidhūsara*). A pumpkin fruit at its upper part becomes greyish-white (*vidhūsara*) by means of a color resembling ash. || 109 ||
O Sage, as King Death approaches, Old Age goes before him with white chowries, while his army of mental and physical ailments follows behind.
"Old age itself, possessed of grey hair, is the white chowrie in that [army] which possesses banners; thus it is described as 'patākinī,' meaning an army.
It is connected with the phrase 'in front of King Death as he approaches. (110)
Within the inner apartments of the body, which are white with the plaster of old age, women remain happily, free from incapacity, affliction, and calamity. (111)
It is a transformation of lime, powder, and so forth. || 111 ||
What is the use of that miserable life held in such a poor grasp, for even one who has reached old age continues to live?
Yet, O dear one, in this world, old age overcomes all people’s desires, even those who have conquered them. (112)

What need is there for much? He says, "What is the use of that?"—meaning that for one who has reached old age, death alone is better than life, which is the locus of manifold torments. Even though one who has reached old age lives as a vessel for many afflictions, what is the use of that wretched life, that miserable grasping, or that miserable obsession with living? For even by world-conquerors, old age remains unconquered; since it assails one's knowledge and other faculties.

Because it bestows great suffering, it sets aside all other desires. The intention is that one whose mind is agitated by the exceedingly great suffering of old age aspires only for the cessation of that suffering, and nothing else. || 112 ||
Even for those who might possess some notion of happiness within this cycle of existence,
time cuts it away entirely, just as a rat gnaws through a thread. (113)

Thus, by means of the preceding textual context, it has been determined that in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which is crowded with hundreds of sufferings, there is no faultless happiness anywhere. Now, even if happiness is admitted, liberation does not exist because of the defect of impermanence inherent in that [happiness] consisting of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the act of enjoyment; this is established by the following textual context.
He establishes this. In that regard, he first states the impermanence of pleasure: "In some cases," etc. The word "vā" (or) is for the purpose of indicating another opinion. || 113 ||
There is nothing here that this all-devouring time does not swallow— the entire world that has been born, just as the submarine fire devours the great ocean.
Now, one might object: "If the class of objects that produce happiness were eternal, then happiness itself could possibly be eternal in the form of a continuous flow.
To this, he says: "Not that... [The word] *ghasmaro* means "one whose nature is to devour. According to Amara, "a devourer (*bhakṣaka*) is called *ghasmaro* or *admaro*. (Verse 114)
Even for the great, our Lord does not provide protection for even a moment;
Time, having become the soul of the universe, has swallowed the entire world. 115.
Regarding the fact that even when there is fear caused by time for the wretched, it does not exist for the great-souled ones, he says here: "Of the great ones" (mahatām). || 115 ||
Those things which are delightful, those which are auspicious undertakings, and even those as massive as Mount Sumeru—
all are swallowed up by Time, just as serpents are devoured by Garuḍa.

He says that even beauty, virtuous action, and being a mine of good qualities do not prevent [the arrival of] Time: "Those which are delightful," etc. Those whose undertakings are auspicious are so described. 116.
(51) Out of self-centeredness, he strives to appropriate for himself everything— from a blade of grass, a particle of dust, Mahendra, and Mount Sumeru, down to a leaf and the ocean. (117)
Now, one might wonder: "In the midst of such a variety of infinite objects, could there possibly be something that has not been swallowed by Time?

To this, he says: "A blade of grass... [and so forth]. "By being *ātmaṃbhari*" means by filling one's own belly; as Amara states: "Both *ātmaṃbhari* and *kukṣiṃbhari* mean those who fill their own bellies. (117)
This is the time when the great trees that are the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), filled with the humming of the mosquitoes that are living beings, have reached the state of falling. || 118 ||
By the phrase "intent on making everything his own," he elaborates upon Time's role as the destroyer of all things.

He states its function as the destroyer of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) during the dissolution of primordial nature (*prākṛtapralaya*): "This is Time. In this context, living beings themselves are the mosquitoes; those [worlds] in which there is the humming sound produced by them are described as such.

The universes themselves are the udumbara fruits; their "oghas" are collections or multitudes; thus, "brahmāṇḍodumbaraugha" refers to those [collections]. Their state of being "bṛhatpādapa" means their condition as massive trees. || 118 ||

Beholding with his sun-like eye, which does not blink day and night, this [Time] devours the fruits of the world like ripe fruit— the fruits that are the guardians of the quarters— just as an old forest decays.

Although it is established that Time possesses the power of destruction within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) once its role as the destroyer of the universe has been stated, [the author] nevertheless describes, at the outset, its destruction of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), showing separately its power to destroy things situated within it, in order to strengthen the conviction regarding its impermanence—beginning with the words "prekṣya" (having observed). [The phrase continues: "ahni vigato... (vanished during the day...).
Since a *nimeṣa* (the blink of an eye) is characterized by the time of sunset for the sun’s eye, that day is therefore called *vinimeṣa*. || 119 ||
Death, like a merchant, gradually casts the jewels of the world— those bound by the qualities (guṇas)— into the fierce hollow of its chest, which is strewn with the dilapidated huts of the universe.
Having described his role as the protector and destroyer [of the guardians], he describes his role as the protector and destroyer of the world itself with the two verses beginning with "jagat."
The world itself is an old hut; in it, he casts those virtuous people who are scattered and dispersed—like jewels—into that very death which is like a casket possessing a fierce hollow or crack. 120.
(52) That very string of world-jewels which is abundantly filled with virtues,
he cuts away again after having placed it upon his body as if for the sake of ornament. (121)
During the period of maintenance, he holds her as his consort; at the time of withdrawal, he cuts her asunder.
While he was thus engaged, the world— like a network of dried jungle— was made into a hunting ground by wretched and deluded throngs of beings and wild animals who were worn out.

He demonstrates another way in which Time is the destroyer of the world through the textual passage beginning with "of this very [Time]" and ending with "the bow flashes forth on all sides. Here, by the word *jāṅgala*, which denotes regions abounding in wind, lands suitable for hunting are indicated. *Jālaka* means a multitude or collection.

The connection [of this work] is with such matters as are set forth in the subsequent body of the text— for instance, that for this very prince named Kāla, who practices the hunt (mṛgayā) as a chase for the herds of living beings within the forest-net of the world, the great ocean of the end of the aeon (kalpa) serves as a pleasure-pool.
It is that [city] in which there is a lotus that is the submarine fire itself; thus, it is "that in which the beautiful submarine-fire-lotus shines forth in one place."
The great ocean at the time of the kalpa’s end was a delightful pleasure-pool, wherein the beautiful submarine fire shone like a lotus in one corner.
The world's morning meal consists of those very same worlds— become pungent, bitter, sour, and so forth— which have become oceans of curd and milk, yet have become stale.

Having shown a lotus pond to dispel the fatigue born of wandering for the hunt, he shows the meal of Prince Kālarāja before his departure for the hunt: "Kaṭu... [and so on]. This refers to those [dishes] in which pungent, bitter, and sour elements are the primary ingredients; that is, with various flavorful vegetable side-dishes (*upadaṃśa*).
He states the reason for the stale condition of the world’s food, which is moistened by the oceans of curd and milk: "by them" (taih).
Whatever worlds existed at the beginning of a kalpa, those very same worlds persist even at the end of the kalpa; this is what is meant by "stale.
*Kalyavarta* means a meal taken at dawn. As Amara states: "Pratyūṣa, harmukha, kalya, uṣas, and pratyuṣas also [denote dawn]."

Caṇḍī, who moves through the four [directions], accompanied by the entire host of Mothers, is stationed in the forest of saṃsāra; she is a tigress who destroys the multitudes of malevolent spirits. (125)
To Time, who was engaged in hunting, he points out the tigress as being like a bitch—saying "Caṇḍī. Caṇḍī means old age. 125.
The earth is the vessel in the palm of her hand, filled with the essence of nectar,
and adorned with a garland of swaying clusters of lotuses, blue water-lilies, and white lilies.
He shows him the vessel placed in his palm for the drinking of wine, saying: "The earth.

The earth—that is, the ground itself—becomes the drinking vessel in the palm of Time; and he says it is no small one: "The earth. It is filled with flavor—that is, filled with the flavor of wine. For the sake of fragrance, it contains a swaying cluster of lotuses, water-lilies, and white lilies.
"Garlanded by a multitude" means intermingled. "Kahlāra" refers to the *saugandhika* lotus. || 126 ||
Roaring, with a formidable slapping of his arms, Nṛsiṃha is within the cage of his own arms;
with a mane and broad, muscular shoulders, he is the lovely pet bird of play.

He points out the bird suitable for his sport, mounted upon the fierce staff-like arms of Time—the great warrior who is skillful at wandering through the hunt of the forest of the world—describing it as "virāvī" (making a sound). It is so called because it possesses a loud cry (*virāva*). *Āsphoṭa* refers to the clapping of the palms against the joined forearms and upper arms; it is *vikaṭa*, meaning deformed or formidable.

"One who has a slapping [of the arms]" is so called. "With shoulders broad and thick with manes" means one whose shoulders (the upper parts of the body) are thick and whose neck-hair (mane) is formidable and misshapen; thus he is "one with formidable, thick shoulders. Alternatively, it means one whose broad shoulders are formidable due to the mane. "Śakunta" means a bird. || 127 ||
Sweet with the lute of the bottle-gourd, possessing the stainless luster of the autumnal sky,
the Lord Mahākāla is indeed the playful protector of the cuckoo.
He states that even the deity named Mahākāla, who exists as an attendant of Rudra like Nṛsiṃha, is a mere instrument for Kāla’s play:
"alābv... As Kṣīrasvāmin has said: "Nandin, Mahākāla, and Bhṛṅgin are the attendants of Rudra.
[The phrase] "alābu-vīṇā-van-madhura" means having a sweet sound like that of a gourd-lute. Alternatively, there is a reading: "madhuradhvanir vyoma," meaning a sweet-sounding sky.
He describes his blackness like that of a cuckoo with the verse beginning "autumn" (śarad). || 128 ||
A bow named Non-conceptualization (Abhāvanā), whose form is an incessant flash and which has discharged a volley of arrows of suffering, vibrates everywhere. (129)

He displays his bow to one who has entered the world’s dilapidated forest and is occupied with the slaughter of the animal-like living beings—[the verse beginning with] "ajasra-": One whose form is constantly manifesting as neither Indra, nor the moon, nor Mount Meru, nor the Vindhya range; [and] he by whom the row (āvali) of arrows consisting of sufferings alone has been discharged (vāntā)—that is, vomited forth.
Likewise: *kodaṇḍa* means a bow; [it belongs] to the Supreme Lord, whose nature is Time. || 129 ||
Having herself become the Night of Doom (Kālarātri), she dances by her own will;
the entire series of the celestial realms serves as the ornament upon her limbs.

He describes the play of the world’s dissolution in another manner, beginning with the words "The Night of Time" (*kālarātri*). By the phrase "shining throughout the great aeons" (*mahākalpeṣu rājate*), it is meant that the power consisting primarily of darkness, which is exceedingly capable of destroying everything, is called the "Night of Time. The connection is as follows: this Supreme Lord, who is the very essence of Time, having himself become the Night of Time, dances. Of him—

He shows the implements of dance with the words "yasyā" (of whom): the series (*āvali*) of various celestial realms—that is, the different divisions of the worlds of the gods—which serves as an ornament upon her limbs; she is Kālarātri—this is how the phrase connects with what precedes. 130.
And Narakālī, a garland of anklets resplendent with a sweet tinkling sound, is threaded upon the string of evil deeds and stands with her feet in the underworld. (131)
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: the row of hell-dwellers (*narakālī*), situated upon whose feet, becomes a garland of anklets (*mañjīramālā*).

*Ālī* means a row; *mañjīra* means an anklet (*nūpura*). The phrase "garland of anklets" establishes a common quality (*sādharmya*) through the description beginning with "kalakala," and so forth. It is radiant and brilliant due to the *kalakala*, which is a tumultuous clamor. || 131 ||
(55) On one [side] there is a long ear like the Himavat mountain, a seal-ring of bone; on the other, indeed, there is the great Meru, lovely as a golden pericarp. (132)
On one ear of hers is a long earring made of bone, white as snow, measuring slightly less than one hundred thousand yojanas in length; *karṇikā* is a specific kind of ear ornament. || 132 ||
Right here, her two dangling earrings are the sun and moon,
her circular cheeks are the Lokāloka mountain range, and her waist-girdle extends all around.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "The moon and sun become her very earrings here. The word "here" (*atra*) refers to the ears mentioned in the preceding verse. The term "swinging" (*lole*) is an epithet qualifying the two earrings. "On the orb of the cheeks" (*gaṇḍamaṇḍale*) means "on the two orbs of the cheeks. "Line" (*śreṇī*) means a row. || 133 ||

Furthermore, they were terrifying with the loud *jhāṃkāra* sounds from the large apertures of their three eyes, and with peacocks that had been killed by youths who wandered about with dangling [limbs]. || 134 ||
Intending to state that it is unnecessary to say that her form brings fear to the world, he says: "Afterwards," etc.

The six words ending in the third case—from *paścātpralamba* up to *khaṭvāṅgabhaṅgaiḥ*—are connected with the phrase *āpūritāmbara*. [The word] *paścāt* means "at the back" or "in the hair-tuft (*kabara*) and so forth.
*Pralambāḥ* means "hanging down," and *vibhrāntāḥ* refers to those peacocks that died in their youth.

"By those [beings] consisting of the six-faced one, the nectar, and the peacock. Regarding "by the eyes": due to the filling of air within the large apertures of the three eyes of the specific heads of Hara, there were many *jhāṅkāra* sounds; by those terrifying [sounds]. (134)

With the heads of Hara, whose long, dangling matted locks and moon were scattered about; and with the chowries of Gaurī’s beautiful, swaying tresses, white as the Mandāra flower, rising aloft. || 135 ||

By those whose matted locks and the moon are long and swaying (*lambalolajaṭācandra*), and who have scattered themselves across the head of Hara; by those [who possess] chowries which are the tresses of Gaurī, wherein beautiful Mandāra flowers are rising up—*kabara* meaning a mass of hair. 135.

With skull-drums as large as the bellies of Bhairava, appearing like mountains in a wild dance, and with alms-bowls formed from the skulls of Indra’s body, which resound through their hundred holes; || 136 ||

By means of those *tumbakas*—that is, bottle-gourds—which are *uttāṇḍavas*, meaning they have rolled about and possess a moving form, and which are the bellies (*udarāṇi*) of Bhairava; or alternatively, *uttāṇḍava* is an epithet for Kālarātri. And by those *indradehas*—meaning the bodies of Indra—which are *raṇat* (resounding), that is, making noise, and which are accompanied by *saśatarandhra*, meaning possessing a hundred apertures.
They [are characterized] by those alms-bowls. || 136 ||
Filling the sky with the snapping of her dry skeletal staffs,
she who brings about the destruction of all terrifies even herself. (137)
Those which are the dried bones produced from the body are themselves the "broken parts of the bed-frame," meaning fragments of the components of the couch. If it is asked,
"But since the peacock feathers (*barha*) and so forth are singular, how can there be the plural form *barhibhiḥ* (with peacock feathers) and so on?"— do not say so.

Regarding the phrase "it shines throughout the great aeons" (*mahākalpeṣu rājate*), this is already resolved by the use of the plural number; for it is possible that there are many peacocks and so forth due to the distinction between different great aeons. [He is] that self by whom the sky, the atmosphere, has been filled. (137)
With a beautiful garland of lotuses that are the wheels on the heads of Viśvarūpa,
she shines as she dances vibrantly throughout the great kalpas.
Thinking, "What is the use of much? Listen to the power of Kālarātri in brief," he says:

"viśvarūpa... etc. By means of the beautiful garlands of lotuses (*puṣkaramālā*), which are actually the multitudes or collections of many millions of heads of Viśvarūpa—well-known from the *Gītās*—which quiver during the *tāṇḍava* dances, that is, on the occasions of those dances; in some places [the text reads] *tatra*.
The syntactical connection is "they move about. In that context, it means "when the tāṇḍava dances are to be performed. || 138 ||
O Great Sage, since these factors such as time and the rest are thus [transient] within this so-called saṃsāra, what reliance could there possibly be here for those like me? (139)

Thus, restating the conduct of Time and the other factors, he clarifies the result of fully understanding their defects: "In this manner," meaning by the method already described; having supplied the words "when such conduct exists," the construction is as follows.
In some versions, it reads "when such conduct of these [factors] exists. In the term "Time and the others" (*kālādi*), the word "others" (*ādi*) includes the Moon and so forth.
The conduct of Time and the others is an illustration of the other previously mentioned defects of saṃsāra. || 139 ||
(57) It is true that the enemies are none other than the sense-faculties, which have fallen into untruth;
the mind itself strikes down the self by means of the self—the mind is indeed the enemy of the mind. 140.

One might object: "If there is no attachment to this misfortune called *saṃsāra*, then let the supreme effort be directed toward its cessation; what is the use of this boasting? Anticipating this doubt, he describes the ease with which factors adverse to that cessation are encountered, and the difficulty of finding those favorable to it, by means of the series of verses beginning with "The enemies" and ending with "the bond of worldly existence. Now, as for the goal to be attained...
If the reality characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth were to manifest directly, what could the enemies that are the senses do?
To this he says: "It is true. The reality characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth has fallen into the state of unreality, taking on the form of the body and other such things.
Now, one might object: if the mind is favorable to us, there should be no fear of the enemies that are the senses; to this he says:
"He strikes": the mind, having become an enemy in its second aspect, strikes itself by means of its own self.
When an object is known as non-existent, the mind is surrendered to the ego;
once existence has been pierced by non-existence, no end to existence is perceived.

He establishes the enmity of the mind with the words, "The Reality (vastu). The Reality, which is characterized as the witness of the aggregate of cause and effect, has been grasped as a non-reality—that is, as having the nature of that very aggregate of cause and effect. Now, one might object: since the Reality can indeed be grasped as the witness of the aggregate, such a mistaken apprehension will surely cease. To this, he says: "It was given."

The intention is that because that mind, agitated by desire, is incapable of discernment (*viveka*), it pursues only the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and not its witness; this is the point. Now, if the mind indeed plunges into an object, then let attachment be bound precisely to those states such as the ego-sense which it plunges into; to this he says: "In the absence... [of objects]. "States" (*bhāvāḥ*).

"Objects are pierced by non-existence" means they are struck by non-existence; that is to say, they are impermanent. If it is argued that, according to the principle that "an object perishing does not perish until reaching a state of immutability," the Self should be known as the limit of destruction, the author says: "bhāva... (of existence). This means that the Self is the end, the terminal ground, of existences—that is, of impermanent objects. Thus, [it is called] "the end of becoming" (*bhavānta*).
In some cases. || 141 ||
O virtuous one, the mind, with its inner depths agitated, suffers in vain;
the disease of passion flourishes, while the person free from passion is rare indeed. (142)

Having stated that when the perception of defects in the non-self occurs and the self is not attained, the result follows, he says: "It suffers" (*tapyate*). [The word] *antarā* means in the interval between the real and the unreal. Now, one might ask: since the cessation of suffering is possible through the total renunciation of all desires, for what purpose does it suffer?
To this he replies: "Passion" (*rāga*). Then, one might suggest that passion could be removed by contact with those who are dispassionate; to this he replies: "The dispassionate one" (*virāgī*).
Through effort, youth passes away; association with the virtuous remains far off; no certain refuge exists anywhere, and truthfulness does not arise. 143.

If it is asked, "In that case, why should one not act with haste now?", he says: "With effort. The intention is that during youth, the body and its instruments possess the capacity to accomplish the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), whereas this is not the case in old age. If it is then suggested, "In that case, let those who know reality (*tattvavid*) be served right now," he says: "Far off. If it is then argued, "Let another means be sought," he says: "The only resort. Now, [an objection]: nanu...

How is it that there is no other recourse? [The author] says "In some place" (*kvacit*) to address the objection that the self, being self-luminous, will manifest by itself through the power of reasoning alone. "Truth" (*satyatā*) means the state of being real; the meaning is the nature of reality (*satyasvarūpa*).

Alternatively, [the author] says "In some place" because if the reality of the world were accepted, there would be another recourse as for the dualists (*dvaitin*); therefore, he says "In some place. Not even in some place...
Reality does not arise in an object existing within the world; the meaning is that it does not appear. || 143 || 144 ||
The mind is as if utterly bewildered within; joy has gone far away.
Compassion does not arise with its usual brilliance; baseness approaches from afar.
A person who is intent on falling and rising alternately goes from steadfastness to instability;
association with the wicked is easy to obtain, but meeting with the virtuous is difficult to find. (145)
To show that equanimity is difficult to attain for one dwelling amidst the wicked in saṃsāra, he speaks of the instability of that state:
"Dhīratā... [Verse 145]. *Pāta* is the fall from sovereignty and the like; *utpāta* is the attainment of it. Alternatively, *pāta* is destruction and *utpāta* is emergence.
(59) Phenomena arise and pass away; the cultivation [of them] binds one to existence.
Only a constant succession of beings is led here and there. 146.

Meditation has the body and so forth as its object. Having thus established that things favorable to human goals are difficult to obtain while those unfavorable to them are easy to find, he states the conclusion: "He is led. He is led onto some path that is devoid of the performance of the means for achieving human goals and is, moreover, an obstacle to those goals. [This occurs] "by fate" (vidhinā).
The remainder. || 146 || 147 ||
Even the Dānavas are torn asunder; even Dhruva’s life is uncertain;
even the immortals are slain—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
For even the directions are no longer seen, nor is any place recognizable by its distinct designation;
even the mountains crumble—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I? (148)

To demonstrate that there is an exceedingly intense desire for immersion in eternal bliss for me—who am consumed by the forest fire of *saṃsāra*—just as one whose head is ablaze desires immersion in water, he elaborates upon impermanence, which was previously stated as "phenomena are subject to coming and going.

A few words are now explained: [the verse begins] "possessing the nature of being designated by another, possessing the word 'fame'... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.]

The meaning is that even a place (deśa) comes to be designated by the word "non-place" (adeśa). Regarding the phrase "partaking of another's instruction" (anyopadeśabhāk), it means that in some cases it partakes only of the instruction of another and is not perceived by itself; the reason is its having perished. || 148 ||
The sky is devoured by non-existence, and the world is likewise consumed; even the earth falls into desolation—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I? (149)
The word division is *asattayā* [meaning] "by way of non-existence. *Vaidhuryam* means non-existence (*asattām*). || 149 ||
Even the oceans dry up and even the stars perish;
even the perfected ones (siddhas) meet their end—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even Parameṣṭhin, though steadfast, is carried away; even Hari, though unborn, is led off;
even Bhava falls into non-existence—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
*Niṣṭhāvān* means "possessing destruction. According to Amarasimha, *niṣṭhā* refers to both completion and destruction. || 151 ||
Even time is driven by another, and even destiny is led away;
even the infinite sky dissolves—what reliance can there be on a person such as I? (152)

By this Supreme Self, [the world] is drawn forth; the meaning is that it is withdrawn. *Niyati* means destiny (*daiva*), which is to say prior karma, or else it refers to the cosmic law (*maryādā*). Thus is *niyati*. || 152 ||
By someone who bestows delusion, whose form is knowledge difficult to perceive, and whose nature is both inaudible and ineffable,
the worlds are being mimicked.

It has been stated that even Time is measured by another; [the author] now shows this other [agent] with the words "inexpressible" (*aśrāvya*). That whose ultimate nature (*pāramārthika-svarūpa*) is a reality that cannot be heard or expressed due to its being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatayā*), is such [a one]. By him whose form (*mūrti*)—that is, whose very nature—is knowledge that is difficult to perceive, [he perceives] that which is difficult to see.

"Having entered into what is hidden," according to the Śruti. They are mocked—that is, they are ridiculed. They are deceived by one who, concealing the truth, displays only that which is imagined; the meaning is "by a magician. || 153 ||

"Today is a festival, this is the season, likewise here is the procession, these are your kinsmen, this is happiness, that is a special enjoyment"—thus, vainly weaving a web of such false imaginings, the world falls away with its fickle and fragile intellect. (154)

He expresses compassion, saying "Today is a festival," for the world perishes by clinging to mere delusion and failing to recognize that deluding one who has been granted [existence] by the Supreme Self as its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). "With a mind as unsteady as a swaying lotus stalk" means that his physical intellect is extremely fickle; "it falls away" means it perishes. (154)

Having wandered here and there to a great distance and entered his home at the close of day, when the sun has set—a day devoid of the virtuous conduct that is the refuge of discerning people—who can find sleep? (155)

Having thus lamented over those who wander in saṃsāra due to their lack of discrimination, [the author] says that one seeking liberation—who dwells in their midst—does not even value natural sleep because of the agitation caused by anxiety and the impossibility of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth in the proximity of those devoted to Brahman, who are dear to him as the sole goal: Thus, having lamented over those wandering in saṃsāra due to their lack of discrimination, [the author] says that one seeking liberation—who dwells in their midst—does not even value natural sleep because of the impossibility of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth in the proximity of those devoted to Brahman, who are dear to him as the sole goal, and because he is overwhelmed and agitated by anxiety. He says:

"From here," [it is said]. Those who possess discernment, the knowers of Brahman, [see] that which is devoid—that is, empty—of the virtuous conduct characterized by hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, which has that [world] as its support and is dependent upon it. || 155 ||
(61) O dear one, sons, wives, and wealth are mentally constructed as being like an elixir;
yet in the end, they all turn out to be nothing more than a most unpleasant fainting spell caused by poison. 156.

[Objection: Surely every person, conceiving their children, wife, and so forth as being like nectar, engages with them; why then should your engagement not be the same regarding hearing [the scriptures] and other such practices? To this, he says: "Children," etc. The word *nātiramyā* is a single compound. The connection is as follows: that which is "not very delightful" (*anatiramyā*)—namely, the very state of being intoxicated by poison—he performs at the end, at the time of death. The word *nāma* [is used here for emphasis].

Regarding the sense of contempt: in some places where it says "where it is exceedingly pleasant" (*yatrātiramyeti*), the meaning here is as follows: when that suffering exists, even the fainting caused by poison becomes exceedingly pleasant; the meaning is that he inflicts such suffering. || 156 ||
When the entire host of enemies has been put to flight and prosperity has arrived from all sides, while one is still enjoying these pleasures, death comes from somewhere or other. (157)

In some cases, even without experiencing the sensual pleasure that results in future suffering, one who is intent on sense objects meets death after undergoing the exertion required to procure them; thus he says: "driven away" (vidrāvita). || 157 ||

Likewise, people who have come from here and there, bound by the same conventions, share a common purpose; the worldly dealings regarding wife and friend are merely a deceptive illusion for men. (158)

When one lives without having entered the jaws of death, even then one’s worldly dealings with wife and so forth—which consist of delusion—are unstable; thus he says: "From this... Those worldly illusions (*vyavahāramāyā*) in which the intention (*bhāva*), that is, the purpose directed toward enjoyment and the like, is bound by a common or shared convention (*saṃketa*). This is the meaning:

Just as momentary pilgrimages (*yātrā*) occur through a universal convention among men— such as "the pilgrimage to Viśveśvara is to be performed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Phālguna"— which fixes their intentions,
so too do [marriages and other rites] occur when intentions are fixed by a common convention pertaining to the time of marriage and so forth.
The delusions regarding worldly dealings such as wife and so forth are momentary. || 158 ||
For Viriñci lives for a duration of kalpas, as he exists through the calculation of the number of kalpa-epochs;
therefore, within the web of time which is garlanded with its parts (kalās), even the notions of shortness and length are unreal.

Now, one might object: "While death may occur for enjoyers such as ourselves only at the time of enjoying what is to be enjoyed, this is not the case for Brahmā and others who live for many thousands of yugas. To this, he says:
*kalpa*... Since the calculation of the number of the multitude of kalpas—that is, the counting of the number of the collection of kalpas—is being performed within this beginningless saṃsāra.

For although the moments that constitute the life-span of Viriñci are indeed what are called "kalpas," and thus his life consists of moments termed "kalpas," nevertheless, in comparison with the short duration of time such as ours, Brahmā is long-lived; therefore, he says "ataḥ" (for this reason).
The sense is that just as there is the delusion of a multitude of years in a single moment during a dream because of its lightness and so forth, so it is likewise in the waking state. || 159 ||
People are attached to desire and intent on various base and unskillful activities; indeed, such a virtuous person is not easily found in this world even in a dream these days.
Every action is beset with suffering and utterly devoid of joy; I truly do not know how this state of existence must be navigated. (160)

Having thus described the nature of saṃsāra, he demonstrates his despondency regarding the lack of a means for its cessation with the verse beginning "jana" (people). "Kukalāḥ" means those of evil learning; what is the use of attaining good people? If it is argued that the human goal (puruṣārtha) should be accomplished through action alone, he replies with the word "kriyā": all action is accompanied by suffering and becomes utterly distressing.
That which is joined on all sides by sufferings is thus described as "distressed by distress"; the meaning is that it is utterly devoid of human purpose (puruṣārtha). || 160 ||
Those were the days; those were the riches; and those were the deeds.
Everything has passed into the realm of memory; from this point on, we must simply go forward.
Thus, having established in detail the impermanence of the category of non-self, he states it concisely in three verses beginning with "The days pass away" (divasāsta). || 161 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all species of living beings alike hasten toward destruction, just as bodies of water flow into the submarine fire.
The Vāḍava fire is the submarine fire. || 162 ||
Calamities come for a moment, and prosperity likewise for only a moment; birth and death each last but a moment—O Sage, what indeed is not momentary? 163.
"What is it like? means "but rather," [as the sense]. || 163 ||
A hero slain by one who is not a hero; many killed by a single individual; commoners have attained lordship—the entire world is being turned upside down. (164)
"By one who is not a hero"—the meaning is clear. || 164 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Thus, when my mind has been scorched by the forest fire of faults, even the celestial beings appear to me as if shimmering in the lakes of a mirage. 165.
Having thus described the defects of saṃsāra in many ways, he states its result—supreme detachment—with the words "iti" (thus).
I do not revile death, nor do I revile life;
I remain free from fever, exactly as I am now. 166.
Even in the absence of desire for enjoyments, there might initially be attachment toward them; therefore, he says: "I do not censure" (verse 166).
But if, O Lord of Sages, it is not treated with a clear intellect, then how indeed could there ever be an occasion for further treatment of the mind? (167)
One might object: "Is it not more appropriate to treat a mind inclined toward sense objects in old age? Why is it treated during youth? To this, he says: "Now" (*atha*).
The meaning of the word *atha* is "immediately following childhood. Alternatively, it may mean "that very mind.
The particle *kila* expresses a lack of conviction [regarding the possibility of such treatment]. || 167 ||
Poison is the inequality of sense objects; poison is not called [merely] the substance *viṣa*.
Sense objects destroy future lives, whereas [ordinary] poison destroys only a single body.

Regarding the question of why this mind must indeed be treated with respect to sense objects, he says: "Poison. In the context of sense objects, "poison" refers to the imbalance consisting of attachment and aversion, characterized by perceiving things as either attractive or unattractive. (168)
Neither pleasures nor pains, neither friends nor kinsmen, neither life nor death serve to bind the mind of the wise man. 169.

Now, one might ask: "What fruit has been obtained by one whose mind has been treated with the medicines of knowledge and dispassion, such that you perform this treatment of the mind? To this he says: "Not pleasures... [referring to] the knower, the one who knows Brahman. 169.
Life is as fragile as water droplets flickering within a mass of clouds scattered by the wind;
enjoyments are as transient as flashes of lightning gleaming amidst the canopy of rain clouds.
Reflecting upon this wondrous torrent of the waters of youthful indulgence, I have indeed today applied a firm seal within my mind for the sake of peace. 170.

Having demonstrated the fruitfulness of the treatment of the mind, he states the result: "Life," etc. *Vitāna* means a canopy. *Saudāminī* means lightning. *Yauvanalālanā* is the indulgence of youth; that itself is the *jalaraya*, the force of water. In some places it is written as *lolā*, which is a feminine designation. In that context, *jalaraya* is a separate word. The force of water is stated as an illustration for the state of instability (*lolatva*).
The meaning is that the seal of dispassion, forged by the blacksmith of discernment, has been impressed upon the mind to prevent it from running after sense objects. || 170 ||
The intellect, dependent upon the individual soul and the Lord, neither remains stationary nor proceeds according to its own desire, like a beloved woman in the house of her lover.

If you have been thus entrusted with the seal (*mudrā*), the task is accomplished; what remains for you beyond this? To that he replies: "Not stability" (*nāvasthitim*). The individual soul (*jīva*) itself, by virtue of its discernment, is the Lord (*īśvara*), the controller;

dependent upon him, subject to him, or else the intellect of the soul—which is inclined toward its identity with the Lord—does not attain stability in the state free from suffering. (In the case of the beloved: *Note: The provided text contains a commentary on a verse concerning the relationship between the individual soul and the Supreme Lord, using the metaphor of a woman's devotion to her lover.*

The Lord of Life is the master and protector. She, too, does not remain at her own will in the house of her beloved—that is, the husband’s home—due to fear or other such causes; nor does she go outside as she pleases. Regarding the word "citta," in some contexts even the intellect (buddhi) is intended there.
