The sense is that in certain pure states, the resting of the mind alone remains as the final residue. || 171 ||
Therefore, what is that excellent state of stability—substantial, effortless, free from conditions, and beyond delusion—in which no doubt exists? (172)

One who possesses such inquiry asks for the sake of establishing a firm position: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Since the mind does not attain stability, therefore I ask. [He asks about that which is] non-trivial (*atuccham*), whose nature is the reality of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-sad-rūpam*), effortless (*anāyāsam*), and free from suffering (*nirduḥkham*). The reason for its being effortless is that it is "free from delusion" (*gata-bhramam*). The reason for its being free from delusion is that it is "without limiting conditions" (*anupādhī*). The limiting condition (*upādhi*) is the mind (*manas*). For the mind...

It is the root of all delusion. Thus it was stated previously and will be stated again: "First, the mind and the views regarding its bondage and liberation; afterwards, the construction of the manifold world and its designations. "Excellent" means beautiful; that is to say, its nature is bliss (*ānanda*). In that state, moreover, there exists no suspicion whatsoever of a connection with suffering.
The word "that" (tat) refers to the connection [with the preceding]. || 172 ||

And how is it that even when falling into the fire of the best of the wise, one is not consumed, just as mercury is not burnt in the fire because it is permeated by the essence of its processing (*vāsanā*)? (173)

Having asked about the place of rest for the mind, he asks—“And how?”—about the means to avoid contact with suffering even when the mind is distracted. “O best of the steadfast” is the address. The qualification “possessing the essence of latent impressions” (*vāsanā-rasa-śālī*) is intended to demonstrate the attainment of burning pain. *Rasa* is that which is tasted, such as clarified butter and so forth; a person who shines (*śālate*) by means of this *rasa*, which is the latent impression itself, is thus described.
By that [means]: even by a person falling into the fire called *saṃsāra*, how is he not burned?

By what means (*kena upāyena*) is he not burned? [The answer is] mercury (*pārada*), the elixir (*rasa*). For it is well known that mercury—whether in the form of milk, or as the volatile *capala* mercury, or as *sūta* mercury—is difficult to burn (*durdāha*). || 173 ||
For it is said, O mighty-armed one, that in this scorched world there can be no existence without the activity of worldly transaction, just as there can be none without water in the ocean.
Since remaining inactive within saṃsāra is itself the means for its cessation, he says: "Because..."
The meaning is that just as it is impossible to remain in the middle of the ocean without contact with water, so it is in this case. || 174 ||
O Blessed One, as you know, please tell me for the sake of dispelling delusion that method by which the virtuous have indeed attained freedom from suffering. (175)
The collection of passages beginning with "yathā jānāsi" (as you know) is clear in meaning. || 175 || 176 || 177 || 178 || 179 || 180 ||
Or else, O Brahmin, if such a logical argument does not exist, or if someone does not clearly state it to me even though it exists; (176)
And yet, he himself does not attain that unsurpassed rest;
therefore, having abandoned all doubt and attained a state free from egoism, I [have done so]. (177)
I shall not eat, nor shall I drink water, nor shall I put on a garment from now on;
I shall not perform any activity such as bathing, giving gifts, or eating.
I do not remain involved in worldly affairs, whether in times of prosperity or in states of calamity;
O Sage, I desire nothing except the abandonment of this body.
Free from all doubt, devoid of the sense of "mine," and rid of envy, I abide solely in silence, as if fixed in a painting.
Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus, Rāma— delightful as the stainless moon, his mind expanded by the awakening of profound discernment—
became silent before the great ones, like a peacock ceasing its cry out of exhaustion from the loud clamor of the clouds. || 181 ||
*kekā* is the cry of a peacock; *nīlakaṇṭha* is a peacock. || 181 ||
Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Illumination of the Faults of the World," in the section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya*.

Thus ends the second canto in the Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā, composed by the venerable Ātmasukha, disciple of the venerable Uttamasukha, the worshipful feet of the teacher of the wandering mendicants of the supreme order (Paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya). || 2 ||
The Third Canto.
Vālmīki said:
While that prince Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, was thus speaking words that bring about the cessation of great delusion, [the sage spoke].
Through the preceding textual composition, dispassion (*vairāgya*) was established by means of the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities (*nityānityavastuviveka*).

With the five and a half verses beginning with "He speaks thus" (*vadaty evam*), [the author] describes its power to captivate the minds of the learned and its rarity, even among those who move through the sky (*khecara*), for the purpose of praising Rāma. This section ends with the words "heard, the elixir of the ears" (*śrutaṃ śrutirasāyanam*).
The textual composition of the subsequent section has a clear meaning. || 1 ||
p.
67) All those present there became filled with wonder, their eyes wide open, as if their hairs stood erect on their bodies to listen to the words with upraised ears. (2)
With the hairs on his body standing erect and his face upturned... || 2 || 3 || 4 || 5 ||
Then, while the lotus-eyed Rāma remained silent, a cry of "Well done!
was uttered by the hosts of Siddhas along with their voices.
Then a rain of flowers fell from the sky like a canopy;

when the shower of blossoms had ceased after a quarter of a muhūrta, those who had assembled there heard these words spoken by the hosts of Siddhas: 4. Then a rain of flowers fell from the sky like a canopy; when the shower of blossoms had ceased after a quarter of a muhūrta, those who had assembled there heard these words spoken by the hosts of Siddhas.
Wandering all around the heavens for an entire kalpa among the hosts of perfected beings (siddhas),
we have heard this unprecedented elixir for the ears.

Because the Joy of the Raghus has respectfully attained the state of supreme excellence, which is beautiful with the nectar of tranquility, we have been instantly awakened by that which he has spoken so appropriately.
With the intention that the speech of one free from passion, when directed toward its essential meaning, bears fruit immediately for the listeners, he says: "Tranquility," etc.

The "state of excellence" (*uttamatāpada*) refers to the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), which is the ultimate station. That speech by which this state of excellence has been attained or reached is described as such. The meaning established here is that those who seek knowledge should approach the virtuous, they should be properly accepted by the virtuous, and one should conduct oneself toward them with complete conformity. || 6 ||
Bharadvāja said:
Now, I wish to hear the conclusion regarding the purifying words spoken by the banner of the Raghus, as it is about to be declared by these great-souled ones. (7)

The section of the text beginning with "pāvanasya" and ending before "iti nādena" is clear in meaning. In some places, certain points are difficult to understand; therefore, they are now being explained. [He was] by Raghuketunā—by the banner of the chariot, like a banner, [and] by the ornament of the Raghus. (7, 8)
Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus,
that entire divine succession of sages, dwelling in their celestial abodes, descended there into that assembly hall.
Then, as this army of Siddhas descended from the sky to the earth,
the assembly hall of the son of Daśaratha rose up, filled with sages.
The earth with its [seven] flavors. || 9 || 10 || 11 || 12 || 13 ||
Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra honored them in an instant;
they, in turn, honored Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra with great respect.
The king honored the hosts of Siddhas with all reverence,
and the hosts of Siddhas likewise greeted the king with inquiries concerning his welfare.
With words, a rain of flowers, and shouts of "Well done!",
they honored Rāma from all sides as he stood bowed before them.
The sages said:
"Oh, how wonderful! By the Prince, words endowed with auspicious qualities, most noble and pregnant with the essence of dispassion, have been spoken. (13)
O best of the twice-born, in this burnt-out world created by the handiwork of fate and unrestrained wickedness, true essence is indeed extremely difficult to find.

And because he possesses unrestrained wickedness and is fashioned by the creation of fate, he is so described; for in that cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), he is endowed with unchecked wickedness and produced by superhuman agency.
By the phrase "fashioned by the creation of fate," his ineffability is indicated. (14–15)
Even if that which causes wonder to the entire world is not pleasing to the mind of Rāghava, then it is clearly we sages ourselves who are of ruined intellect. (15)
When these words had been spoken with a great voice by the multitude of people,
Viśvāmitra addressed Rāma, who stood before him, with affection. (16)

Thus, the text beginning with "not by the impeller" and so forth, up to the conclusion of the section, is clear in meaning. Among those [passages], certain words are now explained. || 16 || 17 || 18 ||
Viśvāmitra said:
O Rāghava, best among the wise, there is nothing further for you to know;
by your own subtle intellect, you have understood everything.
Your intellect, like that of Śuka, the son of the Blessed Vyāsa,
requires only internal rest, even though that which is to be known has already been known.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, how was it that Śuka, the son of the venerable Vyāsa, did not find rest in the Intellect even at the outset regarding the Knowable, and yet found rest therein later? (19)

Regarding the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even with respect to the object of knowledge" (*jñeye 'pi*), it signifies a contradiction: although [the mind] is free from all afflictions and consists of supreme bliss that is self-luminous even prior to the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is contradictory that it has not yet come to rest within that [bliss] by means of the intellect (*dhī*). || 19 ||
Viśvāmitra said:
O Rāma, listen to this account of the son of Vyāsa which I am about to relate; it is similar to my own history and is the cause of the end of successive births.
Udanta means news or an account. || 20 || 21 || 22 || 23 ||
As he was thus reflecting on this worldly course of life within his heart, a discernment arose for him— indeed, for one of truly virtuous intellect— just as it has arisen for you.
Therefore, by means of his own discernment, that high-minded one himself reflected for a very long time upon what is beautiful, and he attained that which is the truth. (22)
Though he stood with his mind not yet at rest regarding the supreme reality already attained by himself, he did not reach the conviction within himself that "this is the reality. (23)
(70) His mind alone ceased its flickering; it turned away from enjoyments fraught with manifold calamities, just as a *cātaka* bird turns away from the clouds. 24.

The *cātaka* is a particular kind of bird that turns its back on drinking water found on the ground. The meaning is: "just as the *cātaka* ceases from the rain-showers immediately after being satisfied by them. (24, 25, 26)
Once, that one of pure intellect, with devotion, questioned his father, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, who was staying in a secluded place on Mount Meru.
O Sage, how has this grand display of saṃsāra arisen?
How does it come to rest? To what extent, by whom, and when does it occur? (26)
Thus questioned by his son, the sage Vyāsa,
who knows the self, explained everything that was to be said clearly and exactly as it is.
"I already knew this before," Śuka then thought to himself; thus, with his auspicious intellect, he did not hold his father's words in high regard.
The venerable Vyāsa, having understood his son’s intention to be such, replied again to his son: "I do not know [this] in its true essence."
There exists on the surface of the earth a king named Janaka;
he knows that which is to be known exactly as it is, and from him you shall obtain everything.
Addressed thus by his father, Śuka departed from Mount Sumeru for the surface of the earth;
he reached the city of Videha, which was protected by Janaka.
O King, that son of Vyāsa, Śuka, having been announced by the staff-bearers to the high-souled Janaka, was informed: "He stands here at the gate."
By those armed with clubs, using their staff-like weapons.
Having said, "Let this remain as it was for the sake of Śuka's inquiry," Janaka then became silent for seven days out of disregard.
His mind was distracted, longing for the sight of Janaka. (33–36)
Then Janaka had Śuka enter the courtyard;
there he remained for exactly seven days in that same state of mindlessness.
Then Janaka caused Śuka to enter the inner apartments;
for seven days, he [Śuka] thought, "The king is not to be seen. (35)
There, Janaka cherished Śuka, whose face was like the moon, with intoxicated women, sumptuous foods, and an abundance of enjoyments.
Those enjoyments and those sorrows did not shake the mind of Vyāsa’s son, just as a gentle breeze cannot move a mountain that has established its foundation.
The seat is bound; the foundation is bound. || 37 || 38 || 39 ||
With a mind solely composed, pure, silent, and joyful at heart, Śuka remained stainless like the full moon. (38)
Having recognized his true nature, King Janaka brought Śuka near; beholding him with a joyful heart, he bowed down to him.
"O you who have completed all duties for the world and attained every heart's desire, what is it that you wish? Thus he spoke to him, having offered a warm welcome.

"Niḥśeṣita" means: he by whom all those actions that exist for the sake of the highest good (*śreya*) in the world have been exhausted (*niḥśeṣita*), leaving nothing remaining (*anavaśeṣita*); thus it is "one who has rendered all actions without remainder. Alternatively, the meaning is "one for whom every task has been completely finished. || 40 ||
Śuka said:
"O Teacher, how has this grand display of saṃsāra arisen? How does it come to rest? Tell me this properly and quickly. (41)
The grand display of saṃsāra; the frantic activity of saṃsāra. 41 || 42 || 43 || 44 || 45 || 46 || 47 ||
Viśvāmitra said:
When questioned thus by Janaka,
Śuka then related that very same thing which had previously been told to him by his high-souled father.
Śuka said:
"I myself previously understood this through discernment;
and this very same thing was declared by my father when he was questioned. (43)
O best among those skilled in speech, you too have stated this very same point;
and this indeed is the meaning of the sentence as it is observed in the scriptures. (44)

Just as this [world], arising from one's own conceptual construction, is exhausted through the exhaustion of that very conceptual construction, so too is saṃsāra destroyed; such is the certainty that it is devoid of essence. (45)
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, tell me this truly and unswervingly;
for the world, with its wandering mind, finds rest only in you.
Janaka said:
O Sage, there is no other certainty superior to this;
you have realized it yourself and have heard it again from a teacher. (47)
In this world, there exists only the one Person whose nature is the uninterrupted consciousness-self, and nothing else;
bound by the power of his own volition, he is liberated when free from volition. (48)

That which is uninterrupted, indestructible, immutable, and eternal is the Self consisting of consciousness (*cidātman*); thus, although the Self is by its very nature non-dual, it becomes bound through the power of its own volition by perceiving itself as having a second. As it has been said by Sureśvarācārya:
"By an attachment to what is unreal, this one deceives his own self, like the father of Somaśarman even though no second object exists."
"Thus": and one who is free from conceptual construction is liberated. 48 || 49 || 50 ||

By this, it is clearly known by you that for that Great Soul, all that is to be known has been realized, such that a distaste has arisen even for enjoyments or for everything visible here in this world. (49)
(73) Everything that was to be attained has been attained by you, whose mind is now full.
O Brahmin, since you do not perceive [any further goal], you exert yourself in vain; you are liberated, so cast off this delusion. 50.
Having been thus instructed by the high-souled Janaka,
Śuka remained silent and rested in the self-abiding, supreme reality.
Instructed by the attainment of knowledge, he remains established as the substrate within the individual soul (jīva), which is like a reflection; thus, he is self-abiding within it. 51, 52, 53.
Free from sorrow, fear, and exertion, effortless and with all doubts severed,
he went to the faultless peak of Mount Meru for the sake of meditative absorption.
Having remained there for ten thousand years in a state of non-conceptual meditative absorption,
he was extinguished within himself like a lamp devoid of oil.

Pure, with the stain of temporal succession removed, that Great Soul attained oneness within his own stainless and purifying self, just as a drop of water merges into the ocean once its latent tendencies have dissolved. (54)

Regarding the term *vyapagata*: *kalanā* means conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*). That very thing is a stain (*kalaṅka*), which is to say, a blemish; as Amara states, "stain (*kalaṅka*) refers to both a mark and a blemish. That from which the stain of conceptualization has departed is thus described; and that is also "pure" (*śuddha*). By the phrase "one from whom the stain of conceptualization has departed," the cessation of subtle ignorance (*tūlājñāna*) is expressed. By "pure," [the cessation of gross ignorance is indicated].
There is the cessation of fundamental ignorance. He states that even Brahman is free from the two adventitious impurities that are beginningless:
"In the stainless Self, which is purifying. (54–55)
Viśvāmitra said:
O Rāma, the mere removal of the impurity of that son of Vyāsa serves you exactly as is required. 55.
For one whose mind has known all that is to be known, this state is surely distinct:
that he no longer relishes the entire multitude of enjoyments. (56)

That the entire multitude of enjoyments no longer tastes sweet nor is pleasing—this is indeed the certain characteristic of a mind that has known what is to be known; for *nūnam* means "certainty" in the sense of a logical conclusion (*tarka*), according to Amara. (56–58)
Through the contemplation of enjoyments, bondage born of unreal things attains firmness;
through that same [contemplation] being stilled, bondage in the world attains attenuation. (57)
O Rāma, the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā) is called liberation by the wise;
the strengthening of the latent impressions regarding objective things is designated as bondage. (58)
He for whom worldly enjoyments no longer hold any appeal in this life, even without causes such as fame and the like, is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 59 ||

He says that one for whom enjoyments do not appeal due to motives such as fame or gain should not be considered liberated while living (jīvanmukta)—namely, "by means of fame and so forth. [This implies] "even without a cause such as fame and the like. 59–65.
When Rāma learns from the mouth of the True One (Sat) that "this thing exists,"...
Upon hearing it, O lords of sages, one surely attains the rest of the mind.
In this matter, let the illustrious and venerable Vasiṣṭha provide the means for the high-souled Rāghava’s mind to find rest.
He is the eternal lord and family preceptor of all the descendants of Raghu;
he is omniscient, the witness of all, and possesses pure vision of the three periods of time.
O venerable Vasiṣṭha, do you perhaps remember that which you yourself [did] in the past, with your great intellect, for the sake of pacifying our enmity and for our ultimate welfare? (63)
The knowledge repeatedly taught by the Blessed One, the lotus-born Brahmā, that very same [knowledge] you should now teach to Rāma, who dwells at your side. (64)
That knowledge, that meaning of the scriptures, and that unimpaired proficiency which is imparted to a virtuous, dispassionate, and excellent disciple—(p. 75)—that is it. 65.
Whatever is taught to one who is not a disciple and who lacks dispassion becomes impure, like cow’s milk poured into a dog’s skin-bag.
A leather bag is a *dṛti*. 66 || 67 || 68 ||
When this was said by the son of Gādhi, those sages, headed by Vyāsa and Nārada, honored him with that very same purpose, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! (67).
Then the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, possessed of great luster, standing by the side of the king like Brahmā’s son Brahmā himself, spoke.
"O Sage, whatever you command me, I shall carry out without hindrance;
for who, even if capable, is able to transgress the word of the virtuous? (69)
"You command" means "you order. || 69 || 70 ||
I remember it all without omission for the sake of pacifying the delusion of saṃsāra—
that knowledge which was formerly proclaimed on Mount Niṣadha by the Lotus-born One.
Vālmīki said:

Having spoken thus, that great-souled Vasiṣṭha, whose speaker’s splendor was enhanced by his firm resolve, declared this for the sake of pacifying ignorance—the sole awakening to the supreme state. (71)

"Thus" (iti). Regarding "the binding of the preparatory equipment" (parikarabandha): he is one by whom the splendor of the speaker has been grasped—that is, accepted—through the binding, that is, the fastening, of those preparations which are useful for the act of salutation;
thus ends the third canto in the section on dispassion within the *Mokṣopāya* of the venerable *Vālmīkīya*. 3.
Thus ends the third chapter [of the work] composed by Śrīmat Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Sureśvarācārya, the disciple of the venerable Uttamasukha Pūjyapāda.
This section on dispassion is complete.
(p. 76) Om, salutations to Śrī Rāma.
The Chapter on the Conduct of the Seeker of Liberation—
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O descendant of Raghu, at all times and in this entire cycle of existence,
everything is attained by everyone through human effort when it is properly applied.

In the preceding section, it was primarily established that the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities leads to dispassion (*vairāgya*), which serves as the seed for the sprouts of tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities, culminating in the fruit of liberation (*mumukṣu*). Now, by means of the subsequent section, the conduct of one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) is described— characterized by hearing (*śravaṇa*) with reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) as its constituent parts, and having tranquility and the rest as its procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*).

It is being established, along with certain incidental points. Regarding this, the venerable Vasiṣṭha offers a rebuttal—taking as his motive the doubt that might arise in other people based on the first verse—that all human effort is dependent on fate and therefore useless, so one should not resort to exertion directed toward objects of deliberation. He says: "All indeed... *Pauruṣam* means human exertion (*puruṣakāra*).
The meaning is "exertion. The word *eva* (indeed) is also connected with the word *samavāpyate* (is fully attained). || 1 ||
Human effort is traditionally held to be of two kinds: that which is contrary to the scriptures and that which is in accordance with the scriptures.
Among these, that which is contrary to the scriptures leads to misfortune, while that which is in accordance with the scriptures leads to the supreme goal.

If everything were obtained through human effort (*pauruṣa*), then even from effort that is contrary to the scriptures (*aśāstrīya*), the attainment of the supreme goal might occur; consequently, such effort would also have to be practiced by one seeking liberation. Anticipating this objection, he says: "That which is contrary to the scriptures" (*ucchāstram*). || 2 ||
Through qualities such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous, practiced sufficiently from childhood, one’s own beneficial purpose is attained by human effort. (3)
He elaborates on this point—that it has been taught for the sake of the ultimate truth—with the words: "From childhood," etc. (3).
Śrī Rāma said:
Just as the web of past latent impressions impels me, so do I remain;
O Muni, I am miserable—what can I do? (4)
(Objection: "Because of dependence on latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one's own purpose cannot be attained through independent activity. Thus he raises this objection.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Therefore indeed, O Rāma, you shall attain eternal welfare through human effort alone,
brought about by your own exertion, and not otherwise.

He refutes this with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). Precisely because of this—namely, because previous latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are not things that can be enjoined—you attain the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) solely through human effort (*pauruṣa*), that is, through human activity brought about by your own exertion. This is the intended meaning: it is not the prior impression that impels the person like a violent wind; rather, [it acts] by way of withdrawing desire, thereby [establishing] independence.
If that were the case, it would grant [the result] because one's own purpose can be attained through independent activity. || 5 ||
O Rāma, the accumulation of latent impressions (vāsanā) is of two kinds— wholesome and unwholesome—
and of these two, either one or the other exists from the past.

Anticipating the question of how the attainment of the highest good (*śreyas*) occurs through human effort alone— effort brought about by one's own exertion— the author demonstrates the existence of the web of past latent impressions (*vāsanā*) through a detailed classification, and therein shows the specific manner [of attainment] by means of the verse beginning with "dvividha" (twofold).

If you are removed from there by a pure flood of impressions, wherein one of the two masses of auspicious and inauspicious latent tendencies has become so extremely diminished as to be virtually non-existent,
then you will gradually attain the eternal state through that very auspiciousness alone.
In that regard, it means "in the midst of those two arrays"; that is the sense of "tattarhi" (then, in that case). || 7 || 8 ||
Moreover, if an unwholesome disposition should entangle you in distress,
then that very disposition from your past must be conquered by you yourself through effort.
The river of latent impressions, flowing along both auspicious and inauspicious paths,
must be directed toward the auspicious path through human effort.

By the word *bhāva*, the flood of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is intended here. Having explained the manner of attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) when the person is impelled by either of the two—the collection of auspicious or inauspicious latent impressions—he now states it even when he is impelled by both: "by the auspicious and the inauspicious" (verse 9).
O best among the powerful, one should, by means of human effort and strength, draw one's own mind away from unwholesome things and establish it only in wholesome ones. (10)
He elaborates on the meaning already stated: "In regard to impurities," etc. This means: by reason of the human goal (puruṣārtha). || 10 ||

The mind of a living being, having moved away from the unwholesome, goes toward the wholesome, and from that [wholesome] state it moves to the other; therefore, one should restrain it by force, as if it were a child. (11)

Demonstrating the fitness for entering into auspicious [states], he concludes what was said with the verse beginning "From the inauspicious" (*aśubhāt*). Some introduce this verse by raising the following objection: "Since an auspicious object, even without depending on human effort (*pauruṣa*), moves the mind of its own accord toward that which is inauspicious, human effort is therefore useless. Anticipating this, they provide the transition as follows. (11)
One should quickly pacify it with equanimity, yet not too abruptly, but gradually;
one should cherish the child-like mind through human effort and exertion.
Since the mind is like a child, [the author] shows the appropriate manner of its movement: "Equanimity" (samatā).
O child-mind, do not grasp at objects that are superior to even poison, both in name and in substance.
[Cultivate] equanimity, characterized by the absence of joy or dejection upon encountering pleasant or unpleasant objects.
"Taking as one's support the desire for the attainment of unsurpassed bliss"—thus [it is said] by way of consolation through equanimity. The word *drāk* means "quickly.
As Amarasimha states: "sadyas, drāk, maṅkṣu, sapadi, and drutam [all mean immediately]. (12)
O crusher of enemies, know that when the arising of latent impressions (vāsanā) born from the power of prior practice occurs within you, then the practice has reached its fruition.

To the question of when the practice of shifting the mind from the impure becomes fruitful, he says: "Previously" (*prāk*). Even in this life, for you who are practicing intensely, [the result arises] by the power of previous practice—that is, by the power of practice in a prior birth—or alternatively, "previously" means in earlier youth; it is said that [this occurs] through what has been sufficiently practiced since childhood. In some places, the reading is "drāk" (quickly). Now, one might object: "In this case, it is not..."
If it is argued that this contradicts what was stated in the previous verse—namely, "suddenly" (*drāk*) and "gradually, little by little" (*śanaiḥ-śanaiḥ*)—it is not so;
for the former was prescribed with reference to the stage of beginning the restraint of the mind, whereas "suddenly" is said with reference to the subsequent state. || 13 ||
Even when [the result] is doubtful, cultivate only that which is highly auspicious;
for, my dear, when auspicious latent impressions increase, there is no fault whatsoever. (14)

Having stated what must be done when the latent impression of the auspicious (*śubhavāsanā*) exceeds or is equal to the latent impression of the inauspicious (*aśubhavāsanā*), he says the same even when there is doubt regarding them: "In the case of a doubtful [impression]" (*sandigdhāyām*). The phrase "in the auspicious one" (*śubhāyām*) is clear in its meaning. || 14 ||
As long as your mind is unrefined and you have not realized that state of reality, practice that which has been determined by the authority of the Guru and the scriptures. (15)

One might object: "Is there not no fault in the increase of auspicious latent impressions (*śubhavāsanā*)? How can it be so? Anticipating this objection—that even these may bring about faults because they are effects of ignorance—the author states in three verses beginning with *avyutpanna* that they are to be adopted until the direct realization of the Self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*), and thereafter abandoned. The term "the unknown state" (*ajñātaṃ tatpadam*) refers to the essential nature of Brahman.
It is "thus" (tathā) because of that [reason]. The word *tu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). As Amarasimha states: "The word *tu* may be used for distinction or for emphasis. || 15 ||

Therefore, by one whose latent impurities have been ripened, who has truly understood the reality, and who is intent on cessation, even this stream of wholesome mental impressions must surely be abandoned. (16)
"By one whose impurities have been ripened"—that is, by a discerning person whose passion and other defilements have been burnt away. || 16 ||

Following that which is most beautiful and practiced by the noble—the auspicious—by means of a mind perceiving it as a delightful state, always attain the sorrowless state; thereafter, having even abandoned that, abide well.

The construction is as follows: "May the mind, following the web of auspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*), reach the state free from sorrow—that which is exceedingly fortunate because its fortune (*bhaga*) or majesty (*māhātmya*) is most beautiful. "Adhigamaya" means "cause it to attain" or "lead it to.

The word division is *manaḥ* and *jñabhāvabuddhyā*. In this context, *jñabhāva* means "the state of being a knower" (*jñatva*); thus, it means "by means of an intellect characterized by that [state]."

Alternatively, "manojñabhāvabuddhyā" is a single compound word. It means: she whose disposition (*bhāva*)—that is, her intention (*abhiprāya*)—is charming (*manojña*) or captivating (*manohara*) is "manojñabhāvā";
she who is such, and who is also intelligence (*buddhi*), [is referred to] by that term. Or, "manojñabhāve" may be a vocative address. 17.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having abandoned within himself the inclination toward worldly existence so as never to grasp it again, and having taken up perfect tranquility and contentment with a noble intellect; || 18 ||

Explaining the statement that "one should practice what has been determined by the authority of the Guru and the scriptures," he describes, in three verses beginning with *apunar*, how the science of knowledge (*jñānaśāstra*) which is to be heard is rooted in a distinguished tradition and brings about the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). [He speaks of] *bhāvanā* as latent impression (*vāsanā*), [qualified] by *udārayā*, meaning great or excellent.
Having made the mind equanimous and focused upon the Self with continuous reflection, one should attend to the investigation of the meaning of the preceding and following statements. (19)

Regarding "supūrva": that which is an excellent investigation (*vicāra*) into the meaning of the preceding and following sentences—that alone is the object (*viṣaya*); [the mind] is directed toward that.

In some places it is read as *svapūrva*; in that case, the meaning is that it is directed toward the investigation of the objects which are the meanings of the preceding and following sentences as determined by oneself (*sva*). The mind is directed toward the object of investigation, [finding] equal flavor (*samarasa*) within itself.
And having performed it with its subsequent rites. || 19 ||
Listen, O Rāma, to that which was spoken of old by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord:
it brings about the destruction of all suffering and is the ultimate consolation for the intellect. (20)
"Listen"—this is the syntactical connection. || 20 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahman, for what reason was this spoken previously by the Self-born One?
And how was this obtained by you? Tell me, O Lord. (21)
"By whom was it said?"—this is the clear meaning of the verse. || 21 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
There exists the one whose nature is infinite splendor, all-pervading, the refuge of all, the space of consciousness, imperishable by nature, and the lamp within all things. 22.

In order to proclaim the greatness of Brahmā, the founder of the tradition of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), and demonstrating his status as having arisen from the supreme cause and his role as the creator of the world, [the author] provides the answer to the two questions beginning with "By whom was this spoken?
through the following collection of verses, starting with "There exists the Infinite... and ending with "...having known which, I remain happy."
The Self of infinite splendor, whose nature consists of infinite effects, is the illuminator and light within all things and objects.
From Him, who possesses the form of both vibration and non-vibration, Viṣṇu was born;
and from the lotus of His heart, Parameṣṭhin was born.
Vibration is the expansion in the form of the world, while non-vibration is its opposite; from their state of being identical in form means from their having an identical nature.
He created the entire creation as a flood of mental constructs, just like the mind;
within this land of Bhārata, it is filled with various calamities. (24)
That which is created is the *sarga*, the world. To dispel the doubt regarding the reality of that which is created, he provides an illustration:
"the flood of conceptual constructions" (*vikalpaugha*). The "flood of conceptual constructions" is a multitude of mental desires. (24) (25) (26) (27) (28)
Having seen the suffering of these people, that Lord, the creator of all worlds, was moved to compassion, just as a father is by the suffering of his son. (25)
"Who could bring an end to the suffering of these whose hopes are destroyed and whose lives are forfeit?
Having reflected thus with one-pointed mind for a moment, he indeed felt great remorse.
Austerity, charity, recitation, and pilgrimage do not lead to the ultimate cessation of suffering;
therefore, for the sake of liberation from that very suffering, I shall now proclaim knowledge.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed Lord Brahmā, seated upon a lotus,
formed this resolve in his mind and brought me into existence.
The Lord, bearing a water-pot, stood upon a lotus with me, who also held a water-pot; together with my rosary, I bowed to him and offered my salutations. || 29 ||
"With a rosary of seeds" is an adverbial modifier of the action. || 29 || 30 ||
"Come, my son," saying this to me, O mighty-armed one, the unborn Lord placed me upon the northern petal of his own lotus and spoke.
O son, for just a moment your mind, as fickle as a monkey, has been entered by ignorance, like a mirror covered with tears. (31)
In this context, "bāṣpa" refers to the heat exhaled from the mouth. 31 || 32 || 33 || 34 ||
Thus, having been immediately cursed by him,
I instantly forgot my entire stainless true nature.
Then, falling into a state of dejection with an unawakened mind, I stood there, scorched by pain and grief like a base person born into the world. (33)
p.
82) Then that Lord approached me and said: "O son, why are you sorrowful?
Ask me for the destruction of your sorrow; you shall be eternally happy. (34)
Then I asked that Blessed One about the remedy for cyclic existence:
"O Lord, how did this cyclic existence, consisting of great suffering, come to be? (35)

To show that only knowledge obtained through the traditional lineage (*saṃpradāya*) grants liberation and nothing else, to inform that for one who knows Brahman there is no duty other than showing grace to the world, and to demonstrate the superiority of Bhāratavarṣa over all others in the accomplishment of the goals of human life, he says: "Then... (verses 35–36).
And how, O Lord, was that knowledge—which has been extensively proclaimed by that Great-Souled One—diminished by him, knowing which I remain happy? (36)
Then the Creator of the world, the cause of all things, spoke these words to me, who had realized what is to be known and was established in my own primordial nature: (37)
The verses beginning with "tato viditavedyam" (then, having known what is to be known) up to "kartavyam asti" (there is that which must be done) are clear in their meaning.
[37] [38] Having brought you to the state of one ignorant through a curse, I have made you an inquirer so that all people may attain the essence of this knowledge. [38]
Now that your curse has been pacified and you have attained supreme awakening,
go, my child, to the surface of the earth situated within Jambūdvīpa.
O virtuous one, for the sake of favoring the world, you shall go there to Bhāratavarṣa; O son, there you shall find those of great intellect who are devoted to the ritualistic portion of the Vedas.

Those whose minds are detached, who are highly wise, and who possess discernment, should be instructed by one established in tranquility through the sequence of the ritual section (kriyākāṇḍa). || 41 ||
O virtuous one, you should instruct them with knowledge that bestows bliss.
Thus commissioned by my father, who was born from a lotus,
O virtuous one, I remain here as long as the succession of living beings endures.
(83) "There is indeed nothing at all that must be done by me here; with the thought 'I shall simply remain,' I am established upon the earth.
With a disposition in which the intellect is perpetually asleep and utterly tranquil, I perform my duties, yet I do nothing at all."

Anticipating the objection that your remaining in the land of action (*karmabhūmi*) for the duration of an eon while obeying the word of your Guru would serve solely for the benefit of the world and not for the sake of completing your remaining tasks, he says:
"That which is to be done" (*kartavyam*). "Atimanāḥ" means one whose mind has transcended; that is, one who has conquered the mind. Alternatively, *atimanāḥ* [means...]
"Of exalted mind. (In some versions it is "of undisturbed mind. In that context, one who is *vimanāḥ* is one who is dejected; he who is not so is *avimanāḥ*.

To the question—"Since you are seen to engage in activities just like an ignorant person, how can you be one who has accomplished all that was to be done?"—he replies with the word "sam-": "In whom the intellect is ever asleep through tranquility"—that is, through a state free from joy and grief upon encountering the desirable or the undesirable.

Having described the state of being an agent of action through that mode of existence—whether from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*) or the perspective of appearance (*prātibhāsika-dṛṣṭi*)—he states its absence from the perspective of ultimate reality with the words "And not... (*na ca*). The "sleepiness" of the intellect (*dhiyaḥ suptatvam*) consists in its having true non-duality as its object. As it has been said by the Teacher: "He who, even while waking, is like one in deep sleep... (*suṣuptavat...*)

"He sees duality, yet even while seeing, he sees through non-duality; likewise, even while acting, he is actionless—he who is thus is the knower of the Self, and no other; this is the certainty here. And: "When one's cognition of 'I' as the Self and the cognition of 'mine' as belonging to the Self are devoid of objective referents, he is the knower of the Self, and no other. And likewise is the word of the Blessed One: "In which [state] they are awake..."
For that sage, as he watched, those very beings became the night. || 44 ||
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
Having first ascertained through the effect whether the speaker possesses knowledge or ignorance, the man who then poses a question is a person of great intelligence. (45)

Having thus related the answers to questions such as "By whom was this said?", and having spoken briefly on matters arising from the context, [the author], desiring to impart knowledge along with its means to Rāma— who had become attentive due to the words "Listen, O Rāma, that which was told of old"— thought: "The dialogue between us two, consisting of a distinguished questioner and speaker, will certainly lead to a fruitful result."
In order to demonstrate this, he characterizes the questioner and the speaker with two verses beginning with "ajñatā" (ignorance). 45.
(84) When one possesses an irreproachable intellect capable of reconciling what precedes and what follows,
a wise person should answer when questioned; not, however, toward a base person who follows the nature of a beast.

When an objection has been raised because the meanings of the preceding and following sentences do not cohere with one another despite having been heard from the teacher, [the teacher should speak] to one whose intellect is capable—that is, competent—to resolve that [objection]. In this regard, the rule is as follows:
it should be spoken only to a disciple whose intellect is capable of resolving the connection between what precedes and what follows, and it should be spoken only to one who is blameless.
And that which has been asked must indeed be answered. || 46 ||
At the gateway to liberation, four gatekeepers are proclaimed:
tranquility, inquiry, contentment, and fourthly, association with the virtuous. (47)

In order to demonstrate the fruitfulness of this dialogue, [the author] describes the duties of one seeking liberation at the beginning of the narrative, by means of the verses beginning with "The door to liberation" and ending with "one should increase.
These [verses] have clear meanings. || 47 || 48 || 49 || 50 ||
These four, or else two or three, should be served with diligence;
they open the door to liberation, just as [the ministers] did at Rājagṛha.
Or rather, abandoning everything else with all one's effort, one should take refuge in a single [virtue], because when that one is brought under control, all four come under control as well. (49)

At the outset, for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra, one should increase wisdom itself through the study of the scriptures, association with virtuous people, and the practice of austerity and self-restraint. (50)
O Rāma, this unbearable cholera-like affliction caused by the force of the poison of saṃsāra is pacified by the purifying Gāruḍa mantra of Yoga. (51)

To the question, "What would result from the further increase of wisdom? he says: "Unbearable," and so forth. Saṃsāra itself is the cholera of the force of poison—the disease known as *viṣūcikā* produced by the force of poison. Yoga is the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self;
it is that very [realization] which is the *Gāruḍa* mantra. This indeed is the meaning of the word "yoga."

From the verse following this one in the *Bṛhad-Vāsiṣṭha*: "And that yoga [is attained] through inquiry into the scriptures with a virtuous person; for it is understood from this that the knowledge of the ultimate reality is certainly obtained.
It has been stated that, for the sake of firm wisdom that cuts through the disease of saṃsāra, one who is endowed with tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities should investigate the Self. || 51 ||

85) This chronic cholera of the poison that is sensory objects is indeed incurable; if it is not treated, it leads inexorably to the experience of the fruits of the multitude of hellish cities, wherein it brings about this [state].
The striking with stones, whetted and dark, like a blue lotus—[in the *Bṛhadyogavāsiṣṭha* it says, "the stone is a sharp fall"].

Now, he describes the unsurpassed suffering for one who does not investigate the self in this way, beginning with the words "This is endless" (*duranteyam*). Sense objects themselves are the cholera of poison (*viṣajaviṣūcikā*). In some places it is called "the cholera of sense objects" (*viṣayaviṣūcikā*); in that case, the meaning is that sense objects themselves are the cholera. It is not...
If that [evil] is treated with medical therapy, then those very hells become their cities;

the collection or multitude of them constitutes the fruit, and being one whose consequence is that fruit—namely, "having the consequence of the fruit of the multitude of hell-cities"—it produces that suffering.
To the inquiry, "What kind of suffering does it produce?", he says: "Where... (yatreti). "Where" means in which [hell].

For those who suffer from the cholera-like affliction of the poisons of sensory objects, the falling of hundreds of sharpened and whetted swords upon their limbs becomes like the striking of blue lotuses. || 52 ||

The burning of fire is for the sake of cooling with snow; the cutting off of limbs is the application of sandalwood paste; falling into hell is an endless shower of spray from a fountain-house for dispelling the summer heat; the severing of the head is the induction of pleasant sleep; and deafness is the sealing of the mouth—a great accumulation of merit. || 53 ||

The word "where" (*yatra*) is connected to every instance. Where there is the burning of fire upon the body, there is the sprinkling of snow; where there is the lopping off of limbs—that is, the cutting away of members—there is the anointing with sandalwood paste; where there are *nārāca* arrows—arrows made entirely of iron—there is the raining down of spray from a fountain-house for the relief of summer heat.

For the purpose of dispelling the heat of summer and destroying the scorching sun, there is the sprinkling of water droplets—showers of fine spray—from water jets propelled by mechanical devices within the house. "The seal of the mouth" (*ānanamudrā*) means the closing of the mouth.
"Accumulation" (*upacaya*) means increase. The intended meaning is this: even such things as the falling of hundreds of swords, which are causes of great suffering—

That which, when perceived as suffering, people nevertheless behave toward as if it were a cause of happiness—that is the unsurpassed suffering which acts like a poison-cholera of the objects of the senses. || 53 ||

(86) Thus, O Rāma, one should engage with the scripture without hesitation; it must certainly be investigated in this manner, and it must be understood in this way, for indeed, awakening arises from the investigation of the scripture. || 54 ||

Since this is so, one should therefore strive for the treatment of the disease of sense-objects; thus he says: "Therefore, in this way... *Avahelā* means disregard, contempt, or sportiveness. Some form of treatment must be performed for the cessation of the disease of sense-objects; regarding that, he says: "In this way..."
The word *kila* is intended to indicate that this is well-known from the Śruti, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas.

The meaning is that one who desires the cessation of all misfortunes and the attainment of the state of supreme bliss must properly engage in the investigation of the meaning of the scripture. || 54 ||
Through the continuous practice of that which brings into harmony one's own experience, the scripture, and the teacher, the Self is perceived.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that spiritual welfare (*śreyaḥ*) arises only through the investigation of the scriptures by means of the investigation of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*); why then does that right knowledge not arise for all those who engage in such investigation? To this, he says: *sva-*. By that person whose [investigation] has reached a continuous state of practice and which accords with the triad beginning with his own direct experience (*svānubhūti*), the Self (*ātman*) is beheld.
It is realized by nothing else. || 55 ||
For those with some degree of refined intellect, there is no other treatise whatsoever that removes ignorance as effectively as this scripture has been heard. (56)
To the question of which scripture’s meaning should be investigated by one seeking the highest good, he says: "Something," etc. It has been stated that scripture removes ignorance. (56)
O Rāma, it is better to wander for alms with a bowl in hand through the streets of the outcaste quarters than to live a life of ruined existence in ignorance. (57)
He states the necessity of abandoning ignorance with the words "Better," etc. (verse 57).
Neither wealth, nor friends, nor kinsmen provide assistance;
neither the movement of hands and feet, nor travel to foreign lands [can help]. (58)

He dispels the doubt that, like the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures, the giving of wealth and other gifts to a worthy recipient is also a highly esteemed means for attaining Brahman—by the words beginning with "not by wealth" (*na dhanāni*). Just as wealth and the like do not bring about the attainment of Brahman, so too investigation does not bring about its attainment; for even among those who possess such investigation...

Anticipating the objection that such attainment is not seen even among many, he says: "merely" (*kevalam*). The sense is that it is precisely due to the absence of mastery over the mind that the attainment of Brahman is not observed in those who engage in inquiry. || 58 || 59 ||
Neither the affliction of time, nor the sacrificial grounds, nor life itself [are the means];
the Supreme is attained solely through the conquest of that mind alone. 59.
Listen now to these gatekeepers at the door of liberation in their proper order;
by devotion to even one of them, one is ushered through the door of liberation. (60)

Regarding those previously mentioned as the "gatekeepers at the door of liberation," for whom the accomplishment of their function was said to be the human goal and the failure to accomplish it was said to be a calamity—the author begins to elaborate upon them with the words: "At the door of liberation. (60)
Whatever sufferings, whatever unbearable cravings, and whatever painful anxieties there may be—all of these perish for those whose minds are at peace, just as darkness vanishes before the suns. (61)
In that regard, he first states the incidental fruit of peace (*śānti*) with three verses beginning with "yāni" [61, 62, 63].
Like a mother, all beings here place their utmost trust in one who is endowed with tranquility, whether they face hardships or gentleness. 62.
A person does not attain such happiness through the drinking of elixirs nor through the embrace of Fortune as they do through inner tranquility.
Having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled that which is auspicious or inauspicious,
he who neither rejoices nor desponds is said to be "peaceful. (64)

Having stated the fruit of peace, he describes its essential nature with the two verses beginning with "śrutvā" [and so forth]. "Glāyati" means it causes the loss of joy; that is to say, it causes despondency. || 64 ||
He whose mind is as clear as the orb of the moon and remains undisturbed even in the midst of death, festivals, or battles, is called "peaceful. (65)

The "cool-rayed one" is the moon. For a person who possesses firm discernment, who has established himself in great dispassion, and who understands the inevitability of future events, there arises an absence of joy and dejection upon encountering pleasure and pain;
that alone is the meaning of tranquility (śama). || 65 ||
Among ascetics, the learned, sacrificial priests, and kings;
among the powerful and those rich in virtues—it is only the man of tranquility who truly shines.
He states another incidental result of tranquility (śama) in the verse beginning with "among ascetics" (tapasviṣu). || 66 ||

Having taken refuge in that supreme state—tranquil, immortal, invincible, and guarded by the Noble Ones—the great-souled ones have gone to the highest goal; O descendant of Raghu, follow that very same path in due order for the sake of perfection.
Demonstrating the great fruit of tranquility (*śama*), he states that it must be practiced because it is upheld by those of great majesty:

"Tranquility," and so forth. Having taken hold of that other nectar which is unassailable and protected by the noble ones, the gods have proceeded to the supreme state. But those of great majesty [have attained] that which is otherwise unassailable—unfit to be stolen—and which is protected by the noble, guarded by the wise.

Having relied upon that supreme nectar known as tranquility (*śama*), just as those who have proceeded toward the highest state in accordance with it, so too for the sake of perfection—that is, for the attainment of the supreme state—maintain, or rather practice, that very sequence which is the means characterized by tranquility;
the meaning is that you should follow the sequence of tranquility, discernment, contentment, meditation, and so forth. || 67 ||
One who knows the cause should constantly engage in self-inquiry with an intellect that is supremely purified by the stainless understanding of the scriptures. (68)

Having explained tranquility (*śama*) in detail among [the virtues] beginning with tranquility, he introduces investigation (*vicāra*) with five verses beginning with "In the scripture" (*śāstre*). Therein, he first enjoins investigation with the verse beginning with "In the scripture."

First, by means of actions dedicated to the Lord, which are supremely purifying; subsequently, by means of the stainless comprehension of the meaning of the scriptures on renunciation (nivṛtti-śāstra); and by one who knows the cause—that is, one who is conversant with causes and effects, knowing "this is the cause of this" and "this is the effect of this. || 68 ||
Having attained sharpness through investigation, the intellect perceives the supreme state;
for investigation is indeed the great medicine for the long-standing disease of saṃsāra. (69)
He states the fruit of inquiry: "From inquiry," [verse 69].
"Who am I, and whose is this cycle of existence?"—this should be reflected upon with effort by the wise man, even in times of calamity, while personally seeking its remedy. (70)

Showing the nature of reflection (vicāra), he clarifies its necessity with the words "Who am I? The term *sapratīkāram* is an adverbial modifier; it means "accompanied by the counteraction of obstacles" (*vighna-pratīkāreṇa saha vartate*). [He reflects] by means of the self, that is, by means of the intellect (*buddhi*). || 70 ||
Investigation is a beautiful eye that sees even what is obstructed—unlost in darkness and unblinded by great splendors. (71)

He praises *vicāra* (discernment) with the words "not lost" (*anaṣṭam*). To establish the quality of having beautiful eyes, there are these three qualifiers beginning with "not lost. "Not lost" means it does not perish like a physical effect; thus it is "not lost. "Not crooked" (*ajihnitam*) means not bent; the meaning is "unobstructed. [The inquiry is: "Who am I? How has this defect called 'saṃsāra' come upon me?"
The reflective consideration "by means of reasoning" is called investigation (vicāra). || 72 ||
He clarifies the nature of investigation with the words: "Who am I? How [am I]? (72).
Vasiṣṭha said:
Contentment is indeed the highest good; contentment is called happiness.
O crusher of enemies, one who is contented attains supreme rest.

He elaborates upon contentment, which was mentioned immediately after reflection, by means of six verses. Therein, he praises contentment with two verses beginning with "Contentment" (saṃtoṣa). By the word "rest" (viśrāma), "repose" (viśrānti) is intended. || 73 ||
For those who have attained peace and satisfaction by drinking the nectar of contentment, even this incomparable splendor of worldly enjoyment acts as a potent poison.

The connection [of the sentence] is: "They have attained satisfaction by drinking the nectar of contentment. It acts like *prativiṣa* (an antidote); *prativiṣa* means poison that is contrary [to other poisons]. || 74 ||

Having abandoned the desire for what has not been attained and having reached equanimity toward what has been attained, he who is free from distress regarding what is unseen is said here to be "contented. (75)
He describes the nature of contentment: "When not obtained... [Verse 75]. "Desire for what is not obtained" refers to the longing for a desired object that has not yet been attained.

"Equanimity toward what is obtained" means being free from mental modification when a desired object is acquired; the meaning is to remain devoid of joy or dejection regardless of whether the enjoyment of the desired object is small or great.
When the mind is rendered helpless by the powerlessness of desire and is devoid of contentment, wisdom does not reflect within it, just as a face does not appear in a tarnished mirror. (76)
He states that since knowledge does not arise in the absence of contentment, one must practice contentment—beginning with the verse "Āśā" (Hope):
"In the powerlessness of being enslaved by hope. The meaning is that one is unsettled due to being under the sway of hope. By the word "withered" (*mlāna*), a state of impurity is indicated.
[Such a person] does not desire what has not been attained; having attained it, he enjoys it in due order.
But he whose conduct is gentle is said to be "contented. || 77 ||

Having stated the nature of contentment, he speaks again for the sake of strengthening the knowledge thereof: "Not... [and so on]. "In due order" (yathākramam) means that which proceeds without transgressing the sequence of conduct (ācārakrama). || 77 ||

O descendant of Raghu, even the best of men and great sages bow down to that stainless one, the king among men, who is adorned here by his equanimity, his wisdom, and his possession of virtuous qualities.

Demonstrating the extreme excellence of contentment, he concludes with the words "by equanimity" (samatayā). The grammatical connection is: "He is well-adorned by equanimity, which is the perspective of those possessed of virtues. || 78 ||
Especially for men in crossing over the cycle of existence, O mighty-armed one, the company of the virtuous is beneficial here in every respect. (79)
He elaborates upon association with the virtuous through four verses beginning with "viśeṣeṇa."
Therein, by the first verse, the fruit of association with the virtuous is described; by the second and third, it is praised;
and by the fourth, service to them is enjoined, preceded by a description of the nature of the virtuous. || 79 ||
The empty becomes crowded; even death turns into a festival;
and misfortune appears like prosperity in the company of learned men. (80)
"An empty place seems as if it has become crowded and teeming with living beings"—the word "as if" (*iva*) should be supplied here as well. || 80 ||

For one who has bathed in the cool, white Gaṅgā of association with the virtuous, what need is there for gifts, what need for sacred fords, what need for austerities, or what need for sacrifices? (81)
It is both cool (śītā) and white (sitā); it is "cool" because it wards off the torments of saṃsāra. Whiteness signifies purity. || 81 ||

Those virtuous ones who are honored by all, whose knots have been severed, and who possess that knowledge—these must be served by every means, for they are indeed the means [for crossing] the ocean of worldly existence. 82.
The "knot" is the ego (ahaṃkāra), because it consists of the knot between the self and the non-self, and because, like a knot, it is difficult to untie. || 82 ||
These four are the stainless means for shattering existence;
those by whom they have been practiced have crossed over the ocean of existence, whose waters are delusion. (83)
"Four" means: the meaning is clear. || 83 ||
Supported by this unimpaired glory of virtues, listen to these words about to be spoken, which remove the delusion of the mind. (84)
To Rāma, who was reflecting, "Am I not distinguished by these [qualities] which enable one to cross the ocean of existence filled with the waters of delusion?
he replied: "You... He then stated what must be done by one embraced by the glory of virtues: "The mind... (84).
O crusher of enemies, for those who listen to this discourse on the means to liberation, a supreme awakening arises by force, even against their will. (85)

The subsequent textual passage beginning with "mokṣopāya" and ending with "girām aviṣayaḥ" is intended to reveal the fruit of hearing the discourse on knowledge that is about to be expounded, introduced by the words "Listen to this. Its meaning is clear; however, certain points are explained here and there. (85)
The defects such as greed, delusion, and the rest sufficiently diminish for the intellect; the mind attains clarity, like a lake becoming stainless in autumn. (86)
Tānava means thinness or attenuation. || 86 ||
(92) Their glances, though filled with the defects of wretchedness and poverty and revealing their inner thoughts,
do not cut into the vital organs, just as arrows fail to pierce one who is clad in armor. 87.

Wretchedness and poverty are indeed the two faults; by means of these, the "riches" of the views—namely, the conceptualizations regarding what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted—are shown their inner gaps, with the opportunity revealed for the piercing of the vital points, even while [the mind] is armored with a fine coat of mail. 87.
The terrifying fears of saṃsāra do not seize his heart;
supreme equanimity arises within him like the ocean when Mount Mandara has been removed.
They snatch away; they cut off. 88 || 89 ||
Like the ocean, there arises in the one who investigates the depth of his being; like Mount Meru, his stability;
and like the moon, the coolness within his heart. (89)

His intellect delights in whatever action comes to him that is not in conflict with true scriptures and the conduct of the virtuous, just as a noble woman finds pleasure in the courtyard of the inner apartments.
The courtyard is without decay. || 90 || 91 ||
That state of liberation while living gradually reaches its full fruition for him;
for one in whom all particularities have been stilled, it becomes beyond the reach of words. (91)
He appears like an ordinary person, following whatever comes to him;
yet, in the attainment of desired or undesired results, his heart remains unconquered.

To explain what kind of person this liberated-while-living (jīvanmukta) is, he says: "He is seen... He is one whose continued engagement—that is, the persistence—of worldly activity as it occurs according to the scriptures and common practice remains as it is; [this is done] with the heart, that is, the mind.
Seated on a comfortable seat, eating as much as is appropriate, and never remaining engaged in activities contrary to right conduct regarding the web of enjoyments; || 93 ||

To show how the means to liberation (*mokṣopāya*) is to be practiced by a person—namely, that it consists of hearing (*śravaṇa*) in this manner—he demonstrates its fruit, which is the direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), through the textual passage beginning with "sukhāsana" and ending with "yoniyantraprapīḍana. That [passage] is clear in meaning. (93, 94, 95)
Reflecting at every opportunity and in every place for the sake of happiness, one should pursue this sequence of discourses on liberation through association with the virtuous as it may occur. (94)
By that through which great awakening, which brings peace to cyclic existence, is attained,
one is no longer born again to suffer the oppression of the machine of the womb. (95)

Even those who are terrified by this much, being sinful and addicted to the taste of worldly enjoyments—those base ones, who are like worms in the excrement of their own mother, are not even worthy of mention. 96.

Having described the fruit for one who performs the hearing of the scriptures accompanied by the necessary subsidiaries of reflection and meditative absorption (nididhyāsana), as well as the procedural requirements such as tranquility (śama) and so forth, he censures those persons who do not perform it, saying: "Even with this much... and so on.

The meaning is that even in a task where the effort—characterized by listening to the scriptures and so forth—is great while the fruit is small, one should proceed according to the principle of sitting in a comfortable posture (*sukhāsana*) and so on. || 96 ||
Through encounters with teachers, those who have attained tranquility, the noble-minded, and the wise, he repeatedly engaged in the practice of acquiring the Dharma and its meaning. || 97 ||

Anticipating the doubt as to how long this inquiry should be practiced, he refutes it by repeating [the objection] along with its supplementary context, beginning with the words "In the scripture" and ending with "the designation of the fourth state. One who has "attained success at intervals"—that is, one for whom the activity of acquiring dharma and artha occurs from time to time—is so described. (97, 98)
The wise one should investigate until he attains rest within himself—
that peace called the fourth state (turyapada), which is freedom from rebirth.

For one who is established in repose in the Fourth State (turya) and has turned back from the ocean of worldly existence—whether living or dead, whether a householder or an ascetic—[this applies]. 99.

Having distinguished the non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpa-caitanya*) which persists like a thread amidst the flowers of the Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña states as they turn away, and having further transcended even the state of the Fourth (*turya*), one who is endowed with repose in the Fourth— characterized by an unwavering state through the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) within that [consciousness] where the web of duality has been shaken off; [for such a person...]
He dispels the lingering doubt regarding what has been done with the words beginning with "turya" (the fourth state), etc. "Of the pratīpa" means of one who is turned away. || 99 ||
There is no purpose served by what is done or left undone, nor by the confusion of the Śruti and Smṛti;
like the ocean without Mount Mandara, he remains just as he is.
Listen now, O Rāghava, as I relate this expansion of knowledge, which is the innermost essence of the core of the intellect. (94)1.

Having declared the fruit of listening to the treatise on knowledge (jñānaśāstra) that is about to be expounded both in brief and in detail, and being about to begin its exposition, he says "Listen" (*śṛṇu*), because the mind must be concentrated upon it due to the vastness of what is to be heard. He says "The intellect... (*buddhi...*) to show that even though it is vast, this [treatise] is not like that which is worthless; therefore, one's mind should be concentrated upon it.
His intellect is "innermost within the innermost," meaning it is the very essence of knowledge at its core. || 1 ||
"A statement endowed with reason should be accepted even from a child;
any other, even if spoken by the Lotus-born Brahmā, should be rejected like a blade of grass. (2)
And he says—“yukti... (verse 2)—that you should not accept a matter out of respect for us, but rather only that which is consistent with valid means of knowledge and endowed with reasoning.
O descendant of Kakutstha, whatever examples I have used here to awaken your understanding, let them all, though possessing their own causes, lead you to that which is truly causeless. (3)

Having explained that even what is spoken by a teacher is not to be accepted if its meaning is untenable due to negligence, he states— by means of the two verses beginning with "yair" (by whom)— the portion to be accepted among the examples about to be presented for the instruction on Brahman, after first demonstrating the disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*).
The word "sat" has Brahman as its object. 3.4.3–4.
Regarding this example of the instruction on Brahman that is told to you here, let it be understood that its similarity applies only to a single aspect. (4)
This being the case, how could that which possesses form serve as an illustration for Brahman, which is formless?
Here, the arguments of the disputants are merely the talk of fools. (5)
"Such being the case" is clear in its meaning. || 5 ||

Surely, having attained the status of a logician, one should not destroy [reality] through impure conceptual constructions that end in the denial of direct experience by means of mere intellectual awakening.

"You must not resort to the conceptual constructions of fools arising from fallacious reasoning, because they destroy right knowledge"—with this in mind, he instructs the disciples who have found the opportunity: "No. Those whose end is the denial of experience are called *anubhūtyapalāpāntāḥ*;
by them, [the constructions] which terminate in the repudiation of direct experience. They are impure because their objects are impure matters.

Is Brahman dual or non-dual? If it is dual, there is a contradiction with one's own established tenet (*apasiddhānta*). If it is non-dual, then because of the absence of a teacher, scriptures, and so forth, knowledge cannot arise. Is Brahman possessed of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or devoid of a means of valid cognition? If it is possessed of a means of valid cognition, there is a destruction of non-duality; if it is devoid of a means of valid cognition, that object of knowledge (*prameya*) cannot be established. By such alternative positions (*vikalpita*), [the opponent argues].
The virtues such as tranquility arise from knowledge, and likewise, wisdom arises from tranquility and the other virtues; they increase one another like two lotus ponds. (7)
The inquiry previously described as a duty for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), which is endowed with tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities,

must be practiced by the seeker of liberation together with the practice of knowledge— of which *nididhyāsana* is another synonym— and not with an outward-turned mind; he states this point along with its supporting reasoning in the two verses beginning with "The qualities" (*guṇāḥ*).

To the extent that one, being inward-turned, perceives the reality of the Self (ātmatattva), to that same extent one becomes possessed of tranquility and the like; and to the extent that one, being inward-turned, becomes possessed of tranquility and the like, to that same extent one beholds the reality of the Self—
this being established by experience through an internal mental modification (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) that has the single form of non-conceptual consciousness (nirvikalpacidekākāra).

The meaning is that one should practice the investigation of the Self, endowed with tranquility and other virtues, together with the repeated cultivation of knowledge regarding the characteristics of the functions [of the mind], which is designated as the "succession of the virtuous" (*satpuruṣakrama*). Alternatively, it has been stated: "The wise know the practice of Brahman to consist in reflecting upon That, discoursing upon That, mutually awakening one another to That, and being solely intent upon That."

He states, with supporting reasoning, that the practice of knowledge and the practices of tranquility and contentment must be performed simultaneously, beginning with the verse starting "The qualities" (guṇāḥ): 7–8. [The verses follow.]
As long as both the path of knowledge and the sequence of the true person are not well-practiced,
not even one of these two will grant success to a person in this world.
This [teaching] bestows fame and long life, and grants the fruits of human goals;
having heard it, you shall by force of the purity of your intellect attain that supreme state.
"This brings fame"—the meaning is clear. [This occurs] from the multitude of great sayings (mahāvākya) through the purification of the intellect by means of hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth. || 9 ||
For this mind of the sage, having known that which is to be known, indeed goes helplessly to the supreme state;
for that which has been realized as undivided and without succession never again abandons the state of such realization.
Lest it be thought that once the knowledge characterized by the attainment of that state has arisen, there might still be a forgetting of it, he says:

"viditavedya" (one who has known what is to be known). The word *padam* ends in the accusative case. One particle (*hi*) is used for emphasis; the second is used to indicate what is well-known among the wise. It goes [to that state] inevitably. He establishes this with the word *yat*: that which has been understood—that is, directly realized—without being fragmented.

The meaning is that the Supreme Self—being undivided by space, time, or substance, and for that very reason non-sequential due to its nature as unobstructed and perfect consciousness—does not forfeit its state of being pervaded by the mental fluctuations of the wise. || 110 ||
Thus ends the first canto in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhavivaraṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the section on the means to liberation (*mokṣopāya*). || 1 ||

Thus ends the chapter on the Conduct of the Seeker of Liberation (*mumukṣuvyavahāraprakaraṇa*) in the *Śrīmad-Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya-vivaraṇa*, composed by the disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Uttamaśloka-pūjyapāda, Śrī Madhvācārya.
(p. 97) Chapter on Origination—
Vasiṣṭha said:
This conduct of those seeking liberation has been proclaimed by me to you;
now, this glorious origin of the world is being proclaimed. || 1 ||
In this section titled "Origination," which is adorned with nine chapters,
the first is the narrative of the one born from space, and after that follows the narrative of the divine play.
In those narratives, the essential point is stated concisely by means of the former.
Having restated the subject matter of the preceding section, he states the purport of the subsequent section: "The conduct of one seeking liberation."

The practice characterized by *śravaṇa* (hearing), which is prescribed in such scriptural passages as "The Self, indeed, should be seen," and which is accompanied by the auxiliary rites of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, and has *manana* (reflection) and *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) as its limbs, is called the "practice of one seeking liberation.
The term "worldly" (*jāgatī*) means pertaining to the world; it is like the appearance of a city of Gandharvas arising from the sky.
The meaning is that the origination of the world from Brahman, which is unperceived due to its being the substratum, is here being described. || 1 ||
That which is called "perception" (pratyakṣa) here—consisting of experience, feeling, and cognition according to its specific designation—is for us none other than the soul (jīva). || 2 ||
The narratives of Karkaṭī, Aindava, and Kṛtrimendra follow in sequence; then the sixth is that of Citta, and the seventh is that of Bāla. || 2 ||
Once the reality of Brahman as the Self has been established for the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*),
and when a doubt arises regarding its perfection due to the suspicion that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)— revealed by means of valid cognition such as perception— is real,
it is necessary to demonstrate the non-existence of the phenomenal world apart from the Supreme Self, which is its cause, in order to dispel that doubt.

Therefore, intending that creation shall be described later, [the author]— anticipating the divergent views of disputants regarding the nature of the individual soul (jīva)— first states his own position on the nature of the soul and then declares its identity with Brahman through the passage beginning with "anubhūteḥ" and ending with "sa eva saṃvit. Alternatively, for the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) who desires to realize the unity of the Self (aikātmya), that very [unity] is...
Intending that what was to be established first must have its creation described afterwards as a subordinate element,

[the author argues that] identity with Brahman— which is remote and contrary to the nature of the individual self— is not possible through that very self, which is immediate consciousness in the form of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) manifesting even prior to the desire to know, and is well-known as the "witness-means of knowledge" (*sākṣipramāṇa*).

Anticipating the objection that [the world] arises [from something else], he states the identity with the inner self (*pratyag-aikya*) by demonstrating that it is of the nature of immediate consciousness (*aparokṣa-caitanya*),
beginning with the words "anubhūteḥ" (of experience). Alternatively,
