rather than stating the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*)— which is what the seeker of liberation desires to know— he [first] addresses the origin of the world, which is not what is desired to be known.

In the sphere of common discourse, that immediate consciousness which is designated by the terms "experience," "feeling," and "realization" is referred to as "experiential perception," "perception of feeling," and "perception of realization," respectively, without deviating from their respective designations.
What is called "perception" (pratyakṣa) is that which has been established by various disputants, each preceded by the insertion of their own preferred qualifications.

Such is the *jīva* for us, the followers of the Upaniṣads. And thus it has been stated by the great ones: "Experience (*anubhūti*), cognition (*vedana*), and realization (*pratipatti*)—that which is immediate consciousness (*caitanya*) is here called the *jīva*. By this, the nature of the *jīva* as otherwise imagined by other disputants is refuted. However, in the case of the *brahman* position, this verse is to be explained as follows:

By the word *anubhūti* (realization), Brahman is denoted; it is that very same [Brahman] which is specified by means of "knowledge" (*vedana*) and "attainment" (*pratipatti*). By "knowledge" is meant the immediate, non-dual cognition of Brahman; by "attainment" is meant that very Brahman as it has ascended upon a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), which is an extraordinary form of perception designated by the term "immediate cognition."

That very [Brahman], when mounted upon the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) through a modification (vṛtti) produced by the eyes and other senses, is called "empirical perception" (laukikapratyakṣa). Since experience consists of both feeling and comprehension, and since Brahman is designated according to its own nature,
the name "perception" (pratyakṣa)— without deviating from its synonymy— is applied here in this treatise on liberation (mokṣaśāstra).

The meaning is that it has been recited. "From the immediate, the immediate eye" (*cakṣur-netram*)—this is the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which establishes perceptible objects. That very one, Brahman known by the name "the immediate," is for us followers of the Upaniṣads the "living soul" (*jīva*), the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) of the word *jīva*. The change in gender is due to the requirement of the correlative being pointed out [in the subsequent clause]. || 2 ||
That very consciousness is the Person (puruṣa), whose nature consists of the notion of "I. When that [consciousness] arises through cognition, it is known as an object. (3)
Then follows the account of Sāmbarika, and after that, the story of King Lavaṇa.
It is a narrative containing a beautiful description of the seven stages. || 3 ||

"That very [Self] is consciousness. That living being (jīva), whose nature is immediate consciousness, is indeed consciousness itself; it is Brahman itself. Now, one might object: even if the identity with Brahman is established by the statement "that very [Self] is consciousness," liberation is not possible for one who desires liberation. For liberation is the abiding in the state of the perfect Self; since that is impossible as long as the phenomenal world (prapañca) exists as something distinct from Brahman—having raised this doubt, [the text says] "of everything..."
He demonstrates that phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is an illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, beginning with the words "That person" (*sa pumān*).

The individual soul (*jīva*), characterized as a reflection of consciousness within the mind, is called the "person" (*puruṣa*). It is called the "I-maker" (*ahaṅkāra*) because it is perceived through the sense of "I-ness.

By the word "that" (*saḥ*), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), whose nature is pure consciousness, is referred to. That Supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness, having first become a person limited by the adjunct of the mind (*cittopādhika*) through its own ignorance (*avidyā*), subsequently becomes the essence of the notion of "I-ness" (*ahantā-pratyaya*).

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood that [the Self] consists of the nature of intellect (*buddhi*) and the nature of mind (*manas*). He says "that" (*sa*) to show that this very [Self] also evolves (*vivartate*) in the form of external objects. "That" refers to the consciousness (*saṃvit*) by which it arises in the forms of jars, cloths, and so forth; the meaning is that it evolves in the form of that consciousness. That is consciousness.

The category of objects characterized as jars, cloths, and so forth is what is traditionally known; for it is the established principle of the scriptures that every object is indeed a manifestation of the mind. (3)
Through delusions such as conceptualization and discursive thought, which create various sequences,
it manifests as the world, just as water manifests as waves and the like. (4)

He clarifies the meaning already stated with the words: "He [is] saṃkalpa... That Supreme Self has a sequence of various states produced by those things beginning with egoism (*abhimāna*), of which *saṃkalpa* (volition) and *vikalpa* (conceptualization)—or delusion (*bhrama*) and doubt (*saṃśaya*)—are the first. Thus, this sequence of states comes to be.

The Supreme Self, whose nature is perfect consciousness, at the time of creation first attains the state of general visibility (*dṛśyatva*); from that, it attains the state of the mind (*citta*); then the state of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*);
then the state of the intellect (*buddhi*); and then the state of the mind (*manas*). This very sequence will become clear later on. || 4 ||
At the beginning of creation, having first manifested as the causeless itself through the play of creation, it quickly became the manifest cause within its own self.

Now, one might object: "If Brahman thus manifests as the world, then the identity of the individual soul (jīva)—which is the opposite of that world—with Brahman, the cause of the world, is untenable. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "prāk" (before).

Brahman is designated as "direct perception" (pratyakṣa) because it is non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman), which is of the nature of the means of direct perception; or else, Brahman is directly named "direct perception" itself, being, according to the maxim that "that which undergoes modification while performing an action is the effect," a non-cause prior to creation due to the absence of action. Alternatively, since causality is illusory, Brahman is indeed a non-cause.
At the beginning of creation, having quickly manifested through the play of creation— which consists of *māyā* and the play of observing the purpose of creation—
for the sake of bringing about the world according to its causes; that is, having manifested within Himself the world which exists in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*),
[He perceives] that which is Himself the cause, or [perceives it] at the beginning of creation.

Regarding the creation, preservation, and so forth, Brahman is "without a cause," meaning devoid of any real auxiliary cause; having first manifested through the play of emanation prior to creation, it becomes the cause of the universe existing within itself by means of Māyā—which effects that causality—and its nature as the causal ground consists in being the substratum of Māyā which evolves into the form of the phenomenal world (prapañca). || 5 ||
The world, agitated by forms, light, mental attention, and objects,
exists within the knower like the movement of wind within a bellows. (6)

In order to indicate that Brahman alone is the cause and that Māyā is the medium, and to point to the Śruti passage stating "He made Himself" (*tad ātmānaṃ svayam akuruta*), the word "Himself" (*svayam*) is used; this [the author] elaborates upon with the verse beginning "form" (*rūpa*). Alternatively, having described the origin of the world from Brahman, he states its subsistence therein with the verse beginning "form. "Mental activity" (*manaskāra*) refers to the mind.

*Ābhoga* is the expansion of the mind; according to Amara, *manaskāra* is the mental application (*cittābhoga*). Form (*rūpa*), light (*āloka*), mental application (*manaskāra*), and other objects (*padārtha*) constitute "form-light-mental-application-objects"; [the mind] is agitated—that is, mixed—with these.
Alternatively, the light of form is its illumination, which is the seeing of form; by this, wakefulness is indicated.
By the word *manaskāra* (mental attention), a dream consisting of mental expansion is intended.

The world, which is agitated by the objects of form, light, mental attention, waking, and dreaming, exists within Brahman—whose characteristic is pure consciousness—in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), whether in a subtle or gross state. Within Brahman...
To make it known that the world exists through identity (*tādātmya*), he provides an illustration, beginning with "vātāntari" (within the wind). || 6 ||
When the pure awareness of the self of all arises, it shines forth as that very essence,
manifesting in the form of bodies with external and internal aspects, as well as directions and time, which have been projected forth.

Now, if Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the world, then it should be perceived in the form of each individual object—such as "the pot is Brahman" or "the cloth is Brahman"—just as water is perceived in the form of waves and the like. But this is not the case; therefore, [it is argued that] Brahman is not the material cause but only the efficient cause (*nimitta*).
To this, he says: "The Self of all. Brahman, whose nature is knowledge and which consists of all things, [is perceived] in whatever manner...

That which arises in the form of an effect is an illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of that very essence; thus, it appears as the nature of that effect. For indeed, "the pot is Being," "the cloth is Being"—in this way, Brahman, whose nature is Being, shines forth through the various forms of those [effects]. Therefore, it is logical that Brahman is also the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). Its body consists of the forms of space and time, both external and internal, which have been projected forth.
By means of the indeclinable *antareṇa*, the immediately following object is intended [to be expressed].

That whose body is its very own nature (*svarūpa*)—the form of those things which are external and internal, yet freed from the distinctions of spatial direction and time, and whose essential nature is dispersed—is thus described.
In whatever way and wherever that Universal Self attains manifestation,
it immediately abides there and shines as if it were of that very form.

He clarifies the meaning already stated with the words "he is the self of all. In whatever place, in whatever manner, and by whatever means it manifests—that is, its unfolding—as the nature of an effect; such is the meaning. (8)
Therefore, this world remains as the Brahma-cosmos, being indeed without a cause;
it is directly perceived as its own creator, while inference and other means of knowledge are merely its parts.

He clarifies the point stated in the passage beginning with "prior [to creation], it was indeed without cause" by saying: "without cause" (akāraṇakam). Since causality does not exist in Brahman except through the medium of Māyā, this world prior to its manifestation is indeed without cause—that is, devoid of any real cause—and exists like the very nature of Brahman, being a state of Brahman in which name and form are unmanifested.

The meaning is that when the world has dissolved into Brahman, which serves as its substratum, it remains with only its residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) and thus its distinction [from Brahman] is no longer perceived. When the time for creation arrives, Brahman itself—being of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa-ātmaka*)—becomes the creator of the world; unlike in the systems of Akṣapāda and others, it is not of the nature of non-manifest consciousness (*aparokṣa-samacid-rūpa*).

In order to demonstrate that the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed immediate consciousness (*aparokṣacaitanya*), it was stated that the soul is precisely the means of valid cognition known as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

In connection with that, he describes the nature of inference (*anumāna*) and the other means of knowledge—beginning with the words "of that" (*tasya*). Alternatively, in order to demonstrate that mediate consciousness (*parokṣacaitanya*) is indeed Brahman, it was stated that Brahman is that which is called direct perception; in connection with that, he describes the nature of inference and the other means of knowledge.

The parts of Brahman—which consists of immediate consciousness—are like the limbs of the direct means of knowledge (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*). Brahman, which is pure, perfect cognition, when reflected in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is called the knower (*pramātṛ*).
That very same [Brahman], when mounted upon a portion of the internal organ produced by the sense organs, marks, and so forth, is designated as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus it is said.
The boundary of Vedānta. || 9 ||
This bondage arises from the existence of the visible; in the absence of the visible, there is no bondage.
Listen now as it is explained how this visible world does not truly exist. (10)

By demonstrating that the entire world is an effect of Brahman, it has been stated that the world, as an effect, is non-existent apart from the causal Brahman; for there is the scriptural text, "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is real," which establishes the non-existence of the effect apart from its cause. Now, regarding bondage and its cessation:

Having first shown the reason, he elaborates upon that very unreality of the visible world—which serves as the cause of bondage—by means of a formal proposition (*pratijñā*), following the scriptural text: "All this is indeed Brahman, for it originates, dissolves, and breathes in That" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.1).
[He does so] because the existence of the visible world about to be described is directly experienced by this [perceiver].

Bondage, characterized by agency, enjoyership, and so forth, comes into being. Now, it is true that bondage does not exist in the absence of the visible; however, he says "it is not possible" [to claim] that this very absence of the visible is impossible.
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of removing doubt. It is now explained how this visible world is not possible.
Listen. || 10 ||
All this that is seen, the entire world of the stationary and the moving, perishes at the end of the eon like a dream in deep sleep. || 11 ||

Regarding the phrase "yadidam" (this which): the object of dispute, the visible world, is non-existent because it is perishable, like a dream; the meaning is that the object of dispute is perishable because it is visible, like a dream. || 11 ||
Then, there remains a certain reality— motionless and profound, neither light nor pervasive darkness, inexpressible and unmanifest. (12)

Anticipating the objection that Brahman might be subject to destruction like the visible world, he says: "Then... Following that, there was neither light nor darkness; rather, there was something—unmoving and immeasurable, nameless and inexpressible because it is beyond the reach of the senses, unmanifest because it cannot be defined as "this. It was something incapable of being determined.
Only the existent Brahman remains, according to the Śruti: "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed the Existent alone. (12)
"Ṛta," "Ātman," "Para Brahma," "Satya," and so forth—these names of that Great Soul have been devised by the wise for the sake of conventional usage. (13)
To the objection that it is incorrect to call it "inexpressible" (anākhyam) because it possesses names such as Brahmā and others, he says: "It is Truth" (ṛtam). || 13 ||
That very self, though remaining as it is, shines forth as if it were something else;
it enters, as it were, into the state of living beings who are free from all distress regarding their future.

Having thus described how the entire manifold of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) finds its resting place in the realization that Brahman is one's own Self, [the text] now shows how, from that very reality which never deviates from its own nature, the world arises at the time of creation—like the appearance of a city of Gandharvas in the sky—and first describes the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha, the collective individual soul (*samaṣṭijīva*), with the words: "He, being such... He remains in that very state, characterized by stillness and profundity.

Thus, that Supreme Self, like the sky reflected in clear water, appearing as if it were something else while shining forth, and expanding as if it were indeed another, enters into a state of "living-ness" (jīvatā)—a condition that is afflicted, distressed, and clouded by the names of future living beings and so forth, which are themselves rendered wretched by their own future states.
The two occurrences of the word *iva* are intended to illuminate the illusory nature (*māyikatva*) of this apparent otherness and so on. Herein lies the sequence of creation:

Prior to creation, the non-dual Supreme Self (*paramātman*) manifests, at the time of creation, first as the mere visible world unqualified by prior distinctions; then as the nature of the universal totality (*samaṣṭi-cit*);
then as the nature of the universal individual soul (*samaṣṭi-jīva*); then as the nature of ego (*ahaṃkāra*); then as the nature of intellect (*buddhi*); and then as the nature of mind (*manas*).

Therefore, it evolves in the form of the subtle elements (tanmātra), the gross elements (bhūta), and their derivatives (bhautika). And so it is stated in the *Bṛhadvāsiṣṭha*: "First arises the conceptualization of the state of being an object; then, from the consciousness of that objective aspect, the mental construction arises from the consciousness of the power of pure awareness (*citiśakti*)."

From that arises the perception of the living skin through consciousness joined with the object of thought; from that arises the perception of the sense of "I" by virtue of being solely intent upon the object of thought.

Then, from the transformation of the intellect (buddhi), the skin (tvak), time (kāla), and the ego-sense (ahaṃtā), this very [unmanifest] comes to possess the nature of the mind (manas) and so forth, as well as the subtle elements (tanmātra) such as sound.

Then that referent of the word "jīva," having fallen into the state of being agitated by mental construction, becomes the mind (manas), the self of the elements; it becomes sluggish through the act of thinking. (15)

This same sequence should be understood in its entirety even in cases where it has not been explicitly stated. Through the medium of the mind (*citta*) which is the object of perception, he describes how the Supreme Self, having attained the state of the collective individual soul (*samaṣṭi-jīva*), attains the state of the collective ego (*samaṣṭi-ahaṃkāra*) and intellect (*buddhi*)—this is expressed by the word "tataḥ" (thence).

Because He is the cause of all beings, He is the "Self of Beings" (*bhūtātmā*); that is the meaning of the term *jīva*. [He then enters into] the state of agitation caused by conceptualization (*kalanā*).

Having become agitated by time and conceptualization, it becomes the mind (*manas*). The qualification of the mind is that it "becomes sluggish" (*mantharībhavat*); that is, through thinking and conceptualization, it becomes sluggish, meaning it becomes gross. || 15 ||
The mind arises from the Great Supreme Self, which is perfectly stable; it takes on an unstable form, like a wave from the ocean. (16)
Having stated it in brief, he says: "The mind. The word "nāma" is used in a derogatory sense. 16.
It itself constantly and spontaneously conceives this [world] at its own will;
by that means, this worldly splendor, like a magical illusion, is extensively spread out. (17)

Demonstrating the nature of the mind, he says "that" (tat), meaning that by means of that collective mind (*samaṣṭimanasa*), the world— a magical illusion characterized by the five subtle elements such as sound, the five gross elements such as space, the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), and other material phenomena— is extensively fashioned. By that mind, it is "pravitanyate," which means it is expanded forth pre-eminently.
It is expanded. || 17 ||
Just as the referent of the word "bracelet" is not distinct from the gold,
nor is the gold distinct from the bracelet, so too the referent of the word "world" is not distinct from the Supreme.

If the world-illusion, which has arisen from the Supreme Self having assumed the state of the collective mind (*samaṣṭi-citta*), the individual soul (*jīva*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), and mind (*manas*), were false, then Brahman—which is non-different from it—would also be false. Since Brahman is real, the world would also have to be real; therefore, he says "just as" (*yathā*). This refers to the meaning of the word *kaṭaka* (bracelet).
Gold is not subject to separation or differentiation from gold; for it is invariably absent when that [separation] is absent, like a snake in a rope.

Furthermore, because it is not perceived as distinct from gold by one whose vision is correctly turned away [from delusion], it is not the case that gold is not subject to separation from a bracelet; for it exists even in the absence of that [bracelet], like a snake in a rope.

Just as in these two examples, so too does the status of being the referent of the word "world" belong to the Supreme, the Highest Self; and the word "higher than" is to be understood as following "the world. Because that which is superimposed depends upon its substratum for existence and manifestation, whereas the existence and manifestation of the substratum do not depend on the superimposed, the aforementioned distinction between Brahman and the world remains exactly as stated. || 18 ||

The world, though non-existent, appears as if real—like a flickering wave upon a scorching river; the splendor of this worldly illusion is spread forth by the mind alone, like a magical conjuration. (19)

If it be objected that it is untenable for the mind to be the generator of the world-illusion because, like a shadow or a piśāca, it is non-existent, he says in response: "By the non-existent itself. Here in this saṃsāra, by the non-existent mind alone—like a flickering wave upon the river of heat (a mirage)—the real splendor of the world-illusion is extensively spread forth. 19.
Ignorance, the cycle of worldly existence, delusion, bondage, illusion, impurity, and darkness—these are the names assigned to it by those who know all things. (20)
He establishes both the falsity and the worthlessness of the world even by means of the designation "the conceptual construction of names" with the words: "It is ignorance."

The phrase "to which the names 'worldly illusion' (jagad-indrajāla) and 'splendor' (śrī) have been assigned" is connected with the preceding term "worldly illusion-splendor" (jāgatīndrajālaśrī). And he will say: "O Rāghava, ignorance, worldly existence, bondage, the mind, delusion, impurity, and darkness—these are the names for the web of mental constructs. This bondage arises from the existence of the visible world; in the absence of the visible world, [there is no bondage].
There is no bondage; however, that which appears as this [world] does not truly exist—listen now as it is explained. || 20 ||
First, listen to this description of the nature of bondage being told;
thereafter, O moon-faced one, you shall understand the true nature of liberation.
He elaborates upon what was stated by this [verse], beginning with "of bondage" and so forth. || 21 ||
The existence of the seer and the seen is called bondage.
The seer is bound by virtue of the seen; in the absence of the seen, he is liberated. (22) [Commentary:

"Of the seen" refers to the phenomenal expansion of duality (*dvaitaprapañca*). "O friend" (*aṅga*) is a term of address. It is called "bondage" (*bandha*) because one is bound by it. Thus it has been said:
Clarifying that when the object of perception is absent, the state of being a perceiver ceases through knowledge, he declares liberation (kaivalya) with the words: "Of the seer... (draṣṭuḥ).
The world, the ego, and so forth—this nature of creation is called the visible (dṛśya).
As long as this persists, liberation does not exist. (23)

"What is that visible object (dṛśya) which serves as the cause of bondage? To this he says: "The world" (jagat). Now, one might ask: "Even if the visible object exists, as it does for the Naiyāyikas and others, why should there not be liberation? To this he says: "As long as...
For according to the scripture, "When he perceives even the slightest difference in this [Self], then fear arises for him," liberation is impossible for those who maintain duality.
The milk of a female tortoise becomes [a reality]. || 23 ||
Just as the seed of a lotus exists within the hollow of a lotus-stamen in the form of a dark-blue stalk, so too does the perception of the visible reside within the seer. (24)

If liberation is not seen as long as any object of perception exists, then why would liberation not occur during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), when all objects of perception are absent? For the scriptures establish the absence of all objects of perception in deep sleep and similar states. If it is argued that this is not so because ignorance (*ajñāna*) exists therein, we say no.

Anticipating the objection that liberation cannot be admitted there because [the seed] is as ineffective as a snake whose fangs have been extracted, he says: "ānīla... The lotus seed, which is the causal seed of a future lotus pond (*padminī*), takes the form of a dark-green creeper (*ānīlavallarī*)—that is, its entire nature becomes a dark-green vine—within the hollow of the lotus seed-vessel.
Just as the lotus and the jewel remain within the interior space in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), so too do the cognitions of the visible objects remain within the seer.
It is called "cognition" (*dhī*) because the visible object is merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*). || 24 ||
Just as a sprout situated within a seed unfolds its radiant body according to place and time, even so does the intellect of the visible unfold.

Now, one might object: "If the visible object exists within the seer in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) during the dissolution and so forth, then why does the manifestation of the visible not occur at that very time from the seer—who is unknown [to others] and variegated by diverse impressions? Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it with an illustration: "Just as... [The sprout] situated within the seed in the form of a latent impression...

Just as a radiant form—characterized by a specific place and time, and possessing the nature of shining through its prominent branches, leaves, and so forth, namely a gross form—extends [itself], in the same way, the intellect (*dhī*) regarding the object of perception also extends a gross form according to a fixed place and time;
for this reason, there is no contingency of the world arising at that very same moment. || 25 ||
Just as a wonder is eternally present within the interior of a substance that is devoid of rising and setting,
so too the existence of the world is inherent within the interior of the substance whose body is pure consciousness (cinmātra). (26)
He concludes what was stated in the passage beginning with "not blue" (*ānīla*) with the words "of the substance" (*dravyasya*).

Just as a wonder or marvel (*camatkṛti*) arises and is produced within the heart regarding a substance such as a lotus seed, so too does that same [wonder] exist eternally within the very interior of that [substance], being free from setting and known as the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the supreme subtle state of the future substance. Thus it is.

Within the belly of the Supreme Self-substance—which has pure consciousness as its body and whose essential nature is pure consciousness—there exists the existence of the world, which is its inherent nature and non-different from its own essence. || 26 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen to this narrative called "The Birth from Space," an ornament for the ears, which is the section known as "Origination," by means of which you shall understand, O Rāghava. (27)
Thus, having first stated that the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is the intended meaning taught by all the Vedānta texts,
[the author proceeds] to refute the doubt regarding the impossibility of their unity due to being possessed of contradictory attributes,
and to refute the doubt regarding the existence of other entities such as space (ākāśa) distinct from them, [he addresses] everything...

Having stated that the manifold world of space and so forth— which consists of contradictory properties and has a real cause— is non-existent apart from Brahman because it is produced from It and so on, the venerable Vasiṣṭha now spoke in order to demonstrate the fruit of the immediate knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self, which is characterized by the cessation of saṃsāra consisting of action and its results.

In this context, by means of the dialogue between Death and Yama, when the fruit of knowledge has been shown to exist in the case of Hiraṇyagarbha among the wise, the author—intending that the same fruit is thereby shown for other wise persons as well due to the equality of the underlying principle—introduces the narrative concerning the one born from space (Ākāśaja) with the words: "This... This is a figurative statement (*abhūtārthavāda*).

This section, titled "The Origin" (*utpatti*), is intended to establish the meaning that cyclic existence—consisting of karma and its fruits—is due solely to the vision of delusion, like the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*); however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it has never existed, does not exist, and will never exist.
Listen to this narrative called "The Origin of Space" (*ākāśaja*), by which, when heard, you shall understand it through the teaching on the origin of space. Indeed, space...
Because of the Vedic scripture stating, "The evolver of name and form. (27)
(108) Here there is a twice-born man named Ākāśaja, who is supremely righteous,
constantly devoted solely to meditation, and ever intent on the welfare of all creatures. (28)

Space is Brahman; because he is born from that, Brahmā is "space-born" (ākāśaja). The conceptualization of his being twice-born and so forth is for the sake of the aesthetic beauty of the narrative. (28–31)
When he lived for so long, Death thought to himself:
"I am indeed imperishable; I devour all beings one after another in due order. (29)
"Why do I not devour this brahmin born of space?
Here my power is blunted, like the edge of a sword upon a stone. (30)
Having reflected thus, he then went to that city to slay him;
for no one who is diligent abandons their exertion in their own task.
Then, as soon as Death himself enters that abode,
fire— resembling the conflagration at the end of an aeon— burns him.
The fire that stands all around in the form of a rampart for the protection of Brahmā’s abode burns this Death;

or else, Agni—who has been served for a long time by the twice-born one born of space (the wind) and who is pleased with him—emerges from the fire-sanctuary and burns this Death who is intent on slaying his own devotee. || 32 || 33 ||
Having burst through the great garland of fire-flames, he entered within;
seeing the twice-born man, he strove with effort to seize him with his hand.
And though he was powerful, he was unable to seize the Brahmin standing before him even with his hundred hands, just as one cannot grasp a person created by mere thought (saṃkalpa-puruṣa). || 34 ||

Even powerful Death was unable—indeed, could not—to seize or restrain [him], even though he was seen before him and held within the grasp of his hundred hands. The root *śak* (in the sense of "to be able") takes the *liṭ* suffix. The particle *api*, meaning "even," is connected with the word *avaṣṭabdhum*. A "man of resolve" (*saṃkalpapuruṣaḥ*) is a mere semblance of a person created by the power of the mind. || 34 || 35 ||
p.
109) Then Death himself, having arrived, questioned the dispeller of doubts:
"O Lord, why am I unable to consume that which is born of space? (35)
Yama said:
O Death, you alone are not capable of killing anyone by force;
it is the actions of the one to be killed that cause their death, and nothing else.

He states the reason why you alone, by your own strength, are not capable of killing even a single living being with the words "of that which is to be killed" (*māraṇīyasya*). The word *tat* refers to the object of killing. The word *iti* is used in the sense of a reason; according to Amara, *iti* is used in the senses of reason, context, excellence, and conclusion. (36)
Therefore, having carefully observed the deeds of this Brahmin who is to be slain, you shall devour him with their assistance.
Among those actions, by means of one or another assistant; "by assistance" (sāhāyyena) is used in some places, where the meaning is "by way of being an assistant. || 37 || 38 || 39 || 40 || 41 ||
Then Death wandered about, intent on searching for that deed, through regions, the ends of the quarters, lakes, rivers, and all directions. (38)
Having thus wandered over the circle of the earth, that arrogant Death did not obtain from anywhere any of those actions born of space. (39)
Having approached him who was skilled in all matters, he questioned him regarding the Dharma;
for the sovereign is indeed the ultimate refuge for his dependents in times of doubt.
"O Lord, tell me where the deeds of one born of space reside.
Then Dharmarāja, having reflected for a very long time, spoke this: || 41 ||
There are no actions whatsoever belonging to one born of space;
for this brahmin is born of space alone, from the void itself. (42)
Relying on the perspective of the learned, he says: "Of that which is born of space. He states the reason for this: "This..."
For it has indeed arisen as a reflection from the very source—the Supreme Self—which is the sky-like void, being entirely devoid of any real auxiliary causes.
This is because it arises from that which is absolute. 42.
He who is born from space alone shall be as stainless as the sky;
there are no auxiliary causes whatsoever for him. (43)
To the question of how there can be an absence of karma for Hiraṇyagarbha, who is a living being (jīva) born from the Supreme Self (paramātman), he says:

"From space" (ākāśāt). That which is born from the Supreme Self—which is devoid of any real auxiliary cause—and is manifested as a reflection, would be like the pure ether (vyoma), free from the impurities of karma and the like; it is born from space.

In reality, it does not differ from its own cause; the meaning is that, while being devoid of any real auxiliary causes, it is produced, like the moon reflected in water. He clarifies this stated point with a verse and a half: "The auxiliaries...
[referring to] that which is produced in the absence of auxiliary causes.
It is experienced that this [effect] does not become different from its own cause. || 44 ||
It is experienced in cases such as reflections and the like. || 44 ||
"Therefore, O Death, do not be so intent on attacking him.
Having heard this, Death was struck with wonder and departed for his own abode. (45)

He states the conclusion: "This [is so]. The meaning is: because this [Hiraṇyagarbha], whose nature is the reflection of consciousness and which is born of space, is in reality the Supreme Self and therefore devoid of karma; thus, by the rejection of its being subject to death, it should be understood that all worldly attributes invariably associated with it are also rejected. Now, [an objection is raised]: "But the elemental self (bhūtātman) is indeed one..."
"Abiding in every being, He is seen as one and also as many,
like the moon reflected in water. According to this statement, since all individual souls (*jīvas*)— along with Hiraṇyagarbha— are equally reflections of Consciousness (*cit*),
are in reality of the nature of the original Archetype (*bimba*), and are equally devoid of transmigratory existence consisting of karma and its fruits, what [is the distinction]?

[The opponent argues: "By taking a specific distinction into account, it is stated that Hiraṇyagarbha alone possesses such qualities as being without karma. To this, we reply: It is precisely by taking his status as a knower of reality (*tattvavit*) as the specific distinction that his lack of karma and so forth are predicated. And thus, scripture declares his very status as a knower of reality: "He (Hiraṇyagarbha) reflected: 'Since there is nothing other than me, from what indeed should I fear?'"

"From that very [source] his fear departs. Having heard this and so forth, the preceding section of the text ending with "Brahmā, indeed, whose body is the supreme ether" is clear in its meaning. Only certain points are here analyzed in detail. || 45 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
This god Brahmā, my great-grandfather, has been described by you;
it is my conviction that he is the self-existent, unborn, singular self, the very essence of consciousness.
The four epithets beginning with "prapitāmaha" are for the purpose of proclaiming the greatness of Brahmā.

"Vijñānātman" is for the purpose of stating his essential nature. The "pitāmahas" are the fathers of the *pitaras*; the "prapitāmaha" is the father of the *pitāmahas*. The meaning is that he is the primordial creator of all beings. In some places, the reading is "tvayā me'tra pitāmaha" (O Grandfather, here by you [I am protected]).
He states the excellence of his manifestation: "the Self-existent" (*svayaṃbhū*). He is called the Self-existent because he exists by himself alone;
for this very reason, he is "unborn" (*aja*), as he is not born from seeds such as semen or blood. He is the "single self" (*ekātmā*) because he alone attains and pervades all effects;

or alternatively, he is the "self of primordial matter" (*pradhānātman*). He is "of the nature of consciousness" (*vijñānātmā*), meaning that consciousness—intellect—is his essential nature; thus, he is of the nature of Brahman.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"It is even so, O mighty-armed one; this Brahman has been described to you.
Formerly, on account of this, Death engaged in a dispute with Yama."
In that Manvantara, when Death became a devourer of all beings and began to consume the creatures,
he attained great strength and personally undertook an assault upon the Lotus-born One.
At that very moment, even though commanded by Yama, the King of Dharma, how indeed could Brahmā—whose body is the supreme ether—not advance? 49.
He states the instruction of Yama in brief: "Brahmā, it is said...

The word "it is said" (*kila*) indicates the inconceivability of the invasion. He whose body (*vapuḥ*), that is, whose essential nature (*svarūpa*), is the supreme ether (*parākāśa*), which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), is thus described. || 49 ||
Just as a person created by imagination appears in the sky with a shimmering form, though devoid of earth and other elements, so too does the Self-born One shine forth. (50)
Now, one might object: "If Brahmā is the body of the Supreme Brahman, how can he possess a four-faced body? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says:

"In that manner, for a person imagined through the mind, his being the body of Brahman is merely apparent (prātibhāsika). In reality, however, like a person created by volition (saṃkalpa), it does not exist at all"—this is the intended meaning. || 50 ||
The self-existent one shines as Brahman—the mere infinite sky of consciousness, without beginning or middle—by the power of its own mind;
yet, though appearing as if possessing form or like a person, in reality it has no body, just like the son of a barren woman. (51)
Clarifying what has been said, he concludes: "The space of consciousness" (cidvyoma). "By the power of its own mind" means by the power of one's own mind;
that is to say, by the power of the perceiving mind. || 51 ||
This body of the Self-born One, O Rāma, is purely *ātivāhika*; a material (*ādhibhautika*) body is not possible for one who is unborn.

Immediately following the verse beginning with "cidvyoma," one should here consider a verse from the *Bṛhad-Vāsiṣṭha* concerning Hiraṇyagarbha who has attained the state of Virāj: "O Rāma, this body of the Self-born (Svayambhū) is purely *ātivāhika*; a material (*ādhibhautika*) body is not possible for the Unborn (Aja). (52)
Śrī Rāma said:
There exists indeed another body, the *ātivāhika*, whereas the *ādhibhautika* belongs to all classes of beings; is there only one [body] for Brahmā? (53)
One might object: "Since Brahmā possesses life, why should he not have a physical body (ādhibhautika-deha) like other living beings? To this, the author replies with the verse beginning *ātivāhika*.
That which is carried or led to various places by the deities residing on the two paths is the subtle body (*ātivāhika*); such is the subtle body [of Brahmā]. || 53 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
For all beings whose nature is causal, there are indeed two bodies;
however, for the unborn [Ātman], because of the absence of causality, there is only one, the subtle body (ativāhika).

He provides the answer—namely, "of all"—regarding how the two bodies of living beings arise from the presence or absence of the elements such as space that constitute the gross body, and how this applies even to Hiraṇyagarbha despite the absence of a gross body for him. [The phrase] "of those whose cause is the Self" means those whose cause is the Self characterized as the material cause (upādāna), which is their very nature (svarūpa). By this...

The existence of the causal substance that initiates the two bodies has been indicated for individual living beings (vyaṣṭijīvas). Because the Unborn (aja) lacks such a cause, there is an absence of the causal substance that initiates a gross body. 54.
For others, the world arises from Brahman as its cause;
for the Unborn, Brahman is the cause, and therefore He possesses a single body.

He clarifies the meaning already stated with the words "of others" (*anyeṣām*). The world, characterized by subtle elements and gross elements, has arisen from the manifestation—that is, produced by the creative will (*saṃkalpa*)—of Hiranyagarbha, who is [the manifestation] of Brahman; by that [world], those two bodies are possessed, as is the ellipsis. But for the Unborn (*aja*), however...
Brahman alone, the Supreme Self, is the cause; it is not the elements.
Brahmā is the Puruṣa of volition, whose form is devoid of earth and other elements;
consisting solely of the nature of consciousness, he is the cause of the existence of the three worlds. (56)

But is it not the case that, according to the doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation as perception), the mind is not admitted to be a modification of the subtle elements, since it is itself a modification of the subtle elements? Furthermore, we have already previously demonstrated the process of the individual soul's creation (*jīvasṛṣṭi*) therein; for in the established system of Vasiṣṭha, "perception alone is creation."

Since there is no contradiction in the entire world, beginning with the subtle elements, being a modification of the mind; and since the scriptural passage, "When one is fast asleep and sees no dream, then he becomes one with this prāṇa alone,
and speech merges into it along with all names," and so forth, indicates that when the mind dissolves in deep sleep, there is as if a dissolution of the entire world.

If it is argued that the Śruti speaks thus with the intention that while the vision itself demonstrates dissolution (*laya*), it actually authorizes creation (*sṛṣṭi*), for surely in deep sleep the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) dissolves as if in a cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), yet it is not perceived due to the absence of the instruments of perception—this is not so. For if dissolution were not established there, it would follow that creation could not be established at the time of the world's awakening; and yet, [the Śruti] does indeed establish it.

The Śruti says: "When he awakens to the awakening of the entire creation, then, just as sparks fly out in all directions from a blazing fire, even so from this Self all the vital breaths (prāṇas) emerge according to their respective stations; from the vital breaths the gods, and from the gods the worlds. And there is another Śruti passage concerning the doctrine of creation through perception (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi).
It comes to be. From that which is non-existent, the mind (*manas*) was created; the mind created Prajāpati; Prajāpati created the creatures.

Indeed, this which exists here—whatever there is—is that supreme foundation. And what [is it]? It is that the imagined duality, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and so forth, having its body consisting of mere appearance, does not, at the time of its appearance, exist apart from the pure Being (*sanmātra*) which is the substrate of its own imagination.

Furthermore, based on the statement of the teacher Vijñānottama that "abiding in its own nature is impossible," and from the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* which says, "One should perceive the entire range of living beings, from space down to the earth, as stirred by the mind of the Self," it follows that [the world] is produced by that [mind]. Much more could be said here, but for fear of prolixity, it is not stated. Since Brahman has the mind alone as its body, [the world] is created by it.

Intending to show that [the world] is indeed non-existent, like a kingdom of the mind, because it is a transformation of the minds of worldly beings, he says: "Brahmā is a man of volition," and so forth. "A man of volition" means equal to a man of volition. He clarifies this very equality with a man of volition by saying: "Devoid of earth and so forth. This means his form is devoid of earth and other elements that constitute a gross body. 56
The entire universe is stretched out by Brahmā, the Self-born, by means of the mind alone;
therefore, this universe which is perceived is composed of mind. (57)
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, tell me clearly what the nature of the mind is, from which this entire cluster of defects is extended. (58)
With the intention that, if the mind were the cause of all things, it would possess existence (*sattva*) like Brahman, he asks:
"O Blessed One. Anticipating the objection that the question is redundant, he says: "Because... (verse 58).
Vasiṣṭha said:
No form whatsoever is seen of Rāma’s mind, except for its mere name, like that of the sky which is empty and insentient by nature. (59)

He provides the answer—that the mind, being a modification, has no existence apart from mere name due to the scriptural teaching that it is a "beginning with speech"—in the verse beginning with "O Rāma" (and the following half-verse). Even in the case of space (*vyoman*), nothing whatsoever of a real nature is perceived by common folk, nor even by those whose minds have been refined by the scriptural teachings such as "beginning with speech. || 59 ||
The mind does not exist as a real entity either externally or within the heart;
know, O Rāma, that it is situated everywhere, just like space.
Now, one might object: "If the mind is not the root of misfortune, then we who strive to uproot that very source will not have achieved our purpose.
Anticipating this doubt, he speaks from the perspective of one with deluded vision: "In every respect indeed," etc. (60).
O virtuous one, know that this manifestation of meaning—whether it pertains to what exists or what does not exist—is the mind itself and nothing else. (51)
With four and a half verses beginning with "O virtuous one," he dispels the doubt that it is untenable for [consciousness] to be present everywhere.
"Pratibhāna" means knowledge. To what kind of knowledge does he refer there? He says: "prathām.
This means having attained renown (*prathā*), that is, the common designation such as "the cognition of a jar" or "the cognition of a cloth. (61, 62, 63)
That which is the manifestation of objects is designated as "mind" (manas);
apart from this, there never exists anything whatsoever called "mind. (62)
Know that the mind is volition; it is not distinct from volition.
Wherever there is volition, there the mind exists—this should be understood. (63)
Volition (*saṃkalpa*) and mind (*manas*) are never distinct from one another; they are indeed the same.
Ignorance, worldly existence, the intellect (*citta*), the mind (*manas*), bondage, and the darkness of the mind (*manastamas*) are all one and the same.
And "ke ca na" is a dual form. || 64 ||
(116) O Rāghava, these are the names for the web of mental constructs (saṃkalpa).
When the web of mental constructs has dissolved, one's true nature remains. || 65 ||

Having thus explained that the mind is the root of bondage and its specific nature, he states that through knowledge there is the cessation of that [mind] along with its root, resulting in the absolute liberation (kaivalya) of the Self: "saṃkalpa... (verse 65).
When everything— consisting of the directions, the earth, and space— is incapable of being manifested,
the form of the light remains as it is, stainless.

When the web of conceptual constructions called the "world" has dissolved, that which remains as the nature of the Self is clarified by means of an impossible analogy—beginning with the words "asaṃbhavati" (it does not exist), etc. The term "asaṃbhavati" is used here in the locative absolute sense (satisaptamī). || 66 ||
When the three worlds, as well as "you" and "I," have attained non-existence within the field of the visible,
the seer of that pure-souled one becomes established in the state of absolute oneness (kaivalya).

The word-break is "asattvam" (non-existence). The meaning is that if the pervasive and motionless light of the sun were to remain when all objects of illumination—such as the directions, the earth, and so forth—have vanished, then its essential nature would serve as an illustration for the nature of the Self in the state of liberation (*kaivalya*). || 67 ||
For when all mountains and other objects have been reflected therein, the nature of the mirror remains as it is—consisting solely of its own essential form. (68)

He also makes known its essential nature by means of a simile involving real entities: "unperceived" (*anāpta*). This means that by it, the reflections of all objects such as mountains and so forth are not perceived. For in a mirror, due to a specific state of being held and the absence of contact with the eyes suitable for the delusion of a reflection, it remains one in which no reflections whatsoever are grasped.
Regarding what kind of mirror-nature exists in that mirror, he says: "It consists solely of the nature of the Self;
it consists solely of the nature of the mirror. (68)

When the agitation of the visible world—such as "I," "you," and "the universe"—has subsided, there arises that state of absolute oneness (kevalatā) wherein the Seer remains established without further perception. (69)

When there is no seeing of that which is to be seen, because of the very absence of such an object, the state of pure isolation would belong to the witness—the seer—who remains devoid of any perception of that object. (69)
The mind spreads this defect consisting of the visible world, which is of the nature of decay;
though unreal, it takes the form of the real, just as one dream follows another. (70)

To show that in the attainment of such non-isolation (akaivalya), the mind alone is the obstacle, and therefore one must apply the supreme effort toward its destruction, he describes its wicked nature in two verses beginning with "the mind" (manaḥ). || 70 ||
It throbs, leaps, moves, begs, wanders, sinks, and withdraws by itself;
it even assumes the state of another; yet the mind merely moves, solely through its flickering power. (71)

Or, "otherness" means the state of being inferior, consisting of non-self forms such as the body and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that it is only the mind that moves due to its flickering power, but not the Self. || 71 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the great dissolution has occurred and all that is visible has reached non-existence at the beginning of creation, only the tranquil [reality] remains.

Since it will be stated that the attainment of liberation previously mentioned occurs through the vision of the Supreme Self, [the author] first establishes the nature of the Supreme Self by relying upon the natural dissolution (*prakṛtika-pralaya*), starting from the verse beginning with "mahāpralaye" and ending before "bhidyate hṛdayagranthiḥ. At the beginning of creation...

At the time prior to creation; or alternatively, "sarga" means that by which something is created, i.e., the cause, at the beginning of the perceptible world. It is indeed Brahman alone—quiescent and changeless. || 72 ||
The unborn, undecaying, and stainless Lord, the supreme Self and Great Lord, who is all, the doer of all, and eternal, remains forever as the unsetting sun. (73)

[Objection: "Is it not logical that, just as the object of perception (dṛśya) is non-existent, the perceiver (draṣṭṛ) is also non-existent? For the Śruti says: 'In the beginning this was non-existent; neither the existent nor the non-existent existed then,' and so forth. To this, he replies: "He exists" (āste). By the negation of the two modifications of being—namely, birth and death—in the words "the unborn" (aja) and "not set" (anastamita), the four modifications of being occurring in the interval are also negated.

These [attributes] are to be understood. He states his non-insentience with the word "the Lord" (*deva*). To refute the notion that his luminosity is merely occasional, he says "the Radiant One" (*bhāsvān*). He wards off the idea of his being subject to suffering with the word "free from affliction" (*nirāmaya*). Alternatively, "eternal" (*śāśvata*) qualifies every single term. He states his fullness with the word "all" (*sarva*). The reason for this is given as "the maker of all" (*sarvakṛt*).
The meaning is that it evolves in every form; or rather, by the term "all-maker" (sarvakṛt), he states its status as the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇatva).
He states that the quality of being the controller of all belongs to Him alone as well, by saying "the Great Lord" (maheśvara). || 73 ||
(118) From which words turn back, which is realized by the liberated;
and for whom designations such as "self" and so forth are merely conceptual constructs, not born of intrinsic nature. (74)

Now, one might object: "If the Supreme Self is the creator of all and the Lord of all, then He must be possessed of conceptual distinctions (savikalpa) due to His dependence on effects and those subject to His governance. Anticipating this doubt, the author intends to show that His nature is in fact devoid of conceptual distinctions (nirvikalpaka), and that His status as the creator of all and so forth is merely due to ignorance (avidyā). With this in mind, he says: "From whence [words turn back]," etc.—thus [the fifteenth verse]. In passages such as "from whence words turn back," there are fifteen [verses].

The words beginning with "yat" (which) should be connected with the preceding [verse] by supplying the word "asti" (it exists), or they should be connected with the word "tasmin" (in that) which will be mentioned later in the phrase "dṛṣṭe parāvare. To the objection that if Brahman is beyond the scope of speech and other senses, it could not then be directly perceived, he says: "He who [is attained] by the liberated... This refers to Brahman, which is beyond the scope of speech.
Regarding the notions such as "How is there a self? and so forth, he says: "Of whom... [etc.]. They are not born of intrinsic nature; that is, they are not inherent. 74.
That person who [sees] the Sāṃkhya views, the Brahman of those who know the Vedānta, and the purely stainless consciousness-only of those who know consciousness; 75.

Now, one might object: "Even though that [Reality] is experienced by the liberated, we have no faith in it because it is beyond the reach of speech and other means of knowledge. Anticipating this doubt, the author says "He who... with the intention of showing that this is not so, since that Reality is accessible through all the scriptures, either in its qualified or its absolute form, as the case may be. Alternatively, [this is said] regarding the Supreme Truth already mentioned.

With the intention that—for those who observe the disagreements among disputants—it is impossible for there to be disagreement regarding a non-existent object, and therefore one must place trust in that [Self] which is established as the very objective support (*ālambana*) of such disagreement even prior to the disagreement itself, he says: "The person who... (*yaḥ pumān iti*).
He states the opinion of the Yogācāryas: "In consciousness... [etc. It is "absolutely pure" (*ekānta-nirmala*), meaning it is pure by way of absolute necessity. || 75 ||

He who is the emptiness of the proponents of emptiness, who is the illuminator of the sun’s splendors; he who is the speaker, the thinker, the enjoyer of truth, the seer, and the one who is always the rememberer. (76)

He states the Madhyamika view: "That which is void... To dispel the doubt that in reality the truth is merely voidness, he says: "...the illuminator. This is based on the Vedic scripture: "By whose splendor the sun shines. He precludes the difference of the Supreme Self from the individual soul—which might be inferred from its being the illuminator of the sun's light—by saying: "...the speaker."

"Ṛtabhoktā" means the enjoyer of the *ṛta*. By the word *ṛta*, the fruit of action (*karmaphala*) is expressed; for in the Vedic text, "The two who drink the *ṛta* in the world of good deeds," the word *ṛta* denotes the fruit of action. The absence of the euphonic junction (*visandhi*) in "mantā ṛtam" is a Vedic archaism (*ārṣa*). In some places it is read as "vaktā mantā svayaṃ bhoktā. (76)
Though present, that which moves as non-existent is far away even while residing within the body;
for this light of consciousness is like the radiance of the sun.

Anticipating the objection that there would be no room for disagreement among disputants regarding the reality that is most directly perceived—even by the light of astrology which establishes all worldly conventions—the author states the following with the intention of showing that such disagreement is possible because, being defiled by passion and other afflictions, their intellects are incapable of grasping subtle objects: [The verse follows: "Just as a person whose eyes are covered by a cloth does not perceive the sun, so too those whose minds are obscured by ignorance do not perceive the Self. (2.10) The meaning is this: just as a person whose eyes are covered by a cloth does not perceive the sun, even though the sun is shining before them; similarly, those whose minds are obscured by ignorance do not perceive the Self, even though the Self is shining before them. Therefore, due to the defect of ignorance, there is indeed room for disagreement among disputants. Thus, it is established that the Self is self-evident. (2.10) Furthermore, the Self is not merely self-evident, but is also the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). To demonstrate this, he says: "Even when the body is destroyed, the soul exists, for its existence is inferred from the activity of the senses; likewise, the soul exists even when the body is absent, for its existence is inferred from the activity of the mind. (2.11) The meaning is as follows: just as the existence of the soul is inferred from the activity of the senses while the body is present, so too its existence is inferred from the activity of the mind even when the body has perished. Therefore, the soul is eternal. (2.11) Moreover, the soul is not only eternal, but is also the agent of actions. To show this, he says: "The soul is the agent, because it is the enjoyer; and since it is the agent, it is also the experiencer. It is the enjoyer because it is conscious, and it is conscious because it is the witness. (2.12) The meaning is this: the soul is the agent of actions because it is the enjoyer of their fruits. And since it is the agent, it is also the experiencer. It is the enjoyer because it possesses consciousness, and it is conscious because it is the witness of all states. (2.12) Furthermore, the soul is not only the agent and enjoyer, but is also omnipresent. To demonstrate this, he says: "The soul is omnipresent, because it is eternal and devoid of parts; and because it is omnipresent, it is without action. It is without action because it is unchanging, and it is unchanging because it is pure. (2.13) The meaning is as follows: the soul is omnipresent because it is eternal and lacks constituent parts. And because it is omnipresent, it is without action. It is without action because it is unchanging, and it is unchanging because it is pure. (2.13) Finally, the soul is not only omnipresent and without action, but is also free from all attributes. To show this, he says: "The soul is free from attributes, because it is beyond the reach of the senses; and because it is beyond the senses, it is without qualities. It is without qualities because it is unmanifest, and it is unmanifest because it is the supreme reality. (2.14) The meaning is this: the soul is free from attributes because it transcends the range of the senses. And because it transcends the senses, it is without qualities. It is without qualities because it is unmanifest, and it is unmanifest because it is the supreme reality. (2.14) Thus, having established that the Self is self-evident, eternal, the agent, omnipresent, and devoid of attributes, he concludes: "Therefore, the wise should always meditate upon the Self, which is the witness of all, the inner controller, and the one who is beyond all darkness. (2.15) The meaning is as follows: therefore, the wise should constantly contemplate the Self, which is the witness of everything, the inner controller of all beings, and which is beyond the darkness of ignorance. (2.15) In this way, the nature of the Self has been fully explained. Now, the means for attaining that Self will be described. (2.16) The means for attaining the Self is the practice of yoga. To explain this, he says: "Yoga is the union of the individual soul with the Supreme Soul; it is attained through the restraint of the mind and the senses, and by the practice of concentration. (2.17) The meaning is as follows: yoga is the union of the individual soul with the Supreme Soul. It is achieved by restraining the mind and the senses, and by the practice of concentration. (2.17) Furthermore, the practice of yoga consists of eight limbs. To enumerate them, he says: "Yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi—these are the eight limbs of yoga. (2.18) The meaning is clear. (2.18) Among these, Yama consists of non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness. To explain this, he says: "Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness—these are called Yama, along with forbearance and the rest. (2.19) The meaning is as follows: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness—these five, together with forbearance and the others, constitute Yama. (2.19) Niyama consists of purity, contentment, austerity, study, and devotion to the Lord. To explain this, he says: "Purity, contentment, austerity, study, and devotion to the Lord—these are known as Niyama. (2.20) The meaning is clear. (2.20) Āsana is a steady and comfortable posture. To explain this, he says: "An Āsana is that which is steady and comfortable; it is mastered through relaxation and meditation on the infinite. (2.21) The meaning is as follows: an Āsana is defined as being both steady and comfortable. It is perfected by abandoning effort and by meditating on the infinite. (2.21) Prāṇāyāma is the regulation of breath. To explain this, he says: "Prāṇāyāma is the cessation of the flow of inhalation and exhalation; it is of three kinds: recaka, pūraka, and kumbhaka. (2.22) The meaning is as follows: Prāṇāyāma is the stopping of the movement of the incoming and outgoing breaths. It is of three types: exhaling (*recaka*), inhaling (*pūraka*), and retaining the breath (*kumbhaka*). (2.22) Pratyāhāra is the withdrawal of the senses. To explain this, he says: "Pratyāhāra is the withdrawal of the senses from their objects, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs; it is accomplished through the power of practice. (2.23) The meaning is as follows: Pratyāhāra is the withdrawal of the senses from their respective objects, just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs. This is achieved through the strength of repeated practice. (2.23) Dhāraṇā is the fixing of the mind. To explain this, he says: "Dhāraṇā is the fixing of the mind on a single object; it is accomplished by the practice of concentration. (2.24) The meaning is as follows: Dhāraṇā is the stabilization of the mind upon a single point. It is achieved by the practice of concentration. (2.24) Dhyāna is continuous contemplation. To explain this, he says: "Dhyāna is the uninterrupted flow of thought toward that same object; it is accomplished by the practice of meditation. (2.25) The meaning is as follows: Dhyāna is the continuous stream of cognition directed toward that very object. It is achieved by the practice of meditation. (2.25) Samādhi is the state of absorption. To explain this, he says: "When that [contemplation] itself shines forth as the object alone, devoid of the form of the knower and the knowing, it is called Samādhi. (2.26) The meaning is as follows: when that very contemplation appears as the object alone, free from the forms of the subject and the act of knowing, it is termed Samādhi. (2.26) When these eight limbs are practiced, the supreme reality is revealed. To explain this, he says: "From the practice of these eight limbs, the supreme reality is gradually revealed; it is the cessation of all mental modifications. (2.27) The meaning is as follows: through the cultivation of these eight limbs,
"Even though present" means: although the Supreme Self is indeed present in the world, it is said in the Śruti that "He is seen by those of subtle vision through a sharp and subtle intellect.

Thus, for those devoid of such distinguished intellect, He becomes as if non-existent because there is no fruit of His existence; and though residing within the body, He remains as if distant. For them, even in ten million billion years—

Because it cannot be reached by them. He states, in two successive verses, that this very Supreme Self is the regulator of the illumination of the insentient: "Consciousness... [Verse 77]. From which conscious Self the light of consciousness—which is experienced in such perceptions as "the jar shines" and "the cloth shines"—has issued forth.
By that wind, the creeper of primordial nature— which has grown in the sky, bears the great fruit of the cosmic egg,
and possesses the mind as its root and the senses as its leaves— dances.

*Prakṛti* itself is the *vratati*, the creeper; for Amara states: "The *vallī*, the *vratati*, and the *latā* [are synonyms for creeper]. That [creeper] is so described because it has the beautiful (*sat-śobhana*) fruit which is the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). || 78 ||
That jewel which shines within the casket of every body,
which floods the agitated *puryaṣṭaka* here and there; (79)

Now, one might object: "Is it not logical that there is a difference between the Supreme Self—who is the illuminator and controller of the world—and the individual soul (jīva), which is the opposite of Him?

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states—beginning with the words "He who is consciousness"—that it is that very same [Supreme Self] who exists in the form of the individual soul, as established by such scriptural passages as: "He entered here," "There is no other seer than He," and "He became the counterpart of every form. Yaścit... (He who is consciousness... [is the Supreme Self].

"Shines forth" means it throbs. "Casket" (*samudgaka*) means a small box. Having stated its nature as a regulator with reference to the divine plane (*adhidaiva*) by the phrase "the natural creeper," he speaks with reference to the internal plane (*ādhyātmika*): "He who floods. He is the one who floods—that is, causes to move—the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body) which is agitated and tossed here and there; the meaning is that he sets it in motion.

The nature of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the city of eight) has been described by the great ones: "Indeed, the five organs of cognition, likewise the other five organs of action, the four beginning with the mind (*manas*), the five beginning with *prāṇa*, the elements beginning with ether (*viyat*), desire, action, and darkness—this is the city of eight. (Verse 79)
He who is pure because he consists of consciousness becomes the void through the contemplation of space;
yet, when presiding over it, he attains the state of being an object through the contemplation of objects, as if becoming a thing itself.

Now, one might object: "If it is the Supreme Self alone that enters the body and undergoes transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), how can there be liberation (kaivalya) for It? Anticipating this doubt, he says "Pure" (śuddha) and so forth, explaining that although the Self is in reality non-transmigratory, its liberation is indeed possible because the transmigratory state—which is brought about by erroneous identification—is capable of being removed through the cultivation of the true nature of reality (tattva-bhāvanā).

Because its nature is consciousness devoid of ignorance and its effects, through the contemplation of the void—that is, the contemplation of being like space—it becomes the void; it becomes like space. Alternatively, that Supreme Self which has assumed the state of the individual soul (jīva) becomes the void—becomes Brahman—through the contemplation of the void, meaning through the contemplation of Brahman. Through the contemplation of objects—that is, through the contemplation of non-self objects—one [becomes] adhi...

He stands established above saṃsāra; or rather, being occupied with or made the object of reflection upon categories (padārtha), he seems to attain the state of being an object, such as the category of space and so forth. || 80 ||
In that which is without limit, the waves of the three worlds— consisting of manifestation and disappearance—
quiver like mirages in a desert.

He elaborates on the statement that [the world] appears as if it were an object through the contemplation of categories with the following two verses beginning with "āvirbhāva" (manifestation). In that ocean of consciousness (*cid-arṇava*), which is exceedingly vast and all-pervading, the waves of the three worlds—characterized primarily by manifestation and disappearance—quiver; that is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). It exists.
The connection is with what precedes; we have already stated that when He is seen, there is no further connection with what follows, as expressed in the phrase "the higher and the lower. || 81 ||
Even while performing here an infinite multitude of great deeds for the worlds, he never does anything at all;
for, with his mind having abandoned the notions of arising and remaining, he stands alone, established in his own self which is non-conceptual and undying consciousness. (82)

Although he creates the multitude—the entire collection—of worlds through *māyā*, in reality he does not create them. He is one whose mind has abandoned arising and persistence; that is, he is one by whom the mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*) of arising and persistence have been abandoned. Alternatively, "tyaktodaya" may be treated as a separate word:
he is one by whom arising—that is, birth—has been abandoned; and "sthitimān" means one who possesses persistence, [meaning] he is immovable within that state.
Abiding in one's own self, which is consciousness free from setting and whose nature is indestructible awareness—this means abiding without any external support. || 82 ||
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are severed, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. (83)
Having thus established the true nature of the Self, he states the fruit of that realization: "It is split asunder," and so forth.

The "knot of the heart" is the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). "In the high and the low" means in the Supreme Self who is both the superior (para), meaning excellent, and the inferior (avara), meaning base; that is, in the Self of all. || 83 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, how is it that this entire visible world—the cosmic egg and the stability of the universe—is not non-existent? And where is Mount Meru within the interior of a mustard seed? (84)
He raises an objection, stating that non-dual knowledge is difficult to attain because it is impossible for everything other than the supreme Self to be merely imagined:
"iyata" (84).
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, if you are devoted to the company of the virtuous and to the true scriptures,
then within days, or at least within months, you shall attain this supreme wisdom.

He offers a rebuttal—saying "Well said"—that non-dual knowledge is very easily attained through the continuous practice of the non-dual scripture preceded by association with those who know Brahman. || 85 ||
This essence of all histories has been declared;
for when this stainless [teaching] is heard, the imperishable state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is attained.
"What is that scripture by which another may attain the supreme intellect? To this, he says: "Of all... [etc.].

He states the reason for its being the essence among the histories (itihāsas) such as those of Bharata and others: "It has been heard" (śrutaḥ). Liberation while living (jīvanmuktatva) is an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) of liberation after death (videhamuktatva). 86.
This very world arises by itself within; reflect upon this! Through inquiry, the visible world that exists comes to its setting. (87)

To the objection that "for the sake of non-dual knowledge (*advaitajñāna*), only the dissolution of duality (*dvaitavilaya*) should be performed through its appropriate means; what is the use of inquiry (*vicāra*)?", he says:

"sthitam" (it is established). The word "eva" (only) is also connected with the word "vicāraṇāt" (from inquiry). The world, which is the object of perception, culminates only in the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) through inquiry alone.

It comes to an end like a ghost conjured by a shadow, but not by means of a blow from a mallet or the like; even in that case, it comes to an end exactly as it was situated, not through the disintegration of its parts or similar means. || 87 ||
For those men who are solely devoted to knowledge and who investigate self-knowledge,
that state of liberation while living arises, which is indeed liberation even while the body remains.
He explains what was stated in the verse beginning with "In this [teaching], it is stainless" (śrute'smin nirmale) by means of the words "Of men" (nṛṇām). || 88 ||
Śrī Rāma said:

O Brahman, tell me the characteristics of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and of one liberated after the body has fallen away (videhamukta), so that I may strive accordingly with a vision guided by the scriptures. (89)
"O Brahmin"—the meaning is clear. || 89 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
He for whom this world remains as it is, even while engaged in worldly affairs, and who has set within the abiding sky—that one is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 90 ||

He states the characteristic of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), which is accessible solely through his own experience, beginning with the word "yathā" (as): Even though he engages in worldly activity through mere appearance or from the perspective of others, for him this world as it exists has, by the vision of reality, come to rest;
it becomes like the void, established in Brahman. Such a person is called liberated while yet alive. || 90 ||
He whose facial radiance neither rises nor sets in joy or sorrow, remaining as he is according to what has come to him—he is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 91 ||

He states its definition, which is also knowable by others: "It does not arise," and so forth. One who remains established in worldly conduct as it has naturally occurred is described in that way. || 91 ||
He who remains awake while established in deep sleep, for whom no waking state exists,
and whose consciousness is free from latent impressions— he is called one liberated while living.
Furthermore, he explains the characteristic that is accessible through one's own experience by means of the three verses beginning with "He who is awake," and so forth.

Because he does not experience duality as a reality distinct from himself, the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) remains as if in deep sleep; yet, just as one in deep sleep remains unmodified even when objects are present, so too this one remains awake because of the perception of the appearance of duality—or rather, because of the direct experience of Brahman itself. Thus it has been said by the Lord of All:

"In that state, the self-controlled one remains awake. His waking does not occur like that of the ignorant; the meaning is that he is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*) or has attenuated latent impressions (*tanuvāsana*), because liberation while living (*jīvanmukta*) is possible only when all latent impressions have dissolved. || 92 ||
Even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and the like, he who is as utterly transparent as the inner sky is called liberated while living. 93.

Even while acting or moving in whatever manner is appropriate and consistent with the mere appearances of attachment, aversion, fear, and so forth— which have arisen through the force of *prārabdha* karma—
the wise person remains, by virtue of this, the very nature of the Self, as utterly transparent and exceedingly pure as the sky. Just like the sky.
The meaning is that one understands that the self is likewise stainless, being free from the impurities of passion and the like. || 93 ||
He whose state of being is not characterized by egoism, and whose intellect is not defiled—
whether he is acting or not acting— he is called one liberated while living. (94)

That wise person for whom there exists no such state of being, no mental conception, and no cognition as "I am the doer"—one who perceives that "the senses operate upon the objects of the senses, but I am not; I, however, am the witness of their activity and am the non-doer"—and whose intellect (buddhi), which is the internal organ, is not smeared and does not become possessed by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)—[he is liberated].
