"I am this... [is the thought of one who is still bound].
He whose mind is not defiled by such thoughts as, "I have committed this forbidden act, I have not performed that which was prescribed; therefore, I shall fall into hell," is not tainted.
He from whom the world does not shrink, and who does not shrink from the world, being liberated from joy, envy, and fear—he is called one liberated while living. (95)
The passages beginning with "yasmāt" and ending with "nirāmayam" have clear meanings; however, certain points are explained in detail here and there. || 95 ||
He whose waves of worldly existence have been stilled, who, though possessing parts, is partless;
who, though possessed of thought, is free from anxiety—he is called one liberated while living. (96)

Though possessing arts, he is free from ignorance; though appearing to have parts, he is in reality partless. Though seemingly possessed of thought—existing together with the appearance of thought—he is in reality free from thought. || 96 ||
He who, though engaged in all kinds of worldly affairs, remains cool as if toward the interests of others, being full in his self—such a person is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 97 ||
Regarding the interests of others—that is, things belonging to another—he is as cool as a mere bystander; the meaning is that he is free from burning heat and free from distress.

This is also an elliptical expression for being free from elation; for in one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and devoid of ego-inflation, neither joy nor dejection can arise with respect to the entire range of objects, whether in their totality or in their deficiency. || 97 || 98 ||
Having abandoned the state of liberation while living when his own body has been surrendered to time, he enters the state of disembodied liberation, just as the wind enters a state of motionlessness.
The one liberated while in the disembodied state (videhamukta) neither rises nor sets, nor does he cease;
he is neither existent nor non-existent, neither far away, nor am I, nor anything else. (99)
The meaning is that the effect is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it the cause. || 99 || 100 ||
Then, neither light nor pervasive darkness remains; there persists a certain reality that is unnameable, unmanifest, tranquil, and profound.
It is neither empty nor devoid of form; it is neither the object of vision nor the act of seeing.
Nor is it a multitude of real entities, for it abides as the eternal infinite.
The meaning is that it is neither empty nor formless. || 1 ||
It is something whose nature is indefinable, possessing a form more full than the full;
it is neither being, nor non-being, nor both being and non-being, nor is it non-existence or even the act of bringing into existence.

The connection [of the words] is: "Something exists as infinite. It is not "existent" (*sat*), because it does not become an existent thing like a jar or the like, since the universal of existence (*sattājāti*) is not admitted there; nor is it "non-existent" (*asat*), because it is not illuminated by the cognition of existence, owing to its being the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārthasvarūpa*); nor is it both "existent and non-existent," because of contradiction. "Non-existence" (*abhāva*) means non-becoming, that is to say, inconceivability (*acintya*). It is not... [the sentence continues].
Meditation is reflection. || 2 ||
Pure consciousness alone, devoid of any object of thought, infinite, undecaying, and auspicious;
that which is without beginning, middle, or end, free from mental affliction, and untainted by disease. (3)
The object of thought is the visible world. That in which there is no beginning, middle, or end is "without beginning, middle, or end.

It is "without mental affliction" (anādhi), meaning free from mental distress; it is "free from disease" (nirāmaya), meaning free from physical suffering. That pure consciousness (cinmātra) which is of such a nature is called "liberation while disembodied" (videhamukta). The word "is said" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 3 ||
O virtuous one, that which exists as the act of seeing among the seer, the seeing, and the seen— you shall understand this very thing through focused attention.
Having thus described the state known as liberation while in the body (videhamukti), which is the nature of ultimate reality, he states the means for its direct realization:

"The Seer" (draṣṭṛ). Among the seer, the seeing, and the seen—the knower, the knowledge, and the knowable—that which is the seeing, which stands as the witness of them all, manifests as the Seer; the seeing manifests; the seen [manifests].

The meaning is that it exists as the non-conceptual, immediate consciousness (*pratyak-caitanya*), which is distinct from them and pervades them in the form of their manifestation (*sphuraṇa-rūpeṇa*)—that is, as the very fact that they "manifest.

"By attention to that" (*tad-avadhānena*) means by one-pointedness of mind toward that; or alternatively, "by attention to that" means by the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the purified meaning of the term *tvam-pada*, through the ascertainment of that [identity]. You understand this very thing.
The meaning is that you now understand the nature of the ultimate reality (paramārtha-svarūpa) which was previously stated and has just been explained. || 4 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
What is the nature of that ultimate reality, which has the form of bliss and consciousness?
Tell me this again in detail for the increase of my understanding. (5)

Rāma asks— "Of the ultimate reality" (paramārthasya)— in order to understand, as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, that very nature of the ultimate reality which was previously established by the passage beginning with "attained during the great dissolution" (mahāpralaya-saṃpannau), and which was immediately thereafter described as the state of disembodied liberation (videhamukti). || 5 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Upon the occurrence of the great dissolution, that supreme Brahman, the cause of all causes, remains; that very thing is now described—listen.
In order to demonstrate the nature of the ultimate reality by means of reasoning that grasps it directly, he says: "At the time of the great dissolution," and so forth.
"That which is described as this": that Supreme Brahman is described as "this"; the meaning is that it is being described perceptibly. || 6 ||
Having destroyed its own self through the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind,
that which is of the nature of existence and inexpressible is the true form of that reality.

In that context, by means of the four verses beginning with "having destroyed," he describes the nature of the ultimate reality (paramārtha-svarūpa) based on the state of meditative absorption (samādhy-avasthā). Since in the state of meditative absorption the fluctuations (vṛtti) of the mind are destroyed while the mind itself is not destroyed, he says: "the complete destruction of the mind's fluctuations. [This refers to] the fluctuations of the mind...
When the forms of sound and the other [objects] are completely destroyed, one destroys one's own self as it exists in the form of the three bodies;

the state of the self being the three bodies, which was brought about by mere conceit, perishes in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon the destruction of that conceit. Therefore, this is stated: "having destroyed one's own self."

Here, the construction [of the sentence] requires the supplying of the predicate (*sādhyāhāra*). Having destroyed its own self and remaining in itself, that which is of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*), which is inexpressible because it is devoid of genus, quality, action, and so forth, and which exists as the witness-form (*sākṣi-rūpa*) upon the cessation of mental modifications—that is called the form, the essential nature (*svarūpa*), of that reality which is Brahman. || 7 ||

That form of the individual soul (jīva), which is by nature consciousness, when turned away from the objects of thought— that pure, stainless, and tranquil state of pure consciousness (cinmātra)— is the very nature of the Supreme Self (paramātman). (8)

That whose nature (*svabhāva*) or essential form (*svarūpa*) is the living soul (*jīva*) is "jīvasvabhāvā. Of that consciousness (*cit*), there is a body or essential form which is turned away from the object of cognition (*acetyonmukha*), that is, turned away from objects (*aviṣayonmukha*). To the question "What is it like?", he says:
"pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), stainless (*vimala*), and tranquil (*śānta*). It is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) and has the singular form of consciousness (*cidekarūpa*).
That form of the Supreme Self, which is free from the two types of adventitious impurities that have no beginning and is changeless, is called its *svarūpa* (essential nature).

|| 8 || Even when wind and other elements touch the limbs, that state of the mind of a living being which exists without the experience of touch and so forth—that is the supreme form of the Self. || 9 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the case of a limb being touched" (*aṅgalagne*): even when there is contact with a part [of the body] such as wind or heat, the nature of the *jīva*—which is consciousness conditioned by the mind (*cetopādhika*)—exists as a state devoid of the experience of touch and so forth, even while that experience of touch, form, and other qualities occurs; this is the true nature (*svarūpa*) of the *jīva* even when it has abandoned the body, which remains devoid of the experience of touch and so forth even when a limb is touched.
To that end, he says: "of the living one. That is the supreme nature of the self, which transcends transmigratory existence. || 9 ||
O Mahāmati, that which is the nature of the long sleep—sleepless, infinite, and non-inert—is the very nature of the Supreme Self. 110.

Regarding the phrase "of that which is without sleep": even waking is included under the term "sleep" because it is a long dream. "Of that which is without sleep" means devoid of both dreaming and waking. "Of that which is non-inert" means devoid of deep sleep (suṣupti).
"Of that which is infinite"—because its object is an infinite reality—and "of that long sleep," meaning the yogic sleep lasting for a vast duration; such is its form.

The passage beginning with "tadrūpam" (of that form) is the same [as before]. This is what is meant: in the yogic sleep characterized by abiding in the fourth state (*turīya*), the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) which is devoid of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) is perceived; that is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). || 110 ||
The experience of sensation, light, the visible, and likewise darkness—that which is beginningless and endless experience is the form of the Supreme Self. || 11 ||
Even while relying upon the state of mental distraction, he describes the nature of the Supreme Self with the three verses beginning with "vedanasya" (of sensation).

The "perception" (*vedana*) refers to that which is characterized as the witness (*sākṣin*), namely the perception of light—which is characterized by the activity of the internal organ, belongs to the sun and other sources, is visible, and consists of sound and other objects of cognition; this is an elliptical expression for the perception of darkness, which is ignorance (*ajñāna*). The rest is as explained previously. || 11 ||

Even for one intent on worldly activity, that state of remaining like a stone is the very nature of the Supreme Self— like the sky possessing the quality of space despite not being the sky itself. (12)

"Of one intent upon worldly activity": even for the individual soul (*jīva*) who is intent upon worldly activity, its state of sitting is, in terms of the actual nature of reality (*vastuvṛttyā*), like that of a stone;

it remains as motionless as a massive rock. Just as the sky-like nature belongs only to that which is not [actually] the sky, so too the appearance of the manifold world (*saprapañca*) is false, while in reality there is only the absence of the manifold (*niḥprapañcatva*). Or else, [it refers to] the sky itself.
From a worldly perspective, it is only that which is not like space that possesses the nature of space; in reality, however, its being like space and so forth is the same [as the previous case]. 12.
That form of the Supreme Self, wherein these three aspects—the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower—arise and set before us, is His very nature. (13)

The triad consisting of the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower—the triad whose forms are knowability, the process of cognition, and the state of being a knower—is directly perceived before us; that form in which this triad arises, originates, and sets, perishes, is the [true] nature. || 13 ||
If the very form of immobile beings were to consist of consciousness, being free from mind, intellect, and the like, it would be comparable to the Supreme. || 14 ||
He explains the nature of the Supreme Self through an unconventional simile: "Of the stationary beings," and so forth.

If the nature of stationary beings, such as plants and the like—which is well known to be naturally devoid of mind, intellect, and so forth—should at any time become composed of consciousness (bodhamaya), that is, possess the very form of consciousness, then that nature may be compared with the Supreme Self (parameśvara). In other words, it is said that it becomes comparable to the Supreme Self. || 14 ||
Brahmā, Arka, Viṣṇu, Hara, Śakra, Sadāśiva, and the rest—during the state of peace, this one supreme Śiva alone remains here;
through the dissolution of all limiting adjuncts, it is of an undifferentiated form, consisting solely of pure consciousness, and free from all worldly attachment.

He summarizes: "Brahman. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara have the qualities (guṇas) such as rajas and so forth as their limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Sadāśiva is the witness of the equilibrium of the qualities. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), Maheśvara and others who have the equilibrium of the qualities as their limiting adjunct are included. "Auspicious" (śivam) means the nature of bliss (ānanda-rūpa). It is of a non-conceptual form, meaning its essential nature is free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa). The reason for this is:
"By virtue of the departure of all limiting adjuncts" means: by virtue of the destruction of all limiting adjuncts, it consists of pure consciousness alone;
its very nature is pure consciousness alone; it has abandoned attachment to the universe, having relinquished all attachments. || 115 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning of the Section on Origination," in the *Mokṣopāya* of the venerable Vālmīki.
Thus ends the first chapter of the commentary composed by the venerable Ātmaprakāśa, disciple of the venerable Uttamasvāmin, the worshipful feet of the supreme Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya.
Chapter One. || 1 ||
(p. 129) Second Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
In this regard, listen to this narrative of the pavilion, which is an ornament for the ears, so that this matter may rest without doubt in your mind. (1)

In the previous narrative titled "The Birth from Space," it was stated that Māyā alone, having become the mind, creates the world out of the Supreme Self whose nature is pure consciousness (cinmātra). Now, in order to strengthen the firm conviction that the world is illusory, he introduces the narrative of the "Divine Play" (līlā) to elaborate upon how Māyā is the cause of many seemingly impossible feats.

Regarding this point: thus it has been stated by the great masters—“In the previous account of the origin of space, it was described that the Māyā of the Supreme Self, which is pure consciousness (cinmātra), becomes the mind and creates [the world]. Through the narrative of His divine play (līlā), the capacity of Māyā to bring about many difficult-to-accomplish feats is elaborated, so that the illusory nature (māyikatva) of this universe may become clear. Such is the text.
The section preceding "the space of the mind" (cittākāśa) is clear in meaning; however, certain points are distinguished here and there. || 1 ||
On this surface of the earth, there once lived a king named Padma, a glorious lord who possessed many sons and was endowed with discernment; he was like a blooming lotus of a noble lineage.

A lotus of the noble family, an ornament of the family. Alternatively, the word *padma* may be masculine; for Amara states: "Or [the word] *padma* is in the masculine. It is one who possesses blossoming, that is, one who possesses fame; or else, one whose face has blossomed, meaning one whose face is perpetually joyful.
He is an ocean for the preservation of moral boundaries, a sun to the darkness of his enemies,
a lake for the swans of virtuous qualities, and a fire for the grass of vices.

An ocean for the preservation of boundaries; that is, he is like the great sea in his observance of limits. Just as the ocean does not transgress its boundary (velā), so too he does not overstep the boundaries of the social classes and stages of life (varṇāśrama-maryādā)—this is the meaning.
He is a sun to the darkness of his enemies; that is, a sun to the gloom of his foes. And those excellent qualities (sadguṇāḥ) are beautiful virtues...
The lake for those [swans] is their pond. "The fire for the grass of faults" means that the faults themselves are the *tṛṇyā*—a collection of grass—and he is the fire (*hutāśana*) for that.
The suffix *ya* is applied to the word *tṛṇa* in the sense of a collection according to the rule *pāśādibhyo yaḥ*. (3)
He had a fortunate wife named Līlā,
a playful woman endowed with every charm, who was like a lotus risen upon the earth.

She whose fortune (*bhaga*) is auspicious is "Subhagā. *Kamalā* means Lakṣmī; *uditā* means arisen or born. *Avani* means the earth. The connection is: "Like Kamalā, she has arisen upon the earth (*avanau*). || 4 ||

When [the master] is anxious, she is deeply anxious; when he is joyful, she is joyful; when he is agitated, she is agitated; when he is overcome by a reflected image, she is likewise overcome; and when he is enraged, she is simply terrified. (5)
When her husband is agitated and distressed, she becomes agitated and intensely distressed. || 5 || 6 ||
Once, she who was endowed with auspicious intentions reflected:
"This lord of the world, my husband, is dearer to me than even my own life. (6)
"How might I, possessing the splendor of youthful exuberance, become free from old age and death? And how might I enjoy myself with this husband for hundreds of eons? (7)
Possessing the exuberance of youth, possessing the fullness of youth. || 7 ||
I shall ask those twice-born ones who are advanced in knowledge, advanced in asceticism, and advanced in learning: "How might death not occur for men? (8)
Knowledge has Brahman as its object; wisdom has the deities, dharma, and so forth as its object.
Having thus brought them and honored the twice-born, she bowed and asked them again and again: "O Brahmins, how may immortality be attained? (p. 131) || 9 ||

In the phrase "ity ānīya," the word *iti* is syntactically connected with what precedes it, namely *cintayāmāsa* ("he thought"). O Brahmins, the connection is that he asked again and again, "How might immortality come to mortals? || 9 ||
The brahmins said:
O Goddess, all the perfections of the Siddhas are attained through austerities, recitations, and restraints; however, immortality is not obtained by any means whatsoever.

The restraints (yamas) are non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness; the perfections of the Siddhas, such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, are the perfections of the Siddhas. || 10 || 11 ||
Having heard this from the mouth of the twice-born, she, terrified of separation from her beloved, reflected once more, relying quickly upon her own wisdom.
If, by fate, my death should occur before that of my husband, then,
liberated from all suffering, I shall abide happily in my own self.
Therefore, I shall establish that [mind] within the Self, whose nature is non-dual bliss, so that it remains there properly, incapable of ever emerging again. (12)
Now, even if my husband should die at the beginning of a thousand years,
I shall do whatever is necessary so that his life-force shall not depart from this house.
The word "atha" (now/then) indicates an alternative position. || 13 ||
While this husband of mine lives, I shall dwell at my ease in my own inner apartment, constantly gazed upon by my lord.
At that time, while the life-force of her husband was wandering—that is, while the life-force of her husband was roaming—in the inner apartment pavilion, the pavilion of the harem.
Starting this very day, for the sake of this purpose, I shall worship the goddess Jñapti Sarasvatī with recitations, fasts, and observances until she is fully gratified.
From satisfaction up to the limit of contentment. || 15 ||
Having thus resolved, that beautiful woman, without even informing her husband,
undertook severe asceticism according to the scriptures, remaining steadfast in her observances. (16)
"Established" means "resorted to. || 16 ||
At the conclusion of every three-night period, she broke her fast, remaining devoted to the worship of gods, twice-born brahmins, gurus, the wise, and the learned. (17)
The wise one (*prājña*) is one who has direct knowledge of the Dharma and so forth; the learned one (*vidvān*) is a knower of Brahman.
In some places, he is described as being devoted to the worship of gods, the twice-born, gurus, the wise, and the elderly. || 17 ||
Her body is constantly engaged in bathing, giving, austerity, and meditation;
she practices all forms of faith and right conduct, and she removes all suffering.

She whose body was constantly engaged in bathing, giving, austerity, and meditation is described as such. She who practiced right conduct with total faith is "one who practices right conduct with total faith. (18)
In this manner, for a hundred three-night periods, that young woman, steadfast in her observances,
remained incessantly devoted to asceticism through arduous exertion.

The ellipsis to be supplied is that he remained, having taken up a state of constant and uninterrupted devotion to austerity; or else, the verb "atiṣṭhat" contains an implied causative sense, meaning "he caused [them] to remain. || 19 ||
Then, having been worshipped and honored with a hundred three-night rites,
the blessed goddess Gaurī, the mistress of speech, being pleased, spoke to her.
"Pratimānitā" means "honored. It is stated that she was "honored" and "venerated" in order to indicate an excess of respect. In some places, it is read as "pratimāgatā. || 20 ||
"O child, I am well-pleased with your uninterrupted austerity and your extraordinary devotion to your husband; accept the boon you desire."
"Exceeding devotion to her husband" means by that which surpasses devotion to her husband. || 21 ||
The queen said:
Victory to you, O moonlight to the defect of the burning heat of the flames of birth and old age!
Victory to you, O sunlight for dispelling the mass of darkness within the heart! 22.

Birth and old age are indeed the flames; the burning by them is the very defect. O you who possess the luster of the moon that quells that [burning], "hārda" refers to that which is connected to the heart. || 22 || 23 ||
"O Mother, O Mother of the World, protect this wretched woman!
Grant these two boons which are being requested by me here. (23)
First of all, let not the life-force of my lord, the King of Videha, depart from this very pavilion of his own inner apartments to my presence. 24.
Of the deceased Videha. || 24 ||
But as for the second boon, O Great Goddess, whenever I pray for a vision for the sake of a favor, then grant me a vision. (25)

The syntactical connection is as follows: "When I pray for the sight of you for the sake of a boon—that is, for the purpose and cause of obtaining a boon—then grant me a second boon, which is that very sight. || 25 || 26 || 27 ||
Having heard this, the Mother of the World herself said, "So be it," and vanished, rising up like a wave in the ocean.
Then that queen, her chosen deity being well-pleased,
became a bearer of bliss, as if filled by a rain of nectar.
Then, as the Wheel of Time— consisting of moments, navel-like centers, and pulsations, flowing through fortnights, months, seasons, days, years, and staffs of time— was turning,
the consciousness of her husband vanished from his body.

"Having fortnights, months, and seasons as its rim," and so forth, are adjectives of the fivefold wheel of time (*pañcakālacakra*). That which has fortnights, months, and seasons as its rim—that is, its navel-girth—is described thus. According to Amara: "The word *kaṭaka*—not feminine—denotes both the slope of a mountain and a rim or wheel. That which has days as its spokes is described thus; the spokes are iron components arranged all around, starting from the hub and extending to the felly.

It is said: in the *varṣadaṇḍaka* (the staff of years), which is the axle of the year, the *nābhi* (navel) is the *piṇḍikā* (pedestal). In the "consisting of vibration" (*spandamaya*), that is, in the nature of vibration (*spandasvarūpa*), the state of being identical with that is expressed because the sun is metaphorically [designated] as such by virtue of its manifesting time. The word "vahati" (it carries) is used in the locative absolute construction (*satisaptamī*). || 28 ||
When that protector of the earth had died, she, afflicted by the torment of grief, fell into extreme desolation like a waterless lotus pond. (29)
Sorrow (*śoka*) is the suffering born from separation from what is desired; distress (*tāpa*) is mere suffering. *Nalinī* means a lotus pond. || 29 || 30 ||
(134) The proud woman, on the verge of death, quickly cried out like a female ruddy goose separated from her mate, and then suddenly became silent as if mute. 30.

Then Sarasvatī, who dwells in the compassionate void, felt compassion for her who was excessively overwhelmed—just as the first rain feels pity for a small fish distressed by the drying up of its lake. (31)
"Excessively overwhelmed" means being utterly under the control of another. *Śapharī* is a specific species of fish;
Amara states, "The word *proṣṭhī* refers to both [the female and male] *śapharī*. Some say it is a small fish. (31–32)
Sarasvatī said:
"Daughter, have I been remembered by you? Why do you bear such excessive grief?
Thus, approaching her presence, Sarasvatī, known as Jñapti, spoke to her.
"O child, having covered this husband of yours who has become a corpse in the Puṣpakhaṇḍaka grove, place him there; you shall obtain a husband once again. (33)
In *puṣpakhaṇḍaka*, meaning in a cluster of flowers. || 33 || 34 || 35 ||
These flowers will merely wither, but he shall certainly not perish;
moreover, he will before long restore you to the status of being his wife.
And this life-force of yours, as clear as the sky, shall not quickly depart from this pavilion within the inner apartments. (35)
Having heard that divine voice and having thus steadied her husband, she called out in her distress; he approached her and spoke.
In the expression "āhvāyayāmāsa," the sense of the causative suffix (ṇic) is not intended here; rather, it means "he called out" (ājuhāva). || 36 || 37 ||
Līlā said:
"Where is my husband staying, what is he doing, and what is he like? Lead me to his side; I cannot live alone. (37)
Jñapti said:

There is the space of the mind (*cittākāśa*), the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), and the third is [ordinary] space (*ākāśa*). Know, O fair-faced one, that the space of consciousness is more void than the other two. (38)

When Brahman is known, there arises— within that very [Brahman] which consists of the cessation of all activity— the capacity to perceive objects that are beyond the reach of ordinary people through yoga; therefore, [it is seen] within the space of the pleasure-pavilion of Līlā’s inner apartments.

In order to establish the capacity for beholding her present husband, the divine Sarasvatī explains the nature of Brahman through the two verses beginning with "The space of the mind" (*cittākāśam*). Now, one might object:
is it not possible for Līlā to attain her goal even without the exposition of Brahman, as was the case with the wife of Vidūratha who will be described later?
If it is asked, "Why does Sarasvatī not grant the capacity to perceive other creations, and why does she proceed with the exposition of Brahman at the very beginning?"— it is said in reply:
because she has not been propitiated by a desire for the fruits of worldly existence, like one who engages in various pastimes, those who are liberated from *saṃsāra* [do not seek such things].

Because it was propitiated with the intention, "May I become [thus]," it proceeds accordingly. The mind itself, due to its clarity, subtlety, and so forth, is like space; thus, the supreme self of consciousness is space, the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).
Furthermore, there exists a third kind of space known as the great element (*mahābhūta*), which is present in the world through its clarity, subtlety, and other qualities.
Among those three well-known [states], know that which is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) to be more empty than the other two, being the absolute void.

Alternatively, it is stated that "space is the third," and by the phrase "more empty than the two," the absence of phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañcatva*) of Brahman is expressed, because there is no phenomenal world apart from the mind and the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*). || 38 ||
O lady of excellent complexion, know that which lies between consciousnesses as they move from one place to another in a single blink of an eye—that is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). 39.

"From space," etc. When consciousness moves from one place to another place, or when it moves from one object to another object, that which is perceived in the interval—the extremely brief duration of a moment (*nimeṣa*)—know that very thing to be the *cidākāśa* (the space of consciousness).
This is what is meant: when the preceding state of the mind has perished and the succeeding state is about to arise, in the interval between them...

Know that to be the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) which is objectless, which serves as the witness to the transition between mental states, and which shines by itself; it is called "the middle" because it is perceived in the interval between two mental modifications (*vṛtti*). And so, on the occasion of describing the seven stages, he will say: "When the mind moves from one object to another, that which exists in the middle..."
Stability: the state of abiding in one's own nature, in which the form of mental activity has been discarded, is called *svarūpasthiti*. And it has been said by the great ones:
"He by whom the junctions and the absences of all mental fluctuations are illuminated through his changeless nature is celebrated as the *kūṭastha* (the immovable). || 39 ||
If you attain a state in which all conceptual constructions have been entirely cast out, then you will undoubtedly reach that peaceful state which is the self of all. (40)

Having thus established the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) as being of the nature of Brahman, he describes the yoga pertaining to it and its fruit, beginning with the words "In that" (*tasmin*). That by which all conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*)—characterized by the cognition of the non-Self—is entirely cast out, without remainder, is so described. "You go" (*eṣi*) means you proceed; this is the second person singular present indicative of the root *iṇ* (to go). You attain.

The meaning is that you shall be liberated by means of attaining realization. And so it has been said: "Having made the mind free from mental modifications (vṛtti) and having unified the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) with the Supreme Self, one is liberated; this is called the primary yoga. And: "When, established in samādhi, one does not perceive any beings, then, become one with the Supreme, he becomes absolute (kevala). || 40 ||
"However, this [state] regarding the world is attained through the realization of absolute non-existence, and not otherwise; by my boon, O beautiful one, you shall attain it. (41)
He states the means for attaining the state that consists of all things: "by the attainment of absolute non-existence."
"By the attainment of the absolute non-existence of the world"—that is to say, by the certainty of its absolute unreality. This word [pada] consists of all this.
The portion of the text beginning with "By my boon, immediately... and ending before "of the Lord" (patyuḥ) is clear in meaning; it has been explained here and there as needed. 41, 42, 43.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess departed for her own divine abode;
Līlā, however, effortlessly entered a state of unwavering meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi).
Then, in an instant, she abandoned her own body along with the cage of the internal organs, like a female bird that has left its nest and flown into the sky. (43)
(137) He beheld his lord situated in that very celestial abode,
the protector of the earth, seated upon his throne in the midst of many kings.
In that very abode of the sky, meaning in the space of his own house. || 44 ||
Seated upon his lion-throne, he was praised with cries of "Victory!
and "Long life!", while an infinite circle of sages, brahmins, and seers stood at the eastern gate.
"Jīva" is the verb. || 45 || 46 ||
The mandala of the king of all kings was situated at the western gate,
crowded with countless chariots, elephants, and horses located at the northern gate.
Then, with great display, she entered that assembly hall of the king, which was crowded with countless women gathered at the southern gate.
He fell and went [to his death]. || 47 ||
He [saw] those regions, their customs, and likewise those very cymbal-players;
and then others as well—unprecedented scholars and friends.
By those words, the places and other objects previously experienced are playfully referred to; the *tālakas* are the bards. || 48 ||
Adorned with great rivers, mountains, cities, and towns, he was a ruler of sixteen years of age, free from the decrepitude of former times. (49)
A *pura* is a branch city; a *pattana* is a primary city, meaning a capital. || 49 || 50 ||
Having beheld all this, that queen was filled with the utmost wonder;
then, rising up, she returned to her own inner apartments.
The queen remembered her petition and saw it standing before her;
Līlā, standing on the ground, questioned the queen who was seated upon an auspicious throne.

"Seated upon a *bhadrāsana*," meaning seated upon a lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*). According to Amara, "that which is a royal throne is both a *bhadrāsana* and a *siṃhāsana*. Thus, [the phrase means] "seated upon an auspicious seat. (51)
Just as this illusory creation has arisen from you, who are formless, so please explain it to me for the sake of dispelling the delusion regarding the world. (52)

King Padma, having ascertained the falsity of the other manifestation that appeared in that very same space of the house at the very moment after his death— due to the absence of suitable place, time, means, and so forth, like a dream-manifestation—
then sought to ascertain the falsity of the world as it was suspected by means of that example. For his husband...

He asks with the verse beginning "Just as the cause of delusion regarding another manifestation," and so forth. This is because once the cause of that delusion is known, it is possible to ascertain the falsity of the entire world, which has that very cause. It is "formless" (*amūrta*) because it does not possess a form—that is, it does not have parts; the reason for its being formless is that it is "of the nature of delusion."
Therefore, the phrase "other than that creation" must be supplied as an ellipsis. || 52 ||
The illustrious Goddess said:
Just as this creation was previously described as being of the nature of mere illusion prior to memory, so too is this second [creation] of your husband; listen as it is told. (53)

This entire phenomenal world is of the nature of delusion alone; since it is established in our doctrine that the production of each subsequent delusion arises from a preceding delusion, just as the prior delusion of the phenomenal world arose from the accumulation of impressions from previous births, so too does the delusion of the phenomenal world occurring after death arise [from its predecessor].

He provides the answer, stating "arisen through the cultivation of a previous birth," with the word "prāk" (previously). Anticipating the objection that the illustrative example itself is not accepted, he says "yathaitat" (just as this...). It is explained in such a way that it becomes clear. || 53 ||
Somewhere within the space of consciousness, there exists a pavilion of saṃsāra;
it is as clear as the sky, yet its form is veiled by a film of glass.

In order to show how Padma and Līlā previously existed as a Brahmin couple in another creation, he describes their former cycle of existence (*pūrvasaṃsāra*) by way of a dilapidated pavilion (*jīrṇamaṇḍapa*), so that it may be rejected—beginning with the words "There is a certain... That which covers is a covering (*saṃchādana*); this is space itself (*ākāśa*).
Because of its blueness, it has a covering consisting of pieces of glass; he whose form is covered by that is thus [described]. || 54 ||
It has Mount Meru as its central pillar, the world-protectors as its statues, and the anthills of the elemental spirits situated in its corners as its mountainous mounds of earth. || 55 ||

Meru itself is the pillar; those who are the wives and householders of Indra and the other world-protectors (lokeśas) situated upon it are the *śālabhañjikās* (statues) of that [pillar]. A pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) that has stood for a long time becomes a clod of earth (*loṣṭaka*) pervaded by an anthill (*valmīka*);
likewise, the pavilion of saṃsāra is a clod of earth in the form of a mountain pervaded by the anthills of the *bhūtas* (spirits) located at its corners. *Loṣṭam*.

A lump of dust. Living beings situated on the corners of the mountains are called "bhūtas" (spirits). The mountains themselves are the clods of earth, and the creatures on the corners are the anthills; that [place] which is pervaded by those mountain-clods is described as such. Alternatively, it is so called because its mountain-clods are pervaded by anthills inhabited by bhūtas. || 55 ||
(139) It is the abode of the Brāhmaṇa Prajeśa, who has grown old with many sons;
it is a mere insect dwelling within the great bamboo-stalk of the path of the wind, situated among the celestial palaces. || 56 ||

*Jaraṭhaḥ* means one possessed of old age (*jarā*). *Anekaputraḥ* refers to one who has many sons, such as Marīci and others. The phrase *anekaputro jaraṭhaśca yaḥ prajeśo brāhmaṇaḥ* refers to that place or abode (*āspada*) of such an aged Brahmin who is a lord of creatures (*prajeśa*). For a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) consists of large bamboo poles extending horizontally supported by upright beams; likewise, he says "vāta... [to describe] the pavilion of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-maṇḍapa*).

Between the path of the clouds (*meghamārga*) and the path of the sun (*sauramārga*), the path of the wind (*vātamārga*) is well known. Having reached that path, the many thousands of elephants hurled by Bhīmasena acted like tufts of cotton. Those who travel in celestial chariots (*vimāna*) are themselves but insects;
he is one in whom those insect-like celestial-dwellers reside within that very great bamboo-stalk which is the path of the wind. 56.
It was filled with the humming of swarms of goblins that were like mosquitoes to the hosts of Siddhas dwelling in the sky,
and agitated by the tumultuous clamor of the playful antics of gods, demons, and other such children.

It was such that a buzzing sound (*ghuṃghuma*) was produced by the swarms of *siddhas* dwelling in the sky, who were like mere gnats; it was agitated by the playful clamor—the tumultuous noise of play—of the gods and others, who were like weak and wicked children. || 57 ||
There, within the interior of a certain corner-room,
on a surface of stone and clods of earth, there was a single pit belonging to a mountain village.

In this regard, the preceding textual passage beginning with "In a certain [place]" and ending with "this has been told to you" is clear in meaning. Certain words therein are now analyzed: *apavaraka* means an inner chamber; *śailaloṣṭatale* means at the base of a mountain-clod;
*girigrāma* is the name of a village. Furthermore, this village is situated in a low-lying area of the mountain, as will be shown.
The word *gartaka* [is used]. || 58 ||
p.

140) In that place, sheltered by rivers, mountains, and forests, there lived a learned and healthy brahmin who maintained the sacred fires along with his wife; possessing cows and milk, he was unacquainted with fear of kings, hospitable to all guests, and devoted to dharma. (59)
"Upagūḍhe" means embraced or kissed. || 69 ||
In wealth, dress, age, occupation, learning, power, and conduct,
he was like Vasiṣṭha, yet his mind was not like that of Vasiṣṭha’s son.

In the phrase "resembling Vasiṣṭha," the word *iva* is used in the sense of restriction; that is, she was exactly like Vasiṣṭha, but not the conscious being who is Vasiṣṭha, nor indeed the individual soul (jīva) related to Vasiṣṭha. The meaning is that she was simply someone else entirely distinct from the well-known Vasiṣṭha.
She became his wife, Indusundarī, by the name of Vasiṣṭhā.
By name she was Arundhatī, the wife; in the earth she was Arundhatī, and in the sky she was Arundhatī.
"By the name Vasiṣṭha"—the word "renowned" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 61 || 62 ||
In terms of wealth, dress, age, occupation, learning, power, and conduct,
she was indeed equal to Arundhatī, but not in terms of the possession of consciousness.
Once, while that brahmin was seated upon the grassy plateau of that mountain covered with *sarala* trees, he beheld the king below.

"On a *sarala-śādvale*": on a green meadow (*śādvale*) consisting of *saralas*, that is, trees known as *pūtikāṣṭha*. According to Amara: "The *pītadru*, the *sarala*, and the *pūtikāṣṭha* [are synonyms]. Although Amara states—"A *śādvala* is a place green with *śāda*"—and thus uses the word *śādvala* for a region green (*harite*) or blue (*nīle*) with *śāda* (young grass), Pāṇini also uses it in the sense of "a place where *śāda* exists."

Although he states the suffix *ḍvalac* in the rule "naḍa-śāda-bhāṣā-ḍvalac," nevertheless, because that specific meaning is impossible here, the word *śādbala* is intended to signify merely the state of being green. || 63 ||
Seeing that protector of the earth departing for the hunt with his entire retinue, he reflected thus: (64)
Ākheṭa means hunting. || 64 || 65 || 66 || 67 ||
(141) "Oh, how delightful is sovereignty, cherished with every fortune!
When shall I become a lord of the earth who fills the groves of the ten directions? (65)
When will the winds, fragrant with the nectar of kunda flowers, blow over my foot-soldiers, chariots, elephants, horses, banners, parasols, and chowries? (66)
"From that time forward, the Brahmin formed this resolve: 'The spray from the fatigue of lovemaking shall fall upon the women of the inner apartments. (67)
Constantly devoted to his own duty and untiring throughout his life,
he was intent on crushing [his enemies] like a thunderbolt from the snowy mountains shattering a lotus.
Because it destroys the lotus-like snow, it is the "snow-thunderbolt" (himāśani). || 68 || 69 || 70 || 71 ||
While that brahmin was thus absorbed in thought, old age approached him;
as his death drew near, his wife fell into a state of withered despondency.
O lady, she propitiated me just as she has you;
yet, realizing that immortality is exceedingly difficult to attain, she chose this boon instead.
"O Queen, lest the life-breath of my deceased husband depart from his very own pavilion, I have therefore accepted his [the king's] proposal. (71)
Then, by the power of time, that brahmin passed away;
yet he remained within that very space of the house as the space of the living soul (jīvākāśa).
"Pañcatva" means death. Amara states: "Pañcatā, kāladharma, diṣṭānta, pralaya, and atyaya [are synonyms for death].

By virtue of being the space of the living soul (jīvākāśatayā), the living soul itself—because it is like space due to its transparency, subtlety, and so forth—is "space" (ākāśa); the state of being that is "tattā. || 72 ||
By the power of his own former, no small, resolve,
that most powerful lord of the earth became, as it were, one whose body was composed of space itself.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: although he was himself already of the very nature of space (*ākāśavapuḥ*), by the power of his previous and abundant resolve, he became a sovereign lord of the earth (*urvīpatiḥ*) endowed with supreme power (*paramaśaktimān*). || 73 || 74 || 75 ||
When that brahmin had become a corpse, his wife, the brahmin woman, being utterly emaciated by grief, her heart broke in two. (74)
Having become a corpse along with her husband and casting off her body far away, she approached her husband by means of her subtle, transportive body (ātivāhika-deha). || 75 ||
There, this brahmin possesses houses, land, immovable property, and other riches;
yet today, having reached his eighth day, his life-force remains within a cave in the mountain village. (76)
*Kandara* means a cave; according to Amara, *kandara* or *darī* is feminine. || 76 ||
That husband of yours has now become a twice-born man who has attained the status of a king;
and she who was the Brahmin woman named Arundhatī, O lady, is you yourself. (77)
"He is your husband": the grammatical connection is that he, having become a king, has today become your husband. 77.
"May you two, a noble couple, rule this kingdom here—like a pair of young cakravāka birds, or like Śiva and Pārvatī born upon the earth. (78)
Śiva and Pārvatī are the Supreme Lord and his consort. || 78 ||
This ancient creation, this delusion of worldly existence, has been described to you;
for creation appears as mere illusion, like the sky itself. (79)
Concluding by dispelling the doubt that our previous worldly existence was real, she states the result with the words "This... (verse 79).

*Bhrāntimātrakam* (mere illusion) is the predicate and *ākāśam* (space) is the subject. The syntactical connection is: "That creation which appears is, according to the reasoning already stated, mere illusion (*bhrāntimātrakam*), for it is space (*ākāśam*) devoid of objective reality. || 79 ||
Līlā said:
O Queen, how has your word come to be so false?
Where is the life of a brahmin in his own home, and where are we standing here? (80)
He challenges what was stated as being incoherent in meaning with the words beginning, "O Goddess, your speech... (verse 80).
(143) How can such other worlds, that earth, those mountains, and those ten directions all fit within this house where we now reside? 81.
"How can these regions where we currently reside, such as foreign lands and the like, fit within the interior of the house of the Brahmin Vasiṣṭha? The meaning is: not at all.
The word 'interior' (antara) is used here in relation to the space of the Brahmin Vasiṣṭha's dwelling. How can my husband fit inside the house?"
"In those [states] in which he is situated"—this is found in some [versions]. (81)
The intoxicated Airāvaṇa was bound within the hollow of a mustard seed;
a battle was waged by a mosquito against a pride of lions within the cavity of an atom.
*Airāvaṇa* is *airāvata*. According to Amarasimha: "Airāvata, abhramātaṅga, airāvaṇa, and abhramuvallabha [are synonyms for the elephant of Indra]. (82, 83)
"Mount Meru was placed within a lotus seed and swallowed by the son of a bee;
this is indeed inconsistent, O Goddess, just as this [present matter] is. (83)
The Goddess said:
I do not speak this falsely; listen to it as it truly is, O beautiful one:
for the subversion of the laws of destiny is not brought about by people such as I. (84)

Because I am the supreme authority (*paramāpta*), he offers a rebuttal with the words "I do not speak falsely," etc., with the intention that this objection is merely a manifestation of [limited] discernment (*parijñāna*). [This refers to] the fixed laws (*niyatīnām*), which are the boundaries of the world (*jaganmaryādānām*). 84.
That soul of the twice-born village-dwellers, in his very own home,
perceives this entire world— the sky, the earth, and the kingdom— as being of the nature of space alone.

The soul of the village-dvijas, the soul of the Brahmins of the mountain-village, is the self of space (*vyomātman*). It has the mind as its body; for it was previously stated that this is the space of the mind (*cittākāśa*) and the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). Alternatively, being the self of space, formless like space itself, he perceives this earth and kingdom—this very earth and kingdom together with its own essential nature—as if one seeing a dream. (85)
(144) That previous memory has been lost, and what arose for you two was otherwise; just as the memory of waking [is lost] in a dream, O lady, so is this death. (86)

[Objection: "In that case, why does the memory of our previous births not persist for us, and why has this contrary activity arisen? To this, he says: *prāktanī* (the former). Just as the memory of objects experienced during the waking state does not arise in the dream state, and instead a contrary perception arises, so it is here.
The memory whose object is things experienced in a previous birth becomes lost in this birth and does not persist.

A different kind of cognition arises due to a particular mental impression (*bhāvanā*) in the previous birth; death is the cause of this, as is understood from the context. For death indeed crushes the seed of memory, which is characterized by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); therefore—
The meaning is that mindfulness does not follow [the object]. || 86 ||
This ground, situated within, is like the imagination and the mirror within the hollow of the sheath of that sky of consciousness which has the appearance of reality. (87)

He clarifies the resolution of the objection—"How do they go within the house?"—with the verse beginning "This" (iyam). That which has the appearance of reality is *satyāvabhāsa*; of that *cidvyoman*, the space of the Supreme Self, the "sheath" (*kośa*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the state of being an individual soul (*jīva*). Within its hollow (*koṭara*), that is, in its interior, lies this "ground" (*bhūmi*).
It stands together with its mountains, forests, and groves. By the word "saṃkalpa," the mental construction (manorājya) of a person who is forming a resolve is understood.
Alternatively, it means "situated within," that is, situated in the mind; in this case, it connects with the words "of him" (*tasya*) and so forth that follow. || 87 ||
"O child, within every atom, within every living being, and within every individual self, there exist worlds within worlds, consisting of nothing but appearances. (88)
One should not think that the world exists only in some places and not everywhere; thus he says: "even in an atom."

In the Brahman that is the nature of consciousness—whether it be the Supreme Soul or the individual soul (jīva)—the latter is considered atomic because it is conditioned by the extremely subtle internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). As the Śruti declares: "The jīva should be known as a part of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold. Within [the Self], there exist worlds of such a nature, which are merely causes appearing within as mental reflections.

Because saṃsāra is beginningless; because the very act of seeing constitutes creation; and because even in the state of dreaming, worlds are seen within the jīva—which, due to its passage through extremely subtle channels, is like an atom—it is logically established that there are worlds within each and every jīva. || 88 ||
Līlā said:
O Supreme Goddess, that brahmin died on the eighth day;
O Mother, many years have passed for us—how could this be? (89)
The two verses beginning with "On the eighth day" have a clear meaning. || 89 ||
The Goddess said:
O fair lady, just as there is no such thing as spatial extension, so too there is no temporal extension;
everything else is merely a manifestation of consciousness, whose sole nature is the play of the intellect.
From that whose sole form is the play of consciousness, and whose very nature is the transformation of consciousness.
O child, hear this sequence of how appearances manifest as they truly are: having experienced for a moment the false delusion of death, the living soul [awakens]. (91)
If so, how then is there a sequence of error designated as "appearance"? To this he says: "As it truly is," and so forth.
The fainting at the threshold of death is "death-fainting"; that [he experienced]. 91 || 92 || 93 || 94 ||
O lady of virtuous vows, having forgotten one's former state of being, one perceives another:
"I am the object to be placed here," and "I am situated within this support," O beautiful one. (92)
One perceives: "This body, consisting of hands, feet, and so forth, is mine";
"I am the son of this father"; "These many years are mine. (93)
"These are my delightful kinsmen; this is my lovely abode"—such is the delusion in this world that arises immediately after the confusion of death. (94)
Līlā said:
"Oh! What a supreme vision has been shown to me by you, O Goddess! Now, as far as I have matured in this vision—" (95)
Desiring to make known to himself the thorough realization of the falsity of everything other than the conscious self (cidātman), he says: "Aho! (Oh!)

Having thus understood the falsity of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) through the words of a reliable authority, Līlā now exerts herself for the sake of strengthening that realization by means of direct perception and other methods regarding the matter already explained: "Until, through this practice, this vision has now reached its full maturity— become ripe and perfected— I shall not reveal this secret wonder."

"Destroy curiosity; rend it asunder! He says "Maheśvarī" (the Great Sovereign) to indicate that you are capable of leading that creation—the world-expansion (*prapañca*)—which is called *sarga* because it is emitted (*sṛjyate*). || 95 || 96 ||
"O Goddess, without practice, you cannot pierce this marvel;
O Maheśvarī, lead me to that creation of the Brahmin couple."
The Goddess said:
Having taken recourse to this supreme, purifying vision, which consists of the nature of non-conceptual consciousness, abandon this form and become stainless. 97.
Observing through Līlā’s gross body the karma that causes the transition to another creation, the Blessed Lady,
perceiving her mass of merit to be intent on bestowing the knowledge of Brahman,
spoke accordingly, beginning with "acetya": that which is "acetya" is the form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) in which perceivable objects (*cetya*), such as sound and so forth, do not exist.
"Consisting of that" means having that as its primary focus; that is to say, "having that as its object. "Vision" (dṛśam) refers to comprehension. || 97 ||
This being the case, we shall behold that [Supreme Reality] along with its unimpeded creation;
this body of yours is a great bolt upon the door to that vision.
Having come together, we shall see [it] without restraint—that is, without obstruction—or rather, without impediment, that is, without any hindrance. || 98 ||
These formless worlds have been perceived by you as if they possessed form through a vain grasping, just as one might perceive golden rings where there are none.
Now, one might ask: "Why is the gross body an obstacle to the soul's departure through the gateway of perceiving other worlds?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The worlds... These worlds are called "amūrta" (formless) because they do not consist of solidified parts.

He provides an illustration for the grasping of the reality of the limbs as having form—which is contrary to the truth—due to the futile obsession and vain attachment of you ignorant living beings: "haimānīti" (as if made of gold). By the notion of a "ūrmi-kā," that is, with the idea of a ring (*aṅgulīyaka*). According to Amara: "aṅgulīyaka" means *ūrmi-kā*. For it is not the case that being made of gold constitutes the state of being a ring.

When examined more closely with the eye, nothing is perceived apart from those [atoms] which have assumed particular configurations; therefore, just as the foolish mistakenly grasp at rings through a distorted perception, so too the world-realms, though formless, are grasped through delusion as having form. Consequently, [there is no such thing as] a corporeal body...
Because it is obstructed by another form, it is logical that it acts as a bolt on the path of going, which serves as the gateway for perceiving other manifestations.
147) O child, without your practice, this form has not attained the state of Brahman.
Abiding as the self whose nature is the form of mental construction, you do not perceive it because of that.

He says "of you" (*tava*) to show that it is not merely the body that acts as an obstacle to entering the gateway to another creation, but also an obstacle to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Your form (*ākāra*), that is, your physical appearance, has not attained the state of Brahman—the nature of Brahman which is the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—without the practice of the knowledge to be described hereafter. Since it does not exist apart from the Brahman that is the substratum, it is [unreal].

"Ascertained" means this very point. "Having the nature of conceptualization as its self" (*kalanarūpātmā*) means that whose self (*ātmā*), or essential nature (*svarūpa*), is that very form of conceptualization (*kalanarūpa*), which is the very essence of imagination (*kalpanā*). For that reason, you do not perceive That Brahman; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Thus it has been said in the *Bṛhadvāsiṣṭha*: "As long as, through the yoga of practice, the fear of duality has not departed from you, surely..."
"so long you do not perceive Brahman as being of a nature other than that. || 200 ||
In this regard, those such as ourselves who have attained proficiency through the repeated practice of the realization of Brahman indeed perceive that state. (1)

Anticipating the objection—"In that case, since obstacles such as the delusion of a body persist for you and others, how can that Brahman be experienced?"—he says: "Therein... Those of us who have attained proficiency in that practice of knowledge through the repeated cultivation (*abhyāsa*) of the realization of Brahman, that is, the knowledge of Brahman.
For we have indeed attained renown; therefore, we perceive and experience that which is to be known.
This is the intended meaning:

through the ripening of the practice of the knowledge of Brahman, there occurs the dissolution of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that serve as the cause for the delusion of identifying the body and so forth with the Self.
Due to the absence of obstacles, the true nature of Brahman as the Self is experienced by people such as ourselves as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand. || 1 ||
p.
148) This body of consciousness belonging to one such as you is indeed purely *ātivāhika* (subtle/transmigratory),
yet it has been grasped through a materialistic intellect due to long-standing habitual tendencies.

Anticipating the objection that the body’s nature as a *kalana* (a subtle instrument of perception) is unestablished, he says: "The *ātivāhika*. That which is carried (*ativāhyate*)—conveyed by an unimpeded movement to various locations—is the *ātivāhika*, the subtle mental body (*sūkṣma-cittadehaka*). It is indeed *ātivāhika*, that is, subtle. And because of long-standing habitual cultivation (*cirabhāvanā*)—that is, due to long-term contrary conceptualization (*viparīta-bhāvanā*)—it appears as the material body (*ādhibhautika*) to such ignorant people.
It is apprehended by a cognition of the form "this is elemental" (ādhibhautika). || 2 ||
When the attenuation of your latent impressions (vāsanā) has indeed reached its firm establishment,
then the subtle body (ativāhika-bhāva) will once again enter this physical frame.
If that is so, one might ask when this innate state of being a *ātivāhika* (conveying body) will pass away from the mental body; to this he says: "The latent impression (*vāsanā*)."

When, through the practice of knowledge, the attenuation of latent impressions—that is, the diminution of the impressions of duality—shall truly attain stability within the body, the subtle state of the mental body, namely the *ātivāhika* nature, will once again return, that is, it will come forth. (3)
The mind, when it has entered into pure being and its latent impressions have become attenuated,
attains the state of a subtle body, just as snow turns into water through heat.

He clarifies what was stated with the words "pure" (*śuddha*). "Pure" means accompanied by *sattva*, not overcome by *rajas* and *tamas*, and following the quality of *sattva*. The meaning is this: even in the waking state, the mind—which exists in the form of the manifold world of the body and so forth, as it does in the dream state—[becomes pure] when, through the practice of knowledge, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have become attenuated.

Abandoning its form as the body and so forth, it attains its own subtle nature, which consists of mere appearance (*pratibhāsa-mātra*). For this very reason, they have declared that in the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), the world is merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*). || 4 ||
Therefore, O blameless one, exert yourself toward the attenuation of latent impressions;
when that [attenuation] reaches full maturity, you will become liberated while living.

Since the density of the mind dissolves when the thinning of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) occurs, one must therefore apply effort characterized by the practice of knowledge (*jñānābhyāsa*) for its accomplishment; thus he says: "Latent impression" (*vāsanā*). When the thinning of latent impressions is extensive, not only does the density of the mind dissolve, but because knowledge arises culminating in direct experience (*anubhava*), even bondage dissolves; thus he says: "In that" (*tasmin*).
(149) As long as this cool moon of awakening has not been fulfilled,
so long must you maintain this body and observe another cycle of creation. (6)

Having thus explained the means for the fulfillment of knowledge, she reminds [the disciple] of what must be done in order to perceive the previous creation prior to that fulfillment—beginning with the words "yāvad" (as long as). Now, one might object: "As long as awakening is not fulfilled, let one remain here in this gross body and observe another manifestation of the phenomenal world"; yet, [the author] says that once awakening is fulfilled, there is no need to maintain the body at all.
It is understood that the perception of another world-process (*prapañca*) is permitted; however, that is not tenable,

because since the departure into the sky and so forth does not arise from perfect awakening (*pūrṇabodha*), it is impossible to perceive another creation with that very same body, even for one possessing perfect knowledge such as Cūḍālā.

This is not a fault, because we observe that other efforts are undertaken for the sake of attaining perfections such as traveling through the sky; for on the path of knowledge, it is stated in that manner in order to generate an extraordinary degree of reverence for spiritual play (līlā).
Līlā said:
Tell me, what is this practice that assists in this matter, or of what nature is it? How does it attain growth, and what occurs when it has matured? (7)

Thus, regarding what was stated in the verse beginning with "Without such practice, O child, the form does not attain the state of Brahman," he asks in sequence about the nature, the method, the cause of its maturation, and the fruit of that maturation of the practice of knowledge which fulfills awakening—starting with the phrase "In this regard" (*atre*). The construction is as follows: "In this fulfillment of awakening, what is that practice which is beneficial?"
The Goddess said:
"The wise know that contemplation of That, the discourse upon That, mutual instruction regarding That, single-minded devotion to That, and the practice of That constitute [true yoga]. (8)

Regarding that, he states the nature of practice: "Reflection upon that" (taccintanam). This means the reflection on that Brahman which has been heard from the teacher, its thorough investigation through reasoning, and the subsequent explanation of it to another disciple endowed with virtuous qualities. (8)
(150) Those who are supreme practitioners, whose intellects are pregnant with the essence of dispassion and the beauty of exalted nobility, and which distill bliss— [for them this is intended]. (9)
Intending to provide the answer to the question "What kind of practice is this? regarding what was called *nididhyāsana*—namely, being solely intent upon this—he says:
"uditā... etc. "Uditaudāryasaundaryā" means that in which nobility (*audārya*), greatness (*mahattva*), and beauty (*saundarya*) have arisen (*uditā*).
It is also "pregnant with the essence of dispassion" (*vairāgyarasagarbhiṇī*). "Ānandasyandinī" means showering bliss (*ānanda*). "Pare" means in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Those who, through reasoning and the scriptures, strive for the attainment of the absolute non-existence of both the knower and the object of knowledge, are the steadfast practitioners of Brahman. (210)
With two verses beginning with "atyanta," he describes the practice of knowledge for the dull-witted and the mediocre practitioners respectively.

Alternatively, intending to provide the answer to the question "Of what kind? he also speaks these two verses beginning with "atyanta. [This refers to] the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), that is, the perceived entity (*dṛśya-padārtha*). (210)
The visible world was never produced even at the beginning of creation; it does not exist at all, always.
"This world" and "I"—the wise know this to be the practice of awakening. (11)

They know that this world and I—the object of perception—are in reality never produced at the beginning of creation or at the start of manifestation; therefore, they understand the practice regarding the Supreme Self to be the practice of realization that "this object of perception does not exist at all times.
This is expressed by the phrase "whose nobility and beauty have arisen."

The best [of aspirants] are those whose minds are immersed in the bliss of Brahman, which is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca), because they have firmly realized the falsity of phenomenal manifestation (prapañca).
The middling are those who, having fully understood the falsity of the visible world, strive for its firm realization.
The inferior are those who strive through scripture and reasoning to understand the falsity of the world; such is the distinction. || 11 ||
When passion, hatred, and the like have been attenuated through the realization that the objects of perception are non-existent,
that delight which arises from strength is called the practice of Brahman.

He provides the answer to the question, "How does he attain nourishment? with the word *dṛśya* ("the visible"): through the realization that the object of perception (*dṛśya*) does not exist in the perceiver (*draṣṭṛ*) even throughout the three periods of time, attachment, aversion, greed, and so forth become attenuated—that is, diminished.
Then, by the power of practice manifested through the force of its own momentum, there arises that delight characterized by the bliss of Brahman; this is the practice of Brahman (*brahmābhyāsa*).
This means that the practice of the matured knowledge of Brahman is being described. || 12 ||
(151) For the realization that the visible object is impossible is called both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
Through the cultivation of that, there is nirvāṇa; thus, cultivation is of great consequence. (13)

Praising the cause for the maturation of the realization that the object of perception is impossible, he provides the answer to the question, "What would happen when that [realization] is fully developed?"—namely, "For the realization that the object of perception is impossible... By "by its practice" (*tadabhyāsena*) is meant by the practice of that realization that the object of perception is impossible; it refers to the maturation of the practice of the knowledge of Brahman preceded by that [realization].

Up to this point: through the attainment of direct knowledge, there arises liberation (nirvāṇa) and absolute isolation (kaivalya). Since from this practice there arises a great emergence—sovereignty characterized by the attainment of the bliss of Brahman—it is called "the Great Emergence" (mahodaya). || 13 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus conversed that night, O beautiful woman,
they went to a place for meditative concentration and remained there with their limbs motionless.
Thus, the verses beginning with "iti saṃkathanam" and ending before "ekārṇavamivocchūnam" are clear in meaning; however, in some places, a certain amount of analysis is provided. || 14 ||
Through non-conceptual absorption, they abandoned their former consciousness;
by that very body of knowledge, the goddess of cognition moved about.

"Jahatuḥ" means they both released. "Pūrvasaṃvidam" refers to the prior cognition, the knowledge existing before the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which takes the form of "I" and so forth. "Jñānadehena" means by means of a body in which knowledge is predominant. || 15 ||
Then that woman, having abandoned her human body, wandered about;
and by means of her consciousness, she ascended to another body the size of a span.

By means of their consciousness (*saṃvit*) and volition (*saṃkalpa*), those two, whose forms were that of the sky and who moved through the void, became possessed of the form of the sky; they took on the form of the sky through their consciousness. Such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). They became possessed of the form of the sky and took on the form of the void. || 16-17 ||
Then those two women, playful in their dalliance and with lovely eyes,
by the very nature of their perception of objects, departed far from here into the sky. (18)

Because of the awareness of the object of thought—that is, the knowledge of the visible—it is understood through its very nature as the awareness of the object of thought to have the nature of the vision of consciousness; for that [vision] sublates all activities. || 18 ||
Having leaped further and further away, they beheld the sky,
which was like a single vast ocean— swollen, deep, and pure within.

He describes [the scene] with the words beginning "a single ocean" (ekārṇavam) in order to demonstrate that within the limited space of the pavilion given by the Brahmin, a vast proliferation (mahā-prapañca) exists, thereby establishing the certainty of its falsity. || 19 ||
It bestows the blissful enjoyment of the touch of the exceedingly gentle breeze,
and its movement and return surpass the course of the wind-mastered by great siddhas through the speed of their minds.

"Komalama" means soft and non-harsh. "Komalamarudāsaṅgasukhabhogadam" means that which grants the enjoyment of pleasure through contact with, or rather, the non-contact with, gentle breezes—that is, it provides the experience of bliss through the touch of soft winds.
"Manovegairjitau vātagamāgamau" refers to that place where the coming and going of the wind—the movement of air—has been conquered by the great Siddhas who possess the speed of thought.

The mastery over the coming and going of the vital air (vāyu) is the cause for attaining the speed of thought. For the Siddhas, who have begun to move through the sky together with the wind, go and return even before [the wind] does, by virtue of possessing the speed of thought; this is the meaning. || 220 ||
The circle of Kūṣmāṇḍas, Rākṣasas, and Paiśācas stationed at the perimeter was,
in some places, made to ripple as if by the dancing throngs of Ḍākinīs.
This is the *paiśāca* [mandala] of the *piśācas*, as well as the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mandala. The *kūṣmāṇḍas* are a specific class of spirits (*bhūta*).
Thus, it is likewise [the mandala] where the *kūṣmāṇḍa*, *rakṣasa*, and *piśāca* mandalas are situated on the periphery. The *ḍākinīs* are a specific class of seizing spirits (*graha*).
"Taraṅgitam" means having waves produced; "pravṛttaiḥ" refers to those [assemblies] in which excellent conduct has been established among the hosts of Yoginīs. || 21 ||
It was filled with throngs of active Yoginīs with the faces of dogs, crows, camels, and donkeys,
who traveled back and forth for hundreds of miles without purpose.
"Uselessly" means "without purpose"; the word "by those who come" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 22 ||
(153) In some places there was the water of the triple-pathed river within and without the hollows dug for the wind-spirits;
in other places were wall-less dwellings where Nārada and Tumburu sang.

Regarding the term *vātaskandha*: it refers to the wind-path (*vātamārga*) situated between the path of the clouds (*meghamārga*) and the path of the sun (*sauramārga*). Those winds which reside there have "skandhas"—meaning shoulders or their upper portions. Alternatively, *vātaskandhas* are specific divisions of the wind;
as stated in the *Kalpataru*: "Skandhas are divisions. Or else, *vātaskandhas* are masses of wind.

And thus Kṣīrasvāmin says: "The word *skandha* [is used] for a shoulder, and also for the *vetasa* tree; when explaining it in the sense of a collection (*samudaya*), as in 'the seven wind-skeins' (*sapta vātaskandhāḥ*). By the force of the word 'also' (*api*), it refers to a military camp (*sainyavāṭa*), as in 'the activity of the army-skein' (*skandhavyāpāraḥ*).
It is also used for a tree, the *japā* flower, the shoulder, a king, a multitude, and understanding. Regarding those [trees], there are pits dug within and without them."
"Tripathagājalam" means that in which the waters of the celestial river flow with their mouths turned downwards. || 23 ||
In some places it resembles a silent cloud at the end of an aeon with forms painted upon it; in other places it is garlanded by a continuous circle of intoxicated mothers.

It is that in which the clouds of the end of the aeon (*kalpāntavārida*), the clouds of dissolution, are like those painted in a picture—having the very same form as figures depicted in a painting—and are mute and silent. The "Mothers" (*mātaraḥ*) are Brāhmī and the others.
It is encircled by a dense, uninterrupted circle of intoxicated Mothers (*nirantaronmattamātṛmaṇḍalamālitaṃ*). By "dense" (*nirantareṇa*) is meant compact.
"Adorned with a mandala" means it has become possessed of a garland; that is to say, it is joined with the circle of the mother-goddesses (mātṛkā) who are like garland-makers. || 24 ||
In some places it extends for hundreds of thousands of yojanas, with terrain difficult to traverse; in other places it is like the interior of a stone, filled with masses of indestructible darkness.

"In some places" means [regions] where living beings are difficult to find for hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*; "in some places" means [regions] devoid of all living beings for many hundreds of thousands of *yojanas* in every direction. The accusative case in the word *yojanalakṣāṇi* is used according to the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge*. The phrase "of the interior of a stone" (*dṛṣadgarbhasya*) means "within a rock. This is the comparison.

In which [the mind] there is a light like that within a diamond; likewise, in which there is a vast and great light that is indestructible—for this very reason, it is comparable to the sun and fire. 25–26.
It is indestructible, vast splendor, resembling in some respects the sun and fire. || 26 ||

O beautiful lady, having traversed the mass of beings contained within the three worlds— which move like gnats inside the hollow of an udumbara fruit— she is now once again intent on returning from the high sky to the surface of the earth. (27)

"Maśakas dwelling within the interior of udumbara fruits" refers to those gnats inside the fruit; "udumbarodaramaśakas" [is a compound] meaning that very thing. Furthermore, it is "that in which there is a multitude—that is, a collection—of beings wandering within the three worlds according to that sequence and by that method.
The preceding verses beginning with "vilaṅghya" and ending with "aho nu parama" are clear in their meaning.
In some cases, something is analyzed in detail. || 27 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, those two women of excellent complexion, having departed from that sphere of the universe, reached another place where that abode of the brāhmaṇa was located.
The two women of excellent complexion were the most sublime of women. || 28 || 29 ||
Then, in that creation, those two perfected women beheld the circle that was the abode of Brahman, invisible to the world.
With its female servants overwhelmed by anxiety and the faces of the women drenched in tears,
its former appearance utterly ruined, it was like a tree consumed by lightning.
That pavilion where the female attendants were distressed by anxiety and deprived of their desired objects was called *cintāvidhuradāsīka*.
It was described as such because the faces of the women there were wet and moistened with tears (*bāṣpa*).
It was likewise described as such because its former position and previous arrangement had been destroyed and disrupted. *Vidyut* refers to lightning; *aśani* refers to a thunderbolt. || 230 ||
Then, through long practice of stainless knowledge, that beautiful woman became like a goddess, possessing the power of true resolve and true desires.
The grammatical connection is that Līlā became like a god, possessing the power of true resolve (satya-saṃkalpa) and having her desires fulfilled (satya-kāma). || 31 || 32 || 33 || 34 ||
He thought: "Let my kinsmen behold me and this goddess for a moment, appearing in the form of an ordinary woman. (32)
Then the household members there beheld two women,
who illuminated the palace like a pair of Lakṣmī and Gaurī. (33)
Having said, "Salutation be to the two forest goddesses," Jyeṣṭhaśarman then cast a handful of flowers along with his household.

And the two goddesses, the most excellent in the worlds, were here as a Brāhmaṇa couple—welcoming all guests, founders of the lineage, and the very pillars upon which the stability of the twice-born rested. (35)

Those two for whom every person was a guest were "sarvātithī. They were "kulakarau," meaning the founders and increasers of their lineage. They were the pillars—the very supports—of the stability of the twice-born, or rather, of the established order of the twice-born; that is, they were the foundation for the residence of the twice-born. || 35 || 36 ||
