Having abandoned their home along with their sons, cattle, and kinsmen, those two, our parents, have gone to heaven; therefore, the three worlds are empty.
Therefore, O two Goddesses, please perform for us now the destruction of our grief;
for the sight of the great is never in vain. (37)
The word "nāma" signifies well-knownness.
When her son had spoken thus, she touched his head with her hand;
by that touch of hers, he [was freed from] the distress of suffering and misfortune.
For that reason, suffering itself is the calamity of misfortune; it is the very oppression of wretchedness. 38–39.
Just as a mountain sheds the heat of summer due to contact with the clouds of the rainy season, so too did another person there cast off grief, which is so difficult to abandon. (39)
Seeing them there on that mountain slope, in that village, within the hollow of that pavilion, those two perfected women then vanished from sight.
The Goddess said:
The knowable has been known in its entirety, and the consciousness of illustrative examples has been seen; such is this reality of Brahman—tell me, what else do you ask? (41)

Regarding the cognition of examples for the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), the recollections of examples have been seen; that is to say, they have been obtained. The existence of Brahman (*brahmasattā*)—existence whose nature is Brahman—is of such a kind: either having the form of a real world or being devoid of the phenomenal world (*niṣprapañcā*).
Līlā said:
"In that place where the soul of my deceased husband rules his kingdom, why was I not seen by them? Why have I been seen here by my son? (42)
The Goddess said:
"O child, O lady of excellent complexion, without practice, your conviction in duality at that time certainly did not come to a complete end."
Without practice, the thought "I am Līlā" did not become established in you;
or rather, at that time, the state of having true resolve had not yet arisen in you.

"‘I am Līlā’—the connection is that when your state of being, the mental cultivation (bhāvanā) that ‘I am Līlā,’ did not come to an end without the practice of knowledge (jñānābhyāsa), then your power of true resolve (satyasaṃkalpatva) did not arise. || 44 ||
"Today you have become one whose resolve is true; therefore, O beautiful one, your cherished wish that 'the son may behold me' has borne fruit. (45)

In non-dual Brahman, because the certainty of duality—which acts as an obstacle to yoga consisting of the cessation of mental fluctuations—has dissolved, you have today become one whose resolve has become true. 45–46.
If you now go into the presence of that husband of yours, then your dealings with him will proceed just as before. (46)
Līlā said:
"Alas! O Mother of the World, I have now remembered you here;
this birth of mine is rajasic, neither tamasic nor sattvic. (47)

Having attained the grace of Sarasvatī, having acquired worldly power through the application of touch, and having recollected the succession of her previous births through a playful act, she—having conceived supreme world-weariness (nirveda)—describes her former lives with the words beginning with "Aho" in order to demonstrate instantly, by means of herself, the worthlessness of cyclic existence (saṃsāra). "Hanta" expresses grief. This...
The present birth is characterized by passion (*rājasa*), being produced from the quality of passion (*rajo-guṇa*). || 47 ||
(157) "Since my descent from Brahmā, eight hundred births have passed for me through various wombs; now, as it were, I behold them once again. (48)
[This is] from Brahmā, who has descended from his lotus-seat at the beginning of this kalpa. || 48 ||
O Goddess, in a certain part of the circle of saṃsāra in the past, I was a Vidyādhara woman, a bee among the lotuses of other worlds. (49)
In relation to the world of humans, the abode of the Vidyādharas is another world; that itself is the lotus (*abja*).
The "bee" (*bhramarī*) therein is the "bee of the lotus of the other world," meaning she is a resident of the world of the Vidyādharas. || 49 || 250 ||
Then, defiled by evil latent impressions, I became a human woman;
in another cycle of worldly existence, I was the beloved of the Lord of Serpents.
Then I became a Śabarī woman, dwelling in a grove of Karañja, Jambīra, and Kadamba trees;
dark-complexioned, I wore leaves as my garment. (51)
*Karañja* is the tree known as *naktamāla*. According to Amara, *cirabilva*, *naktamāla*, *karaja*, and *karañjaka* are synonyms.
In the forest of the enemy’s snares set by Vihaṅgī,
they were severed with great difficulty, like base latent tendencies.

"By me, a female bird (vihaṅgī), being truthful, [the trap] set by the enemy—the net (vāgurā) set by the hunter—is [seen]. The meaning 'a snare for binding deer' is not accepted here because it is impossible. In the forest-land (vipināvanau), that is, on the ground of the wilderness. || 52 ||
She rested together with her soiled companion upon beds in the centers of the lotuses,
and enjoyed herself in secret within the hollows of the lotus buds, having consumed the filaments.

The *karṇikā* is the seed-vessel situated in the center of a lotus. The "laps of the *karṇikās*" are their central regions; these themselves are the beds, thus they are "beds in the laps of the *karṇikās*. Upon them, I rested, having become a bud with my filaments already enjoyed—that is, my garland of filaments already consumed. (53)
Then, as a result of the ripening of my actions as one who bestowed the fruit of the *astrī* tree, I became a glorious king in the Surāṣṭra lands for a hundred years. (54)
The attainment of manhood from womanhood is the very fruit for those who grant it, lasting for equal years.
I immediately experienced the poverty of swinging upon the swing of a blade of grass with a mosquito; I remained there together with that mosquito.

The ground was verdant, covered with young grass, and likewise swaying with blades of grass; thus, "śādvalīdaladolā" refers to that [ground] swaying with the movement of the blades of grass, and "āndolanadaridratā" refers to its state of being destitute of such swaying. || 55 ||

I have wandered through various wombs, filled with hundreds of manifold sufferings and agitated by many violent collisions, following the course of the boat upon the irresistible wind across the surging waves of the long river of saṃsāra. (56)
*Vimarda* means wandering. *Laharyā* means by a wave; here, the "wave" intended is the wave of the river of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) characterized by craving for sense objects.
That which has an irresistible wind is *durvāravātā*; it is both that and a boat (*taraṇī*), and its *saraṇa* is its movement.
By that sequence—that method—of a long river being tossed about by extremely treacherous and flickering waves.

The meaning is that he has wandered through various wombs—which are like whirlpools—within the long river of saṃsāra, tossed by the waves characterized by craving for sense objects, according to the analogy of a boat moving in the midst of a violent wind. || 56 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus conversing, those two women of graceful form flew far into the sky by means of the methods of yogic movement.
They rose up from the Brahma-maṇḍapa and ascended upwards; their movement was a yogic progression performed by means of those steps.
Then, having emerged from that creation, they saw a second creation within the inner apartments as if it had appeared instantaneously.
"Having reached" means having attained; "the second" refers to that which belongs to King Padma. || 58 ||
[She saw] the great corpse, the Great King, standing there covered with a profusion of flowers.
Then, emerging once more, the divine Yoginī remained established in yoga. (59)

Furthermore, the textual composition beginning with "Then again" (*tataḥ punar*) and extending until the conclusion of the narrative is for the purpose of demonstrating the engagement and attainment that result in strengthening the certainty regarding the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) for Līlā and Sarasvatī; it is for the most part clear in meaning. In that regard:
Some points are now being analyzed. It should be understood that even though the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is characterized by manifold and great agitation, it is shown to be illusory;
therefore, the description of the grand battle that took place within another world-system inside the sky of King Padma’s pavilion is intended as a subject for poetic depiction. || 59 || 260 ||
Līlā, endowed with consciousness (jñapti), entered the worldly existence of her husband within that circle on the adorned earth. 260.
A certain king, whose power surpassed that of his neighboring vassals,
launched a surprise attack upon a certain vast forest as terrifying as a second sky.

"Attacking" means an invasion or the depletion of the kingdom. "Surpassed by neighboring kings" (sāmantodrikta) means one who has grown powerful due to his neighbors; such a person is a ruler of the earth (bhūmipa), and thus he is so described. || 61 ||
The two armies were undisturbed, resembling two calm oceans;
they were dense with great undertakings and contained two kings stationed in their midst.
"Ghana" means dense; "mahārambhaghana" means dense due to the cause of a great undertaking, namely, a beautiful and gentle commencement of a great battle. || 62 ||
And Līlā and the goddess Jñapti, stationed in the sky, beheld him who was ready for battle, exalted, blazing like a wondrous fire.
"Ready for battle" means equipped and prepared for combat;
"blazing" means radiant. || 63 ||
Then the clash of weapons between the two armies began violently, with the speed of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution, scattering sparks like flashes of fire.

With speed and impetuosity, he scattered—that is, he cast about—fires and lightnings; for the fires produced by the clashing of weapons were called "lightnings" because they took the form of lightning. || 64 ||
(160) The waters were agitated by the earth shaking from the falling intoxicated elephants,
and the sky-dwellers were driven far away by the flood of mechanical stones and wheels. || 65 ||
In that encounter, the waters flowed as the earth was shaken by falling elephants in rut;
likewise, in that encounter, the sky-dwellers—the gods and others—fled far away due to stones propelled by machines and floods of discuses. || 65 ||
The sky was starred with fragments of swords flashing as they flew high,
and the armor of excellent warriors was crushed by the impact of diamond-hard fists.

It was such that the sky was "star-spangled"— that is, filled with stars— by those fragments of swords which, having flown far and risen high, were glittering and expanding; and it was such that the armor of excellent warriors had been ground into powder by the crushing blows dealt by fists as hard as thunderbolts.
"In which he was thus": *uracchada* means armor (*kaṅkaṭaka*), as in Amara’s lexicon: "armour, *ajagara*, and *kavaca* are not feminine. (66)

The tumult of battle became like the end of an aeon: a mass of clouds intoxicated by the flood of heroic warriors and the rain of excellent iron arrows caused headless trunks to dance like peacocks; it was encircled by mountains of elephants whirling with speed.

The showers of iron arrows (*nārāca*)—arrows made entirely of metal—are themselves excellent rain-clouds; those who give them are thus "givers of excellent rain-showers of iron arrows. The floods of heroes (*vīrapūra*) are masses of warriors, and these are like intoxicated clouds.
Thus, due to the agitation of those "intoxicated cloud-like floods of heroes" which are givers of excellent rain-showers of iron arrows, they were made to dance.

In that tumultuous battle, there were headless trunks (*kabandha*) acting as peacocks (*barhiṇa*); thus, it was "one in which headless trunks served as peacocks. Alternatively, it refers to that [battle] in which headless trunks danced (*vinṛtta*) with frantic energy due to the cause of intoxicated clouds (*mattābhra*). A *kabandha* is a headless body still possessed of motion; the word *kabandha* is not feminine.

"Kriyāyukta-apamūrdha-kalevara" means "a body whose head has been severed," according to Amara. It is "balitaḥ" (connected/bound) by those "mātaṅga-śailas"—elephant-mountains—which are "vivartamānāḥ" (whirling) with speed. || 67 ||
Thus, in that exceedingly tumultuous battle, crowded with warriors brandishing their weapons, he—
possessing a form sweetened by majesty that remained as an eighth part of his original ten-fold power— [stood there].
Struck by the blow of the weapon, he became emaciated like a hero struck down by the sun. || 68 ||

That which has eight parts of a day—where a day is divided into thirty parts—is "eight-parted" (*aṣṭabhāgā*). That sun whose remaining state (*daśā*) consists of those eight parts is "one whose remaining state is eight-parted" (*aṣṭabhāgadaśāśeṣa*). He is further described as such because he possesses a sweet form despite his intense heat. Alternatively, the "state of eight parts" (*aṣṭabhāgadaśā*) refers to the condition of dissolution; that which has this as its remainder is "one whose remaining state is eight-parted. And [he is] that very one.

And that which is majesty (*pratāpa*); he whose appearance or form (*ākṛti*) is sweet and beautiful because of that is so described. In the case of a hero, however, *pratāpa* is the power that generates fear in enemies even from afar. That which has eight parts is "eight-parted" (*aṣṭabhāga*).
That of which death (*daśā*)—the final stage—is the remainder is "death-remaindered" (*daśāśeṣa*). And that which is both eight-parted and... [is so].

"Daśāśeṣa" means one for whom the remainder of the period (*daśā*) consists of eight parts; he is thus described as "one whose form is sweet with majesty. Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: that period (*daśā*) in which there are eight parts is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) of that hero. Or else, the period (*daśā*)—meaning the state of dissolution—is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) of his majesty, and by that [majesty] he is "sweet" (*madhurā*).
He whose appearance is beautiful is described as such. || 68 || 69 ||
Then, after Senā and Dinātha had deliberated together with their ministers,
they dispatched messengers to one another, saying, "Let the battle be withdrawn."
Then the kettledrums resounded, their echoes filling the quarters of the sky;
and a pair of elephants began to emerge from the forest of battle.
"Śamū" is the third person plural form of the optative (liṅ) derived from the verbal root "upaśamana" (to pacify). || 170 ||
Then, like a hero, the sun, reddened by time, set;
thereafter, the dead of night arrived, with its vanguard being the mass of darkness.
The hero too becomes red because he is drenched in blood. That king of the night is so described as one whose vanguard—the front of the army—is the mass of darkness, a flood of gloom. || 71 ||
The noble-souled Lord of Līlā, appearing as if somewhat dejected in mind,
quickly deliberated upon his morning duties with his ministers, who were experts in counsel.
In him, the noble-souled one possessed the most excellent mind. || 72 || 73 ||
(162) He began to sleep for a moment in his palace, which was as bright as the rays of the moon;
then those two divine yoginīs entered the king’s house. 73.
By its power, the inner apartments of the king were lulled into sleep by the gentle breeze from the Mandara trees, which was soft, pure, and fragrant.

Regarding the word *komala*: "mṛdu" means soft, "komala" means gentle, and "amalasaugandhya" means possessing stainless fragrance; the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: that house in which the breeze from the *mandāra* flowers is both soft and gently fragrant is described as such. || 74 ||
Refreshed by the floods of light from their bodies, which were as cool as the radiance of the moon,
the king awoke as if sprinkled with nectar.
In this context, "niṣpanda" means a ray; "āhlādita" means made happy or blissful. || 75 || 76 ||
Then that king, having reflected for a moment with a mind filled with great wonder, beheld two women resting upon two seats. (76)
He rose from his bed like the wielder of the discus and mace rising from Śeṣa;
he took up a handful of flowers as one would grasp a blossoming garland of flowers.
One for whom there is a garland (*hāra*) of flowers is a "flower-garlanded" one (*puṣpahāra*). In some places it is read as *puṣpādhāra*; in that case, the meaning is "a florist.
*Utphulla* means blossomed or fully opened. || 77 ||
On the pure ground, the king sat in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), possessing the moon-like luster that dispels the defect of the burning distress of worldly existence. 78.
"In a place devoid of clothing" (*vivasane vivastre*) means in a place lacking garments or coverings. Regarding "the wretchedness of people" (*janadausthitya*):

the wretchedness of people is the state of their minds being corrupted by defects such as envy; the "burning" is the affliction caused by that [wretchedness], which is like a fire. [The two goddesses] possess the luster of the moon that pacifies that [fire], and the luster of the sun that dispels external and internal darkness.
Having spoken thus to them, he offered a handful of flowers at their feet.

"External and internal" (bāhyāntara) means: the solar radiance that dispels the darkness of ignorance regarding external and internal objects; the connection "of those two feet" is intended distributively for each one. 79, 180, 81, 82.
Then, in order to describe her birth as a king for the sake of sport, the Sovereign Goddess Sarasvatī, through her creative will (*saṃkalpa*), enlightened the minister standing at her side. (180)
Seeing those two yoginīs, he prostrated himself, offered a handful of flowers at their feet, and, bowing low, entered before them.
The queen said, "O King, how, whose son, and when was he born here? Having heard this, the minister spoke these words: || 82 ||
O two goddesses, by your grace, I am able to speak even before you;
therefore, let this birth of my lord be heard.
The connection is that the thought "I am able to speak" arises through your grace. || 83 ||
There was a lotus-eyed king belonging to the lineage of Ikṣvāku,
the illustrious one named Kunda-ratha, whose shadow from his arms covered the earth.
The earth covered by the shadow of his arms—the meaning is that the ground was properly protected by the shadow of his arms. || 84 || 85 || 86 || 87 || 88 || 89 || 190 || 91 ||
He had a son named Bhadraratha, who possessed the luster of the moon's orb;
his son was Viśvaratha, and his son was Manoratha.
Viṣṇuratha was his son, and Bṛhadratha was his son;
Sindhuratha was his son, and Śailaratha was his son. || 86 ||
His son was Kāmaratha, and his son was Mahāratha;
this lord of ours is his son, possessed of a perfectly pure form.
Through great accumulations of merit, he was born of his mother Sumitrā as one renowned by the name Vidūratha, like a second Guha born of Gaurī.
When he was ten years old, his father gave him the kingdom and departed for the forest;
from that time forward, he protected the surface of the earth in accordance with righteousness. (89)
When the minister had spoken thus and remained silent,
and likewise the king stood with palms joined in reverence, face bowed down, and seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana).
"O King, remember your former birth through discernment," saying this herself,
Sarasvatī touched him on the head with her hand.
Then the darkness of delusion within the heart of this king came to an end;
he remembered his former history as if it were still throbbing within him.
The qualification "māyā" is used to demonstrate that darkness (tamas) causes many difficult-to-accomplish things. || 92 ||
"Alas, this vast world-process within myself, which possesses sovereignty over other bodies and is accompanied by the play of divine sport, is indeed an illusion. (93)

Endowed with the playful charms and graceful gestures of his wife Līlā—thus possessed of Līlā’s playful charms—I have now, through the grace of the two goddesses, fully realized and understood everything here.
O Goddesses, what indeed is this, that for me who am as if dead, even a single day has passed? (94)
Seventy years have passed for me born here today;
I remember many deeds, as well as friends, kinsmen, and attendants. (95)
Jñapti said:
O King, immediately after the fainting fit caused by the great delusion of death, in that very world which had passed for you, at that very moment— || 96 ||
It is called "loka" because it is perceived (lokya); [it refers to] the body, within which [the self resides]. || 96 ||
In that very house was born a creation with the delusive appearance of a vast flood;
at that very moment, it arose within your mind, which is as pure as the clear sky.
"Sphāra" means extensive or abundant. He clarifies the meaning expressed by the word "eva" (only/just) with the phrase "tadaiva" (at that very moment). || 97 ||
This eloquence has arisen, though it is spread across the delusions of worldly convention; seventy years of my life have already passed. (98)

The phrase "vyavahārabhramātatam" means pervaded or overspread by the delusions of worldly activity. He shows this very appearance even slightly with the verse beginning "vayasaḥ" (of age). The connection is as follows: the intuition arose that seventy years—belonging to a lifespan of which it is said, "A man indeed lives for a hundred years"—have already passed. || 98 || 99 ||
Just as the delusion of a hundred years may occur within a single moment of a dream, so too does this delusion in the world arise through the playful manifestation of Your Māyā. 99.
In reality, you have never been born, nor have you ever died;
you are of the nature of pure consciousness and abide as peace within the Self. (200)
In response to the inquiry, "What then is the actual state of things?", he says this in two verses beginning with "But in reality... and so forth.
You perceive all this, yet you do not perceive anything at all;
by virtue of being the self of all, you shine eternally within yourself through yourself.
Relying on the vision of reality, he says: "And yet you do not see. You shine forth; you manifest. (1)
For one who is dull-witted, deluded, and not established in the expansive state,
this world— which is like the essence of a diamond— exists as if it were real, though it is actually unreal.
Now, for the purpose of praising the vision of the wise as presented and for the purpose of abandoning the contrary vision,

he describes the vision of the wise with the textual passage beginning with "He whose mind is impure" and ending with "the long dream. [The phrase] "not established" (*na rūḍhaḥ*) means not well-known or not firmly rooted in the "vast expanse" (*vitata*), that is, in the reality (*vastu*).

In reality, the world is indeed non-existent; yet, from the perspective of that deluded person, it appears as existent, as if possessing the ultimate reality of the essence of a diamond (*vajrasāra*).
That which has a firm core, like the essence of a diamond, is described as such. (2)
Just as a ghost causes suffering to a child until his death, so does this world, though unreal, appear real to the deluded mind. (3)
In this context, a Vetāla superimposed upon one's own shadow by a child is intended as an illustration.
Just as that [Vetāla], which causes suffering ending in death and bestows misery culminating in death, appears as if real, so too does the world appear real to the deluded mind. (3)
Just as a mirage appears to thirsty deer as water even though it is only heat, so too does this world appear real to the deluded mind even though it is unreal. (4)
The heat belongs to one who has gone to a desert land; [it arises] from the wandering of one who wanders. || 4 ||
Just as for one who is untrained in the nature of gold, there is only the cognition of a bracelet in a golden bracelet, and not even the slightest thought of it being gold. (5)
In the case of gold, which serves as the substrate for the conceptualization of a bracelet,

for one who is untrained— that is, for one in whom no such cognition has arisen— there exists only a contrary cognition regarding the bracelet made of gold, namely the thought "this is a bracelet," and there is not even the slightest notion of it being gold. This is not a bracelet [in reality].
However, the meaning is that there is no cognition [establishing] that "it is indeed gold. || 5 ||

Likewise, for the knower, there exists only this very perception of the visible world— resplendent with ancient dwellings, mountains, and the lords of serpents— and no other perception of ultimate reality.

Just as in this illustration, so for one who knows [the truth] but is not yet fully realized of the foundational Brahman (adhiṣṭhāna-brahman), there exists only this perceived object and the perception of it—a delusion regarding the visible; there is no other vision of ultimate reality (paramārtha-dṛṣṭi). The meaning is that there is no such valid cognition (pramiti) as "this is not the visible world, but rather Brahman alone. A *naga* is either a mountain or a tree; a *nāga* is either an elephant or a serpent of the Kadrū lineage. || 6 ||
This entire universe, joined with mind, ego, and so forth, is a long dream;
herein, other dream-people exist just as these [dreamers] exist while awake. (7)

Having thus shown the view of the ignorant which is to be abandoned, he elaborates upon the view of the knower of reality which is to be adopted, beginning with the words "a long dream" (dīrghasvapnam). Just as in this world other persons seen in a dream are false relative to the dreamer, so too these other persons are indeed false relative to a person who is awake. (7)
There exists the all-pervading, tranquil, and pure essence of the ultimate truth, whose form is pure consciousness beyond the reach of thought— an expansive supreme space.
The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is that which is solid and uninterrupted; thus, it is the "vault of the ultimate reality" (*paramārthayanam*).

Having a body consisting of pure consciousness that cannot be an object of thought, and having the nature of pure consciousness that is beyond all objects, it is the supreme space (*paramākāśa*), the supreme Brahman, omnipresent.
It is described as "spread out" (*ātata*) in order to express that it is unrestrained (*niraṅkuśa*). (8)
(167) That [Reality] is all-pervading, possessed of all powers, everything itself, and the self of all;
wherever and in whatever manner it arises, it truly abides in that very place in that very manner.
"Omnipresent" (*sarvaga*) means that it goes to and knows everything; thus, "all that" (*tatsarvam*) is a grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) used in the sense of negation.
"Consisting of all" (*sarvātmaka*) means that its essential nature (*ātmasvarūpa*) is woven through all things as their underlying self. || 9 ||
Thus, O King, have you been described for the sake of this play.
May it be well with you; we two shall now depart, having attained the realization of both the seen and the unseen.

O King, this [account] was described by you for the sake of *līlā*—that is, for the purpose of establishing the illusory nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) through the attainment of illustrative examples; or else, for the sake of *līlā*, meaning for the pleasure of *līlā*. "Illustrative perspectives" (*dṛṣṭānta-dṛṣṭayaḥ*) refers to the perceived certainties regarding illustrative examples concerning the illusory nature of the phenomenal world; the meaning is that they have been obtained. || 210 || 11 || 12 || 13 || 14 ||
Vidūratha said:
O Goddess, even my own vision becomes fruitless toward those who do not seek [you];
how much more so would yours be, you who bestow great fruit? (11)
O Giver of Boons, tell me truly: when shall I cast off this body and go to that body named Padma? (12)
The Goddess said:
O King, you must now die in this excellent battle;
this kingdom which was yours in a former life is now manifestly before you.
Vasiṣṭha said:
While the two sweet-spoken lovers were thus engaged in their private conversation, a man entered in great agitation and, standing upright, spoke: (14)
O Lord, the great army of the enemy, raining down spears, discuses, swords, maces, and iron clubs, has arrived like a surging single ocean. (15)
A *paṭṭiśa* is a specific type of weapon with edges on both sides; a *parigha* is a club bound at its base. || 15 ||
In the city, which resembled a mountain, a fire broke out, pervading the horizons;
burning with crackling and popping sounds, it brought down the finest houses.
A mountain is a *nāga*. || 16 ||
Like great mountains of smoke in the sky resembling jars of clouds at the end of an eon, they began to rise up with force like Garuḍas. || 17 ||
They are like jars [filled with] the clouds of the eon and like masses of clouds at the time of dissolution; "proḍḍīyanam" means rising up preeminently. || 17 ||
Even as the man was speaking thus with agitation,
a great clamor arose outside, filling the quarters with its harsh sound.
A harsh, rough, and all-pervading sound arose—that is, it emerged—whose roar was harsh; the quarters are the directions. || 18 ||
Of bows drawn forcibly to the ear and raining arrows, and of powerful, highly intoxicated elephants trumpeting loudly; 19.

Of those swelling and roaring; of those possessing *taras*—for Amara states that *draviṇa*, *taras*, *sahas*, *bala*, *vīrya*, *sthāma*, and *śuṣma* are synonyms for strength—or alternatively, of those possessing speed (*tarasvin*), for Amara states that *raṃhas*, *taras*, *rayas*, and *syadas* are synonyms for velocity;
and of the fires (*jātavedas*) blazing with crackling sounds in the city.
With the great tumultuous cries of the citizens whose wives had been burned.

*Caṭacaṭa* and *halahala* are imitative sounds (*śabdānukāra*). The connection with the preceding verse is that a tumultuous clamor arose from the *caṭacaṭa* crackling of bows and the *halahala* shouting of elephants. || 220 ||
Then, from the window, the two queens, the minister, and King Vidūratha beheld the great city resounding with loud clamor in the dead of night.
A *vātāyana* is a window; "a *vātāyana* is a window, not feminine," according to Amara. || 21 ||

It was filled by the supreme force, which possessed the momentum of the seven oceans agitated by the winds of cosmic dissolution, and which surged with waves like fierce clouds at the end of an eon. (22)
It is "ekārṇava" because it is one (eka) and a single ocean (arṇava). It is "saptaikārṇava" because it is seven (sapta) and a single ocean (ekārṇava);

its "raṃha" is like the speed (raṃha) or velocity of that [ocean]. That supreme army is "ugrakalpameghataraṅgi," meaning it possesses waves whose form is equal to those fierce clouds (ugrakalpamegha) of the dissolution (pralaya). By that [army]... // 22 //
Resplendent like Mount Meru or Mandara melting in the fire at the end of an eon,
it was being consumed by masses of great flames that filled the sky.

Resplendent like Mount Meru and Mount Mandara melting from the fire at the end of the eon; that is, it possesses a nature of radiance like those two mountains, Meru and Mandara, which are melting because they have been consumed by the fire at the end of the eon. || 23 ||
With the fierce roars of great clouds that could be grasped by the fist, with threatening and violent sounds, and with the harsh, clamorous chatter of bandits; (24)

By those [threats] which are like the roars and thunders of great clouds that can be grasped by the fist—by those powerful and intensified threats; or rather, by those powerful threats which are like the roars of great clouds graspable by the fist. By clamorous sounds, by the noises of tumultuous shouting. "Kolahala" means a confused noise, according to Amara.

"Kalakala" is an imitation of sound. "Māṃsalaiḥ" means "dense. The connection is that [the place was] "terrible" due to "clamorous sounds" and "the prattlings of bandits. Alternatively, the construction is: "terrible" because of the "dense clamorous sounds," which are caused by "the prattlings of bandits. || 24 ||
The sky was made turbulent by fierce stars resembling fragments of flickering firebrands,
while men and women wailed piteously as they fell upon heaps of glowing coals.

"Tarad-ulmuka" means: that city in which the sky (ambaram) is tossed and agitated by those fierce stars (ugratārā), which are fragments of burning embers (ulmukakhaṇḍa) that cross over or leap across it. As Kṣīrasvāmin says:
"preṅkholitaḥ, taralitaḥ, lalitaḥ, and also lolitaḥ. [It is] fierce for the men and women falling into heaps of glowing coals.
In which there is weeping; thus it is so. || 25 ||
In the meantime, the queen, intoxicated by her youth and overwhelmed with fear, entered followed by her female companions. (26)
Together with her female friends and women. || 26 ||
Then one of her companions informed the king: "O Lord, the queen has arrived, having fled from within the inner apartments. (27)
She made known; she informed. This is from the root *jñā* (to know/understand) in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense. || 27 ||
All these guardians of the inner apartments, brought before the royal gate by powerful men with raised weapons, were crushed by the arrogant enemies. (28)
"Ground" means pulverized. || 28 ||
"Our city has been seized by enemies who have approached unsuspected from afar"—hearing this and looking out, he [the king] will go forth to battle with his two queens. (29)
That action in which no doubt exists is "without doubt" (aśaṅkam). "Brought away" means carried off. "O two Goddesses" is an address. || 29 ||
"May this wife of mine, who is a bee at your lotus-feet, be protected by you," having said this, the king departed with his eyes agitated by anger. || 230 ||
The six-footed one is the female bee. || 230 ||
Then Līlā beheld Līlā, whose form was identical to her own, like a lion emerging from a forest cave shattered by a rutting elephant.
[The suffixes] dūr and yaḥ [are applied] after the word *kandara*. || 31 || 32 ||
She was beautiful to behold, appearing like a reflection in a mirror.
Prabuddhalīlā said:
"O Goddess, tell me, what is this? Why am I standing here? How is it that she who was formerly 'I' is now standing here as 'this'? (33)
"Why is this woman standing here? Why is she standing here as if she were my equal?"—this is the sense.
Now, one might suspect that she is not a beautiful woman with a human body produced by the power of yoga; anticipating this doubt, he says: "She who... (verse 33).
Jñapti said:
In whatever state your husband was when he died in that city at that time,
in that very same state and with respect to that very same object, he indeed saw him once again.
However, because your husband has been permeated by the meditation upon you and has thus fashioned a playmate who is similar to you, the sport remains equal to yours;
intending this as the answer, he says: "yādṛg" (of such a kind). The meaning is:
"tatsadṛśam evārtham" (an object that is indeed similar to that). || 34 ||
That very form of all objects which is non-deceptive is reflected as such in the mirror of the mind. (35)

Raising the objection: "If this *līlā* (divine play) is imagined, why does no contradiction arise in it, as is the case with nacre-silver and the like? he says: "Non-contradictory" (*avisaṃvādī*). This means that its nature—which consists of all objects that are non-contradictory, i.e., devoid of contradiction (which is synonymous with sublation) during the state of empirical transaction—is reflected in his mind.

That very same thing, which had appeared in such a way in your husband’s mind, being non-contradictory, reflects in the mirror of the mind at a later time. The meaning is that what was previously experienced as non-contradictory exists in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and manifests in the mirror of the mind exactly as it was, at a subsequent time. || 35 ||
Dream is unreal in the waking state, and the waking state is unreal in the dream;
death is unreal in birth, and birth is likewise composed of unreality in death. (36)

Now, one might object: "In the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), since there is no contradiction [between perception and subsequent experience], the very fact that things are imagined (*kalpitatva*) remains unestablished.
Anticipating this doubt, he establishes the falsity (*mithyātva*) of everything that is perceived on the grounds of its variability, beginning with the words "In a dream" (*svapne*). || 36 ||
Thus, this is neither existent nor non-existent; it manifests as mere delusion.
Yet these experiences arise from some prior experience. (37)

Having first demonstrated the variety of worldly delusions, he clarifies the previously stated point— that the novel play is grasped by a corresponding delusion— by means of the verse beginning with "anubhūtayaḥ" and so forth.
Certain experiences arise as errors through the medium of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from previous experiences. || 37 ||
(172) Some are of unprecedented experience, some are equal, and others likewise unequal;
she is of your character, of your conduct, of your lineage, and of your form, O virtuous lady. (38)

Some, however, are of unprecedented experience; those for whom prior experiences do not exist as causes are "of unprecedented experience. Some are equal, meaning similar: "of your character" means having a character like yours;
"of your lineage" means having a lineage like yours; "of your form" means having a body like yours. (38)
Thus this play appears as a reflection born of creative intuition;
O lady, this Vidūratha is indeed your husband, who has cast off his body.
The connection is as follows: this reflection of your husband, born as a reflection (*pratibimba*), appears as "play" (*līlā*). || 39 ||
Having reached that very inner apartment, he will become such a self.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these words of the goddess, Līlā, who resided in that city, stood before her with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words while bowing low. (41)
That city was Vidūratha’s city; she whose abode or place [of origin] was that city is thus described. She joined her palms in reverence, having made an añjali. || 41 || 42 ||
The goddess Bhagavatī Jñapti has been constantly worshipped by me;
O Mistress of Gods, O Mother, you are exactly like her in every respect.
Therefore, out of compassion for my wretched state, grant me this boon, O fair-faced one:
that I may cast off my body in battle where my husband stands.
He who endures great humiliation for the sake of extreme greed is a wretch; compassion for such a wretch is "pity for the wretched" (kṛpaṇakāruṇya); therefore [one should avoid it]. 43–49.
When the Goddess said, "May this be so— that I shall remain there as her wife with this very body," Pūrvalīlā then spoke.
(173) Pūrvalīlā said:
O Sovereign Lady, tell me why I was not led by this very same body to that mountain village in this other world? (45)
The Goddess said:
"O lady of excellent complexion, I do nothing for anyone;
it is the will of living beings themselves that swiftly brings about everything."
While you were propitiating me, such was your resolve: "May I be liberated. For that reason, you were awakened by them through those various means.
"Requested by her for this very purpose, I granted it;
thus does the resolve of men bear fruit through the grace of the Lord."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Vidūratha, adorned with great jewels, emerged from his palace surrounded by a vast retinue.
Beholding the hosts of heroes, he ascended his excellent chariot,
which was shaped like a gabled pavilion and adorned with pearls and rubies.

A *kūṭa* is a mountain peak; a house situated like a peak is a *kūṭāgāra*. He whose form is equal to a *kūṭāgāra* is so described. Alternatively, it refers to that which has a form equal to a *kūṭāgāra*, meaning a house made of a peaked roof. || 250 ||
Then there arose the fierce sound of kettledrums, filled with the roar of various unrestrained clouds and intensified by echoes from the mountain walls.

*Udapatat* means he rose up. *Uddāmanānābhraravanirbharaḥ*: "filled with the roar of various unrestrained clouds"; *uddāmāni* refers to unrestrained, *nānābhrāṇi* to various clouds (various rain-clouds), and *ravavannirbharaḥ* means a fullness like their roar; that is to say, dense. *Śailabhittiṣu*:
on the mountain walls, i.e., the side-walls of the mountains; *pratidhvānaiḥ*: by means of echoes; *dāruṇaḥ*: terrible or horrific.
Terrible with the echoes from the mountain walls. || 51 ||
With the tinkling sounds of networks of small bells, with the clanging of weapons striking one another,
with the crackling sounds of bows, and with the whistling songs of arrows; (52)

By the clanging sounds produced by the striking together of weapons—the *hetis* being weapons, as Amara states: "The rays of the sun, weapons, and flames of fire are all called *heti*"—[the sky was filled]. 52.
With the mutual challenges of the warriors and the tumultuous weeping of the captive women,
the sound filled the entire cavity of the universe, as solid as a mountain of stone.
A *bandī* is a woman abducted by force; as Kṣīrasvāmin has said: "A *bandī* is a woman forcibly carried off.

A *śilāghana* is a stone with dense internal structure. That by whom the entire cavity of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) was filled and occupied by such *śilāghanas* is so described. A *kuhara* is a hollow or cavity. [He did this] everywhere with an exceedingly great sound.
The meaning is that the cavity of the universe was filled, as if packed solid with stone. || 53 ||
Bhīma became graspable by the hand, filling the groves of the ten directions;
meanwhile, thick dust arose, obscuring the sky.
A *kuñja* is a place whose interior is covered by creepers and the like. The ten directions (*daśāśā*) are themselves the ten *kuñjas* of the belly of the universe;
he who fills them is the "filler of the ten-directional *kuñjas*" (*daśāśā-kuñja-pūraka*).
Folly, like darkness, reached its full intensity through his youth;
the king entered the enemy's army as Mount Mandara enters the Ocean of Milk.
Solidity, density. || 55 ||
The conflagrations produced by the clashing of weapons blazed like flaming torches;
the heroic clouds rumbled as they rained down torrents of arrow-showers. || 56 ||

They blazed; they acted as fire. "Jvalana" means fires; according to Amara, synonyms for fire are *kṛpīṭayoni*, *jvalana*, *jātavedas*, and *tanūnapāt*. They roared; they made a thundering sound. || 56 ||
Cruel weapons fell like herons upon the limbs of the heroes,
and the clashing of weapons in the sky produced a sharp *paṭapaṭa* sound.

The *kaṅka* is the bird known as the *lohapṛṣṭha*; indeed, Amarasimha states that "the *lohapṛṣṭha* is the *kaṅka*. They flew, meaning they performed the act of flying. "With a *paṭapaṭā* sound" is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). "Crushing" (*niṣpiṣṭayaḥ*) refers to the acts of grinding or pounding. || 57 ||
In that march of Yama, rows of headless trunks rose up; the dust was settled by the blood, and the darkness by the fires of the weapons. (58)
The darknesses and the terrors of noise were gradually pacified and stilled by the rays of his weapons and fires.
Due to their single-minded focus on battle and their certainty regarding death, they were free from fear of noise; there was only the combat itself, devoid of foul words and confusion.
Through their singular focus on battle and their certainty regarding death, they became silent, as if to ensure that no ill-omened sound was heard.

With floods of arrows rushing together in equal combat, with *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons falling amidst a clatter of *ṭaki-ṭaki* sounds, and great missiles colliding with a ringing *kaṇa-kaṇa* noise, that battle was as difficult to cross as the ocean inhabited by sea-monsters (*timi*).

"Samasamam" is an imitation of sound (*śabdānukāra*). It means that in which battle the flood of arrows was falling together (*saṃvahan*) in such a way as to be "equal-to-equal" (*samasamaram*). Alternatively, it refers to that [battle] in which there were words of mutual equality (*samasama-vaccha*) of equal speed (*samāḥ* = *samajavāḥ*), and floods of arrows were falling together. Or else:

In that [battle], showers of arrows were carried along—either evenly and very straightly, or simultaneously and with a great roar; or "ṭaki-ṭakita" is an imitation of sound, or "kalakala. A *bhuśuṇḍī* is a particular kind of weapon.
The illustration regarding the mere quality of being difficult to cross is "like a whale and the ocean," meaning like the sea. || 260 || 61 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
While this terrible tumult of battle was occurring, the two Līlās spoke thus to the divine Goddess: || 61 ||
"O Goddess, why does our husband suddenly lose in battle?
Speak, for even though you are pleased with us, this elephant has fled. (62)
Regarding the word "devī": "no" means "not" for us; "no" here signifies negation. The connection is with the phrase "in the battle where the elephants have fled and been made to dissolve. || 62 ||
The Goddess said:
I have been long propitiated by that King Vidūratha, the enemy of [my] foe, for the sake of his daughters' victory, but not by King Vidūratha himself. (63)
Therefore, he alone triumphs and Vidūratha is not defeated;
for I am possessed by the thought: "By this [act] I shall surely be liberated. (64)
Therefore, O child, liberation will come to you in the form of inspired eloquence;
however, this enemy of yours shall be victorious and rule the kingdom. (65)
She is of the nature of creative intuition and consists of mind. || 65 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
While the goddess was speaking thus and as the two armies were engaged in combat,
the sun rose from the mountain of sunrise, as if to witness the marvel.
While the two were engaged in combat. || 66 ||
The world shone as if it had emerged from an ocean of collyrium;
the rays of the sun fell like beautiful streams of molten gold.
Kajjala is lampblack; kanakaniṣpandāḥ are golden rods. || 67 ||
In the meantime, all the armies met their destruction;
the battlefield became as if empty, with only a few soldiers remaining on either side.
The soldiers are assembled in the army. || 68 ||
Having reached the city of his enemy, King Sindhudvīra, with his neck held high,
strung his bow, making the quarters of the sky resound.

He drew his bow—the bow named Sindhu—so that its neck was raised high; that is to say, he stretched the bowstring. It was an action in which the quarters of the sky were made to resound on all sides. || 69 ||
Like the shore of the mountain of the immortals being shattered by the gale at the end of an aeon,
the powerful king cast off [his grief] in the morning, as if shedding the rays of the sun.
In this context, *āsphoṭa* means striking; *amaragiri* is Meru; and *karān* refers to rays. || 270 ||
The sharp, exceedingly painful-to-touch flights of arrows were such that even the ocean possessed only the lightness of being pierced through. (71)
*Śilīmukhas* are arrows. || 71 || 72 ||
Thus the mighty-armed Sindhurāja, having sported for a long time at the head of the battle,
afflicted Vidūratha with showers of arrows.
With his banner severed, his chariot shattered, his horses broken, and his charioteer slain;
with his bow and armor cut to pieces, and all his limbs mangled, he was utterly overwhelmed.
*Kārmukam* means a bow; *varma* means armor. || 73 ||
Having pierced his chest— [a place] with a broad stone-slab-like surface and a firm, thick head—
with arrows as hard as thunderbolts, he caused him to fall to the ground.
That heart whose upper portion—the head—is as firm and thick as a broad and expansive stone slab; such is its nature. || 74 || 75 ||
"The king is slain! The king is slain by a rival king in battle!"—when these words arose, the kingdom fell into great agitation. || 75 ||
A multitude of wagons was fleeing with heavy loads of vessels and household goods,
while a great throng of citizens fled along with their wives who were crying out in distress.

"Bhāṇḍopaskara" means: that kingdom whose multitude of carts was fleeing with loads of vessels, utensils, and implements; that [kingdom] whose mass of womenfolk was distressed and weeping on all sides due to their crying; and [the city] of the citizens who were fleeing and running away.

That which has a heap (*utkara*)—meaning a pile (*puñja*)—of the inhabitants of the city is described thus. According to Amara, "a collection (*nikāya*), a heap (*puñja*), and a mass (*rāśi*) are synonyms; *utkara* and *kūṭa* (the latter being neuter) also denote a heap. (76, 77, 78)
In the meantime, seeing her husband before her rendered unconscious with only his breath remaining, Līlā spoke to Sarasvatī.
"O Mother, this husband of mine has set out here to cast off his body;
I shall follow my husband. Have mercy, O Maheśvarī! (78)
Having spoken thus, by virtue of her knowledge and meditative absorption, she, possessing great power, instantly leapt into the sky like a bird of delicate form. (79)
"Pupluve" means she performed a leaping motion; this is from the root *plu* (to go) in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). "Pelavākārā" refers to her whose form was delicate and slender;
according to Amara, "pelava" means sparse, thin, or slender. || 79 || 280 ||
Then, having crossed the paths of the clouds and further the regions of the winds, he emerged from the path of the sun and passed beyond the path of the stars. || 280 ||

Having ascended to and reached the abode of Brahmā and the shell of the cosmic egg, and having then pierced the shell of the cosmic egg as well as the coverings of water and the other elements; || 81 ||

The shell of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa-kharpara*) is the site, that is, the skull of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa-kapāla*). According to Amara, "kharpara" and "kapāla" are synonyms and are not feminine.
Having meditated with extreme speed, he leaped forward and reached the interior of the great sky of consciousness, whose far boundaries and limits were unseen.
The great consciousness itself is the sky known as the Supreme Self; its interior, its middle, is the interior of the sky of great consciousness.
Fearing that even the Great Self might have a limitation like the coverings of earth and so forth, he says: "unseen," etc. (Verse 82).
Even for Garuḍa, though he were to search in every direction for hundreds of millions of kalpas,
there exist therein countless and abundant lakhs of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
The connection is that even by Garuḍa its further limit and boundary could not be seen. || 83 || 84 || 85 ||
Like fruits in a great forest that have not seen one another, they were there,
with one standing before them within an extensive enclosure.
Having pierced through, she entered within and reached the city of Padmapura;
having arrived there at that pavilion, the Goddess was augmented by her Śakti.
Having entered and stood near the corpse of Puṣpagupta, she beheld it and reflected with a heart whose very essence was trembling: || 86 ||
"With a throbbing self" means with a nature that has been set in motion; that is to say, with a nature blossoming in wonder. || 86 || 87 || 88 || 89 || 290 ||
(179) "This man shall surely become my husband, for he is the foremost among the best of heroes; and by the grace of the Goddess, I have arrived here first. (87)
Having reflected thus, Līlā, possessing charming youth, took the beautiful fly-whisk in her hand and fanned the king of kings.
Vasiṣṭha said:
In the meantime, with their divine vision, the two queens beheld the life-force of the king who had fallen upon the earth, situated in the sky.
Then, from that [place], the triad consisting of Jīvakalā, Līlā, and Jñapti flew away;
however, Jīvalekhā did not see those two Yoginīs.
Following him as he passed from one creation to another,
they reached Padmarājapura and the pavilion of Līlā’s inner apartments.
In an instant, they both entered at their ease, and Jīvalekhā went ahead;
then they saw the two goddesses lying on one side of the bed of the corpse.
In the meantime, while Līlā had set out before Vidūratha and arrived first,
Jñapti again approached the son of Vidūratha, Jīva.
Vaidūratha means belonging to Vidūratha.
Then, as she restrained the movement of her mind through volition,
Līlā, with her beautiful eyes, spoke to the Blessed Lady.

With a resolve characterized by the thought, "Let this living soul not enter the corpse; let it remain instead in the sky," she obstructed it, that is, she brought about its confinement. She was one whose eyes were *lalita*—that is, beautiful. 94 || 95 ||
O Goddess, why is that former body of mine not seen? || 95 ||
Jñapti said:
Listen, O great-souled one, to what happened to your body during your play;
while you were absorbed in meditative concentration, your physical frame [remained behind]. (96)
She whose intention (abhiprāya) is a great resolve (mahā-āśaya) is so described; that is the address: "O Mahāśaye! (96, 97, 98).
Lifeless, fallen upon the ground like a withered leaf, he has become like a block of wood or a wall—a corpse as cold as frost. (97)
Then the ministers, having arrived and being certain that he was dead,
threw him onto the funeral pyre and burned him with sandalwood logs and ghee.
Now, seeing you arrived here in personified form, it will be a great marvel that you have come from the other world. 99.
Now you are seen with a subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), consisting of mere appearance, augmented by the power of yogic success (yogarddhi).
By means of the *ātivāhika* body, that is, the *liṅgaśarīra*; he whose form consists of mere intuition, that is, mere cognition, is such [as described].

That body of yours has been forgotten due to the complete exhaustion of latent impressions; through the established vision of the subtle body (*ativāhika*), the physical (*ādhibhautika*) aspect subsides. || 1 ||

The body is gross (*sthūla*). By means of the "perfected subtle-body perspective" (*rūḍhātivāhika-dṛśā*), that is, by means of the firm conviction (*dṛḍha-pramā*) that there is no physical body (*ādhibhautika-deha*) distinct from the mind—just as in the case of a dream-body—the latent impression of the gross body (*vāsanāyāḥ sthūladehavāsanāyāḥ*) [is destroyed]. Therefore they say: "The body of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) is merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*). || 1 ||
Therefore come, O Līlā; by means of our creative will, let us both manifest ourselves to Līlā so that worldly activity may proceed.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: "As long as I manifest myself through the play of volition—that is, through the sport of volition—let worldly activity proceed. Alternatively, the word *yāvat* may have the same meaning as the word *tāvat*. || 2 ||
(181) Just as we thought, "Let Līlā see these two," then Līlā, her eyes darting about, appeared there by the power of the goddess Jñapti.
The grammatical connection is as follows: "When the Goddess Jñapti thought, 'Let these two of us be seen by Līlā,'" [they appeared]. (3, 4, 5)
He beheld the house, radiant with a mass of that splendor;
having looked at the house before him, he beheld Līlā and Jñapti.
Rising up in agitation, she fell at their feet;
then Jñapti and Līlā sat down upon the seats.
Jñapti said:
"O you two who walk with the grace of swans, O playful ones with lovely eyes!
Let us raise this king once again from his bed of corpses."
"Moving with the grace of a swan," "moving with a charm captivating like a swan," and "O playful ones, O lovely-eyed ones"—these are vocative dual forms in the nominative case. (6)
Having spoken thus, she released her life-force like a lotus releases its fragrance;
taking the form of a gust of wind, it went near her nostrils.

"That fragrance which captivates the mind by its far-reaching pervasion is called *āmoda*; that which is exceedingly diffusive is called *vāsi*," says Amara. The breeze, like air entering the hollow of a bamboo flute, quickly entered the space of the nostrils;
it attained the splendor of the mouth of the living being residing within him.
Gradually all his limbs shone with vitality;
he expanded his limbs, which were full of rasa and soft.
They shone; they produced radiance. He expanded it; he made it manifold. || 9 || 310 ||
He opened his eyes, which brought forth pure light,
and rose up with a radiant body like the Vindhya mountain come to life.
He asked with a deep and resonant voice, "Who stands there?
Then Līlādvaya spoke before him, saying, "Let it be commanded."
"Let the command be given—let it be ordered—in a manner that possesses a deep and resonant sound. 11 || 12 ||
Looking about, he asked, "Who are you? Who is she? And from where has she come?
To him, Līlā said, "O Lord, listen to what I shall tell you. (12)
"O Līlā, I am your former companion;
this woman here is your second Līlā, created by me through my divine play."
*Mahilā*, *vanitā*, *pratīpadarśinī*, *vāmā*, *mahilā*, and *vanitā* are synonyms; thus says Amara. (13)
This auspicious image made of reflected form, which has been acquired for your sake,
is seated here upon this great golden throne at the head of the bed.
"For your sake" means for the purpose of your own interest. || 14 || 15 || 16 ||
"This auspicious Goddess Sarasvatī is the mother of the three worlds. Having heard this, the king rose up at the lotus feet of the one who grants knowledge. (15)
Having become composed, he fell down, saying, "O Sarasvatī, salutations be unto you!
To him who had spoken thus, Sarasvatī spoke after touching him with her hand. (16)
May all calamities, along with all evil deeds and wrong views, go away from you toward auspiciousness and infinite bliss;
may the people always remain joyful, and may the great ones in the kingdom be steadfast and ever flourish. 17
The populace is a multitude of people. || 17 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Sarasvatī, having said "So be it," vanished right there amidst the deep,
resonant, and tumultuous sounds of the chanting of "Jaya," "Maṅgala," and "Puṇyāha."

"Ghuṃghuma" is an onomatopoeic imitation of sound. It refers to that [place] in which there were "ghuṃghuma" sounds along with shouts of victory and the sounds of auspicious and meritorious proclamations (*puṇyāha*). || 18 || 19 || 320 ||
(183) Thereupon the royal palace became crowded with joyful and well-nourished people;
then the brahmins, ministers, and kings consecrated him. 19.
Līlā, Līlā’s husband, and the king— all of great intellect and liberated while living—
delighted in recounting their past adventures as if they were amorous dalliances.
That king, fully awakened by the knowledge of realization and endowed with the two-fold play,
ruled an irreproachable kingdom there for eighty thousand years.
"Fully awakened by the knowledge of realization" means that he was perfectly enlightened through the words of wisdom taught by the Goddess Jñapti.

Having thus established a kingdom free from all thorns, those of pure consciousness, being liberated while living (jīvanmukta), attained the state of liberation beyond the body (videhamukti). || 322 ||

Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Narrative of Līlā," within the "Narrative of the Pavilion" in the "Section on Origination" of the *Mokṣopāya* (The Way to Liberation) by the venerable Vālmīki. || 2 ||

Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Narrative of Līlā," in the *Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Yogavāsiṣṭha* composed by the venerable Ātmasukha, disciple of the most worshipful feet of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Uttama. || 2 ||
The Third Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
This sinless narrative of Līlā has been told to you, O Rāma, for the purpose of removing the defect of the visible world; abandon the density of the universe.

He introduces the following [verse] in order to state briefly for easy comprehension the meaning that has been explained in detail through the two discourses titled "The Birth from Space" (Ākāśajākhya) and "The Play" (Līlākhya): "This... (etad). For the sake of removing the defect of the visible world—that is, for the removal of the defect consisting in the perception of the visible world itself as being real—he speaks of its "solidity," which means its density or reality. 1.
p.
184) Here exists Brahman, which is pure in essence yet appears as the non-existent;
it is expanded, vast, the embodiment of conscious Bhairava, imperishable, and named Bliss. || 2 ||

"Non-existent appearance" (*asadābhāsam*) means that from which there is the appearance or manifestation of the unreal, indeterminable phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Alternatively, it means that in which the appearance—the object of perception—is non-existent or not present. "Pure self" (*acchātman*) means having a transparent nature.
He states two meanings for the word *brahman*: "expanded" (*prabṛṃhitam*), meaning augmented by the illusory phenomenal world; and "pure" (*accham*).
"Augmented" (*prabṛṃhitam*) means endowed with great magnitude that is vast and unrestrained.

There is no contradiction between "vastness" and "augmentation" being present together in one [subject], namely through the perspectives of reality (*tattva*) and its opposite. "Consciousness" (*cit*) has the nature of pure awareness (*jñapti*). "The form of Bhairava" (*bhairavavapuḥ*) means a terrifying form. [As it is said: "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear the sun rises."

This is because of the Vedic revelation, "He is the Sun," and also because of the words of the Blessed One: "Out of fear of Him this wind blows; out of fear of Him the sun burns; out of fear of Him Agni is kindled along with the mountains; and the earth does not sink. || 2 ||
That which is equal, perfectly full, pure being, and unmarked— undefinable even for those who know it— that is the peaceful, supreme state.
If such a Brahman exists, then let it be pointed out by distinguishing it as "this is that"; to this he says: "Of that, which...
It is equal, being of one and the same form throughout the arising and destruction of the visible world; or rather, it is equal within all beings.
It is unmarked, being without any stain or characteristic. Even for those who possess knowledge (*vidas*), it is indefinable and inexpressible, like the sweetness of milk.

It is peaceful and changeless. By the phrase "the supreme abode of Viṣṇu," he indicates that this [reality] is established by scriptural authority (śruti), such as the aforementioned Vedic texts. || 3 ||
O Rāghava, know that the Jīva is that slight vibration of Brahman which is like [the movement] of an ocean without wind, or like that of a lamp in a windless place. || 4 ||

The true nature of Brahman has been stated; he now clarifies it through superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and negation (*apavāda*) by means of seven verses beginning with "The vibration of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ sphuraṇam*). The word *atha* introduces a new topic; *api* indicates conjunction.
Just as there is no movement in a windless ocean or in a lamp situated where there is no wind, so too, whatever slight vibration or motion exists in Brahman—[that is what is being discussed].
Know it as the living soul; do not bring it [into doubt]. || 4 ||

That very [consciousness], through its dense awareness, gradually attains the state of "I-ness" (ahantā), just as a spark of fire, due to an abundance of fuel, reaches its own full capacity for illumination. (5)
That very [consciousness], through that same manifestation— by means of a dense perception (*ghanasaṃvitti*), that is, by means of a thick volition (*sāndrasaṃkalpa*),

meaning by means of the cultivation of a dense ego-sense (*nibiḍāhaṃkārabhāvanā*)— becomes the "atom of fire" (*vahnyaṇu*), which is a subtle portion of fire, of the element *agni*, characterized as the state of "I-ness" (*ahantā*), the nature of the ego (*ahaṃkāratā*). || 5 ||
When it turns toward conceptualization, that very [Self] indeed becomes the ego (ahaṃkāra),
known by such names as citta, cetas, manas, māyā, and prakṛti.

The word *uta* has the sense of *api* (even/also). One should supply the ellipsis and connect it as follows: "When the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) has turned toward conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*), that is to say, when it is oriented toward mental ideation (*manobhāvanā*), it becomes the entity designated by such names as 'mind' (*citta*) and so forth. || 6 ||
For this very reason, the mind first arose from that [Supreme Cause];
consisting of thought and possessing expansive capacity, it stretches out this world.
In the sequence thus described, the mind first arises from the supreme cause, Brahman;

and that mind, consisting of reflection (manana) and consisting of volition (saṃkalpa), is "all-encompassing" (ābhogi). It is called all-encompassing because it possesses fullness (ābhoga)—that is, because it pervades the world, which is its own effect. || 7 ||
Through the surging waves of consciousness, which extend across the shoreless expanse of the near and the far,
this very Self manifests as the single ocean of consciousness.

He clarifies what was stated regarding its state of being effortless (*abhogitva*) with the verse beginning "apāra" (boundless). "Pāra" means the further shore; "avāra" means the near shore, according to the statement:
"pārāvāre" refers to the distant and the near shores. Those whose expanse (*vistāra*) is boundless on both sides are "apārāvāravistārāṇi.
Consciousness itself—synonymous with volition (*saṃkalpa*)—is the water; these are the waters of consciousness (*saṃvitsalila*). And they are those which are boundless on both sides.

The grammatical connection is as follows: these waters of consciousness and those [elements] together constitute this very Self as a single ocean of consciousness; having become the mind, it expands itself in the form of the world within its shoreless and boundless expanse through the surging waves of the waters of consciousness. || 8 ||
Due to the power of the mind, this state called saṃsāra has entered into a long-lasting sleep;
because of incorrect vision, there is a firm conviction of it being a person, just like the perception of a man in a tree trunk.
The phrase "a long dream" has a clear meaning, based on such scriptural passages as, "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name," and so forth. (9)
(186) Just as duality does not exist between consciousness and the self, nor between consciousness and the individual soul, so too there is no difference between the individual soul and the mind;
and just as there is no difference between the individual soul and the mind, so too there is no difference between the mind and the creation. || 10 ||

Just as there is no duality or difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—the two aspects of the reality of consciousness (cid-ātmatattva)—which stand in the relation of effect and cause, so too there is no difference between the individual soul and the mind, which likewise stand in the relation of effect and cause. In this same way, there is also no difference between the mind and the phenomenal world (prapañca), both of which are essentially the causal Self. || 10 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
In this very context, they cite this ancient history,
containing the entire web of great questions spoken by the Rākṣasī.

He introduces the narrative of Sūcī regarding the point already stated with the words "atraiva" (right here). It should be understood that this story is intended to show that even for those of a *tāmasa* nature who take pleasure in violence, the path to liberation may somehow arise through an extraordinary prior effort that is not connected to violence. The term "āvalitākhilam" means having encompassed everything.
On the northern side of the Himavat mountain, there is a fierce female statue named Karkaṭī, like a carved figure on a mountain of collyrium paste.
She appeared like a wooden statue upon the mountain of ink-paste to the north of the mountain of soot-paste. || 12 ||
Her eyes were like steady streaks of lightning, her knees like the trunks of date-palm trees;
the tips of her nails were like sun-crystals of beryl, and she was a body composed of sinews and knots of bone.

She whose eyes are like steady streaks of lightning is described as such; this is an *abhūtopamā* (hyperbolic simile). She whose knees are like a date palm (*kharjūra*)—a specific type of tree characterized by long grass-like stalks and which is both tall and crooked—is described as such. She whose tips of the nails are like the sun made of *vaidūrya* gems is [described as such].

She whose nails are like the sun upon lapis lazuli; in some places it is read as "vaidūryasūryogranakhā. She is "snāyvasthigranthidehinī," one whose body is joined by the knots of sinews and bones—the sinews being the *vasnasā*, the bands that envelop the limbs. || 13 ||
(187) Because her body was so vast and because her own food was difficult to obtain,
the fire of her stomach remained unsatiated, like that of the ocean’s shore. 14.
Like the submarine fire (vaḍavānala) produced from the ocean-foam of his own food—consisting of human flesh and the like—his internal digestive fire remained insatiable. || 14 || 15 ||
That large-bellied woman never attained satisfaction;
like the tongue of the submarine fire, she once reflected thus: (15)
I swallow all the people dwelling in Jambudvīpa as well,
incessantly and without breathing, just as the ocean swallows a mass of water.
I swallow, I devour; incessantly, continuously. || 16 ||
"Like a mirage quenched by a cloud, my hunger is thus appeased;
I shall perform supreme austerity with an undaunted mind.
Having reflected thus, she [proceeded] with the desire to destroy the multitude of all living beings. (17)

"By clouds," [it is said]. For a mirage, that is the shimmering heat of a desert, is quenched by the sprinkling of clouds. That [deed], however, was performed with the intent to kill the entire multitude of living beings, with the desire to slaughter the whole assembly of creatures. 17–18.
Then, for the sake of penance, she remembered the mountain Bhūtadurgama;
having gone there and bathed, she resolved to perform austerities.
With her eyes flickering like the moon and the sun, she stood on one foot;
thus the days, fortnights, and months passed for her in succession.

She whose eyes follow the pulsations and movements of the moon and the sun is "Candrārkaspandalocanā. This means that because her gaze is fixed upon the moon and the sun, her eyes move in accordance with their motions. || 19 ||
To her who remained unattached amidst cold and heat, as if she were carved from a mountain,
the Grandfather (Brahmā) came after eight thousand years.
As if fashioned from the very substance of the mountain itself, she remained there as if established by that material cause. || 20 || 21 ||
(188) Even among the lowly, severe austerity arises for the sake of attaining success;
having bowed to him with her mind alone, that virtuous woman remained just as she was. (21)
"Who is capable of removing this hunger?"—thus he became absorbed in thought.
Then it occurred to him: "O Lord, I shall request this one boon. (22)

*Alam* means capable (*śakta*). *Ā* is used for recollection; according to Amara, *ā* is used in the sense of recollection (*smṛti*) and in a sentence (*vākya*), as well as being a *pragṛhya* vowel. || 22 ||
"May I become like a needle made of iron, yet as if not of iron—a 'living-needle'—so that I may swallow all people according to this one's desire. (23)

"May I be like a needle made of iron, though not of iron; may I be as if made of steel, though not of steel—a 'living-needle' for living beings, a suture for them. With this boon, may I swallow the world in due order for the destruction of hunger, according to their desires"—this is the connection [of the verse]. || 23 ||
"Gradually, for the destruction of hunger, the destruction of hunger is the supreme happiness;
I shall enter the hearts of all living beings here.
To her, as she was reflecting thus, the Dweller of the Lotus (Viṣṇu) said:
"Together" means together with the vital breaths (prāṇas). As he will say: "Having entered the heart with the vital breaths. || 24 ||
"O daughter Karkaṭikā, you who wear a garland like a cloud upon the mountain of the Rākṣasa clan!
Arise; I am pleased with you, so accept a desired boon. (25)
The race of Rākṣasas is indeed a mountain; O you two who are like clouds upon that mountain of the Rākṣasa race! O you two, cloud-like ornaments of the mountain of the Rākṣasa clan! 25.
Karkaṭī said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, if you will grant me this boon, O Ordainer, may I become a needle for living beings—not made of iron, but made of steel. (26)
O Creator, O Viriñca! || 26 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having said to her, "So be it," the Grandfather spoke again:
"You shall become a female needle, and you shall be accompanied by the affliction of *viṣūcikā*."

Desiring that the entire world, which is indicated by the term "living being" (jīva) established in common usage, should not be submerged in an unprecedented ocean of suffering due to the gift of the *karkaṭī* fruit,
[the Lord], following the dictates of acquired karma, wished to bestow upon her the state of the disease of cholera (*viṣūcikā*) which exists spontaneously in the world.

The Blessed One, the Grandfather, spoke again: "Sūcikā with an upasarga. Because she exists together with this prefix *vi*, she will become *sopasargā-sūcikā*. He shows her as precisely such a *sopasargasūcikā*: "Viṣūcikā" (the cholera-demoness). 27–28.
"You shall indeed commit violence against those who eat poorly, those who undertake evil deeds, fools, those in miserable circumstances, those dwelling in wretched lands, and the wicked. (28)
Having entered the heart along with the vital breaths, by afflicting the lotus-like spleen and other organs,
you shall become the disease of cholera, consisting of a streak of wind.

"Padma" means a disease called *padma*, namely splenomegaly (*plīhā*) or abdominal tumors (*gulma*); because you will be afflicted by *padma*, *plīha*, and so forth, you shall become a person suffering from cholera (*viṣūcikā*), known as "Vātalekhā. (29–30)
"You shall encounter both those with qualities (saguṇa) and those without qualities (nirguṇa).
This mantra is spoken by me for the purpose of treating those who possess qualities."

Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ rāṃ, obeisance to the power of Viṣṇu! O Blessed One, Power of Viṣṇu, come! Seize, seize! Burn, burn! Strike, strike! Cook, cook! Grind, grind! Destroy, destroy! Drive far away, drive far away, svāhā! O Viṣūcikā, go, go to the Himavat mountains; live within the essence of the lunar orb!
"Gato 'si svāhā. Having thus applied the great mantra upon the palm of his left hand, the practitioner, remaining self-controlled, should wipe away the fourfold form with that hand.

O Viṣṇu-śakti! O Viṣṇu-śakti! The afflicted one is addressed: "O Jīva, you have gone to the nectar-filled lunar orb, svāhā! The meaning is: "May it come here of its own accord; may the lunar orb itself go to the oblation consisting of the living soul (jīvātman) being offered by me. [The practitioner recites] the mantra, the great mantra.
"Among mantras, the great mantra. "In the palm of the left hand" means in the inner region of the left hand; that is, on its surface.

"Having placed [it]" means having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). The practitioner of mantras (*māntrika*), having written the syllables of the mantra with his right hand upon the palm of his own left hand—this is the meaning. "The form of the afflicted" means the appearance of one who is diseased. "Restrained" means self-controlled. || 31 ||
One should visualize that Karkaṭī, who has been held back while facing the snowy mountain— harsh, enraged, and crushed by the mallet of the mantra. (32)
She has been crushed by that very mantra, which acts as a mallet.
One should meditate upon the patient as being situated within the moon at the heart of the elixir (rasāyana),
liberated from old age and death, and freed from all mental anxieties, physical diseases, and delusions.
Within the heart of the elixir, inside the nectar. || 33 ||
For the practitioner, having become pure, having sipped water for ritual purification, and being well-composed, cuts through all colic pains by means of this sequence. (34)
"Having sipped water" means having properly performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth. || 34 || 35 ||
Having spoken thus, the Lord Creator vanished right there;
then she appeared as one the size of a span, and thereafter in the form of a finger's breadth.
Then she became equal in size to a black gram or a śamī seed, and subsequently she became a needle, [piercing] the helpless body of someone who was emaciated and infirm. (36)

"Equal to a *māṣa*-bean" means equal to a *māṣa*-pod; that is to say, equal to the shell of a *māṣa* seed. According to Amara, "the word *śamī* [is used for] a pod (*śimbā*)," with three genders in the subsequent cases. || 36 ||
Having entered within, it becomes an internal wind-needle, causing extreme piercing pain (viṣūcikā) in some person whose body is afflicted, distressed, and impaired. (37)

A "wind-needle" (*vātasūcī*) is a needle consisting of wind; it becomes an "excessive colic" (*ativiṣūcikā*), a disease that surpasses ordinary colic. This occurs in one whose body is thin, whose body is emaciated, who is impaired—that is, who is unwell. || 37 ||
Once it has entered and become indicated by the vital breath (jīva), internal piercing pain (viṣūcikā) arises.
The locative case in "jīvasūcitve" is used in the sense of a cause (nimitta-saptamī). || 38 ||
Thus, for many years, she who was solely intent on destroying the lives of living beings wandered through the sky and likewise upon the surface of the earth with two bodies. (39)

"By means of two bodies" means that since her body in the form of a *rākṣasī* had perished, she [existed] by means of two bodies in the form of needles. As it is stated in the *Bṛhadvāsiṣṭha*: "She became another, small, a living *viṣūcikā* (a needle-like affliction), consisting of space, without food, with a body whose activity was like space; thus her body was born here as a pair of needles."

With her body as delicate as cotton-garment made of moonbeams and frost, she entered the hearts of men with that slender form; thereafter, that cruel one wandered through the ten directions, causing torment. (39)
Then, after a long time, the forest-rākṣasī Karkaṭī felt inner despondency: "Alas, what misery! What is this that has been done? (40)
"Nirveda" means detachment (vairāgya). "Dhik" is used in the sense of censure; as Amarasimha states: "Dhik is used for both reproach and censure. || 40 ||
"Have I been born as a needle? What indeed could enter a needle?
This needle is filled by a mere particle of blood and flesh. (41)
The word *iva* in the phrase *kim iva* is for the purpose of poetic ornament (*vākyālaṃkāra*). *Yāsyati* means "will enter" or "will be included. || 41 ||
Alas! This needle of craving within my heart is exceedingly difficult to bear;
O evil-minded one, where have those expansive limbs of mine gone? (42)

"Hanta" expresses dejection; as Amara states: "Hanta is used in joy, compassion, the commencement of a sentence, or dejection. Like thirst, it is a "thorn of thirst" (tṛṣṇāsūcī) because it causes suffering. || 42 ||
As vast as dark clouds, yet utterly shattered like leaves,
they do not occupy even a needle-point of space, for all hope has been destroyed.
*Manāk* means "slightly" (*īṣat*). According to Amara, *īṣan* and *manāk* have the same meaning. || 43 ||
