Thinking, "This is a mouthful of delicious meat and broth, or even fat and blood," he withdrew from his mind the intent to kill people and went once more to that very peak of the Himalayas to perform austerities. (44)

A morsel endowed with the flavor of delicious meat is a "morsel of delicious meat-flavor" (svādumāṃsarasagrāsa). Fat is *vasā*; according to Amara, "fat" (*vapā*) and "heart-fat" (*hṛnmedas*) are synonyms for *vasā*. "Killing people" (*janamāraṇa*) refers to the intention to kill people. || 44 ||
Withdrawing her mind from everything, filled with the essence of world-weariness and agitated by her needle-like body, she performed most rigorous penance.
She whose womb was filled with the essence of world-weariness (*nirveda*)—the very core of dispassion (*vairāgya*)—was agitated and tormented;
that is to say, she performed ascetic penance (*tapas*). || 45 ||
Free from conceptual construction, abstaining from food, and consisting of a mind without waves,
she then, at the end of a thousand years, attained the supreme state. (46)
She consists of a mind free from waves, having a mind devoid of modification as her primary characteristic. || 46 ||
By means of her asceticism, Sūcī became stainless, her impurities exhausted;
through that very wisdom, she herself came to know all that is to be known.

"Stainless" (nirmalā) means free from passion and other such afflictions. The reason for this is "one whose impurities have been destroyed" (kṣīṇakalmaṣā). "One who has known what is to be known" (viditavedyā) refers to her by whom the identity of Brahman and the Self—the object to be known—has been realized. By her, who is thus well-known... [47] [48] [49] [50]
Then, for thousands of years, she remained in a state of thoughtlessness,
contemplating in her heart that the entire cycle of worldly existence is to be abandoned.
Knowing her to be such, established in the supreme state, the Blessed Lord approached and said: "O daughter, O Rākṣasī Karkaṭī!"
Having attained that very same body, move about in the world in happiness;
you are liberated while living, my child, for the darkness within your heart has dissolved.
Those who are deluded, those who undertake evil deeds, those who are fools, those who are ill-situated, and those who dwell in improper places—they all stand as food for [the wise]. (51)
The deluded are those who do not know Brahman; the foolish are those devoid of discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful. || 51 ||
Having spoken thus, the Creator vanished; thereafter she became a Rākṣasī.
Internally she became composed of pure consciousness, free from external waves [of distraction].
Thereafter, she remained for a long time in unwavering meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi).

"Then," meaning immediately thereafter; "devoid of external waves" means she is free from those very waves—which are the great surges belonging to the internal organ—that have set out toward external non-self objects. || 52 || 53 ||
Then, after a long time, having experienced a vibration of the mind, she became composed of external activity; she then remembered that hunger once again.
(193) "For as long as the nature of the body does not cease for a living being, she reflected thereupon: 'A morsel of food appropriate to my birth is what is right for me. (54)
"As long as there is *sattva*, as long as there is life. According to Amara, "Even though *sattva* refers to substance, vitality, or resolve, it is used [here] in the masculine to mean living beings.
That which is swallowed is a *grāsa*, meaning food. || 54 ||
Thinking, "I shall search for those fools fashioned by the Creator," she rose up from that mountain peak.
The grammatical connection is that "the deluded morsel was fashioned by the Creator. I investigate; that is, I search for it. || 55 ||
He entered a circle of Kirāta people situated at the foot of the mountain;
there, in a certain great forest, he then made his dwelling.

It stands at the foot of the mountain, that is, on the bordering hills (*pratyantaparvata*); for Amarasimha states, "The *pādas* are the bordering hills. Alternatively, *śailapādastham* means situated at the base of the mountain. || 56 ||
In the meantime, there in that circle of Kirātas, the night became as black as a mass of darkness that could be grasped by the hand. (57)
The black night is the Night of Doom (Kālarātri). || 57 || 58 ||
On that terrible night, the king,
noble in his valor, entered the forest with his minister to practice the life of a hero.
In the forest, that cucumber, losing its composure, saw those two— the king and the minister— as they were wandering about, their eyes upturned in the sight of the Vetāla.
She by whom fortitude is maintained is "one who possesses maintained fortitude. || 59 ||
Then she thought: "Ah! I have found two victims to devour;
these two fools are ignorant of the Self, for their bodies are indeed a burden."

For these two who do not know the Self—since the body, which has been grasped as the Self, must necessarily be protected, and since its protection is difficult because it is beset by calamities from all sides—the body is a burden; that is to say, it causes suffering like a heavy load. || 60 ||
In this world and the next, the fool lives for the sake of suffering and for his own destruction;
therefore, he must be destroyed because he is the cause of the accumulation of evil. (61)
"For destruction" means for the ruin of the goals of human endeavor; that is to say, for the non-attainment of happiness. || 61 ||
And at the beginning of creation, a rule was established by the Lotus-born One:
"Let [the flesh] of predatory animals be for food; he who eats it is deluded in soul and lacks self-control. (62)
Of the violent ones, those whose nature is to inflict injury; "one who lacks self-mastery" means one whose mind is unconquered. || 62 ||
Therefore, these two, having become my food, must be eaten by me this very day;
for one who is unworthy indeed disregards a faultless object that has come into his possession. (63)
"Bhavya" means fit or capable; as Kṣīrasvāmin has said: "Bhavya means fit. "Abhavya" is the opposite of that. || 63 ||
These two noble-minded ones shall never again be endowed with such virtues;
for the destruction of such beauty does not please my very nature. (64)

"Never at any time. Here, the word "yadi" (if) is to be supplied. The ellipsis is: "If these two were never at any time endowed with virtues and possessed of noble character, then they would be fit to be eaten by me. 64 || 65 || 66 || 67 || 68 || 69 || 70 ||
Therefore, having thoroughly examined these two, if they are endowed with such qualities, I shall not eat them; for I never harm those who possess virtue.
By one who desires unartificial happiness, fame, and long life,
those endowed with virtuous qualities should be honored by granting all that is desired.
Even if I must perish with this body, I shall certainly not enjoy that which is fraught with the qualities [of worldly existence];
for the virtuous bring more joy to the heart than even life itself. (67)
One should protect a virtuous person even by the gift of one's own life;
for through the medicine of association with the virtuous, even death attains the state of friendship.
If even I, a rākṣasī, protect this man who is endowed with virtues, then who else would not hold him in their heart like a pure necklace? 69.
Those embodied beings who dwell here endowed with noble qualities are moons upon the surface of the earth; through their association, they cool [all things] intensely. (70)
Death is the rejection of virtue, while life is the reliance upon the virtuous;
the fruit of relying on the virtuous throughout one's life is heaven, liberation, and so forth. (71)

The disparagement of the virtuous—one who possesses qualities such as humility and is a knower of Brahman—is "death" itself, for it destroys the very fruit of life. Taking refuge with the virtuous is "life" itself, for it is the root of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*). He whose refuge is the taking of shelter with the virtuous...
From that life, the fruit such as heaven and so forth arises. || 71 ||
Therefore, I shall examine these two lotus-eyed ones through some playful inquiry, [asking] "What is the extent of their knowledge? (72)
"Kiṃmātra" refers to that knowledge whose measure (mātrā) or extent (parimāṇa) is "what" (kiṃ); those two [ears] are described as such. || 72 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then that ogress, a blossom upon the forest of the Rākṣasa clan,
let out a deep roar like a streak of cloud in the darkness.
The race of Rākṣasas is indeed a forest, and she is its blossoming cluster. 73.
At the end of his roar, he spoke these words harsh with the sound "huṃ," like the crash of thunderbolts following a peal of thunder.

"Huṃkāreṇa paruṣam kaṭhoram" means harsh and severe due to the sound "huṃ. Regarding "garjitena": *karakāḥ* are hailstones; *karaka-aśani* is a thunderbolt consisting of hailstones. Speech that is perceived as being like the sound produced by a hailstone-thunderbolt immediately following a roar is what is meant here. || 74 ||

O you two, the moon and the sun, who traverse the path of the sky in this terrible forest; you who are like insects dwelling within the hollows of the stone seat of the darkness of great illusion! 75.

The path of the sky is like a terrible forest; the moon and sun are its [two] pillars. Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) is indeed the stone-pedestal of darkness, the very foundation of the gloom; its hollow is the cavity, and the two insects therein are the "two insects in the cavity of the stone-pedestal of the darkness of Great Illusion. (75)
(196) Who are you two of great intelligence, or rather, of evil intellect, who have come together and fallen into my range as prey, destined for death in an instant? (76)
My place of consumption is my locus of consumption. || 76 ||
The king said:
"O you creature! Who might you be, and where do you dwell in this body? Show yourself! Who would fear the sound of your voice, which is like the humming of bees? (77)
The meaning is that of the sound of the female bee (*alinī*), that is, the sound of the female bumblebee (*bhramarī*). || 77 || 78 ||
When the king had spoken thus, she reflected, "A charming thing has been said," and though her composure was revealed, she cried out and laughed loudly at the two of them.
Then the two of them beheld her, filling the quarters of the sky with sound, her form revealed from afar by the flood of light from her such laughter. (79)

She whose form was revealed from afar by the flood of light from such a fierce laugh—that is how she is described; for when a laugh is uttered, the luster of the teeth spreads forth, and thus she is called "Hāsaprabhā" (She of the Laughter-Light).
[79] Like a mountain slope struck by a thunderbolt at the end of an aeon.
Beholding her, the two great heroes remained just as they were, unperturbed.
Resounding—that is, making a noise—with a sound resembling the thunderbolt at the end of an eon, like the thunderbolt of universal destruction. || 80 || 81 ||
The minister said:
O great Rākṣasī, why is this agitation of yours fruitless? Or perhaps it is a display of agility; yet even in agility, there is excessive haste.
Abandon this agitation; this undertaking does not become you.
For wise men, seeking to accomplish their own purpose, engage only within their proper domain. (82)
Abandon—restrain—your agitation, ostentation, or anger regarding the object, that is, the matter worthy of accomplishment.
The word *hi* indicates the reason. || 82 ||
O frail woman, thousands like you are to us like mosquitoes; they are swept away by the gale of our fortitude like blades of grass and leaves. (83)
"Carried by the gale of fortitude" means they were specifically borne—that is, shaken—by that very gale of fortitude, which is a whirlwind. || 83 ||
Having cast off the fever of agitation, the wise man accomplishes his own purpose through an even and clear intellect,
as well as through practical reasoning.
"Vyavahāriṇī" means she who engages in worldly activity; that is to say, she who is conducive to worldly transactions. || 84 || 85 ||
"Tell us what is desired by you, and for what purpose you come as a petitioner;
for no seeker who has not obtained his object ever passes before us, even in a dream. (85)
Having been addressed thus by him at that time, the rākṣasī reflected:
"Aha! How pure is the conduct and the character of these two lions among men! (86)
Sattva is intelligence. || 86 || 87 ||
I do not consider these two to be common; this is a marvelous wonder:
words, faces, and eyes themselves announce the internal certainty.
Desiring to become the substratum for one another through the channels of speech, the mouth, and the eyes,
the waters of the rivers merge together like flowing currents.
By means of movements and revolutions. || 88 ||
"By these two, my state has for the most part been fully understood;
and by me, these two are not to be destroyed, for they are themselves indestructible. (89)
He demonstrates his own intended view—that there is indeed a mutual unification of intentions and inclinations—with the words "by these two.
They are themselves indestructible, because their nature is that of the indestructible Brahman. || 89 ||
Therefore, I ask you these two things regarding a doubt that has arisen;
those lowest of men who do not consult a wise person when they encounter a doubt are truly base. (90)

Therefore, regarding the phrase "some doubt" (*kiṃcitsaṃdeham*), the word *kiṃcit* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). This is because it is listed among the group of indeclinables meaning "slightly," "a little," or "in some measure. The term *saṃdehataḥ* means "from doubt"; that is, *saṃdeha*. || 90 ||
Having reflected thus, she then spoke these words concerning the principles for the sake of inquiry;
restraining her laughter, which sounded like the roar of clouds at the end of an aeon, she said: (91)
It is so described because its roar was like the roar of the clouds at the end of an unseasonable aeon, the clouds of a premature dissolution. 91–92.
"Who are you two, O steadfast men? Tell me, O sinless ones. (92)
The minister said:
"This is the king of the Kirātas, and I have attained the position of his minister;
we are prepared to subdue people such as you by means of a night-raid. (93)
The connection is that [the two of them] were intent upon the suppression of people such as yourself. || 93 ||
The duty of kings, day and night, is the suppression of wicked beings. || 94 ||
*Divam* (day) and *rātram* (night) are indeclinables. The syntactical connection is: "The subduing of wicked beings day and night is the duty of kings. 94.
The Rākṣasī said:
O King, you are a wise counselor; a king does not become such by means of a wicked counselor.
A wise king becomes so through his counselor, for a king is defined by his wise counselor. || 95 ||

A king whose minister is wicked is one with a wicked minister; he would not be a king of evil counsel. A king whose [minister] is virtuous is a good king, and his minister would likewise be a good king—this is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). The phrase "he would be joined with a good minister" is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).
At the outset, the king himself must be joined with discernment by a wise minister;
for as the king attains nobility through him, so too do the subjects. (96)
Intending to show that the king's association with good ministers must be viewed as particularly significant, he says: "The king alone," and so forth.
This should be applied by the elders. || 96 ||
Sovereignty and impartial vision belong to the king through the science of kingship;
he who does not know this is neither a minister nor a king. (97)

"By the royal science" means by the thorough knowledge of statecraft (*rājanīti*); or alternatively, it is the "king of sciences," which is the science of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), according to the traditional teaching: "It is the royal science and the royal secret. This very meaning is clearly understood from this verse in the *Bṛhadvāsiṣṭha*:
"Among all the networks of qualities, the knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātmajñāna*) is supreme; one who knows that becomes a king among kings."
Therefore, he is both a minister and a knower of mantras. || 97 || 98 ||
(199) "If you two are virtuous experts in that matter, you shall attain prosperity; otherwise, there will be the fault of misfortune, and I shall devour you both because of your nature."
"By a single means you two shall escape from my side, provided that you hold fast in your intellects the essence of the cage of my questions. (99)
Therefore, then: "O children" is the address. 99 || 100 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the Rākṣasī began to answer the questions.
When the king said, "Let them be told," she replied: "O Rāghava, listen to these. (100)
The Rākṣasī said:
Within a single atom, which possesses manifold numbers, hundreds of thousands of universes dissolve like bubbles within an ocean. (1)

"Of one": like bubbles within the ocean, or like bursts of water, millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) dissolve—that is, go to their dissolution—within which minute atom? He qualifies that atom: "of one, who is beyond all number.
What is it? Is it space, or is it not space? Is it nothing, or is it indeed something?
Who is it that does not go while going, and who is it that stands still while standing? || 2 ||

What entity is space, and what entity is not space? What entity is nothing at all, and what entity is something? Who stands while not standing at all? The meaning is: he who stands while being non-existent. || 2 ||
Who is conscious even though they are like stone, and who is the painter of the sky?
In whom do the worlds abide, as trees reside within a seed? (3)

From this interrogative statement, the following answer is understood: "A stone is like a stone," which means it is insentient. The illustration for its abiding in identity with a single tree is "like a seed in a tree.
In that regard, it must be admitted that the effect exists within the cause in a subtle form prior to its production. In that case—

Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that one could not observe the rule that a specific effect arises from a specific cause alone. Yet, such a restriction on production is observed: oil is produced from sesame seeds alone and not from sand; clarified butter from milk alone; and a jar from clay alone.
Thus, since many trees exist within the very belly of a single seed, the tree exists in the seed itself.
Thus, what was stated is established. || 3 ||
Why is it that nothing whatsoever exists as separate from the great ocean, like waves and the like? And why does duality also exist as non-separate from the great ocean? (4)

Having asked about that which is distinct by taking up the notion of difference—asking why even the slightest thing does not exist as separate—he asks about duality by taking up the notion of distinction: "Dvaitam" (duality). || 4 ||

"If you two, upon immediately investigating these questions of mine with your intellect, are indeed unable to fathom them, then you shall, in an instant, without obstacle, instantly become fuel for the fire of my stomach.
(5) [The author] refutes the invalidity of the questions on the grounds that their meanings are contradictory—by the words "my questions" (*matpraśnān*). In that case, then:
The belly is the stomach. "You two shall instantly become fuel for the digestive fire"—the word "in a moment" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 5 || 6 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
When this great question had been posed by the daughter of a great rākṣasa in the great forest at the dead of night, the great mantra-master gave his reply.
The minister said:
"O lotus-eyed lady, by this very turn of speech, which is fit for awakening those who know Brahman, you have described this Supreme Self. (7)
He provides a general answer to all the questions with the words "bhavatyā" (by you). "Bhaṅga" means disjunction; that is to say, a part. || 7 ||
Because it is ineffable, because it is unapproachable, and because it abides as the sixth sense-organ, the mind—
the atomic self consisting of pure consciousness alone— is thus subtler even than space.

Intending to show that the oneness of the Supreme Self is real according to the scriptural statement, "One only, without a second," and that its manifoldness is illusory according to the scriptural statement, "Indra, by means of his powers of illusion (māyā),
appears in many forms," he provides the answer to the first part of the question with the following two verses beginning with the words "Because of being ineffable" (anākhyatvāt).

Or, because it is "inexpressible"—that is to say, because the mind lacks the capacity to express the meaning of words—by the reasoning thus stated, the Self is atomic like an atom due to its partlessness, and like space; thus he says: "from space."

"Due to the transition of power (*śakti-paryāya*), there is a transcendence of the power of persistence (*sthiti-śakti*). *Paryāya* means transition; *atikrama* means transcendence; in that [context], *atipāta* and *upātyaya* mean the same. (Amara-kośa).
By this, it should be understood that the eighth question has also been answered. || 8 || 9 ||
Within the supreme atom of consciousness, millions of bubbles of world-systems arise, persist through repeated cycles of existence, and dissolve again by the turn of Śakti. (9)
Space is [called] "external emptiness" because it is empty of external objects, and it is "non-space" because of its nature as consciousness;
it is "nothingness" because it is indefinable, yet it is "something" because it is the reality of existence. (110)
He answers the second question with the words: "Space."

Because it is empty of externals—that is, empty of objects existing outside itself—and because it is consciousness, being of the nature of *cit*, the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) is not the non-ether (*anākāśa*). He answers the third question with the words: "It is nothing" (*akiñcit*).

If, because the reality of Brahman is indefinable and inexpressible, it therefore becomes nothing at all—that is to say, it does not become "something" consisting of mere ultimate existence—then that is the meaning. || 110 ||
This conscious one, whose nature is luminosity, is like a stone due to the absence of any object of perception;
yet within the pure sky of the Self, he is the painter of the unfolding of the world.

He answers the sixth question with the words, "He is conscious. The answer is given out of sequence for the purpose of testing the intellect of the Rākṣasīs. Because this Supreme Self is of the nature of the light of consciousness, He is therefore conscious.

Furthermore, because there is an absence of an object of knowledge—that is, in reality, an absence of anything to be known—and because He remains changeless even in the presence of imagined objects of knowledge.
He becomes like a stone. He answers the seventh question with the word "ātmani" (in the self). "Unmeṣaḥ" means manifestation. || 11 ||
This entire universe is merely that [Brahman]; therefore, it does not exist apart from it.
Even the diversity of the world is its manifestation; thus, even difference is composed of that.

He states the answer to the ninth question: "tadbhāvamātram" (it is merely its being). This entire world is "merely its being," meaning it is nothing but the consciousness of Brahman; that is to say, its existence is impossible apart from that Brahman-consciousness. Alternatively, "tadbhāvamātram" means it is merely a false appearance of that substratum; for this reason, it does not exist separately from it.
It may be so. He states the answer to the tenth question: "The world," etc. The meaning is that it is composed of that, having its very nature as that, and does not exist apart from it. || 12 ||
Pervading all and connected to all, it does not go because there is no going;
it does not exist because of the absence of a substratum, yet it exists because its nature is real.

He states the answer to the fourth [objection] with the words "all-pervading" (*sarvaga*). For the fruit of going is indeed the connection with that which is to be reached. And the Supreme Self is connected with every object to be reached; therefore, it is all-pervading.
Yet, due to the absence of motion, because its omnipresence renders motion impossible, and because there is in reality no destination to be reached, it does not go.
He states the reply to the fifth [objection]: "That does not exist. For whatever exists in the world is indeed manifestable and possesses a support.

That Supreme Self, because it is not manifestable by anything else and because it is without support, is said to "not exist. Nevertheless, because it is of the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*)—that is, because it is of the nature of ultimate reality—it also "exists. || 13 ||
Having heard these words of the minister, the Rākṣasī took up speech:
"Now, indeed, the utterance of the highest truth from you, my minister, is purifying. (14)
Having heard this, the one and a half verses have a clear meaning. || 14 || 15 ||
Let this king, whose eyes are like lotus petals, speak now.
The king said:
For one who is awake, they say that supreme state of consciousness arises from the absence of [ordinary] cognitions;
it is the renunciation of all volitional thoughts and the grasping by the mind of that which is beyond.
Since the minister has already provided an answer in accordance with the manner of the question, [the author], setting that aside, speaks by resorting to another method:

"Of one who is awake," etc. Of that Brahman which is *paraṃ* (supreme) because it is the means for attaining the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), *pratyayaṃ* (cognition) is knowledge; [this belongs] to the person who is *jāgrataḥ* (awake), that is, the discriminating person.

They say that [non-duality] arises from the absence of the notion of duality—that is, from the absence of the notion of real duality—because the notion that duality is a real entity acts as an obstacle to the knowledge of non-duality. It is logical that the knowledge of non-duality arises even for a discerning person while awake, because that [notion of real duality] is absent for them. Regarding the phrase "the absence of the notion for one who is awake," the meaning in some contexts is as follows: for a discerning person who is awake...

That which is the absence of cognition—the absence of the cognition of real duality—is what they call "cognition" (pratyaya) for someone, because it is the cause thereof. Alternatively, even for one who is awake and perceiving directly, there occurs an absence of cognition regarding the objects of duality;
for the Witness does not undergo transformation into the form of the cognition of duality, owing to its immutability (kūṭasthatva). It is of such a person that they say "he has cognition."

"Supreme" (*param*) is as explained previously. Alternatively, they say that for whom the cognition—which is the consciousness of one's own nature (*svarūpacaitanya*)—is supreme, transcending transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

Here, the word "for whom" (*yasya*) is connected with what is to be said later by supplying the correlative word "him" (*tam*). In the same way, the connection with the word "for whom" (*yacchabda*) should be understood in subsequent instances as well. [The term] "with the mind" (*cetasā*) refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The renunciation of all conceptual constructions, the abandonment of attachment to the cognition of all duality, and non-conceptual samādhi—this constitutes the "acceptance" (parigraha) of that Supreme Self, because it is the cause for its realization. || 16 ||
That which, through its contraction and expansion, brings about the dissolution and creation of the universe,
which is the ultimate goal of the Vedānta scriptures, and which is beyond the reach of words— [that is Brahman]. (17)
By means of its contraction and expansion; that is to say, by means of the dissolution and arising of its conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa-vikalpa*).

It is the culmination—the final ground reached through the function of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—of the Vedānta statements. Furthermore, because of the absence of universals (*jāti*) and other grounds for the application of words, it is beyond the reach of speech. Or else:

It is the object of that [word] because it is pervaded by the mental modification (vṛtti) produced by the sentence; it is not the object of that [word] because it is not pervaded by the result produced by that [modification]. || 17 ||

Now, that which abides in the interval between the two extremes, yet consists of those very two extremes—for whose play, consisting of consciousness, this entire world of moving and non-moving things exists. (18)

Regarding the phrase "between the two extremes": Brahman, which abides in the interval between the two extremes of duality and non-duality, is distinct from those two extremes of duality and non-duality—which are themselves conceptually constructed through their mutual dependence—and stands as their neutral ground by virtue of being their substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Alternatively, it abides in the interval between the two extremes of existence and non-existence, according to the Lord’s statement: "It is said to be neither existent nor non-existent."

Whether it resides within the interval between cause and effect, or within the interval between the seer and the seen, or within the interval between the original object and its reflection; or whether it resides within the interval between bondage and liberation,
or within the interval between the governed and the governor— since all these are merely conceptual constructs, [Brahman] is distinct from them.
By virtue of being devoid of specific characteristics (*vilakṣaṇatayā*), its existence as that which stands between [the two extremes] is established. Now, it consists of the two extremes;

moreover, by means of *māyā*, it possesses the nature of the two aforementioned extremes, and for this substratum, the world—consisting of the mind as its illusory transformation (*vivarta*)—is its playful manifestation (*līlā*). || 18 ||
O auspicious lady,
that which, despite being the soul of the universe, is never divided into even a single fragment—
that you call the eternal Brahman, pure existence. (19)
The meaning is that although He is the self of all and the essence of everything, His state as a single mass—His unity of nature—is not fragmented.
That is to say, even through the illusory identity with the manifold and multiform universe, His reality and His state of being a single essence are not impaired;
this is what is being stated by you. || 19 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this from the mouth of the king, Karkaṭī, the forest-monkey-woman, stood with her purpose understood; she abandoned her envy and fickleness.
In order to demonstrate that the realization of Brahman as the Self has direct perception as its fruit, the two verses beginning with "iti rājamukhāt" have a clear meaning. || 120 || 121 ||
Having attained inner coolness, she found that rest,
like a peahen at the onset of the rainy season, or like a night-blooming lily under the moonlight.
The Rākṣasī said:
Oh, how wonderful!
This intellect of yours shines with such purity, illuminated by the sun of awakening whose essence never sets.

The textual passage beginning with "Aho bata" and extending to the end of the narrative is intended to show that even for one in whom consciousness has arisen, provided there is no lapse in their spiritual practice, a taste for the true path (sanmārga) persists until the fall of the body. That passage, too, is clear in meaning. Nevertheless, certain words therein are now explained. "Bata" expresses satisfaction. "Śemuṣī" means intellect (buddhi).
"Buddhi, manīṣā, dhiṣaṇā, dhī, prajñā, śemuṣī, and mati" are synonyms according to Amara.
"Anastamitasāreṇa" means by one whose essence has not set, that is, by one whose capacity is undiminished. || 22 || 23 ||
(205) I consider those like you, who possess discernment and are honored by the world, to be worthy of service;
for through association with the great alone, suffering no longer afflicts one again. (23)
For who, holding the flame of a lamp in hand, would be overcome by darkness? By my power, you two have reached Jāṅgala like suns upon the earth.
Jāṅgala is a forest in a desert region. || 24 || 25 ||
Therefore, O auspicious ones worthy of worship, tell me quickly what you desire.
The king said:
I entreat you, O jasmine-blossom of the forest that is the race of Rākṣasas:
let it be so that your life shall never again be taken by anyone. (26)

The race of Rākṣasas is indeed a forest, and you are its blossom. O blossom of the forest that is the race of Rākṣasas, the connection with the preceding verse is as follows: "I entreat you that henceforth the life of no one whatsoever shall be harmed by you."
Pleased, the Rākṣasī Karkaṭī Vanamarkaṭī said:
"Certainly, O Lord; from this day forward, I shall act exactly thus, without fail."
That action in which there is no falsehood or untruth is "avitatha" (not false). According to Amara, "vitatha" means untruthful speech. (27–28)
Indeed, nothing at all should now be hated by me.
The king said:
"If this is so, O lotus-eyed one, what would be the purpose of maintaining your body while you remain intent on my desire, which consists solely in the enjoyment of another's body? (29)
*Phullam* means blossoming or blooming. *Bhṛtyai* means for the sake of maintenance. *Matsamīhite* means in what is desired by me or sought after by me. || 29 || 30 ||
The Rākṣasī said:
After a long time, O King, as I awoke from my meditative absorption, a desire for food arose within me; however, I did not take that into account. (130)
Now, having ascended the summit and remaining motionless through her former meditation,
she sat happily for as long as she desired like a living statue.
I shall sit down. "Śālabhañjikā" means a doll; the sense is that she is like a doll. || 31 ||
Having bound the dhāraṇā until death, I maintain this little body;
it is my intention that I shall cast it off at whatever time I desire.
"Āmṛtim" is an archaic (ārṣa) form; it means "until death" (āmṛtiṃ mṛtiparyantam). Alternatively, the reading may be "āmṛteḥ. || 32 || 33 || 34 ||
"O King, from this moment until the abandonment of my body, I shall not harm the lives of others, for I behold Śiva as all-pervading. (33)
When the night-stalker woman, having thus conceived affection for them,
had dismissed them and set out to depart, the king then spoke these words.
You ought not to render our affection and friendship in vain;
for the friendship of virtuous people increases by the mere sight [of one another]. (35)
"Sauhārda" means the state of being a friend. "Vitathīkartum" means to render false; that is to say, to make it futile. || 35 || 36 ||
Having assumed a charming form endowed with youth and good fortune,
come to our house, O blessed lady, and stay there at your ease.
The Rākṣasī said:
Are you able to give food to one who has assumed the form of a beautiful woman? With what can you satisfy me, who am bearing the nature of a Rākṣasī? (37)
You satisfy and you gladden [them]. || 37 || 38 ||
(207) This [food] is indeed for my satisfaction as a destroyer of demons, not the food of ordinary people;
this innate nature, established from before, does not depart from me until the end of this body. (38)
The king said:
"O blameless one, remain in my house for some days in the form of a woman, adorned with garlands of golden flowers, for as long as I desire. (39)
Wreathed with golden garlands, golden necklaces, and encircled by golden threads— thus adorned with golden garlands—
I have brought together from the prisons hundreds of thousands of wicked thieves deserving of death and given them excellent food for you. (140)
Abandoning your lovely form and taking them all without exception, lead them to the peak of the Himalayas; there, enjoy yourself as you please.
For those who eat excessively, eating in solitude indeed brings comfort; having attained some degree of satiety and sleep, become once more possessed of meditative absorption. (42)
Slightly; even a little. || 42 ||
Having desisted from concentration, they returned once more at another time, saying:
"Lead away others who are even more fit for slaughter; for this [practice] is not their dharma. (43)
The phrase "being performed according to dharma" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Alternatively, "according to dharma" means according to the *dharma-śāstra*. 43, 44, 45, 46.
For indeed, even violence performed according to one's own duty is equal to great compassion;
you shall surely come to me, O you who are detached from meditative absorption.
Even among the wicked, a firmly rooted friendship does not cease.
The Rākṣasī said:
"What you have said is right, O King; I shall certainly do so, my friend.
For who would not honor the words of one who acts out of friendship? (45)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, that playful Rākṣasī became manifest there;
O King, saying "Come, let us go," she addressed the king and his minister. (46)
Having set out for their own hermitage, she followed them during the night;
then, having reached the king’s palace, they spent that night together in private.
"Rajanīm" means the night. The connection is: "they spent the night. "Mithaḥ" means mutually, one with another. || 47 ||
They spent their time with great respect in that beautiful house, conversing;
at dawn, she remained in the inner apartments amidst the playful activities of the women.
A *purandhrī* is a married woman. || 48 || 49 || 50 || 51 || 52 || 153 ||
The Rākṣasī and the minister-king each performed their respective duties.
Then, within eight days, the king had [the materials] accumulated.
Then, from the cities of other kings as well as from his own circle of vassals,
he gave her those three thousand condemned men.
At nightfall, she became that very same fierce black rākṣasī;
she seized those thousands of victims within the circle of her arms.
Having taken leave of the king, she departed at that very moment for the summit of the Himalayas;
from that time until today, she remains in the region of the Kirāta people.
Having arisen from meditative absorption, she comes and seizes those who are to be slain. || 153 ||
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Narrative of the Needle," in the section on Origination within the *Śrīmokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Śrīmad-Ātmabodha*, composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Uttamaśukha Pūjyapāda.
(p. 209) Fourth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
All this has been told by means of the narration of the story of Sūcī;
the Self alone is the supreme reality, and there are no other perceptions of worldly existence. || 1 ||

He introduces another narrative to elaborate on how the world is a mere play of the mind, preceded by a restatement of what has already occurred, beginning with the words "All this has been told to you," and so forth. He says, "The Supreme Truth," [to show] that the Self is not something other than Brahman;
for "Truth" is Brahman. The "visions of saṃsāra" are the delusions of saṃsāra. || 1 ||
For all this creation manifests in this manner as nothing but the mind itself.
In this regard, listen to the narrative known as Aindava, which is an ornament for the ears.

Why is it that views of saṃsāra do not exist? To this he says: "For all... The word *hi* (for) indicates the reason. It is this mind alone which, when creation is to be performed, flashes forth as everything—the entire world—precisely in such a manner.
In this regard, concerning the fact that the world is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the mind, there is the narrative of Aindava, [the story] of the sons of the Brāhmaṇa named Indu.
The narrative of the Aindavas. || 2 ||
O Rāma, I shall relate to you that irreproachable narrative, from which you may ascertain that the world is the manifestation of the power of consciousness (cit-śakti). || 3 ||

Since, from hearing the narrative called the Aindava, you ascertain that the world is the manifestation (*samullāsa*) of the power of consciousness; [the text explains: *māyā* is the power of the Supreme Self, which is Consciousness (*cit*), and its "manifestation" refers to its unfolding (*vijṛmbhaṇa*) when it has assumed the state of the mind (*manas*). The meaning is that it is an illusory transformation (*vivarta*). Alternatively, *citiśakti* refers to the mind, being that which possesses the power (*śakti*) within consciousness (*cit*), that is, within knowledge (*jñāna*). || 3 ||
Due to a lack of awakening, the fool of a mind falsely perceives the world as a demon;
once awakened, he beholds his own supreme, stainless form.
He states the purport of the narrative with two verses, beginning with "The child-mind" (*cittabāla*). The "child-mind" (*cittabāla*) is the mind itself that is like a child.

The "world-ghost" (*jagadyakṣa*) is the world itself that is like a ghost; [the verse says] "him. Just as a child, being unenlightened, perceives his own shadow as a false ghost, so too the mind, characterized by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), being unenlightened, perceives the world as false. But when it is enlightened...
The meaning is that he perceives a dwelling place free from affliction. || 4 ||
Mind alone is indeed saṃsāra when defiled by the afflictions such as passion; that very same mind, when liberated from them, is called the end of existence. (5)
The end of existence is called the end of saṃsāra because it is the means for achieving that [end]. || 5 ||
Once, at the end of the day, having withdrawn the entire creation,
the Lord Brahmā, with one-pointed mind, passed that night in sleep.

The textual composition beginning with "Sometimes the entire creation... and extending to the conclusion of the narrative is clear in its meaning. Nevertheless, certain words therein are analyzed here. Regarding the word "entire" (*akhila*), although Maharloka and the other higher worlds remain during the occasional dissolution (*naimittikapralaya*), the term refers only to a limited scope [of destruction].
At the end of the night, having awakened and performed the twilight rites according to the rules,
the Unborn One directed his wide-open eyes toward the sky in order to create living beings.
In the case of a large [object], it is great. || 7 ||
Then, in that vast expanse of space, he beheld with his mind various great undertakings— creations whose maintenance was unimpeded.

Those [worlds] in which there is activity involving great undertakings are so described. They are called *sargas* because they are created; these are the cosmic expansions (*prapañcas*). "Unobstructed in their maintenance" means those whose maintenance is free from impediment. According to Amara, "unimpeded" (*abādha*) is a synonym for "unobstructed" (*nirargala*). (8)
Beholding them with his own supreme, pure splendor, he was struck with great wonder, thinking, "What is this? How can this be? || 9 ||
Now, the word "uta" (also/even) is used in the sense of [an alternative]. 9 || 10 || 11 || 12 || 13 ||
Then, after gazing for a long time at the sun in the sky with his mind alone,
he brought that single sun from the mass of worlds and questioned him.
"Who are you, O one of great splendor, and how was this web of the world born?
If you know, O Blessed One, then tell me this, O sinless one. (11)
Having been addressed thus by the Creator with a mind bowed in devotion, the Sun-god paid his respects and spoke these words in a voice of irreproachable eloquence. (12)
You have always been the cause of this phenomenal world;
therefore, you do not know me—why then, O Lord, do you question me? (13)
Now, O omnipresent one, if your sport consists of the composition of my words, then hear from me as I speak of my own inconceivable birth. 14.
"My own arising" is an illustration that includes the arising of the entire web of the world as well. || 14 ||
Thus, on the Kailāsa mountain, in a single corner of Jambudvīpa,
there is a place named Suvarṇataṭa, which has been brought to splendor by your sons.
By your sons, Marīci and the others. || 15 || 16 || 17 || 18 || 19 ||
A magnificent maṇḍala, beautiful with abundant happiness, was prepared;
there dwelt a most virtuous Brāhmaṇa, the best among the knowers of Brahman.
Indu was a man of exceedingly peaceful soul, born in the lineage of Kaśyapa;
he had a wife who was as dear to him as his own life, and from her, that great-souled one [begot a son].
No son was born to him, like a tree in a desert wasteland;
consequently, that distressed couple went to the mountain to perform austerities for the sake of a son.
Devoted to pure vows, the two ascended Mount Kailāsa;
in that hollow of Kailāsa, which was empty and unoccupied by spirits, they remained.
Those two performed severe penance, subsisting on water and remaining upon a tree;
then the God who bears the digit of the moon became pleased with them.
Those two whose staying is like that of a tree are "tree-stayers" (*tarusthitī*); subsisting on water is well known in the case of trees. (20, 21)
Then he came to that place where the brahmin couple were;
"O brahmin, accept a boon quickly, for I am pleased," he said to him. (21)
The Brahmin said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, may my ten sons once again become highly intelligent and auspicious, so that sorrow no longer afflicts me. (22)

"Bhavyāḥ" means capable or worthy. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "May that [state] come to pass by which, through the birth of ten sons, grief shall no longer afflict me. Alternatively, the singular number in "yena" is not intended; thus it refers to "by whom," meaning by those sons. (22) (23) (24) (25)
Then, having said, "Let it be so," the Lord vanished;
thereafter, the couple, satisfied with having obtained the boon, went home.
Then, in due course of time, the blameless Brahmin woman gave birth to ten sons; those ten boys gradually attained maturity.
Then, after a long time, those two parents of theirs, being skilled in knowing the destination [of beings], abandoned their bodies and went to their own state. Thereupon,
those ten brahmins were left bereft of their mother and father.
Abandoning their home on the peak of Kailāsa, they went there dejected;
bereft of their kinsmen, they reflected there in great agitation.
Alternatively, "weary" means suffering; "agitated" means possessed by agitation; and "bereft of kinsmen" means those whose kinsmen have departed. || 26 ||
"What would be the supreme good here? What here would be free from suffering? How limited is this sovereignty of men, for even a vassal is indeed a great lord. (27)
What indeed is the perfection of a vassal? For kings are indeed great lords;
what indeed is the perfection of subordinate rulers? Here, the universal emperor (*samrāj*) is the great lord. (28)
Kings are lords of their respective realms; he who rules by the command of a king is called a *samrāj* (emperor). According to Amara, he who rules by the command of a king is a *samrāj*. (28)
What indeed is the imperial sovereignty of Indra compared to theirs, for whom Maheśvara is their lord? What indeed is that status of Mahendra which lasts but a moment of Prajāpati? (29)

The connection is that what indeed is called sovereignty is prosperity—that state of being Indra which lasts for a single *muhūrta* of Prajāpati. For during the day of Prajāpati, there are fourteen Indras; among them, each one rules over the three worlds for only the duration of a *muhūrta*. || 29 || 30 ||
And that which perishes at the end of an eon—what good could there be in that here? (30)
The eldest said:
"O brothers, that which remains indestructible until the end of the kalpa among all forms of sovereignty—that state of Brahmahood is what pleases me here, and nothing else. (31)
"Bhrātaraḥ" (O brothers) is the form of address; "me" means to me. || 31 ||
The others said:
"What you have said, dear father, is fitting—it is the wiping away of all suffering.
Teach us the truth; today we shall attain the state of Viriñci. (32)

The word "tāta" is used to address the eldest brother because of his equality with a father. "Sarvaduḥkhāpamārjanam" means the remover of all suffering; "śādhi" means "give instruction," that is, provide guidance. || 32 ||
The eldest said:
May there be for you long-lasting meditation upon the radiant Brahmā seated in the lotus posture, [thinking] "I am he," with the thought, "By my splendor, I create and I withdraw. 33.
"Bhāsvān" means radiant; "tejas" refers to power, majesty, brilliance, and strength—as Amara states: "Tejas is used for power, majesty, brilliance, and strength;
it is also used for semen, and thus [the word] applies to all three. || 33 ||
Having been told "So be it" by their elder brother, those excellent ones, their minds intent on meditation, remained there like figures depicted in a painting. (34)
*Bāḍham* is an indeclinable used in the sense of acceptance. *Lipikarma* is the work of painting. 34 || 35 || 36 ||
With their minds fixed inwardly, they reflected with reverence:
"I am Brahmā, the creator of the world, the agent, the enjoyer, and the Great Lord. (35)
Together with the cities of the world-protectors, these fourteen worlds have been created by me; I abide within them. (36)
Then those brahmins, having thus firmly established the contemplation of the Self as Brahman,
forgot their former bodies that had been projected by their previous state of being. (37)

They forgot those things that ought to have been remembered; they made them objects of forgetfulness—meaning they rendered them into objects of perception—or alternatively, "arpitān" means "samarpitān," that is, they were given. || 37 || 38 || 39 ||
Then all those bodies, having withered over time due to the winds and the heat of the sun, fell away like decayed leaves.
This tenfold appearance of creation arose for them;
through the ripening of their meditative cultivation, those ten attained the state of Brahmā. (39)
These ten formative forces (saṃskāras) reside within the ether of the mind;
I, Bhāskara, am the maker of day and night for each one of these. (40)

He states its own function: "The maker of day and night" means that the sun (bhāskara), being unobstructed by Mount Meru, creates the day; but when obstructed by it, it creates the night. And it is said in the *Bṛhadvāsiṣṭha*: "Just as the sun, creating day and night, displays various forms, so too Consciousness (citi), creating the existent and the non-existent, displays various forms. (40-41)
Having spoken thus to the Creator, Bhānu departed for his own abode;
Virañci, the lord of gods, likewise became intent upon his own duties. (41)
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Narrative of Aindava," in the section on Origination within the Means to Liberation of the glorious Yogavāsiṣṭha.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Liberation," from the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*, composed by the venerable Śrī Vidyāraṇya Svāmin, disciple of the holy Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Uttamaśloka Pūjyapāda.
Fifth Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
For the mind is the creator of the worlds; for the mind is the supreme person. In this world, that which is done by the mind is truly done; that which is done by the body is not considered done.

He demonstrates the meaning established by implication through the preceding narrative with these two verses beginning with "mano hi" (for the mind). The phrase "manaskṛtam" means "done by the mind"; I consider it to be well-done.
The sense is that I know only what is done by the mind to be meaningful. || 1 || 2 ||
Having been ordinary Brahmins, it is said that through the cultivation of the mind they attained the state of Brahmā; behold the power of the mind! (2)
For the body, when meditated upon by the mind, attains the state of being embodied;
yet, when liberated from the conception of a body, it is no longer afflicted by the attributes of the body.

Anticipating the objection that it is untenable to claim that actions performed by the body are purposeless—since it is established through perception and other means that actions performed by the body possess fruit—the author says: "By the mind" (*manasā*).
For indeed (*hi*), because the body, when being conceived by the mind, attains the state of being embodied and becomes the performer of actions appropriate to a body.

Having stated the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "By the contemplation of the body" (*dehabhāvanayā*). The meaning is that a person liberated through the contemplation of the body is not afflicted by the attributes of the body, such as cold and heat, honor and dishonor, and so forth. || 3 ||
Due to his inward-turned state, the yogi does not experience pleasure or pain within the body;
the story of Indra with Ahalyā serves as an illustration here.
To the question, "Where is this perceived? he says: "Not by way of inward-turning. This is the meaning:
when there is mental ideation (*manobhāvanā*), activities such as eating—which result in physical effects—are observed in the body;
whereas in its absence, during the state of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) or the state of dreaming, they are not observed.
Furthermore, since we observe that acts such as eating— which consist of a body made of mind alone— result in fruits such as satisfaction,
we conclude through the discrimination between what is possible and what is impossible that any fruitful action perceived to be performed by the body is actually performed by the mind alone,
just like actions performed by the dream-body. Thus, it is the mind alone that creates pleasure and pain, not the body.
In order to clarify this matter by means of another narrative for the purpose of prescribing an extraordinary effort toward its suppression, he says:
"Of Indra... From here until the conclusion of the narrative, the textual composition is clear in meaning. Among those [passages], some words are analyzed. *Udanta* means a report or account. (4) (5)
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, who is Indra to you, or who else is esteemed here, such that upon hearing news of them, my purifying vision may come to me? (5)
Vasiṣṭha said:
For it is heard, O Rāma, that in ancient times there was a lord of the earth among the Magadhas known as Indradyumna, who was like a second Indra.

"Indradyumna, indeed. He was formerly a king of Pāṇḍya, the best among the Draviḍas, renowned as Indradyumna and devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu; such is one Indradyumna well-known from the Purāṇas. But this [other] stands here like another Indradyumna. (6–7)
He had a lotus-eyed wife named Ahalyā, who was like a reflection of the moon's orb, just as Rohiṇī is to the Moon.
In that very city lived another man named Indra, a *ṣiḍga* who was the crest-jewel of all *ṣiḍgas*, beloved by the women of the town.
The crest-jewel of the assembly of Siddhas, the ornament of the multitude of libertines. || 8 ||
Having heard from the historical epics what occurred in the past between Indra and Ahalyā along with Sāhalī, she conceived a deep affection for that Indra.

He felt affection; he developed a deep attachment. || 9 || 10 || 11 || 12 || While the two of them were engaged in unrestrained activities due to their exceedingly intense love, that incident of misconduct reached the presence of the king. || 10 ||
Having observed their mutual attachment in this way, the king issued instructions to them through many means of separation.
Both of those evil-minded ones, having cast themselves into the reservoir of water, were satisfied and laughed there; they did not experience any distress.
Bound by their feet to the legs of elephants, they did not succumb to exhaustion;
though their bodies were struck with whips, they felt no pain whatsoever.
By means of various divisions or modes; they are strung together and bound. || 13 ||
Though being consumed by the flames, those two stood as if upon slabs of ice. Then the king asked them: "Are you perspiring, yet you do not seem distressed? (14)
The form *stha* is the second-person dual of the present indicative (*laṭ*) from the verbal root *as* (to be), meaning "you two are. *Durmatī* is a vocative. || 14 ||
Then, with joyful hearts, the two of them said to the protector of the earth:
"We have remembered each other's irreproachable beauty of countenance here. (15)
In this context, "intention" (āśaya) refers to the mind (citta). 15 || 16 || 17 || 18 || 19 || 20 || 21 ||
O protector of the earth, though we were born as one with each other’s essence, we did not recognize our own selves; we remained deluded even when our own limbs were being cut away.
O King, mental states arising from the body are not able to disturb a steady mind that has long been fixed upon a desired object.
O Lord of the Earth, we two do not understand that which was contemplated with such intense speed by our minds, for we were born as beings whose very essence was one another. (18)
He sees all that very thing, but not the movement of the body,
nor any actions whatsoever, O King, even those resulting from the curse of a sage and the like.
O King, the minds of the wise, when intent upon a single task, are endowed with such intense momentum that they are indeed impossible to shake.
And it is not moved, like Mount Meru, even by hundreds of obstacles. || 21 ||
O King, the formations of bodies arise in vain; for the mind is the cause among these little bodies.
Know, O Great-souled One, that the mind alone is the primary body here, just as water is the principal element among all the juices of the creepers in every forest grove.
(22) "Formations of bodies" means the conceptualizations of bodies. "In all the juices of the creepers in every forest grove" refers to all those...
And the essences of the forest thickets and the forest-region creepers are indeed the material cause (upādānakāraṇa) for those gross bodies within these female elephants. || 22 ||
When the body is intact, the mind quickly creates various new bodies one after another, like in the realm of dreams;
but when the mind is destroyed, the body indeed accomplishes nothing at all. Therefore, protect the jewel of the mind. (23)

Now, one might ask: "In the case of the bodies, why should it not be the reverse—that the mind is the cause [of the body]? To this he says: "In the body, the senses... [and so on]. [This occurs] in the realm of dreams, that is, on the ground of dreaming. 23–24.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed in this manner by those two, that lotus-eyed king spoke to the sage named Bharata, who was standing by his side.
O Blessed One, Knower of all dharmas, Your words—which touch the essence of the ultimate truth—truly delight even the minds of those blinded by desire. (25)
They touch the essence of the ultimate truth; their domain is the core of the ultimate truth. || 25 ||
"Having instructed these two according to the scriptures, I shall now banish them.
Having said this, that tiger among kings banished both of them. (26)
I banish; I expel. He banished; he expelled. || 26 ||
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Narrative of Indra," in the section on Origination within the *Śrīmokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Narrative of Indra," in the section on Origination within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhacandrikā*.
p. 218) The Sixth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
This has been told to you, O Rāma, by me through the play of narration:
all embodied beings in this world possess two bodies. (1)
He summarizes the meaning established in detail by the preceding narrative, saying: "This has been told to you," and so forth.
The one [entity] is the mental body, which acts swiftly and is always mobile;
the other body, composed of flesh, is incapable of action. (2)
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, you should explain in detail to me, who am dull-witted and devoid of form, how the mind has ascended to the state of conceptualization.

Thinking that once the cause of the disease of saṃsāra is correctly understood, its treatment becomes easy to perform, Rāma asks, "in detail. [The world] is "devoid of form" because it is, in reality, "without intrinsic nature. The reason for this is stated: "of the insentient. He establishes its insentience with the words, "of this," meaning "of the object of perception. That by which a conceptual construction has ascended [is the mind].
"Having ascended to volition" (tadārūḍhasaṃkalpam) means that volition is predominant; or rather, it is so called because volition has ascended [to the state of being primary] within it. || 3 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
They know that form of the infinite reality of the Self, the Great Soul who possesses all powers, which is inlaid with the power of volition, as the mind.

Showing that the nature of the mind is inexpressible, [the author] says in the three verses beginning with "of the Infinite" (*anantasya*) that one should make that mind—characterized by contemplation and so forth from deep sleep until death—inclined toward the means of liberation. [The term *sarvaśakteḥ* means:
He whose power is Māyā, which is the cause of all; or else, [it means] all powers (*sarvāḥ śaktayaḥ*) because they reside in all objects.
That in which [all things] are perceived is thus described. They know that imagined form, which is conjoined with the power of volition (*saṃkalpa*), to be the mind (*manas*). || 4 ||
That which wavers between existence and non-existence for men, moving and tending toward conceptualization— that they know to be the form of the mind.
"Bhāva" means an object or state. Alternatively, by the word "bhāva," which denotes intention, its cause is indicated.

That disposition of men which is inherently fickle and wavering, having reached a state of being oriented toward conceptualization—that is, oriented toward volitional thought—moves between the existent and the non-existent; it oscillates between the self and the non-self, bearing the burden of manifoldness.
For the Self, mounted upon the mirror of the mind, assumes the relationship of seer and seen between itself and the non-Self;
for in deep sleep, when the mind is dissolved, that relationship of seer and seen between the Self and the non-Self is not observed. || 5 ||
Whatever mind arises from whatever source, one should always apply it toward liberation for the sake of one's own release through the methods of liberation. (6)

Because it has arisen from some cause that is charming only so long as it is not investigated, it is therefore merely something "whatever-it-may-be," charming only so long as it is not investigated. When, however, it is subjected to investigation, it falls apart like a ghost conjured by a shadow.

The word *hi* (for/indeed) is intended to indicate what is well-known among the learned. Regarding the arguments for liberation (*mukti-yuktiṣu*), that is, the logical demonstrations of the attainment of release.

One should employ that very mind in the means to liberation, characterized by such contemplation and the like. Thus, it has been stated that the mind alone—the cause of saṃsāra, which appears attractive only so long as it is not investigated—is fragile when subjected to inquiry; therefore, for its cessation, that same mind must be applied to the methods of liberation. || 6 ||
In this regard, O sinless one, I shall relate to you this narrative concerning the mind,
which was told of old by the Blessed One, the lotus-born Brahmā.
Now, introducing this very same subject by means of the exposition on consciousness (cittākhyāna), he elaborates upon it: "In this regard, this... (verse 7).
There is a vast forest called Rāmāṭavī, empty, unpeaceful, and extremely terrifying,
in which only a single corner can be discerned for a hundred yojanas.

There exists the Rāmāṭavī (the Forest of Rāmā). The venerable Vasiṣṭha himself will explain these verses of hidden meaning; nevertheless, we shall provide an exposition for the sake of facilitating understanding. It is called an *aṭavī* because living beings wander (*aṭanti*) within it; it is the path of *saṃsāra*. It is *sphārā*, meaning vast and extensive. It is *śūnyā*, devoid of all objective entities, because those entities therein are illusory (*māyika*). It is *aśāntā* (unpeaceful) because...

Word-separation: Alternatively, it is said to be "empty" (śūnyā) to demonstrate its *tāmasa* nature; "peaceful" (śāntā) to demonstrate its *sāttvika* nature; and "extremely terrifying" (atibhīṣaṇā) to make known its *rājasa* nature. || 8 ||
For in this [city] there stands a single man, with a thousand hands and eyes,
of terrifying appearance and deformed form, his mind agitated.

He lies in the city (puri) of the body; he sits much (purusīdati), or rather, he sinks down much (avasīdati)—thus he is called *puruṣa*. He is the mind (*manas*), possessing a thousand hands and eyes, with infinite hands and eyes. Here, the infinite modifications (*vṛtti*) taking the form of objects are intended to be expressed as his "hands and eyes. As it is said in the *Bṛhadvāsiṣṭha*: "That which is described as the man’s possession of a thousand eyes and hands..."
For it has been demonstrated that the mind indeed possesses infinite forms. || 9 ||
Taking up many iron clubs with his thousand arms,
he flees away by himself while striking his own back. (10)

They are called "arms" (*bāhu*) because they carry one away (*bāhayanti*), that is, cause one to reach various wombs; by means of a thousand such "arms," which are false conceptualizations, they strike all around—these being the "iron bars" (*parigha*).
Taking up these causes of internal and other sufferings, he strikes his own back;
the meaning is that he afflicts himself with the causes of internal and other sufferings, which are grasped through delusion. He flees.
The meaning is that he fears the causes of suffering brought about by wrong conceptualizations. || 10 || 11 || 12 ||
Striking himself with his own self by means of firm blows,
that one of terrifying nature flees even for hundreds of yojanas.
Crying out as he fled, having gone far away here and there,
he became exhausted, helpless in appearance, with his feet and limbs shattered.
Helpless indeed, he quickly fell into a great blind well, terrifying with the darkness of the black night, deep as the hollow of the sky. (13)

"Blind" means devoid of discernment (*viveka*). "In a blind well" refers to a dense hell; it is so called because of the etymology of the word *kūpa*—a place where contemptible sufferings are cast. It is a cavity or hollow, as deep as the sky and immeasurable, containing an internal space, which is what is described by that term. (13–14)
Then, after a long time, he emerged from the blind well;
striking with blows once more, he fled from himself to himself.
Having gone even further, he entered a thicket of Karañja trees covered in thorns, like a moth entering a flame. || 15 ||
In that context, "a thicket in a forest of *karañja* trees" is intended to signify human birth;

for the state of being a lowly plant born from the soil (*udbhijja*), denoted by the word "thicket" (*gulma*) within a *karañja* forest—which is synonymous with *naktamāla*—is productive of unhappiness.
Therefore, having emerged from that thicket of karañja trees as if in an instant,
he again flees from himself by himself while striking with blows.
Having gone even further, [he reached] that which was cool as the rays of the moon. || 17 ||
As if laughing, he entered the lovely grove of plantain trees,
and in an instant, he emerged again from that cluster of plantains.
The grove of plantain trees is heaven, because it is similarly delightful at first sight. 18 || 19 || 20 || 21 ||
Striking himself with his own blows, he flees from himself;
then, having gone even further away, that blind man returns once more to that very same blind well.
Having entered with haste, his limbs and form shattered,
he rose up from the blind well and entered a grove of plantain trees.
From the plantain grove to a thicket of *karañja* trees, from the *karañja* forest to a well, and from the well to another plantain grove. (21)
Having entered [the body] and striking [the senses], he remains established in himself;
having observed such conduct of his own for a long time, I [have seen it]. (22)

By the word *vasiṣṭha*, "splendor" (*tejas*) is expressed. Since the etymology of the word *vasiṣṭha* is "one whose nature is supreme splendor," the word *mayā* (by me), which denotes Vasiṣṭha, is intended here to signify supreme discernment (*viveka*). || 22 ||
Having been forcibly awakened for a moment by being seized, he was asked:
"Who are you? What is this? And for what purpose are you doing it? (23)
He states this point—that the mind has been forcibly and suddenly overcome by discernment—in the words: "Having been seized by force alone, he was awakened for a moment" (23).
"Furthermore, what could be your desire? Why do you run about in vain?
Thus questioned, O descendant of Raghu, he said this to me: (24)
In vain; uselessly. || 24 ||
(223) "I am nothing, nor indeed is this anything; O Sage, I do nothing at all.
I have been shattered by you; alas, you are my enemy! (25)

He demonstrates exactly what was said by the mind regarding discrimination (*viveka*) with the words beginning "I am not" (*nāham*): O Sage, the meaning is that the mind—which is delightful only so long as it is not investigated—along with its effects and so forth, becomes truly non-existent once it has been crushed by discrimination. || 25 ||
"I have been seen by you; I am lost, both for sorrow and for joy. Having spoken thus, he looked at his own limbs with agitation and was dissatisfied. (26)
"I have been seen and brought under control by you, Discrimination; I am ruined for both pleasure and pain.
The meaning is: "I am incapable of producing either pleasure or pain. || 26 ||
Distressed, he wept with a loud cry like a rain-showering cloud;
yet in a mere moment, having ceased his weeping there,
he looked at his own limbs and laughed violently for a long time.
Because its discrimination was only half-attained, the mind, being unable to renounce enjoyments, experienced great distress;
the author expresses this point with the words "He wept" (*ruroda*). That which has sound (*ārava*) on all sides is *āravī*;
having perceived that its own limbs—characterized by the notions of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) and "mine" (*mamakāra*)—were being suppressed by perfect discrimination (*pūrṇaviveka*), [it wept].
He says that the mind attained contentment by virtue of having reached supreme bliss: "Beholding his own limbs... and so forth.
Then, at the conclusion of her loud laughter, she suddenly cast off those limbs of hers one by one from all sides before me.

When full discernment has arisen, he describes the process of the dissolution of the mind along with its conduct in two verses, beginning with "Then, up to the loud laughter" (*athāṭṭahāsaparyanta*). The meaning is: "in my presence," that is, in the face of discernment. (28)
First his most dreadful head fell,
and after that his arms, then his chest, and following that his belly.

The head of that mind is characterized by egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), and it is most cruel and extremely terrifying. Immediately after that, the arms, characterized by false conceptualizations (*kukalpanā*), fell; subsequently, the chest and other parts, characterized by the hope for objects (*arthāśā*), fell.
Thus it is said in the *Bṛhadvāsiṣṭha*: "When the limbs have fallen apart..."
They have vanished from before his eyes. Thus it is demonstrated: "How can the hope for an object be stilled without him?
Here, "hope for an object" (*arthāśā*) serves as an illustration for both egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and false conceptualization (*kukalpanā*). || 29 ||
Then, in an instant, that man, having abandoned his own limbs as they were, was compelled by the power of destiny to depart for some unknown destination. (30)

From the expressions "according to each" (*yathāyatham*), "as before" (*yathāpūrvam*), and "on all sides" (*samantataḥ*), and now from the expression "according to each" (*yathāyatham*), this meaning is understood: he has prepared offerings for his own respective limbs from their respective directions, such as the east, and is now ready to depart; thus it was stated for the sake of the beauty of the narrative.

This is to be understood: the meaning is that he was manifested in the form of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*) through the power of destiny (*niyati*) or fate (*daiva*). By stating that he "prepared to go but did not go," his state of being liberated while living (*jīvanmuktatva*) is indicated. || 30 ||
Then, in another secluded spot, I saw yet another man striking himself and wandering about with an extremely agitated mind. (31)
"paryākulatarāntaram" means one whose interior (antara), that is, the inner part (abhyantara), is extremely agitated; he is described as such. || 31 ||
I questioned him face-to-face, and he indeed answered me exactly so;
having wept and then laughed in that very same sequence. (32)
Having reached a state of disintegration through his limbs, he was barely discernible;
likewise, I saw another man in a secluded spot.
"It has become exceedingly unmanifest; it has reached a state of invisibility"—by this it is indicated that he has attained the state of liberation while in the body (videhamukti). || 33 ||
Fleeing, I indeed fell into a blind well that was utter darkness;
there I dwelt for a very long time, waiting for him.
Then, even after a very long time, that rogue did not emerge from the well;
he saw yet another falling here and there. (35)

"Now, after a very long time" means that the mind, being possessed of great sins, fell into the hell called the "Blind Well" (andhakūpa) and did not emerge from that well even after an exceedingly long period of time. || 35 ||
Having quickly seized him in that very manner, I spoke to him for a long time:
"O fool of wicked mind, you do not understand anything at all."
Having said, "Go away, O evil-minded one," he became intent on his own business. || 36 ||
He says that the mind—devoid of even a trace of purity and ignorant of the Self—overpowered its own discrimination:
"The evil-minded one... The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "That evil-minded one, having said 'me,' became intent upon his own activity.
He explains what is referred to by the word "iti" with the words beginning with "O fool," etc.: "O foolish, wicked twice-born one, you do not know anything at all."
Go away; depart from my presence. || 36 || 37 ||
Thus, many such men remain wandering in that great forest; even today, that wilderness still exists.

That terrifying and dreadful forest, its body crowded with various thorns and dense with thick darkness, is nevertheless resorted to by people who have not attained their own true awakening, as if it were a bower of flowering shrubs.

"She is terrifying" (*bhīṣaṇā*): she is so described because her limbs possess a manifold, narrow confinement (*saṅkaṭa*) characterized by thorns, which is to say, sufferings. She is "thick with dense darkness" (*ghanatamogahanā*), meaning difficult to enter due to dense ignorance (*ajñāna*). Even though she is thick with dense darkness, she is [nevertheless] [accessible] to people who have not attained self-awakening—that is, those who have not obtained knowledge of the Self (*ātma-jñāna*).
Having attained tranquility and obtained happiness, living beings are served from all sides; "gulmakas" are specific types of small shrubs. || 38 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahmin, where is that great forest, and how is it seen, O sinless one?
Who are those men there, and what do they intend to accomplish? (39)
The composition of the text from "What is this great forest? up to the end of the chapter is clear in meaning; however, certain points are here analyzed in detail. || 39 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed Raghunātha, listen; I shall tell you everything:
that great forest is not far away, O Rāma, nor indeed are those men. (40)
And those men are certainly not far away; this [phrase] continues [from the previous verse]. || 40 ||
This path of accumulation, deep and with its far-reaching hollows, know it, O Rāma, to be that great forest rich in the transformations of emptiness. (41)
Abounding in the transformations of emptiness, and abounding in the doctrine that the effect is non-existent [in the cause]. || 41 || 42 || 43 || 44 || 5 ||
Know that those large-bodied men wandering about there are indeed the minds fallen deeply into suffering. (42)
O Mahāmati, that "I" who am the observer of these [minds] possesses discernment;
for it is by means of discernment that those minds are awakened by me. (43)
O Mahāmati, having attained supreme awakening through my grace,
some minds have reached the highest tranquility.
Deluded, some do not welcome me or my solitude;
due to their contempt for me, they fall headlong into wells. (45)
O descendant of Raghu, those dark wells and dense forests are for you hells;
the plantain grove is heaven, and the karañja tree is the realm of mortals.
The Karañja is the circle of mortals. || 46 || 47 ||
But those fears that have entered into the interior of blind wells and emerged are always present in hell for those joined with great sins. 47.
That thicket of karañja trees, turbid with the passion for one's wife, is human existence—painful, crowded with thorns, and filled with manifold desires. (48)
He explains what was stated in the verse beginning with "that thicket of karañja trees": "turbid with the passion for a wife" means defiled by attachment to women. (48)
By those ignorant men who insulted me, saying "O wicked Brahmin," their own discernment was insulted by their minds that lack self-knowledge. (49)
"I have been seen by you! I am ruined! You are my enemy!"—these words spoken so hastily were the lamentation of one possessed by the sense of "mine," uttered by a distracted mind. (50)
By means of a distracted mind, that is, a mind directed toward sense objects. || 50 || 51 || 52 ||
O Raghava, that great wailing which was heard there among men was the weeping made by the mind as it renounced the web of enjoyments.
For one who has attained partial discernment but has not yet reached the stainless state,
a sense of distress indeed arises when the mind renounces enjoyments.
But that laughter which brings joy to men arises from awakening; it is the satisfaction produced in the mind by one who has attained discernment. (53)

The two words *tadavabodhataḥ* mean "from the awakening" or "by means of awakening. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: that very thing which constitutes the satisfaction of men—whose minds have attained discernment (*pariprāptaviveka*)—through the awakening to that [truth], which is the blissful laughter of battle, is precisely this. || 53 ||
For one who has attained solitude and abandoned abiding in saṃsāra, bliss indeed increases as the mind relinquishes form. (54)
Form undergoes transformation characterized by conceptualization and discursive thought.
When he was seen by me with great effort as he stood firm, it was shown that discrimination forcibly seized the mind. (55)
When a person strikes himself with a torrent of blows against his own self,
it is the mind that strikes itself there with the blows of its own conceptual constructions.
When a person flees while striking at his own self,
it is because the mind itself is fleeing here and there from the blows of its own latent impressions (vāsanās).
