Through the very nets of its own volitions and latent impressions,
the mind incurs bondage by means of playful attachments, just like a silkworm in its cocoon. (58)

He states the intended meaning of the section concerning the past as follows: "By the webs of volitions and latent impressions" (*saṃkalpavāsanājālaiḥ*). Volitions themselves are called "latent impressions" because they are the root of latent impressions; [the phrase means] by their own respective webs.
Just as the silk-worm, having become attached to a wood-apple tree or similar object, constructs a cocoon for its own dwelling—
The meaning is: even while attempting to close the door of departure, he is bound by bonds consisting of divine play (līlā).
Thus has this supreme narrative concerning the mind been told to you, O Rāma;
having perceived all this through the mind alone, remain steadfast in the renunciation of the mind.
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Narrative of Citta," in the *Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭhasāra*, within the means to liberation.
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Narrative of Citta," in the section on Origination within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhacandrikā*.
(228) Seventh Canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, for those who are awakened, this mind is indeed Brahman alone and nothing else—
the Supreme Brahman, which possesses all powers, is eternal, perfectly full, and imperishable.
At the end of a past creation, the mind comes to be bound like a silkworm;
because this illustration is employed and because the mind is designated as something to be abandoned, and since it is impossible to abandon what is non-existent, its reality is established.
And if that [mind] is real, then the reality of the world, which is its modification, follows—thus for all duality.
Anticipating the objection that this [world] might be real, he introduces the following in order to demonstrate its worthlessness through the pretext of a story told to a child:

"Of the awakened," and so forth. The meaning is: for the awakened ones—the knowers of Brahman—this mind, which expands in the form of this world, is Brahman itself; it is not other than that, nor even non-different from it; rather, it is merely insubstantial (*tuccha*).

The grammatical coordination in the phrase "the mind is Brahman" (*mano brahma*) is used in the sense of sublation (*bādhā*). The word "hi" (for/indeed) is intended to indicate the well-known [notion] of the void (*śūnya*) and so forth. Having raised the doubt as to why the mind and other [faculties] possess the nature of Brahman—that is, why they are nothing but that—he states: "possessing all powers" (*sarvaśakti*). [This means: because it is the cause of everything, including the mind...
Or [it means] "in which"; it is an indeclinable meaning free from decay. || 1 ||
There is nothing that does not exist within that expansive Self;
by whatever power it manifests, that [power] attains its manifestation. (2)

Now, one might object: "Since among the various manifold objects it is possible for some to be non-works of Brahman, how can everything be Brahman and nothing but that? To this he says: "There is nothing else" (*na tadasti*). In that pervasive Self, which is the substratum, whatever effect does not exist—that is not the Supreme Brahman, which possesses all powers; for [Brahman] is that in which all powers reside.

He states that those [powers] mentioned as being grounded in Brahman are perceived indistinctly in their respective effects, beginning with the words "by whichever power He shines forth": this Supreme Self shines forth—that is, manifests through transformation—by means of whichever power among His own manifold powers rests within Him. (2)
O Rāma, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) of Brahman is perceived in bodies;
the power of motion (spandaśakti) is in the winds; and likewise, the power of solidity (dārḍhyaśakti) is in stones.
To the question "Where is that power perceived?", he says: "The power of consciousness," and so forth. On a stone (*upala*) means on a rock (*pāṣāṇa*). || 3 ||
Furthermore, the power of fluidity resides in waters, the power of burning in fire,
the power of emptiness in space, and the power of destruction in that which is perishable.
The power of emptiness is the power of producing the formless. || 4 ||
Just as a peacock exists within its egg, so does all this exist within the Self;
just as a tree— possessing fruit, leaves, creepers, flowers, branches, boughs, and roots—
is contained within the seed of the tree, so too is this world situated within Brahman.

At the time of dissolution, the entire range of duality exists within Brahman alone in a state where name and form are unmanifest. When the time of creation arrives, it unfolds gradually from that very source—like [the world] emerging from the waters within the cosmic egg—by means of the magician (māyin). Even there, since creation is nothing but perception, it unfolds precisely through the sequence beginning with the mind (manas). And that [sequence] beginning with the mind...

Duality, which appears as if real during the state of non-investigation—much like the meaning of an inconsistent story told for the sake of consoling a child—is utterly trivial upon the determination of reality;
this entire point is stated in the passage beginning with "phalapatre" (the fruit and leaf). Here, "latā" means a tender branch. In this context, the word "viṭapa" is used to avoid redundancy.
The trunk of the tree is grasped. || 5 ||
In some places, at times, and in certain ways, powers arise from that [source],
just as rice sprouts from the surface of the earth due to the variety of place and time. (6)
"Somewhere," etc. The meaning is that from that Brahman they arise, manifesting in the form of effects. "From the surface of the earth" means from the ground. || 6 ||
O Rāma, that Self is all-pervading and possesses an eternally manifest great body;
when it assumes even a slight power of thought, it is called the mind.

"That Self, O Rāma, is all-pervading. The Self, whose great body is eternally manifest, shines by itself at all times as full. Whenever it assumes even slightly a thinking power—that is to say, a power characterized by thought—then, through the process of evolving thought, it becomes delimited by that power;
at that very moment, it is called "mind" (manas). || 7 ||
First is the mind, then the views of bondage and liberation, and afterwards the construction of conceptual proliferation known as the world;
for this entire state of affairs has become established like a story told by fortunate children. (8)

First, by "mind" (*manas*), the collective form is intended. Thereafter, immediately following that, the two perspectives of bondage and liberation—the cognitions of bondage and release—arise. For if these two were not to arise, there would be the undesirable consequence that creation could not occur for the sake of experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*). It is recorded in tradition that creation exists for the purpose of experience and liberation: *...for the sake of experience and liberation...* (Sāṃkhyakārikā 41)

"The omnipresent Lord created the sense organs, the mind, and the vital breaths for the sake of the objects of the senses, for the sake of worldly existence, and for the sake of the self's non-conceptualization. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the intellect (*citta*) and so forth are included. "O Subhaga" is either a vocative or a single compound word.
This state of duality—such as that told in the aforementioned narrative concerning Subhaga-bāla-jana and Suśrīka-bāla-jana—is [described] by such passages.
It has attained a state of stability through immovability; the meaning is that, due to the absence of further deliberation, it has become the object of a firm conviction regarding the truth. || 8 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O best of sages, why is this sequence of the narrative concerning the boy mentioned?
Please explain to me in due order the reason for this description of the mind.
The verses beginning with "What is said? and continuing until the end of the chapter are clear in meaning. In some places, a certain point is further analyzed:

"the cause for the description of the mind. This refers to the cause for the description of the mind—that is, for the awakening to the true nature of the mind—in which the mind, though accompanied by its play (*savilāsa*) and being insubstantial (*tuccha*), appears as if real to those whose minds are devoid of inquiry. || 9 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, a certain child of innocent mind asked his nurse:
"Nurse, tell me quickly some entertaining story. (10)
To the *dhātrī*, the foster-mother; speak, say. 10, 11.
O Great-minded One, for the amusement of that child, his nurse told him a narrative composed of clear and sweet syllables. (11)
In a certain place, where there was no city at all, there were three auspicious princes of great soul, righteous and exultant in their valor. (12)
He specifies the city for the sake of establishing the equality of the Unequalled. "Extremely non-existent" means "insubstantial. (12) 13.
Two were not born, and likewise one did not even remain in the womb;
nevertheless, for the sake of a supreme gain, those three auspicious ones [met] at once. (13)
Having emerged from their own empty city, those of pure intention saw trees laden with fruit while traveling through the sky.
Intention (āśaya) is purpose (abhiprāya). || 14 || 15 ||
Resting again and again among them and eating that delicious fruit, those three princes traveled happily with playful ease. (15)
Then they reached a triad of rivers garlanded with surging waves;
there, one was completely dried up, while not even a drop of water remained in the other two. (16)
"Āseduḥ" means they arrived or came. "Mālitaṃ" means it has become garlanded; that is to say, it was joined with waves (kallola) as if by garland-makers. "Manāk" means even slightly. || 16 ||
In that very lake which had become utterly parched, they bathed with great devotion;
after sporting in the water for a long time, they drank the water which was like milk.
They bathed; "payas" means water. || 17 ||
Then, at the end of the day, the three of them reached the city that was about to come into being—
a city whose joyful clamor could be heard from afar and where the circles of citizens were sporting.

"Samullāpa" means mutual conversation spoken aloud. That city where such conversation was heard from afar was "dūraśruta-samullāpa. "Khelannāgaramaṇḍala" refers to a city in which the multitude of living beings born within the city were sporting; it is described as such because it contained a circle of playful inhabitants. (18, 19, 20)
There they beheld three beautiful mansions;
one was without walls and without pillars, while the other two houses were unproduced.
Those princes entered the beautiful,
wall-less palace and there found three vessels fashioned from refined gold.
There, two of them turned into shards and one turned into powder;
those of pure intellect took the vessel that had turned into powder. (21)
The state of being a skull-cup, that is, the state of being a severed head-bowl. || 21 ||
In that [vessel], three *droṇas* were cooked; however, when it was deficient by three *droṇas*, the blind man was then fed by the twice-born, who were great eaters and had finished their own meals.

Eight *āḍhakas* are called a *droṇa*. As it has been said: "A *pala*, a *prakuñcaka*, a *muṣṭi*, and a *kuḍava*—the latter being four times the former; four *kuḍavas* make a *prastha*, and four *prasthas* make an *āḍhaka*."

"Eight *āḍhakas* make a *droṇa*, and two *droṇas* are called a *śūrpa*. In some regions, however, the common usage is that four *āḍhakas* constitute a *droṇa*. That which was cooked by the princes as "three *droṇas*" was actually slightly less than three *droṇas*. (22, 23, 24) [p. 233]
The blind man ate what remained after the Brahmins had finished their meal;
for those three princes were destined to be born in that very city. (23)
"O son, those who engage in the practice of hunting remain only in happiness.
O Rāma, thus was this auspicious tale concerning the boy told by the nurse.
That boy reached a firm conviction through his non-discerning intellect.
This, O Rāma, is the story of the boy that has been told to you. (25)
This construction of saṃsāra belongs to those whose minds are devoid of inquiry;
thus has this narrative called "The Child" come to pass. (26)
The story of Bālaka is as follows: the syntactical connection is "and thus is the story of Bālaka. || 26 ||
"The entire world is merely the fabrication of the web of conceptualization; because of the fabrication of the web of conceptualization, it is a play of the mind.

Abandoning mere conceptualization, take refuge in the state free from conceptualization (nirvikalpa), and having attained certainty, O Rāma, obtain peace. Thus [it is said]: "The entire world is merely the fabrication of the web of conceptualization," meaning it is simply the delusion of a mass of conceptual constructions.

Regarding what is meant by "the fabrication of the web of conceptualization" (saṃkalpajālakalanā), he says: "From the fabrication of the web of conceptualization" (saṃkalpajālakalanāt tu). He states the resulting conclusion:

"It is mere conceptualization" (saṃkalpamātram) [which takes on] the form of the object that is beyond conceptualization; or rather, it is the non-conceptual, doubt-free certainty regarding the reality of Brahman as the Self. [This leads to] peace (śāntim), which is the cessation of saṃsāra. || 27 ||
Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Narrative of the Story of the Boy," in the section on the Means to Liberation within the *Śrīyogavāsiṣṭhasāra*.

Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Narrative of the Boy," in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā*, composed by the venerable Ātmasukha, disciple of the venerable Uttamasukhapūjyapāda, the foremost wandering mendicant of the supreme order (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka*). 7.
(234) The Eighth Canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:

Under the influence of one's own volitions, the fool falls into delusion, but not the wise man. With an intellect characterized by inquiry and free from the agitation of delusion, investigate with that intellect what is real and indeed abandon what is unreal. (1)

Having raised the doubt as to what must be done in order to rely upon the previously mentioned foundation of non-conceptual certainty at the end of the preceding creation, he states—with justification and by means of the verse beginning with "By the power of one's own volition" (svasaṃkalpavaśāt)—that the inquiry into Brahman, characterized by truth and so forth, must be undertaken. Indeed, inquiry itself is dharma; like other forms of dharma, it should be practiced constantly.
The wise person does not fall into delusion by means of that intellect which is free from the agitation of delusion and free from the ostentation of delusion. || 1 ||
Having said that the unbound is bound, why do you grieve in vain?
How, by what means, and in what manner can the infinite reality of the Self be bound?
Now, one might object: "I am bound; like a bird caught in a snare, what can I do? To this, he says: "Unbound," and so forth.
In vain; for naught. || 2 || 3 ||
In the infinite, dense mass of consciousness and bliss, which is of a single non-conceptual nature, since nothing else exists, who is bound and who is liberated? (3)
Therefore, O Rāma, it is merely the vibration of the mind that has attained the state of bondage; when the mind is stilled, nothing remains but liberation.
He states the conclusion regarding the fact that, in reality, bondage is impossible: "Therefore," etc. [Bondage] is merely the manifestation, merely the unfolding, of the mind. || 4 ||
Within his own playful pastimes, he makes an eon appear as a moment and brings a moment to the state of an eon, even for the mind that perceives a cow’s footprint as a league-long expanse.
Now, one might object: "If, in reality, there is an absence of bondage, how can the mind possibly be the cause of bondage?
Anticipating this doubt, the author speaks of its power to accomplish the impossible in order to explain that point, beginning with the words "goṣpadam" (a cow's footprint).
For the mind, when engaged in its own inherent pastimes, even a multitude of *yojanas* becomes a mere cow's footprint; indeed, even a collection of *yojanas* [is thus reduced].
The meaning is that it expands like a cow’s footprint; it should be understood that even a cow’s footprint can become an array of leagues (*yojanavyūha*).
For indeed, in dreams and the like, an illusion regarding the length of space and time is observed. (5)
(235) Listen here as I shall tell you this supreme account,
of how the splendor of the world’s illusion resides within the mind. (6)

The mind, which is illusory in nature, brings about even that which is impossible; having introduced the narrative to clarify this stated meaning, [the author] elucidates it with the words "In this matter, listen to you," and so forth. The remainder of the sense is: "You shall know how the worldly state—that which pertains to the world—is situated within the mind, by what manner [it exists]. || 6 ||
On this surface of the earth, there is a great and prosperous region named Northern Pāṇḍava, which is filled with various forests.
A flourishing and prosperous country is a *janapada*. || 7 || 8 ||
There was a king named Lavaṇa, supremely righteous,
born of the lineage of Hariścandra, like a sun upon the earth.
With the circles of their shoulders made white by the crest-ornaments of their flowers of fame, all the mountains shine resplendent like necklaces from which pearls have been shaken loose.

*Uttaṃsa* means a crest-ornament (*śekhara*). As Kṣīrasvāmin has said: "That which rests upon the head is a *śekhara*; *uttaṃsa* is also used in this sense. Those whose circles of shoulders (*skandhamaṇḍala*) are white—that is, bright—due to those very flowers that are the fame of Lavaṇa acting as crest-ornaments, are called *yadyaśaḥkusumottaṃsapāṇḍuraskandhamaṇḍalāḥ*.
For it is well known in the world that the circles of tree trunks become white due to the falling of pollen from flower-ornaments.
"Proddhūlitāḥ" means made stainless; the intended meaning is that his fame pervades the ends of the quarters. || 9 ||

He who does not recognize ambiguity, by whom greediness has not been observed, and by whom nobility is maintained according to the expression as it is designated—[such a person is a true reciter]. 10.

*Jihmatā* means deceitfulness. *Gṛdhnutā* is the state of one whose character is characterized by greed (*gṛdhru*) or longing; it is derived from the root *gṛdh* (in the sense of "longing") with the suffix *knu* according to the rule *trasigṛdhītyādinā*. *Udāratā* means generosity or munificence, or else greatness.
It is either denoted by a signifier (*vācaka*), or expressed by a speaker (*vaktrā*), or it is the function known as *abhidhā*—that is, the operation called direct denotation (*abhidhāna*). 10–11.
p.
236) Once, he was seated upon the lion-throne in the assembly hall; while he, the foremost among those who know the science of statecraft, was sitting there at ease— (11)
A certain magician entered the assembly with arrogance;
he bowed to the protector of the earth, whose shoulders were as noble as mountain peaks. 12.
"With pride" means with agitation. "One whose neck is noble"—that is, excellent—like a mountain peak (śikhara) or a horn (śṛṅga), is described as such. || 12 ||
Like a bee toward a lotus, he spoke to the king who stood with his neck upraised:
"O Lord, behold for a moment this one extraordinary feat of the ass,
which is like the rising of the moon upon the earth."

"With neck upraised" means with the neck raised. "One principal" [refers to the primary trick]. Regarding the phrase "the art of harsh play," the practice of the science of sorcery (indrajāla-vidyā) is intended here. || 13 ||
Having said this, he whirled his peacock-feather broom, which causes confusion,
the seed of various manifestations, like the Māyā of the Supreme Self.
The peacock-feather fan (picchikā) here is a bundle of peacock feathers; it is the seed for various arrangements and the cause for various creations. || 14 ||
The protector of the earth beheld that assembly hall, resplendent with particles of light; then, at that very moment, he entered it along with his vassal kings.
Then, immediately after the appearance of the peacock-feather whisk, at that very moment, the Saindhava vassal—the feudal lord of the Sindhu region—entered the assembly hall. || 15 ||
And that gentle horse, possessing supreme speed, followed right after him;
then the provincial governor, taking up the horse, spoke to the king.
The meaning is that the king fell into the delusion that the horse was following after that neighboring king; the same should be understood for what follows hereafter. || 16 ||
"O lord of the earth, this jewel among horses, resembling Ucchaiḥśravas, has been sent to you by my master, the sovereign of the circle of the world. (17)
Uccaiḥśravas is Indra’s horse; "resembling that" means having its likeness. "Sent" means dispatched. || 17 || 18 || 19 ||
(237) "For the auspicious splendor of the objects of the great shines forth through their renunciation"—
when he had spoken thus, that magician replied: || 18 ||
"O Lord, mount this noble horse and roam the world.
The king looked at the horse, and it spoke thus to him. (19)
Then the king, whose form was like a painting, gazed at the horse with an unblinking eye, as if it were fixed in a work of art.
He remained for two muhūrtas as if absorbed in meditation upon the Self;
then those members of the assembly, overcome with wonder, fell into deep reflection.
A pair is a couple. Those present in the assembly are the members of the court. || 21 || 22 ||
The ministers remained there, submerged in an ocean of doubt;
the great clamor of the people in the assembly hall subsided.
While the lord of the earth stood with eyes motionless, that multitude— stupefied by wonder, paralyzed by fear and delusion, and despondent— bore the luster of a forest of lotuses with closed buds.
When the lord of the earth stood with his eyes fixed in a state of wide-open astonishment— a state characterized by great wonder and a certain crookedness like that of a magician—
the multitude of people, dejected and distressed by fear and delusion, [beheld] a forest of lotuses closed like buds.
Splendor and beauty were maintained. || 23 || 24 || 25 || 26 || 27 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after two muhūrtas, the lord of the earth awoke;
having awakened, he trembled upon his seat.
Then, supported by those walking before him, the king’s mind became utterly agitated;
thereupon, the members of the assembly and the ministers questioned him. (25)
But since you have attained perfect awakening, why does your mind—pure and endowed with respectful humility—sink into such agitations? (26)
The mind assumes delusion, not the manifestation of greatness;
then the king, opening his eyes in wonder, said: (27)
O members of the assembly, listen today to this wonderful narrative: having seen this peacock-feather whisk being whirled around by that rogue, I [laughed]. (28)
"By the fool, who acts without reflection. According to Amara, "a fool (jālma) is one who acts without reflection. || 28 ||
Mounted upon this horse, with my own mind bewildered, I set out alone at great speed for the hunt. (29)
With extreme speed and excessive velocity. || 29 ||
"O horse, by this extremely restless one, I have been led far away, just as an ignorant and deluded man is led astray by his own mind, which is dulled by the habitual pursuit of enjoyments. (30)

Stupefied by the habit of enjoyment—that is, by the mental state of experiencing sensual pleasures—he is dull-witted; therefore, he is ignorant of other goals of human life, being stupefied by the habit of enjoyment. Thus, being ignorant, he does not know the Self; being deluded, he is devoid even of worldly wisdom like a beast.

Then, with my mount exhausted, I reached a vast, boundless forest— a place as terrifying in its stillness as the world consumed by the fire of universal dissolution, devoid of birds, trees, and water, and filled with dense, spreading mist. (31)
That forest in which there was a vast and abundant mist of frost is described as such. || 31 ||
Then, having reached that forest, my mind was overcome with distress; I spent the day there until the sun set, wandering about in exhaustion.
"Until the end of the sun" means up to the time of sunset; "prākramta" means having wandered extensively. || 32 ||
Then, having passed through that forest with great difficulty and exhaustion, he reached the Jāṅgala region, just as a man of discernment leaves behind the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra). (33)
Jāṅgala is a specific type of forest. || 33 || 34 ||
In those regions abounding with rose-apple and kadamba trees, where birds warble sweetly in the groves like kinsmen for travelers. (34)
There, I reached the ground of a cluster of rose-apple trees; there, I grasped a creeper that was entwined with the trunk.
The *jambīra* is the tree known as *dantaśaṭha*. "Creeper" (*latā*) means branch, according to the statement of the learned: "The creeper is the branch of trees. (35) (36) (37)
While I was hanging there, that horse galloped away,
just as the accumulation of one’s evil deeds departs when a man clings to the Ganges.
Exhausted from traveling a very long road, I rested there;
for me, submerged in delusion, a night passed there that was equal to an eon.
I had not bathed, nor had I performed worship, nor had I eaten at that time; rather, the night had simply passed for me as I stood at the forefront of calamities. (38)
That night; or "sāpadām" may be considered a single word [meaning "of those with calamities"]; "dhuri" means on a burden. || 38 ||
Accompanied by the whistling sounds of her rows of teeth chattering from the cold,
that night passed away along with the masses of darkness.

The night passed away— having been spent together with the masses of darkness, as well as with the clattering sounds of my teeth and the whistling sighs produced by my row of teeth while I was afflicted by the cold. || 39 ||
Having set out for that vast region, I then proceeded toward the plateau;
not a single living being was to be seen there in that desolate wilderness.
"Bhūta" refers to the class of living beings; "jaraṭhajaṅgala" refers to a particular type of withered forest. || 40 ||
Just as a mere fragment of virtue might appear in the body of a fool,
[so too do these qualities exist] entirely without suspicion, flickering with partial delusions. (41)
Partial wandering is incomplete wandering. || 41 ||
The birds moved about uttering the sounds "cī-cī" and "ku-cī," when the lord of the day had reached the eighth part of the sky.
"Cīcīkucī" is an imitation of sound. The meaning is: when the lord of the day, the sun, has reached—that is, arrived at—a region that constitutes one-eighth of the thirty parts of the sky. || 42 ||
As I was wandering about, I saw a young girl carrying boiled rice;
she had large, sparkling eyes, a dark complexion, and was dressed in white garments. (43)

A young girl (*dārikā*) or maiden (*bālikā*); "one whose eyes have pupils that are like stars" refers to one whose eyes possess black spots in their centers and whose pupils are moving within the *taratāraka* (the space between the iris and the pupil). Thus she is described. (43–44)
I arrived there like the moon at night;
O child, this boiled rice is of great importance to me in my current distress. (44)
"O girl, wealth expands when given away to those who remove the suffering of the destitute; yet this great hunger within me has reached full growth. (45)
Having expanded, she has attained a state of vastness; she has arrived. || 45 || 46 ||
Not even by that begging of mine was anything given to me in this manner,
just as wealth is not given to a wrongdoer by Fortune, even when she is entreated with great effort.
Only after a long time did she, following me most closely, fall from one fragment to another as I stood before her like a shadow.
The locative case [in "khaṇḍe"] is used because [the fruit] falls upon another piece from the collection of trees and so forth belonging to that same fragment. || 47 ||
She said, "Know me to be a Caṇḍālī adorned with necklaces and armlets;
by merely begging from me, O King, you shall not obtain food. (48)
The name is "Possessing Necklaces and Armlets. || 48 ||
When Līlāvanitā had spoken thus, as she was walking, moving step by step, and resting in the bowers, she said: (59)
In the groves and thickets, she sat down intensely with the desire to grasp fruits and the like;
[the variant reading] "in the *guñjaka* shrubs" means that she was intent on the *guñjā* berries either hanging from her own neck or lying outside. || 49 ||
"I give you this food if you become my husband;
here, my father, a Pukkasa, is driving my two oxen. (50)
The two oxen are tamed, disciplined, well-trained, and strong; they are on the field that has been ploughed with a plough—thus [the locative case] is used in the sense of location (saptamī).
This food belongs to him, for it is given while he remains in the state of a master;
indeed, beloved men are to be honored even at the cost of one's life.
Then I said to her, "O lady of virtuous vows, I shall become your husband; for in times of distress, who takes account of caste, lineage, or family tradition? (52)
Then half of that rice was offered to me;
I drank the juice of the jambu fruit and ate that cooked rice from the hamlet. (53)
By the word *pakkaṇa*, which denotes the dwelling of the Śabaras, the house of the Pukkasa is indicated. || 53 || 54 ||
And while I was resting there, my mind having been carried away by delusion, he then seized me by the hand as if I were life itself standing outside [the body]. (54)
He approached his father, who was of hideous appearance, evil conduct, and terrifying, with a massive form like the Avīci hell of torment.
"Of stout form" means having a plump appearance. "Avīci" is a specific type of hell. || 55 ||
By her, who was [my] companion, I was introduced to Mātaṅga:
"O father, let it be pleasing to you that this man shall be my husband. (56)
*Mātaṅga* means a *caṇḍāla*. According to Amara: "Caṇḍāla, plava, mātaṅga, divākīrti, and janaṅgama [are synonyms]. (56)
Having said "Certainly" to her, when the end of the day had arrived,
he released the two tamed [elephants] that were bound, like the servants of Kṛtānta (Yama). (57)
The indeclinable *bāḍham* signifies acceptance or agreement. || 57 ||
When the quarters were as if covered in rising dust, being ruddy with frost and clouds,
we departed at the end of the day from that place where the Vetāla had been bound.
In the quarters that were tawny with frost-clouds—frost-clouds being showers of snow and sandhyā-clouds—the connection is that they appeared as if covered in dust while moving.
From that forest, known as Vetālabandhana, which is a haunt of Vetālas (where Vetālas are bound). *Note: According to Amara, *kaḍāra* means tawny (*kapila*), reddish-brown (*piṅga*).*
In an instant, they reached the hamlet from the Dīrghajaṅgala forest at twilight;
it was filled with slaughtered boars, horses, monkeys, cocks, and crows,
and with birds swooping down upon the nets of moist entrails spread out for drying.

*Jaṅgala* is a specific type of forest. By way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the three qualifiers of *pakvaṇa*—beginning with *vikartita*—refer to the dwelling of the *pukkasa*. That [dwelling] is so described because in it boars and other animals have been variously cut up (*vikartita*). Here, *āmnāṇi* refers to the veins (*sirā*). Those very moist intestines (*ārdrāntrāṇi*) which have been spread out and scattered for the purpose of drying are what is meant.
It was that [place] where birds and winged creatures fell into a web of tendons—tendons of moist entrails spread out for the purpose of drying them. || 59 ||
It was filled with the buzzing of flies attracted to lumps of raw flesh held in the hands of children,
and it contained many pieces of plantain leaves scattered about in a state of agitation.

*Kravya* means flesh; *palalam* is flesh, *kravya*, and *āmiṣa*—so says Amara. It refers to that [place] where flies were buzzing—that is, making a sound—over the morsels of flesh held in the hands of children. || 60 ||
I remained there in my new father-in-law’s house,
together with my mother-in-law, who was squint-eyed and possessed blood-red eyes.
"Upahitam" means presented or offered. "Kekarākṣī" is a name. 61 || 62 ||
"This man is my son-in-law," she said, and that was welcomed by him.
What need is there for much more to be said here? Then, on a certain day— (62)
And that girl, who was a source of fear, was given to me by him—she who was dark-complexioned like a wicked deed resulting in torment. (63)
The connection with the preceding [phrase] is "by him who was black in color. || 63 ||
There, the outcastes, having drunk their fill of flowing, potent liquor, roared impetuously on all sides;
like great heaps of their own evil deeds personified, they were full of revelry, beating their drums with skillful strokes.

*Sarabhasam*, *sasambhramam*, or *savegam* means with impetuosity, agitation, or speed. *Abhitaḥ* means on both sides. *Vineduḥ* means they uttered a distinguished roar. *Madirāsavāḥ* refers to those from whose mouths great quantities of wine (*madirā*) and spirits (*āsava*) had flowed forth; *āsava* refers to spirituous liquors such as *surā* and *madirā*. *Surā* is wine with a delicious taste, as it is said: [citation].
According to Kṣīrasvāmin: "madirā" means having a sweet taste. "Śvapākāḥ" and "śvapacāḥ" [mean] dog-cookers (outcastes). 64 || 65 ||
The king said:
From that time forward, I became a well-nourished Pukkasa there;
at the end of the seven-night festival, eight months passed by in succession.
Having blossomed, she then became pregnant;
subsequently, she gave birth to a daughter who brought misery, like a calamity that brings about suffering.
She has blossomed, she has come into fruition, she has become possessed of the menstrual flow. || 66 ||
That girl grew quickly, becoming stout like the thought of a fool;
after three years, she gave birth again to an unlovely son. (67)
Pīvarī means plump. || 67 ||
Then that Pukkasi, of wicked intellect, gave birth once more to a son who was like a calamity and a creator of the snares of hope.

It is "durbuddhi" because it is both wicked and an intellect; "āśāpāśavidhāyaka" means that which ordains or produces the snares of hope, since these [hopes] are themselves snares due to their being the cause of bondage. || 68 ||
(244) Together with her, many years were spent by me there,
rendered helpless by the afflictions of cold, wind, and heat in that other state of existence. (69)

For years that were equal [in length]. "In the interval of the *daśā*" refers to a specific division of time; the connection is that [he remained] in the interval of the *daśā*, rendered helpless by the afflictions of cold, wind, and heat. || 69 || 70 ||
With a mind struck by anxiety for wife and family, and being consumed by it, he saw his arduous undertakings as if the very quarters of the sky were ablaze. (70)
Then, as time passed and my life was worn out by old age,
I grew a beard like the flickering flames of a fire made of straw.
Regarding the phrase "arising from grass": for the flame of a fire produced from grass is indeed white. || 71 ||
There, a great famine occurred where the grass was completely withered; it was like a sudden, untimely death, or a swarm of fierce Caṇḍālas flying up all at once.

"Unseasonable" (*akāṇḍa*) means there is no opportune time; "famine-time" (*durbhikṣakāla*) refers to that period, and death caused by it is "untimely death" (*kāṇḍamaraṇa*). From that cause, [the army] has "flown up" (*uḍḍīna*), meaning it has surged forth. According to Amara, "caṇḍa" means "extremely wrathful. The analysis of the compound is: "that which is both a flight from untimely death and a circle of fierce outcasts (*caṇḍāla*). (72)
Then he went to the Vindhya forest, which was devoid of food, grass, leaves, and water;
while the masses of clouds did not rain and people were seen and lost from sight here and there. (73)
"Vindhya-kakṣa" refers to the water-abundant region of the Vindhya mountain. According to Amara, "kaccha" denotes a marshy place (anūpa) rich in water, and is used in the masculine gender. (73)
While the sky was filled with masses of glowing embers and the wind blew,
a terrifying and violent forest fire suddenly broke out.
The time of famine is untimely and lacks any proper occasion. To the question "What is that 'untimeliness' like?", he says:
"Terrible," and so forth. That in which there is a wild forest fire (*davapāvaka*)—that is, one unrestrained and without restraint—is "one with a wild forest fire" (*uddāmadavapāvaka*).
When that painful reversal of fate was occurring, in which all thickets were withered away and only ashes remained of the grass and reeds; (75)

*Ulapa* means a creeper (*latā*). According to Amara, "a creeper is that which spreads [by tendrils], such as *vīrud*, *gulminī*, and also *ulapa*. That [place] is described as such because its grasses and *ulapas* remain only as ashes. *Vidhiviparyaye* means in the reversal of fate, that is, in the turn of misfortune. || 75 ||
Some people, having gone out, departed together with their friends;
some were crushed right there, while others entered the fire;
some fell into pits, and some became as if wishing for death.
In chasms and cavities. || 76 ||
Taking my wife and accompanied by my three children, I emerged slowly from that place of distress along with her.
From hardship and from exertion. || 77 ||
Having reached the edge of that region,
he set down his sons from his shoulders beneath a palm tree there, as if they were formidable calamities.
"Ulbaṇān" means manifest; "sphuṭa," "pravyakta," and "ulbaṇa" are synonyms, according to Amara. (78, 79)
I then rested there, as if having emerged from the Raurava hell;
and so it was when the Caṇḍāla girl had rested at the foot of the tree. (79)
While she slept in the cool shade, embracing her two sons, this son of mine named Pṛcchaka stands here before me. (80)
"Dārakau" means two young boys. According to Amara, "dārakau" refers to two children who break [their vows]. (80) (81) (82) (83)
"My youngest brother, with his charming speech, is extremely dear to us," he said to me, his soul distressed and his eyes filled with tears. (81)
"Father, give me flesh quickly, and blood to drink in an instant!
Thus my young son spoke again and again. (82)
Having reached a state bordering on death and crying out again and again, I, burdened by extreme sorrow upon beholding his agony, [acted]. 83.
(246) Unable to endure that intense calamity, I, with a ruined soul, made a firm resolve within myself to die, seeking a friend in death. (84)
To Atimitra, the kinsman who appeared at the opportune time. || 84 || 85 || 86 ||
There, having gathered wood, I piled up a funeral pyre;
and the pyre stood there, crackling with the sound of *caṭacaṭa*, longing for me.
Just as I was about to cast myself upon that funeral pyre, the king suddenly rose from this lion-throne;
then he was awakened by the sound of trumpets and shouts of victory. || 86 ||
"Thus has this delusion been produced for me by the sorcerer, just as ignorance produces for the living soul a state accompanied by hundreds of conditions. (87)
By a magician, a performer of illusions. || 87 || 88 || 89 ||
When Lavaṇa, the lord of kings of immense splendor, had spoken thus,
that sorcerer vanished on the spot in an instant.
Then they spoke thus, their eyes wide with wonder:
"O Lord, this man is no juggler, for he has no desire for wealth. (89)
This is some divine illusion that makes one perceive the existence of the world;
for within it, the world is perceived as a transformation of the mind. Indeed, the mind and the universe are the play of the omnipotent and infinite [Brahman].
Because the world is an evolution of the mind, the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of "mind" and "world" as "the mind is the world" is logically established. || 90 ||
Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Juggler," in the *Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha*, within the section on the means to liberation.

Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Juggler," in the *Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Yogavāsiṣṭha* composed by the venerable Ātmasukha, the disciple of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Uttamasukha. 8.
Ninth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
O Raghava, know that whatever is done by the mind is truly done;
O Raghava, know that whatever is abandoned by the mind is truly abandoned.

Thus, through various narratives, it has been established that the entire mass of duality—the source of all misfortune—is false, consisting as it does of the play of the mind which is a transformation of *māyā* resting upon the Supreme Self; whereas its substratum, the reality of Brahman-Ātman alone, is true.
Now, although [this realization] has arisen from such an exposition...

The realization of the true nature of Brahman as the Self does not culminate in direct experience due to the absence of one-pointedness of mind; therefore, for the sake of achieving that one-pointedness, the cessation of its outward-turned activity must be performed. Although this has been established in various places, the author states "yatkṛtam" (whatever is done) here specifically to establish it once more. The word "nāma" [is used]...
In the case of what is well-known. || 1 ||
O sinless one, he whose mind has attained freedom from fickleness and is devoid of conceptual thought is followed by meditation on the unsurpassed state.
[He attains] lack of fickleness and lack of instability. He states the very essence of lack of fickleness: "devoid of mentation.

This means devoid of volition and so forth. This person becomes followed by, or endowed with, the unsurpassed state—the supreme means—namely meditation, which is characterized by the mind's reduction to pure consciousness alone. Therefore...
Because it yields great fruit, one becomes endowed with the necessity of achieving steadiness of mind;
therefore, the meaning is that because it yields great fruit, steadiness of mind must be achieved. || 2 ||
Through the restraint of the mind, the delusion of saṃsāra attains peace,
just as the great ocean of milk becomes still when Mount Mandara ceases its churning.
One might ask: "Even by means of the fruit of meditation, what would happen to one desiring liberation from saṃsāra due to the restlessness of the mind?
To this he says: "From restraint. The word should be split as *aspandatām* (into a state of motionlessness). || 3 ||
Whatever fluctuations of the mind there are— those delusions consisting of the intention for enjoyment— they alone are the rows of sprouts of the poisonous trees of saṃsāra.

Having first demonstrated that mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) taking the forms of sound and so forth are the cause of hundreds of transmigratory bodies, he states the means for their cessation with the three verses beginning with "The fluctuations of the mind" (*manaso vṛttayaḥ*). Enjoyments are merely conceptualizations of sense-objects; these are the delusions (*vibhrama*). The fluctuations of the mind that arise by means of those causes—the delusions consisting of conceptualizations regarding enjoyment—are [what must be restrained].
The grammatical connection is that the functions [of the senses] regarding sound and so forth are precisely those having sound and so forth as their objects. || 4 ||
(248) Listen, I shall describe the supreme medicine for the treatment of this great malady of the mind; it is within one's own power, easy to accomplish, pleasant, and certain. (5)

He establishes the superiority of this medicine with the words beginning "svāyatta" (dependent on oneself): In the world, some medicine cannot be accomplished by itself without assistance; he says this is not so—“svāyatta” means dependent on oneself, that is to say, accomplishable by oneself alone. Furthermore, some things that are dependent on oneself are difficult to procure; he says this is not so—

It might be argued that this is not so; therefore, he says "sweet" (*svād*). Even such a medicine might have an uncertain result; thus he says "certain" (*niścitam*), meaning determined by its fruit. || 5 ||
He who remains free from affliction while renouncing objects of desire has already conquered the mind by abandoning its outward wandering.

"Abandoning the desired and cherished object" means being free from affliction, that is, devoid of remorse. "By one casting off the outward flow" means by one abandoning the movement of the mind toward external objects. || 6 ||
Alas, that wretch of a man, for whom the renunciation of what is desired—though entirely beneficial and within one's own power—has become difficult to perform! 7.

He censures one who does not undertake this in order to generate encouragement for the renunciation of desired objects: "svāyattam" (dependent on oneself), etc. "Ekāntahitam" means beneficial by necessity; the meaning is that it never becomes harmful at any time. "Svepsitatyāgaḥ" is the renunciation of one's own desired objects, for that itself is the "knowledge" (vedana), since it is the means to knowledge. || 7 ||
O Sage, with the mind itself— sharpened by contact with the scriptures and heated by the fire of contemplation—
cut through the iron-like mind as if with an iron tool.
If the renunciation of desired objects is indeed the means for victory, then what is the means for that renunciation? To this, he says: "By the Teacher," and so forth.

"Association with the scriptures" refers to listening to the treatises on the supreme self (*adhyātma-śāstra*) and so forth; or alternatively, "association" means association with the virtuous (*sādhu-saṅgati*). Just as a blacksmith cuts iron heated by fire with a cutting tool made of steel—such as a whetstone—which is the opposite of [the iron] and serves as its support, and is skilled in cleaving—by means of that association.

In the same way, cut through the mind of the undiscriminating person, which is scorched by anxieties for acquisition and preservation, with a mind possessed of discernment that remains unagitated by such anxieties. 8.
Without the mere pacification of the mind— accomplished solely through one's own human effort and consisting in the relinquishment of what is desired— there is no auspicious rebirth. (9)
Anticipating the objection that the attainment of the goals of human life might occur even without the restraint of the mind, he says: "One's own... and so forth.
Because it is accomplished by the relinquishing of what one desires for oneself, it is [figuratively] described as having the nature of the relinquishing of what one desires for oneself.
When the mind has been severed by the weapon of non-conceptualization and has come to rest, it then attains Brahman, which is all-pervading and tranquil. (10)

To the question, "What is that auspicious state? he says: "All. Conceptualization (*saṃkalpanam*) is characterized by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the beautiful and the ugly; the absence of that is non-conceptualization (*asaṃkalpanam*), and that alone is the weapon.
For it is through the superimpositions of the beautiful and the ugly—denoted by the term "conceptualization"—that attachment and aversion arise; therefore, upon their abandonment...
Because those two do not arise, the mind becomes truly conquered; thus it is said that non-mental-construction itself is the weapon. || 10 ||
Dwelling for a long time in that singular, indescribable Great State, having made the mind devoured by consciousness, become even beyond the mind. 11.

Since there is no attainment of a favorable rebirth without the restraint of the mind, he states that its restraint must be practiced for that purpose in the following three verses beginning with "That great path" (*tāṃ mahāpadavīm*). By "great path" (*mahāpadavī*), Brahman is meant;
for that is the great path upon which infinite living beings move simultaneously and without obstruction—meaning, in some way that is inconceivable.
"Abiding" means having ascended and dwelt [therein]; the meaning is that one should fix the mind upon it. "Devoured by consciousness" means seized by reflection;
the meaning is that one should make the mind such that only pure consciousness remains. || 11 ||
Freed from worldly existence through meditation and endowed with supreme intelligence, remain undistracted and hold the self; thereafter, seize the mind.
Fix the self, which is the mind, upon Brahman; thereafter, the mind becomes free from the grasp of thought. || 12 ||
Relying upon supreme human effort and having brought the mind to the state of non-mind, enter that great path where you neither exist nor does anything else. (13)

"Thinking 'I am a man, the son of such-and-such, the doer, the enjoyer,' you exist not where—that path upon which you do not abide and wherein no world other than yourself exists; go, enter that very great path called Brahman, which is non-dual. (13)

Freedom from agitation is the root of prosperity; from freedom from agitation proceeds the conquest of the mind by a living being, through which the conquest of the three worlds becomes as a blade of grass.

Even now, the conquest of the mind (*manojaya*) may not be accomplished because distraction obstructs that conquest; therefore, it must not be abandoned by one engaged in the conquest of the mind. Thus he says: "without agitation" (*anudvega*). Accordingly, it was said by the Blessed One: "That yoga must be practiced with a resolute mind and a heart free from despondency. By such a conquest of the mind, the conquest of the three worlds is as a blade of grass; even the conquest of the triple world—
The meaning is that it appears like a blade of grass. || 14 ||
Through meditation, by means of the continuous flow of the wheel of consciousness within the space of the heart, kill the mind without hesitation; then mental afflictions will no longer bind you. 15.

He speaks again of the means for restraining the mind: "by meditation" (dhyānataḥ). By means of the stream of the wheel of consciousness—that is, the stream of the wheel of knowledge—set in motion through meditation upon the object of consciousness, which is perceived as the witness of the existence and non-existence of the modifications of the internal organ within the space of the heart, and of their junction. || 15 ||
If that which was pleasant has been perceived by you as unpleasant through your own awareness, then it is my conviction that the limbs of the mind have indeed been severed. 16.

Now, one might object that because the mind by its very nature tends toward external objects, self-meditation is simply impossible; therefore, he says: "If... [yadīti]. This means: if you, being discerning (vidā), have perceived an attractive (ramya) or delightful object as unattractive—that is, as something devoid of delight—meaning, if what was grasped by the intellect as delightful has been known by you to be unattractive.

Therefore, by the cessation of the superimposition of attractiveness upon objects—which is rooted in passion—passion itself ceases, and the modifications (vṛttis), which are the limbs of the mind, become truly severed. || 16 ||
"This is he," "I am this," "this is mine"—the mind consists of nothing more than these [notions].
By the mere non-contemplation of them, it is cut away as if by a sickle. (17)

He elaborates upon what was stated—that [the mind] is severed by the weapon of non-conceptualization—by first describing the nature of the mind, beginning with the words "This... and so forth. "This am I" and "That am I" refer to recognition (*abhijñā*) and re-recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
One should apply this logic to such cases as: "this is a proximate object," "that is a remote object," and "this is my object," and so on.

"Of this much extent" means of such a measure; it is cut down—that is, completely severed—by that mere non-contemplation, by mere lack of volition, which is to say, by the abandonment of volition, as if by a sickle or a scythe, which are instruments for cutting. || 17 ||
Just as a mass of clouds in the sky is dispersed by the wind in autumn,
so too is the mind dispersed within by means of non-conceptualization.
By means of non-conceptualization and non-mental construction. || 18 ||
Let the winds at the end of the aeon blow, let the oceans become one, and let the twelve suns blaze; for one who is free from the mind, there is no injury. (19)
The verses beginning with "kalpānte" and so forth are for the most part clear in their meaning. || 19 ||

Abiding firmly in that state, remain in the empire of non-conceptualization, which is accomplished solely by the absence of volitional thought, which bestows all perfections, and which transcends all conceptualization.

In the supreme sovereignty of non-conceptualization— wherein non-conceptualization is itself the samādhi of the non-discursive, and that very state is the "supreme sovereignty" (atisāmrājya), meaning a sovereignty that transcends all others— you, having firmly established yourself in that state and having taken hold of the nature of Brahman, are conquered by the chariot of the mind through its power consisting of mere volition, by means of the manifestation of various objects.
Having conquered the mind through the power of mere contentment—which is ever-arisen and free from longing—attain happiness.
Having conquered the mind with a mental state whose sole wealth is contentment—a state that is eternally arisen because it shines at all times due to its self-luminosity;
the meaning is "by means of the fourth state" (turya). Its qualification is "nirīpsitena," meaning by that which is free from desire. || 21 ||

May that unborn state which remains— [attained] through the most purifying, snow-cold equanimity, through the realization of those who know the Self, through tranquility, and through the measured destruction of inner enmity— be mine. 22.
Demonstrating that equanimity (*samatā*), like contentment, is also a limb of mental restraint, he concludes with the words:

"by the supremely purifying. This means by means of equanimity—characterized by the absence of joy or dejection upon encountering the desirable or undesirable—which is esteemed and approved by the views of those who know the Self; that is, by the practice of meditation preceded by that [equanimity]. By this [equanimity]...

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "May that state which remains [after] the limited 'I-ness'—the ego-sense—has been stilled, measured, and made true, be yours. The meaning is: when the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) has been stilled through the practice of meditation preceded by equanimity (*samatā*), that which remains—the non-dual form known as the Fourth (*turya*)—may that be yours. || 22 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Indeed, a mind devoid of restlessness is nowhere to be found;
restlessness is the inherent nature of the mind, just as heat is the nature of fire. (23)

The verses preceding the one beginning with "nāhi cañcalatāhīnam" (not devoid of fickleness) up to "yattatsadasatormadhyam" (that which is the middle between being and non-being) are for the most part clear in meaning. || 23 || 24 ||
For know that this flickering power of vibration, which resides within the essence of consciousness, is the mental power whose nature is the phenomenal display of the universe. (24)
That mind which is free from restlessness is called nectar;
that alone is called austerity, scripture, the final doctrine, and liberation. (25)

That very immortality of the mind is the scripture; the hearing of the scripture is [the means], for it is the established conclusion (siddhānta) accepted as authoritative because it is the fruit thereof. That alone is called liberation (mokṣa), because it is the means to that [liberation].
O Rāma, this very restlessness of his is called ignorance (avidyā);
destroy it—also known by the name latent impression (vāsanā)—through inquiry. 26.
It is called ignorance because it is the effect of ignorance; or it is known by the other name "impression" because its root is impression. (26)
By means of that ignorance, which is a latent impression (vāsanā) existing within the mind,
once it has dissolved through the power of renunciation, the supreme good is attained. (27)

"By virtue of renunciation"—that is, by virtue of abandoning desired objects—[the mind] becomes dissolved. And it was said previously: "He who remains free from affliction while abandoning a desired object, having cast off its external expansion, has indeed conquered his mind. (27)
That which is between existence and non-existence, that which is between the clarity and dullness of the mind—that, O Rāma, is called the *manas*, its form oscillating between the two. (28)

Having stated that the mind is to be "slain" solely through the practice of knowledge (*jñānābhyāsa*), he describes its essential nature and how it is brought to completion through such practice by means of the four verses beginning with "That which [arises] from being and non-being... and so forth.

The meaning is that, just as in the world a mediator (*madhyastha*) stands between existence and non-existence and is favorable to both parties, so too the mind is favorable to both the Self (*ātman*) and the non-Self (*anātman*); therefore, it must be conquered by means of a specific method. He further states that the mind is favorable even to the two attributes of the Self and the non-Self, namely consciousness (*caitanya*) and insentience (*jāḍya*).

"—that which is the middle between mental dullness and [clarity]. Its form is "swinging between the two," meaning that because its nature is to undergo transformation into the two modes of activity consisting of "I" and "this," its form or appearance is thus swinging between the two mentioned states. || 28 ||
For the mind, when seized by the contemplation of dullness and kindled by its nature as dullness, indeed attains a state of inertia through the power of firm habituation. (29)

The mind, captivated by the pursuit of dullness and brought under the sway of thoughts of insentience, attains a state of dullness—that is, it reaches a condition of insentience—by means of its own nature of dullness, which has been kindled, ignited, and increased through the power of firm habitual practice. The meaning is that it becomes dominated by the inert body and so forth. For this is indeed observed.
The minds of ordinary people are of such a nature. || 29 ||
Through the continuous contemplation of pure awakening, the mind, by virtue of its essential nature as a portion of consciousness,
attains oneness with consciousness here in this world by the power of firm practice.
"Vibodha" means distinguished awareness; the witness (*sākṣin*) is that which is one in that [awareness].
"Vibodhaikānusaṃdhāna" is the continuous connection within that very one; from this, the qualifier "consisting of the aspect of consciousness" (*cidaṃśa*) must also be drawn over here.

That whose nature (*svarūpa*) is a mind whose aspect is consciousness—that is, whose aspect is not "this" (*anidamaṃśa*)—is "that which consists of the aspect of consciousness" (*cidaṃśātman*); the state of being such is "the nature of that" (*tattā*).

The meaning is that, through continuous contemplation by means of that [meditation], "I am Brahman," one abides in the form of the mind-made fire (manaścit), whose true nature is not perceived as distinct from the conscious reality (sac-cit). || 30 ||
By means of human effort, the mind is joined to that very state;
for by means of practice, having attained that state, one becomes [that state] itself. (31)
He clarifies what was stated [in the previous verse] with the words "by human effort" (pauruṣeṇa). "In the state" (pade) means in the reality (vastuni). || 31 ||
Therefore, relying on human effort and mastering the mind with the intellect, take hold of the sorrowless state and remain steadfast, free from fear.

He states the conclusion: "Therefore" (ataḥ). With a "discriminating mind" (cetasā) means with a discerning consciousness (cittena). "Free from fear" (nirātaṅkaḥ) means free from affliction; that is to say, free from calamity. || 32 ||
The mind alone is indeed capable of firmly restraining the mind;
for what king, O Raghava, would be capable of restraining another king?
Anticipating the doubt that the mind might be assailed by something other than itself, he says: "The mind alone," and so forth. || 33 ||
For those seized by the grasp of craving and falling into the ocean of saṃsāra, being carried away by its whirlpools, their own mind alone is a boat far off [to rescue them]. 34.
The connection is as follows: for those being carried far away by the crocodiles that are the grasping [for existence] and by the whirlpools that are wives and so forth. || 34 || 35 ||
Having severed with the mind alone the noose of the mind, that supreme bond, deliver yourself from worldly existence; for one cannot be delivered by another.
Whatever latent impression called "mind" arises, permeating the inner self, the wise person should abandon each one; through that, the destruction of ignorance occurs.

He explains the very manner of cutting through the mind by means of the mind itself, both briefly and in detail, with the two verses beginning with "yathodeti" (just as it arises). By the term "vāsanā," a mental modification (*vṛtti*) rooted in latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is understood. That which has perfumed—that is, conditioned—the interior, the region of the mind, is called "vāsitāntarā. For it is by means of this modification that [the mind is affected].

The Vedāntins declare that when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has perished, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced; the logicians (*tārkika*), however, maintain that it is produced by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) itself, which is termed "knowledge.
Therefore, "by abandoning the cognition of difference" means having abandoned the internal distinction between existence and non-existence as distinct entities;
that is to say, having abandoned the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding those objects. (36–37)
Having abandoned the sole latent impression of worldly enjoyment, abandon the latent impression of duality;
then, having relinquished both existence and non-existence, become free from conceptual construction and happy. (37)
This indeed is the destruction of the mind and the destruction of ignorance itself;
it is the complete relinquishing of whatever has been perceived by that [mind]. (38)
The two [verses] beginning with "this very... have a clear meaning. "With effort" means by means of the abandonment of the superimposition of attractiveness upon sense objects. || 38 || 39 ||
For non-reliance is indeed nirvāṇa, while the grasping at reliance is suffering;
by this very effort, one attains Brahman in an instant. (39)
Ignorance exists only as something non-existent among those whose wisdom is destroyed;
it assumes a form through mere name alone—how could it exist for one of perfect wisdom? (40)

One might object: "Since ignorance (avidyā) exists, its cessation through knowledge is impossible—just as [the cessation of] the mind [is impossible while it exists]. Therefore, the presentation of the restraint of the mind and its means for the sake of attaining the knowledge that would remove it is useless.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: *avidyā*. The word should be split as *a-vidyamānā* (non-existent).
For indeed, the primary meaning of the word "name" is precisely the absence of name, which is itself ignorance. || 40 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, tell me again: how can this dense blindness of a person, which arises from the expansion of ignorance, be destroyed? (41)

To elaborate on the meaning of the statement "From where does that [ignorance] belong to one who possesses right wisdom," he raises Rāma’s question with the words "Avidyāvibhavaprottham" (arisen from the power of ignorance), which means "produced by the sovereignty of nescience."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Meanwhile, it causes the embodied beings, together with their own selves, to oscillate amidst the dense thorns of suffering upon the trees of the abysses of saṃsāra. (42)
In those precipices of saṃsāra—which are like thorny trees, being densely covered with branches of suffering—he causes [the mind] to oscillate. || 42 || 43 ||
As long as ignorance has not arisen that brings about its destruction,
there exists within oneself the desire to perceive the Self, which bestows the complete cessation of saṃsāra. (43)
For one who perceives that which is beyond this [duality], the destruction of the self occurs;
for when all-pervading consciousness is seen, this [ignorance] dissolves of its own accord. (44)

Beyond this ignorance, which remains in the form of that which is left over (śiṣṭa), [he perceives] the Supreme Self. He clarifies what was stated in the first half [of the verse] with the words "seen" (dṛṣṭa). || 44 ||
This ignorance is merely desire; its destruction is called liberation.
And that [destruction], O Rāghava, is accomplished by the weapon of non-mental-conception (asaṃkalpa). 45.

Having raised the doubt as to what the means for the vision of Brahman—designated as the all-pervading consciousness—is, [the author] states "merely desire" with the intention that since even hearing and other such practices would be useless if there is desire for sense objects, freedom from thirst (vaitṛṣṇya) toward them alone is the means to that [vision]. Then, to the question "By what, then, is the destruction of desire accomplished?", he says "And that... regarding sense objects.
The superimposition of attractiveness is volition (saṃkalpa); its absence is non-volition (asaṃkalpa), which is itself the weapon; by that [weapon]. || 45 ||
When the night of latent impressions (vāsanā) in the sky of the mind comes to an end even slightly, the dark veil (kālikā) becomes attenuated through the radiance of the sun of consciousness.
With the intention of showing that even a slight degree of detachment leads to such a fruit, what need is there to mention full detachment? He says:

"Vāsanā alone is the night; when even a small portion of it has perished, consciousness itself becomes the sun, and through its illumination, the darkness of ignorance attains thinness—that is, it becomes attenuated. (46)
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahmin, whatever is seen here is ignorance, and that ignorance is destroyed by the cultivation of the Self; what, then, is this Self said to be like? (47)
The phrase "whatever it may be" has an unclear meaning. || 47 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
That reality of consciousness which is free from the pursuit of objects, all-pervasive in its generality, and inexpressible—that is the Self, the Supreme Lord. (48)

The meaning is that the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), being devoid of following after objects of thought and empty of tracking knowable objects, follows after knowables such as sound and so forth; the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*) does not follow after them in that way. The essence of consciousness is the all-pervading, uncontradicted nature of consciousness, which exists through its very equality and without any state of deficiency or excess.

Because everything is non-existent, it is "all-pervading" (sarvagata) and thus inexpressible; or rather, it is inexpressible because there is no ground for the application of words. Even in the presence of objects, it is changeless.
The meaning is that the Self is that consciousness which is entirely devoid of all particularities, perfectly full, and real. And of that—
He excludes any difference from Brahman by stating: "the Supreme Lord. (48)
Indeed, all this is Brahman—eternal, a mass of consciousness, and immutable;
there exists no other mental construction whatsoever called "mind. (49)
It excludes both the delimitation of objects and the delimitation of time, as expressed by the words "all indeed."

The term "immutable" (*avyayam*) excludes decay. The grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "all this is Brahman" occurs through sublation (*bādhā*); for this very reason, he says: "another conceptual construction. Since every conceptual construction is merely a play of the mind, it is described as being "named the mind. (49)
Nothing whatsoever is born or dies here in the three worlds;
nor does the existence of the modifications of being exist anywhere at all. (50)

Now, one might object: since the birth and so forth of non-existent things such as the son of a barren woman are not observed, how can the world—which is perceived as possessing the sixfold modifications of existence (bhāva-vikāra) beginning with birth—exist therein? To this, he says: "It is not born."
Since the world is unfit for any definition of its origin and so forth, it is rightly said that its existence does not exist. || 50 ||
Only pure consciousness exists here—absolute, appearing as absolute, the universal commonality, imperishable, and devoid of any dependence on objects of thought. 51.

He summarizes: "merely" (kevalam). "Merely" means non-dual (advitīya). "Appearing merely" (kevalābhāsam) means it appears—that is, it shines—merely as its own manifestation, even without the operation of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); the meaning is that it is self-luminous (svayaṃprakāśa). "Universal to all" (sarvasāmānyam) means it is equally common to everything.
The meaning is that it exists without deficiency or excess among all things from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.

It is devoid of "following after objects of cognition" (cetyānupāta), which refers to the transformation into the form of those objects of cognition—the knowables such as sound and so forth—and is thus empty of that. || 51 ||

In that which is eternal, pervasive, pure, consisting of consciousness alone, free from affliction, tranquil, characterized by an even distribution of experience, and whose self has arisen as changeless— (52)

Having restated the nature [of the Self] as previously described, he speaks of that substratum with the three verses beginning with "In that," concerning the conceptualization of the duality of misfortune which is its opposite: "In that," etc. "Tate" means pervaded; "samasamābhogam" refers to that whose fullness (*ābhoga*) or perfection is entirely equal; in that [substratum], the Self—whose very form (*svarūpa*) has arisen and shines forth as being free from modification—is [described].
That self, arisen from that which is changeless, is within it. || 52 ||
That which, having itself conceptualized what transcends its own nature, runs forth; that consciousness, though itself unfading, is called "mind" (manas) because of its thinking (manana). 53.

Regarding the phrase "yaiṣā": having conceptualized that which has transcended its own nature—that is, having gone beyond the essential nature consisting of truth, knowledge, and so forth—as being something other than its own nature, namely the insentient and other forms of the object of thought (cetya) or the visible (dṛśya), that consciousness which, characterized by both the sentient and the insentient, pursues only its own conceptualized object of thought and not the underlying pure consciousness (adhiṣṭhāna-cinmātra), is itself [the one] that does not wither. By itself...

Because it is of the nature of Brahman, it is free from decay and free from afflictions; yet, due to its association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is perceived as if it were decaying, and is thus described in this way.
This is because it possesses those adjuncts, according to the Vedic scripture: "It is called *manas* because it reflects. (53)
From this all-pervading deity, the great-souled one who possesses every power,
the capacity for conceptual differentiation has arisen, like a wave rising from water.
The power of conceptualizing division, the power of conceptualizing differentiation, arose from the waters in the form of Manu, like a wave emerging from a ripple.

Therefore, this [delusion] accomplished by volition perishes by volition alone; it is destroyed by that very thing from which it was born, just as a flame of fire is extinguished by the wind. || 55 ||
Having thus demonstrated that duality is the root of all misfortune, he states the means for its destruction with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Since this power of conceptualizing division, known as the mind, is devoid of a suitable cause—given that the changeless reality of Brahman cannot possibly be its appropriate cause—it is therefore established through volition and established through mere appearance. And that [power]...

By means of the very resolve (saṃkalpa) about to be described—namely, that "everything is Brahman"—it perishes. The verses beginning with "yenaiva" and ending with "mano yadanusaṃdhatte" have clear meanings. || 55 || 56 || 57 || 58 || 59 || 60 ||
The mind is bound by the firm conviction that "I am not Brahman"; the mind is liberated by the firm conviction that "all is Brahman. (56)
"I am emaciated," "I am extremely miserable," "I am bound," or "I possess hands, feet, and so forth"— it is through such worldly discourse, corresponding to these mental states, that one is bound.
"I am not suffering, nor do I have a body; for what self could bondage exist?"—by such conduct in accordance with this realization, one is liberated. (58)
"I am neither flesh nor bones; I am other than the body, the Supreme.
One who possesses such certainty within, whose ignorance has been destroyed, is liberated. (59)
Thus, O Rāghava, this ignorance is merely imagined, consisting of the conception of a self in that which is not the self; it belongs to the unawakened person, not to the awakened one.
Whatever the mind intends to connect, all the functions of the senses accomplish that in an instant, just as ministers carry out the command of a king.

It is not only by its nature as volition that the mind acts as a binder; it does so also by setting the senses in motion toward the objects of those volitions. Thus he says: "The mind follows which... (verse 61).
Relying upon supreme human effort and with the highest intelligence,
one should thus uproot from the mind the cultivation of hope for enjoyments, together with its very roots.

Since the mind possesses binding power only when the latent impression of passion (*rāga-vāsanā*) is real, and not when it is unreal, he says "the supreme human effort" (*paraṃ pauruṣam*) to indicate that it must be abandoned. [The phrase] *samūlām* means that which exists together with its root, namely the latent impression of enjoyment (*bhoga-vāsanā*), characterized by superimposition (*adhyāsa*). || 62 ||
"My sons, my wealth, this is I, this is mine"—
this very latent impression (vāsanā), like a magical illusion (indrajāla), leaps forth with great force. (63)

Then, raising the doubt as to what must be done for the purpose of uprooting the root characterized by habitual practice, he says—beginning with "My sons"—that the uprooting of that root-vāsanā must be performed. In the phrase "by means of the magician's trick" (*indrajālena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the manner of being (*itthambhāve*). The description of the nature of the magician's trick is provided by the half-verse beginning with "My sons. (63–64)
Do not be ignorant; become wise. Abandon the latent impressions of saṃsāra.
Why do you weep like an ignorant man by perceiving a self in that which is not the self? 64.
O Rāghava, what is this dull and mute body of yours?
For its sake you are helplessly overcome by pleasure and pain. (65)
"What is your [suffering]?"—the meaning is clear. || 65 ||
Oh, how strange it is that the true Brahman has been forgotten by men, while that which is unreal, called ignorance, leaps about before them! (66)
Under the guise of compassion, he encourages [the listener] for the sake of dispelling ignorance: "O, how wonderful! (verse 66).
While you remain engaged in your duties, let there be no coloring by passion,
just as a crystal assumes various reflections while receiving them.

He says "tiṣṭhata" (remain) to show that one who is striving to dispel ignorance should not harbor attachment even while performing unavoidable activities such as eating; "rāgānurañjanā" means the persistence of attachment. 67–68.
Vālmīki said:
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, the high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
Rāma’s inner heart was opened, and he then took up speech.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Aha! How wondrous it is that mountains are bound together by threads produced from lotuses;
by that knowledge which does not exist, the entire universe has been rendered a wasteland. (69)
"What wonder is seen here [in this] that is equal to binding a mountain with lotus fibers?
To this he says: "avidyamāna... and so forth. "Khilīkṛtam" means made empty; the meaning is that it has been rendered devoid of human purpose (puruṣārtha). || 69 ||
p.
261) This very thing has attained the state of a vajra here in the three worlds;
for even by means of ignorance, that which is called "creation" is indeed a fetter-binding. (70)

"Sarga" means the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). The words "api" and "nāma" are used in a derogatory sense. The syntactical connection is as follows: since even this creation, though brought about by ignorance, is called a "bondage like an iron chain," therefore these three worlds—which are not even worth a blade of grass—have attained the state of being a thunderbolt. 70.
Furthermore, O Great-souled One, this doubt dwells within my heart:
what was the name of that illustrious Lavaṇa who attained that station? (71)
And there is something else that remains to be asked; this is the sense. || 71 || 72 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
In this regard, listen as I shall tell you this wonderful account: how that Lavaṇa was born and how, through a delusion of mind, he attained the state of a Caṇḍāla.
The mind is the agent that experiences the fruit, not the body which is the product of action;
since you perceive this, O Raghava, listen now to the truth of it.
He states the purpose of narrating the account about to be told: "The mind... || The mind alone, together with its appearances (*sābhāsa*), is the agent;
it alone experiences the fruit, the result of action, and not the body. Listen—that is, hear—that activity by which [this occurs]. || 73 || 74 ||
O sinless one, in former times, Lavaṇa, born of the lineage of Hariścandra,
sat alone in solitude and reflected for a long time in his mind.
My grandfather was a great officiating priest at the Rājasūya sacrifice;
born into his lineage, I mentally perform that sacrifice for him.
The grammatical connection is: "I sacrifice the Makha rite; I perform it. || 75 ||
Having thus reflected in his mind and prepared the necessary materials beforehand,
the lord of the earth entered the initiation for the Rājasūya sacrifice.
The word "manasā" (with the mind) is also connected with the phrase "in initiation" (dīkṣāyām); here the locative case is used in the sense of the accusative. 76–77.
Having brought the officiating priests face to face with the deities,
he summoned the gods and kindled the sacrificial fire. (77)
As he was thus performing the sacrifice, more than a full year passed for him within the garden of his mind while honoring the celestial sages and the twice-born.
