Thus addressed, the Blessed One Kāla, the course of the world, as if smiling,
took Bhṛgu by the hand with his own hand, as the sun takes hold of the moon.
Then the two gods, Kāla and Bhṛgu, set out from a cave in Mount Mandara to go upon the earth to the bank of the river Samaṅgā.
In an instant, the two of them arrived there at the wavy river Samaṅgā;
then, on a certain bank of it, Bhṛgu beheld his son.
Beholding the son of Bhṛgu, whose senses were stilled, who was established in meditative concentration, and whose deer-like mind was motionless, Death became filled with resolve.
Thinking, "Let him awaken," he ceased from his meditative absorption;
opening his eyes, he beheld before him the two lords, Kāla and Bhṛgu.
Then, rising from their seats of *kadamba* creepers, they bowed to one another; having performed their mutual salutations, they sat down upon a rock. (75)
Then, on the bank of the Samaṅgā, that twice-born one spoke these peaceful words:
"By the sight of you both, I have attained peace today. (76)
"That delusion of my mind, which could not be destroyed by scripture, austerity, knowledge, or learning, has perished through the sight of you two."
The visions of the stainless nectar do not gladden the inner self as much as these visions of the great ones cause it to rejoice. (78)
"O you two of immense splendor, who are you that have purified this region with your feet, as the moon and sun purify the sky? (79)
To him who had spoken thus, Bhṛgu said to his son from another birth:
"Remember your self; you are awakened, you are not ignorant," O scion of Raghu. (80)
Awakened by Bhṛgu, he remembered his own state in a previous birth within a mere moment, his eyes opened through meditation.
Then, with a face smiling with wonder and a joyful mind, that best of speakers uttered words slow with reflection: (82)
Oh, some kind of vision consisting of delusion expands within the mind, by the power of which this expansive web of the world proceeds! (83)
That which was to be known has now been known; that which was to be seen has been seen unimpaired.
Long exhausted, I have finally come to rest; apart from pure consciousness, there is nothing at all.
"Arise, dear one, let us go; I wish to behold that body of Niyati situated on Mount Mandara. I am curious to see it;
for here, there is nothing desired by me, nor is there anything undesired. (85)

"Arise!"—this is the statement consisting of one and a half verses. "I wander, that is, I go, to behold the curiosity and the playful manifestation of destiny (*niyati*), which is the course of fate (*daivagati*). For me, there is nothing desired (*samīhita*) nor anything undesired (*asamīhita*). (85–86)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Investigating the courses of the world, they are known as knowers of reality.
The three reached a cave of Mount Mandara on the banks of the Samaṅgā river;
there Bhārgava beheld his body born of a previous birth.
And he said this: "O father, this body of hers is indeed withered, she who was formerly cherished by you with the enjoyments of pleasure. (88)
Behold how he sleeps happily in the forest, his doubts stilled, all curiosity vanished, and the web of conceptual constructions cast aside! (89)
With the arrival of autumn for the mist of delusion caused by the fever of all desires,
I see no other welfare for living beings than the state of being free from mental distraction.

"Of all"—that is, of all the causes for hope, of the delusions of fever, and of the delusions of suffering, it is the autumn that brings about the cessation of the mists and the frosts. "Distraction" (vicittatva) means being despondent or distracted in mind.
Those very ones of great intelligence, who had attained wisdom, have now reached the limit of the enjoyment of happiness, having become despondent. (91)
"By good fortune, I behold this body of mine in the forest—freed from all states of suffering, established in a state free from fever, and beyond mental agitation. (92)
Then, having interrupted his speech, Kāla said to the descendant of Bhṛgu:
"O virtuous one, enter this body as a king enters a city."
"You must show respect to the lords of the asuras by this [action].
May it be well with you both; we shall now depart for our desired direction. (94)
Having spoken thus, as they both shed tears, he vanished;
when that Blessed One had departed, Bhārgava, subject to the power of destiny, [remained].
Having abandoned that body, he entered the body of the bird Samaṅga;
once the life-force had entered that body of his son, the great sage [departed].
He performed a nourishment rite with mantras using the waters from his water-pot;
thereupon, all her veins, which had been thin, shone forth, now full.
Then Śukra arose, his vital breaths flowing freely;
he saluted his father, who was of purifying appearance, standing before him. (96)
Then, in that sacred forest, Bhrigu and Bhargava remained with their minds liberated, like two lakes free from waves.
Thus has the narrative of Bhārgava been described to you, O delighter of the Raghus;
having reflected upon it firmly in your heart, do as you wish.
Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Narrative of Bhārgava," in the section on Stability within the *Mokṣopāya*, the essence of the *Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha*.
Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Narrative of Śuka," in the section on the State of Being within the *Vasiṣṭha-vivaraṇa*, known as the *Saṃsārataraṇī*. 1.
p. 296) Second Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
For a person who has practiced inquiry, whose mind’s fluctuations have dissolved, who constantly abandons discursive thought, and whose self has attained some degree of transformation— (1)

Previously, in the narrative of Bhārgava, it was shown that the world is composed of the mind (*cittamaya*). Here, however, in the narrative of Dāma and others, it is established that this mental world is stilled through discernment (*viveka*) when the mind is pacified, whereas in the absence of discernment, it increases.
To demonstrate the necessary conditions for the clarity of the mind (*cittaprasāda*), he says [the following] with five and a half verses beginning with "of the living being" (*jantoḥ*).
"Of one whose mind has its functions flowing away": that is, one whose mind is such that impure functions are flowing away from it;
for him, "thinking" means volition (saṃkalpa). || 1 ||
For one who abandons the visible as something to be rejected, who attains that which is to be accepted, and who perceives the eternal Seer who is not an object of sight; || 2 ||
That which is to be accepted is mere seeing; the seer is the Self. (2)
(297) While one is awake regarding the supreme reality that must be known,
yet remains asleep on the path of saṃsāra, which consists of dense delusion; || 3 ||
Of one who is asleep and devoid of reflective awareness. || 3 ||

When the knots of the heart have been severed by the force of dispassion— rendering even the most exquisite flavors tasteless due to ultimate maturity in detachment— and when the web of worldly tendencies has been torn asunder like a bird-net by a mouse; (4)

The reason for this state of sleep is "due to extreme maturity of dispassion. When the snare of worldly latent impressions (*saṃsāra-vāsanā*)—which is like a net for birds set by a rat or mouse—is torn asunder and severed by the force of dispassion, both toward the "flavors" (*rasa*) of worldly objects consisting of meager gusts of pleasure and toward the "flavors" of otherworldly objects consisting of abundant gusts of pleasure; and when the knot of the heart (*hṛdaya-granthi*) has been cut...
And when the knot in the form of egoism has become loosened, || 4 ||
Just as water becomes clear upon reaching the *kātaka* fruit, so too does one's own nature become perfectly serene through the power of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*). || 5 ||

The grammatical connection is as follows: having obtained the *kātaka* fruit, just like water, one's own nature—that is, one's true form—becomes completely serene through the power of discernment (*vijñāna*). That *kātaka* fruit is that by contact with which turbid water becomes clear. (5)
Free from passion, free from attachment, free from duality, and free from dependence,
the mind emerges from delusion like a bird from a cage.

"Free from passion" (nīrāgam): passion (rāga) is a particular kind of desire; that which is devoid of it is "free from passion. For this very reason, it is "without attachment" (nirupāsaṅga), meaning free from attachment to sense objects. And for this reason, it is "beyond the pairs of opposites" (nirdvandva), meaning it has ceased from the pursuit of the distinctions between pleasure and pain. Consequently, being "without support" (nirupāśraya)—that is, without any objective basis—the mind emerges from delusion, which is the bondage of ignorance. It is like a bird.
"Or like [a bird] from a cage, etc. (6)
With its wickedness and doubts stilled, and with its restless wanderings and delusions gone,
the mind, its interior completely full, shines like the full moon.
"Peaceful" (śānta): that from which the wickedness and corruption of doubts have been stilled; that from which the delusion and playfulness of curious conceptualizations have departed. (7)
For one whose own nature has been fully known through inquiry and whose self has arisen,
even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara become objects of compassion in this world. (8)

Regarding the phrase "by means of discernment" (vicāreṇa): for one who has fully understood the true nature [of reality], who has directly realized the essence of the Self, and who, for that very reason, has arisen as the Self—that is, whose own nature is perfectly complete—even Brahmā and the other gods become objects of his compassion. The meaning is that, alas, these beings are constantly suffering; thus they become worthy of pity. || 8 ||
As long as one has not inwardly investigated "Who am I? and "How is this?", the spectacle of saṃsāra remains like a thick darkness.

He states the fault in the absence of inquiry: "Who am I? Inquiry concerning the Self is "Who am I?"; that concerning the world is "How is this? "Within" means within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). || 9 ||
He truly sees who perceives both himself and the other as nothing but the light of consciousness, through a vision that is eternally undivided. 10.

He shows the nature of *vicāra* (investigation) through three verses, beginning with "The Self" (*ātmānam*). He who perceives— through the vision of knowledge (*jñāna*)— his own self and other persons as eternally non-different, always devoid of distinction,
and perceives the entire world as nothing but the light of consciousness (*cij-jyotis*), as nothing but pure sentience (*caitanya-mātra*), that person devoted to investigation sees [the truth].
The meaning is that one directly realizes reality (tattva). || 10 ||
He who perceives that which is omnipotent, infinite in essence, dwelling within all beings, non-dual, and pure consciousness—that one truly sees. || 11 ||

"Of all"—he who sees that the Puruṣa, who abides within all beings, who is the inner controller of all things, and who is omnipotent; who is the infinite Self, whose nature is undivided; and who is therefore non-dual because of the absence of any entity distinct from Himself, and whose form is pure consciousness alone—[he sees truly]. 11.
"I do not exist, nor does anything else; only Brahman exists, free from all affliction.
He who perceives the middle between being and non-being in this way—he truly sees.
"No. There is no "I"—no object delimited by egoity or conditioned by adjuncts—and there is no other visible object distinct from itself;

rather, there exists only Brahman, which is free from affliction and change. In this manner, between existence and non-existence, the Self and the non-Self, lies the state of pure consciousness (cinmātratva), devoid of the limiting conditions of being the seer or the seen. 12.
Just as the eye falls upon objects such as the directions that present themselves effortlessly without any attachment, so too does the intellect of the wise man fall upon its objects. (13)

Regarding the phrase "without effort" (ayatnena): when objects situated in the directions—that is, in the various quarters—have come before the eye, the sense organ of sight, without any effort at all, the mind's longing or attachment toward them falls away; likewise, the intellect (dhī) of the wise who know Brahman proceeds toward their necessary duties entirely free from passion. 13.
For when enjoyment is consumed with full understanding, it leads to contentment;
and when a thief is served after being recognized, he attains friendliness and no longer acts as a thief.

"Having fully understood" means this: here, the specific excellence of enjoyment for one who possesses knowledge is that enjoyment, when consumed after being fully understood, leads to contentment and not to affliction. For just as a thief, even while being served, does not harm one who recognizes him, but rather assists him out of a friendly disposition, so it is in this case. || 14 ||
Just as a village procession encountered unexpectedly by travelers is watched with curiosity,
so too is the splendor of enjoyment observed by the wise.

"Aśaṅkitā" (unexpected): Just as a village procession—a multitude of people proceeding for a great festival such as a wedding—is encountered unexpectedly and without being anticipated by travelers on the road, even so the splendor of enjoyment is perceived by the wise, those possessed of knowledge, as entirely free from attachment. 15.
Even that slight enjoyment of play which belongs to the restrained mind, though it has not attained expansion, is regarded as great because of its intensity. (16)

Regarding the phrase "of the mind" (manasaḥ): even a slight enjoyment (*līlābhoga*), that is, a disregardful indulgence, of the mind that has been restrained—that is, suppressed—by the limbs of yoga such as withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the rest, the mind regards that very enjoyment as great, because it is afflicted and, being suppressed, has not attained expansion. || 16 ||
A ruler of the earth who is bound by fetters is satisfied with merely a morsel of food;
yet one who is neither bound by others nor oppressed does not value his kingdom highly. || 17 ||
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "bandha" etc. [The phrase] "by mere feeding" means by the mere giving of food and drink. || 17 ||
Pressing hand against hand, grinding tooth against tooth,
and crushing limb against limb, one should first conquer one's own mind.
There is no other way out of the ocean of worldly existence than through the conquest of the mind.

He states the means for restraining the mind: "The hand," etc. The essential meaning is that one should conquer one's own mind through Haṭhayoga by means of mastering the vital breath (pavana). || 18 || 19 || 20 ||
On this entire surface of the earth, those men are truly fortunate and possess virtuous minds who are counted among the subjects of human discourse for having conquered themselves by their own will.

I bow to that immutable one, whose mind has attained peace, wherein the serpent of the mind— with its earrings formed in the hollow of the heart and its virulent poison of restless fancies— has been subdued.
Vasiṣṭha said:
In the empire of the great hells, the elephants of evil deeds are intoxicated;
the enemies that are the sense-faculties are difficult to conquer, for they are bristling with the arrows and shafts of desire. (21)
Regarding the phrase "the great hell" (*mahānaraka*): the hells themselves are the empire, because they are the locus of enjoyment for the senses and so forth.

Misdeeds alone are the intoxicated elephants, because they are the cause for the activity of the senses. Hopes and desires are the arrow-shafts—arrows in the form of shafts—because one is driven by them. (21)
For one whose mental pride has been destroyed and who has subdued the enemies that are the senses,
the latent tendencies for enjoyment wither away like lotus ponds in the winter.

He states the fruit of the tranquility of the mind and the mastery of the senses with the verse beginning "prakṣīṇa": "the latent impressions of enjoyment" refers to the repeated longings for enjoyment. || 22 ||
So long do the Vetālas of latent impressions dance within the heart, as long as the mind has not been conquered through firm practice on the single Reality. (23)
"Up to that point" means: from the firm practice of a single principle—that is, from that meditative practice which is firmly rooted in the single reality of the Self (ātmatattva). || 23 ||

He is a servant because he performs what is desired; a minister because he accomplishes the proper task; a vassal because he has overcome the senses; and a guru because of his bestowing of knowledge. (24)

He says in two verses that a mind which has been brought under control benefits many living beings: "As a servant... and so forth. The meaning is that because it performs the tasks of a servant and the like, the mind assumes the form of a servant and so on. Because it spontaneously performs beneficial deeds for the virtuous (*sat*), it is a minister (*mantrī*) of the senses.

Because it impels knowledge, action, and the instruments by means of its own pervasion and its quality as an instigator, it is like a feudal lord (sāmanta) who sets various types of authorized persons into motion. || 24 || 25 ||
I consider that for wise men, a tender woman is [their] mind through her fondling, a father is their mind through his protection, and a friend is their mind through his trustworthiness. (25)
Beheld by the vision of the scriptures, realized by one's own intellect, and experienced through one's own direct perception,
the father of the mind bestows supreme perfection once it has abandoned the sense of self.

"Self-illuminated" (svālokita) means well-observed through the knowledge of the scriptures, which is established by inquiry; "experienced by oneself" (svānubhāvita) means brought to a firm certainty through one's own intellect and personal experience. Since it is said that the mind is the father because it protects and purifies, the mind itself is the father; having abandoned the [limited] self and dissolved itself, it leads to the Supreme.
It bestows perfection and liberation; the sense is: "Who else could assist in this way? || 26 ||
Well-seen, well-firm, clear, beautiful, and perfectly awakened, the jewel of the mind shines in the heart, delightful and exalted by its own qualities. (27)

"Clearly seen" (*sudṛṣṭa*) means correctly perceived; for that very reason, it is "well-firm" (*sudṛḍha*), being unshakable due to the absence of doubt and error. Furthermore, it is "clear" (*svaccha*), meaning stainless; "beautiful" (*sukānta*), meaning endowed with noble desire (*subhecchā*); and "well-awakened" (*suprabodhita*), meaning brought to a correct awakening by its own quality of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth.
The excellent jewel of the mind, being powerful and sublime, shines within the heart. || 27 ||
O Rāma, having thus washed the jewel of the mind— which is stained by much mud— with the water of discernment for the sake of perfection, become possessed of light.

Thus it is said: Having washed this jewel of the mind—which has been stained by much mud, that is, defiled by many impure latent impressions—with the water of discrimination, which is the wisdom born of inquiry, become one who possesses light, a knower of reality, for the sake of attaining perfection, which is liberation. 28–29.

Relying firmly upon discernment and perceiving the truth with your intellect, cross over the enemies that are the senses; having crossed them, be one who has transcended the ocean of worldly existence. (29)

O Great-minded One, having thoroughly cast aside with your own intellect that vain conviction of "I am this," rely upon that which is other than it; go to that state, drink, and eat, for you are not bound when you are without the mind (amanaska).
"This" refers to that false certainty, which is a contrary determination whose object is a limited form, such as "this is I.

Having thoroughly cast that aside by means of your own intellect, and having taken refuge in that other state—which is consciousness unconditioned by egoity—conduct yourself as you wish while remaining without the mind (amanaska). The meaning is that when this is so, you will not be bound. || 30 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Raghava, let not the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa be yours; through the firm standing of Bhīma and Bhāsa, may you possess complete freedom from sorrow.

"Dāma," "Vyāla," and "Kaṭa"—these are names of Daityas; may their conduct, which is devoid of discernment, not be yours. "Bhīma," "Bhāsa," and "Dṛḍha"—these are also Daityas; through their state of being, may you possess freedom from sorrow. || 31 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, you who remove the torment of worldly existence, what have you said regarding the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, and the firm standing of Bhīma and Bhāsa? 32.
"Dāma" means: he whose nature it is to remove the heat of existence—that is, the sufferings of saṃsāra. || 32 || 33 || 34 ||
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, hear the maxim of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, which is firmly established in the Mīmāṃsā; having heard it, do as you wish.
In the cavern of the netherworld (Pātāla), which was enchanting with all forms of sovereignty,
there was a lord of Daityas named Śambara, who was a great ocean of the jewels of illusion (māyā).
That primordial God of gods, possessing a form both formidable and fierce,
had a vast asuric army that was the destroyer of the gods.

Regarding the word "tasya" (of him): the *ādidevas* are the ancient gods, the Daityas; he was born as their god (*deva*). He is one whose form (*ākṛti*) is hard, fierce (*uḍḍāmara*), and terrifying (*bhayaṃkarā*). || 35 || 36 ||
While that Māyābala was asleep and likewise gone to another land,
the gods, having found a vulnerability, indeed swiftly struck down his army.
Then, for the sake of protection, the Daitya Śambara appointed Muṇḍika, Aṅka, Drumā, and others as ministers and vassals within his own armies.
Regarding the word "atha" (now): "Muṇḍikāṅkadrumādayaḥ" means those for whom Muṇḍika, Aṅka, Druma, and others are the first [in the series]. 37, 38, 39.
Having reached their midst, the terrifying gods slaughtered them as well;
then, out of anger, Śambara himself came to the city of the gods.
Terrified by the power of his illusion, those gods vanished, constrained by the weight of fear within the groves and thickets of Mount Meru. (39)
He beheld heaven empty, like the world at the end of an eon, with the hosts of minor gods wailing and the faces of the women drenched in tears.
Having stayed there, enraged and reeling with the intoxication of his staff-like arms, he burned the city of the world-protectors and returned to his own abode. || 41 ||
When the enmity between the Dānavas and the gods had thus become even more firm, the gods abandoned heaven and vanished from sight in all directions. (42)
Then, whatever army commanders were appointed with great effort by the Daitya Śambara, those gods, intent on their own efforts, slew them all.
When Śambara became greatly agitated and filled with intense anger,
he created by means of his illusory power three terrible and exceedingly powerful asuras.
Created by means of illusion, terrifying like mountains shaken by a storm,
the great illusions Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa rose up.
Devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā) and the conceit of self (ātmābhimāna), those who first emerged knew neither how to fall down, nor how to leap up, nor how to flee. 46.

Regarding the term *vāsanā*: they are devoid of both the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the conceit of selfhood (*ātmābhimāna*), as well as the worldly impressions (*lokavāsanā*) and the conceit of the body (*dehābhimāna*).

Since they have emerged first—having arisen from the Supreme Self alone through the power of *māyā*—they do not perceive, that is, they do not know, either the *abhipātam*, which is the charging toward enemies, or the *āpātam*, which is the arrival of enemies. 46, 47, 48.
There was neither life nor death in that battle, nor victory or defeat;
they were merely intent on slaying the enemy soldiers as soon as they saw them before them.
Then Śambara, his mind completely satisfied, reflected:
"For these [ascetics] have indeed been liberated from those latent impressions consisting of likes and dislikes. (48)
"Having thus resolved that these do not flee even when struck by the gods, the lord of the Daityas [sent] Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa... (49)
He dispatched an army capable of slaying the forces of the Lord of the Gods;
the Daityas, armed with weapons, emerged from the thickets by the ocean and from the mountain caves.
Then, with the playful gait of winged mountains, the gods rose up from the groves and the caves with terrifying roars and by force.
Like formidable mountain lords moving forward, the hosts of the celestial dwellers advanced;
thus did the battle between those two armies, bearing the banners of gods and asuras, commence. (52)
While that terrible turmoil of battle was then unfolding within the world— an event as fearsome as the dissolution of the universe at an untimely hour— (53)
With their limbs and weapons fallen here and blood flowing forth,
the divine armies fled like scattered waters.
Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, though they had long been hidden,
followed after them with a loud roar, just as fires follow their fuel.
Although they searched with great effort, the Asuras did not find the gods;
and since the hosts of immortals were unattainable, Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa likewise [remained].
With joyful hearts, they went to the Lord residing in the treasury of Pātāla;
then those deities, being despondent, consoled themselves for a moment and departed.
When they had been conquered by Dāma and the others, Brahmā of immeasurable splendor appeared before them— red in color, with the luster of a red seat.
Those gods bowed down to him and fully related everything that had been done by Śambara, as well as the sequence of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.

Brahmā said:
"Come now, O gods, at the end of a thousand years, Śambara's army must be conquered in battle; wait for that time. (61)
"O lords of the immortals, fight these Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa! While fighting, you must flee and then return once more for the sake of battle. (62)
Through the power of practice in battle, this wondrous display of egoism will enter into his heart like a reflection in mirrors. (63)

Regarding the word *yuddha*: "From the power of repeated practice in battle—that is, from the frequent engagement in combat—the wonder in the form of ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which is a particular cognition, will attain the status of a reflection within the interior, as it were, of the mirrors. This is the syntactical connection. (Verses 63–75)
For these demons Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa have taken up latent impressions;
they will be easily conquered by you, like birds caught in a net.
The wise know that mere attachment is the source of endless sufferings; they know that mere non-attachment is the source of all-around happiness.
Bound by the threads of latent impressions (vāsanā), this world indeed revolves;
when that [vāsanā] has increased, it leads to extreme suffering, but when it has reached its cessation, it leads to happiness.
Though steadfast, though possessing vast knowledge, though advanced in age, and though great, a living being is bound by craving, just as a lion is bound by a chain. (67)
Having spoken thus, the divine Lord vanished on the spot; and the gods, having heard those words, departed for their desired destination.
They raised a roar from their drums resembling the sound of clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
Then, by those Daityas who had risen from the depths of Pātāla in the great sky, [the battle was joined].
A terrible battle that delayed the end of time broke out once more;
the gods fled again and fought yet again. (70)
In this way, O best of gods, they caused a delay in the battle through various means for the purpose of deluding the Daityas.
And after such a length of time, through the firm practice of egoism, Dāma and the others, with disciplined minds, took up the conviction that "I am [the body]. (72)

Seized by the latent impressions of worldly existence, joined with the latent impressions of delusion, and bound by the snares of hope, they have consequently fallen into a state of wretchedness. (73)
"May my body remain firm; may my wealth lead to happiness"—thus, the fortitude of those with aged intellects vanished within.
Therefore, in that battle, the Daityas fell into a state of despondency, their hearts stricken with the thought, "We shall die! We shall die! (75)
Then, their courage failing, they were unable to strike the soldier standing before them, just as fires cannot consume an oblation when their fuel is exhausted.
What is the use of saying more here? With their minds terrified of death and having flight as their sole refuge, those enemies of the gods were utterly destroyed.
O high-minded Rāma, I speak this for your awakening so that the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa may not occur through mere playfulness. (78)
Due to its persistent lack of discernment, the mind effortlessly embraces such a calamity for the sake of the endless sufferings of existence. (79)
Rāma said:
O Brahman, you ought to sever my doubt as it truly is: how did the tamer, the bull, and the serpent arise from the Supreme State? (80)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as Dāma and the others, O Rāma, were of the nature of mere appearances, so too are we; they do not exist anywhere externally. (81)

"Just as... || Just as Dāma and the others, being fashioned by *māyā*, consist of mere appearance and possess illusory bodies, so too we here consist of mere appearance; we do not exist anywhere at all outside the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).
Your existence is indeed false, and my existence is indeed false;
even the existence of Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others is indeed false. (82)
A certain power of the living soul (*jīva-śakti*) belonging to the Supreme Self, consisting of manifestation, was agitated by the meditation on Śambara and attained a threefold expansion. (83)

Pratīti: From the Supreme Self, that certain power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), consisting of manifestation, being agitated by the meditation on Śambara, attained a threefold expansion in the form of Dāmā and the others. || 83 ||
Therefore, neither we nor Dāma and the others exist anywhere as real entities;
rather, reality is pure consciousness, the stainless sky of awakening. 84.
Therefore: "The entire manifold of difference is unreal; only pure consciousness, which is the mere space of consciousness, is real. (84)
Truth is all-pervading, peaceful, and free from rising or setting;
the world exists as merely the manifestation of its power. (85)
The intended meaning of these two verses is that this world exists as the manifestation of the power of that pure consciousness alone. || 85 ||
Everything exists everywhere as it truly is, yet nothing whatsoever exists here that has been experienced;
this peaceful, single, face remains thus, free from doubt and devoid of division— therefore, remain as you are.

"Everywhere": according to experience—that is, in accordance with what has been experienced—everything exists everywhere, yet nothing exists apart from that which is experienced. The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "if. If it is not experienced, then nothing whatsoever exists anywhere. This entire universe, being of the nature of the One Reality which is Peaceful and Pure Being, thus pervades and extends; it exists as this world and appears in the form of the phenomenal realm. Therefore, you... [should realize this].
The meaning is: remain at ease, having abandoned all suspicion, as well as the sense of non-duality or duality arising from one's own doubts.
Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Narrative of Dāma and Others," in the Section on Stability within the *Mokṣopāya* of the glorious *Vālmīkīya*.

Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Narrative of Dāma and Others," in the *Samsarataraṇi*, a commentary on the *Vāsiṣṭha*, composed by the learned teacher Śrī Mummaḍideva, son of the illustrious Allālasūri, who had gazed across the ocean of grammar, logic, and epistemology. || 2 ||
The Third Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
"May this be mine, may that be mine"—such is the thought, O Mahāmati;
yet due to one's own misfortune and wretchedness, reality does not manifest.
Previously, in the narrative of Dāma and others, it was stated that worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) increases through the notions of "I" and "mine" arising from a lack of discrimination (*viveka*).

Now, in the narrative of Bhīma and others, it is established that the absence of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) regarding the body and so forth conduces to the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Regarding this, he first teaches what is beneficial: "This... [The entire world exists only within the Self.]

The Self is the essence of all. This being so, because of that miserable state—the thought "I am unfortunate" arising from one's own wretchedness—the Truth, which is Brahman, does not approach, does not remain present, and does not manifest for the sake of that intellect which thinks, "May this son and so forth be mine," and "May this field and so forth be mine. This is the meaning. || 1 || 2 ||
All calamities abandon that noble-souled one who always regards even the three worlds as a blade of grass, just as deer flee from withered grass.
The lords of the world protect him within whom the wonder of truth constantly vibrates, like the indivisible cosmic egg of Brahmā.

"Parīti": The lords of the world protect that person—like they protect the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa)—because he contains the essence of Brahman, for within him the wonder of truth, the constant contemplation of Brahman whose nature is truth, perpetually shines forth.
The meaning is that they hold [them] in high esteem. || 3 ||
Those who find contentment in virtues, those whose passion is for sacred learning, and those who are devoted to truth—these men are [truly] human; all others are but beasts. (4)
"Of those who... means: those men, persons, who are indeed endowed with the aforementioned qualities; others, however, are like beasts—this is the meaning. (4) (5) (6) (7)
Furthermore, one must never proceed with haste toward a calamitous end;
even Rāhu died while drinking the nectar in such a hasty manner.
Those who are naturally uncontrollable come under control, and all calamities go to their destruction;
for one by whom fame has been purchased through virtues, well-being becomes inexhaustible.
Who does not achieve success by applying the supreme human effort, undertaking excellent exertion, and acting according to the scriptures without despondency? (7)
One who dwells according to the scriptures should not be in haste for the attainments;
after a long time, the supreme attainment becomes fully ripened and yields abundant fruit.

Regarding the word "yathā": the grammatical connection is that accomplishment (siddhi), having been ripened over a long period and being possessed of a nourishing fruit, shall become supreme—that is, most excellent. || 8 ||
Let worldly affairs be conducted according to the scriptures— free from sorrow, fear, exertion, greed, and constraint— so that they do not come to ruin.
"Vīta" means free from greed (agardham), that is, without longing; this is derived from the verbal root *gṛdh* in the sense of "desire.
It also means free from constraint (apayantraṇam), that is, devoid of crookedness (*kauṭilyam*). 9, 10, 11, 12, 13.
The attainment of wealth leads to misfortune; a flood of enjoyments brings about the disease of existence;
all prosperities are calamities; and victory everywhere is characterized by a lack of concern.

For one whose conduct is beautiful through right behavior, whose life is secluded, and who does not hanker after the states of suffering that result from the pleasures of worldly existence, his lifespan, fame, virtues, and prosperity flourish together for the sake of good fruit, like a spring creeper in full bloom.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Neither austerities, nor sacred fords, nor the recitation of scriptures can indeed carry one across the ocean of saṃsāra without the service of the virtuous.
He whose greed, delusion, and anger diminish day by day, and who conducts himself in his duties according to the scriptures—he is a virtuous person. (13)
When the sense of "I" is not fully understood, it is stainless within the sky of ultimate reality;
but when the sense of "I" is fully understood, it becomes the very sky of ultimate reality.
"I" [is as follows]: the meaning of the word "I" (ahaṃśabda) when not fully understood is like a stain or blemish in the sky of ultimate reality, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).

When fully understood, the object of "I" (ahamartha) becomes indeed supreme; it becomes the very sky of ultimate reality. The sense is that this occurs because of the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman. || 14 ||
As long as the moonlight of consciousness remains shrouded within by the dense cloud of egoism,
it cannot cause the night-lily of ultimate reality to blossom.
"O moonlight! [This refers to: "The night-blooming lily of the ultimate truth," that is, "ultimate liberation. 15.
The sense of "I" is the sprout of those trees of birth that are imperishable in nature; the extensive branches of these trees are the thoughts "this is mine," which bear only worthless fruit.

"I" [means]: the very sense of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*) is the sprout of those trees that are births; the sense of "this is mine" (*mamedam*) is their state. The branches of those trees of birth bear fruit that is non-existent—that is, fruit that is suffering. Rāma said: [verses 16–21]
What is the form of the ego, O Lord, and how is it abandoned?
Is it embodied or bodiless, and what occurs when it is relinquished? (17)
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Raghava, there are three kinds of egoism here in the three worlds;
two are excellent and the other is to be abandoned. Listen, and I shall tell you. (18)
"I am this entire universe; I am the Supreme Self, the Infallible One.
There is nothing else"—having reflected thus, that indeed is the supreme egoity. (19)
This [identification] does not exist at all for one liberated while living as a cause of bondage;
I am distinct from everything, imagined to be as small as a hundredth part of the tip of a hair. (20)
Thus, this very consciousness is the auspicious second form of ego;
it leads to liberation and not to bondage, for such [an ego] exists in one who is liberated while living.
"This 'I' consists merely of hands, feet, and so forth"—this conviction is the third kind of egoism; it is worldly and utterly trivial. (22)
This wicked-souled bulb is to be avoided, for it is the root of the continuity of saṃsāra; by means of this, a living being is carried away and runs further and further down.
By long abandoning this wicked egoism through its very essence,
a living being, possessing the refined ego, quickly becomes fit for liberation.

"By this... || By means of this—that is, by having long since abandoned that false egoism (durahaṃkṛti) which consists in regarding the Self as limited to the body—and by virtue of the remaining intention (bhāva), one who possesses the two remaining forms of egoism—namely, "I am the Self of all" and "I am beyond all"—and who manifests them, attains liberation. || 24 || 25 || 26 || 27 || 28 ||
Having accepted the first two forms of egoism as being super-mundane,
the third form of egoism— the mundane one that bestows suffering— should be abandoned. (25)
This [woman] must indeed be abandoned; having renounced her, who brings only suffering, in whatever manner a man abides, to that very extent he attains the Supreme.
If he remains contemplating these two previously mentioned views of the ego, the sinless person attains the supreme state. (27)
Then, having abandoned even those [notions] and being devoid of all egoism, he remains thus and ascends to that exceedingly lofty state. (28)
The state of the body is of great merit due to the abandonment of egoism;
this alone is the ultimate supreme good, the highest station. (29)

Regarding the word *śarīra*: by abandoning "bad egoism"—that is, having abandoned the previously mentioned false sense of self—that state of the body is "highly meritorious," meaning it is the cause of great merit because it is a means for the practice of yoga; it is the "supreme good" (*paramaṃ śreyaḥ*), and it is also the "highest station" (*paraṃ padam*). It is this alone and nothing else, because all other things are merely its means. 29–37.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Now listen, for I shall tell you what happened even after Dāma and the others had departed: that Śambara, whose mind was arrogant, had his army defeated by the gods.
Again the Dānava reflected upon a means for slaying the gods:
"Those [beings] such as Dāma and others who were previously created by me through my power of illusion—" || 31 ||
Out of delusion, their intellect has been conditioned such that their internal ego-sense is purely false; now, through my supreme power of illusion (māyā), I shall create other Dānavas.
I shall also make those who know the inner sciences (adhyātma-śāstra) possess discernment;
then, through the thorough knowledge of reality, they will be freed from false conceptions.
"They shall not fall into egoism and they shall conquer the gods"—
having reflected thus, the lord of the Daityas [sought] such Dānavas with his intellect.
By means of his illusory power (māyā), he brought them forth like bubbles from the ocean—
beings who were omniscient, knowers of all that is to be known, free from passion, and devoid of sin.
Those supreme ones who had cultivated their selves were performers of deeds exactly as they occurred;
they were distinguished by the names Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Dṛḍha. (36)
Perceiving the entire world as mere straw, those of pure intent,
having received the words of the lord of the Daityas,
covered the sky and fought against the gods for many groups of years.
As long as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) "this is mine" arises within them, so long will this "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) not reach untruth through inquiry. (38)

Regarding the phrase "of them": for those such as Bhīma and the others, as long as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) that "this is mine" or "I am this" arises within, for that duration that impression passes into unreality by means of inquiry—that is, by reason of inquiry into one's own true nature. The meaning is that because they possess the knowledge of Brahman, these notions of "this" and "I" are not stable. (Verses 38–46)
Then, by those heroes who were free from ego, fearless of old age and death, who accomplished their goals, and who followed the conduct of the present; || 39 ||
By those who are free from passion, devoid of hatred, and always possessed of an even vision. || 40 ||
That divine army was slain, devoured, wounded, and scorched by Bhīma, Bhāsa, Dṛḍha, and the others, just as the beauty of one's own food is destroyed by its eaters. || 41 ||
Then the army of the gods, violently crushed by Bhīma and Bhasa,
fled with speed like the Gaṅgā falling from the Himavat.
That army of the Asuras went for refuge to the God who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk, just as a row of clouds driven by the wind seeks a mountain for shelter.
Then, in that most terrible battle, those Daityas were utterly consumed by the flames of the discus-fire and sent to the city of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O Rāma, the mind is bound by latent impressions and liberated when free from them; quickly attain the state of being free from impressions through discernment.
Through the correct perception of the Truths, latent impressions (vāsanā) dissolve;
and upon the dissolution of latent impressions, the mind becomes stilled like a lamp without oil.
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Narrative of Bhīma and Others," in the Section on Stability within the *Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-sāra*.

Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Narrative of Bhīma and Others," in the *Samsarataraṇi*, a commentary on the *Vāsiṣṭha* composed by the learned teacher Śrī Mumadi Deva, son of the illustrious Allālasūri, who had reached the further shore of the ocean of grammar, logic, and epistemology. || 3 ||
The Fourth Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
For this suffering of saṃsāra, which causes every kind of affliction, there is only one remedy: the restraint of one's own mind. (1)

Previously, in the narrative concerning Bhīma and others, it was stated that the renunciation of egoism conduces to the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Now, in order to substantiate that, the illusory nature (*māyikatva*) of the world's existence is clearly established. In this regard, he first teaches the means [to liberation] with the words "of this" (*asya*). The term *duḥkha* refers to the suffering of saṃsāra, so called because it causes one to suffer (*duḥkhayati*).

The meaning is "the cause of suffering. That is to say, [it refers to] the cause of suffering in the form of saṃsāra. The reason for its being suffering is that "it brings about all calamities. "Means" means the means for cessation. || 1 || 2 ||
Listen to the essence of all knowledge, and having heard it, let it be firmly grasped:
bondage consists solely in the desire for enjoyment; its renunciation is called liberation.
What is the use of other collections of treatises? Let this alone be done:
whatever is pleasant here, let all that be viewed as like poison or fire. (3)

"What is it? [The answer follows: Whatever object in this world is perceived as sweet and dear to the mind, let all that be viewed like poison or fire; let it be considered harmful because it is a cause of torment. (3-4)

Having repeatedly investigated with the mind that sense objects are fraught with perilous enjoyments, one should completely renounce them; yet when cultivated [with discernment], they bring about happiness.
The rise of the mind is its destruction; the destruction of the mind is the great awakening.
The mind of the wise man goes to its destruction, for the mind of the ignorant is indeed a shackle.
Regarding the phrase "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*): the "exaltation of the mind" (*manaso 'bhyudayaḥ*) means its rising on all sides; that is to say, its expansion.

That exaltation of the mind is actually its destruction, because it is the cause for the non-perception of one's true nature. However, the destruction of the mind is the "great exaltation" (*mahodayaḥ*) of the Self, because it is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
For the knower (*jña*), the wise one, the mind reaches its destruction; but for the ignorant one, the mind itself is a fetter. (5)

The wise know that the mind of the knower is neither blissful nor devoid of bliss, neither moving nor unmoving, and neither stable; it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor even the middle between these.
"No. The mind of the knower cannot even be defined as "what it is," because it is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*) and yet remains the cause of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*).
To explain: it is not of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), because it is insentient (*jaḍa*); nor is it devoid of bliss, because it is the cause of the experience of bliss;
it is not moving, because it is solely established in the Self; nor is it unmoving or stable, because it manifests externally in whatever manner is appropriate.

It is not existent, because its effects, such as volitional thought (*saṃkalpa*), are absent; nor is it non-existent, because the sense organs are still active toward their objects. Nor can there be a middle state between these two—bliss and the absence of bliss—for when two things are mutually contradictory, no third alternative can arise.
Therefore, the meaning is that the wise know the mind of the knower to be indefinable (*anirvacanīya*). || 6 || 7 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, tell me again for the sake of increasing my understanding how this universe is situated within the conscious Self that transcends the universe.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as space, though all-pervading, is not perceived due to its subtlety,
so too the partless nature of consciousness, though all-pervading, is not perceived.

Indeed, in order to demonstrate that the entire universe exists as a phenomenal manifestation (*vivarta*) of the conscious self (*cidātman*), and to define the nature of consciousness, [the author] first states its difficulty of being perceived, beginning with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). Just as the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), which is illumined by consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), cannot be perceived due to its subtlety and lack of parts, so too is the reality whose nature is consciousness (*cidbhāva*).
Even though it is everything, it is not perceived because it is partless.
Free from all volitional constructions and devoid of all conceptualizations,
this very consciousness, whose nature is indestructible, is designated by such names as "one's own self" (svātman).

The two verses beginning with "sarvā" constitute a single sentence. Although this very consciousness is in reality devoid of all designations, it has been given names such as "Self" (svātman) and so forth; the meaning is that it is designated by imagined names such as "one's own" (svam), "the Self" (ātman), and "the conscious one" (cetana). || 9 ||
(317) More subtle than a hundredth part of space, she exists in all things of knowledge in an undivided form;
she perceives the single self-nature within the entire, stainless cycle of existence. || 10 ||

"Clearer than space by a hundredfold" means it is a hundred times more transparent than space. Among the "knowers," that is, among the wise, she is "of an undivided form," meaning her nature is stainless. Since she was previously described as residing in the ignorant who possess all parts (*sakala*), she is "with parts" (*sakalaṅkā*) among the ignorant; therefore, she perceives the single self as being of the nature of impurity (*mala*) and transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Here, "impurity" is ignorance and "transmigratory existence" is its effect.

The meaning is that she reveals the Self as having become one—that is, attained identity—with its own essential nature (svarūpa), thereby showing the Self to be non-different from ignorance and its effects.

This is the same meaning even in the reading "malasaṃsārasvarūpeṇātmadarśinī" (revealing the Self by way of the essential nature of impurity and transmigratory existence); [it refers to] by way of the essential nature of impurity and transmigratory existence.
It shows itself as non-different [from the self]. || 10 ||
Just as the vast diversity consisting of waves and so forth in the ocean of water does not appear as something distinct from it, even though it spreads out [from it]. (11)

The two verses beginning with "taraṅga" form a single syntactical unit. Just as in the ocean there is a manifold variety—consisting of waves, foam, bubbles, and so forth—which spreads out according to its movement, yet manifests as non-different from that ocean; [so it is with consciousness]. || 11 ||
This vast and manifold world, consisting of the states of "thou-ness" and "I-ness," shines forth in this manner within the ocean of consciousness;
it appears thus precisely as non-different from pure consciousness alone.

Likewise, the connection [of the verse] is as follows: although this expansive manifoldness consisting of "thou-ness" and "I-ness" is conceived as diverse, it shines forth within the ocean of consciousness (cid-arṇava) as nothing other than non-different from pure consciousness (cin-mātra). || 12 ||
Among the ignorant, she is the womb containing the multitude of the inherently fierce cycle of existence;
among the wise, she is of the nature of pure light, the single reality that comprises all things.

The three verses beginning with "ajñeṣu" form a single syntactical unit. Among the ignorant, she is of an unreal nature due to the impurities of passion, hatred, and so forth; thus, she is of the nature of suffering. For this very reason, she is "pregnant with the multitude of the fierce cycle of existence" (*ugrasaṃsāragaṇagarbhiṇī*), meaning she carries within her the womb of the terrible mass of transmigrations—her sense being that she is the cause of the succession of worldly existence. Among the wise, however, she is of the nature of light.
She is indeed the embodiment of pure wisdom, the single essence of all things, existing everywhere with an undifferentiated nature. || 13 ||
By virtue of experience, she is eternally the illuminator of karma and the other factors;
she is the savorer of all existents, the one to be meditated upon by those who enjoy worldly existence. (14)

Regarding the term *anubhūti*: by virtue of experience—that is, by virtue of the experience of various respective objects—she is the illuminator of the factors of action (*karmādīnāṃ kāryakārakāṇām*); she is the savorer, the cause of the knowledge of taste for all states (*sarvabhāvānām*), meaning all objects of enjoyment; she is the object of contemplation (*bhāvanī*) for those who enjoy existence (*bhavabhoginām*), meaning the cause of their worldly activity. Consciousness (*cit*) is of such a nature. 14.
The consciousness neither sets nor rises, neither arises nor remains;
it neither goes nor comes, neither is here nor is not here.

It neither sets nor rises, because it is eternal; it neither arises nor remains, because it is changeless; it neither goes nor comes, because it is actionless; it does not exist here, because it is without support; yet it does not not exist here, because it is all-pervading. || 15 ||
This very consciousness, pure in form, established by itself within itself, expands as this Rāghava through the phenomenal world known as the universe. 16.
Thus [it is said]: This very consciousness previously described, whose form is stainless, abiding within its own self alone, thus unfolds as the manifold expansion known by the name "the world. (16)
By its own nature, it is named Consciousness; it is all-pervading, arisen as the Self, manifest and yet unmanifest, partless and yet bearing parts. || 17 ||

The phrase "tat" (that) refers to a statement consisting of three and a half verses. That aforementioned supreme reality, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), [manifests] through a light that is all-pervading, perfectly full, risen in its own essence, and non-setting; which is both manifest and unmanifest, consisting of knowledge and ignorance;
which is partless yet assumes parts, being both without and with limbs by virtue of its own conceptualization (*svakalpanā*) and through the power of its own volition (*svasaṃkalpa*).

Having itself abandoned its own state of abiding in its true nature— the state of the infinite— it goes through the cycle of transmigratory existence by means of its own nature called "consciousness," which has attained the condition of a limited individual soul (jīva) through the ignorance of the state of the Unknowable and through the conceit of assuming forms imposed by the notion "I am this. || 17 || 18 ||
(319) By one who,
abandoning the infinite state through the application of his own conceptualization,
proceeds slowly toward the state of pure consciousness with the thought "I am this," [the goal is reached]. 18.
When this diversity has increased through the process of worldly existence,
and [the self] has come to abide in the state of grasping and abandoning existence and non-existence,
the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka) acts and does not act by means of hundreds of vibrations.

When diversity has increased, and when one has come to abide in the state of grasping and abandoning— consisting of the apprehension of existence and non-existence in the form: "this is of the nature of existence," "this is of the nature of non-existence," "this is grasped," and "this is abandoned"— then, through hundreds of fluctuations consisting of conceptual constructions, the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), whose characteristics will be described hereafter, [arises].
It neither creates nor does not create the subtle body, because in reality there is an absence of a cause. || 19 || 20 ||
In this manner, all these successions of worldly existences, possessing stable forms of power, come forth from and return again to Brahman by their very nature.
Just as rivers are perceived in the sky during the heat of summer within a mere appearance of consciousness,
even so are these perceptions of creation perceived within the nature of the mind.

"In the sky" means: just as streams of rain are observed in the sky immediately after the summer heat, so too, within the essence of consciousness—which is devoid of appearance and stainless—there are perceptions in the form of creation; this is the meaning. || 21 ||

Just as, under the influence of intoxication, the self appears as something other than itself, so too, due to the ignorance of consciousness, that very same self remains established as "not-self. (22)

Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): For just as the self, through intoxication—the blending of delusion and bliss produced by liquor—appears as if it were something other than itself due to the power of that intoxication, in exactly the same way, due to the ignorance (*avidyā*) of consciousness—that is, because of the non-knowledge of its own conscious nature—that very self remains as if it were non-existent, as if it were other than itself. 22.
O Raghava, that by which you perceive sound, taste, form, and smell—this is the Self, the Supreme Brahman, which exists pervading everything. (23)

"By which": that consciousness which, having issued outward through the channel of the external senses, perceives objects such as sound—this very Self, whose nature is such consciousness, is the Supreme Brahman;
that same Self exists, pervading all things. 23.
(320) This world exists as Brahman alone by name; there is no impurity here other than that.
The water of the ocean manifests through its multitude of surging waves, yet no dust [of duality] exists. || 24 ||

"Brahman" means that this world exists as Brahman alone, through the various distinctions of names such as "space" (*viyat*) and so forth; the meaning is that it exists in the form of the world. Here, there is no other impurity—consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects—that is distinct from Brahman. To illustrate: just as water alone manifests through the multitude of waves of the ocean, and not dust (where "dust" is used as an illustration for anything else), so it is here.
The meaning is that another object manifests. || 24 ||
O scion of Raghu, no second conceptualization exists here at all, other than Brahman alone, just as there is nothing other than heat alone in fire. (25)

"Regarding 'the second': just as there is no conception of a second thing apart from heat in fire, so too in this world, there is no conception of a second thing apart from that which is the nature of Brahman, consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss. || 25 ||
At first, one should instruct the disciple through qualities consisting primarily of tranquility and self-control;
afterwards, one should instruct him that "all this is Brahman" and "you are pure. (26)
Having thus established the non-difference between the manifest world of the sentient and insentient and Consciousness, because it is an illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of Consciousness,
[the author] says "At first" (*ādau*) in order to show that this meaning shines forth only for such a qualified seeker (*adhikārī*).
At first, having examined the attainment of the fourfold means beginning with tranquility (*śama*), [one examines] the qualified seeker afterwards.
The meaning is "he should awaken. || 26 ||
He who says "everything is Brahman" to one who is ignorant or only half-awakened casts that person into the snares of the great hells. (27)
But he states that there is a great transgression in causing one who is not qualified to understand [the teaching], saying "of the ignorant" (ajñasya). That ignorant person, by that instructor.

For one whose intellect is awakened, whose desire for enjoyment has perished, and who is free from expectations—for such a person as you alone is it within the range of experience that the stain of ignorance does not exist. (28)

"Awakened" (prabuddha) means that the realization—that the impurity of ignorance does not exist for one such as you, who is free from desire and devoid of conceptual construction—is the proper object of experience; that is to say, it is suitable for you. || 28 ||
When consciousness exists, the world is like light in a lamp, like day in the sun,
and like fragrance in a flower.
This world appears only as a manifestation; it does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality.

"Regarding the word 'satī' (being existent): because consciousness and the world stand in a relationship of cause and effect—just like a lamp and its light—there is no mutual separation between them; rather, they exist in a state of inseparability (*ayutabhāva*).
Rāma said:
Awakened by your diverse and profound words, which possess a cool and stainless luster like the interior of the Ocean of Milk; (30)

The two verses beginning with "kṣīroda" form a single syntactical unit. The construction is as follows: "Like a day characterized by cool breezes and the onset of heat, and possessing clouds that flicker during the rainy season—the time of the monsoon—in which the clouds are flickering, I attain a momentary darkness and a momentary state of brightness. (30–31)
For a moment I fall as if into blindness, and for a moment I attain clarity, like a day with its shifting clouds during the cold season, the heat, and the rainy season. (31)
How has the conceptualization of that which is infinite, immeasurable, all-encompassing, singular, luminous, and whose essence never sets come to be? 32.

Regarding the word "anantasya" (of the infinite): how has *kalanā*—ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause of bondage—come to that which is infinite, whose nature is everything, which is one and without a second, radiant, eternally manifest, whose essence never sets, and whose power is never lost?
The sense is that for such a luminous being, the obscuration of darkness is impossible. || 32 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:

All my utterances have meanings that accord with reality; they are never ineffective, nor do they possess contradictory meanings, for they are free from internal inconsistency between what precedes and what follows. (33)

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): all my utterances have meanings and sentence-meanings that correspond exactly to reality; they are indeed non-contradictory in their meaning. They are not incapable, nor are they inconsistent in meaning; furthermore, due to the absence of contradiction between what precedes and what follows, they are neither discordant in meaning nor contrary in meaning. || 33 ||

When the vision of knowledge has become clear and awakening has dawned extensively, you, established in yourself, will understand exactly as it is the strength and weakness of the power of my words and views. (34)
If this is so, then why is it not perceived in that way? To this he says: "jñāna... [and so forth].

The strength and weakness of my speech and vision—that is, the strength and weakness, as well as the validity and invalidity, of my words and of the vision or knowledge that serves as their basis. || 34 ||
O Rāma, that knowledge which removes all defects is attained through ignorance itself— the highest [ignorance]— which arises from the effort to destroy one's own self.

"By ignorance" (avidyayā): This refers to the highest, fully matured ignorance, which arises from the effort toward the destruction of one's own self—that is, it is produced by that effort directed toward the destruction of one's own essential nature.

Although this ignorance takes the form of the final direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), it must be understood as arising from the effort toward the destruction of one's own self, because ignorance itself is a transformation of knowledge (*vidyā*). || 35 || 36 ||
For a weapon is quelled by a weapon, impurity is washed away by impurity;
poison is neutralized by poison, and an enemy is slain by an enemy. (36)
Such is this illusion of existence (bhūtamāyā), which gives joy through its own destruction;
its true nature is not perceived, for it perishes the very moment it is observed.
"Such as this" means: *bhūtamāyā* is the ignorance (*avidyā*) of living beings. In the reading *bhavamāyā*, *bhava* refers to saṃsāra;

[she is] such by virtue of the *māyā* that is its root. She, having herself perished through her own destruction, bestows joy—that is, she grants the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*). Her true nature (*svarūpa*), however, can be perceived but cannot be seen, because:
The meaning is that it perishes even while being perceived, because of its unreality. || 37 ||

"By kindling this meditation that 'this does not exist in the ultimate sense,' you will become a knower; through the attainment of the object of knowledge, you shall understand its true intention. (38)

"It does not exist" [means]: through the attainment of the object of knowledge—that is, through the attainment of the identity of Brahman and the Self—[one abandons] the "abode," which is the inherent nature, of this ignorance. || 38 || 39 || 40 ||
However, until you attain awakening, let there be a firm and unshakable conviction in my words alone: that ignorance does not exist. (39)
He who possesses the internal realization that "all is Brahman" is indeed a partaker of liberation;
this perception of duality is ignorance—one should abandon it in every way. (40)
O Rāma, it is said that the further shore of the river of ignorance cannot be reached except through the attainment of the Self; for that state is called the imperishable.

Regarding the term "ignorance" (avidyā): apart from the attainment of the Self—that is, without the direct realization of one's true nature—the further shore of the river of ignorance cannot be reached;
the meaning is that the cessation of ignorance is not accomplished. For this reason, that very state which is beyond ignorance is called the imperishable station, liberation (kaivalya). || 41 ||
O Rāma, let there be no deliberation for you as to "whence has she been born?"; let your deliberation be only this: "how shall I kill her? (42)
The three verses beginning with "From where? constitute a single statement. Let there be no inquiry as to "from where this ignorance has arisen," for such an inquiry would be purposeless.
Rather, let your inquiry be only this: "How shall I destroy this ignorance so that it will not again subject you to the sufferings of birth? For only this inquiry is purposeful. || 42 ||
O Raghava, when this [illusion] has set and ceased, you will know from where it came,
what it was, and how it perished, without any flaw in your understanding.

He states that this indeed has a purpose: "When she has set," etc. When this ignorance (avidyā) has been exhausted and has gone to its setting, you will know everything without exception—whence this ignorance arose, what its true nature is, how it perished, and so forth. || 43 ||
Therefore, exert yourself in the medical treatment of this infirmary, so that she will not further involve you in the sufferings of birth. (44)

Therefore, for that reason, the syntactical connection is: "Exert effort in the treatment of this ignorance, which is the abode of diseases and the like within the 'sickroom' of worldly existence. (44)
Just as the wind moves within the sky by itself,
so too does the Self experience agitation within its own self solely through its own power.

Regarding the phrase "in the Self": just as the wind moves within the sky by itself, without another support, by its own nature, and not by any other cause, so too the Self, through its own power—which is non-different from itself, namely the power of consciousness—attains restlessness in its very self, taking on the form of the world. The meaning is that the Self alone is the locus, the material cause, and the efficient cause of the universe. || 45 ||
The transparent ocean of consciousness flashes within itself through its own vibrations;
let it be firmly internalized that this [ocean] is a single, indivisible unity. (46)

Regarding the phrase "in its own self": the ocean of consciousness, through its own vibrations—which are the displacements of its own nature—manifests within itself alone; for this reason, that reality, which is of a single essence and indivisible, should be firmly contemplated and investigated as being internal. || 46 ||
That power of consciousness, slightly agitated in the great ocean of consciousness,
flashes forth as something transparent within that very [ocean], like a wave in the sea.

"Something" means: that power of consciousness (cicchakti), which is of the nature of ignorance within the great ocean of Consciousness, being in a state of slight agitation, flashes forth right there—consisting of that very same Consciousness and having the form of Consciousness—just like a wave in the ocean. || 47 ||
In that moment, as that Goddess flashes forth through her universal power,
she draws forth her companions— the powers of space, time, and action.
Regarding the word *kṣaṇam*: that Goddess, whose nature is consciousness, because she possesses all powers—that is, because she is of infinite power—manifests in such a way for a moment (*kṣaṇam*).

She draws forth, impels, and sets into motion for the sake of creation her companions—the powers of space, time, and action—as if they were her female friends (*vayasyāḥ*) or confidantes (*sakhīḥ*). || 48 ||
Having realized her own intrinsic nature, she remains even at the highest level of infinity; yet, though she is undifferentiated, she manifests form through limited means.

"Her own... || This Goddess of Consciousness (ciddevī), although having known her own nature (svabhāva) and her own form (svarūpa) and being established in the exceedingly lofty, infinite state—the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya)—remains unmanifested, heedless, and devoid of inquiry, and thus she conceives of her own form through a limited and circumscribed self. || 49 ||
As soon as that most beautiful woman had thus contemplated form,
at that very moment, visions consisting of names, numbers, and so forth, followed her.

Regarding the phrase "yadā" (when): when the supreme beloved goddess has thus contemplated form as being limited, at that very moment, the visions—consisting of names, numbers, and so forth—become attendant upon this goddess. || 50 ||

O mighty-armed one, the form of consciousness— which possesses an aspect constructed by conceptualization and which is the locus of space, time, and action— is called the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña). (51)

In order to elaborate upon the very distinctions of name, number, and so forth, he says in three and a half verses beginning with "vikalpa": vikalpasamaye 'nyatra yad rūpaṃ dṛśyate sphuṭam | tadeva rūpaṃ bhavati svapne vyāmohajālake || 1 || At the time of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), whatever form is clearly perceived elsewhere, that very same form appears in the dream-state, which is a web of delusion. || 1 || svapnānte caiva yadrūpaṃ dṛśyate bhrāntisaṃbhave | tadeva rūpaṃ bhavati jāgraddaśāsu sarvadā || 2 || And whatever form is seen at the end of a dream when delusion has arisen, that very same form occurs at all times during the waking state. || 2 || jāgraddaśāsu yadrūpaṃ dṛśyate viṣayātmakam | tadeva rūpaṃ bhavati maraṇānte sukhāvaham || 3 || Whatever form consisting of sense-objects is perceived during the waking state, that very same form becomes the bringer of bliss at the end of death. || 3 || maraṇānte ca yadrūpaṃ dṛśyate mokṣasādhane | tadeva rūpaṃ bhavati nirvāṇe paramārthataḥ || 4 || And whatever form is seen at the end of death in the means of attaining liberation, that very same form exists in *nirvāṇa* from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). || 4 || Thus, by means of these four verses, he has shown the identity of form across the various states. Now, in order to show the identity of number, he says: ekasaṃkhyāprabhedena yathā saṃkhyā pravartate | tathā saṃkhyāpravṛttiṃ tu vakṣye 'haṃ śṛṇu sāmpratam || 5 || Just as number proceeds through the distinction of the number one, so too I shall now explain the operation of number; listen! || 5 || dvayasaṃkhyāprabhedena trisaṃkhyā ca pravartate | catuḥsaṃkhyāprabhedena pañcasaṃkhyā pravartate || 6 || Through the distinction of the number two, the number three proceeds; through the distinction of the number four, the number five proceeds. || 6 || pañcasaṃkhyāprabhedena ṣaṭsaṃkhyā ca pravartate | saptasaṃkhyāprabhedena aṣṭasaṃkhyā pravartate || 7 || Through the distinction of the number five, the number six proceeds; through the distinction of the number seven, the number eight proceeds. || 7 || navasaṃkhyāprabhedena daśasaṃkhyā pravartate | daśasaṃkhyāprabhedena ekādaśa pravartate || 8 || Through the distinction of the number nine, the number ten proceeds; through the distinction of the number ten, eleven proceeds. || 8 || ekādaśaprabhedena dvādaśa ca pravartate | dvādaśaprabhedenaiva trayodaśa pravartate || 9 || Through the distinction of eleven, twelve proceeds; through the distinction of twelve, thirteen proceeds. || 9 || trayodaśaprabhedena caturdaśa pravartate | caturdaśaprabhedena pañcadaśa pravartate || 10 || Through the distinction of thirteen, fourteen proceeds; through the distinction of fourteen, fifteen proceeds. || 10 || pañcadaśaprabhedena ṣoḍaśa ca pravartate | ṣoḍaśaprabhedenaiva saptadaśa pravartate || 11 || Through the distinction of fifteen, sixteen proceeds; through the distinction of sixteen, seventeen proceeds. || 11 || saptadaśaprabhedena aṣṭādaśa pravartate | aṣṭādaśaprabhedena navadaśa pravartate || 12 || Through the distinction of seventeen, eighteen proceeds; through the distinction of eighteen, nineteen proceeds. || 12 || navadaśaprabhedena viṃśatiśca pravartate | viṃśatyā ca prabhedena ekaviṃśati pravartate || 13 || Through the distinction of nineteen, twenty proceeds; through the distinction of twenty, twenty-one proceeds. || 13 || ekaviṃśatiprabhedena dvāviṃśati pravartate | dvāviṃśatiprabhedena trayoviṃśati pravartate || 14 || Through the distinction of twenty-one, twenty-two proceeds; through the distinction of twenty-two, twenty-three proceeds. || 14 || trayoviṃśatiprabhedena caturviṃśati pravartate | caturviṃśatiprabhedena pañcaviṃśati pravartate || 15 || Through the distinction of twenty-three, twenty-four proceeds; through the distinction of twenty-four, twenty-five proceeds. || 15 || pañcaviṃśatiprabhedena ṣaḍviṃśati pravartate | ṣaḍviṃśatiprabhedena saptaviṃśati pravartate || 16 || Through the distinction of twenty-five, twenty-six proceeds; through the distinction of twenty-six, twenty-seven proceeds. || 16 || saptaviṃśatiprabhedena aṣṭāviṃśati pravartate | aṣṭāviṃśatiprabhedena navaviṃśati pravartate || 17 || Through the distinction of twenty-seven, twenty-eight proceeds; through the distinction of twenty-eight, twenty-nine proceeds. || 17 || navaviṃśatiprabhedena triṃśaccaiva pravartate | triṃśaccaiva prabhedena ekatriṃśat pravartate || 18 || Through the distinction of twenty-nine, thirty indeed proceeds; through the distinction of thirty, thirty-one proceeds. || 18 || ekatriṃśatprabhedena dvātriṃśacca pravartate | dvātriṃśatprabhedenaiva trayastriṃśat pravartate || 19 || Through the distinction of thirty-one, thirty-two proceeds; through the distinction of thirty-two, thirty-three proceeds. || 19 || trayastriṃśatprabhedena catustriṃśat pravartate | catustriṃśatprabhedena pañcatriṃśat pravartate || 20 || Through the distinction of thirty-three, thirty-four proceeds; through the distinction of thirty-four, thirty-five proceeds. || 20 || pañcatriṃśatprabhedena ṣaṭtriṃśacca pravartate | ṣaṭtriṃśatprabhedenaiva saptatriṃśat pravartate || 21 || Through the distinction of thirty-five, thirty-six proceeds; through the distinction of thirty-six, thirty-seven proceeds. || 21 || saptatriṃśatprabhedena aṣṭatriṃśat pravartate | aṣṭatriṃśatprabhedena navatriṃśat pravartate || 22 || Through the distinction of thirty-seven, thirty-eight proceeds; through the distinction of thirty-eight, thirty-nine proceeds. || 22 || navatriṃśatprabhedena catvāriṃśacca pravartate | catvāriṃśatprabhedena ekacatvāriṃśat pravartate || 23 || Through the distinction of thirty-nine, forty indeed proceeds; through the distinction of forty, forty-one proceeds. || 23 || ek

The form of consciousness (cit) which possesses a shape constructed by conceptualization (vikalpa), a shape conditioned by volition and imagination (saṃkalpa-vikalpa), and which is the locus of space, time, and action—being delimited by space, time, and so forth—is called the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña). The knower of the field is the individual soul (jīva). || 51 ||
Even while perceiving latent impressions (vāsanās), he again falls into the state of egoism (ahaṃkāra).
Egoism is the determiner; when it is stained, it is called the intellect (buddhi).

Even that *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), while fashioning and cultivating latent impressions (*vāsanā*), attains the state of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). Egoism, too, having become stained by latent impressions, becomes the determiner and the cognizer, and is called "intellect" (*buddhi*), according to the statement: "Intellect is of the nature of determination. 52. Intellect, fashioned by volitional constructs, proceeds to the locus of reflection (*manana*).
The mind, which consists of dense conceptualization, gradually attains the state of the sense organs;
the wise know that the hands, feet, and so forth constitute the body and the senses. (53)

The intellect (*buddhi*), too, being conditioned by volitions and the like, undergoes vibration as the locus of reflection. And the mind (*manas*), becoming dense with conceptualization—that is, thick with discursive thought—attains the state of the senses, namely, the nature of the external organs. The senses, moreover, are known to consist of the body made of hands and feet; the meaning is that the senses themselves are the body. (53)
Thus, indeed, the individual soul, ensnared by the rope of volitional tendencies and latent impressions, its self enveloped in a web of suffering, gradually descends to a state of degradation. (54)

"Thus" means: in the manner described, being bound by the rope of the latent impressions of volition (*saṃkalpa-vāsanā*), the individual soul (*jīva*) alone, its self enveloped by a web of suffering, gradually descends to a low state. || 54 ||
Thus, the mind, consisting of latent impressions (śakti), having attained a state of dense egoism,
enters into bondage by its own will, like a silkworm in its cocoon.

"Thus" (iti) means: in the manner previously described, the mind—which consists of the power of volition and possesses manifold powers—is consciousness itself; yet, becoming a dense egoism, it enters into bondage by its own will alone, like a silkworm. || 55 ||
(326) That which consists merely of one's own imagination and remains within the net falls into a state of supreme helplessness, like a lion bound by chains. (56)

"By itself" (sva): that very mind, having become situated within the net of the subtle elements—sound and the rest—which are conceived by itself, falls into a state of supreme helplessness, like a lion bound by chains. || 56 ||
