In some places it is called the mind (manas), in some the intellect (buddhi), in some knowledge (jñāna), and in some action (kriyā);
in some it is simply the ego (ahaṃkāra), and in some it is known as the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka). || 57 ||

The phrase "in some places" refers to the three verses [57–59]. The meaning is that this very consciousness, which has been described as possessing manifold powers, attains a state of multiplicity in the form of the mind, intellect, and so forth. || 57 || 58 || 59 ||
In some places it is called *prakṛti*, in others it is conceived as *māyā*; in some places it is declared to be *mala*, and in others it is established as *karman*.
In some places it is clearly called "bondage," in others it is explicitly called "mind" (citta);
in some places it is called "ignorance" (avidyā), and in others it is agreed upon as "desire" (icchā). || 59 ||
Just as a banyan seed contains within itself a banyan tree that is devoid of fruit, so too does this entire cycle of existence contain within it the binding snares of hope.

The phrase "imam" (this) refers to the two and a half verses that follow. Just as a banyan seed (*vaṭadhānā*) is the agent that produces a banyan tree, so too does this [seed] hold within its interior this worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), which, like the tree, creates the snares of hope and is devoid of fruit—possessing only perishable results. || 60 ||

O Rāma, rescue the mind— which is scorched by the flames of the fire of anxiety, devoured by the python of anger, struck by the waves of the ocean of desire, and has forgotten its own grandfather— just as one pulls an elephant from the mud. 61.

Uplift this mind, which is like an elephant, from the mire of worldly existence— this mind that has been consumed by the flames of anxiety, chewed and devoured by the serpent of anger, and struck down by the waves of the ocean of desire, such that it has forgotten both itself and the Grandfather (Brahmā).

O Rāma, he who does not feel compassion in his own heart for this world— which is swooning with the distress of blazing old age and death, and whose form is struck down by the spreading flow of the auspicious and inauspicious— is a demon in human form. (62)

Regarding the word *jvalat*: he in whose own mind compassion—the desire to uplift—does not arise toward one who is fainted by the blazing sorrows of old age and death, and whose form is struck down by the expansion of the auspicious and inauspicious, that is, merit and demerit; such a person, though having human form, is indeed a *rākṣasa*. || 62 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
In this way, living beings are states of consciousness, impelled by the ideation of worldly existence;
they are imagined forms of Brahman, numbering in the hundreds of thousands and even in the tens of millions.

Thus, with nine verses, the statement is made: From Brahman, accompanied by *māyā* and possessing imagined forms, like torrents of water from a mountain cascade, there arise hundreds of thousands and millions of manifestations of consciousness in the form of individual souls (*jīva*), accompanied by the worldly tendency (*bhava-bhāvanā*) or the latent impressions of transmigratory existence. 63.
Innumerable [beings] were born in the past, they are being born even now on all sides, and others will also be born, like torrents of water from a mountain spring. (64)

Innumerable beings have been born in the past, are being born even now, and will continue to be born; and they, distinguished by the sequence of their times of birth, by the relative degrees of merit and demerit, and by the diversity of their knowledge, are divided in many ways according to their status as first or last, as gods, humans, animals, and so forth, and as insentient matter. (Verses 64–68)
Some have had only one birth, some more than a hundred births;
some have had innumerable births, and some are within two or three existences.
Some were kinnaras, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas;
some were Arka, Indu, Varuṇa, Tryakṣa, Adhokṣaja, and Padmaja.
Some groups consist of Brāhmaṇas, kings, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; others subsist on meritorious medicinal herbs, leaves, fruits, roots, and insects. (67)
Some were kadamba, jambīra, śāla, tāla, and tamāla trees; others were the Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Mandara, and Meru mountains.
Some were vast reservoirs of alkaline water, curds, milk, ghee, and sugarcane juice;
some were expansive quarters of the sky, and others were rivers of great velocity.
Some dwell on high, yet they fall and spring up again;
incessantly struck by Death as if by a hand, they are like balls.
Having experienced thousands of births, some ignorant ones fall once again into the perils of saṃsāra, even after attaining discernment.
The collective meaning is that they fall into the perils of saṃsāra. || 71 ||

This ceaseless, pervasive illusion of delusion regarding the construction of the three worlds exists, perishes, and increases in vain through the currents of worldly states; it is like a wave in the ocean within the supreme state.

"Unceasingly" (avirataṃ): The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: like a wave in the ocean, Māyā—which consists of the construction of the three worlds and which deludes—exists, increases, and perishes in vain within the Supreme Abode, Brahman. || 72 || 73 || 74 ||
Rāma said:
O Brahman, tell me quickly and in detail how the individual soul (jīva), having attained the state of the mind, reached the state of Virañci, and how everything else came to pass.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O mighty-armed one, to the sequence of the assumption of a body pertaining to Brahmā;
by that very illustration, you shall understand the condition of the world. (74)
The reality of the Self, unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, assumes through its own power a body delimited by space and time, solely as a matter of sport. (75)

The two verses beginning with "dikkāla" constitute a single sentence. The reality of the Self (ātmatattva), which is the agent unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, assumes—that is, takes upon itself—a body characterized by space and time, solely as a sport (līlayā) and by virtue of its own power (svaśakti). || 75 ||
Thus, by the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), this very [consciousness], as a modification of the individual soul (jīva),
becomes the restless mind (manas), intent upon both conceptualization and non-conceptualization.

This very form, which is a modification of the living being (jīva) and denotable by the synonymous term "living being," becomes, solely through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), the fickle mind; indeed, it is only by the power of latent impressions that it becomes so. || 76 ||
At the outset, the power of the mind, as it impels [the process], instantly brings about the pure contemplation of space,
which is oriented toward the essence of the seed-syllable of sound.

"Kalayantī" means: the power (śakti) whose form is the mind (manas), being "kalayantī"—that is, deliberating—first [becomes] "ādyācchām," meaning directed toward the essence of the seed of sound (śabdabīja).

"Śabda" itself is the "seed" (bīja); the meaning is the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra). "Rasa" refers to the aesthetic flavor (bhāvanā) which has that as its object; "tad-unmukhīm" means directed toward that, or dependent upon it. The meaning is "preceded by that."

He meditates upon such a meditation on space; the meaning is that having first meditated upon the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), he subsequently meditated upon the meditation on space, because the subtle element of sound is the cause of space.
Then, having attained density through the process of dense vibration,
the mind conceives the vibration of the wind, which is oriented toward the flavor of the seed of touch.
"Then" means immediately thereafter; that mind, having attained density, through the process of dense vibration, becomes oriented toward the essence of the seed of touch (*sparśa-bīja-rasa*).
Preceded by the contemplation of the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*), it brings about the vibration of the wind—the movement of air. || 78 ||
From the friction of those two—space and air—which, by virtue of firm practice, possess the natures of sound and touch, fire is born. (79)

"From those two": by means of the friction arising from the force of firm practice with those two—space and air, whose natures are sound and touch—the mind itself is produced as fire; the meaning is that having meditated upon fire, one becomes of its form. In the reading "vaśāttataḥ," it means that from that [friction], fire is produced from the mind.
Such is the grammatical connection (anvaya). || 79 ||
The mind, having attained such qualities, experiences the subtle element of taste; in an instant it perceives the coldness of water, and from that arises the consciousness of water. (80)

Regarding "the mind": when the mind, possessing such qualities—that is, endowed with the qualities of sound, touch, and form—contemplates the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra), it gradually perceives and contemplates the coldness of water; from that contemplation, the consciousness of water arises. || 80 ||
Then, the mind, having attained such qualities, contemplates for a moment; from this arises the subtle element of smell, and from that, the perception of earth occurs. (81)

"From that": the mind, endowed with such qualities—that is, possessed of sound, touch, form, and taste—contemplates the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*). Immediately thereafter, from this contemplation, the consciousness of the earth arises. (81)
Then, enveloped by the subtle elements (tanmātras) that have become thus, he beholds his body— shaped like a spark of fire, throbbing and casting off its grossness— in the sky.

Now, regarding the word "atha": after the creation of the gross elements (*mahābhūta*), in this manner—that is, by this process—the creator beholds and contemplates a body shaped like a spark of fire, which has manifested in space (*vyoman*) through a sequence of stages; for that very reason, it has abandoned its state of *tanutā* (extreme subtlety), having been enveloped by the gross elements and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). || 82 ||
Endowed with a portion of egoism and accompanied by the seed of the intellect,
that is called the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), which is like a bee within the lotus-heart of living beings.
"I am"— thus [it is]. Endowed with the aspect of ego (ahaṃkāra-kalā), joined with the eleven organs which are portions of the ego,
accompanied by the seed of the intellect (buddhi-bīja), and associated with both the intellect and the subtle elements (tanmātra),
that manifested body has become the bee in the lotus of the heart, abiding within the white lotus of the hearts of all beings.
It is called the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka). || 83 ||
By meditating upon that radiant form with intense spiritual urgency,
the mind reaches full maturity and attains solidity, just like a bilva fruit when it is ripe.

Regarding the phrase "in that": by abiding in that city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka), through the cause of intense momentum of the mind—that is, through the connection with intense latent impressions—one fashions a radiant body; then, by the power of ripening, like a bilva fruit, it attains grossness. || 84 ||
(331) That radiance, shimmering in the stainless sky with the luster of molten gold within a crucible, then assumes a particular configuration according to its own inherent nature. (85)

The two verses beginning with "mūṣā" constitute a single syntactical unit. Now, immediately thereafter, [the light] resembling molten gold situated within a crucible— where a "crucible" (mūṣā) is a hollow earthen form fashioned for the purpose of making images and the like—
[and] which is similar to that molten gold located therein, shines forth in the pure sky as the light whose nature is the *puryaṣṭaka*.
Precisely by virtue of their own intrinsic nature. || 85 ||
Above it consists of a mass for the head, and likewise below it consists of the feet;
on the two sides is the position of the hands, and in the middle is that which has the nature of the belly.
Above, it assumes a form consisting of the head; below, one consisting of the feet; on the sides, the position of the hands; and in the middle, that which has the nature of the belly. || 86 ||
In time, having attained full development, he becomes one of stainless form,
established in intelligence, purity of being, strength, enthusiasm, discernment, and sovereignty.

"By time"—this is a sentence consisting of one and a half verses. The construction is as follows: that aforementioned *saṃniveśa* (embodiment), having attained clarity through time, becomes the Lord Brahmā—the grandfather of all the worlds—possessing a stainless body and endowed with intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest.
His "intellect" (*tad-buddhiḥ*) is the wisdom at that moment which is the cause for what ought and ought not to be done; "being" (*sattvam*) is resolve; and "power" (*balam*)...

Physical capacity; enthusiasm, which is effort according to one's own will toward supramundane tasks; specialized knowledge, which is cognition in the form of direct realization of the Lord; and sovereignty, such as *aṇimā* and the other powers—he is established and firmly rooted in these. (Verses 87–93)
That very Blessed One Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, having gazed upon his own most excellent and beautiful form, [spoke]. 88.
The Blessed One, whose vision is stainless regarding the three periods of time,
enters into reflection upon this supreme ether, which consists of the singular nature of pure consciousness.
(332) Having just been born, Brahmā, whose vision perceives the stainless Self, reflected: "In this world whose beginning and end are unseen, what was there in the beginning? (90)
Beholding all the multitudes that have passed away in great numbers,
he then remembers all the successive sequences of the qualities of every dharma.
In sport, he fashions diverse beings born of his own volition,
with their various activities and undertakings, like a city of Gandharvas.
For their sake, for the purpose of attaining heaven and liberation, and for the accomplishment of dharma, desire, and wealth,
he composed infinite and diverse scriptures.
O Rāma, this very creation has thus attained stability within this world-process,
like the beauty of flowers from the mind of Brahmā in the form of Virañci, as if from the springtime.
"Creation" (sṛṣṭi) means in the world of emanation; "creation" refers to the phenomenal universe being brought forth. 94 || 95 || 96 || 97 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
All gods, asuras, humans, and immortals are created by one's own volition;
upon the cessation of that volition, they are extinguished like a lamp without oil.
O one of great intelligence, behold the entire world as being like space, manifested solely through the expansion of conceptual construction, like a very long dream that has arisen. (96)
Nothing whatsoever is ever born or dies from the perspective of ultimate reality, O wise one; rather, everything that exists is merely illusory.
Abandon this treasury of the serpents of desire, this ostentation of saṃsāra;
knowing it to be unreal, do not fix your heart upon it. 98.
"Treasure chest"—do not place your affection here; do not fix your heart or intent upon this ostentatious display of worldly existence (saṃsāra). || 98 ||
Whether for the sake of a city of Gandharvas—whether it be adorned or ruined—or by means of sons and so forth who are but portions of ignorance, what sequence of pleasure and pain can there be? (99)

Regarding the term *gandharva*: just as there is neither pleasure nor pain when the object denoted by the word "city of the Gandharvas" is either embellished or destroyed, so too there is no sequence of pleasure or pain regarding sons and other such things imagined through ignorance. 99 || 100 || 1 || 2 || 3 (p.
Suffering is appropriate for one who does not strive when wealth, wife, and elders are present;
but when delusion and illusion have grown old, who here would undergo such exertion? (100)
By those very objects of enjoyment which, when increased, give rise to passion in the fool, it is by those same objects that detachment arises in the wise man. (1)
Therefore, O Raghava, you who know the truth and abide in worldly affairs,
disregard what is lost as lost, and accept what is gained as gained.
Not desiring future enjoyments and experiencing those that have arrived without artifice—this is the characteristic of a wise person. (3)
For one whose attachment in the form of the thought "this is mine" has ceased with respect to all things,
unreal ignorance does not embrace that omniscient one.
Regarding the phrase "of whom": for him in whom the attachment that "this might be" toward all things has ceased, that unreal ignorance does not embrace nor obscure him—the omniscient one. 4.
Having grasped with the intellect that pure state which lies between existence and non-existence, do not grasp at the visible world— both external and internal— and do not abandon it either.
"Pure," it is said. Having taken hold with the intellect of that pure, stainless state—the middle between existence and non-existence, which are cause and effect;

the middle between consciousness and its objects, which consists of both cause and effect—that reality whose nature is pure consciousness alone, do not grasp at the visible world with its exterior and interior, nor abandon it. The meaning is: remain indifferent to it. || 5 ||
For the wise man who stands engaged in action, neither desire nor aversion exists;
his discernment is not smeared by it, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.

Regarding the phrase "of whom": for the wise man who is established in knowledge—that is, one who abides in the state of necessarily performing his duty—desire does not arise toward sense objects because they are not seen as means to what is desired; nor does aversion arise, because he lacks the cognition that they are means to what is undesired. His wisdom is not smeared by joy, sorrow, and the like, nor does it become attached to them, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by waters. || 6 ||
p.
334) O Rāghava, if that splendor of the senses and their objects does not please your heart, then you have realized true knowledge and have crossed over the ocean of worldly existence. || 7 ||
Regarding the word "yad": it means "svadate," which signifies performing the act of tasting. || 7 ||
O Rāma, by means of supreme wisdom, separate the mind from the multitude of latent impressions for the sake of the highest state, just as one extracts noble fragrance from a flower.

"Highly" (uccaiḥ) means: for the sake of the high state, which is liberation (kaivalya), one should extract the mind from the web of latent impressions (vāsanājāla) by means of wisdom (prajñā)—that is, by the excellence of wisdom; such is the meaning. || 8 ||
In this ocean of saṃsāra, flooded with the waters of latent impressions (vāsanā), those who have boarded the boat of wisdom have crossed over; others remain suffering.
Regarding "in saṃsāra": the sense is that as long as wisdom has not ascended [into the mind], there is never any transcendence from saṃsāra. || 9 ||
Those people who know the further and the near shore neither abandon nor desire the worldly activities arising from the world; they simply conform to everything.

"No. The meaning is as follows: those who know the "far shore" and the "near shore"—that is, those who know that *vidyā* (knowledge) is the cause for crossing to the far shore of the ocean of *saṃsāra*, and that *avidyā* (ignorance) is the near shore which is the cause of *saṃsāra*. 110 || 11 || 12 || 13 ||
They do not despond even in the midst of emptiness; they frequent the celestial gardens;
and like the suns, these great beings do not abandon their destined course.
Vālmīki said:
Thus, by the pure speech of the sage whose intention was pure, Rāma appeared as if fully nourished;
having been considered through that sweet nectar of knowledge, he attained a coolness like that of the full moon.
Rāma said:
Tell me, is creation of a single kind, or is it manifold? By knowing that, the nature of Māyā will become very clear. (13)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Sometimes the creations belong to Śarva, sometimes they arise from the lotus-born [Brahmā],
sometimes they belong to Viṣṇu, and sometimes they are fashioned by the sages.

With six and a half verses beginning with "kadācit," he demonstrates the lack of fixed order in the process of creation (*sṛṣṭikrama*). Among these, he states the lack of fixed order regarding the creator with the word "kadācit" (sometimes). "Śārvyaḥ" means those related to Śiva;
"padmajodbhavāḥ" means those born from Brahmā; "vaiṣṇavyaḥ" means those arisen from Viṣṇu; and "muninirmitāḥ" (created by sages) refers to those created at other times. 14
Sometimes he is born from a lotus as Brahmā; sometimes he is born from the waters;
sometimes he is born from an egg; and sometimes he is born from the sky.
He states in the fifteenth [verse] that even the place of manifestation is not fixed.
At one time, at the beginning of creation, the earth was densely crowded with trees;
in some places it was packed with men, and in others it was covered by mountains.
He states in verses sixteen and seventeen that even the intrinsic nature of the earth is not fixed.
At one time the earth was made of clay, at another it was made of stone;
at one time it was made of gold, and at another it became composed of flesh.
Sometimes it first attains stability in space;
sometimes first in earth, sometimes first in water;
sometimes first in fire, and sometimes first in wind. (18)
He states, with the eighteenth verse along with its half, that even the temporal sequence of ether and the other elements is indefinite.
This origin has been told by me for the sake of illustration regarding the creation of myself alone as the Prajāpati; however, this is not a universal rule that applies everywhere. (19)
The distinction is that the nineteenth [verse] concludes the previously stated lack of restriction. || 19 ||
Again there is the Kṛta age, again the Tretā, again the Dvāpara, and the Kali;
all this occurs again and again, but that which is not [of this nature] does not exist there. (120)

"Again" (punar) means that all four ages (*yuga*) revolve again and again. In this way, all of this indeed revolves repeatedly. However, there is no such thing as an immutable, eternal entity (*kūṭastha-nitya-vastu*) that remains exactly as it is even at other times. 120 || 21 || 22 || 23 || 24 || 25 || 26 || 27 || 28 ||
O Rāma, listen as I describe the narrative of Dāśūra, which is told by way of illustrating the true nature of the world's illusion (māyā). 21.
On this surface of the earth, there is a great and glorious region known as Māgadha, famous for its trees bearing variegated blossoms.
Its forests were filled with the sounds of cranes spreading through the kadamba groves;
it was enchanting with every wonder, due to the flocks of various birds. || 23 ||
There, on a certain mountain slope thick with *karṇikāra* trees,
it shone with dense groves of plantains and clusters of *nīpa* shrubs.
There was a certain sage named Dāśūra, whose soul was supremely devoted to dharma and who possessed great ascetic power, endowed with the practice of intense penance.
His father was indeed known as Śaraloma;
like a second Brahmā to Rāma, he dwelt upon that very mountain.
He had an only son named Kaca, who was like the preceptor of the gods;
together with that son, he spent his life in the forest.
Then, having eaten only śaraloma, he passed through many ages;
casting off his body, he went to the abode of the gods, like a bird abandoning its nest.
In that very forest, Dāśūra alone wept piteously,
like a kurara bird whose father has been snatched away by fate.
His heart was tormented by grief due to his separation from his mother and father. || 29 ||
"Ten" means one whose father has been removed by the "ten. The "ten" refers to the final stage of the period of life; he is one whose father has been removed by that [stage].
A *kurara* is a specific type of bird named *utkrośa*. 29 || 130 || 31 || 32 || 33 || 34 ||
Then that boy, dejected in spirit, surely fell into a state of withering like a lotus in the winter,
as he was left in the forest by the forest deity.
O Rāma, O highly wise son of a seer, having been thus consoled by her whose body was invisible, she said: "Why do you weep like one who is ignorant? (31)
Why do you not understand the flickering nature of saṃsāra?
O virtuous one, the condition of saṃsāra is always thus, ever-fickle. (32)
One is born, one lives, and afterwards one inevitably perishes;
therefore, do not indulge in useless despondency over the death of your father. (33)
"The setting of one who has been born is inevitable, like that of the sun"—hearing these bodiless words, his eyes became bloodshot with rage. (34)
Śikhaṇḍin regained his composure as if from a peacock at the sound of thunder;
rising and performing the necessary duties that followed, he, out of reverence for his father,
resolved with firm intent upon penance for the sake of the highest perfection.
"Utthāya" refers to the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika) performed for one who has passed away. 35.
Through his brahminical deeds while practicing austerities in the forest,
he attained the status of a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya) characterized by infinite resolve.

"By means of the Brāhma [state]" means: it consists of infinite volitions (*saṃkalpa*). For the sake of asceticism (*tapas*), there must be such a pure state; and there must be such purifying means (*sādhana*)—thus it is abundant with infinite volitions.
"Being a *śrotriya*" means being learned in the Vedas (*chāndasa*). 36–49.
(338) But because of his state as a true śrotriya— one whose intellect seeks to know what is yet unknown—
his mind found no rest even upon the pure surface of the earth. (37)
Seeing all this entire surface of the earth as utterly impure, though it was in fact perfectly pure, he indeed found no delight anywhere at all.
Then, by means of mere volition and with the mind of volition alone, he [perceived] that very tip of the tree to be perfectly pure; "In this place, my staying is appropriate. (39)
Now, performing fierce austerities among the trees,
he attains a state like that of a bird, dwelling upon the branches and the leaves.
Having reflected thus, he kindled an exceedingly brilliant fire and offered as an oblation the flesh he had cut from the surface of his own shoulder.
Now, let not the entire throats of the host of gods be reduced to ashes by the Brahmin’s flesh held in my mouth. (42)
Having reflected thus, the seven-rayed Lord of that deity appeared before him,
blazing like the sun, as if he were the Sun himself appearing before the Lord of Speech.
He spoke these words, which were most pleasing to the young brahmin:
"O virtuous one, accept this excellent boon offered by me, like a fine jewel placed within a casket. (44)
Having honored that god, who was adorned with half-applied flowers, with words of praise after he had spoken thus, the young brahmin said:
O Blessed One, because I do not attain the sanctifying circle of the earth that was once filled with beings, may my station be upon the tops of trees. (46)
When the son of the sage had spoken thus, the Lord Śikhin (Agni), the mouth of all the gods, said,
"So be it for you," and vanished from sight.
When that god had vanished in an instant like a twilight cloud,
there appeared [the mountain] situated in the midst of the forest, kissing the circle of the clouds. (48)
The best of the twice-born ascended the kadamba tree, which acted as a pillar supporting heaven and earth; there, upon the tip of a sprout on a branch reaching toward the sky, he took his place.
Free from all doubt and established in one-pointed ascetic practice, he entered [the hermitage];
then, having sat down there upon a soft seat of tender leaves.
For a moment, out of playful curiosity, he gazed at the quarters of the sky,
which were beautiful with rivers as their single strings of pearls and the great mountains as the buds of their breasts.
With hair as dark as the stainless sky and locks like shimmering blue clouds,
they stood for a moment in that bower of creepers, gazing toward the quarters of the horizon.
Having firmly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), with the self withdrawn from the directions, he remained engaged in mere ritual action, not knowing the supreme reality. || 53 ||
With a mind characterized by stinginess regarding the sacrificial fee, he performed the sacrifice;
there, for ten years, he worshipped the gods through his mind alone.

When his expansive mind had attained purity over time through sacrifices such as those involving cows, horses, humans, and other animals, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), [he beheld the Lord].
By the power of his own serene confidence, he forcibly descended into inner knowledge;
then, with his veils shattered and the impurity of latent impressions dissolved,
he once beheld her standing before him within that creeper.
The sage spoke to that forest goddess of faultless limbs and large eyes, who was dressed in garments of swaying flowers and whose face was cast down in modesty.
"Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, who agitates the God of Love with your splendor?"—
when this was said, Gaurī, the deer-eyed one with full breasts, [replied]. (58)
The charming sage spoke these words in sweet syllables:
"Whatever things there are on the surface of the earth that are difficult to obtain and desired," (59)
Those various [objects] are quickly obtained only through the requests of the great;
here, in this place filled with trees and adorned by your *kadamba* grove, (I shall dwell). 160.
O Brahmin, in the forest that is the abode of the playful charms of Lakṣmī, there was a forest deity who,
on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra during the festival of Smara, [acted].
A gathering of forest goddesses took place in the Nandana grove;
there, O Lord, I went to that assembly of the beauties of the three worlds.
There, at the festival of love, I saw all my friends accompanied by their sons;
because I was childless, I was therefore deeply distressed. (63)
While you, the great wish-granting tree for the caravan of all seekers, stand here, how indeed can I, like one who is orphaned and childless, truly grieve? (64)
"Give me a son, O Blessed One; otherwise, I shall offer my body here as an oblation into the fire for the sake of quelling the burning pain caused by the loss of a son. (65)
Having spoken thus to that slender woman, the preeminent sage smiled and,
filled with compassion and love, gave her the flower held in his hand.
"Go, O slender-limbed one with eyes free of impurity; in one month you shall give birth to a lovely son, just as a fine creeper brings forth its flower. (67)
However, that son who was requested by you through a stratagem involving the onset of death—he shall not possess the knowledge attained with such great difficulty. (68)
Having spoken thus to the slender woman, whose countenance was bright with joy, the sage dismissed her as she made this request: "I shall perform service for you. (69)
"Thus" (iti) means: she whose speech was uttered in the form of a prayer, that is, spoken as a supplication. 69 || 170 || 71 || 72 || 73 ||
She went to her own abode, and the sage, intent on his own purpose,
passed the time in due order, marked by the seasons and the years.
Then, after a long time, that very same lotus-eyed woman approached the sage, bringing with her a son who was twelve years old.
Having bowed and sat down before the sage, she whose face was like the moon spoke with gentle words, like a female bee to a mango tree.
"O Blessed One, this is that son of ours, the prince who is worthy;
indeed, I have made him proficient in all the arts. (73)
O Lord, he has attained only this much auspicious knowledge;
therefore, he is helplessly tormented within this machine of saṃsāra.
"O Lord, you alone must now compassionately instruct me in this knowledge.
To her who was speaking thus, that sage said, "O weak woman, [this is] my disciple, my son. (75)
"Establish him right here," she said, and dismissed her;
once she had gone, he [acted] by virtue of his status as his father's pupil.
The wise one remained self-restrained before him, like Aruṇa before the sun;
and then, he [the king] [expounded] the knowledge to be attained for that purpose through various eloquent expressions. (77)
For a long time, that sage instructed his son there with hundreds of stories and narratives, using examples drawn from both empirical experience and philosophical insight.
The phrase "for that purpose" refers to two and a half verses as a single syntactical unit. [He taught] by means of hundreds of *ākhyāyikās* and *ākhyānas*.
An *ākhyāyikā* is a narrative whose subject matter has been perceived through direct observation; an *ākhyāna* is a narrative concerning events that occurred out of one's sight.
[These were taught] by means of those fabricated according to [his own] views—that is, fashioned from his own knowledge. (Verses 78, 79, 80, 81, 82)

Likewise, through accounts from the Itihāsas, and through the certainties of the Vedas and Vedāntas, one should [teach] constantly and in detail, according to the proper sequence, with a manner that causes no agitation. (79)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Once in the past, having become invisible, I went through the path of the sky by means of that noble path to bathe in the river flowing from Kailāsa.
Having emerged from the midst of that circle of sages into the sky,
O wise one, I reached the lofty Dāśūra tree during the night.
I heard a voice from the hollow of a bough in the forest,
like the humming of a bee dwelling within a lotus bud.
Dāśūra said:
Listen, O son of great intelligence, to this parallel account of this matter;
I shall relate to you a single, most wonderful narrative. (83)
"Listen," he says. The syntactical connection is: "I shall describe this narrative (ākhyāyikā), which is equal to—that is, similar to—the account of this matter. 83.
There is a king of great heroism, renowned throughout the three worlds, the illustrious one named Svottha, who is capable of subduing the universe. (84)

"It exists. Following his son's question, Dāśūra himself will explain this narrative, whose meaning is concealed by various names such as "arising from oneself" (svottha) and so forth. Nevertheless, something is said here regarding that [matter]. 84 || 85 || 86 || 87 || 88 || 89 ||
The instructions of whom all the leaders in every world bear upon their heads with great reverence, like a supreme crest-jewel. (85)
This great-souled one, who delights solely in daring feats and dwells in various wonders, has not been brought under control by anyone in the three worlds. (86)
(343) He whose thousands of undertakings are fully capable of bestowing both pleasure and pain—
who is able to enumerate them, any more than the waves of the ocean? (87)
The prowess of that one of great valor could not be overcome by anyone— neither by weapons nor by fires— just as the sky cannot be grasped with a fist within his abode.
Even Śakra, Upendra, and Hara do not imitate in the slightest that extensive and playful manifestation of his, which is radiant with its own creative power.
The three qualities of that mighty-armed one, capable of sustaining the directions of his body, remain pervading the world—superior, inferior, and middling. (190)

"Three" refers to the three bodies—consisting of the qualities of *sattva* and so forth—which belong to that very [Self] arisen from itself and are capable of filling the directions, meaning they have the power to pervade the quarters of space. 190.
Born within that very vast expanse of space as one possessing three bodies,
he remained right there, moving like a bird by means of the flight of sound.

Regarding the phrase "in the sky" (*vyomani*): this one, arising from itself, possesses a threefold body (*triśarīraka*), meaning he whose bodies are the three forms of *sattva* and so forth. He is born in the sky alone—that is, in the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*)—and attains his station right there. Furthermore, he is a "faller of sound" (*śabdapāta*); for "sound" (*śabda*) refers to the sky (*vyoma*) in the sense that it is "that in which sound resounds," and he falls therein like a bird. For just as a bird manifests in the sky alone...
The meaning is that it likewise remains and dissolves. || 91 ||
Right there, at the very edge of the shoreless ocean, he fashioned a city with fourteen great thoroughfares and adorned with three divisions.

"In that very place" refers to the two and a half verses [beginning with] "the city. Regarding "the city": it is within the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa), wherein the fourteen worlds themselves constitute the great thoroughfares. It is adorned with three divisions, being divided threefold by the distinction of the upper, lower, and middle worlds. || 92 ||
Abounding with groves and rows of pleasure gardens, well-situated upon playful peaks,
whitened by strings of pearls, adorned with seven ponds,
and illuminated by two inexhaustible lamps consisting of cool and warm light. (93)
It is well-supported by the pleasure-mountains such as Meru and Mandara; it is whitened by the rivers which are like strings of pearls;
it is adorned by the seven oceans which are like lotus-pools; and it is illuminated by the two lamps, the moon and the sun, which are cool and warm in nature and never-failing. || 93 ||
In that very same vast city, by that wandering king, groups of charming apartments were constructed. (94)
"In that" refers to a sentence consisting of three and a half verses. "Apavarakas" are inner chambers in the form of bodies. (94)
Some are stationed above, some below, and some in the middle;
they are covered with dark veils and adorned with nine gates.
The "black covering" refers to the hair-form grass; there are nine gates, beginning with the ears. || 95 ||
They were provided with many windows through which the wind blew incessantly;
they were illuminated by five lamps, supported by three pillars, and constructed of white wood.

The windows are the nostrils and other such apertures. The five lamps are the three pillars or supports—namely wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*)—and because they sustain the body, the white wood is the bones. (96)
By that high-souled king, through his power of illusion (māyā), were constructed streets crowded with rows of houses, soft with smooth plastering. 97.

Those whose plastering consists of clay are [the mountains]. Therein, the "plastering" (ālepa) is the outer skin; the "clay" (mṛd) is the flesh. The "streets" (pratolī) are the pathways in the form of limbs such as the arms. || 97 ||
They are protectors with great wings, yet they are constantly afraid of the light.
The "great wings" are the ego-constructions (*ahaṃkāra*). Their fear of light is due to the fact that they are to be dispelled by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). 98 || 99 || 200 ||
Then, as the throngs of inner apartments moved about, that lord of the earth engaged in various diversions, like a bird in its nests.
Possessing three bodies, he dwelt for a moment among them with those yakṣas and his little son, languid with play; then, quickly emerging again, he departed.
O child, at times a firm desire arises in that one of restless mind: "I shall go to some city yet to be constructed. (1)
"Of him" (tasya) means: the city of future emanation (*nirmāṇa*) is another future body. [Verses 1–10]. 210.
As if possessed by a spirit, he rises up with impetuosity and runs;
he reaches even that city, which is as if constructed by the Gandharvas.
O child, sometimes a desire arises in that one of unsteady mind, "I shall bring about destruction"; by that [desire], he is quickly destroyed.
It arises again swiftly, like a great wave from the water in the sky;
it expands worldly activity intensely, yet again becomes sluggish in its undertakings.
Through its own very activity, it sometimes suffers deep distress.
"I am ignorant, I am suffering"—thus he grieves;
yet at times, attaining joy, he spontaneously returns to a state of plumpness.
He drinks, he moves, he leaps, he yawns, he quivers, and he shines, assuming a radiant form; that lord of great majesty, like the lord of waters agitated by the force of the wind, is the son. (6)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, at the dead of night in Jambūdvīpa, the son of pure intent questioned his father, who was situated upon the leaf of a kadamba tree.
Who is this king renowned as Svottha, whose form is like that of his father?
Tell me truly: what is this that you have told me? (8)
Dāśūra said:
Listen, my son, as I tell this to you exactly as it is, so that you may realize the true nature of this wheel of saṃsāra. (9)
I have thus described this structure of saṃsāra, which is devoid of substance, vast in extent, and an undertaking arisen from the non-existent. (210)
The volition born from the supreme ether is said to arise from itself;
it is born by itself alone and dissolves by itself alone. (11)
This entire expansive universe exists as the very nature of that [Reality]; when it is born, the world is born, and when it is destroyed, the world perishes.
They know Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the others to be merely his limbs;
by him, this triple-world city was fashioned within the void of space.
By the mere act of following after appearances, [he reached] that which was spun out,
wherein these fourteen worlds, the repositories of light, are spread out.
Where there are rows of forests and groves, a succession of pleasure gardens, and sporting mountains such as Sahya, Mandara, and Meru; (15)
The moon and sun are lamps of coolness and heat, unharmed by fierce winds;
they possess lofty pearls in the form of waves, shimmering like the rays of the sun.
There, rivers flow, moving like strings of excellent pearls,
with waters of sugarcane juice and milk, and possessing sprouts of precious gem-stalks.
In this very world, in that city of the Lord of Resolve, there are ponds containing the Aurvānala fire and lotuses, as well as the seven great oceans.
For his own amusement, various body-cells were created;
some, named "Gīrvāṇas," were stationed in the upper [cells] alone. (19)
Certain beings, such as humans, nāgas, and others, are stationed in the middle and below;
made of flesh and clay, they move by means of the flow of the vital-force machine (prāṇayantra).
(347) Some have white bones for their timber, with smooth, unblemished surfaces from the application of oily skin;
others possess the beauty of a covering fashioned from the lush growth of hair-lichen.
They are endowed with nine principal gateways, such as the ears, eyes, and nose,
and are provided with a multitude of windows such as the ears, nose, mouth, and palate.
O Great-minded One, the streets and other parts of the body, as well as the lamps of the five sense-faculties, are constructed by means of illusion through mental construction. (23)
The great yakṣas of egoism, terrifying due to their supreme radiance, dwell within the inner chamber of the body along with the factions of great egoism. (24)
Together with those [elements] arisen from the unreal, it plays excessively within that very [body];
for a moment it rises, and for a moment it subsides, like a lamp. (25)
In the houses of the body, volition is like a wave in oceans;
even while yet to come into being, it attains the manifestation of that city.
When one perceives an object that has been mentally constructed in an instant,
it perishes quickly by itself through mere non-attention.
It never leads to infinite self-suffering nor to bliss;
rather, by means of its own existence, it expands this pervasive suffering of the world. (28)
Just as the absence of light destroys the dense twilight gloom, he weeps because of his own very actions that bring him suffering. (29)
A mere fragment of the bliss of his resolve remains in the upper throat; from that lack of mental construction (amati) arise three bodies—low, high, and middling.
Tamas, sattva, and rajas—these are known as the causes for the persistence of the world;
for volition, which is of the nature of tamas, is ever characterized by natural activity.
Falling into extreme wretchedness, it goes to the state of worms and insects;
for volition, when its nature is pure (*sattva*), is devoted to righteousness and knowledge. (32)
The state of absolute liberation (kevalībhāva) stands as if it were a sovereign empire;
for volition, which consists of passion (rajas), is characterized by worldly transaction. (33)
O Mahāmati, one who is enamored with wife and children wanders in saṃsāra; however, having abandoned these three forms, one transcends it. || 34 ||
Having abandoned all views and restrained the mind with the mind, one's volition reaches the supreme state upon the dissolution of the self. (35)
Bring about the destruction of all volitional thoughts, whether they reside within or without;
even if you perform rigorous austerities for thousands of years.
Whether situated in the netherworld, on earth, or even in heaven, that [state] is yours;
there is no other means [to attain it] than the cessation of mental constructs (saṃkalpa). 37.
Exert yourself to the utmost through human effort toward that supreme, most purifying bliss which is free from affliction, changeless, and characterized by the cessation of all volitional constructs.
O sinless one, all states of being are indeed strung upon the thread of volition;
when that thread is severed, I know not where those fragile things go. (39)
Be free from volitional constructs and devoted to worldly activity as it arises; for when volitional constructs are extinguished, consciousness indeed turns toward the inconceivable. 240.
Having attained the state of ultimate reality and having forcefully cast aside the entire web of conceptual constructions,
realize that peerless state for the sake of expansive bliss, with the activities of the mind stilled as in deep sleep.
The son said:
"O Father, O Lord, what is the nature of this volition? How does it arise?
How does it increase, and how does it perish? (42)
Dāśūra said:

They know that which is the consciousness’s orientation toward an object of cognition—the sprout of volition—belonging to the infinite reality of the Self, whose nature is the universal existence. (43)

Regarding the phrase "of the infinite": they know that very state of the infinite *ātmatattva*—which consists of the universal form of existence (*sattāsāmānya*) and is all-pervading—and of consciousness (*caitanya*), which is its own essential nature (*svarūpabhūta*), that is directed toward objects (*cetyonmukhatva*), i.e., its outward orientation (*bahirmukhatva*), which is the sprout of volition (*saṃkalpa*) in its subtle form. (43)
Having attained existence even in a slight degree, that very [intellect] gradually reaches a state of density;
filling the consciousness-principle (cittattva), it becomes firmly solidified through dullness, like a cloud.

Regarding the word *leśa*: that very sprout of volition (*saṃkalpāṅkura*), which has attained existence and acquired its own form even in a mere trace—that is, by way of a subtle portion—consisting of the state of being oriented toward consciousness and the object of consciousness, gradually fills the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*) firmly; and for the sake of insentience, for the sake of transformation into the nature of the insentient phenomenal world (*jaḍātmakaprapañca*), it attains density.

It attains a state of condensation like a cloud. The meaning is that just as a cloud, having first acquired existence in a subtle form, gradually fills the sky and reaches a state of density for the sake of coldness—that is, for the manifestation of dullness—in the same way [the mind does]. || 44 ||
The consciousness, while contemplating the object of thought as if it were distinct from itself,
attains a state of volition, just as a seed attains the state of a sprout.

"Contemplating" (bhāvayantī) means: while contemplating consciousness (cit)—the sentience of the Self—as if it were the object of cognition (cetya), visible, and as if distinct from the Self, it becomes, as it were, the state of volition (saṃkalpatā), just as a seed becomes a sprout. The meaning is that volition is the contemplation by consciousness of an object of cognition as being separate from itself. || 45 ||
For volition indeed arises by itself;
it increases spontaneously and swiftly, leading only to suffering and not to happiness. (46)
By the phrase "it comes as if," he shows that this is merely imagined through delusion and does not exist in ultimate reality; thus it is called "conceptualization" (*saṃkalpanam*).
For because conceptualization is indeed the imagining of what is non-existent, it arises by itself, appearing independently of any other cause, and it grows rapidly by its own nature alone. However—
Accompanied by conceptualization, it leads only to suffering and never to happiness; therefore, the meaning is that it must certainly be abandoned. || 46 ||
Do not form a mental construction; do not contemplate existence in its state of persistence.
By this much alone, through such a disposition, you become fit for your own well-being.

He teaches the means for its abandonment: "Mā" (Do not). Do not form a *saṃkalpa* (volitional resolve); do not set it in motion. Do not cultivate—that is, do not direct your intent or purpose toward—*bhāva* (the state of being) in the maintenance of the world (*jagatsthiti*). By this much—by a state of mind that is free from volitional resolve and devoid of concern for the maintenance of the world—you will become fit, that is, you will become worthy, for prosperity, which is to say, for liberation (*mukti*).
No further effort is required for the destruction of mental construction; indeed, this construction is overcome merely by the absence of contemplative cultivation. 48.

Regarding the resolution (*saṃkalpa*): a great effort does not suffice for the destruction of mental construction (*saṃkalpanā*). For this reason, because mental construction exists, there would be some disturbance even in the crushing of a flower from a well-arranged garland, merely by the non-existence—that is, the mere non-activation—of that very mental construction or imaginative ideation (*bhāvanā*).
It is easily accomplished merely by [the absence of] that [state], but not in the destruction of conceptual construction.

Regarding the word *sumanaḥ*: *sumanaḥ* refers to the jasmine flower (*mālatīpuṣpa*). Even upon its *āmarde*—that is, even with slight crushing—there would be some degree of *vyatikara*, meaning a small difference in effort. But in the destruction of a mere mental construction (*saṃkalpa*), there is no *vyatikara* whatsoever;
there is no difference in effort at all. Why? Because by the mere absence of that which is easily accomplished, even a task that is easy to accomplish ceases to exist.
Because volition is to be removed by equanimity alone. || 49 ||
O sage, having severed thought by means of thought itself and the mind by means of the mind itself, abide within your own self; what is so difficult in this? (250)
Regarding the phrase "by means of *saṃkalpa*": therein, the distinction is that by means of an inward-turned *saṃkalpa*, the outward-turned *saṃkalpa* is severed;
and by means of a mind cooled through the study of the scriptures, the mind scorched by anxiety is severed. || 250 ||
p.
351) Just as this sky is empty, so indeed is the world empty; for both of these are extended from conceptual constructions consisting of what is non-existent. (51)
In order to bring about the cessation of the outward-turning nature of conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*), he declares the world to be as empty as space—beginning with "yathā" (just as).

Because these two—the world and the sky—arise from a conceptual construction consisting of ignorance, being produced solely from a mental construction (*vikalpa*) composed of non-existence (*asanmaya*), they are both extended (*tate*). Therefore, the meaning is that because there is no distinction between the two in their being merely imagined (*kalpitatva*), both are empty. || 51 ||
Just as the husk of rice or the blackness of copper is destroyed by processing, O son, so too is the impurity of a person removed.

Anticipating the objection as to how an innate impurity can be removed by human effort, he provides a justification by means of an illustration, stating: "Of the rice-grain," etc. Here, just as the husk of the rice-grain is destroyed by actions such as threshing, and the blackness of copper is destroyed by washing with sour liquids, salt, and so forth, so too—
The discernment is that the destruction of the impurity consisting of ignorance occurs for the person through the activities of hearing, reflection, and so forth. || 52 || 53 ||
This [knowledge] utterly destroys even the innate impurity of the soul, just as [the husk is removed from] a grain of rice; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, be diligent. (53)
Let there be no vain delusion within you that my teacher’s splendor and your own brilliant amusements are distinct;
for you too possess those same extensive amusements, and this entire universe shines as the reality of the conscious self.

"Mine!"—let this delusion that the brilliant amusements of the great masters and their abundant wealth are "mine," that they belong to me, not arise in vain within the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa). You too are [that], and these extended amusements as well—all this is simply the reality of That (Tadātmatattva) which shines forth. 54–59.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard that conversation between the two there at night, [he said]:
"O descendant of Raghu, moon in the sky of the Raghu dynasty! (55)
Having fallen with a thud at the tip of the kadamba tree, which was thick with leaves, flowers, and fruit,
Dāśūra saw that I had arrived and offered me a respectful welcome with the arghya offering.
When the leaf-seat had been spread out, he honored us both there with the highest devotion through various conversations with one another.
That night passed away like a mere moment for the two lovers;
then, having bid farewell to Dāśūra, I went to the celestial river.
O descendant of Raghu, this story of Dāśūra has been told to you;
let it be contemplated that this entire world is indeed the story of Dāśūra. (259)
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Narrative of Dāśūra," in the section on the Means to Liberation within the *Śrī-Yogavāsiṣṭhasāra*.

Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Narrative of Dāśūra," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Vāsiṣṭhavivaraṇa* named *Saṃsārataraṇi*, composed by the venerable scholar-teacher Mummaḍideva, son of the illustrious Allālasūri, who had reached the further shore of the ocean of grammar, logic, and epistemology. || 4 ||
Fifth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Of infinite time, what portion is a hundred autumns? How can one who possesses a lifespan of merely that much duration place his trust in it? (1)

Previously, in the narrative of Dāśūra, the illusory nature (*māyikatva*) of the world's existence was explained. Now, the purport of this section on existence is set forth in brief: "Of that which is infinite... [etc. A hundred autumns means a hundred years; how small is that duration? One whose lifespan is merely that much—a hundred years—what reliance can there be [on it]?
Or what support does he take up as he runs after and pursues [it]? (1)
Having abandoned all intermediate states, O Bhāvaśrī, who consists of pure contemplation, remain as you truly are in this world and sport at your ease, O sinless one. (2)

"Antar" means: being one who takes refuge in the glory of existence—that is, the state of pure being—within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and having thus abandoned reliance on that which consists of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) or volition (*saṃkalpa*), you remain in a state of mindlessness (*nirmanaskatā*).
The meaning is: "Whoever you are, whatever form you remain as, that indeed you are; you are of that very nature. || 2 ||
Just as light proceeds from a jewel that remains without desire,
so too does this multitude of worlds proceed from the Divine by His mere existence alone.

Regarding the phrase "niricche" (in the desireless): just as light proceeds even when it remains devoid of the desire "let me proceed," so too this multitude of worlds proceeds by the mere presence of His proximity, even though the Divine Supreme Self remains desireless.
Therefore, both agency and non-agency reside in the Self.
Because it is devoid of desire, it is not an agent; yet it is an agent by virtue of its mere proximity.
O sinless one, these two natures—agency and non-agency—are found within the self;
relying upon whichever of these causes you wonderment, remain steadfast therein.
"Those two"—whatever wonder or delight you find therein, whether it be agency or non-agency—rely upon that and remain steadfast. (5-6)
By means of this firm cultivation that "I am a non-doer in all circumstances," one is not tainted even while performing actions that have fallen into the stream of worldly life.
A living being falls into a state of flavorlessness due to the lack of activity of its own mind;
therefore, by kindling the contemplation that "I am eternally a non-doer," that very equanimity known as the supreme nectar remains.

The phrase "he goes" constitutes a verse and a half. Because his own mind no longer functions, he attains an internal state of saplessness; "sap" (rasa) here refers to longing for sense-objects, and he becomes devoid of that. For that reason, through the eternally established contemplation that "I am a non-doer," only that equanimity remains, which is of the nature of supreme nectar. || 7 ||
(354) Now, O Rāma, if you desire that state [of liberation] through that [state] of being the Great Agent, thinking "I do everything," they know that too to be the highest.
"Now" (atha) means "then" (tarhi). That [great agency], namely even that egoism (ahaṃkṛti), [is abandoned]. || 8 ||
Wherever I produce this entire worldly delusion, therein exists the sequence of attachment and aversion; for it is impossible for these to belong to anyone else.

"I am [the doer]. Wherein—in which state of being the Great Agent—there arises the conceit, "I alone create this entire worldly delusion," how could attachment, aversion, and the like exist there? For it is impossible for there to be any other agent. || 9 ||
Since my body was burned by one person and cherished by another, it is simply our own undertaking; therefore, what room is there for either grief or joy? (10)

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): that my body was cherished by one [such as] mother or father, and burned by another [such as] a son, is merely the beginning of our own birth, growth, decay, and so forth—it is simply the ripening of our own karma. For this reason, what room is there for sorrow or joy? What scope is there for them? || 10 ||

When the expansion of my own pleasure and pain occurs, and when the destruction and arising of the net of the world take place, who within me would think "I am the doer"? What room is there for the sequence of sorrow and joy? (11)

"Maditi": Thinking within myself, "I alone am the agent of the destruction and arising of this web of the world—which is but the expansion and manifestation of my own pleasure and pain"—what room is there for grief or joy? (11)
When one's own volition has dissolved through the sole agency of one's own self within the playful manifestations of joy and sorrow, only equanimity remains.

He becomes weary. When one’s own agency—which exists as a single, unbroken, and true reality throughout all the play of weariness and joy—is dissolved into one's own volition (saṃkalpa) in the form of "this must be done" and so forth, then only equanimity, that is, the intellect of indifference (upekṣā-buddhi), remains. || 12 ||
That state which is equanimity toward all things and is devoted to the truth—
the mind established in that state shall no longer be subject to birth. (13)
Regarding "equanimity": That equanimity which exists toward all things is a state devoted to truth and devoted to Brahman.
A mind established in that equanimity shall not undergo birth again. (13–14)
Alternatively, O Rāghava, having abandoned everything— both the state of being the doer of all and the state of being a non-doer— and having drunk in the mind, remain firm as you truly are.
"This is I," "this is not I," "I do this," or "this is not [done by me]"—a vision consisting of such conceptualizations does not lead to contentment. (15)

"This one" refers to Yajñadatta, whereas "I am not. The meaning is that a vision consisting of the mental synthesis of distinctions—such as "I perform only this limited task, but I do not perform this other task performed by Yajñadatta and others"—is not conducive to satisfaction, that is, to the bliss of Brahman. || 15 ||

That which is the path of the Kālasūtra hell, that which is the snare of the Mahāvīci hell, and that which is the row of sword-leaf forests—all these are the state of "I" established within the body. (16)
Thus it is said: Kālasūtra, Mahāvīci, and Asipatravana are specific types of hells. || 16 ||
She should be abandoned with every effort, even when total ruin is imminent;
she must not be touched by a noble man, any more than a Pukkasi woman is touched by dog-meat. 17.
"She" refers to that conception of the body as the self. "By the fortunate one" means by the seeker of liberation. "Pukkasī" is a Caṇḍālī. || 17 ||
When that film-like layer of vision has been cast far away,
the supreme vision arises like moonlight freed from clouds;
O Rāma, by its arising, this ocean of worldly existence is crossed.
The phrase "by her" constitutes one and a half verses. By means of a film (*paṭala*), which is a disease of the eyes that obstructs vision, [one sees].
(18, p. 356) Having clearly understood within oneself: "I am not the agent, nor is this [world] me; he is [the agent]."

Having realized with certainty that "I am indeed the doer of everything" or "I am this," or having resolved that "I am someone" or "I am no one at all," remain established in your own supreme state, where the virtuous who know the path abide as the highest of all. 19.

Regarding "the agent" (*kartā*): the first contemplation (*bhāvanā*) is that "I am neither an agent nor limited. The second is "I am the agent of all and the self of all. The third is "I do not exist as anything at all characterized by agency and so forth; rather, I am simply some indescribable reality that transcends all conceptual constructs (*vikalpa*). Among these, relying on whichever one you prefer, abide in your own supreme state, wherein—
Thus stand the knowers of the path, the wise, and the virtuous. || 19 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
For bondage is indeed the bondage of latent impressions (vāsanā), while liberation is the destruction of latent impressions.
Having abandoned latent impressions, you must also abandon the very desire for liberation.
Regarding the word "bondage": abandon even the desire for liberation, because that too is a specific kind of latent impression (*vāsanā*). || 20 ||
First, having abandoned mental impressions perfumed by sense objects,
take up the stainless impressions known as the meditations on friendliness and the rest.

Regarding the phrase "mental": having first abandoned the mental impressions (*vāsanās*) perfumed by sense objects—that is, those impressions consisting of identification with them—take up the stainless impressions known as friendliness and so forth. When that is done, clarity of mind arises.
As the venerable Patañjali said: "Friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity..."
The cultivation of objects pertaining to pleasure and pain, merit and demerit, is the clarification of that mind. || 21 ||
Having completely renounced even those [external objects], and even while dealing with them,
remain inwardly possessed of the most profound peace and free from attachment, with consciousness alone as your latent impression.

"Even those" means: even while dealing with those [qualities] such as loving-kindness (maitrī) and so forth, having internally abandoned them as well, being most profoundly peaceful and free from affection, and having all desires ceased, remain as one whose latent impression is pure consciousness alone. 22.
Then, having abandoned even that [intellect] together with the mind and the faculty of discernment, remain in the remainder with firm concentration; abandon that by which you abandon. (23)

"Even that" means: having abandoned even that latent impression of pure consciousness (cinmātra-vāsanā) which is accompanied by the mind and the intellect, and having become firmly established in meditative absorption (samādhi) within the remaining form of consciousness (cidrūpa) which is entirely free from all impressions, abandon even that specific effort by which you renounce [everything else]. 23.

The forms of the mental constructs of consciousness, such as light and darkness, as well as the latent impression and the one who is impressed, are preceded by the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 24 ||

The two verses beginning with "cid" constitute a single sentence. Having abandoned—along with their roots—the conceptualization of "consciousness," "this mind," and so forth, as well as the latent impressions (vāsanā) regarding those objects, the one who possesses those impressions, and the cause of those impressions, including the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa-spandana) preceded by that vibration; and being as serene as the sky and possessing a perfectly tranquil intellect, you are that which you truly are.

"Whatever you are, you are venerable; in reality, you are exactly that"—this is the meaning. In this context: *cit* is the consciousness of one’s own nature; *manas* is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); *kalanā* is ignorance (*avidyā*); *ākāra* is the phenomenal world (*prapañca*);
*prakāśa* is light; *timira* is darkness; and by the word "etcetera," jars and other objects are included. || 24 || 25 || 26 ||

Having abandoned everything along with its very root, you who are as serene as the sky and possessed of a tranquil intellect—O one of noble understanding, may you truly become that [Reality] in essence. (25)
O Mahāmati, he who remains free from agitation, having completely renounced everything from his very heart, is liberated and is the Supreme Lord.

Whether he practices meditative concentration or performs actions—or whether he does not—such a person of supreme disposition, having cast aside all mental objects through the heart, is indeed liberated. (27)

Regarding "samādhim" (meditation): let him not practice meditation, or else let him not perform actions; or let him perform them—whosoever has cast away all longing from his heart and abandoned all regard for the visible world, he is one of supreme intent and is indeed liberated. 27.

For one whose mind is free from latent impressions (vāsanā), there is no purpose served by inaction (naiṣkarmya), nor any purpose served by ritual acts (karman), nor by meditative absorption (samādhi) or the recitation of mantras (japa). || 28 ||

Regarding the phrase "by means of inaction" (naiṣkarmyeṇa): the meaning is that for one whose mind is free from latent impressions (nirvāsana), there is no purpose whatsoever served by inaction and the like. Inaction (naiṣkarmya) is the renunciation of actions performed with desire for rewards. || 28 ||
(358) The scriptures have been sufficiently investigated and long debated among one another;
yet there is nothing superior to the silence born of the abandonment of latent impressions. (29)
"Thus it has been investigated": the scripture has been thoroughly investigated, mutually discussed in private, and contemplated by one's own intellect;
yet, apart from silence arising from the abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is no other supreme or ultimate reality. || 29 || 30 ||
Having wandered and wandered through the ten directions, everything that is to be seen has been seen;
yet only a few people perceive things as they truly are. (30)
Whatever undertakings there may be, whatever sequences of action for people, they all serve only the purpose of the body; nothing at all serves the purpose of the Self.
"Ya" means for one's own sake; that is, for the sake of one's own bondage and liberation. || 31 ||
Everywhere there are the five elements; a sixth does not exist anywhere.
Where, then, can one of steadfast intellect find delight—in the netherworld, on the earth, or in heaven? (32)
"Everywhere": the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) everywhere consists solely of the five elements. And those elements are perishable and insentient.
Therefore, where can the intellect of the wise and discerning person find delight or rest? The meaning is: you ought to find delight only in the true nature of the Self. || 32 ||
For one who conducts himself according to reason, saṃsāra is like the footprint of a cow;
but for one who has utterly abandoned reason, it is comparable to a great whirlpool in the ocean.
"By means of reasoning" (yuktyā) means by means of the great yoga consisting of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the complete Brahman. 33–34.
None of these worldly phenomena can please one who knows reality, just as the women of a wretched village cannot please a refined city man who loves a noble lady.
All the great mountain ranges are but foam upon the vast, stainless ocean of Brahman;
the splendors of the world are but a mirage within the great radiance of the sun of consciousness.

He expands [the vision]: the world-glories are like mirages shimmering within the heat and light of the Great Radiance of the Sun of Consciousness; the meaning is that all worlds are fashioned as mere play of consciousness (cid-vilāsa). || 35 ||
(359) Listen, O Rāghava, to these purifying verses concerning this very subject which were sung by Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, as his ancestors spoke them. (36)
"In this very [work]" means by the Bārhaspatya, the offspring of Bṛhaspati. || 36 || 37 || 38 || 39 ||
Once, Kaca, rising from his meditative absorption with a joyful mind, spoke these words in private, alone and with a faltering voice: || 37 ||
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? What shall I grasp? What shall I abandon?
The entire universe is filled by the Self, just as it is by the waters at the end of a great aeon. (38)
Within the body, both externally and internally, below and above, and in all directions—from here the Self and from there the Self; there is nowhere anything that is not composed of the Self.
There is nothing that does not exist where I am, and there is nothing that does not exist within me;
what else could I desire, since everything exists as consisting of consciousness? (40)

"That does not exist" means that whatever object did not exist when I was not present does not exist; for it is said, "Having created that, He entered into it," because the Self has entered into everything. And whatever object is not in me does not exist, because the entire phenomenal world is superposed upon the Self. Therefore, everything consists of consciousness; what else, then, could I desire?
Thus end the verses of Kaca. Vasiṣṭha said:
For those, O Raghava, who are established in the quality of goodness (sattva) and born with great virtues upon this earth,
are always risen and joyful, like moons in the sky.

The phrase "ye hi" (for those who) consists of five and a half verses. Those established therein are devoted to knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*). They are those who possess great qualities such as tranquility (*śama*) and the like. || 41 ||
They do not succumb to weariness even in times of adversity, just as the golden lotus does not wither at night;
they desire nothing other than their natural state and delight in the path of the virtuous.
They do not strive for, nor do they depend upon, anything other than what is naturally incumbent. || 42 ||
They never abandon their internal state of eternal fullness, which is as beautiful as the moon and remains undisturbed even in times of adversity, just as the moon does not lose its coolness. (43)
"Of the moons" is the plural form. || 43 ||
By their very appearance, they shine with the beauty of virtues such as loving-kindness;
they are equanimous, of uniform flavor, gentle, and always of righteous conduct. (44)

"By those lovely with virtues such as loving-kindness" means by those lovely with the virtues characterized by loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā). "Equal" means free from attachment and aversion. "Of equal flavor" means those whose essence (rasa) is the same, all-pervading Brahman; they are thus described. || 44 ||
Those of expansive mind remain steadfast within their boundaries like the ocean;
therefore, O mighty-armed one, pride and calamity are not seen in them. (45)
"Unobserved by calamities" means not being looked upon by calamities. || 45 || 46 || 47 ||
One should always follow this and reflect upon it when in the ocean of calamity:
"Who am I? How has this impure, expansive cycle of worldly existence come to be? (46)
One should investigate with effort together with a wise and virtuous person;
one should not plunge headlong into actions, nor should one dwell with one who is ignoble.
The destroyer of all must be beheld; death is not to be treated with levity.
Having abandoned the body, consisting of bone and flesh, along with the blood and other impurities, it is no longer beautiful. (48)

The three verses beginning with "draṣṭavya" form a single syntactical unit. "With disregard" means without respect. "The body" refers to that which consists of bone, flesh, blood, and so forth; therefore, the construction is: "having abandoned this unattractive body. || 48 ||
One should behold the thread of the pearl necklace of reality as pure consciousness alone, which is like a radiant sky that adorns the vast expanse of the firmament of consciousness. (49)
The thread of the pearl necklace of the elements is woven through all beings. (49–50)
Whether situated in the hollow of the earth or within the cavity of an insect,
whether existing in a tamasic or rajasic birth,
or even any other kind, the virtuous, by the power of their own effort, attain the state of a sattvic birth.
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Instruction," in the section on Stability within the *Mokṣopāya* of the *Yogavāsiṣṭhasāra* composed by the venerable Vālmīki.

Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Narrative of Instruction," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Vāsiṣṭhavivaraṇa* named *Saṃsārataraṇi*, composed by the learned teacher Śrī Mummaḍideva, son of the illustrious Allālasūri, who has gazed across the ocean of grammar, logic, and epistemology. || 5 ||
This fourth chapter, on Abiding, is completed.
Chapter One: The Section on Quiescence (Upaśamaprakaraṇa)
— The First Canto (Prathamaḥ Sargaḥ)
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, this long-lasting illusion of saṃsāra is perpetually maintained by men of rajasic and tamasic nature, just as a pavilion is supported by sturdy pillars.

Previously, it was stated that the mind alone is the cause for the origin and maintenance of the world. Now, this section is commenced for the purpose of its pacification. In this regard, there are ten narratives: Janaka, Puṇya-pāvana, Bali, Prahlāda, Gādhi, Uddālaka, Suraghu, Bhāsa-vilāsa, and Vītahavya.

And there is the absence of such things as traveling through the sky for one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). In that regard, he prepares the introductory framework (*pīṭhikā*) in order to introduce the account of Janaka, beginning with the words "long" (*dīrgha*), etc. [He says] "by those characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*" (*rājasatāmasaiḥ*), meaning those in whom *rajas* and *tamas* predominate. Regarding the definitions of *sattva* and the others: "Sattva is held to be light, illuminating, desirable, supporting, and mobile."

In the Sāṃkhya system, *rajas* is heavy and *tamas* is purely obstructive; in the Gītā, it is stated that *sattva* is knowledge, *tamas* is ignorance, and *rajas* is declared to be a mixture of both. (1)
By steadfast men like you, who are established in goodness and enriched by virtues,
this matured illusion is cast off with ease, just as snakes shed their skin.

Regarding the word *sattva*: those whose birth (*jāti*) or origin is established in *sattva*—meaning they are dominated by the quality of *sattva*—are "augmented by qualities" (*guṇabṛṃhitaiḥ*), that is, increased by qualities such as friendliness (*maitrī*) and so forth. [He spoke] with ease, that is, playfully. His "bark-garment" (*tvakkañcukaḥ*). || 2 || 3 ||
All this is indeed Brahman; this entire extended universe is the Self.
O sinless one, abandon the delusion that "I am one" and "this is another."
O Rāma, within that eternal, dense mass of Brahman, no conceptual constructions arise; just as in the ocean, various forms of division are not truly real.

Regarding the word "tataḥ": when Brahman has become a solid mass (*ghanībhūta*), the "divisions" (*vicchittayaḥ*)—that is, the arrangements of distinctions such as waves and so forth—are "consisting of Being" (*sanmayāḥ*). They are "consisting of Being" because they are *sat* (Being), meaning ultimately real, and they are *mayaḥ*, meaning "dispersions" (*vikṣepāḥ*). [The root] *ḍu miñ* means "to cast. Otherwise, because the suffix *mayaṭ* is marked with *ṭi*, it would have to be *sanmayyaḥ*. || 4 ||
There is no sorrow, there is no delusion, there is no birth, and there is no one who is born.
That which exists here is indeed that alone; be free from the fever of anxiety, O Rāghava. (5)
"No. Here, whatever exists and whatever is the reality of pure consciousness that exists in the ultimate sense—that alone exists; that alone is perceived as being.
Therefore, become free from fever, that is, free from the threefold affliction. || 5 ||
Free from dualities, ever established in purity, devoid of acquisition and preservation, self-possessed, without a second, free from sorrow, and without fever— be thus, O Rāghava.

"Free from dualities": free from dualities means having emerged from the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat. "Constantly established in the quality of sattva. "Without acquisition or preservation": *yoga* is the attainment of what is desired; *kṣema* is the warding off of what is undesired; he is devoid of these. "Self-possessed": one whose mind is vigilant. "Without a second": devoid of the notion of duality. "A sorrowless self": one whose mental happiness has destroyed all subsequent grieving.
O Rāghava, be equanimous, self-abiding, firm-minded, tranquil, peaceful in spirit, silent, pure as a precious gem, and free from the fever of passion.

"Sama" means one who has become tranquil, having desisted from the path of worldly activity; one whose mind is peaceful, whose heart is stilled; a sage (*muni*) devoted to contemplation, as pure as a gem born from a mine, stainless like a choice jewel. || 7 ||
By experiencing whatever has been obtained, by not desiring anything anywhere, and by relinquishing both rejection and acceptance, become free from the fever of passion, O Raghava.
