"Yathā" means: because you experience that which has already been obtained—namely, the fruit of karma already set in motion—and because you have no desire for anything not yet obtained, be free from fever by abandoning both taking and giving. 8.
O Great-minded One, just as pure pearls enter an excellent bamboo tube, so do stainless sciences enter one whose final birth is this.
"Of whom" (yasya): the latter [term] is the final one. Beyond this, because there is no further birth, the "sciences" (vidyāḥ) are the causes of knowledge.
Nobility, amiability, friendliness, gentleness, liberation, and wisdom—these are the qualities.
They always resort to him, just as women resort to the inner apartments. || 10 ||

He states those very qualities: "nobility," and so forth. Nobility (*āryatā*) is the state of being established in the tradition of right conduct (*sadācāra*). Charm (*hṛdyatā*) is being universally esteemed.

Benevolence (*maitrī*) is compassion for all living beings. Gentleness (*saumyatā*) is inner coolness. Freedom (*muktatā*) is the state of being unattached. Wisdom (*jñatā*) is steadfastness in knowledge. (10–11)
All people desire him whose conduct is sweet with grace, just as forest deer long for the flute with its sweet resonance in the woods. (11)
This general sequence has been declared for all living beings;
now hear this other specific detail, O lotus-eyed one. (12)
"This" refers to the aforementioned sequence, the sequence of liberation, which is common and universal to all living beings.
This [sequence] is that which will be described hereafter. 12–19.
O Rāma, for those embodied beings born into this turmoil of saṃsāra, these two excellent methods are capable of leading to liberation. (13)
First, one [type of mantra] is declared to bestow perfection either gradually through practice as taught by the guru over the course of a single lifetime or even over many lifetimes. (14)
The second [type of person] quickly attains knowledge by himself alone, even though his mind is somewhat undeveloped; it is like the falling of a fruit from the sky. // 15 //
For the sake of attaining knowledge, which resembles the falling of fruit from the sky, listen here to this ancient account as I relate it to you. (16)
Vasiṣṭha said:
There was a powerful king of the Videhas named Janaka, whose noble intellect had brought all calamities to an end and caused prosperity to arise.
A wish-fulfilling tree for the multitudes of supplicants and a sun for the lotuses that are his friends,
he once went to a lovely grove during the springtime, which was radiant with the joy of intoxicated cuckoos, just as Indra goes to the Nandana garden. (18)
In that delightful grove, fragrant with the scent of *kesara* flowers, he then wandered through the thickets, his attendants remaining at a distance. (19)
Then, in a certain thicket of tamāla trees, he heard words uttered by invisible siddhas during their own conversation.
The word "atha" (now) introduces the two verses as a single syntactical unit. || 20 ||
O lotus-petal-eyed one, these songs, which consist of the meditation upon the Self, were sung by those who dwell eternally in solitude and roam the mountain caves. (21)

These verses summarize the meaning of the Gītā Upaniṣad. They are "contemplations on the Self" (gītātmabhāvanāḥ), meaning those in which the contemplation of the Self described in the Gītā—the manner of one's own internal inquiry—is contained; that is, those in which there is the contemplation and definition of the essential nature of this very Self as delineated in the Gītā. || 21 ||
We worship that vibrationless state, arising from the reality of one's own self, which is the certainty of the bliss of consciousness resulting from the union of the seer and the seen. 22.

Thereupon, the first perfected one (siddha) said: "The Seer" (*draṣṭṛ*). From the conjunction of the seer and the seen—that is, from the union or contact of the Puruṣa, the seer, with the object of sight which is dear to the vision—there arises a certainty of the bliss of cognition (*pratyayānanda-niścaya*), which is the manifestation of bliss within the cognition (*pratyaya*, i.e., the intellect). This [bliss] arises from the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). Of the Self...

We worship— that is, we contemplate— the very Self as the motionless and unmoving God, who has arisen and become manifest through the reality of the individual soul (jīva) as the nature of Brahman, consisting of such bliss.
When the mind has ceased its activity because the desired object has been attained, the bliss that arises in the Self is the bliss of Brahman.
Such is the meaning. || 22 ||
Having abandoned the seer, the seeing, and the seen, along with all latent impressions,
we worship the Self as the first manifestation of perception.

The second [teacher] says: the seer, the seeing, and the seen—the seer is the "I-maker" (ahaṃkartṛ), the self (ātman); the seeing is the functional cognition (vṛttijñāna) conditioned by the activity of the eyes and other senses; the seen is its object. Having abandoned all three of these, along with their latent impressions (vāsanā), that which is the first appearance of seeing, distinct from seeing—that is, from functional cognition—[is the Self].
We worship that Self which first appears, which shines prior to everything, and which illuminates all things by its own radiance alone. || 23 ||
We worship the Self of all luminous beings, which eternally abides between the two positions of "existence" and "non-existence," and which is the manifestation of all manifestations. (24)

The third [teacher] says: "Of the two. We worship that Self which stands between both positions—namely, "it exists" and "it does not exist"—because it possesses the nature of being (*sadrūpatva*) and because it is formless (*nirākāratva*). It is common to both positions, serving as the cause of cognition for the illumination of all lights—whether solar, lunar, or electric—as well as for the illumination of inert objects. || 24 ||
We worship our own Self, which is together with its head, established in all forms beginning with the letter *ha*, and which is incessantly uttering itself. 25.

The fourth [verse] says: "With the head" (*saśiraskam*). We worship our own Self, which exists in all forms, abiding as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) within all bodies—those of gods, humans, animals, and so forth; which is "with the head," meaning ending with the letter *sa* (the head); and which incessantly utters the *haṃsa*-mantra beginning with the letter *ha*. || 25 || 26 ||
Those who, having abandoned the Lord of the heart-temple, go to another deity,
are like those who desire a jewel after casting away the Kaustubha gem held in their own hand.
Truly, by renouncing all desires, this fruit is obtained,
whereby the very root-stalks of the poisonous creepers of longing are severed.

"By all"—by that seeker of liberation who, having completely renounced all hopes, that is, all desires concerning both this world and the next, attains this fruit which consists of the worship of the Self. By this worship of the Self, hope itself—which is like a poisonous creeper because it is the cause of torment—is cut down at its very root; that is, the continuum of ignorance, which is the root of those hopes, is severed.
It is cut. || 27 ||
That dull-witted man who, despite having understood the ultimate tastelessness of all objects,
again forms an attachment to them, is no other than a donkey.

"Even having understood... etc. A person of dull intellect (*durmati*), one of little understanding, who—even after having understood the "insipidity," that is, the lack of essence (*niḥsāratva*) due to the absence of prior existence and destruction at the beginning and end of things—still binds further *bhāvanā*, that is, latent impressions (*vāsanā*); such a man is not a non-ass; he is indeed an ass. (28, 29, 30)
Again and again, one should strike down these enemies of the senses— whether they have arisen or not— with the staff of discernment, just as Indra struck the mountains with his thunderbolt. (29)
Pressing hand against hand, grinding teeth against teeth,
and crushing limb against limb, one should first conquer one's own mind.
Through the power of tranquility, the virtuous mind attains peace and brings forth the purifying bliss of *upaśama*.
For one whose mind is thus pacified, there arises for a long time an excellent abiding in the bliss of its own true nature.
He brings about tranquility. One who desires liberation should first acquire—that is, accomplish—the pure and faultless happiness of tranquility (*upaśama*).

Then, through the power of tranquility, by virtue of the efficacy of the happiness of tranquility, the mind properly attains calmness and peace regarding the pleasures of the sense objects. And thereafter, for the person whose mind is pacified, there arises the supreme [bliss] in the happiness of its own true nature.
Stability endures for a long time. || 31 || 32 || 33 || 34 || 35 || 36 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this song uttered by the hosts of Siddhas,
the lord of the earth immediately fell into despair, like a coward at the roar of battle.
Having dismissed his entire retinue to their respective abodes,
the king entered all alone, like a lion entering a mountain.
There, beholding the movements of the world as flickering as the wings of birds eager to fly upward, he lamented thus in his distress: || 34 ||
"Alas, what misery!"—thus, amidst these miseries, I myself roll about like one stone against another upon stones out of delusion, while the fickle gaze of the world looks on. (35)
(368) Only some infinitesimal fraction of infinite time is lived by me; yet I fix my affection upon it—shame on me, of such base mind! (36)
How insignificant indeed is this kingdom of mine, lasting only as long as my life!
Why do I remain here in vain, like one whose intellect is destroyed? || 37 ||

"How much? means of what measure; that is to say, extremely small. For this reason, what is the use of this kingdom? It means there is no purpose whatsoever. "Like one whose intellect is destroyed" means as if one's understanding were lost; thus I remain in this kingdom in vain.
Whatever object there may be, whatever is delightful, and whatever is noble and unartificial—
Since that [object] does not exist here at all, upon what is this resolve of mine based?

Regarding the word "yat": whatever object in this world is real, beautiful, faultless, noble, excellent, and uncontrived or uncreated—none such exists at all. Upon what, then, is my steadfastness and love based? Upon what does it rest? 38.
Then those who stand at the pinnacle of the great fall downward within days;
alas, O mind, what kind of misplaced confidence is this in greatness? 39.
"Now," thus [it begins]. "O mind! is the address. 39 || 40 || 41 || 42 ||
Those great enjoyments of immense wealth and those virtuous, affectionate kinsmen have all come within the path of memory; while this [present moment] endures, what stability can there be? (40)
Where are the riches of kings, or where are the worlds of Brahmā? They have all passed away as mere material things; what then is this confidence of mine? (41)
Tens of millions of Brahmās have passed away, and successions of heavens have gone by; kings have departed like dust. What stability is there in my life?
If one continues to maintain attachment toward this empty delusion of a body within the nightmare of the night of saṃsāra, then let me be cursed for such instability! 43.

Regarding "saṃsāre": Saṃsāra itself is a night because it consists of darkness; therein, like a bad dream, there is a delusion in the form of the body composed of suffering. If one persists in clinging to that, then fie upon my lack of stability, fie upon my lack of self-restraint!
The meaning is: "This instability of mine is a misery. (43-44)
Days have come and gone incessantly even until this very day;
yet not a single day has been seen that possesses the nature of an indestructible, singular reality. (44)
Whatever is pleasing in the middle, at the end, or upon first sight—all that is indeed impure, defiled by destruction and filth. (45)

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): in the middle, during youth, it is the body and so forth that is charming; at the end, it is the mango fruit and so forth that is charming; and at the first encounter, it is the jasmine flower and so forth that is charming. || 45 || 46 || 47 ||
Day by day, the dull-witted person in this world encounters a condition that is ever more sinful, ever more cruel, and ever more distressing. (46)
Struck solely by ignorance in childhood, struck by women in youth, and in the remainder of life preoccupied with his wife and wealth—what can this dull-witted man ever do? 47.

Existence stands at the pinnacle of non-existence; even in what is pleasant, there is unpleasantness at its peak; and amidst pleasures, sorrows stand at their summit. To which single thing, then, should I resort? (48)
"Of the existent" (sataḥ) means of an existing entity. "On the summit" (mūrdhni) means at the limit. || 48 ||
There exist such persons for whom the closing and opening of their eyes constitute the dissolution and creation of the worlds;
what need is there even to count those like me?
"Of whom" means: of those [gods] beginning with Brahmā. "Closing and opening the eyes" refers to their sleep and awakening. (49)
Even those various prosperities, if they are approved by the mind,
are, alas, I believe to be great calamities, for they entail great undertakings.

Regarding "prosperity" (saṃpada): even various prosperities, if they are approved by the mind of one who is suffering due to the separation from a son or other such misfortunes, then they are great undertakings. I consider even those great prosperities to be great calamities, according to the maxim that "when the mind is distressed, everything is unbearable. || 50 ||
Even those various calamities, if they are approved by the mind, I consider them to be great undertakings— indeed, I deem them to be riches within the mind. (51)

Having forcibly cast out from within the false flashings of "I am this" and "this is mine," I slay my exceedingly powerful enemy, the mind, and attain tranquility; salutations to you, O Discrimination! (58) Regarding the verse beginning with "Calamities": if even diverse calamities are approved by the mind because they culminate in great prosperity, then I consider those very calamities to be all forms of success. (51-52)
It is said that saṃsāra itself is the very limit of sufferings;
how, then, can happiness be found in a body fallen within it? (52)
It is established that the mind is the root of this tree of worldly existence, which abounds with thousands of sprouts, branches, fruits, and shoots. (53)

Regarding the word *sahasra*: it refers to that which shines forth (*śālate*) by means of thousands of [elements] beginning with sprouts (*aṅkura*). In this context, the "sprouts" are passion, hatred, and so forth; the "branches" are sons and so forth; the "trunk" (*skandha*) is the body itself; the "fruits" are pleasure and pain; and the "tendrils" (*pallava*) are the causes thereof. 53, 54, 55.
I consider that to be nothing but volition; therefore, by the cessation of volition, I shall dry it up so that the tree of saṃsāra reaches its withering.
I am awakened! I am awakened! I have seen the thief within myself;
I shall slay this one named "mind" here with my mind, for I have long been slain by the mind.
For all this time, this pearl of my mind remained unpierced;
but now it has been pierced and is worthy of the string. (56)
I have been well enlightened by the wise, the virtuous, and the perfected ones;
I follow after my own Self, which is the means to supreme bliss.

"Of such extent" means this much. "Unpierced" means untrained; "pierced" means well-trained. "Quality" (guṇa) refers to qualities such as tranquility (śama) and so forth. Elsewhere, "pierced" means perforated; "quality" (guṇa) refers to the thread used for stringing. 56–57.

Having forcibly cast out from within the false manifestation that "I am this" and "this is mine," I slay the exceedingly powerful enemy, the mind; I attain tranquility. Homage to you, O Discrimination! 58.

"This one" (ayam iti): The syntactical connection is as follows: "Having forcibly cast off the pervasive untruth that flashes within through the two forms of ego-inflation—'I am this' and 'this is mine'—I shall slay the exceedingly powerful enemy, the mind. (58–60)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, Janaka became silent;
with his restless mind stilled, he was like a figure depicted in a painting. (59)
Then, having remained silent for a long time, Janaka, the sustainer of the people,
rose up and reflected with a mind endowed with tranquility.
Janaka said:
What is there to be accepted here that I should strive to accomplish?
For what conceptualization can I have regarding the stable and pure consciousness? (61)

"What is it? [The answer is: For me, who am consciousness itself—pure, stainless, stable, and of the nature of existence—what conceptualization could there be? The meaning is that nothing at all is to be conceptualized. (61) (62) (63) (64)
I do not long for what has not been attained, nor do I abandon what has been attained; I abide in my own pure Self—whatever may come to me, let that be mine.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, Janaka rose to perform his duties as they arose,
remaining unattached, just as the sun rises at the beginning of the day.
He does not connect with the future, nor does he dwell upon the past;
rather, he follows the present moment as if laughing.
O lotus-eyed Rāma, by the power of his own discernment alone, he has attained everything that is to be attained; it cannot be reached by any other means.

"By oneself" (sva): for that reason, by means of the power of one's own inquiry alone, the supreme reality—which is to be attained by every seeker of liberation without exception—has been attained; it has not been attained by any other effort, nor by any other action. || 65 || 66 || 67 || 68 || 69 || 70 || 71 ||
O Rāma, by means of one’s own beautiful intellect—that is, wisdom alone—as one’s companion, the supreme state is attained; it is certainly not attained through any other action. (66)
The very same effort that people exert in acquiring external objects should first be applied toward the increase of wisdom. (67)
One should destroy the dullness of wisdom—the boundary of all sufferings, the supreme treasury of calamities, and the seed of the trees of saṃsāra. (68)
This wisdom is a wish-fulfilling gem residing in the heart-casket of the discerning person;
like a celestial creeper, it bestows the fruit of whatever is desired.
Faults arising from the multitude of desires do not afflict the discerning man who is undeluded and wise, just as arrows do not strike one who is clad in armor.
The vast and dark cloud of ignorance, which is the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), acts as a veil over the supreme sun;
it is cast down by me through the wind of wisdom. 71.
For one who desires to attain the peerless state of a Buddha, this very intellect must first be cherished;
for surely, by the farmer who longs for fruit, the earth itself is tilled first.
Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Narrative of Janaka," in the Chapter on Quiescence within the *Śrī Mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Narrative of Janaka," in the section on Quiescence within the *Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa*, known as the *Śrī-saṃsārataraṇi*. 1.
The Second Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
When that Supreme-Non-Supreme (Parāvara) is seen, the fists of the seeds of delusion, the various views that lead to calamities, and all false views come to an end.
Previously, the pacification of Janaka’s mind was described as resulting from the accidental hearing of a perfected being’s song, like the falling of fruit from the sky.

Now, the stilling of the mind through the realization of the Self by means of recollecting many past births is set forth by way of the narrative known as "The Purifying Merit" (Puṇyapāvana). In that regard, he first teaches the means for the pacification of the mind: "Muṣṭi... (The Fist).

By such [statements] as these: "Fists" (*muṣṭayaḥ*) are hands with fingers clenched, which are the causes for sowing seeds; "sights" (*dṛṣṭayaḥ*) are the causes for seeing; "bad sights" (*kudṛṣṭayaḥ*) are delusions. Both of these two terms—*muṣṭayaḥ* and *dṛṣṭayaḥ*—should be understood as qualifiers of "bad sight" (*kudṛṣṭi*). (1) (2) (3) (4)
For one who constantly reflects within and perceives the world as flickering, the Self becomes serene of its own accord over time, just as it did for Janaka. (2)
Neither destiny, nor actions, nor wealth, nor kinsmen provide refuge for men terrified by worldly existence, except through their own effort. (3)
When this contraction of "I am this very [person]" has dissolved,
an expansion arises that pervades all worlds.
When the destruction of this night of the thought "I am this very one" has dawned,
there arises of its own accord the all-pervading, expansive self-illumination.

"This" refers to the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*) in the form "I am merely this much, limited by the body. That very [ego-sense] is "night" because it consists of darkness. When that [night] has waned and dawned, the all-pervading, expansive self-luminosity—the knowledge of the reality of the Self—fully proceeds. || 5 ||
O Rāma, know that the mind’s pursuit of what is to be acquired and its absolute avoidance of what is to be abandoned—this is bondage, and nothing else. (6)
"To be accepted" (upādeya): here, it should be understood that this distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted is from the perspective of ordinary people. || 6 ||
Do not indulge in grief regarding things to be abandoned; do not be intent on things to be accepted.
Having relinquished the views of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, remain steadfast, established in that which remains. (7)
"Me" [is the self]; "remaining in the remainder" means abiding in the vision of equality. || 7 ||
Hopelessness, fearlessness, constancy, equanimity, and knowledge;
effortlessness, actionlessness, gentleness, and freedom from conceptual construction. || 8 ||
He states the qualities that serve as signs for one who stands in right vision (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). The two verses beginning with "freedom from desire" (*nirāśatā*) constitute a single syntactical unit.

Freedom from desire (*nirāśatā*) is the cessation of craving for future objects, such as thinking, "May this be mine. Freedom from fear (*nirbhayatā*) is the cessation of one's own fear resulting from granting safety to all beings. Constancy (*nityatā*) is the state of an eternal self distinct from the body. Equanimity (*samatā*) is the vision of the Perfected One (*paripūrṇadṛṣṭi*).

Knowledge is the state of being established in wisdom. Effortlessness is the absence of engagement even toward that which is desirable. Actionlessness is the lack of concern even for that which is undesirable. Gentleness is the quality of being delightful. Non-conceptuality is one-pointedness of mind. || 8 ||
Fortitude, friendliness, contentment of mind, gentleness, and softness of speech—
these abide in the wise one who is free from what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, and who is devoid of latent impressions.
Steadfastness is the state of being unshakable. Benevolence is the disposition of friendliness toward all. Contentment of mind is satisfaction with whatever is obtained.
Gentleness is the state of having a non-harsh mind. Soft-spokenness is the quality of speaking kindly. || 9 ||
The turbid water of saṃsāra has spread forth, its net of latent impressions being the fish caught by craving; it is stretched wide by the threads of anxiety.

The two verses beginning with "gṛhīta" form a single syntactical unit. It refers to that net of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in which the fish of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) have been caught; it is spread out in the waters of *saṃsāra*—that is, in the water called worldly existence—and is extended by the very threads of anxious thoughts. || 10 ||
O dear one, cut through [this] with this sharp probe of intelligence;
having severed the web of clouds with a whirlwind, remain in the far-reaching state. 11.

Cut with the sharp probe of the intellect; having cut through the net—that is, the collection—pertaining to the clouds, as one would cut through a mass of clouds by means of a whirlwind—that is, a gale of wind—stand firm in that expanded state. This is the connection [of the verses]. 11–12.
Having severed the mind with the mind alone, as one would cut down a tree with an axe,
and having attained the state of purity, become steady this very moment. (12)
Whether standing, walking, sleeping, waking, breathing, rising,
or falling, resolve within yourself that "this world is indeed unreal" and abandon all attachment to it.
The meaning of "standing" (tiṣṭhan) and so forth with these three [verses] is: having ascertained the non-existence of the world even in all its states, abandon attachment to it.
The mind, being inherently inert by its very nature, pursues the state of consciousness, just as a cat in the forest, out of greed for meat, pursues the lord of beasts. 14.
"Mind" (manaḥ): the meaning is that [the mind] pursues the lion, which has slain the elephant, out of greed for its flesh; that is, it pursues the nature of consciousness (citsvarūpa). || 14 ||
The follower of the lion eats the meat obtained through the power of the lion’s prowess;
likewise, the mind resorts to the objects of perception obtained through the power of consciousness’s prowess. 15.

It "roars" (siṃheti). Just as even a jackal or similar animal, though itself incapable, eats meat by following a lion, so too the mind—though inherently insentient—becomes capable of grasping objects through the reflection of consciousness; this is the meaning. || 15 ||
If you take refuge in this visible world, then you possess a mind and are bound;
if you renounce this visible world, then you are without mind and possess liberation.

"Regarding the term 'the visible' (dṛśya): the very locus of the visible is the state of possessing a mind (sacittatva) and the cause of bondage. The abandonment of the visible is the state of being without a mind (acittatva) and the cause of liberation; this is the meaning. || 16 ||
Meditating that "I am not the object of knowledge," remain forever immovable within the Lord of the Heart, with a heart resembling the infinite sky.

"No. Meditating upon the indivisibility of the Self and the non-existence of the world, becoming as firm as a mountain, with a heart as stainless as the infinite sky, abide in the Lord of the Heart. 17.
Within yourself and within the world, amidst the various states of the seer and the seen, always contemplate your own self as that which is called "vision"; thus become [that). 18.

Regarding the word "ātmanaḥ" (of the self): that vision which exists within—between—the self and the world, abides in the state of either the seer or the seen; having reached the state of the seer or the state of the seen, it exists as pure consciousness alone.
Constantly contemplating your own self, whose very nature is such a vision, remain [abide] thus. 18.
Meditating constantly on that which is abandoned by the tasted and the taster, situated between the tasted and the taster, and abiding within the act of tasting— become one with the Self. (19)

He states this very same point by means of two verses in a different manner, beginning with "svādya" (the object of tasting): "The object of taste (*svādya*) is that which is to be relished, such as a drink; the taster (*svādaka*) is the one who experiences it. That reality which consists of the experience of flavor—the act of tasting itself—is situated between those two, being completely abandoned by the agent and the object, and is purely unconditioned. Meditating upon that..."
Become one with the Supreme Self. || 19 ||
Relying upon that which is itself the constant experiencer of what is experienced through passion,
and which is supportless, remain steady in the middle within the middle.

Regarding "rāge" (in passion): taking as your support that intermediate state which is the very nature of experience—devoid of support and untouched by the relationship of agent and object, and existing between the beloved and so forth who are to be experienced and enjoyed, and the one who experiences and enjoys—remain steadfast in that middle. 20.
Having severed this unmeritorious state consisting of the sense of "I" by means of the very probe of the "non-I" state,
and having cultivated one's true nature on the ground that marks the end of existence, one attains the glory of all beings who have overcome worldly becoming.

"Cutting this"— meaning, having cut through this self-conception consisting of egoism with the very probe of non-egoism, which is the realization "I am not," and having become one for whom all the power of the elements has been stilled, abide on the shore beyond the ocean of worldly existence (saṃsāra). 21–22.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, this speech of yours is indeed exceedingly profound, in that you say to me, "Do not grasp at the thirst of egoism. (22)
(377) "O Lord, if I renounce the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra),
then I shall completely abandon this configuration known as the body. (23)
"If" [is used] because, since the bondage of the body is based on conceit (ābhimānika), if one were to abandon its form, it would mean the abandonment of the body itself—this is the meaning.
When egoism (ahaṃkāra) perishes, the body indeed necessarily perishes, just as a great tree does when its root is cut by a saw. 24.
Vasiṣṭha said:

O lotus-eyed Rāma, the abandonment of all latent impressions (vāsanā) is said by the knowers of truth to be twofold by name: that which is to be meditated upon (dhyeya) and that which is to be known (jñeya). || 25 ||
"I am the owner of these objects, and they are my very life;
I am nothing without them, and indeed, they cannot exist without me. (26)
Among the two—namely, the abandonment of latent impressions regarding the object of meditation and the object of knowledge—he states the definition of the former with three verses:
"When, preceded by inquiry, one has mentally abandoned [the notion of] the body and other such objects, and it is realized that there is no connection whatsoever between them and 'I'... (26–27)
Having thus abandoned internal conviction and deliberated with the mind,
when it is cultivated that "I am not the object" and "the object is not mine," [then one attains liberation].
O Rāma, that which is truly the abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā)—performed as a mere play by one whose intellect is cooled within—that is declared to be the object of meditation. 28.

For one who performs actions with an intellect that is cooled within and free from passion and hatred, the relinquishing of latent impressions (vāsanā) is proclaimed as this very object of meditation (dhyeya). || 28 ||

Having brought about the destruction of latent impressions through an all-encompassing intellect, one who is free from the sense of "mine" abandons the body; this is to be known as the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanākṣaya). || 29 ||

He defines the second [type], the abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanātyāga*), with the words "all" (*sarvam*). That exhaustion of latent impressions which, having been accomplished by means of an all-encompassing intellect free from differentiation, causes one— being free from possessiveness (*nirmama*) and devoid of the sense of "I" and "mine" (*nirgata-ahaṃ-mamabhāva*)—
to abandon or cast off the threefold body (distinguished as gross, subtle, and causal), that is to be known as the abandonment of latent impressions.
Thus it is said. || 29 ||
He who, having effortlessly abandoned the latent impression that is the companion of egoism,
remains as one who has renounced all objects of meditation, is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 30 ||

The two types of renunciation mentioned are distinguished with respect to liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*) by means of two verses beginning with "I am" (*aham*): [verses 30, 31, and 32].

O descendant of Raghu, know that he who has abandoned rootless mental construction and reached equanimity toward latent impressions, being composed of the renunciation of all objects of knowledge, is liberated.
O Raghava, these two types of renunciation are equal and established in the state of liberation;
both have attained the nature of Brahman, and both are free from the fever of worldly distress.
He who neither rejoices nor desponds when pleasure and pain incessantly arrive in their due time is said to be liberated.
With the four verses beginning with "In calamities" (āpatsu), he describes the characteristics of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 33 ||
He for whom neither the desired nor the undesired exists within his perceptions of objects,
and who moves like one in deep sleep— he is called liberated.
Regarding views on entities, that is, regarding the perception of the desirable and the undesirable. || 34 ||
He who is not internally touched by joy, resentment, fear, anger, desire, miserliness, or false views is said to be liberated while living.
*Amarṣa* here is envy in the form of intolerance; *krodha* is the inflaming of the mind by insults from others and the like; *kāma* is longing; and *kārpaṇya* is wretchedness. || 35 ||
He who remains always awake with a mind whose mental fluctuations have been stilled as if in deep sleep,
and who is always attended by joy like the moon accompanied by its digits— he is remembered here as one who is liberated.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: that seeker of liberation remained characterized by a mind in which the fluctuations of mental states had been stilled, even during the waking state as if in deep sleep, with the fluctuations of states such as joy and dejection having ceased. || 36 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, craving arising from the latent impressions of external objects is called "bound";
craving freed from all latent impressions of objects is said to be "liberated. (37)
Regarding the word "external" (bāhya): it is produced by the latent impressions of external objects and is predominantly composed of the latent impressions of external things. || 37 ||
"O Raghava, O high-minded one, know that this internal notion, 'Let this be mine,' is craving; it is a chain and a mental construction. (38)

He states the essential nature of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) with the words "this" (*idam*). Know that craving to be a chain; and as for "mental construction" (*kalanā*), it is that very same mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) which is craving, and that itself is bondage and the cause of bondage—this is the meaning. (38, 39, 40)
Having completely renounced this [notion] regarding all things, whether they exist or do not exist, at all times, the one of great mind attains the state of supreme magnanimity. (39)

Abandoning the state of bondage and the state of liberation, as well as the conditions of pleasure and pain, and even the attachment to existence and non-existence, remain like the undisturbed great ocean.
Furthermore, O virtuous Rāma, a fourfold certainty of vast scope arises in the mind of a person who reflects. (41)
With the six verses beginning with "anyaśca," he describes the fourfold ego (ahaṃkāra). || 41 ||
"From head to foot, I am created by my mother and father"—this is the single conviction, O Rāma, which leads to bondage through the perception of what is unreal. (42)
Among those, the first is the notion "I am this very body from head to foot. || 42 ||
"I am more subtle than even the tip of a hair, transcending all existing things"—this second conviction arises in the wise for the sake of liberation. (43)
"I am beyond all and supremely subtle"—this is the second [meditation]. || 43 ||
"I am the very self of all things in the web of the world, and I alone am imperishable"—
O best of the Raghus, such is the third certainty, which leads precisely to liberation. (44)
"I am the self of all"—this is the third [meditation]. || 44 ||
This world is unreal and empty, always equal to the empty sky;
such indeed is the fourth certainty for the attainment of liberation. (45)
"I" and "the world"—all this is indeed empty; therefore, like space, I am beyond all conceptual constructions. This is the fourth [state]. || 45 ||
Of these, the first is said to be bound by craving;
the three with pure craving are clear and sport as those liberated while living. (46)

Among these, the first is for the sake of bondage alone, because it is pierced by craving (tṛṣṇā) that is fit for bondage; however, the other three, being endowed with pure craving, manifest only among those liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 46 ||
O Mahāmati, having grasped the certainty that "I alone am all this," your mind shall no longer fall back into despondency.

Regarding even the three things to be accepted, he says that the conviction "I am the Self of all" is best: "All," etc. The grammatical connection is: "He who has the conviction that 'all' and 'I' are indeed the Self. (47)
It is called emptiness, primordial nature, illusion, and the realization of Brahman;
it is also described as Śiva, the Puruṣa, the Lord, and the eternal Self. || 48 ||
To dispel the suspicion that this is a doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda), he states "It is empty" (*śūnyam*) and so forth, explaining how these terms are in some sense synonyms for the Self:
"It is empty" (*śūnyam*). In this regard, it is called "empty" because it is formless; "primordial nature" (*prakṛti*) because it is the material cause of the world;
"illusion" (*māyā*) because it is the cause of various diversifications; "Brahman" because of its expansion; and "pure consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because its nature is pure knowledge.
Because he is of auspicious form, he is Śiva; because he fulfills [all desires], he is Puruṣa; because he exercises lordship, he is Īśāna—in this way, the Self alone is eternally described. || 48 ||
Through the playful manifestation of the world by means of the emergence of duality and non-duality, it is the power consisting of the Supreme Self that expands as non-duality alone. (49)

Regarding the term *dvaita*: the state of two is *dvitā*; *dvitā* itself is *dvaita*, which is to say, duality. *Dvaita* (duality) and *advaita* (non-duality), as well as their union—by these modes, that *līlā* (divine play) consisting of the creation of the universe;

by means of that, the supreme power (*śakti*) identical with the Supreme Self, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), is indeed non-dual everywhere, being of the nature of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*).

Because its own nature (*svarūpa*) is uninterrupted, it unfolds and shines forth as non-different; the sense is that even amidst the diversity of waves and so forth, there is the unity of the ocean. In this regard, in some cases a duality between cause and effect is perceived, as for example in the statement, "a scorpion is born from cow dung. In other cases, there is non-duality, as for example, bracelets, earrings, crowns, and so forth [are produced] from gold.
In some cases there is both duality and non-duality, as in the case of curd and so forth arising from milk. 49 || 50 || 51 || 52 ||
Whether belonging to oneself or to another, in all things at all times— whether when they are lost or increased, whether in action, pleasure, or pain— do not grasp them as "mine. (50)
Taking as his object the state that transcends all, with a mind as cool as the full moon,
neither agitated nor overly elated, he does not despair within saṃsāra.
One who is impartial toward both enemy and friend, endowed with compassion and courtesy, and who always performs his duty as it arises, does not perish within saṃsāra. (52)
He neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires; freed from likes and dislikes, he does not sink in the cycle of existence. || 53 ||
No, indeed. For that seeker of liberation who does not rejoice in pleasure when it is obtained, nor approves of its means;

who feels aversion toward pain and its means when they are encountered; who does not grieve when what is desired perishes; and who does not crave for the unobtained object of desire—he, being liberated from the desirable and undesirable, from the sought and the unsought, does not sink in the cycle of worldly existence.
He is not distressed by the sufferings of birth and so forth. || 53 ||
One who speaks what is pleasing to all, who is eloquent when exhorted, and who understands the intentions of living beings, does not perish in saṃsāra. (54)

Regarding the word *sarvasya*: by nature, he is one who possesses gentle speech and speaks softly. When urged by others as to what he intends to do (*kimīhitam*), being thus questioned, he speaks only that which is desired and appropriate for everyone. The suffix *kan* here has the sense of habit (*tācchīlika*). Consequently, because the rule "na lokāvyaya... prohibits the genitive case when used with a *kṛt*-formed word, the accusative case in *abhimatam* is appropriate.
Regarding how there can be certainty concerning what is desired, he says: "And [he is] the knower of the intentions of beings.
"Intention" (āśaya) means purpose (abhiprāya). || 54 ||

O Rāghava, firmly grasping the perfect vision that delights in the relinquishing of all objects of meditation, remain established in yourself through the state of liberation while living, and wander in the world.
With six verses beginning with "pūrṇam," he describes the conduct of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*): "the abandonment of the object of meditation" (*dhyeyatyāga*).

The abandonment of the previously mentioned latent impressions (vāsanā) consisting of the ego-sense is the abandonment of the object of meditation; by means of that, one attains the "sportive," radiant, and full vision—the meaning being the vision of Brahman. || 55 ||
Internally having renounced all expectations, free from passion and devoid of latent impressions,
yet externally maintaining all conventional conduct, wander through the world, O Rāghava.
Regarding "within": hope concerns the future, attachment concerns the present, and latent impressions concern the past; [the Self] is free from these three. || 56 ||
Displaying outwardly a feigned agitation while being inwardly free from all agitation, act as an agent on the outside but a non-agent within; thus, O Raghava, move about in the world.

"Outwardly" means possessing artificial agitation, which is the imagined transformation of passion, hatred, and so forth. "Free from agitation in the heart" means being without transformation due to the absence of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*). || 57 ||
Having abandoned egoism, with a mind as tranquil as one in deep sleep, and as beautiful as the sky,
wander through the world, O Rāghava, free from the mark of blemish.

"Tyakta" (abandoned): "one by whom stains and marks have not been taken up"—that is, by whom neither stains (*kalaṅka*) nor marks (*aṅka*) have been assumed. Among these, *kalaṅkas* are defects of the mind; *aṅkas*, however, are blemishes that cause the threefold cycle [of rebirth]. || 58 ||
O Rāghava, conduct yourself in the world with noble and gentle behavior, following all proper modes of conduct, while inwardly renouncing everything.

He brings them forth: one whose conduct is gentle, whose behavior is mild, who conforms to all modes of conduct, following the conduct of everyone; that is to say, he approves of it, according to the principle: "The wise man, being disciplined, should perform all actions while remaining engaged. || 59 ||
Having taken up inner desirelessness while directing your outward conduct toward worldly desires,
wander in the world, O Rāghava, being cooled within while burning without. (60)
"Antar" means one who is intent upon external objects, whose efforts are directed toward worldly desires. || 60 ||
"This one is a kinsman, and this one is a stranger; this is I, and this is you"—O Rāma, may such false views now vanish from you. (51)

"This one," [it is said]. "This is a kinsman, but this one is a stranger; this one indeed is I, but this one is you"—may such false views, those perceptions of duality, now dissolve; may they now dissolve and perish for you who have awakened. 61.
"This one is a kinsman, this one is not"—such is the calculation of those with small minds;
but for those of noble conduct, the entire earth is indeed their family.

"This one" refers as follows: for those of small mind—those whose consciousness is fixed upon the body, which is limited and perceived by them as their own soul—the calculation occurs that "this alone is a kinsman, this is not. But for those of noble conduct—those whose character is established in the noble, great, and perfect Brahman, namely the ones steadfast in Brahman (brahmaniṣṭhā)—it is the earth itself [that is their kin].
The entire manifold of conceptual proliferation (prapañca) is one's family; the meaning is that it consists of the objects and materials for enjoyment. || 62 ||

In this world, which is filled with the agitation produced by hundreds of diverse births, the perception of "friend" and "enemy" appears only as a state of delusion; in reality, the three worlds are neither eternally friendly nor eternally hostile.

Regarding the word *vividha*: in this world, which is filled with agitation by hundreds of births in various forms such as gods, humans, and animals, and in which errors have been fashioned, the perception that "this one is a kinsman" or "that one, on the other hand, is not a kinsman," appears merely as a state of delusion; it is simply the manifestation of a state of error. However, when investigated from the standpoint of ultimate reality, even a kinsman may become a non-kinsman, and even a non-kinsman may become a kinsman.
It may be so because of the difference in births; the sense is that there is no fixed rule regarding relationships when viewed in light of the difference in births. || 63 || 64 || 65 ||
On this very point, they cite this ancient history:
the conversation between two sons of sages on the banks of the triple-pathed river (the Gaṅgā). (64)
In a certain corner of this Jambūdvīpa,
there is a mountain named Mahendra, the great crest-ornament of the forest array.
On a certain part of that delightful mountain peak, covered with jewels,
there lived one of noble intellect, a mass of asceticism whose wisdom had fully dawned.
There was a sage named Dīrghatapas, who stood as if he were the very embodiment of asceticism;
that sage had two sons, as beautiful as the moon.
He lived for a long time together with those two sons, Puṇya and Pāvana, who were like the two locks of hair of the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati).
Then, in the course of time, one of those two sons became possessed of knowledge;
O Rāghava, the elder of them was named Puṇya, and he was the most eminent in virtues.
He became like a newly blossomed lotus at the morning twilight;
having strayed far from wisdom due to folly, he stood as if upon a swing, having failed to reach a firm footing.

Regarding the term *pāvana*: the "morning lotus" refers to the lotus of the morning twilight; it is "half-awakened. [The subject] has "passed beyond" due to ignorance—that is, because of its absolute non-existence—and has thus "transcended" it. He is "one who has not attained the state," meaning one who does not abide in the state of Brahman.
Then, when time—whose causes have been grasped—has flowed on unmeasured, he abandons delight in saṃsāra, his life worn out by old age. (71)

The phrase "tataḥ" introduces a statement consisting of two verses. "In him by whom the causes of birth and so forth have been fashioned" means: in him by whom the causes of birth and so forth have been fashioned—that is, impelled. || 71 ||
The sage Dīrghatapas abandoned his body— the nest of the bird of Time—
within the dwelling of a mountain cave, just as a porter discards a burden.
The "nest of the bird of conceptualization" (kalanā-pakṣiṇī-nīḍam): conceptualization (kalanā) is the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti); that itself is the bird, and its nest is its dwelling place.
A "carrier of burdens" (vaivadhikaḥ): a *vivadha* is a carrying-pole; one who carries such is a carrier of burdens. || 72 ||

(385) He attained that passionless state, where the activity of mental construction has been stilled, which is the abode of consciousness free from objects of thought, just as the fragrance of a flower pervades the sky. 73.

"Tranquil" means that in which the commencement of mental construction (*kalanā*) has been stilled; for constructions such as volitions (*saṃkalpa*) are the causes of bondage. That state in which the onset of constructions has ceased is the abode of consciousness freed from objects of thought (*cetya*).

He attained that passionless state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), which is the very foundation of consciousness liberated from objects of thought, just as the fragrance of flowers pervades the atmosphere.

For the fragrance of the flower, having emerged from the confinement of the bud, pervades the atmosphere. (Verses 73–79) When that father had passed away, while the funeral rites were being performed, Puṇya alone remained unperturbed; though he was purifying, he experienced sorrow. (Verse 74)
With his mind struck by grief, wandering through the forest paths and disregarding all principles of right conduct, Pāvana lamented.
Then, having performed the funeral rites for his father, that most righteous and meritorious one returned to the holy forest, which was purifying yet filled with intense grief.
Puṇya said:
Why, my son, do you direct your steadfastness toward grief, which is the sole cause of blindness?
Your father, O highly wise one, has gone as the foremost among the intelligent. (77)
Since he has attained his own supreme state, known as liberation, which is his very own nature, why do you grieve for your father? (78)
O son, thousands of mothers and fathers have passed away for you, as have multitudes of sons and kinsmen, in birth after birth. (79)
O son, if parents and children are to be mourned out of affection, then why are those thousands who have passed away not mourned incessantly? (80)
In the vast desert of ignorance, this world of manifold forms flickers like water in the mirage of its own latent impressions, tossed by the shifting waves of good and evil karma. (81)

Regarding the phrase "through ignorance": Ignorance itself is a vast desert region. Within it, the water of the mirage-rays of the heat of one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—where the heat is the very heat of one's own latent impressions—is imagined as water in the form of a mirage.
This world, possessing infinite forms through waves consisting of the vibrations of the auspicious and inauspicious, manifests itself. (81–82)
This phenomenal world is spread out merely by means of one's own mental constructs, consisting as it does of the states of affection for kinsmen and friends, hatred, and delusion. (82)
One who is cultivated as a kinsman becomes a kinsman; one who is cultivated as a stranger becomes a stranger.
In this world, one's state of being is bound by one's own mental cultivation, just like the states of poison and nectar. 83.

Regarding "bandhutva" (the state of kinship): it is like the state of poison and nectar. In this context, the state consisting of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of otherness and non-otherness is like the state of poison;

however, the state consisting of the contemplation of kinship is like the state of nectar. The meaning is that one is bound by that *bhāvanā*, which is so called because it binds through contemplation (*bhāva*). || 83 ||
Since the self, being omnipresent, exists as a single unity, from where does this conceptualization arise that "this one is a kinsman" and "that one is a stranger"? (84)

Regarding "oneness": since the Self—which exists as the ultimate reality, is truly existent, and is all-pervading—is one and without a second, from where could this conceptualization arise, such as "this is a kinsman" and "that is a stranger"? (84)
"O son, investigate by yourself with your mind: 'Who am I?'—apart from this body, a mere collection of blood, flesh, and so forth, and nothing more than a cage of bones. (85)

Regarding the word "raktā" (blood): although this body is not the self because it consists of a collection of blood, flesh, and so forth, nevertheless, the meaning is that you should investigate, starting from such a body as this, by asking, "Who might I be? || 85 ||
But from the perspective of ultimate truth, there is neither you nor even I; it is only this false cognition that prances about, thinking "this is meritorious" or "this is purifying. (86)
Let this effort of investigation rest; rather, let this ultimate perspective be adopted here, as he says:

"By [the vision]" (dṛṣṭyā). When examined by the ultimate vision, which is intent upon thorough reflection, there is no entity whatsoever that is "you," nor is there any that is "I. What then? This is merely false knowledge (mithyājñāna). It is merit... [text fragment].
The meaning is that the notions "I am pure" and "you are purifying" are mere delusions, because they are constructed by false knowledge; thus it "dances" and "quivers" [in the mind]. || 86 ||
They were born as deer in many auspicious places; they were your numerous kinsmen and paths—why do you not grieve for them? (87)
"They became" means: paths related to deer. 87 || 88 || 89 || 90 || 91 || 92 || 93 ||
Upon the peaks of great mountains shrouded in massive clouds, there were many lions who were their kinsmen; do you not grieve for them as well? (88)
Then he became a monkey living in the forest in the Daśārṇa country;
in Tuṣāra he was a prince, and in Puṇḍra he was a crow living in the forest.
Among the Haihayas he was Mātaṅga, and among the Trigartas he was Gardabha;
among the Śālvas he was Saramāputra, and in the Sarala tree he was Patatrī.
In these and many other various births among living beings,
you were born previously in this Jambūdvīpa hundreds of thousands of times.
Countless fathers pass away, and countless mothers pass away,
for men wandering in this worldly existence like leaves upon a tree in the forest.
Free from existence and non-existence, devoid of old age and death—remember the Self with an undistracted mind; do not become deluded in intellect. 93.

Within the center of the heart-lotus, by means of this very son— the Self— possessing a pure nature and free from the stain of all the diseases of worldly longing, O one of great intelligence, abandon all agitation and find complete contentment within the Self.

"O all!"—the construction is as follows: having completely abandoned agitation by means of the self, that is, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is free from the stain consisting of desires for objects such as sons and wives, and which is endowed with a pure state, being possessed of a clear nature, attain contentment within the Self alone. || 94 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus awakened by that Puṇya,
Pāvana then attained enlightenment and radiance, like the surface of the earth at dawn.
"Thus" means: at dawn, the earth-surface (bhūtalam), as the agent, [attains] luminosity, that is, the state of being manifest. || 95 ||
Then both of them, having attained perfection and reached the further shore of knowledge and realization, wandered blamelessly through that forest in this manner. (96)
"Both" means those who have reached the further shore of *jñāna* and *vijñāna*; *jñāna* and *vijñāna* refer to the knowledge of Brahman that is indirect and direct, respectively. 96.
Thus, for bodies previously experienced, there have been endless births among kinsmen and relatives;
O sinless one, why should hope be grasped from them, or why should they be abandoned? (97)

"Thus. He asks his younger brother for the sake of providing an intellectual resolution as to what should be grasped from those infinite hopes born of people and kinsmen, which relate to bodies experienced in previous births—that is, bodies belonging to former lives: "In this matter, what is appropriate: the grasping of hope or its abandonment? The underlying sense is that abandonment alone is appropriate. || 97 ||
Thought increases through thinking, just as fire grows with fuel;
it perishes through non-thinking alone, like a flame without fuel. 98.
Regarding "reflection" (cintana): reflection is the inquiry as to how one's desired goal may be accomplished; it is the repeated recollection of things perceived through the senses. 98.
Mounted upon the chariot of abandoning all objects of meditation, beholding the world with a gaze noble with compassion for those in distress, remain steadfast; arise, O Rāghava! (99)
"Dhyeya" means: remain established in ease; arise and exert yourself for the sake of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 99 || 100 || 1 ||
This is the state of Brahman: self-abiding, free from desire, and devoid of affliction.
Having attained this, O mighty-armed one, even one who is deluded is no longer deluded.
Taking solitude as his only friend and mature discernment as his only companion, he wanders in this manner and is not deluded by mental constructions. (1)
For one from whom all resources have been withdrawn and whose kinsmen have been cast aside,
nothing can rescue him from this peril except his own fortitude.

"Vinivārita" means that from which all objects—that is, all worldly purposes—have been warded off; and "from whom the kinsmen have been cast aside," meaning removed by the hand. The grammatical construction is as follows: apart from one's own fortitude—that is, without one's own discernment, dispassion, and courage—one is not rescued from even the slightest distress, namely, from the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). || 2 ||
Then, through detachment, by means of the scriptures, and also by qualities such as greatness,
one should with effort uplift one's own mind for the sake of warding off calamities.
It has been stated that one's own fortitude alone delivers one from distress. Now, he describes the method for cultivating fortitude:

"By means of dispassion," etc. For the purpose of averting calamities and for the cessation of worldly existence (saṃsāra), one should by oneself uplift the mind through such means as dispassion; that is to say, one should make it endowed with fortitude. || 3 ||
Neither from sovereignty over the three worlds, nor from a treasury filled with jewels,
is that fruit obtained which is attained from the mind when it is augmented by greatness.

"No. The construction is as follows: that fruit in the form of liberation which is attained from the mind when it is augmented by greatness—that is, elevated by qualities such as greatness—is not attained even through sovereignty over the three worlds and the like. || 4 ||
When the mind is full, the entire world is filled with the flow of nectar;
indeed, for one whose feet are covered by shoes, the earth is as if carpeted with leather.
"Full" (pūrṇa) means that when the mind is full and satisfied, the entire world arises as a source of happiness, as if filled with the liquid essence of nectar. || 5 ||
Through dispassion, the mind, following the power of its own dissolution, attains fullness;
yet through desire, it becomes turbid, like the water of a lake in autumn.

Regarding how the mind attains fullness, he says: "Through detachment" (*vairāgyāt*). It is only through detachment that the mind reaches fullness; however, one who follows the dictates of desire never attains fullness. As Pārāśara has said: "Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects; rather, like a fire fed with clarified butter, it only increases all the more. (6)
The heart becomes empty, its hollow exposed,
like the ocean swallowed by Agastya for those whose minds are overwhelmed by longing for the quarters of the world. (7)
The exposure of the hollow within the heart is, in fact, the manifestation of an excess of craving. || 7 ||
Neither does the full moon shine thus, nor the full ocean of milk, nor the lovely face of Lakṣmī, as does the mind free from longing. 8.

"No," [it is said]. The meaning is that the splendor of the full moon and such things is impermanent because it is subject to waning and waxing; however, the splendor of a mind free from desire is eternal, as it is never subject to joy or dejection. || 8 ||
Just as a streak of cloud defiles the moon, or as ink defiles a plaster of nectar,
even so does the demoness of desire corrupt a man within.
Regarding the word "yathā": a streak of clouds (*abhralekhā*) is a row of clouds; a plaster of nectar (*sudhālepa*) is a coating of substances such as lime powder and the like. || 9 ||
O Great-Souled One, having cast off the bonds of existence, become one whose mind is liberated, with all desires stilled.
When the wicked hopes—the ropes that fetter the mind—have fallen away, who is not liberated? 10.

"Having attained tranquility": having pacified all desires (*eṣaṇā*), cast off the bond of worldly existence, and become one whose mind is liberated. For this reason, the base hopes (*kadāśā*)—consisting of the desire for sons, wife, and so forth—which reside in the mind, are like fetters and ropes;
they are chains that, like ropes, cause bondage. Therefore, when these have fallen away, who [would remain bound]?
He is not liberated; the meaning is that everyone is indeed liberated. || 10 ||
Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Narrative of Puṇya and Pāvana," in the Chapter on Tranquility within the *Mokṣopāya* of the venerable *Vālmīkīya*.
Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Narrative of Puṇyapāvana," in the section on Quiescence within the *Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa* named *Śrī-saṃsārataraṇi*.
The Third Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
Alternatively, O full moon of the sky known as the lineage of Raghu, may you attain pure knowledge through the discernment of the intellect, like Bali. (1)

Previously, the pacification of the mind through the knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpajñāna*) by means of recollecting many past births was described. Now, it is established through the story of Vālī that even sensual pleasure (*vaiṣayika-sukha*), when attained through the excellence of merit, may lead to the pacification of the mind. In this regard, he states with two verses beginning with "atha" that a distaste for enjoyments arises from long-term indulgence in them.
Śrī Rāma said:
O All-pervading Lord, please speak again of the attainment of knowledge like that of Bali for the further increase of my awakening; for the virtuous do not feel weary toward one who is humble.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Within this treasury of the world, in a certain corner of the quarters,
there exists a realm situated beneath the earth, renowned as Pātāla.
Upon that [throne], whose great weight was supported by the pillar-like arms of the Asuras,
there reigned as king Bali, the son of Virocana.
Having effortlessly conquered the entire expanse of the world as his sole ornament,
he ruled the kingdom of the Daityas for ten crores of years.
Then, as many ages passed away in their cyclical revolutions, amidst the great floods of gods and demons rising up and falling down; (6)
Regarding the phrase *āvartavṛttiṣu*: an *āvarta* (whirlpool) is the swirling of waters; those whose movement is like that movement are *āvartavṛttayaḥ*, and [the term refers] to them.
Although he had incessantly enjoyed all the pleasures existing within the belly of the three worlds,
Bali, the leader of the Dānavas, felt a sense of revulsion toward them.
Agitation and aversion. || 7 || 8 || 9 ||
Once, while standing upon the pinnacle of his palace, he reflected: "By means of my great kingdom, which causes wonder throughout the three worlds... (8)

What indeed is gained by this food, so heavily laden with abundant enjoyments, which is sweet only for a moment and must inevitably perish? What kind of happiness does this mere indulgence in sensory enjoyment bring me? (9)
The beloved is embraced again and enjoyed once more;
this is like the play of children, yet it brings great shame to the wise.
For the sake of modesty; the sense is that what has been left over by the great is unfit for further enjoyment. || 10 || 11 ||
Why does the wise man not feel ashamed as he performs again and again, day after day, that very same flood of activities which has become tasteless once enjoyed? (11)
Again a day, again a night, again a succession of duties;
again and again, I consider this to be the mockery of the wise man.
"Again" (punar) means: "I think that this repeated activity of those who think 'again and again' is a mockery of the wise"—this is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). || 12 ||

Even by this constant performance of ritual action, once it has been completed and its purpose achieved, what goal could there be such that no further action would ever need to be performed again? (13)

"By that which has been done" (kṛtayā): even by this action, though it has been performed and its purpose accomplished, what kind of goal could there be that is eternally achieved such that, by virtue of that goal, no further action would exist? The meaning is that there is no action whatsoever that serves as a cause for having already accomplished all that is to be done. || 13 ||
"What else could that imperishable wealth be, other than enjoyment? I shall reflect upon this quickly. Having thought thus, Bali meditated.

Regarding the phrase "from enjoyment" (*bhogāt*): having reflected upon and determined that apart from enjoyment—that is, excluding the pleasure derived from sense objects—what other indestructible substance could there be, Bali meditated; such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). || 14 ||
p.
393) Then the king of the asuras said, "Ah! It is remembered," and in an instant, knitting his brows, he fixed his mind upon the matter within his own self. (15)

"Now," [it is said]. Immediately thereafter, Bali, the king of the asuras, fixing within his own mind—the very faculty of his intellect—the matter he had contemplated, while knitting his eyebrows (a gesture indicating the focus of his deliberation), exclaimed after a moment, "Ah! It has been remembered.
The phrase "knitting his eyebrows" is a dramatic representation of the gaze of reflection; "Ah! is an indeclinable particle signifying remembrance. || 15 ||
It is said that in ancient times, the Blessed One Virocana— my father, who knew the reality of the self and had perceived the higher and lower worlds— was questioned here by me.

He restates what was previously mentioned with the words "In the beginning," and so forth. He has seen the higher and lower worlds; the "higher" (para) is the ultimate cause, and the "lower" (avara) is the initial cause. || 16 ||
O Great-minded One, tell me, what is that ultimate limit where all delusions, as well as all sufferings and pleasures, are stilled? (17)
He repeats the manner of his own question: "O Father"—"O Father, let it be told: what is that which is called the limit, the ultimate boundary, of all worldly pleasures and pains? (17)
Where has the delusion of the mind been stilled? Where have all desires passed away? Father, where is that long-lasting rest which is free from passion? (18)
He elaborates upon the very pacification of all delusions with these two verses as a single statement: "Where...
In which reality there arises a long-lasting repose, a bliss of rest, free from detachment and devoid of aversion;
in which reality my own form—exceedingly expansive, beautiful with bliss, and indescribable—is present in some way.
Tell me of such a place; staying there, I shall attain long-lasting rest—this is the syntactical connection. || 18 || 19 ||
Tell me of some place where there is that which is beautiful with exceedingly vast bliss; staying there, I shall find long-lasting rest. (19)
(p. 394) My father said:
"O sons, there is an exceedingly vast region with a wide hollow, wherein even many thousands of triple-worlds find room. (20)

He repeats his father’s reply, beginning with "My father": "Where there is no earth, nor sky, no oceans, nor mountains; no forests, no sacred fords, no rivers, and no lakes—therein the country is liberation, the king is the Self, and the minister is the mind. (21)
There is but one great king there, possessed of immense splendor;
he is the doer of all, the all-pervading, the all, and he remains established in silence.
Immediately after Bali's question, Virocana himself will speak.
The minister, directed by him, being intent upon counsel on all sides,
quickly brings about what was impossible and thoroughly dismantles what was possible.

The phrase "by him" (*tena*) constitutes two verses. By that king, he was appointed; he, having been conceived merely by the king’s desire to create—as expressed in the thought, "Let me now create the worlds"—is a minister fashioned by mere intention. He brings about all those royal affairs, even those that are difficult to accomplish (*aghaṭam*) or impossible, through deliberation and the intent to counsel. Furthermore, he renders even an already well-accomplished task undesirable.
If it causes disintegration; that is to say, it destroys. || 23 ||
He is unable to enjoy anything and knows nothing at all;
yet for the sake of the kingdom alone, he performs every act with incessant exertion. (24)

He is unable to eat anything at all, nor does he perceive anything; the sense is that this is because the mind is insentient. He alone is the sole performer of all the king's duties, while the king himself remains established in his own state, entirely alone.
Bali said:
O Mahāmati, what is that land free from mental and physical afflictions?
How is it reached, and by whom was it attained, O Lord? (26)
Who is that such-like minister, or even a king of great power,
who has not been conquered by us, even though he effortlessly cut through the nets of the world? (27)
Virocana said:
O son, that powerful minister there cannot be overcome even slightly, even by the hosts of gods and asuras combined, though they were multiplied a hundred thousand times.
There, weapons such as swords, clubs, darts, thunderbolts, discuses, and maces become blunted, like the striking of a lotus against a stone. (29)
If that minister is conquered there by that lord alone, then he is easily subdued; otherwise, however, he is as immovable as a mountain.
"O son, if he is approached with the proper method, he will come under control in an instant;
without the method, he burns like a fierce, venomous serpent. (31)
Listen, my son; I shall first reveal to you that country which, by its name as spoken by me, is liberation itself, the destroyer of all suffering. (32)
But there, O Mahāmati, the Blessed One himself, who transcends all states, became the king; by him the wise one named Manas was made his minister.
O son, regarding all sense objects in every respect,
this supreme lack of reliance is indeed the method for the conquest of the mind.
This alone is the supreme method; by this very means, the great elephant of one's own intoxicated mind is swiftly subdued. (35)
One should fill two parts of the mind with enjoyments, one part with the scriptures, and one part with service to the teacher, for one who is unlearned in the noble tradition. (36)
He describes the sequence for conquering the mind according to the distinction of practitioners in three verses, beginning with the words "of the mind" (*cittasya*).

Having divided the time for worldly activity into four parts, one who is unskilled—that is, untrained—in the practice of knowledge regarding that true sequence should first fill two parts with enjoyments, meaning with the enjoyment of sense objects; the meaning is that he should spend two portions of time in this way.
One should fulfill one part by means of the scripture—that is, the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra); and one should fulfill a fourth part through service to the teacher. || 36 ||
One who possesses some degree of proficiency should fill one part with enjoyments,
two parts with service to the guru, and one part with reflection on the meaning of the scriptures. (37)

"Something" means: one who possesses some degree of proficiency should spend one period of time in enjoyments, two periods in service to the teacher, and the fourth period in reflecting upon the meaning of the scriptures. || 37 ||
For one who follows the path of thorough understanding, he should daily fill two parts of his mind with the scriptures and dispassion, and two parts with meditation and the worship of the Guru.
Regarding the phrase "cultivation" (*vyutpatti*): for one whose mind is properly cultivated, there are two periods of worldly activity;

these two periods should be fulfilled through the scriptures and detachment—namely, by reflecting on the inner sciences and by reflecting on the objects of the senses as things to be abandoned—and also by means of the worship of the Guru accompanied by meditation. || 38 ||
O son, through the power of wisdom and discernment, one should always bring about tranquility itself, as well as the vision of the self and the complete relinquishing of craving. (39)

Regarding "wisdom" (prajñā): Thus, by means of the power of wisdom and the power of discernment, through both wisdom and discernment, one should bring about—that is, accomplish—tranquility, which is the calming of the mind; the abandonment of craving; and the perception of the self. || 39 ||
From reflection comes the censure of enjoyments, and from the censure of enjoyments comes reflection;
these two fulfill one another like the ocean and the clouds.

Regarding "vicāra" (investigation): through the censure of enjoyment—that is, by perceiving the defects in the pleasures of sense-objects—the investigation into the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) is fulfilled.
And from the investigation into the goals of human life, the censure of enjoyments is fulfilled, as they are seen to be non-ends of human life and to have base purposes;
thus, these two—investigation and the censure of enjoyment—fulfill one another. Just as the ocean is filled by the clouds through the medium of rain.
The meaning is that, in the same way, the clouds are filled from the waters of the ocean. || 40 ||

O dear one, acquire wealth through righteous means with little reproach, and first of all, win over virtuous people with honor; for by disregarding the objects of the senses arising from such association, and through the power of thorough discernment, you shall attain the realization of the Self. (41)
He teaches: "Earn wealth by means of modest reproach, minor faults, proper regional conduct, and the customs of the land.
And with that wealth, acquire the company of virtuous people with honor and respect.
Through the disregard for sense objects arising from that association—namely, through the detachment from sense objects born of the company of the virtuous—"
And by the power of right investigation, you will attain self-realization; such is the syntactical connection. || 41 ||
Bali said:
"This was previously told to me by my father, who is of beautiful discernment;
now, by good fortune, it has been remembered, and I have attained full awakening. (42)
Regarding the word "this": the grammatical connection is that "this which was previously told to me by my father has now been remembered. || 42 ||
Today, this clear aversion toward enjoyments has arisen within me;
by good fortune, I enter the bliss of tranquility, which is self-abiding and cool as nectar.
The indeclinable *diṣṭyā* is used in the sense of joy. || 43 ||
"Oh, how truly delightful is this land of tranquility, so cool within!
For in tranquility, all perceptions of pleasure and pain proceed equally. (44)
"Ah! [Thus: "The ground of peace is the state of tranquility. 44.
"Who am I? What might this 'self' be?"—desiring to behold the Self, I shall surely ask my lord Uśanas for the sake of pacifying ignorance. (45)

"Who am I? The syntactical connection is as follows: I ask the meaning of the word "I" and the nature of the self—namely, "What might this self be?"—to my teacher and lord, Uśanas, who beholds the self. || 45 || 46 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, the powerful Bali, whose eyes were half-closed,
meditated upon Śukra, the lotus-petal-eyed one whose abode is the sky.
Then the lord Bhārgava, whose self is all-pervading and infinite consciousness,
brought his own body along with that of Bali to the jeweled window. (47)
"Now," [it is said]. Then that descendant of Bhṛgu brought his own body to the jeweled window, which served as the location for Bali’s residence; the meaning is that he arrived there. (Verses 47–51)
Then, with offerings of precious gems and their value, heaps of mandāra flowers,
and by prostrating at his feet, he honored that descendant of Bhṛgu.
Bali said:
O Bhārgava, this intuition arising from your grace impels me to speak before you, just as the light of the sun impels one to perform a task. (49)
"What is here? How much is this? Or is it only this?
Who am I? Who are you? Or what are these worlds? Tell me this quickly. (50)
Śukra said:
What is the use of saying much more here? O Indra among all the lords of the Dānavas, I am striving to go to the sky; hear the essence in brief.
For here there is only consciousness; this is indeed composed of consciousness alone.
Consciousness, the state of being consciousness, I am consciousness, and these worlds are consciousness—this is the summary. (52)

"Cit" means pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), the very form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), and consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*), having consciousness as its material cause (*citprakṛtika*). The meaning is that nothing exists apart from consciousness. || 52 || 53 ||
If you are capable, then you will certainly attain all of this from this;
if not, then even though much has been spoken to you, it is like an oblation poured into ashes.
Bondage consists in being determined by the object of consciousness; liberation is said to be its freedom from that.
"The Self is indeed consciousness, devoid of objects"—this is the summary of all established doctrines. (54)

Regarding the word "cit": Consciousness (cit) itself, when unperceived as an object of thought (cetya), is called bondage; whereas consciousness alone, having abandoned the object of thought, is liberation. The summary is this: the Self is consciousness itself, which is beyond being an object of thought and untouched by objects of thought. 54–58.
Having thus adopted this certainty, behold with an illumined intellect;
you shall yourself, by means of the self, attain the state of the infinite. (55)
I am going there; these seven sages have assembled here for some mission of the gods, and I must indeed dwell there.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed Śukra ascended to the vault of the sky;
Bali, for his part, reflected that this world is composed of consciousness.
Bali said:

What was spoken by the Blessed One is indeed appropriate: "This triple world is consciousness alone; I am consciousness, these worlds are consciousness, the quarters are consciousness, and this activity is consciousness. (58)
Freed from the seen and the seeing, possessing a solitary and stainless form,
eternally risen and devoid of appearance, I am the Supreme Lord, the Seer.

"Is seen" (*dṛśya*): free from the seen and the seeing. The "seen" refers to the elements (*bhūta*) and elemental derivatives (*bhautika*).
