The "sees" (*darśana*) refers to the means of knowledge (*jñāna-sādhana*). He is free from these, meaning distinct from them; and for this reason, he possesses a form that is absolute and stainless. He is eternally risen, eternally luminous. He is without appearance (*nirābhāsa*), being independent of any other illuminator. He is the Seer, the witness of all.
"I am the Supreme Lord. || 59 ||

I am the Great Consciousness, whose nature is consciousness liberated from the object of thought, which fills the entirety of the universe on all sides, in which everything perceivable has been completely stilled, and which is pure awareness alone.

Thus it is said: "I am pure consciousness alone—free from the object of thought (cetya), whose nature is consciousness, consisting of pure awareness; pervading everywhere within and without, filling the entire universe; in which all that is perceivable has been stilled, and all latent impressions of sense-objects have ceased; great and perfectly full. 60.
Reflecting thus, the highly wise Bali remained absorbed in meditation,
contemplating the meaning of the half-mora of the syllable *oṃ*. (61)

Thus: having extracted the meaning of the half-mora from the Praṇava—the syllable Om—and remaining established in meditation while contemplating that very meaning of the half-mora as the form of the Supreme Brahman. || 61 ||
With all volitions completely stilled and the multitude of mental constructions pacified,
he is free from doubt, with the thought of "object" cast far away, and his contemplation is devoid of conceptualization.

The two verses beginning with "saṃśānte" form a single syntactical unit. By the phrase "by which [the triad]—the object of thought (cetya), the thinker (cintaka), and the act of thinking (cintana)—has been cast far away, as if beyond doubt," the absence of outward-turned distraction is expressed. || 62 ||
Devoid of the meditator, the object of meditation, and the act of meditating, Bali— his mind dissolved and his latent impressions stilled—
became like a lamp in a windless place, having attained the supreme state.
With this desire fully stilled, perfected, and freed from the state of the fault of mental reflection,
Bali shone with stainless being, like the autumn sky with its cloudless clarity.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then those Dānavas, the followers of Bala,
instantly ascended that lofty crystal palace there.
O Great-minded One, having remained for a long time in non-conceptual meditative absorption,
Bali awoke there in their presence.
Then Vairocana,
there, through his mind— which was composed of the abandonment of meditation— performed all the duties of the king.
By the phrase "devoid of the meditator, meditation, and the object of meditation," he states that even when turned inward, there is no distraction—beginning with the word "atha" (now).

With a mind consisting of the abandonment of the object of meditation—that is, the abandonment of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as "I" and "mine"—he performed the duties of the king in this manner. (67–68)
Seeing both adversity and prosperity with equanimity, he perceives them as the same;
his wisdom neither sets nor rises in the face of pleasure and pain.
Thousands of conjectures and refutations, and hundreds of instances of existence and non-existence have been scrutinized by the Mighty One; where, then, can he find consolation? (69)

"Ūha" is the contemplation of the means to achieve what is desired; "apoha" is the contemplation of the avoidance of what is undesired. Although thousands of such categories of objects and hundreds of their positive and negative states were perceived by Bali, nevertheless, where could that Bali find any consolation or confidence? The meaning is: nowhere at all. That is to say, he ruled the kingdom entirely unattached. || 69 ||
Restrain this mind that runs hither and thither, wallowing in worldly pursuits, and establish it within the hollow of the heart.

He instructs Śrī Rāma on what is beneficial— [in the verse beginning] "dhāvamānam": having restrained this mind— which is running here in this world and there in the next world, rushing with speed out of a desire for the pleasures of sense-objects, and wallowing, that is, deeply attached, to worldly activities such as the acquisition of wealth and other mundane pursuits— by means of discrimination, detachment, and so forth.
"Establish [it] in the hollow of the heart, in the lotus of the heart"—the meaning is: make it intent upon the contemplation of the Self.
From whichever objects the mind sinks, like a child,
one should indeed pull it out from each of those and fix it upon reality.
By thus practicing this discipline and binding the intoxicated elephant of the mind with one's whole being, the supreme good is attained. (72)
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Narrative of Bali," in the Chapter on Quiescence within the *Śrī Mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Narrative of Bali," in the section on Quiescence within the *Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa* named *Śrī-saṃsārataraṇi*.
(p. 402) The Fourth Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, O Rāma, listen to this supreme sequence for attaining higher knowledge, just as Prahlāda, the lord of the Daityas, attained perfection through his own self. (1)
It was previously stated that, due to the excellence of merit, even sensual pleasure sometimes leads to the tranquility of the mind.

Now, it is established through the narrative of Prahlāda that the realization of the reality of the Self occurs only through the grace of the Lord. In this regard, he introduces the account of Prahlāda with the words "Now," and so forth. (Verses 1–5)
While his enemy Hiraṇyakaśipu was slaying the hosts of the thirty gods,
Prahlāda, his mind agitated by grief, reflected as follows.
All these foremost of asuras, including Tāta and the others, have been slain by Viṣṇu,
like the principal mountains by the turbulent wind at the end of a kalpa.
By him, many terrifying battles were practiced together with our grandfathers, in which mountains were mutually hurled about in the fervor of combat.
When those various most terrible rows of Asuras have been arrayed,
what need is there to mention that he who is not afraid now will experience fear?
Therefore, I clearly believe that against the assault of that most heroic Hari, there exists no counter-measure other than fleeing from him.
With one's whole being, with all one's intellect, and with the full force of all one's exertion—that Lord alone is the refuge and the goal here; it cannot be otherwise.
From this very moment onward, I have eternally taken refuge in the unborn Nārāyaṇa;
for everywhere, I am indeed composed of Nārāyaṇa.
The mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" accomplishes all aims;
it does not depart from the treasury of my heart, just as the wind does not depart from the sky. (9)
One who worships Viṣṇu while not being Viṣṇu himself shall not partake in the fruit of that worship.
Having become Viṣṇu, one should worship Viṣṇu; for I am established as this very Viṣṇu.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus reflected and assumed the form of Nārāyaṇa, Prahlāda again meditated upon the enemy of the asuras for the purpose of worship.
From this body of Viṣṇu, this other one— the supreme and yet lower form of the Maruts—
is situated externally through the flow of the vital breaths.

In this regard, the two verses beginning with "tatra vapuṣaḥ" form a single syntactical unit. He who is "parāvaraḥ"—meaning that from whom even the supreme ones such as Brahmā and others are "avare," or inferior—is this Viṣṇu.
Outside of this Vaiṣṇava body, there exists another who, through the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the exit of the wind, is "marunmūrtiḥ," having the form of air. || 12 ||
I shall quickly worship him, together with his retinue,
with a mental offering delightful with all necessary requisites.
The syntactical connection is: "I worship this very Viṣṇu who exists in the form of wind. || 13 ||
Thinking "This is Prahlāda," he worshipped Mādhava, the husband of Kamalā, with a mind laden with the weight of his accumulated spiritual provisions.
"Prahlāda"—this consists of two verses. "Saṃbhāra" refers to the requisites for worship; "saṃbhārabharabhāriṇā" means by one who bears the weight of those requisites.
With layers of jeweled offering bowls, with ointments such as sandalwood paste, with incenses, lamps, purifying substances, and various ornaments of great splendor. || 15 ||
Then, in that temple, the lord of the Dānavas worshipped Janārdana with an offering complete with external objects.
Now, "with worship" means by means of the ritual procedure for worship. 16–24.
From that time forward, Prahlāda worshipped the Supreme Lord every day with complete devotion in that very same manner. (17)
Then, from that time forward, all the Daityas in that city became Vaiṣṇavas through devotion; for the king is indeed the cause of conduct.
Then the slayer of enemies went through the air to the world of the gods and announced:
"The Daityas, having abandoned their hatred for Viṣṇu, have taken refuge in him with devotion. (19)
O Raghava, Śakra and the other gods, together with the hosts of Maruts, were filled with wonder, asking:
"How is it that the Daityas have indeed taken hold of devotion to Viṣṇu? (20)
In the Ocean of Milk, seated upon the coils of the serpent, the gods, filled with wonder,
abandoned the sky and approached Hari, who was resplendent in battle.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, what is this? Those Daityas who were always your adversaries have now attained identity with you;
our amazement grows. (22)
Where, indeed, are the utterly wicked Dānavas who have shattered the mountains, and where is devotion to Janārdana, which is obtainable only through a great birth in the West? (23)
"O Blessed One, this report that a common man has been born with [divine] qualities is like a garland of flowers out of season; it brings neither happiness nor anything but agitation. (24)
Where is that base, vulgar, and ever-minded-to-lowly-acts Dānava, a wretch of insignificant birth; and where indeed is Vaiṣṇava devotion? (25)
"Where? "The wretched one, the pitiable one. 25 || 26 || 27 ||
The Blessed One said:
"O wise ones, do not be despondent because Prahlāda is a devotee;
this is his final birth, O subduers of enemies, for he is worthy of liberation."
They know that "the virtuous has become devoid of virtue" is an unfavorable sequence;
they say that "the one devoid of virtue has become virtuous" is the sequence that bestows success.
"O best of immortals, depart to your own various worlds; this [earth] belonging to Prahlāda, produced from the qualities, does not lead to unhappiness. (28)
"Belonging to herself" means: *prāhlādī*, belonging to Prahlāda; *guṇitā*, endowed with qualities, having arisen from excellence, and possessing superior power.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord vanished there amidst the waves of the Ocean of Milk, like a cluster of *tāpiccha* flowers on its shore.
Thus: like a cluster of *tāpiccha* (blackberry) blossoms, like a bunch of *tamāla* flowers. || 29 || 30 || 31 || 32 || 33 ||
Having fully worshipped Hari, that host of gods departed through the sky;
thereafter, the deities felt affection toward Prahlāda.
Vasiṣṭha said:
The devoted Prahlāda worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, every day with his mind, his armor, and his speech. (31)
Then, for him who was devoted to worship, his mind— due to its inclination toward renouncing enjoyments— found no rest in the visible world, as if it were a mere patch of land in a lotus pond.
Having renounced enjoyments and the like, his mind had not yet attained rest; it remained as if suspended upon a swing. (33)
From his abode in the Ocean of Milk, the divine Lord Kṛṣṇa perceived that state of Prāhlādi with his all-pervading and supremely beautiful intellect.

Regarding the verse beginning with *prāhlādīm*: the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that, while remaining in the abode of the Ocean of Milk, he perceived [the daughter of Prahlāda] by means of an all-pervading intellect. In the phrase "from the abode" (*mandirāt*), the ablative case is used according to the rule "there is an addition [of the ablative] when expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in the elision of a *lyap* suffix. 34.
Then, proceeding by way of the netherworld (pātāla) with his vanguard delighted, Viṣṇu arrived at the temple of worship belonging to that Prahlāda.

"Now," [it is said]. Viṣṇu arrived at his temple for the worship of the deity by way of the netherworld (pātāla). The meaning is that he submerged himself in the Ocean of Milk and emerged from that temple of the deity's worship. "With his vanguard delighted" means that his retinue was fully satisfied because he was intent upon bestowing grace upon his devotees. || 35 || 36 || 37 ||
Having recognized that the god had arrived, the lord of the Daityas honored the lotus-eyed one with redoubled devotion and worshipped him with great respect. (36)
Prahlāda, being deeply delighted, praised with nourishing words Lord Hari, who was present in person within the sanctuary of worship.
Prahlāda said:

I take refuge in Hari, the unborn, the infallible Lord, the sovereign who is the beautiful treasury of the three worlds, who removes every blemish, and who is the supreme, worthy refuge for those without shelter. 37.

Then, with eight verses, Prahlāda praises Viṣṇu, beginning with "tribhuvana...": "The three worlds themselves are the dwelling; its delightful treasury is like a mass of wealth, for it is the source of sustenance for all. (38)

I take refuge in Him who resembles a mountain of blue lotus petals, who is like the hollow of the stainless autumnal sky, who has the luster of bees, darkness, and collyrium, and who bears the lotus, the discus, and the mace. 39.

A mountain of blue lotus petals, a heap resembling a mountain, appearing like that; having the luster of the collyrium of bees and darkness, it is collyrium in the form of *añjana*. The specific epithets are employed because there are many varieties of the substance *añjana*, which serves as the means for clarifying the eyes. (39)

I take refuge in that lake of the lotus of my own heart, whose limbs are as tender as a cluster of stainless lotus buds, which possesses a conch shell with the luster of a white-petaled lotus bud, and where the bee-like Brahmā hums with the sound of the Vedas. 40.
"Vimala" means: that [place] which resounds with or causes the Vedas (śrutis) to ring out like a *viriñci*—that is, a bee (*cañcarīka*);
and which is like a reservoir for the lotus of one's own heart, specifically the heart of Prahlāda, serving as its support. 40.

I take refuge in Hari, who is like the autumnal sky: his broad moon-like face is white with a smile and studded with pupils as bright as white nails; he is the Gaṅgā of the mass of rays from the jewel upon his chest. 41.
"Sitā" means: he whose Gaṅgā—the Mandākinī—is the very mass of rays from the pearls situated upon his chest, [acting as] the Gaṅgā formed by the network of rays from the jewel in his heart. || 41 ||

I take refuge in Hari, the white lotus in the lake of the three worlds, the foremost lamp for dispelling the darkness of delusion, the clearly manifest, non-inert reality of consciousness, who removes the suffering of the entire world. (42)

"O Tribhuvana... etc. The three worlds themselves are a lotus-lake; in that lake, he is the white lotus. His whiteness is intended with reference to his incarnations as Narasiṃha and others. He is a lamp for the delusion that is like darkness—meaning, like a lamp that dispels the delusion which resembles darkness because it obstructs knowledge. || 42 ||

I take refuge in Him whose limbs are adorned by a body as pale-gold as the pollen of a newly blossomed lotus, who has applied a crimson unguent like the twilight at the end of day, and who is made beautiful by garments resembling gold. 43.

"Navaiḥ" means: whose limbs are adorned by the body of Śrī, who dwells upon the chest of Kamalā and is fair like the pollen of a newly blossomed lotus; and whose cosmetic ointment on his limbs is as red as the twilight at the time of day's end.
I take refuge in that Child who plays at the creation of the universe without ceasing, who is eternally unborn, undecaying, and vast;
whose noble body has grown old through hundreds of ages, and who now lies upon the leaf of a tree.

Regarding the term *avirata*: here, an apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*) is perceived, for the following attributes are contradictory when applied to one who has incessantly performed the play of universal creation: being eternally unborn (*ajatva*), being vast despite not having grown (*avardhana-viśālatva*), and being both aged (*jaraṭha*) and yet possessing a noble body as well as childhood (*arbhakatva*).
"Not having grown" (*avardhana*) is "vast" (*viśāla*); even in the absence of growth, it is expansive by its very nature due to its all-pervasiveness.

One whose noble body has become weathered by hundreds of ages—meaning one whose noble body, though aged and worn out after hundreds of ages, remains beautiful—and who lies upon the leaves of trees, that is, who reclines on the leaf of a banyan tree. || 44 ||

I take refuge in the All-pervading Lord, who is the frost-fall for the lotus-pond of the sons of Diti, the ever-rising solar orb for the lotus-pond of the gods, the flood of water for the lotus-pond of Brahmā, and whose abode is the lotus in my heart. 45.

Regarding the phrase *diti-sutā*: the daughters of Diti are themselves the lotus-pools (*nalinī*); they are like frost-falls because they are the cause of destruction [to those pools]. Brahmā, born from the lotus (*kamalaja*), is himself a lotus-pool (*nalinī*) because he possesses many lotus-faces; he is the reservoir (*jalāśaya*) filled with water. [The Lord dwells] within that, in the heart-lotus-pool. Here, the word *nalinī* refers simply to a lotus. In the heart—that is, on the chest—is the lotus, which is the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*).
Thus praised with words abounding in virtues by him, Hari— the destroyer of asuras, whose shoulder is the seat of Śrī—
being pleased like a peacock at the sight of a cloud, replied to the lord of the asuras, who was himself being gratified, his body dark blue like the petal of a water-lily.
The Blessed One said:
O treasure of the lineage, O priceless great jewel of the Daitya race,
accept once more whatever you desire for the sake of pacifying the suffering of rebirth.
Prahlāda said:
O All-pervading Lord, you who grant the fruits of all intentions and abide within all worlds—
teach me that which you know to be the most sublime.
The Blessed One said:
O sinless one, may your inquiry lead to the ultimate fruit—the complete pacification of all agitation—and culminate in rest in Brahman. (49)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to the lord of the sons of Diti, Viṣṇu vanished like a wave of the ocean that has produced a gurgling roar.
When the god Viṣṇu had vanished, the western Dānava cast aside the handful of flowers adorned with jewels and gems for the purpose of worship.

Regarding the word "viṣṇau": it means "belonging to the west," that is to say, forming part of the rite of dismissal (udvāsana). It is "adorned with excellent jewels," meaning embellished with the finest gems. || 51 ||
Although seated in the lotus posture, he sat joyfully upon a lower seat;
at the conclusion of the ritual recitation of the hymn, he reflected with deep contemplation.

"Padma" refers to the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), which has been defined as follows: "O best of Brahmins, placing both soles of the feet upon the thighs—this shall be the *padmāsana*, honored by all. Regarding the rule for the recitation of hymns here, it concerns the hymn mentioned previously. (52, 53)
"I have been told by the Lord, the enemy of Māra:
'May you remain one who possesses discernment.
Therefore, within myself, I shall perform the investigation of the self. (53)
Am I truly that which, within this grand display of the world, speaks, goes, stands, exerts itself, and wanders about? (54)

"What? [This] "I speak," and so forth, is an illustration of the activity of all the sense organs. The commencement of the inquiry is: "What would I be, who conceives of the activity of all the sense organs in the form of 'I speak,' and so on? || 54 ||
This world, including trees, grass, and creepers, is not "I";
since that which is external is utterly insentient, how indeed could I be it? (55)
This world is not I; the meaning is that it is so because of its externality and its insentience. || 55 ||
This body, which has arisen from the non-existent, is mute and quivering like the wind;
it dissolves in a short time. I am not this insentient thing.

"It is non-existent" means that it has arisen as something non-existent in reality, being merely imagined. Since the aggregate of the elements and the senses is designated as the "body," [one realizes] "I am not the body," because it is insentient and inert. Why is it insentient?
The meaning is: because it arises from what is non-existent, because it is mute, and because it is impelled by the vital wind. || 56 ||
Being produced by the insentient ear-cavity, which lasts but a moment, sound is empty in form and born of emptiness; it is not I, for I am not insentient. (57)

"By means of the insentient," etc. [The Lord] has a void form because He is formless; He has a void origin because He originates from space. Here too, as before, the relationship between the probandum and the probans is to be applied. || 57 ||
This [Self] is attainable through the skin that perishes in an instant, yet otherwise it is unattainable;
having realized the Self through the grace of consciousness, I am not the insentient sense of touch.

"By the skin": by means of the sense organ of touch (*tvagindriya*), because it is not perceivable through any other mode; [it is perceived] by the grace of consciousness (*citprasāda*) which, acting as the impeller of the senses, has extended outward. "One whose self is apprehended" means one whose essential nature has been manifested. || 58 ||

I am not the insentient taste, which has acquired its nature through the tongue, which is trivial, characterized by flickering existence, possesses only slight movement, and is dependent upon material substances. (59)
"Obtained" (labdhā): by that [intellect] whose existence is fickle and momentary. || 59 ||
Dissolved in the seer—the one who remains when the seen and the act of seeing have perished due to their momentary destruction—is the form that has ceased; "I am not the insentient. (60)

"Visible" (dṛśya) refers to objects such as a jar; "vision" (darśana) refers to the eye. These two are dissolved—that is, merged—into the solitary Seer (draṣṭṛ), where they cease to exist. The inclusion of the term "solitary" (kevala) is for the purpose of excluding that which is conditioned (upahita). || 60 ||
I am not the insentient odor, which is imagined by the decaying nose—stolid toward fragrance—and which is fragile and possesses a fixed form. (61)
"Destroy it!"—the meaning is: by means of the Gandhavatī river, which is dull with fragrance, and by means of [her] dullness. "Pelava" means sparse or thin.
It is of an indeterminate form because, in another moment, a different fragrance manifests. || 61 ||
Free from possessiveness, free from mental constructs, peaceful, and with the delusion of the five senses gone, I am indeed pure consciousness alone, devoid of all parts and their manifestations.

To the question "Who are you, then?", he replies: "I am without 'mine' (nirmama). In this context, by the phrase "one whose delusion regarding the five senses has departed," he excludes identification with the sense organs such as the eyes and so forth. By "without thinking" (amanana), he excludes the nature of the mind (*manas*); for thinking is indeed the function of the mind. By "without 'mine'," he indicates the absence of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*); *mama* is an indeclinable [expressing possession], and one from whom the conceit "mine" has departed is "without 'mine'."
Because: "Devoid of parts and their aggregation" means free from connection with *māyā*. || 62 ||
I alone am the illuminator, pure consciousness devoid of the object of thought;
pervading both the external and the internal, I am partless, stainless, and composed of bliss.

And he excludes the state of being a living soul (jīva) with the word "cetya": "niṣkalāmalasanmayaḥ" means having the nature of that reality which is partless (niṣkala), without divisions, and stainless (amala). || 63 ||
p.
411) Now I have remembered: all this is truly so.
I am the all-pervading Self, this manifestation of non-conceptual consciousness. (64)
"Ā"—this is an indeclinable (avyaya) indicating recollection. The syntactical connection is: "I have recollected this entire form, which is the Truth and the Self of all. (64)
By me alone, as the conscious principle, all these things, from jars and cloths up to the sun,
are illuminated, just as by a lamp of supreme brilliance.

He shows that very form to be non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) with the words "by me alone," and so forth: "By me alone"—that is, by the conscious lamp—these things, from pots and cloths up to the sun, are illumined. This is according to the Vedic scripture: "By its light all this shines. (65)
It is by me alone that these various functions of the senses throb here,
through the internal light of my splendor, just as rows of sparks [throb] from fire.
"By me alone": these various functions of the senses also flash forth by my own internal luminous power, just as pieces of wood contain fire within them. || 66 ||
Even at the end of a kalpa, my form withdrew its station beyond the abode of Viriñci;
yet even today, my form continues to expand and does not turn back.

"Viriñci" means: my form, which is consciousness (caitanya), brought about—achieved and extends even beyond Satyaloka, the abode of Viriñci, and even at the end of a kalpa; it does not return even today. The meaning is that because it is unlimited by space and time, my essential nature (svarūpa) is fully complete everywhere. || 67 ||
How could this internal thought, "I am named so-and-so," be without support?
For this [ego], which has no limit to its form, was indeed my own smallness. (68)
"This" refers to the following: the delimitation of the undelimited Self as "this" is without support and without cause; such is the meaning. || 68 ||
This pure vision, consisting of consciousness, which possesses infinite blissful enjoyment and is characterized by supreme tranquility, triumphs over all other visions. (69)

Regarding the word *anantā*: the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows—this vision of mine, characterized by supreme tranquility, which experiences infinite bliss among all visions—that is, among all perceptions of objects—is victorious, for it consists of pure consciousness (*cinmayī*). || 69 ||
Salutations again and again to me alone, who am the self of consciousness, free from the object of thought, abiding within all beings, and whose nature is inward awareness. (70)
"Salutation to all": According to the Vedic scripture (*śruti*), "The Self alone is all the deities," and since the Self is non-dual, it is logical that this salutation is directed toward oneself.
Salutation to me, the inner self (*pratyagātman*), who is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all things, whose nature is pure existence (*sadrūpa*), and who is untouched by sense objects. (70)
The various powers are fashioned by the supreme consciousness, which is pure by its very nature, immutable,
and free from the stain of impurity.

By the supreme consciousness itself—which is pure, equanimous, changeless, and free from the stain of impurity—various powers conducive to the creation of the world and other such acts, as well as forms such as Brahmā and others, are fashioned. || 71 ||

Through the indifference toward the three times and the absence of inferiority, as well as through the non-binding of the mind—which has become indifferent to the object of thought—only equanimity remains. (72)

Regarding "time": that consciousness which disregards—meaning does not connect with—the past, future, and present times, is deprived of its objects of cognition (cetya), such as joy, sorrow, and so forth. For that consciousness which disregards the diversity of perceived objects (cetya-dṛśya-bheda), only equanimity and fullness remain. [This refers to] "the one who disregards."
The form [is derived] by adding the feminine suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* after a word ending in a *tṛn* suffix. || 72 ||
For she, being inaccessible to words, remains as if eternally non-existent,
as if having reached the state of the established doctrine of selflessness.

"She indeed" means: for she, having attained equanimity, because she is inaccessible to speech and mind and because she is indefinable, remains as if she has reached an eternal state of equanimity—the stage of the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya-siddhānta*), the condition of the doctrine of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādi-siddhānta*), and as if she has entered the very nature of emptiness (*śūnyarūpatā*). || 73 ||
Enveloped by impurities consisting of both effort and non-effort, that consciousness is indeed unable to leap upward, like a bird bound by a snare. (74)

That consciousness which is enveloped and surrounded by the defects of the mind—impurities rooted in passion and hatred consisting of effort and non-effort—is like a bird bound by snares; it is unable to fly up or become liberated. || 74 || 75 ||
(413) By means of the delusion of dualities arising from desire and aversion, living beings have reached the same state as insects clinging within the crevices of the earth. (75)
Salutations to myself, to me who am the unbroken consciousness-self;
O Lord, the jewel that illuminates the world and the non-world, after a long time I have finally attained You.
Regarding "of the self" (ātmanaḥ): He who illuminates—that is, makes manifest—the worlds is the Lokāloka; he is both the "Lokāloka" and a "jewel" (maṇi), and this is his address. 76.
You have been grasped, you have been found, and you have arisen before long;
you have been extracted from conceptual constructions—you who are what you are, homage be to you!
"Thou art grasped": thou hast been grasped—that is, thou hast been thoroughly investigated—by the words of the Śruti and the preceptor.

Therefore, thou hast been extracted from conceptual constructions, that is, from imagined forms. And therefore, thou hast arisen; thou hast become manifest in thy own nature characterized by truth, consciousness, bliss, and so forth. And therefore, thou hast been attained through oneness.
"You have been directly experienced as 'I am He. Thus, you who were previously such and possessed such a form, even now you remain in that very same form;
having abandoned all imagined forms, you abide by your own true nature. To You who are thus situated, let there be salutation"—this is the grammatical connection. || 77 ||
Salutations to me and to you, O Infinite One; salutations to you and to me, whose nature is auspiciousness. Salutations to the God of gods, the Supreme, the Supreme Self.

"Mahyam iti": Because of the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman), "to me"—that is, to You who are my own form—salutations; "to You"—that is, to me who am Your own form—salutations. Salutations to the Supreme Self, the highest deity of all deities. || 78 ||
Like the orb of the moon when the clouds have vanished, [the Self] is its own true nature, free from the veil of mental constructs (*kalana*).
Within my own joyful body, I myself bow down to that which is established in itself, arisen by itself, self-dependent, and self-manifested.
Regarding the word "vanished" (*gata*): it means the veil of ignorance (*avidyā*) has ceased; therefore, it is "cloudless" (*gataghana*).
It stands like the full orb of the moon; within its own joyful and blissful body—its very nature—and not in any support external to itself; by itself alone, and not through any other cause;
established in itself, being its own essential form, and not having a state of existence consisting of action; it has arisen and manifested by itself alone.
I bow to my own very nature, which is self-dependent and not reliant on anything else. || 79 ||
For even while standing, he is not seated; even while walking, he does not walk.
Though engaged in worldly activity, he remains peaceful; even while acting, he is not defiled. (80)

"Standing," it is said: because he is devoid of action, even while standing he is not "seated," due to his lack of identification with the stationary body. Even while going—that is, pervading another place—he does not go, because the act of going resides in the body and the Self is distinct from it. Even though he is peaceful—meaning his mind is free from modification—he remains engaged in worldly activity.

Because it is the activator of all the senses, even while acting and engaging in worldly affairs in this manner, the Self is not smeared by merit or sin; it is not clung to by them, because egoism has ceased to exist. || 80 ||
He agitates the minds just as the wind stirs the sprouts;
he drives his own row of senses like a charioteer driving a team of horses. (81)

Regarding the word "manāṃsi": *manāṃsi* refers to the internal organs, such as the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*). The "row of senses" (*akṣapaṅkti*) refers to the collection of external sense organs.
This very [Self] is always to be sought, praised, and meditated upon;
by means of this, one transcends old age, death, and delusion, and proceeds [to liberation]. (82)

"This" refers to this very Self that must always be sought. For the Śruti declares: "That is to be sought; that is to be desired to be known. This being so, by means of this Self, one crosses over the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) characterized by old age, death, and delusion, and attains one's true nature. 82–84.
This [Self] is exceedingly easy to attain and easy to conquer, like a kinsman;
it is like a bee within the lotus-cavity of the body for all beings. (83)
I have no desire for the maintenance of enjoyments, nor do I have any desire for the renunciation of enjoyments;
let that which comes come, and let that which departs depart. (84)
"For so long a time, I have been robbed of my entire wealth of discernment by this enemy that is ignorance, and utterly crushed in solitude. (85)
"Etāvantam" means: in such a way that it was entirely unknown to others; "avapothitaḥ" means struck or harmed. || 85 ||
When the mind has been severed within the mind and egolessness has been attained;
when existence has dissolved through being, I abide as the solitary Self, established in my own nature.

"By the mind": when the mind—that particular modification of mental activity refined by the scriptures—has been severed within the heart (the consciousness) that was steeped in transmigratory existence, and has attained a state free from egoism; and when the disposition (bhāva) directed toward the world has dissolved through the disposition (bhāva) focused on the non-duality of Brahman, I remain alone and pure. || 86 ||
Free from objective manifestation, free from ego, free from the functioning mind, and free from desire,
my body abides in the pure Self alone, which is vibrationless.

Regarding "nirbhāvam" (without manifestation): the phrase beginning with "nirbhāvam" is an adverbial modifier of the verb "tiṣṭhati" (he stands). "Bhāva" refers to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of saṃsāra. || 87 ||
Having severed the multitude of craving’s ropes from the cage of my own body, I know not where the bird of wicked egoism has flown away. 88.
Though the splendor of an object may exist, it does not abide in you who are unstable, just as the beauty of a woman's form does not remain for one whose eyes have been lost. 89.
Victory to you of formidable form! Victory to you who are devoted to peace!
Victory to you who transcend all scriptures! Victory to you who are the foundation of all scriptures! 90.

With two verses beginning with "Victory!", he praises himself: "He whose form is *proḍḍāmara*—terrifying—as Bhairava and so forth, because he transcends all limbs [of the body] and is devoid of name, caste, and so on; he is the abode of all scriptures (*sarvāgamāspada*) because he is accessible through the synthesis of all Upaniṣads and because he is the self of all; thus he possesses the nature of being born, unborn, and so forth. (90–93)
Victory to you, O Born; victory to you, O Unborn! Victory to you, O Wounded; victory to you, O Unwounded! Victory to you, O Being;
victory to you, O Non-being! Victory to you, O Conquerable; victory to you, O Unconquerable! 91.
Vasiṣṭha said:
While reflecting thus, Prahlāda, the slayer of enemy heroes,
attained a state of meditative absorption characterized by non-conceptual supreme bliss.
Established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, he appeared as if depicted in a painting;
for five thousand years, with broad shoulders and a fixed gaze, he remained motionless.
And during this time, that entire circle of the netherworld became kingless, harsh, and oppressed by the "law of the fish" (the strong preying upon the weak). 94.
"Thus much" means that it is harsh and abounds in violence. The "law of the fishes" (mātsyanyāya) refers to the oppression of the weak by the strong;
for large fish swallow small fish. 94.
Then Hari, whose body maintains the order of the entire web of worlds,
was reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk.
Regarding the word "atha": he is the embodied one for the sake of protecting the entire web of worlds, their succession, and the boundaries of the duties of castes and stages of life. || 95 ||
The one who is like a sun to the lotuses of the three worlds reflected thus,
now that Prahlāda had come to rest in his station and the lord of Pātāla had departed.
The Lord’s reflection is expressed in eight verses. The sequence of this reflection is as follows:
since Prahlāda has found rest in his own state, the leader [Hiraṇyakaśipu] has gone to Pātāla; consequently, those residing there are in a state of ruin due to being without a protector. (96)
Alas, this creation has for the most part reached a state devoid of Daityas. In the absence of Daityas, the host of gods has fallen into a state of desirelessness;
the pairs of opposites will subside, and they shall attain the state known as liberation.
Abandoning the desire to conquer the ranks of the gods, being tranquil, one should seek liberation. || 97 ||
When the flood of gods has attained peace, all sacrificial and ascetic rites on earth will become fruitless and will undoubtedly come to rest. (98)

Consequently, since there would be no heaven as a realm for experiencing the fruits of those deeds, virtuous actions such as sacrifices and austerities—which have heaven as their fruit—would perish on earth. || 98 ||

Furthermore, when ritual actions have been stilled, the world of the earth will come to its end; thereafter, even regarding the remaining objects of experience, there will be no further involvement in saṃsāra. (99)

Then, because Dharma would not function and the world of mortals would also cease to exist, there would follow the consequence of no further saṃsāra, since there would be nothing left to protect. || 99 ||
Therefore, I too, having established peace of mind in this void where the moon, sun, and stars have vanished, shall abide in that state.
May I too rest in my own state. || 100 ||
Since the world has thus come to such an untimely end, I see no good in this; I think it better that the Dānavas should live. || 1 ||
Therefore, since there would be a dissolution at such an untimely moment, I consider the mere continued existence of the Dānavas to be better. || 1 ||
Then, due to the exertion of the Daityas, the gods' rites of sacrifice and austerity were [interrupted];
by that, the order of worldly existence was established, whereas otherwise there would have been no such sequence of saṃsāra.

Therefore, through the exertion of the Daityas and the gods' desire for victory, when they engage in sacrificial rites and other such activities, the stability of the world-order (*saṃsāra*) is maintained; it could not be otherwise. (2) (3) (4) (5) (6)
"One must dwell here with this very body until the end of the kalpa;
for such is the fixed destiny ordained by the Supreme Lord. (3)
Having reflected thus, the Soul of All emerged from the Ocean of Milk,
reached the city of Prahlāda, and entered the terrace of the palace.
Seated upon the throne of Vainateya, with Lakṣmī waving the fly-whisks for him,
surrounded by his own weapons and attendants, he was saluted by divine sages and holy ascetics.
"O Great-souled One, awaken! Thus Viṣṇu spoke, blowing his conch Pāñcajanya and making the quarters of the sky resound with its sound.
By that great sound, born from the life-breath of the Vaiṣṇava,
the lord of the Dānavas gradually regained consciousness. (7)
"By the great one" means by that which is born from the life-force connected to Viṣṇu—that is, produced by the vital air associated with Viṣṇu. || 7 ||
Then the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti), having risen from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
gradually pervaded the demon from all sides through the channels (nāḍīs).

Regarding the phrase "brahmarandhra": Now, after awakening, the power of breath (prāṇa-śakti) and the power of consciousness (caitanya-śakti), which had previously remained in that very Brahma-aperture during the time of samādhi, having risen from there, slowly caused the vital air (asu) to pervade all the channels (nāḍīs). || 8 ||
Then, as the vital breaths proceeded through the apertures and the mouth,
his consciousness became oriented toward objects of thought, reflected within like an image in the mirror of the internal breath.

Regarding the phrase "in the vital breaths" (*prāṇeṣu*): while the nine vital breaths—that is, the nine sense organs—were active within the nine apertures and mouths, her consciousness (*cit*) became oriented toward objects of perception, reflected in the mirror of the internal vital breath; that is, it was mirrored within the very mirror of the internal sense organ. || 9 ||
O Rāghava, the consciousness, becoming intent upon the object of thought, attained the state of mind and intellect;
it became twofold, like the beauty of a face reflected in a mirror.

Regarding the term *cetanīyā*: "that which is to be perceived" (*cetya*), "the object of perception," and "the visible" (*dṛśya*) are synonyms. Consciousness (*cit*) directed toward that which is to be perceived becomes the perceived object because it is reflected in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). That consciousness thus attained the state of the mind, the nature of the mental faculty (*manas*).
It is like the beauty of a face—the splendor of the countenance—which, when transferred to a mirror or reflected in a looking-glass, appears as a duality, as if it were a different form.
When the painting had slightly sprouted forth and his eyes were about to blossom,
they gradually became dark-edged like blue lotuses.
As his consciousness moved through the hollows of the channels touched by the inhaled and exhaled breaths,
a throbbing arose within him, like that of a lotus afflicted by the wind.

"Prāṇa... etc. For one whose consciousness within the cavities of the channels has been touched—that is, awakened—by the prāṇa and apāna, a vibration arose like that of a lotus moved by the wind. (12–15)
In a mere twinkling of an eye, his mind attained fullness;
then he shone forth with his eyes, mind, breath, and body all blossoming. (13)
His mind became full-blown with joy and grew expansive;
the Lord of the Three Worlds addressed her, as a rain-cloud addresses a peacock.
O virtuous one, remember Mahālakṣmī; remember your own form.
Why do you bring about the cessation of your body so abruptly? 15.
For you who are free from the conceptualization of what is to be rejected or accepted, what harm can there be from the presence or absence of bodily states? Remain as you are; now arise! 16.

"Hey! [Thus: For you who are devoid of the mental constructs regarding objects to be abandoned or accepted, what harm or loss can there be from the presence or absence of things—whether desired or undesired—pertaining to the body? Therefore, remain in the state of one liberated while living; arise from your meditative absorption. 16.
Remaining indeed in the kingdom as one liberated while living,
you must cast off this body without agitation until the end of the kalpa.
"Living," [it is said]. The *kṣepaṇī* (the throwing stick) is to be set in motion. "Free from agitation" means devoid of fear. 17–18.
The twelve suns have not risen, nor have the mountains melted;
the world has not been consumed by fire, O virtuous one—why indeed do you abandon your body in vain? (18)
"I am emaciated, deeply distressed, and deluded"—these and other such thoughts rob one's intellect; for such a person, death is glorious. (19)
"Emaciated" means that for one whose fortitude has been utterly destroyed by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of suffering such as poverty and the like, death alone is fitting. 120.
For one who is bound within by the snares of hope and led here and there by the flickering movements of the mind—for him, death shines forth with splendor.

"Āśeti" means: because one is bound by the snares of desire within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), being led here and there like a beast by the flickering movements of the mind, there is an absence of even a trace of happiness; therefore, death alone is better—this is the meaning. || 120 ||
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not defiled, and who is equal toward all beings— for him life is truly glorious. (21)

He says in three verses that for one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta), life itself is truly glorious: "Of him... and so forth. He whose internal state—the functioning of the inner organ—is not characterized by egoism, being devoid of the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so on; whose intellect is not smeared—that is, not touched—by joy, sorrow, and the like; and who is equal toward all beings, seeing with an even eye: for him...
Life shines forth. || 21 || 22 ||
He who, with an inner mind cooled and free from passion and hatred,
beholds this very life like a witness— his life indeed shines.

For one who, having correctly understood through thorough discernment that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be adopted, has placed the mind within the mind—that person’s life is truly glorious. (23)

"By which" means having fully understood; the remainder is "the reality of the self. "The mind has been offered into its own self" means it has been placed in the end of the mind, that is, in the locus where the mind dissolves; the meaning is that it has been made dependent upon that. || 23 ||
When the relationship between the grasped and the grasper has utterly ceased, tranquility arises;
this tranquility, having attained stability, is designated by the name "liberation. (24)

Regarding the term "grāhya" (the graspable): when the relationship between the graspable and the grasper has ceased and the perception of distinctions such as the graspable and so forth has subsided, that peace which arises—the mind's state of changelessness—is itself called liberation (*mokṣa*) once it has attained stability. 24, 25, 26.
Therefore arise, O Lord of Asuras, and take your seat upon the throne;
I myself shall soon bestow the consecration upon you.
May the Siddhas, Sādhyas, and hosts of gods, who have come to me upon hearing the sound of the Pāñcajanya conch, grant you prosperity. (26)
Then Hari [sprinkled] him with the waters of the great oceans, such as the Kṣīroda,
and with the floods of rivers such as the Gaṅgā, as well as with the waters of all sacred fords (tīrtha).
While being praised by the gods and asuras, Madhusūdana spoke these words to Prahlāda, who was himself being praised by the gods and asuras after his consecration: (28)
O sinless one, as long as Mount Meru endures, as long as the earth remains, and as long as the orbs of the moon and sun exist, so long shall you, O King, be praised for your unimpaired virtues.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one, together with the humans, gods, and kinnaras,
vanished on the spot like a second dissolution.
Rāma said:
O Blessed One, how was the mind of the high-souled Prahlāda awakened when it had been transformed into the state beyond, by means of the sounds of the Pāñcajanya conch? 31.
"In the supreme state" means in the supreme state, Brahman; it has reached maturity, having attained identity [with it]. || 31 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Like a withered seed, devoid of the sprout of further birth,
pure latent impression (vāsanā) dwells in the hearts of those liberated while living.
"Fallen" means like a withered seed; therefore, being devoid of the sprout that is rebirth, pure latent impression (vāsanā) dwells in the hearts of those liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 32 ||
Purifying, supremely noble, and following after pure being,
she consists eternally of self-meditation and remains as if in deep sleep.

He qualifies that very [pure impression] as "purifying" (pāvanī). It is purifying because it is free from the stain of sin; supremely noble because it bestows the bliss of absolute liberation (kaivalya); and following pure *sattva*—meaning it conforms solely to the quality of *sattva* unmixed with *rajas* and *tamas*—that pure impression (*śuddhavāsanā*), consisting of meditation on the Self, belongs to one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
It remains latent, like the latent impressions (vāsanā) of one who is in deep sleep. || 33 ||
Even at the end of a thousand years, they awaken with that very same intermediate state while the body still exists; how could they do so gradually from a state of extreme swelling? (134)

"Even so": by that very same latent impression (*vāsanā*), which—due to some cause—is gradually swollen and increased during the intermediate state, they awaken even at the end of a thousand years while still in the body. 134.
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Narrative of Prahlāda," in the Section on Quiescence within the *Mokṣopāya* of the venerable Vālmīki.
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Narrative of Prahlāda," in the section on Quiescence within the *Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa*, known as the *Saṃsārataraṇi*.
Fifth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
This illusion called saṃsāra is endless;
it comes under control only through the conquest of one's own mind, and not otherwise.
Previously, it was stated that through the grace of the Lord alone, by means of the realization of the reality of the Self, there is the cessation of what is called saṃsāra.

Now, in order to demonstrate that the illusion of the world (*jaganmāyā*) does not subside without the conquest of the mind (*cittajaya*), and to establish the manifold nature of *māyā*, the story of Gādhi is related, just like the story of Lavaṇa. [This begins with] the words "O Rāma," and so forth. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.
O sinless one, listen attentively as I relate this history for the purpose of understanding the manifold variety of the world’s illusory expansion. (2)
On this surface of the earth, there is a province named Kosala;
therein lived a certain virtuous man of Brahmin lineage known as Gādhi. (3)
Having resolved in his mind upon some task to be accomplished,
he departed from the company of his kinsmen and went to the forest to perform austerities.
There, that king of brahmins reached a lake filled with blossoming lotuses;
submerged in the water up to his neck, he performed austerities there.
Eight months passed while he remained submerged in the waters of that lake;
then, one day, Hari approached him as he was consumed by his ascetic penance.
The Blessed One said:
"O Brahmin, arise from the midst of the milk and take your desired boon;
your course of disciplined observance has been completed, endowed with its intended fruit. (7)
Gādhi said:
Salutation to Viṣṇu, who is like a bee within the hollow of the heart-lotuses of countless living beings in the world, and who is the singular lake for the lotus-pond of the three worlds.
"Immeasurable" (asaṃkhyeya) means: to the inner ruler of all beings and the substratum of the entire world. || 8 ||
O Blessed One, I desire to behold this supreme illusion fashioned by you, which is wondrous and known by the name of saṃsāra. (9)
"Mayā" means belonging to the Supreme Self (pāramātmikī), that is, related to the Supreme Self. 9, 10, 11, 12.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"You shall see this illusion; if you wish to abandon it, then abandon it.
Having said this, Viṣṇu vanished like a city of the Gandharvas.
When Viṣṇu had departed, that lordly Brāhmaṇa rose up from the water;
his soul was completely satisfied by the sight of the Lord of the Universe.
Then, some days passed for him in that forest,
filled with the joy of beholding Hari and engaged in the duties of a brahmin.
Once, he began his bath in a lake filled with blooming lotuses,
reflecting in his mind upon the words of Viṣṇu as if he were a great sage.
"Once upon a time" (ekadā): like a great sage at Lake Mānasa, known as Mānasa. || 13 ||
At the edge of the water, he performed the rite and entered beneath the waves;
during that underwater ritual, his mind forgot its meditation and mantras. (14)
"Of the water": in that rite, namely the rite of bathing. 14 || 15 ||
Distressed, he saw his own self dead in his own house,
released from the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths and having vanished.
He was surrounded by distressed kinsmen; his wife clung to his feet, and his mother held him by the chin, which was marked by the impressions of a new fan.

Regarding the word "āvṛtam" (covered): the grammatical connection is that [the chin] was grasped by his mother out of affection—that chin which is marked by the nine types of secondary sexual characteristics (*vyañjana*) due to fresh youth, and distinguished by a newly grown beard on its lower part. || 16 ||
Then, with gestures agitated by cries like the surging waves of that moment,
they led him to the cremation ground— a place stained with the mire of fat—
and there, in a blazing fire, they reduced that corpse to ashes.
"Now" (atha): by means of these verses, there is a demonstration of Gādhi’s successive states, beginning from his entry into the womb. || 17 ||
Then Gādhi, with his own mind made weighty by contemplation, beheld those dwelling in the vicinity of villages on the borders of the Hūṇa territories.
"Now" (atha) means: by one who was swollen with her own mental anguish—that is, thick with the suffering of her own mind. [Verses 18–26]
The wives of the Śvapacas [perceived] themselves agitated in their wombs;
in due time, a Pukkasa woman slowly gave birth to one of dark complexion.
In the house of a dog-cooker (śvapaca), there was a child, a favorite of the dog-cookers,
who had reached sixteen years of age, having passed beyond the state of being twelve years old.
With stout limbs and noble shoulders, he was like a cloud thick with rain,
surrounded by a Śvapaca woman as if by a dark tamāla creeper.
Adorned with clusters of breasts as her blossoms and possessing hands like fresh sprouts,
she rested in forest thickets and slept within mountain caves. (22)
She had hidden herself within the thickets of leaves, made her dwelling among the shrubs,
and now gave birth upon the mountains to sons who were the sprouts of her own lineage.
Though he possessed a wife and was prosperous, his youth had faded;
yet he remained like a lordly sage, having constructed a small hut of leaves at a distance.
Then Gādhi beheld his son, who was becoming decrepit with age, following after him, as well as his wife.
His wife was entirely carried away by Death;
thereafter, his soul overwhelmed with grief, his face distorted by lamentation, [he remained]. (26)
Leaving his own country, he departed with tearful eyes;
filled with grief and consumed by anxiety, he wandered through many lands.
Once he reached the illustrious city of Kīra, which was densely crowded with vassal lords, women, and citizens.
There he reached a royal road resembling the path to heaven,
which had gates fashioned from jewels and gems, and where auspicious elephants stood.
He saw him wandering here and there for the sake of the kingdom after the king had died— unsteady like the world of transmigration, yet appearing like the stainless lord of mountains.
Taking him who was looking on with his very beautiful hand,
he respectfully placed him upon his own neck, like the sun upon the slope of Mount Meru.
When that [arrow] reached his throat, victory-drums resounded on all sides;
a roar from the people arose across the earth, "The King is victorious!",
like the cry of birds awakening together.
There, excellent women chose him for the sake of adornment;
thereafter, all the subjects approached him who was such as he was. (33)
Thus that outcaste attained sovereignty within the city of Kīrapura,
his lotus-feet being rubbed by the lotus-palms of the Kīris.
With royal majesty spread abroad and his commands established in every direction, having within a few days secured the administration of the conquered territories,
and having fully laid down the entire burden of sovereignty upon his ministers, he became the king there by the name of Gavala.

"Parīti" means: one whose royal power has spread abroad, whose radiant majesty has extended in every direction; "one for whom the settlement of the country was accomplished in a few days" means he by whom the settlement of the country—the boundaries of the realm—was accomplished in just a few days, established by his mere will alone.
He by whom the entire burden of sovereignty—of the state—has been borne by his ministers and other natural allies. || 35 || 36 || 37 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Surrounded by playful women, honored by the circle of ministers, saluted by all the vassal lords, and graced by the royal umbrella and fly-whisks; (36)
A Cāṇḍāla ruled over the parrots for eight years;
once, by chance, he remained there having cast off his ornaments.
With that same attire, he went out alone to the outer courtyard;
there he saw a group of outcaste dog-cookers, dark as clouds and stout.
"In that regard" (*tatra*): "a pack of dog-cookers" (*śvapacapeṭakaḥ*) means a multitude of dog-cookers (*śvapaca*). [Verses 38–47]
Striking the lute-string with the playful grace of his sprout-like hand, there arose from it a single being, aged and red-eyed. (39)
Suddenly addressing the lord of Kīra as "O Kaṭañja," he said this to the king of Kīra: "O friend, O Kaṭañjaka! (40)
Where have you been staying? By good fortune you are seen today after so long, O kinsman! Where did you spend all this time within the depths of the forest?
Even as the outcaste spoke thus before the king, the king,
by his very demeanor at that moment, showed him contempt.
Meanwhile, the beloved women who had gone to the windows likewise fell into a state of extreme dejection upon realizing, "This is a dog-eater. (43)
Then the ministers, the citizens, and the women quickly entered the inner apartments, where the people were dejected, to see that lord of the earth.
Just as people do not touch a corpse even when it stands right in their own house,
so too did he remain alone, even while situated in the midst of the multitude.
Like a traveler separated from his caravan and other groups in a foreign land, we have all now been defiled by the dog-cookers for a long time. (46)
"We shall not be purified by expiatory rites; we shall enter the fire," thus resolved the citizens and the ministers in the city. (47)
Having caused the fire to blaze on all sides, the king—whose intellect was purified by association with virtuous people—entered it together with his kinsmen. (48)
Alone, with his mind agitated by grief, he reflected: "For my sake, this calamity has come to pass while I remain in this land. (49)
Furthermore, having resolved, "What use is the suffering of life? Death shall be my great festival," Gavala [stood] before the blazing fire. (50)
Like a moth, he offered his body as an oblation without any agitation. In the meantime, Gādhi, agitated by the fire, woke up from his delusion. (51)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Within two moments, Gādhi became free from his delusion, wondering:
"Who am I? What am I seeing? And what indeed have I done? (52)
Reflecting thus, he rose up from the midst of the water;
for such is the constant state of embodied beings amidst their endless wandering in delusive perceptions.
"Like a tiger maddened by passion ranges through the forest thickets, so does the mind wander";
having determined that this was mental delusion, Gādhi led him away.
While he was staying for some days in his own hermitage,
once a certain most beloved guest arrived from Gādhi.
Having attained supreme satisfaction by feeding on the juices of fruits and flowers,
both of them then performed their evening prayers and completed their recitations.
Having gradually reached their bed, they engaged in purifying conversations;
then Gādhi questioned that guest with words that arose spontaneously in the course of their talk.
"O Brahmin, why are your limbs so emaciated? Why are you so overcome with fatigue? (58)
The guest said:
On this surface of the earth, in a bower of the northern quarter, there is a great and glorious country renowned by the name Kīra. (59)
There I dwelt for a month, being honored by the people of the city; once, on a certain occasion during the course of conversation, it was said there by one person: (60)
(429) "O twice-born one, there was once a king here named Śṛpacas for eight years; he was recognized by me at the end as the very same person who had entered the blazing fire with speed. (61)
"Then hundreds of twice-born men entered the fire here.
Having heard this from his mouth, [the king] emerged from that circle.
"O twice-born one, having performed penance such as bathing and recitation at Prayāga, today I shall break my fast at the end of the third Cāndrāyaṇa. (63)
I have come here because of that; therefore, I am weary and exceedingly emaciated.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this from the mouth of the Brahmin, Gādhi reflected with a mind overflowing with wonder: "Such is this account of my own life. (65)
"Therefore, with an undaunted mind, I shall go to see the account of that outcaste dog-cooker.
Then, having departed and traversed many lands, the one of great intelligence—
He reached the Hūṇa region with such conduct, and by that very disposition, he reached his own dwelling among the Śvapacas.
Thus he saw other settlements here and there;
remembering his former deeds as a dog-eater, Gādhi thought, "I have been born thus. (68)
With his head trembling in astonishment, he reflected upon the movement of the constituent elements;
abandoning the Hūṇa region, he went to the land of the Kiras.
Then he beheld those places in the city which he himself had previously experienced, seen, and frequented, as well as those of which he had heard from people.
"This indeed was a great illusion shown to me by that wielder of the discus; now I have clearly remembered it in its entirety. (71)
Having reflected thus, Gādhi departed from that abode of people and,
reaching a mountain cave, remained there like a lion. (72)
There, for a year and a half, that one of great splendor performed austerities while subsisting on handfuls of water, for the sake of pleasing the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then he arrived at the cave of the lord of mountains, the abode of the twice-born,
bearing his discus and mace, his own complexion as white as a rain cloud.
The Blessed One said:
"O best of brahmins, you have seen my most powerful illusion while performing austerities on the mountain slope; what else do you desire? (75)
Having offered the guest-water, strewn flowers, and prostrated with circumambulations of the body,
the twice-born spoke these words to Viṣṇu, as a cātaka bird addresses a rain-cloud.
Gādhi said:
"O Lord, this illusion consisting of profound darkness has been displayed by you;
I do not understand its secret—how did this delusion become reality? (77)
The Blessed One said:
O Brahmin, the earth and other elements reside within the mind and never exist externally;
this is experienced by everyone in the objects of dreams and illusions. (78)
Regarding the word *vipra*: the world, consisting of earth and the other elements, resides within the mind alone, because the mind itself is the cause of the world;

it does not exist externally. The meaning is that, in reality, there is no external object. And this point is indeed experienced by everyone in states such as dreaming, since in dreams and similar conditions, it is only the phenomenal world residing within the mind that manifests. || 78 ||
If that mind, by which the infinite web of worlds is sustained, manifests the state of a dog-cooker (outcaste), what cause for wonder is there in this? (79)

Regarding the phrase "yatreti": Since the entire web of infinite worlds is situated within the mind, what cause for wonder is there if even the state of a dog-cooker (an outcaste) is manifested by that mind which encompasses all phenomenal expansion? || 79 ||
Just as you perceived the state of being a dog-cooker through the power of appearance,
so too did you see the guest who had arrived in your agitation. (80)

"Having understood" means: just as the state of being a dog-cooker (a *śvapaca*) was understood through the power of appearance and the power of delusion, so too has a guest arrived; thus, "I have seen the entire delusion" is understood precisely through the power of appearance. 80, 81, 82.
Rising up in that very same way, I departed; I reached the realm of the Hūṇas, and there I found this former, well-constructed house of Kaṭañja.
In that very manner, you arrived at the city of Kīra, and it was told to me:
"In Kīra, you beheld the state of being a king of the Śvapacas, free from all delusion. (82)
By a chance occurrence, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow, the state of being a *śvapaca* was reflected in the minds of all the Hūṇas and Kiras in that very same way. (83)

"O crow!"— the sense is that just as the state of being an outcaste (śvapaca) resides in your mind, so too, by chance, the state of being an outcaste is reflected in the minds of all the Hūṇas and Kīras as well, due to the manifold nature of delusion. At times, a single intuition arises even for many people.
For the movement of the mind is indeed as diverse as the occurrence of the "crow-and-palm" coincidence. || 84 ||
He who was formerly that outcaste named Kaṭañjaka in the land of the Hūṇas, he became exactly like that again through that very same disposition. 85.
In that very same way, having encountered a failure of his ritual duties, he went to another country;
he became the king of the Kiras and subsequently entered the fire. (86)
At that time, the state of the Kaṭañja custom appeared in your mind solely as something belonging to yourself, through such a manifestation. (87)
The one who lacks self-knowledge sinks, thinking "this is I" and "that is mine";
but the knower of reality does not despair, realizing that "all this is indeed I. 88.

"This," [he says]. One who lacks self-knowledge (*anātmavān*), being ignorant of the Self, meditates on duality—thinking "I am this," "I am that," "this is mine"—and thus sinks into the ocean of *saṃsāra*, becoming submerged. But the knower of reality (*tattvajña*), meditating on non-duality by thinking "all is indeed I" and "I alone am all," does not perish within *saṃsāra*. || 88 || 89 ||
O Brahmins, this illusion called saṃsāra has no end;
it comes to an end only through the contemplation of the Self, and not otherwise. (89)
He does not grasp at objects as having a conceptualization of division;
therefore, he who knows reality does not sink into delusions and errors. (90)

"No," [it is said]. Because the knower of reality does not grasp the notion of division among categories—that mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) concerning division which is a cause of misfortune—by that reason, this knower of reality does not sink into delusions (*moha*), which are the causes of error and consist of ignorance (*ajñāna*). || 90 ||
Because your knowledge is incomplete, you are unable to restrain the delusions of the mind;
therefore, you are instantly overcome by them one after another.

"Of knowledge" means: because knowledge of the reality of the Self is incomplete—that is, because its object is limited—you are unable to ward off the delusion of the mind; for that very reason, by that very mental delusion, you are assailed and overcome. || 91 ||
The mind, it is said, is the hub of this wheel of illusion here;
if one stands having stepped upon it, nothing can cause one harm.

Regarding the word "mind" (*cittam*): the mind alone is indeed the hub—the central cavity—of this wheel of illusion (*māyā-cakra*) which takes the form of the world; for it is well known that the hub is the cause of the wheel's rotation. Karma stands having completely pervaded and restrained such a mind, which has become the hub of the wheel of illusion, in every respect and everywhere.
If one remains established in that which is consciousness and free from modification, then that wheel of māyā does not obstruct anything whatsoever, not even in the slightest degree.
Arise! For ten years, with a weary mind, perform penance in a grove on the mountain; thereafter, you shall attain infinite knowledge.
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one vanished on the spot;
Gādhi, for his part, attained supreme detachment born of discernment. (94)
With a heart moistened by compassion, he went to the Lord of the Earth for the sake of religious observance;
having cast aside all worldly intentions, he performed intense penance there.
For ten years, he indeed attained self-knowledge through him.
Thereafter, having regained his own true nature, the Great-Souled One, free from grief and devoid of desire for the realm of enjoyment,
remained ever-expansively liberated while living, as serene as if he were the Absolute itself.
Śaśāṅka’s mind was unsteady and agitated. || 97 ||
He rejoiced (*aramateti*). Having attained his own perfect existence, the Great Being (*mahāsattā*), he took delight; the ellipsis "in himself alone" is to be supplied.
His mind was unswerving and full; "unswerving" means undeluded. || 97 ||
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Narration of the Story of Gādhi," in the Chapter on Tranquility within the *Mokṣopāya* of the venerable Vālmīki.
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Narrative of Gādhi," in the section on Quiescence within the *Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa* named *Śrī-saṃsārataraṇi*.
The Sixth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
In this way, O descendant of Raghu, this vast and difficult-to-comprehend illusion, which produces great delusion, is exceedingly perilous and reaches to the very limit of the Self.

Previously, the variety of illusions was described for the sake of calming the mind. Now, it is established through the narrative of Uddālaka that even the flickering mind becomes calm through the practice of yoga on a firm ground—beginning with the words "In this way" (*evam*). It is "pertaining to the Supreme Self" (*pāramātmikī*) because it is of the nature of the power of the Supreme Self.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, I say: this treacherous illusion daily entangles the heedless-minded person in calamity. (2)
But without the supreme medicine of the mere conquest of the mind, the great disease of saṃsāra is not pacified even through effort. (3)
When the mind, for a moment, attends to the present that has arrived in its natural sequence with an outward-directed intellect,
yet does not attend to the past or the future, it attains the state of non-mind (acittatā).

Regarding the phrase "the present": by attending for a mere moment with an indifferent external intellect to the present task alone—that which has arrived in its proper sequence through the force of the order of castes and stages of life—one does not attend to past or future tasks; thus, the mind, by not attending [to them], attains the state of non-mind, which is the state of being free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpatā). || 4 ||
If you abandon the pursuit of intentions and desires at every moment,
then you have indeed attained that purifying state of mindlessness.
He intends: "I shall do exactly thus"—this mental action is *saṃkalpa* (volition). "May this be mine"—this longing is *āśā* (hope). Recollection of the past is *anusandhāna* (recollection). || 5 ||
Indeed, consciousness devoid of the mind is called direct consciousness;
however, in that which has the nature of being without mind, there is no stain of conceptualization.

Regarding the term "consciousness" (*cetana*): consciousness devoid of the mind, free from conceptual construction, is called *caitanya*, the inner consciousness—the consciousness that is the very nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*). In that inner consciousness, because its essential nature is without a mind, there is no stain consisting of mental fabrication (*kalana*), which is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). || 6 ||
That is truth, that is auspiciousness, that is the supreme state of the Self;
that is omniscience, that is contentment—in which indeed the mind is extinguished.
It is thus: in whatever state the mind is wounded—that is, destroyed—that very state is truthfulness, which is to say, freedom from modification;
it is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). That itself is the state of Śiva, which is liberation after death (*videhamukti*). That alone is the supreme state of the Self.
And that alone is omniscience, as well as contentment and the nature of bliss—this is the meaning. || 7 ||
Having withdrawn the mind from its lack of discernment through disciplined resolve, one should forcibly unite it with the scriptures and the conduct of the virtuous. (8)
"Due to non-discrimination" (avivekāt): by means of determinations accompanied by effort— that is,

by determinations joined with enthusiasm (*utsāha*) which serve as the causes for discriminating between the Self and the non-Self, namely valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*)— one should withdraw the mind's activity from non-discrimination, that is, from the identification (*abhimāna*) of the Self with the body and so forth, having extracted it by force through human exertion.
It should be combined with the traditions of the scriptures and the virtuous, with the inner spiritual treatises, and with the sequence of conduct of those who know the Self.
Whether speaking, releasing, grasping, opening, or closing the eyes—
having cast aside the mind, remain intent upon pure consciousness alone in the Infinite.

Now, with five verses, he teaches the contemplation of the Self—beginning with "pralapan" (while prattling). Be intent solely upon that which is pure consciousness, infinite, and free from conceptual construction—the witness of all, the impeller of prattling and other such activities through its mere presence. 9.
Having completely abandoned all latent tendencies such as "this is mine," "that is this," and "I am he," become intent solely upon the pure consciousness residing within through one-pointed devotion.

"Regarding 'mameti' (this is mine): having abandoned the latent impressions of duality—such as 'this is my birth,' 'I am that one,' or 'this is I'—become intent upon the internal pure consciousness alone, through the firm conviction that Brahman is the one and only substratum of all, by virtue of being established in the One. 10. Having cast off the impurity of the object of cognition, purify the mind further.
Having severed the fire of the noose of desires, become one who consists of self-awareness.

Regarding "impurity" (mala): Having completely severed the bonds consisting of desire, and having cast off impurity—which is the very object of perception and the visible world—purify the mind further until it is stainless, and become intent upon your own self-awareness. 11.

Free from the conventions of "pure" and "impure," with the poison-dart of hope completely stilled, and with the vision of the desirable and undesirable destroyed—you become one who is devoted to the essence of pure consciousness. 12.

"Regarding 'impurity' (aśubha): You are one for whom the convention of 'pure' and 'impure' does not exist, and for whom the conceptualization of distinctions—the convention that there is 'pure' and 'impure'—is absent; you are one whose cholera-like affliction consisting of longing has been stilled, and for whom both the perception of the desirable and the perception of the undesirable have perished. As such, become intent upon the essence of pure consciousness. || 12 ||
Having abandoned both selfhood and otherness, remaining free from conceptualization while the world persists,
support yourself like the sacrificial pillar and remain steadfast. (13)

"Regarding the Self": having abandoned the notion of duality within this phenomenal world consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, remain firm and free from conceptual construction, contemplating only the absolute Self alone, like a sacrificial pillar. 13–14.
Then delusion, the cause of the wandering in saṃsāra, is utterly destroyed when one abides in pure, desireless self-awareness. 14.
O Rāma, for one who contemplates the true nature of reality and abides in the state consisting of self-bliss, even a delicious elixir acts like a potent poison.

Regarding the phrase "one's own nature" (*svabhāvam*): for that person who beholds—that is, directly realizes—their own nature (*svabhāva*), which is the very essence of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*), and whose state of being is therefore composed of bliss (*ānandamayī saṃsthitiḥ*), even a delicious and sweet elixir (*rasāyana*) or flavorful substance acts like poison (*prativiṣāyate*), becoming as adverse as venom. This is in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "Other beings subsist on only a fraction of this very Bliss."
When the lack of self-knowledge has long since reached full maturity within the mind, the splendor of light vanishes on all sides, like when a great cloud has arisen. (16)

"From afar," etc. When the mind has attained bulkiness—that is, grossness—due to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of saṃsāra, the knowledge of the Self recedes to a great distance. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that it is like the beauty of light [vanishing] when a vast, immeasurable cloud has arisen; that is, like the consciousness of illumination. || 16 ||
Through the notion of a self in what is not-self, by means of an intellect that clings to the body alone,
and through children, wife, and family, the mind attains fullness.

In response to the inquiry as to how the mind becomes "plump" (*pīvara*), he describes its stoutness with five verses beginning with *anātmani*: "By means of that intellect which, through the cause of regarding what is not-self— such as the body and so forth— as the self, has an attachment— that is, a concern— for the mere body, [the mind attains] stoutness, that is, bulkiness, by way of children, wife, and other dependents who constitute the circle of those to be nourished."
He goes. || 17 ||
Through the transformation of egoism, through the playful impurity of "mine-ness," and through the notion that "this is mine," the mind becomes swollen with attachment. (18)
