Regarding the term *ahaṃkāra*: through the transformation of the form of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), by means of a state of being characterized as "this is mine" (*idaṃ mama*) and so forth, the mind becomes swollen—that is, it attains fullness—by that play or sport (*līlā*, *helā*) of the impurity consisting of possessiveness (*mamatā*). || 18 ||
Through the play of mental and physical afflictions, through finding solace in the cycle of existence,
and through the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, the mind attains fullness.
"Ādhīti" means by means of consolation and by means of a virtuous resolve. || 19 ||
Through affection, greed for wealth, the gain of jewels and women, and that which is pleasant at first sight, the mind becomes swollen with attachment.

Regarding the phrase "by affection" (*sneheneti*): the mind becomes swollen by that greed for wealth which is set in motion by affection for children, wife, and so forth—which is pleasant at first sight but delightful only when unexamined—as well as by the acquisition of jewels and women. || 20 ||
By drinking the milk of false hopes, by the force of the wind of enjoyments,
and by the movement of consolation, the serpent of the mind grows fat.

Regarding the term *durāśā* (evil desire): just as a snake attains corpulence through drinking milk, by the power of its movement in the air, by being properly fed, by being reassured, and by wandering at will—so too does the mind [attain growth] through evil desires and the like. This is the meaning. || 21 ||
O wise one, having repeatedly resolved with your intellect that this body— composed of the five elements— is like a plucked and withered *uddālaka* flower, contemplate it deeply within yourself.
"Like Uddālaka. That which is *ālūna*—meaning cut off on all sides—and *viśīrṇa*—meaning shattered and scattered—is thus described. (Verses 22–33)
Rāma said:
O Blessed One, by what sequence did the sage Uddālaka, having dissected those five elements, investigate them within? || 23 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O Rāma, how in former times Uddālaka attained the supreme, unimpaired vision through the investigation of the multitude of beings.
It is said that on the mountain-king named Gandhamādana, there is a certain plateau strewn with flowers and grey with the pollen of camphor trees.
There, on a certain suitable plateau covered with fruit-bearing trees,
lived a sage named Uddālaka, a practitioner of intense austerities.
At first, he was of little wisdom and lacking in discernment;
thereafter, through the gradual practice of austerity, the meaning of the scriptures, and the observances of niyama and yama, [he became wise].
Having come to solitude, he then reflected thus:
"What might be that supreme goal to be attained, reaching which one no longer grieves? (28)
When shall I find long-lasting rest in that supremely pure state where the mind has been abandoned, like a cloud upon the peak of Mount Meru? (29)
When will these flickering perceptions of enjoyment within me reach peace—those restless thoughts that say, "Having done this, I must do that other thing"? (30)
When shall I, by means of the supreme ship that is wisdom, have completely crossed over this intoxicated river of craving with its many surging waves? (31)
Free from desired and undesired actions, devoid of that which is to be rejected or accepted, when shall I attain well-being, established in the state of self-luminous reality? (32)
With my mind completely stilled, I shall attain a state of equality with a stone in a mountain cave through non-conceptual meditative absorption.
When will the forest maidens build a nest of grass upon my head, as I remain silent, resting in partless meditation? (34)

"Partless" (niraṃśā): for one who is silent through resting in partless meditation, "partless meditation" refers to non-conceptual samādhi (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). "Made of grass" (*tārṇa*) means consisting of grass. A "nest" (*kulāya*) is a bird's nest. "Forest-girls" (*vanaputrikā*) are forest female insects; the honey produced by them is called "putrika-honey. (34, 35, 36)
Thus, the twice-born Uddālaka, overcome by anxiety in the forest,
sat down again and again and practiced meditation.
But as his mind, as restless as a monkey, was being led away by sense objects, he did not attain that state of meditative composure which bestows joy. (36)
Sometimes, immediately after abandoning external contacts,
the monkey of his mind moved toward the accumulation of internal contacts.

"Sometimes" (kadācit) [is used]. "Touches" (sparśāḥ) refers to objects (viṣayāḥ). By abandoning external touches—that is, by abandoning external objects—one [attains] the accumulation of internal touches, which are the multitudes of objects imagined through the mind's desires (manoratha-parikalpita). || 37 || 38 ||
Sometimes, due to an internal touch, he grasps an external object;
then his mind flies away like a frightened bird. (38)
Sometimes he perceives a pervasive radiance resembling the rising sun;
sometimes he sees only empty space, and sometimes dense darkness.

"At some time" means: when *rajas* predominates, one sees an expansive light resembling the rising sun; when *sattva* predominates, however, one sees only the void; and when *tamas* predominates, one sees dense darkness—this is the distinction. (39–43)
Thus, with his mind agitated and tossing about in various states of meditation,
he wandered upon the mountain, his heart deeply distressed and devoid of delight.
Once, having reached a cave that was difficult for all people to find—a place where all movement had completely ceased, like the state of liberation—[he dwelt there]. (41)
The righteous-souled one entered that cave of Mount Gandhamādana;
he prepared a seat with unfading leaves, its interior filled with clusters of blossoms.
He spread a beautiful deer-skin upon his back;
there he sat down, bringing his mind to a state of attenuation through intense absorption.
Having assumed the lotus posture very firmly like Budha, facing north,
and holding his testicles with both heels, he formed the Brahma-añjali.
"Like Budha" means as follows: this is the lotus posture (padmāsana) intended here, as stated in the *Agastya-saṃhitā*:

"When both feet are properly and evenly placed upon the two roots of the thighs, that is indeed the lotus posture, praised for all ritual acts. Therefore, having supported the testicles with the two heels—that is, the back parts of the feet—...

The phrase "having restrained" is thus justified by the statement, "he formed the *brahmāñjali*. The so-called *brahmāñjali* is the positioning of the two hands, turned upward and facing each other, at the time of meditating upon Brahman;
and this constitutes a limb (*aṅga*) of this *padmāsana*. As it is stated in another scripture: "The left foot is placed upward upon the right thigh..."

One should place [the feet] thus: one should set the left foot, turned upward, upon the right thigh. In the middle of that, one should place the two hands, turned upward and extended, with the left hand on the left [thigh] and the other on the right; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Standing with steady gazes, one should look at the tip of the nose. This they call the *padmāsana*, the foremost among practices such as meditation. And so it is said:

Kālidāsa: With the upper body made steady by the paryaṅka posture, and both shoulders bent forward in a straight, extended manner, he resembles a full-blown lotus in the center of his lap due to the placement of his two palms turned upward. (44–46)
Having drawn out the agitated deer of the mind from its habitual tendencies (vāsanās), he undertook this investigation for the sake of non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi). (45)
O fool, what purpose do you have for the activities of worldly existence?
The wise do not pursue actions that result in suffering in the end. 46.
He who pursues enjoyments after having abandoned the elixir of tranquility is like one who,
having left behind a grove of *mandāra* trees, goes toward a poisonous desert. (47)
"He runs after" means: a forest abounding in poisonous thorns and poison trees. 47–48.
Whether you go to the subterranean realm or even to the world of Brahmā,
you shall find no peace there without the nectar of cessation.
These various mental constructions, consisting of existence and non-existence, lead only to suffering and terrible fear; they never lead to happiness. (49)

"Imāḥ" means conceptual constructions (*kalanāḥ*, *kalpanāḥ*). "Consisting of existence and non-existence" (*bhāvābhāvamayātmikāḥ*): because they have existent and non-existent things as their objects, their nature (*ātman*) or essential form (*svarūpa*) consists of both existence and non-existence; these are such [constructions]. "To the fierce one through fear" (*bhayogrāya*): to him who is formidable (*ugra*) by virtue of his fear. (49)
O fool, what is the use of these [senses] directed toward sound and other objects, which have their functions destroyed?
Why do you not pursue that state of tranquility of mind, O fool, from which you might obtain something and in which you might find contentment? (50)

"Sound and so forth" (śabdādīti): "Sound-and-so-forth-going" (śabdādigāḥ) refers to those [senses] which go toward objects such as sound; by means of them. "Since" (yasmāt): since from that tranquility (śama) you obtain some purpose in the form of liberation (kaivalya). "In which" (yasmin): in which tranquility being present you carry—that is, attain—contentment (nirvṛtti), which is the bliss of one's own nature; why do you not place your foot upon that tranquility?
You do not run after it, nor do you bind yourself to it. || 50 ||
O fool, having come here to the state of being a listener, do not go to ruin like a deer through a mind that merely follows sounds, nourished by futile exertions. 51.

"Having come"—having attained the state of being the faculty of hearing (*śrotratā*), which is augmented by a useless exertion through the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) that follows sound with a desire to hear; do not go to your destruction like a deer attached to the song of a hunter. 51.
O fool, do not be bound by that skin which, having come under your power, is intent on contact for the sake of suffering; do not approach it like the lordly elephant lusting after a female elephant.

"O skin! Do not come to this state of being bound by becoming the sense-organ of touch (*tvagindriyatva*), which leads only to suffering through such a longing for touch—that desire for the experience of pleasure worthy of touch—just as the lordly elephant, lusting after a female elephant, meets his destruction. (52)
Having come into the presence of the tongue, do not go to your destruction through greed for those who are blind with craving, like a fish greedy for a baited hook. (53)

Regarding the verse beginning with *rasanā*: O tongue, having assumed the state of the gustatory sense-organ through greed—that is, through the longing for the taste—of bad food (*durandhas*), do not go to your destruction like a fish greedy for a baited hook (*baḍiśapiṇḍī*). A *baḍiśa* is a fish-hook; a *piṇḍī* is the small lump of meat attached to it. || 53 ||
Relying on the visual function that tends toward the accumulation of light-forms, O fool, do not meet with destruction like a moth greedy for radiance. (54)

"And *cākṣuṣīm* (visible to the eye)" means: intent upon the accumulation of the form of light—that is, attentive toward the apprehension of the accumulation of a form endowed with beauty through its radiance. || 54 ||
Resorting to the path of the nose within the hollow of the lotus-body, do not take up bondage out of a longing for fragrance, like a bee.

Regarding the word "ghrāṇa": the construction is that, by being oriented toward fragrance, you should not resort to bondage within the hollow of the lotus of the body by taking recourse to the path of the nose. || 55 ||
The deer, the bee, the moth, the elephant, and the fish are each destroyed by one [of these senses];
O ignorant one, how can there be happiness for one who is beset by all these calamities? 56.
"Kuraṅga" means: one by one, with each individual object of the senses, such as sound and so forth. 56.
If that net of mental impressions (vāsanā) which binds you on all sides within existence is stilled by being abandoned, then your victory shall be infinite. 57.

He addresses the mind: "O mind, for your very bondage, a web of latent impressions (vāsanā) spreads out on all sides. If you abandon that web of latent impressions and become tranquil, then you shall achieve infinite, boundless victory. || 57 ||
(443) For what purpose, then, do I perform this instruction of yours,
since for a person possessed of discernment, even the state of being a mind does not exist? 58.

"I am doing [this]. For a person possessed of inquiry—who investigates what this so-called "mind" is apart from the Self—the mind itself does not exist. The meaning is that, because it is not established through inquiry, it does not manifest as a distinct "this. || 58 ||
The subtle abiding of the infinite reality of the Self within the mind is not possible, just as it is impossible for an elephant to reside within a wood-apple fruit. (59)

Regarding the phrase "of the infinite": just as it is impossible for an elephant to reside within the interior of a *bilva* fruit, so too it is impossible for the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is unlimited by space, time, and other such factors, to abide in the subtle mind; this is the meaning.
From the big toe up to the head, it has been analyzed down to its very atoms;
that which is called "I" has not been found—what could this be that stands as "I"? (60)

"Regarding 'the foot': Starting from the big toe up to the head, I have examined [the body] bit by bit. Therein, within the body from the feet to the tips of the hair, the referent of the word 'I' was not found. This is the inquiry directed toward the mind: 'What could be the entity that exists as "I"? (60)"
I perceive that one [reality] which fills every corner of the directions within the three worlds—a consciousness that is itself beyond being perceived, its nature pervading everywhere. (61)

The two verses beginning with "bharita" form a single syntactical unit. The connection is as follows: I perceive that one consciousness alone—which is such that its limits and so forth are not seen, which is thus unperceivable by other means of cognition, and which is not illuminated by any other light—filling every corner and nook of all directions. 61.
Of which no limit is perceived, nor indeed any conceptual construction;
neither unity nor plurality, neither grossness nor subtlety. (62)

Limitation (*iyattā*) is the state of being circumscribed. Unity (*ekatā*) is the connection with the number one. Multiplicity (*nānātā*) is differentiation. Coarseness (*sthūlatā*) and magnitude (*mahattā*) are specific types of dimension (*parimāṇa*). || 62 ||
"Since you are easily perceived by me because of your nature as a feeling, you— the cause of my suffering—
are destroyed by me through this awakening born of discernment. (63)

"Because it is of the nature of feeling. O mind, because I am self-cognizable and self-luminous due to being of the nature of knowledge—that is, being of the nature of feeling—you arise as the cause of my suffering; therefore, for that reason, you are destroyed by me through this awakening born of discrimination.
"This is flesh, this is blood, these are the bones in the body;
these are your breath-winds—what is this that is called 'I'? Such is the state of things. (64)

"This" refers to this: among the flesh and other such things perceived as "this," what is the referent of the word "I"? None at all; for there is a contradiction between "this-ness" and "I-ness. || 64 ||
O mind, flesh is one thing, blood another, and bones yet others; consciousness is one thing and movement another—what then is this state of "I"? (65)
"Regarding 'flesh': since flesh and the like are perceived as distinct from the self, the notion of 'I-ness' (ahantā) is not tenable; this is the meaning.
In that context, 'cognition' (bodha) refers to the function of the sensory organs. || 65 ||
"This is the nose, this is the tongue, this is the skin, these are the ears, this is the eye, and this is the movement—what is this state of 'I'? (66)

"This" refers to the following: since the sense organs such as the nose and so forth are also perceived as "this," they are not the referent of the word "I. In that context, "spanda" (vibration) refers to the group of action organs (*karmendriya*), which are the cause of activity. || 66 ||
"I alone indeed exist everywhere, or else I do not exist as anything at all here"—such is the vision consisting of pure Being; no other sequence exists.

"I am"—in this world, whether it be the view that "I alone am perceived everywhere" or the view that "nothing whatsoever perceived here is I," that very [view] is composed of Being (sanmayī) and is real. The other sequence, which consists of the notion of "I" directed toward limited objects, does not exist;
that is to say, it is not real. || 67 ||
For a long time, I have been crushed by the ego-sense, which is like a haughty wolf in the forest crushing a young animal, acting as a rogue through ignorance. (68)

"For a long time" (ciram iti): In this manner, I have been struck—that is, harmed—by the rogue named Ignorance (ajñāna), who for a long time has been delimited by the ego-sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā). He is like a proud wolf that destroys the young of livestock, such as cattle, in the forest; such is the meaning. || 68 ||
By good fortune, this thief of ignorance has now been fully recognized by me;
I shall never again take refuge in it, for it robs one of the true nature of reality. (69)
"By good fortune!"—the meaning is: "Now, by good fortune—that is, by my merit—this thief in the form of ignorance has been recognized.
I shall no longer take refuge in this thief of ignorance, which robs one of its very nature, for its nature alone is the true wealth. || 69 || 70 || 71 ||
Even devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā), this sense-faculty such as the eye functions by itself toward its own external object; latent impressions are not the cause here.
Therefore, O all of you, having abandoned the foolish senses and your own internal latent impressions, perform every action; thus you shall not encounter suffering.
O childish senses, you have been ruined by craving alone, in vain,
just as silkworms are destroyed by the thread spun from their own bodies.
"By craving alone": like silkworms by the very thread produced from themselves, you have been pointlessly destroyed by craving alone, which was born of yourselves. || 72 ||

O mind, you are the treasury of all the senses; therefore, having surely attained oneness with all the senses, behold the Self as being of an unreal nature, and abide in Nirvana, which is singular, stainless, and pure consciousness. 73.
"O Citta!"—O Mind, you who are the sheath of all the senses, to be relied upon by all [the organs] beginning with the eye like a protective covering;

therefore, for the reason previously stated, having attained oneness with all the senses, and having perceived—that is, investigated—your own self, your own form, as being non-existent in its nature (*asatsvarūpa*), meaning its essential being is non-manifest (*avidyamānasvabhāva*), [you shall attain] the stainless, singular awakening (*ekāmalabodha*); "one" (*eka*) means absolute (*kevala*).
Remain in nirvāṇa, with all activity ceased, so that there may be stainless awakening. || 73 ||

Having skillfully cast off the endless cholera of the poison of sense-objects— the latent tendencies for existence— through the application of the mantra that abandons what is desired, become the Lord of prosperity, a ground beyond all fears.

"Regarding the objects [of sense]: O mind, having skillfully cast away the cholera of the poison of objects—an endless cholera consisting of objects and produced by objects—as well as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of egoistic persistence, through the application of mantras in the form of abandoning desired things; become the Blessed One (*bhagavān*), free from worldly existence (*vigata-saṃsāra*) and no longer a ground for fears. (74)
Uddālaka said:
Having cut down the forest of the mind—the tree of volition and the creeper of craving—and having reached the vast expanse of the ground, I dwell in happiness as I please. (75)

I have cut down that forest of the mind, in which volitions alone are the trees and cravings alone are the creepers; having reached the vast ground whose nature is the space of consciousness, I dwell there at ease. 75.
I follow that very path; I am alone, I am victorious.
I am extinguished, I am partless, I am effortless, and I am free from desire.
Regarding the word *padam*: since I am alone due to being without a mind (*nirmanaskatva*), I have therefore attained that state, which is the nature of Brahman.
Consequently, through the cessation of the threefold suffering, I am extinguished (*nirvāṇa*). Because of my perfection, I am partless (*niraṃśa*);

and because my desires are fulfilled, I am free from longing (*nirīpsita*); and because of that, I am effortless (*nirīha*); and because of that, I am victorious—this is the connection [of the verses]. || 76 ||
Purity, vigor, existence, loveliness, truthfulness, and wisdom;
bliss, tranquility, honor, and joyous emergence. || 77 ||

"Transparency," etc., constitutes a group of three verses forming a single syntactical unit. The meaning is that Transparency and the other qualities are my beloveds, the dear ones of my heart, who delight the heart during the state of worldly emergence (*vyutthāna*). In this context, "transparency" (*svacchatā*) is the absence of impurity in the mind;

"vigor" (*ūrjitatā*) is the absence of dejection; "existence" (*sattā*) is the nature of being real; "loveliness" (*hṛdyatā*) is being dear to all; and "truthfulness" (*satyatā*) is the state of being uncontradicted.

*Jñatā* is the state of being a knower; *ānanditā* is the nature of bliss; *upaśamitā* is the state of being changeless; *sadoditā* and *muditā* are joy and delight in meritorious deeds; *pūrṇatā* is pervasiveness; *satyā* is real, vast, and supreme excellence; *kāntimattā* is the radiance of the face that manifests the mind of Brahman; *ekatā* is the absence of duality; *matā* is that which is esteemed; [all this is] the oneness of all.
The state of being the self of all; fearlessness is confidence; the cessation of the conceptualization of duality is the absence of conceptual constructions such as duality and so forth.
Fullness, magnanimity, truthfulness, radiance, and oneness are considered [the qualities of the Self].
Oneness with all, fearlessness, and the cessation of the conceptualization of duality [are its further characteristics]. (78)
These women, eternally risen, established in their own nature, beautiful, and dawning with auspicious fortune, are forever my beloveds, dear to the heart of me, whose self is one. 79.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus resolved with that pure intellect, the sage remained seated in the lotus posture with his eyes half-closed.
He uttered the syllable Oṃ with a piercing sound whose resonance rose upward,
like the ringing of a bell struck firmly by its clapper.

"Oṃkāram iti": His tail was struck and beaten correctly so that a staff-like [stiffness] hung from its middle; therefore, like a bell-pitcher—meaning like a bell in the shape of a bowl—he produced a sound that pervaded the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), a resonance with a loud tone of the syllable *oṃ* whose upward-moving vibration resounded on all sides.
As he utters "Om," while his consciousness is directed toward that [reality],
it extends upward into the Omkāra, which is situated above, expansive, and pure in its essence.

The phrase "omiti" refers to three verses. As that Uddālaka was uttering "om," while his consciousness-principle—his own essential self-awareness—was directed toward it and following the resonance of the *oṃkāra*, and while that pure Self remained situated above, facing upward, expanded and all-pervading, for as long as the *oṃkāra* lasted—that is, until the completion of its continuous recitation—[the vision occurred]. || 82 ||
When the first of the three and a half measures of the *praṇava* has become clearly resonant, when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is thoroughly agitated, and the body is vibrating with sound; (83)
Of that [Oṃkāra] whose nature consists of three and a half measures— meaning those measures whose essence (ātman) is three parts together with a half;
the meaning is "consisting of three measures plus one half-measure"— of that Praṇava, the Oṃkāra, when the vital breath is perfectly agitated (*samākṣubdha*), it is equal (*sama*).

When the first portion, consisting of the letter *A*, is characterized by a single mode of vibration, the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—the life-force wind—is undisturbed; and when that first part possesses a distinct resonance, with its body made resonant by a manifest sound, (p.
During the process known as *recaka*, the sequence of the departure of the vital breath emptied his entire body,
just as Agastya emptied the ocean by drinking its waters.

Regarding *recaka*: the process of the exit of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) known as *recaka* emptied the entire body, like Agastya [emptied] the ocean of yellow water. Furthermore, this fact that the *praṇava* consists of three and a half measures is established by the statement in the *Atharvaśikhā Upaniṣad*, "Exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*)," and by the words of Yājñavalkya regarding exhalation and the other [breath-controls].
It should be understood that the manifestation of those whose nature consists of the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*—which are the constituent parts of the *praṇava* (OM)—is logical. || 84 ||
The vital breath remained in the sky filled with the essence of consciousness, and the fire of the heart, with its blazing flames, consumed the impure body. (85)

"He remained" means that the vital breath (prāṇapavana), filled with the essence of consciousness (cidrasa) within the space of the ether (ambare), remained there. The meaning is that the prāṇa, expelled by the exhaling breath (recaka), remained restrained in that very same space. And the fire of the heart (hṛdayāgni), kindled by the recaka and possessing blazing flames, burnt away the impure body consisting of sin. || 85 ||
This state continued as long as desired during the first stage of the *praṇava*;
it did not occur through force, for *haṭhayoga* indeed brings suffering. (86)
"Up to this point": this is the state of the *praṇava* (the sacred syllable Om) during the first stage of *prāṇāyāma*, consisting of exhalation (*recaka*).
It continued "as long as desired," meaning for as long as the will persisted; it did not occur through force or compulsion.
Why? Because *haṭhayoga* is painful. *Haṭhayoga* is defined as follows: [text continues]
Through the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) and other methods, the mind is restrained by means of forcibly arresting the vital breath (prāṇa). || 86 ||
Then, at the time for the other parts, while he remained established in the *praṇava*,
there occurred a sequence of the vital breaths known as *kumbhaka*, which is motionless. (87)

Now, "atha" (then): after the cessation of the space filled with the essence of consciousness by the vital breath (*prāṇapavana*), when he was established in equanimity— that is, in that state where the mind remains steady— at the occasion of the other parts of the *praṇava*, during the moment of meditating on the form of the second part consisting of the syllable *U*, as Uddālaka was uttering "Om," there occurred a motionless, unshakable *kumbhaka* (retention of breath).

The sequence of the vital breaths occurred. The meaning is that, within that very space previously filled with the essence of consciousness (*cidrasa*), the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) was restrained; then, by the power of that effort, it took on the form of *kumbhaka* (retention) therein. And here, because the *praṇava* consists of the three phonemes beginning with *a*, [the sequence of those...]

It should be understood that the sequence of breath control (prāṇāyāma), beginning with exhalation (recaka) and so forth, is being set forth through the repetition of the Praṇava preceded by meditation on the respective forms [of the deities], since they possess the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. || 87 ||
Neither outside nor inside, neither below nor above, nor in the intermediate directions were they found;
their breaths did not falter, remaining as motionless as air confined within a leather bag.
He describes that very state of motionlessness of the *kumbhaka* with the word "not" (*na*). "Outside" means outside the body;

"inside" means within the body. "Below and above" means below and above that space-body (*ākāśadeha*) in which the breath is restrained. In that *kumbhaka*, [it is like] in a leather bag (*dṛti*). || 88 ||
The fire that had consumed the city was extinguished in an instant like a thunderbolt;
only white ash was seen, the body turned pale as snow. (89)
The two verses beginning with "dagdha" form a single syntactical unit: "By him, the city in the form of the body was burnt; that fire was extinguished in an instant like a thunderbolt. (89)
Where the bones of the body are seen white and motionless, as if they had slept comfortably upon a bed of camphor. (90)

The grammatical connection is as follows: the body became invisible like ashes—that body upon which the bones of the frame were seen, appearing as if they had slept comfortably on a bed of camphor amidst white ashes. || 90 ||
The wind carried that ash along with the bones, and the wind joined them together;
tossed by that fierce gale, it covered the sky in an instant.
Like a cloud or mist in autumn, the liquor vanished somewhere into ashes and bones.

Regarding the word "tat": that bone-laden ash, having been carried upward by a fierce wind, covered the sky like a cloud accompanied by frost in autumn—a mere vapor—and in an instant vanished somewhere. || 91 ||
This state of the *praṇava* continued for as long as desired through the subsequent stage;
it did not occur by force alone, for haṭhayoga is indeed a source of suffering.
"As long as" means: this state of the *praṇava*—which is essentially the *praṇava*—and of the *prāṇāyāma* in its subsequent form of *kumbhaka*, continued for as long as he desired. || 92 ||
Then, on the third occasion, during the tranquilizing of the *praṇava*, there arose the process known as "filling" (*pūraka*), which consists of filling the vital breaths. (93)

Regarding the word "tataḥ": after that, following the *kumbhaka* (retention), during the occasion of the third part of the *praṇava*—the syllable *oṃ*, which consists of the letter *m*—and at the moment of meditating on its form situated in that third portion, because of the filling (*pūraṇa*) of him who is uttering *oṃ*, the sequence of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) known as *pūraka* (inhalation) came into being. || 93 ||
At that moment, the vital breaths, dwelling within the nectar of consciousness,
attained a coolness in the sky as beautiful as the touch of snow.

Regarding the phrase "In that": at that moment, during the phase of inhalation (*pūraka*), the vital breaths—the *prāṇa* winds—having entered the midst of the nectar of consciousness within the ether, and being situated in the center of that which is consciousness itself as nectar, attained a beautiful coolness through the touch of frost. || 94 ||
Gradually, situated in the midst of the sky, the smokes attained the state of lunar discs, like cool clouds abiding within the expanse of the firmament. (95)

"Gradually," it is said: those vital breaths (*prāṇas*), situated in the midst of the sky, gradually attained the state of the lunar orb, just as smoke residing in the expanse of the sky attains the state of cool clouds. (95)
Within that lunar disc, complete with its full array of digits,
the vital breaths have become great streams of elixir. (96)
Regarding the word "kāla" (time): those vital breaths (*prāṇavāyu*) have become great streams of the nectar of the elixir (*rasāyana*).

The meaning is that they have attained the form of streams of ambrosia (*sudhā*). Although the stream is singular, the term "became" (*saṃpannāḥ*) is used with the intention of emphasizing the plurality of the constituent vital breaths, just as one says "the Brahmins have assembled."
The plural number. || 96 ||
That stream fell from the sky onto the ashes of Śiva’s body,
like the life-restoring river that fell long ago upon the head of Hara.

It fell—this elixir, a stream consisting of nectar—from the sky, as in the past the river Bhāgīrathī fell upon the head of Hara; it fell upon the remaining ashes of the body. 97 || 98 || 99 || 100 || 1 || 2 ||
That auspicious body of Uddālaka, possessing four arms and shining like the orb of the moon, arose as Nārāyaṇa. 98.
The vital breaths, consisting of the elixir of life, filled his body;
then, with great care, they filled the Kuṇḍalinī within.
Then, seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), having made the stability of the body firm,
he bound the five senses as one binds an elephant to its tethering post.
With his mind, he forcibly restrained the heart— fickle as a bee— in the lotus of his chest, just as a dam holds back rushing water.
She closed her eyes, which were beautiful with full lashes and motionless pupils,
like a lotus at twilight.
Maintaining silence, he brought serenity to the movement of the prāṇa and apāna breaths in his mouth;
with great effort, he withdrew the senses from their respective objects.

"Saumyatayā" (with gentleness): being silent, he brought the force of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*—in the form of inhalation and exhalation—to a state of gentleness, that is, to tranquility. He withdrew the senses from the objects of the senses; the meaning is that he drew them back. || 3 ||
That man of steadfast intellect completely abandoned external contacts at a distance;
by relinquishing his visual perception, he caused internal contacts to dissolve. (4)
Regarding the word "external": it refers to objects of touch. "Vision" refers to functioning cognition (vṛttijñāna). || 4 ||
Then, by contracting his anus, he obstructed the winds of the nine gates,
just as a jar with its mouth covered blocks the other apertures of its interior.
"Rurodha" (he restrained): Then, by means of the vajrāsana and other postures, through the contraction of the anus and the obstruction of the *mūlādhāra*, he restrained the winds of the nine gates.

"Mukhe" (in the mouth): His mouth was sealed (*saṃsthagita*), that is, covered, like other cavities with apertures. The meaning is: just as the wind is restrained within the subtle apertures of a jar when its mouth is sealed, so it was here. [Verses 5–6]
The hero bore his neck— richly adorned with the light of the reality of the self, clear, and marked by the flower (the moon)— like the peak of the summit of Mount Meru.
He bore within the space of his heart a mind that had attained self-restraint,
like a rutting elephant subdued by skillful means within a pit in the Vindhya mountains.

"He sustained" (babhāra): he sustained—that is, held—his mind, which had attained and reached self-restraint (*saṃyama*) and training (*śikṣā*), within the space of the heart known as the *dahara*, like an intoxicated elephant brought under control by means of skillful methods and placed in a pit or cave of the Vindhya mountains.
Then, having attained a stainless clarity and gentleness like that of the autumnal sky,
he washed away the floods of conceptual constructions that had appeared as mental images.
Like autumn, he washed away—that is, he cast out. || 8 || 9 ||
As the mental images appeared again and again according to his desire,
the hero cut them down with his mind, just as one cuts down enemies with a sword in battle.

When the flood of conceptual constructions had been severed by the Supreme, he beheld within his heart that which was shrouded in darkness, where the sun of discernment was eclipsed, and which was as black as flickering lampblack.
He conceptualizes: "Tamas" is ignorance, which serves as the cause of conceptualization; it is dark like flickering lampblack or like crushed ink—deep black and of a soiled hue. || 110 ||
He also destroyed that [darkness] with the sun of his perfectly clear mind;
when the darkness had ceased, he beheld a lovely mass of light.
He trampled the forest of land-lotuses like a young elephant. || 11 ||

"Even that," he says: even that darkness (tamas) he dispelled by means of the discernment residing within his own internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Then, when the darkness had ceased, he beheld the light, which is the modification of the quality of goodness (sattvaguṇa) in the form of radiance. And having seen it, he shattered—that is, cut through—even that light.
When the light had ceased, the mind of the sage began to whirl.
He fell asleep like a night-lotus, but he quickly shattered even that sleep.

Regarding the phrase "in the fiery [state]": when the functioning of the *sattva* quality within the fiery state has ceased, his mind, reeling and finding no rest, again enters the tamasic state of sleep. This is because the qualities of *sattva* and the others undergo transformation through mutual suppression. As it is said in the Sāṃkhya: "They consist of pleasure, pain, and despondency..."
Their purposes are illumination, activity, and restraint; and the qualities (guṇas) function through mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship.
Upon the departure of his sleep, the consciousness of space arose within him;
when that consciousness of space had vanished, his mind became bewildered.
This noble-minded one purified even that deluded mind of his. || 13 ||
Sleep is consciousness in the form of space, appearing as a void; it is a state of consciousness that is deluded and inert due to a lack of cognitive engagement. 13.
Then, having attained a certain indescribable state entirely free from light, darkness, sleep, delusion, and the like,
his mind rested for a moment.

"Then" means: having attained a certain state—a state free from light, darkness, sleep, delusion, and so forth, since light and the rest are merely transformations of the qualities such as *sattva*—that state being non-conceptual and the state of *samādhi*, the mind found rest; it remained established in the Self. || 14 ||
Having quickly found rest, he fell into a state of consciousness of his own limbs that assumed universal forms,
like the water of a lake dammed by a bridge flowing backward toward its own source.
"Rests" (viśrāmyati) means: she who possesses all forms, whose essence is everything—the consciousness of the limbs, which is filled with the consciousness of one's own true nature;

that is to say, the consciousness of the identity of Brahman and the Self. Like the water of a lake obstructed by a dam, which, having turned back against its flow, returns to its own source, the lake that serves as its original location. || 15 ||
Through long-continued inquiry and from the relishing of his own consciousness,
his mind attained the state of pure spirit, just as base metal attains the state of a golden anklet.

It took a long time. Through the power of long-term contemplation on his own true nature, by tasting—that is, relishing—the consciousness of the bliss of his own self-awareness, his mind attained the state of being composed of pure consciousness (cinmaya), just as [the dust] attained the state of a golden anklet. || 16 ||
Then, having completely abandoned its state as mind, the mind attained the nature of pure consciousness; it quickly became something entirely different, just like mud remaining inside a jar.

Regarding the phrase "the state of being mind" (*cittatvam*): immediately thereafter, the mind as an agent, having completely abandoned the state of being mind—that is, the form of the mind—became something entirely different upon attaining *cit-tattva*, the ultimate reality of consciousness. The meaning is that it became consciousness itself.
Just as the mud situated in a jar, through the passage of time, abandons its form as mud when the water has dissolved;
Just as a potter's wheel returns to the state of a clod of earth, so it is in that case. || 17 ||
Having completely abandoned the object of consciousness, the pure consciousness attained the state of universal consciousness,
just as the ocean, having abandoned distinctions such as waves and the like, becomes a single mass of water.

Regarding the term *cetyam* (the object of consciousness): having abandoned the object of consciousness (*cetya*), the Cit—the conscious agent—becoming pure, attained the state of *cit-sāmānya*, which is the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) that persists through all things, because it has cast off distinctions such as waves and the like. Just as the ocean, being the single object of a uniform cognition (*ekadhī*), becomes the *vāḥ-sāmānya*, the state of pure water. || 18 ||
Then, having abandoned the mental preoccupation with the flood of enjoyments, he attained awakening and became the great Viśvaṃbhara, the pure space of consciousness. || 19 ||

"Having abandoned": having attained awakening, which is the direct realization of one's own true nature (*svarūpasākṣātkāra*), he became the pure, great space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), the sustainer of the universe, which is free from the mentalization of the flood of enjoyments—that is, in which the functions of all external and internal senses have been completely relinquished.
There he attained bliss, free from both the seen and the seeing;
it was infinite, of supreme flavor, like an ocean of elixir.

In that regard: there, in the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), he attained an elixir in the form of nectar, like an ocean, devoid of both the seen and the seeing, possessing supreme savor, infinite bliss. 120.
Having completely transcended the body, he reached a certain state;
being one whose self is the nature of pure existence, he became an ocean of bliss.

"From the body" means having transcended the body, having emerged from the state of being a living soul (jīva), [he reached] some ground whose nature is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 21 ||
This swan of the consciousness of the twice-born, remaining steady in the lake of bliss,
stayed in the autumn-clear sky like the moon full of its digits.

Regarding the word *dvija*: "the swan of the consciousness of the twice-born" means the conscious being who has attained the state of the Supreme Self-swan (*paramātma-haṃsa*) while appearing in the form of the twice-born Uddālaka. "The boat" refers to the moon. || 22 ||
He became like a lamp sheltered from the wind, resembling a figure depicted in a painting;
he was like the ocean of the Avīci hell, remaining as silent as a cloud that has finished raining.

"He became" (babhūva) means: his state was like that of a cloud which has ceased raining and become silent—that is, a cloud that has finished its downpour and is now mute and soundless. 23 || 24 || 25 || 26 || 27 ||
Then Uddālaka remained for a long time in this great world;
he beheld numerous Siddhas and even immortals moving through the sky.
Various nets of supernatural powers arrived from all sides;
yet that twice-born man paid no heed to those multitudes of siddhis.
Disregarding the caravan of supernatural powers (siddhis), he then remained for six months in that temple of his own bliss, like the northern peak of a mountain.
That state of liberation while living which that twice-born man attained is where the Siddhas, Suras, Sādhyas, and Brahmā, Hara, and others reside. (27)
Because bliss has been transformed, he has reached the state beyond bliss;
neither in bliss nor in the absence of bliss did that consciousness then manifest. (28)

"Ānandeti" means: because that Uddālaka had attained the state of non-bliss—a state devoid of bliss distinct from his own essential nature—due to being transformed into bliss, that is, having been transformed into the form of bliss; for that reason, his consciousness did not shine, meaning the consciousness of Uddālaka did not manifest as having bliss as its object within that state of non-bliss.
Because there is no bliss apart from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), that which is devoid of bliss did not appear as an object consisting of a blissless entity;
for it is the very essence itself that manifests everywhere in the form of bliss. || 28 ||
That is the state, that is the goal of Śambhu; that is the eternal and auspicious supreme good.
Having attained that state, the virtuous remain for a moment or for a hundred years.
"That state" (tatpadam) refers to the state consisting of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 29 ||
They enter into the vision of the visible, yet it does not produce further rebirth. || 130 ||

"Regarding 'dṛśya' (the visible): it refers to the perception of the visible, which is the cause of saṃsāra, which brings about rebirth, and which is the manifestation of conceptual proliferation (prapañca)."
Having dwelt there for six months, with his ground for supernatural powers far removed, Uddālaka woke up and beheld the Siddhas bearing the forms of the moon.

"Uddālaka. In this state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the ground of supernatural powers (*siddhibhū*) has been cast far away—that is, by him, the realm of heaven and other such attainments has been distantly expelled and rejected. [They were] bearing moon-like forms, as enchanting as the moon itself. 31–37.
Then they spoke to that high-souled Uddālaka Muni, who was surrounded by Vidyādhara lords and Vidyādharīs.
Out of grace, at the conclusion of this salutation, O Blessed One, look upon me;
having ascended this celestial chariot, come to the city of the gods.
For heaven alone is the ultimate limit of the riches of worldly enjoyment; O Lord, enjoy for an entire kalpa those desired pleasures that are appropriate to you.
When the Siddhas had spoken thus, the sage, having honored those guests according to the rule, remained composed and free from agitation. (35)
That man of steady intellect did not rejoice in it;
he abandoned that prosperity, saying, "O Siddhas, go away," and became intent upon his own practice.
Then, after only a few days, the Siddhas themselves approached that venerable one, who was devoted to his own duty and had attained a lack of interest in worldly enjoyments.
And that sage, liberated while living, wandered at his pleasure as long as he desired through the forest regions and the hermitages of sages.
Sometimes after a day, sometimes after a month, sometimes after a year,
and sometimes after a succession of years, he, absorbed in meditation, awoke.
Through the intense practice of the singular essence of consciousness, he attained the state of the Great Consciousness;
through long-term practice of universal consciousness, he reached the state of universal existence.

Regarding the term *cittattva*: from the intense and uninterrupted practice (*ghana-abhyāsa*), that is, the continuous contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) of the single reality of consciousness (*cittattva*); from that, one attains *mahācittva*, the state of the perfectly full consciousness.
He himself will later explain that *cit* is the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*) following Rāma’s question. || 140 ||
With his mind completely stilled through the attainment of the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), his worldly lamentations dissolved, and the oscillation of doubt extinguished,
he bore his own body— tranquil like an autumn day, expansive, powerful, manifest, and stainless— as one devoid of [discursive] mind. (41)
It is equanimity; it is the state of the flavor of equality, the state of liberation while living. 41 || 42 ||
Rāma said:
O Lord, are you the sole sun for the day of self-knowledge, the forest fire for the grass of my doubts, the moon that cools the burning of ignorance, and the universal existence itself? (42)
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the mind is completely dissolved through the cultivation of absolute non-existence,
then there is the state of universal existence for that which has the nature of universal consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "yadā" (when): because of the continuous contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of the absolute non-existence [of the world]—that is, due to the constant reflection based on scripture, reasoning, and personal experience that the object of perception does not exist in reality even throughout the three periods of time—the mind is thoroughly dissolved and merges;
at that time, the Self, whose nature is universal consciousness (*cit-sāmānya*), attains the state of universal existence (*sattā-sāmānyata*).
The meaning is that, due to the absence of the mind which is the cause of distraction, only the existence of the self's own essential nature remains. || 43 ||
When consciousness, devoid of the aspect of "this," dissolves into itself,
it then becomes the generality of existence (sattāsāmānyatā), exceedingly transparent and appearing as if non-existent.

"Surely," [it is said]. When the mind has dissolved, the consciousness reflected in the fluctuations of the mind (citta-vṛtti)—being devoid of the objective aspect (cetyāṃśa) because of the absence of the mind that acts as a container, and thus free from connection with any object—becomes utterly transparent and, as if non-existent (asadrūpavat), merges into the Self; then, for the Self, which is dense consciousness (ghanībhūta-cit), [there remains only pure being].
The state of universal existence is accomplished. || 44 ||
When the mind dwells having negated all this— whatever exists, including the internal and external aspects— then it abides in the state of universal existence (sattāsāmānyatā).

Regarding the verse beginning with *yadā*: when the mind (*cetas*), as the agent, having negated and removed all this—consisting of both the external and internal—having determined that "it does not exist," then it abides in the Self, meaning it merges into it; at that time, there is the state of pure Being-in-general (*sattāsāmānyatā*). || 45 ||
Just as the limbs of a tortoise disappear into itself, so too do all visible objects dissolve into the Self by the Self when they are no longer conceptualized;
that is the state of pure Being-in-general.

Regarding the term "kūrma" (the tortoise): objects of perception, because the mind is turned inward, remain unmanifested and indeed unperceived. When they dissolve within the self by the self alone—just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs—without any effort, then there is the state of pure universal existence (*sattāsāmānyatā*). || 46 ||
This indeed is the supreme vision, which always exists for both those with bodies and those without bodies who are liberated; it is designated as the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). (47)

Regarding the term "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*): this supreme vision is the state of knowledge designated as the plane beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*). It is indeed possible for both those who possess a body and those liberated from the body. The witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) that persists through the three states beginning with waking is the "fourth" (*turya*), in comparison to the consciousnesses that identify with the waking and other states in the forms of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña.
The meaning is "the fourth. However, this state of knowledge, because it transcends that tetrad, is designated by the term "beyond the fourth" (turyātīta). || 47 ||
O sinless one, this [state] occurs for both the one who has emerged [from meditation] and the one established in samādhi;
it belongs solely to the knower, whereas it does not occur at all for the ignorant person born of [mere] awakening.

"Of one who has emerged" means this aforementioned vision, born of awakening—that is, produced by the knowledge of one's own true nature—belongs solely to the knower, whether he is emerged from meditation or established in it; for the ignorant person, however, it does not exist at all. 48.
Established in this vision, O Rāghava, all those on earth who possess the great essence—ourselves and others such as Nārada and the rest—are liberated. (49)
"In this [world]" means: on the earth, like the six flavors (rasas). 49 || 150 || 51 || 52 || 53 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, and the others are established as having beheld her; by taking recourse to this state, which destroys all fear, [they have attained their goal]. 150.
This Uddālaka resided in the house of the world for as long as he desired;
then, after a great length of time, his mind became awakened.
"I shall remain as one liberated while living (videhamukta) after casting off this body"—
thus he thought with unwavering resolve, seated on a bed of young leaves within a mountain cave.
He stood in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) with his eyes half-closed. || 53 ||
Restraining the nine gates with his mind by means of the suppression of the anus,
he investigates the contacts of the sense-objects, his own self having been cultivated as a mass of consciousness.
The phrase "saṃyamya" (having restrained) introduces a passage of four and a half verses. "Mātrāsparśān": that by which objects are measured are the *mātrās*, namely the senses;

those which touch are the *sparśas*, namely the objects. Restraining both the *mātrās* and the *sparśas*—that is, withdrawing both the senses and the objects—one becomes one whose own self is a concentrated mass of consciousness (*bhāvitasvātmacidghana*). Here, "the self is cultivated" (*bhāvitaḥ svātmā*) means...
By which [he is] a mass of consciousness, whose very nature is his own self. || 54 ||
Having restrained the vital breaths, with his neck held in a straight posture,
his face radiant as the root of the tongue touches the interior of the base of the palate. (55)

"Samasaṃsthānakandharaḥ" means one whose neck (kandharā) has a symmetrical (sama) and straight (akuṭila) configuration (saṃsthāna), that is, a particular arrangement (saṃniveśa). "Tālumūlāntarālagnajihvāmūlaḥ" means one whose root of the tongue (jihvāmūla) is attached to the space between the two roots of the palate (tālumūla)—that is, the regions at the base of the soft palate; by this, the *nabhomudrā* [the seal of the sky] is indicated.

It has been shown; for that which is called *khecarī* is indeed this. As it is stated in the *Vivekamārtaṇḍa*, beginning with: "The yogi who knows the *mahāmudrā*, the *nabhomudrā*, the *uḍḍiyāna*, the *jālandhara*, and the *mūlabandha* is a vessel for [spiritual] accomplishments"—and continuing: "The tongue enters the hollow of the skull and moves in reverse."
The gaze directed between the eyebrows is the mudrā known as khecarī. || 55 ||
With his mind and vision focused neither externally nor internally, neither below nor above, neither on an object nor on emptiness, he kept his teeth from touching one another. (56)

"Not externally" means that one whose mind and vision are joined with another object remains thus toward an object that is empty of future form and of the nature of non-existence. Furthermore, "not touching the teeth with the teeth" is also stated as being in accordance with the Khecarī mudrā.
His complexion was as clear and bright as the cessation of the flow of vital breath. || 57 ||
With his body’s hair standing on end from the arising of the consciousness of the awareness of the limbs,
he attained the state of universal consciousness through the practice of that very awareness of the limbs.

"One whose body is characterized by horripilation arising from the consciousness of the awareness of the limbs" means: the "awareness of the limbs" (aṅgacitsaṃvit) refers to the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of the consciousness that is the true nature (svarūpa) of the awareness of the limbs; its "arising" (utthāna) is its emergence. One whose "body" (aṅgabhūḥ)—that is, the physical frame—is "characterized by horripilation" (romakaṇṭakitā), meaning it has become bristling with joy due to the bliss of the direct realization of one's own true nature.

Through the practice of the consciousness of the limbs and through the uninterrupted contemplation of one's own true nature, he attained the universal consciousness—the mere essence of consciousness—which persists throughout all things. || 58 ||
Through the practice of that, one attains the supreme vibration of internal bliss;
by savoring that, the sequence of the state of the dissolved universal consciousness is reached. (59)

The word "that" (*tat*) constitutes half of the sentence. "From the practice of that" means from the continuous contemplation of the equilibrium of consciousness (*citsāmya*). "Then" (*tadā*) means from the savoring of that, which is the experience of supreme bliss (*parānanda*); it refers to the sequence of the state of dissolved universal consciousness (*līnacitsāmānyadaśākrama*), the throbbing of the dissolved mental fluctuations (*vilīnacidvṛttisphuraṇa*). 59.

Through the practice of pure conscious awareness, he attained the universal consciousness (citsāmānya), which is the commonality of existence (sattāsāmānya) whose self is infinite and which sustains the universe.
He attained the state of universal sustainer, perfectly full, infinite in essence, undivided, and the commonality of pure existence through Māyā. || 160 ||
He remained, his full extent of equanimity and tranquility having attained supreme rest. || 61 ||
"He stood" constitutes one half-verse. "The expansion of equal tranquility" means the extension of tranquility in a single form. || 61 ||
Then, having attained that stainless state, his facial radiance became utterly charming with a bliss that is not merely worldly joy, and he experienced horripilation born of perfectly tranquil bliss.
"Anānandā" consists of two and a half verses as a single syntactical unit.

The radiance of his face was utterly charming with a bliss born of the cessation of that which is devoid of bliss; for, due to the stilling (*śama*) of that reality which is without bliss (*anānanda*) and beyond joy (*nirānanda*), the luster of his countenance was appropriately "bliss-charmed"—that is, composed of bliss and enchanting.
Although the glow on the face is produced by bliss, because there is an absence of physical manifestations of bliss such as horripilation, it is not perceived as being "born of bliss."
This is the meaning. Even though it was blissful, because of its state of being changeless (*nirvikāratā*), it was as if devoid of bliss; such is the sense.

"Comparable to a figure depicted in a painting" is the illustration for its changelessness. "Equal to the autumnal moon" refers to its nature as consisting of luminous bliss (*prakāśānandamayatva*). || 62 || 63 ||
With the delusions of existence, such as conceptualization and the like, long since exhausted,
that Great Being became like a figure depicted in a painting.
Within a few days, he gradually became tranquil in his own stainless self,
having transcended the state of birth, like the sap of a tree in the pure heat of the sun's rays at the end of autumn. (64)

"He became tranquil" (upaśaśāma): that Uddālaka, having transcended the state of birth and having passed beyond the condition of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), became tranquil in his own stainless Self, in his very own station, which is his true nature. It is like the sap of a tree at the end of autumn, [subsiding] in the stainless rays of the sun, in the solar radiance itself; for according to the traditional teaching, "from the Sun rain is born. [This refers to] the sap of the tree.
Dissolution into its own cause, the splendor of the Sun, is logical. || 64 ||
With all conceptual constructions gone, delighting in the changeless, his form liberated from the limiting conditions that destroy all fear,
he attained that primordial bliss in which the splendor of Indra is swept away like a blade of grass in a mass of water. (65)

"He has gone" (gateti): He has reached that primordial state in which even the splendor of Śakra is perceived as being as insignificant as a blade of grass in a mass of water—that is, it is so conceived through its insignificance. 65.
Pervading the infinite expanse of the sky and extending through all directions, full, possessing the nature of sustaining the worlds, and served by many fortunate souls;
having described its qualities, it is said to be beyond them— the Truth, the primordial Bliss, the beginningless, the immortal, the infinite Brahman.
There was. || 166 ||

Regarding the word "aparimita" (immeasurable): because there was a sense of dissatisfaction due to the perception of duality in the previous verse—where it says he "attained happiness"—this verse establishes non-duality by stating that "he became the full happiness of Brahman. || 166 ||
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Narrative of Uddālaka," in the Chapter on Quiescence within the *Mokṣopāya* of the venerable Vālmīki.
Thus ends the sixth canto in the Section on Quiescence within the Means to Liberation of the glorious Vasiṣṭha-Rāmāyaṇa. || 6 ||
The Seventh Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
Dwelling by this sequence and investigating the self by means of the self, O lotus-eyed one, attain rest in the expansive state. (1)

It has been stated previously that through the firmness of practice in yoga, there arises the repose of the mind (*cittaviśrānti*), and that this alone is the supreme state of *samādhi*. Now, it is established by means of the narrative of Suradhūpa that this very repose of the mind is the limit of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). In that regard, he first teaches what is beneficial, beginning with the words "in due order" (*krameṇa*). By this sequence...
According to the previously mentioned procedure for the conduct of Uddālaka. || 1 || 2 ||
One should investigate with the mind, guided by the scriptures and their meaning,
for as long as it takes to attain that state through the practice of dissolving all objects of perception.
The meritorious state is attained through detachment, practice, the meaning of the scriptures, wisdom, and the sequence of preceptors and observances; or else, it is attained by wisdom alone.

Regarding "by dispassion" (*vairāgya*): dispassion is freedom from craving; practice is the constant contemplation of the dissolution of all that is seen; the meaning of the scriptures is knowledge of the reality of the inner self (*adhyātma-śāstra-tattva-jñāna*); wisdom (*prajñā*) is the investigation of the true nature of things throughout the three periods of time; the teacher is the instruction of the teacher; and the sequence of restraints is the sequence of *yama*, *niyama*, and so forth—by these [means]. Regarding "by wisdom alone": [it refers to] by means of wisdom itself.
The meaning is that the supreme state is attained through wisdom alone by one whose inner organ has been fully ripened. || 3 ||
An intellect that is fully awakened, sharp,
and free from blemish attains the eternal goal, even if it lacks all other favorable conditions.

In order to establish that [liberation occurs] by wisdom alone, he says: "thoroughly awakened," etc. "Sharp" means that which discerns the true nature of things. "The totality of all factors" refers to the previously mentioned detachment and so forth. (4)
Rāma said:
O Blessed One, knower of the past and the future, there is someone who has attained meditative absorption;
though engaged in worldly affairs, he remains as rested as one who is fully awakened.

"O Blessed One," with these two verses, the question is posed: A certain seeker of liberation who has attained samādhi, having at some time experienced the bliss of samādhi, even while engaged in worldly activity—like one awakened from sleep or risen from slumber—remains rested and delights solely within his own self. (5)
(464) Someone, having resorted to solitude, remains established in the discipline of meditative concentration.
O Blessed One, tell me: which of these two is superior?
But another, having resorted to solitude and established himself in the discipline of meditative concentration—tell me, which of these two is superior? (6)
Vasiṣṭha said:
For one who perceives this collection of qualities as being without self,
that inner coolness which arises is called samādhi.

Regarding the phrase "this": for the person who perceives this phenomenal world—which consists of a collection of qualities (guṇas), namely the aggregate of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest—as not being the Self, that internal coolness which arises, like one submerged in an ocean of nectar, and which is the cessation of all torment, is called *samādhi*. || 7 ||
Having resolved that "I have no connection with visible objects," one person remains cool while engaged in worldly affairs, while another remains established in meditative absorption.

The two verses beginning with "dṛśyaiḥ" form a single syntactical unit (*vākya*). Since the fruit of infinite austerity is precisely inner coolness, therefore, when there is inner coolness, there is complete identity between the two; this connects back to the preceding [verse]. (8–9)
O Rāma, these two are happy if they are cool within;
that which is inner coolness is the fruit of infinite austerity.
If the mind of one established in the state of meditative concentration is still flickering with mental activity,
then his so-called "concentration" is no different from the frantic dancing of a madman.

He states, in two verses beginning with "samādhi," that the primary importance belongs precisely to the tranquility of the mind, which consists of its cooling nature, by means of both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): "That [mind] which is flickering in its fluctuations and agitated by joy, sorrow, and so forth...
as it was said by the Blessed One: "He who sits restraining the organs of action, yet continues to dwell upon objects with the mind..."
"One whose self is deluded regarding the objects of the senses is called one of false conduct. || 10 || 11 ||
If the mind of one engaged in the frantic dance of the madman has its latent tendencies (vāsanā) exhausted,
then his mad dancing is equal to the meditative absorption (samādhi) of a Buddha.
The one who is awakened while engaged in worldly affairs and the one who is awakened while dwelling in the forest—
these two are truly equal, having reached a state beyond doubt.

Regarding the term "one who conducts worldly affairs" (*vyavahārī*): he is the awakened one, one who has realized the true nature of the Self (*ātmatattva*). This refers to the state beyond doubt, the indubitable reality of the Self, according to the Vedic scripture: "All doubts are cut asunder. (12)
Even while performing an action, this mind with its subtle latent impressions (vāsanā) acts as if it were not the agent,
just like a person whose mind is far away while listening to a story.
"Non-doer" (akartṛ): Even though the mind possesses subtle latent impressions (*vāsanā*), even though it acts, and even though it sets the body and senses in motion, it is as if non-doing.
Just as a person whose mind has wandered far off while listening to a story does not hear at all, even though he is hearing the ancient tale because of its proximity. (13)
Even though it was not acting, the mind appeared as if it were the agent, with its latent tendencies fully awakened,
like one standing on the brink of falling into a chasm in a dream while the limbs remain motionless.

"Even though it does not act": if the mind possesses the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of striking, then even while not acting, it is as if it were the agent. For example, in a dream, when one is standing at the edge of a precipice, upon the perception "I am falling into a pit"—such as an old well—even though the body remains motionless and the mind does not produce any physical action, the mind is nonetheless as if the agent because it is the cause of fear, trembling, and so forth; it is just like that. || 14 || 15 ||
That which is the non-agency of the mind is the supreme concentration;
know that to be the state of absolute oneness, that auspicious and ultimate liberation. 15.

The supreme cause of the mind's wavering and unsteadiness is said to be [the lack of] meditation; therefore, make that very mind the sprout of non-attachment toward both meditative absorption and its objects.

"Mind" (ceta) means that the mind itself, through its lack of flickering, is the cause of the vision of meditation; through its flickering, it is the cause of the absence of the vision of meditation—this is the meaning. This follows the principle that the order of meaning is more powerful than the order of recitation. "Without sprouts" means free from latent desires (nirvāsana).
That very mental meditation is declared to be without substrate and stable;
it is itself the state of isolation (kevalībhāva), and it is always peace itself. (17)
Regarding the term "without latent impressions" (*avāsanam*): the meaning is that its constant state of tranquility itself is that very steady mind; thus, "tranquility" is the intended sense.

According to the maxim that pronouns bring about identity between that which is being pointed out and that which is subsequently referred to, and that they take on the gender of the latter in turn, the adoption of the masculine gender (the gender of the predicate) in the phrase "that very state of isolation" (*sa eva kevalībhāvaḥ*) is employed.
In this context, it should be understood that the mention of the gender of the subject is intended to indicate that very state as "quiescence. || 17 ||
It is said that the mind with subtle latent impressions (vāsanā) strives for the highest state;
therefore, by making the mind free from impressions, that state is attained. 18.
By means of two verses beginning with "tanuvāsanam," one should cultivate the state of agency—the attenuation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—which is the very nature of the mind's agency. (18–19)
This mind, which consists of dense latent impressions (vāsanā) and the notion of agency, bestows all suffering; therefore, one should bring those latent impressions to attenuation. (19)
Having completely renounced with your mind the sense of self-identity toward all things,
remain as you are— whether on a mountain or in a house.
"By means of the mind" (cetaseti): [this refers to] the cultivation of the self-nature of all existents, or the latent impression (vāsanā) which consists of the self-nature of all existents. 20–21.
For householders whose minds are well-composed and whose faults of egoism have been stilled, the home itself is like secluded forest lands. (21)
Just as people in a marketplace, though dwelling there,
remain as if they were not there due to their lack of attachment, so too, for the wise man, even a village is like a forest because of his lack of connection to it.

"Yathā" (just as): Just as the people in the marketplace—those situated in the commercial streets—who, though moving about, are like non-existent beings (*asatsamāḥ*) and do not assist a traveler who has arrived from another land; why? Because of a lack of connection (*asaṃbandhāt*), due to the absence of any relationship with them; likewise, even a village for a wise man (*jña*) or one possessed of knowledge (*jñānin*) is comparable to a forest (*vipinopamaḥ*). It is like a wilderness (*araṇya*); it does not [benefit him].
The meaning is that it is the cause of distraction. || 22 ||
With his mind always turned inward, though asleep, awakened, walking, or dancing,
he perceives a city, a district, a village, or even a forest as if they were [mere appearances].
Everything attains the state of space through constant abiding within.

The phrase "antar" refers to half a verse. The syntactical connection is as follows: since everything attains the state of space (*ākāśatā*) through abiding within [the internal], therefore he perceives the entire city and so forth as if it were a forest. || 23 ||
When inner coolness is attained, the world becomes cool;
for those scorched by internal thirst, the world consists of the burning heat of a forest fire.
"Antaḥ" (within): the meaning is that when the mind is cool, the world becomes cool; when it is heated, it becomes heated. || 24 ||
Whatever exists within all living beings is situated outside as well:
heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions;
these are but portions of the reality of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-tattva) appearing as if they were external. (25)

To establish this very point, he says: "It becomes," which constitutes one sentence consisting of three halves. Because that which exists internally within all living beings becomes situated externally; even the heavens and so forth are merely portions of the reality of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-tattva*) appearing as if they were external. Therefore, the meaning is that the modification of the internal organ alone is primary. "Heaven" (*dyauḥ*) refers to the celestial world (*svarloka*).
Ākāśa is the intermediate space. || 25 ||
But he who, finding delight only within himself, performs actions with his organs of action, and is not under the sway of joy and sorrow— he is said to be composed.

"But he who," etc. The syntactical connection is as follows: but he who, even while performing action with the senses, is one whose delight is in the Self and who is established in the Self alone, and who—by reason of joy and sorrow—is not under their sway, that is, does not become dependent upon the means for those [emotions], he is "composed" (samāhita). 26, 27, 28.
He who, by his very nature and not out of fear, regards all beings as himself and the wealth of others as a clod of earth— he truly sees.
Whether death comes this very day or at the end of the eon,
he certainly incurs no stain, just as gold does not become defiled even when it is situated in mud.
All is utterly tranquil, unborn, one, without beginning or middle, luminous, consisting of mere self-experience, and an inconceivable mind.
"Everything is utterly tranquil"—this view consisting of words is indeed for the sake of awakening; for this "Om" is truly in vain. (29)
"Everything" (*sarvam*) means the Ābhāsvara [heaven], which shines everywhere, consisting solely of self-savoring, and being the cause for the tasting of all flavors.

Fearing that non-duality (*advaita*) might be undermined due to its connection with the many qualifiers in the first half of the verse, he says: through the qualifiers beginning with "everything is utterly tranquil," that verbal vision which delineates duality exists only for the sake of awakening.

For [the world] is indeed imagined; therefore, for that reason, it is merely in vain. Consequently, all this should be expressed as "Om" alone, because the syllable Om itself establishes the nature of the Supreme Brahman. || 29 || 30 || 31 || 32 || 33 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
In this very context, they cite this ancient history concerning the story of Suraghu, the lord of the Kirātas, which is a source of great wonder. (30)
On this mountain range of snows there is a peak, a mountain named Kailāsa;
at its base dwell the Kirātas known as Hemajaṭās.
Among them there was a noble-souled king named Suraghu, a conqueror of cities, powerful, and the destroyer of the pride of the gods' warriors and others.
He performed the duties of kingship through the sequence of punishment and favor;
however, his mind was overwhelmed by the pleasure and pain arising from those very acts.
Why should I thus crush all these beings with my power, like sesame seeds in a press? This suffering of mine arises from [the suffering] of all living creatures. (34)
"For what purpose? [The answer is: "In this way, like a machine devised in the world for the extraction of oil, such as a sesame-press. (34)
Or rather, I shall bring about the destruction of this world without him;
for without him, these subjects cannot subsist, just as a river cannot flow without water.

Now, regarding the word *atha*: Alternatively, it means "I shall inflict the punishment that has been reached. That is to say, I shall inflict upon each person that specific punishment which is prescribed as the law in the scriptures according to their fitness. For, without this restraint, the subjects do not abide in their own path—just as water does not remain in a riverbed or a channel without a dam—and they proceed to mutually afflict one another through lust, anger, and other such passions.
Because it has come into operation. As Kāmandaka said: "This world, being forcibly submerged in hell by desire, greed, and the like, is held up by the king through punishment. (Verses 35–43, p.
Thus the king’s mind, swinging to and fro, found no rest;
then one day the sage Māṇḍavya came to his house.
Tamasu honored that great sage and asked him:
"O Sage, by your arrival I have attained peace. (37)
Today, O Lord, I stand at the forefront of the blessed by virtue of my dharma.
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, you have long been weary. (38)
Therefore, dispel this doubt of mine as the sun dispels the darkness;
for whose affliction is it not destroyed by association with the great? (39)
Those who know suffering say that doubt is the highest form of affliction;
yet these [doubts] arise from restraint and favor, and they reside within the body of my servant.
Anxiety drags me away, as the claws of a lion drag away an elephant;
therefore, let it arise within me with equanimity, like the all-pervading rays of the sun. (41)
O Sage, there is no one else more venerable to me than you; please show me compassion.
Māṇḍavya said:
O King, this flimsiness of mind dissolves like snow through one's own effort, established in oneself, and by one's own means. (43)
By one's own inquiry alone, the impurity within the mind is quickly pacified:
"Who am I? How did this come to be? What is it? And how do birth and death occur? (44)
By reflecting within yourself alone, you shall attain the state of the Great Ones;
for you, whose true nature has been fully realized through such inquiry, [this will come to pass]. 45.
Having abandoned its own nature, the mind will attain peace, free from fever; O sinless one, even while remaining in its form as the mind, it will be relinquished by you.
For a wretched mind, O King, sinks even into a trivial matter,
just as an aged mosquito sinks into the water of a cow’s footprint.
O mighty-armed one, to the very extent that the other world remains as nothing but the Supreme Self, to that same extent everything else is abandoned by oneself. (48)

"As for the word 'yāvat' (as much as): to whatever extent the entire visible world—whether small or large—is abandoned by oneself through the realization that it is something else, and is itself disregarded, to that same extent the Supreme Light, the supreme radiance which is the Supreme Self alone, remains, corresponding to the degree to which the visible world has been relinquished. || 48 ||
As long as everything has not been completely renounced, the Self is not attained;
when all things have been relinquished, that which remains is called the Self. (49)
The meaning is that when the visible object is abandoned, only the seer remains. || 49 ||
O virtuous one, as long as something else has not been relinquished, the reality remains merely a generality; what then need be said regarding the attainment of one's own true self? (50)
