"As long as" means: as long as another object has not been relinquished, even a common or shared thing—such as a jewel, gold, silver, or the like—is not obtained. For what reason? Because when one's own self is attained, what need is there to speak of anything else?
The meaning is: why is it said that "another object must be relinquished"? Indeed, when intent upon another, the object desired to be accomplished [is not reached].
The sense is that even the slightest thing is accomplished. || 50 || 51 ||
Therefore, for the sake of beholding the Self, one should renounce everything;
for having renounced all this, that which remains is the supreme state. (51)

Having completely cast aside the succession of all causes and effects—the manifestation of things existing within the world—and having likewise thoroughly shaken off one's own body, let that which is auspicious prevail. 52.
"Entirely," [it is said]. Having cast away the mind—which is permeated by the reality of the world consisting of cause and effect—by rejecting it as not-self;
and having shaken off one's own body from that state and delimited it as not-self, let that alone be the auspicious reality which is established.
52 Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to Suraghu, O descendant of Raghu, the Blessed One,
Māṇḍavya, departed for his own beautiful circle of silence.
When the supreme sage had departed, the king went to a secluded and blameless place and reflected within himself with his intellect: "Who indeed am I? (54)
I consider myself to be nothing more than the body, joined with hands, feet, and so forth;
I do not perceive that [Self] within it, even though it is close at hand. (55)
Therefore, in this regard, I am not this flesh and bone which are insentient;
I am not the organs of action, nor do the organs of action belong to me. (56)
I am not the insentient sense organs, nor am I their nature;
I am not the body and so forth, for I perceive all that remains as distinct from them.
Therefore, I am the pure consciousness, free from conceptual construction;
I am like the wind within the cosmic egg and likewise within the multitude of all living beings. (58)
That very Blessed One, the Self, exists like a thread within pearls;
this is that very stainless power of consciousness (cicchakti), devoid of the affliction of the object of cognition.
She fills all the quarters of space like jars and assumes a terrifying form. || 59 ||
Pervading all states of being, subtle, and free from existence and non-existence,
she dwells within the entire universe up to the realm of Brahmā, containing the treasury of all powers.
Whatever is seen here as this entire visible world, it is merely a portion of the vibration of consciousness; nothing else exists there eternally.
"All this" means: everything perceived in the world is merely a vibration (*niṣpanda*) of consciousness. A vibration of consciousness is its manifestation;
it is nothing but a part of that. There is no other eternal entity whatsoever. 61.

Free from passion, abiding in the objectless state, having transcended the delusion of existence and abandoned all striving, I have attained the state of steady deep sleep; therefore, I dwell in the Self in equanimity.

"Free from attachment" (*vigata*): it refers to one whose state is free from the object of passion. That by which one is colored is "coloration," namely the web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). He from whom that coloration has departed is "free from coloration. For this very reason, his state has emerged from objects; thus he is "one whose state is free from objects. Being both free from coloration and having a state free from objects, he is described as such. He has attained the stage of stable deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
I have attained the state of profound deep sleep; together with tranquility, I abide within the Self in my own true nature.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus Hemajaṭādhīśa attained the unsurpassed state,
just as the son of Gadhi (Viśvāmitra) attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa through discernment and resolute effort.

Thus [ends the section]. "Gādhija" refers to Viśvāmitra. For it is explained in detail in the Rāmāyaṇa and other texts that he, competing with Vasiṣṭha, attained the status of a Brahmarṣi through his austerities. 63–64.
He shone with a mental state possessing the characteristics of the stage of deep sleep. || 64 ||
He was neither pitiless nor compassionate, neither dualistic nor free from envy;
he was neither wise nor unwise, neither a seeker of wealth nor a seeker of its absence. || 65 ||
It was stated that he shone with a mental state free from modification, like the state of deep sleep. He describes that very absence of modification as follows:

because his nature consists of the desire to eliminate the suffering of others, and because that [desire] is devoid of passion (*rāga*) and other such afflictions; for this very reason, he is without envy (*amatsara*), free from hatred (*dveṣa*), and both "well-minded" (*sudhīra*) and "wise" (*sudhī*), because he is devoid of all cognition of the auspicious and the inauspicious. He is neither a seeker of objects (*arthī*) nor a seeker of non-objects (*anarthī*).
Because of the non-existence of passion and hatred, it should be understood that he thus became free from the pairs of opposites. || 65 || 66 ||
Now hear this wonderful dialogue between Suraghu, who had then awakened, and the royal sage Parṇāda.
There was a king of the Pārśikas, a slayer of enemy heroes, renowned by the name Parigha; he was like an iron bar (parigha) upon his chariot. || 67 ||

"He became," [it is said]. "Like a *parigha* on a chariot": by the etymological derivation that a *parigha* is a specific type of weapon because "one strikes all around with it" (*parito hanyate 'nena*), the meaning is that just as it is renowned for striking down enemy heroes on a chariot (*syandana*), so too was he. 67–68.
O descendant of Raghu, Suraghu became his supreme friend.
Once, there suddenly appeared a great circular halo around his iron club.
There, many people perished, their lives destroyed by hunger;
seeing that suffering and being powerless to provide a remedy, Parigha [was overcome]. (69)
He renounced his entire kingdom and went to the forest for asceticism;
practicing penance with a tranquil mind, he subsisted on withered leaves.
From that time forward, he became known as Parṇāda; then, after a thousand years of asceticism performed with a formidable spirit, [he attained his goal]. (71)
By the power of practice, he attained the knowledge born of self-purification;
he became free from dualities, free from disease, and possessed of equal vision. (72)
He wandered at will through this small monastery of the three worlds;
once, the lord of Hemacūḍa went to his abode.
There, those two former friends said this to one another:
"My heart has attained supreme bliss by the sight of you;
oh, how truly my purifying merits have borne fruit! (74)
Parigha said:
"O sinless one, this very knowledge has been attained by me, just as it was by you;
do you indeed practice it with a wise, serene, and profound mind? (75)
Having observed your auspicious undertakings and deeds, O lord of men,
I hope that this vine of your body is free from mental and physical afflictions.
Do you perhaps not sink into enjoyments that are charming only at first sight? And do you perhaps [dwell] in that state free from conceptual construction, the abode of supreme rest? (77)
You practice the concentration that is the highest tranquility and the supreme good. || 78 ||
Suraghu said:
O Great-souled One, tell me: when does that ignorant person, who always conducts himself in silence or through speech, ever become one whose mind is concentrated? (79)

Regarding the word "ya" (who): that person who is ignorant—that is, one who does not know the Self—when can he ever be of concentrated mind, whether remaining silent or engaged in worldly activity? The meaning is: never. The sense is that for the ignorant person, concentration itself is impossible. In the reading *asamāhitacitta* (one of unconcentrated mind), the word division in the phrase *yo'jñaḥ* is *jñaḥ* (the knower). [The question is: when is the knower [not concentrated]?
"He has an unconcentrated mind" means never at any time; the sense is that for the wise person, there is always only meditative absorption (samādhi). || 79 ||
Because their minds are perpetually awakened, even while performing worldly activities,
those who are established in the single reality of the Self are always in a state of perfect meditative absorption. (80)

He establishes this very point through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the words beginning "eternity" (*nitya*). Those who are established in the single reality of the Self (*ātmaikatattva-tanniṣṭhāḥ*) are those whose steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*) lies in that Brahman which is denoted by the word "That" (*tat*), a reality that has attained oneness (*aikya*) with the Self (*ātmanā*)—that is, with one's own self. As stated in the *Gītā*: "The designation of Brahman is traditionally remembered as threefold: *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*."
Even for one who has assumed the lotus posture and joined his palms in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, what is *samādhi* and how can it exist for one whose very nature is restless? (81)
"Having bound" (baddha): even for one by whom the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) is bound—that is, for one who has assumed the lotus posture.

In the reading *baddhapadmāsanasthasya*, it would not be consistent [to interpret this] as "even for one who has formed the *brahmāñjali*," because the hands of one in the bound lotus posture are employed in grasping the thumbs. As Yājñavalkya says:

"O best of Brahmins, having placed both soles of the feet upon the thighs, one should bind the two big toes with the hands in a reversed manner; this is the Padmāsana, honored by all. The characteristics of the simple Padmāsana and the Brahmāñjali have been described previously. (81-83)
O Blessed One, the realization of reality—which is a fire that consumes the grass of all desires—is what is designated by the term "samādhi," and not merely remaining in silence. (82)
O virtuous one, that which is concentrated, eternally satisfied, and perceives the meaning of things as they truly are, is called supreme wisdom by the wise under the term "samādhi. (83)
Unshaken, free from egoism, and not following after the pairs of opposites—the state that is more stable than Mount Meru—is designated by the term "samādhi. (84)

"Unperturbed" (akṣubdha): the word "of Meru" (meroḥ) ends in the ablative case. Furthermore, that very state of the conscious principle which is most stable therein is declared to be *samādhi*. || 84 ||
Free from anxiety, devoid of longing, and abandoned of both the rejectable and the acceptable, the complete movement of the mind is designated by the term "samādhi. (85)

"Free from anxiety" (niścintā): the movement of the mind is devoid of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted; it is free from the conceptualization of duality such as "this is to be rejected" and "this is to be accepted. For this very reason, it is free from desired objects, and thus it is free from anxiety. That very same movement of the mind, when fully perfected, is *samādhi*. || 85 ||
Just as Time never ceases to forget the movement of its own moments,
so too the intellect of the wise never ceases to forget its own self.

"No," [he says]. Just as time does not forget its own movement—consisting of units such as *kalās* and *kāṣṭhās*—so too the intellect of the wise person (*prājñadhī*) does not forget its own self, its own true nature. 86.
Just as the ever-moving wind does not forget its course anywhere,
so the intellect of the wise, having ascertained pure consciousness, does not forget it.
No; for the wind moves constantly. 87.
The great ones, whose intellects are eternally concentrated and who are perfectly equanimous, abide free from the distinctions of the transformation of effects;
therefore, where indeed is that false proliferation of speech which arises through the distinction between the unconcentrated and the concentrated?

"Always" means: the great ones are of the nature of perfect knowledge (*paripūrṇajñāna*). They are "freed from the differentiation of the transformation of effects"—the transformation of effects consists of modifications in the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth; they are freed from the differentiation that is the conceptualization of duality (*bhedabhāvanā*) arising therefrom. Therefore, they are perfectly equanimous, seeing all things with an equal eye. Consequently, they remain with their intellects perpetually concentrated (*samāhita*). By that—

By means of the analytical deconstruction of the distinction between the "unconcentrated" and the "concentrated," that verbal proliferation which is falsely proclaimed through such conceptualization of difference—where indeed does it exist? The meaning is: nowhere at all. "O Supreme One! is an address. 88, 89, 90.
Parigha said:
O King, you have surely awakened; you have attained that state, with an inner heart thoroughly cooled and a profound, manifest intention.
Stainless, expansive, full, and free from the distress of egoism, you appear established in yourself everywhere, O King; you shine everywhere.
Enough with these excessively extensive elaborations of speech; this single view proclaimed here is for the sake of happiness.
If the mind within is joyful, equanimous, and its passions stilled, that is the unsurpassed foundation.

"Enough," it is said. When this [state] is examined in the final verse, if the mind—the agent—has its emotional flavor stilled (having ceased its longing for sense objects) and is therefore equanimous (possessing a state of evenness), and if it is thus delighted and satisfied within the bliss of its own self, then this inward-turned vision alone is declared to have arisen for the sake of happiness; and this very vision is unsurpassed.
The meaning is that it is the supreme foundation, even liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 91 ||
Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Narrative of Suraghu," in the Section on Tranquility within the *Mokṣopāya* of the venerable Vālmīki.
Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Narrative of Suraghu," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhavivaraṇa*.
p. 477) The Eighth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus reflected upon the course of the world, Suraghu and Parigha honored one another; satisfied, they each returned to their respective duties.

It has been stated previously that the very resting of the mind is the limit of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). Now, the dialogue between Bhāsa and Vilāsa is presented to demonstrate that in the absence of such rest, there is manifold effort. || 1 ||
He who is eternally absorbed in the inner self, eternally turned inward, and eternally happy; he who is perpetually engaged in the contemplation of consciousness—he is not afflicted by sorrow. (2)

"Yaḥ" (he who): "Adhyātmamayaḥ" means that which pertains to the self (*ātmani adhi*); *adhyātma* refers to the science of the self, and one who is absorbed in that, intent upon its contemplation, is "adhyātmamayaḥ. || 2 ||
Bound by hundreds of snares of desire, greedily longing for the bait of enjoyments, bearing the heavy burden of great suffering, and lying in the pond of delusion. (3)

The three verses form a single syntactical unit. "Bhogolapasulālasam": *bhogas* (objects of enjoyment) are so called because they are enjoyed; these alone are the *ulapas*, meaning spreading grasses, and it is "sulālasam," meaning intensely longing for them. "Rogāvalidaṣṭam": it is bitten by the swarm of stings that are the diseases themselves. "Tṛṣṇāvaratrayā": *tṛṣṇā* (thirst/desire) itself is the *varatrā*, a leather thong or rope, and by that [it is bound].
"Dragged" means pulled along. "Evil action" (*kukarma*) is sin; that itself is the "mud" (*kardama*), and by that he is "smeared.

"Lying in the pond of delusion" (*mohapalvalaśāyin*): that in which one becomes deluded is "delusion" (*moha*), which is *saṃsāra*; that itself is the "pond" (*palvala*), a small lake, and he is lying within it. || 3 || 4 ||
Bitten by the swarm of disease-stinging insects, dragged by the rope of craving, smeared with the mud of evil deeds, and wandering in the forest of saṃsāra; || 4 ||
O Rāma, rescue this bull of a living being from the pond of saṃsāra, which has not yet found the cool shade [of liberation] and is parched by the thirst of coming and going.
Exerting the utmost effort, one should rescue [the other] by force for a long time. || 5 ||

One should, employing the supreme effort previously described through the application of qualities such as the "flood" (ogha), cause this ox-like form of a living being— which has not yet attained cool shade and has not reached a place of rest— to cross over the pond of saṃsāra. || 5 || 6 || 7 ||
O Rāma, through association with those of great spiritual power, a clear method for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra is obtained, just as a boat is obtained from a navigator.
In whatever region or mountain there is no wise man who is like a tree of the virtuous—
bearing fruit and providing cool shade— a person of intelligence should not dwell there.
Neither wealth, nor friends, nor scriptures, nor kinsmen can assist men when they have sunk and seek their own deliverance. (8)

"No," [it is said]. In the matter of uplifting one's own self that has been submerged—namely, in ascertaining through discrimination the true nature of the self which has attained identification with the body, senses, and so forth while immersed in saṃsāra—wealth and other such things do not provide assistance. || 8 ||
Having reflected upon something together with the mind alone—his constant companion and friend—the self is liberated. (9)

To the question "In what way, then, does it assist?", he says: "By means of the mind alone. Having reflected upon something and investigated such questions as "Who am I?", the Self becomes uplifted. || 9 ||
By this alone, O Lord of Gods, the Supreme Self is understood:
when the body is regarded as being equal to wood or a clod of earth. (10)
"By this much" means that by the very ascertainment of the body's lack of selfhood—just as in the case of wood and so forth—the nature of the Self as the Supreme Self is understood. || 10 ||
Resembling the full ocean, it does not enter the range of speech;
it admits no comparison and does not pursue worldly allure.
"Parīti" means that it does not take up any comparison, for the Śruti declares: "Neither its equal nor its superior is seen.
It does not run after, nor does it depend upon, any object that is pleasing, attractive, or embellishing. || 11 ||
If the fourth state (turyā) is attained—a vision which consists solely of the portion of the light of consciousness and has reached stability—then it is compared with that [state]. || 12 ||
He states that even a comparison can occur based on slight similarity: "Only..."—this consists of three verses forming a single syntactical unit.

When the dissolution of the mind and the ego-construct occurs, that supreme blissful body of the Supreme Lord—which abides within all states of being—emerges as one's own true nature. That body is endowed with a portion of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*);
it is endowed with a portion of consciousness (*cit*) in the form of its luminosity, and it attains stability through another aspect characterized by that very luminosity.

If the fourth vision (*turyā-dṛṣṭi*) is attained, then it is compared by means of that vision. That state of the Supreme Self-nature—vast like the splendor of the sky, full in form, and complete in form—is characterized by a slight resemblance to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), due to its proximity in similarity as being mere changeless consciousness (*nirvikāra-cinmātra*). || 12 || 13 || 14 ||
Deep sleep is characterized by a resemblance that is not far removed [from its true nature];
that state is full in form, as vast as the splendor of the sky. (13)
When the mind and the ego dissolve, that supreme bliss which arises, abiding within all states of being, is the body of the Supreme Lord.
She, perfected by yoga herself, is as if in deep sleep yet not far from being realized; she is beyond the reach of words, O Rāma, and is experienced only within the heart.

She is so. That aforementioned state of the Supreme Self, perfected through yoga—that is, through meditative absorption—is experienced within the heart itself as being not far removed from the state of deep sleep; it is manifested through its similarity to deep sleep in terms of proximity. It is not accessible to words. || 15 ||

When this entire infinite reality of the Self is firmly established within the matured mind, and all external [distractions] have been stilled, the God of gods—who is the soul of all moving and unmoving beings—is indeed experienced by oneself. 16.

The entire infinite universe is the reality of the Self; it is indeed the very nature of the Self. For this reason, when the mind—which is characterized by firm transformation and abounds in latent impressions (vāsanās), and is thus subject to intense and manifold modifications—is stilled through the power of meditative absorption (samādhi), the God of gods, who dwells within as the inner controller of all, is experienced by oneself even externally as the soul of all moving and non-moving beings.
Thus, it shines forth by itself alone, because of the dissolution of the discerning consciousness. || 16 ||
Following that, there is the destruction of the latent impressions of sense objects; following that, the auspicious and supremely lucid light [arises];
and following that, by virtue of equanimity, there occurs for the great ones a transformation into their own true nature, which is inconceivable in form. (17)

Thereafter, following the vision of the Supreme Self both internally and externally, comes the destruction of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of sense objects—that is, the destruction of the residual traces of those objects. Thereafter, following the destruction of the latent impressions of sense objects, there is the clear manifestation of the auspicious Supreme Self in its true nature; and thereafter, by virtue of equanimity, [one abides] in the inconceivable form of one's own essential nature.
Dedication (pariṇamana): the meaning is that, by virtue of one's own state as the Supreme Self, one attains abidance in one's true nature alone. || 17 ||

If the Self is not perceived after cutting through the mind with the mind itself, then the suffering of the world will not perish; for when the mind is severed, there arises the realization of the blissful Self. (18)

"By the mind alone": by means of the mind itself—discriminating and refined by the scriptures—one cuts through the mind, that is, the consciousness attached to worldly existence, by means of the mind alone. (18–19)
Vasiṣṭha said:
In this very context, they cite this ancient history, a dialogue between two friends, Bhāsa and Vilāsa, on a peak of the Sahya mountains.
With its extreme height it has surpassed the sky; with its peak it has surpassed the surface of the earth;
with its base it has surpassed the netherworld; that Sahya mountain is truly transcendent.

Regarding the term *atyutsedha*: *utsedha* means height. *Jita* means pervaded. A *pīṭha* is a broad mountain region above the earth by which it pervades the surface of the ground. A *tala* is the portion of the mountain base submerged in the earth. The *Sahya* is a principal mountain range (*kulācala*). As it is stated in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa: "Mahendra, Malaya... [and so forth].

Sahya, Śuktimān, Ṛkṣaparvata, Vindhya, and Pāriyātra—these are the seven principal mountain ranges here. (20) There, on the northern slope of a mountain where trees bear abundant fruit, lies the glorious and great hermitage of Atri, which removes the fatigue of the perfected ones. (21)
In that great hermitage of Atri, there were two ascetics who were like Śukra and Bṛhaspati in the path of the sky.
Then, those two, sharing a single dwelling, had two sons there named Vilāsa and Bhāsa, who gradually attained maturity. (23)
Let alone their mutual affection, like a pair of deeply in love spouses;
their minds were so perfectly one that they had attained a kind of unity within duality. (24)
Then their two parents, having abandoned their bodies, departed; there, having performed the funeral rites, they broke into lamentation.
Free from passion, they spent their time separately in the forest;
with all their limbs withered by asceticism, they reached the highest state of detachment.
In this manner, days, months, and even years passed for the two of them;
then, on one occasion, having come together, they spoke thus to one another.
Vilāsa said:
O fruit of the foremost tree of life, ocean of the nectar that refreshes the heart, O great kinsman in this world, Bhāsa—welcome to you! 28.
"Jagati" means: while the world exists; O Great Bond, companion of rest. 28.
"O virtuous one, tell me where you have spent these many days—not few—separated from me; has your asceticism been fruitful? (29)

"Etāvantaḥ" (so many): the meaning is, "Where have so many years—more than a few (*analpa*), that is, very numerous—been spent? Since the context of the question concerns time extending up to immeasurable years, it is days, months, and years that have passed; for if the question were concerned with days alone, the expression "more than a few days" (*dinānalpāḥ*) would be inappropriate. [This is because] of the word *dina*...
Because it is neuter, even if masculinity were admitted, there would be no application of *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination). || 29 || 30 || 31 || 32 ||
Is your intellect free from fever? Are you born with self-mastery?
Have you borne fruit through your learning? And are you well? (30)
Bhāsa said:
"O holy man, welcome today! By good fortune you have been seen, O giver of honor.
How could there be well-being for us who remain here in this cycle of worldly existence? (31)

As long as the object of knowledge has not been realized, as long as the realm of the mind has not been exhausted, and as long as cyclic existence has not been crossed, how can there be any well-being for us? (32)
As long as the hopes born of the mind have not been cut down entirely, like creepers with a sickle, how can there be well-being for us? (33)
"Āśā" refers to spreading creepers and climbing vines; this, indeed, is a marvel here. 33.
As long as knowledge has not been attained, as long as equanimity has not arisen, and as long as awakening has not dawned, how can there be any virtue for us? (34)
"Up to this point": knowledge (*jñāna*) is indirect cognition produced by the scriptures; realization (*vijñāna*) is awakening; and awakening (*bodha*) is direct intuition. || 34 || 35 ||
O holy one, without the attainment of the Self and without the great medicine of knowledge, this cholera-like plague of miserable transmigratory existence arises once again. (35)
Falling into various kinds of pleasure and pain, shattered by the vast precipice of old age and death,
this person rolls upon the mountain of the world’s belly and, like a sapless leaf, reaches a state of decay.

"Much indeed! [This means: shattered—having met with ruin—in the very precipices of the widespread sufferings of old age and death; rolling and wandering within the mountain that is the belly of the world, like a leaf whose sap has vanished, like a withered leaf. || 36 ||
Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Dialogue with Bhāsavilāsa," in the section on Tranquility within the *Mokṣopāya* of Vālmīki.
Thus ends the eighth canto in the section on tranquility. 8.
The Ninth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, having exchanged inquiries regarding their welfare with one another, they attained pure knowledge in due time and reached liberation. || 1 ||
It was previously stated that in the absence of the mind’s resting, there is manifold exertion.

Now, by means of the narrative of Vītahavya, it is established that for the sake of achieving the mind’s rest, one must practice the abandonment of attachment, the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), and meditative absorption (samādhi). || 1 || 2 ||
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, I say that for a mind bound by attachment, there is no way to cross the ocean of worldly existence other than through knowledge. (2)
The mind that is unattached and stainless is clearly liberated even while wandering in saṃsāra; but the attached mind, even if engaged in long-term asceticism, remains bound by extreme fetters.
In this regard, he introduces the renunciation of attachment with the words "unattached" (asaktam). Attachment and non-attachment have their definitions to be stated later. || 3 ||
The living being (jīva), free from internal attachment and possessing a sweet disposition,
is never anywhere an agent or an enjoyer, whether it is externally performing actions or not.

"Antar" means: one who possesses the conduct of a *madhura* (honey-gatherer). A *madhura* is a honey-bee (*madhukara*), so "possessing the conduct of a *madhura*" means possessing the behavior of a honey-bee. For that bee, while gathering honey from flowers according to its availability, dwells happily without attachment;
the meaning is that his conduct is like that. || 4 || 5 ||
Rāma said:
O Blessed One, what kind of attachment is it, and what is said to lead to the bondage of men?
What is said to lead to liberation, and how is this [attachment] to be treated?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Because it is cultivated by completely abandoning the distinction between the body and the embodied self,
trust placed in the body alone is said to be attachment, which is worthy of bondage.

"Deha" (the body): the meaning is "having abandoned the singular distinction between the body and the embodied one," that is, having abandoned the single discernment as to what is the body and what is the embodied self. "Trust in the body alone" means the attachment consisting of the conceit of "I" and "mine" directed toward the body itself;
and that [attachment] is said to be worthy of bondage. || 6 ||
When the infinite reality of the Self is determined to have limits,
that internal desire for pleasure is called attachment, which is fit for bondage. (7)

When there is the determination of limitation—that is, the determination that the reality of the Self, which is infinite and undelimited by space, time, and so forth, is measured by the body—then that desire for pleasure, namely the longing for sensual enjoyment, within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), is attachment; and that is said to be "worthy of bondage," meaning it is the cause of bondage. || 7 ||
"All this is the Self alone; what shall I grasp, and what shall I abandon?"—know that this state of non-attachment is the arising of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).

"All this" means: this world and I am all indeed the Self alone. This being so, what should I desire and what should I renounce? Thus, abiding in a state where there is no longer anything to be rejected or accepted, that is not a state of attachment. And that [state] abides in those who are liberated while living; such is the meaning. || 8 ||
"I do not exist, nor does another exist; let there be happiness or let there be none"—a man who is thus internally unattached is said to be a possessor of liberation.

"No. There is no "I," nor is there any entity denoted by the word "I," because the Self is unlimited (*aparicchinna*) and the sense of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) has a limited object as its domain. Nor is there anything else, because there is no reality apart from the Self.
One who is unattached within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) does not desire that pleasures should arise or cease to be.
One is said to be a partaker of liberation. || 9 ||
He who does not rejoice in inaction nor clings to actions,
who is perfectly equanimous and has renounced the fruits of action— he is remembered as one who is unattached.
"No," [he says]. "Freedom from action" (naiṣkarmyam) means the renunciation of action. "Well-balanced" (susamaḥ) means perfectly equanimous toward success and failure.
"One who has abandoned the fruit" (phalatyāgī) is one who is free from longing for the results of action. || 10 ||
The skillful renunciation of all karmic fruits and the like by means of the mind alone, and not by means of action—that is remembered as "non-attachment. (11)
"All" (*sarva*) refers to all actions, fruits, and so forth. "Actions" (*karmāṇi*) refer to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices; "fruits" (*phalāni*) refer to heaven and other results.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the fruits of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), the intermediate fruits of the eight limbs of yoga such as *yama*, and [the results mentioned in passages] such as "the abandonment of enmity in his presence. All these—actions, fruits, and so forth—are [to be understood] by the mind alone.

That skillful renunciation which is not [accomplished] through action is known as "unattached" (*asaṅga*). By the etymological derivation *paritas tyāgo yasya* ("one whose renunciation is all-encompassing"), the word *parityāga* denotes the person who possesses such renunciation; otherwise, it would be impossible for it to stand in grammatical apposition with the word *asaṃsakta*. In that context, what is called "renunciation by means of the mind" is as follows:
It is the absence of attachment to fruits; furthermore, the renunciation of actions should be understood as the non-performance of those actions that serve as the means for attaining fruits. || 11 ||
O dear one, when all activities and various manifestations are performed without attachment,
they become treated [as medicine] and bring about the highest good. (12)

Regarding the phrase "by non-attachment": all activities, whose various manifestations—that is, whose diversions and displays—are of many kinds, become treated by the aforementioned non-attachment and bring about the highest good, which is liberation (kaivalya). || 12 ||
These aged multitudes of beings, being born again and again, become worms and insects; this is the manifestation of attachment to worldly existence. (13)
Having stated that attachment is the cause of bondage, he demonstrates this with two verses, beginning with "kṛmi" (worm).
"Janatāḥ" means groups of people; "saṃsaktiḥ" means attachment. || 13 ||
That infinite beings arise again and again and dissolve like waves in a river is the manifestation of attachment to that [world]. (14)
O Taraṅgiṇī, in the ocean; previously, attachment was indeed described as the cause of bondage. || 14 ||
Attachment is said to be of two kinds, O Raghava: the barren and the venerable.
The barren is found everywhere among the ignorant; the venerable is innate to those who know the truth.

Now, in order to define attachment (*saṅga*) as the cause of liberation, he says: "Attachment" (*saṃsakti*). It is "barren" (*bandhyā*), meaning fruitless; it is "to be revered" (*vandya*), because it bestows liberation and is thus worthy of praise. || 15 ||

Attachment arising from objects such as the body, which is devoid of the realization of the true nature of the self, is called "barren" because it is firm and repeatedly bestows further worldly existence.

In this context, that very attachment (saṅga) which was previously described as being subject to bondage is called "bondage" (bandhyā) or "clinging" (sakti). Although its essential nature has already been defined, he describes it again by way of a different formulation: "The self... [etc. "Firm" means having persisted for a long time. || 16 ||
Through the realization of the true nature of the self, attachment born of discernment becomes real; indeed, it is said that such attachment is venerable and is further free from saṃsāra. (17)

"Regarding 'ātmeti'": by means of the awakening to the reality of the Self—that is, by the cause which is the ascertainment of the Self's true nature; "born of discrimination" means having arisen when the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self has occurred; "become real" means having attained or become the object of that which is real—the uncontradicted reality of the Self; this is the meaning of the root *bhū* in the sense of "attaining. Such [knowledge] is further—
Attachment that is free from cyclic existence is said to be "vandyā" (worthy of homage). || 17 ||
With conch, discus, and mace in hand, his body manifesting through various modes of movement, he protects the three worlds by virtue of being attached to those worthy of worship. 18.

Attachment to the body is attachment to the barren; however, attachment to the Self is worthy of worship—this is the distinction. By way of proximity, he first illustrates attachment to that which is worthy of worship with the verse beginning "śaṅkha... [The body] named Śrī Viṣṇu’s form, with conch, discus, and mace in hand, [is characterized] by various activities (*īhā*) set in motion through incarnations such as the Fish and others.
The accomplished masters of consciousness and likewise the world-protectors remain within the multitude of worlds due to their attachment to that which is to be revered. (19)

Regarding "vijñāna": those whose "gati" (course) is consciousness—meaning those for whom Brahman, which is of the nature of consciousness, is their goal, their final resort, and their place of rest; and by the phrase "standing in the multitude of worlds," it is meant that their course is unimpeded throughout all worlds. || 19 ||
The mind falls upon sense-objects like a vulture upon scraps of meat, due to the power of attachment to the barren and through the vain suspicion that they are delightful. (20)

Now, he illustrates attachment to that which is barren (the futile): "The mind," etc. Regarding enjoyments—that is, sense objects—it is by the suspicion of their being delightful, meaning by the imagination that they are delightful; in other words, by the conceptualization of their loveliness. || 20 ||
These delightful grounds of the inner apartments belong to those whose power is barren;
they are fashioned as the hells named Raurava, Avīci, Kālasūtra, and so forth. (21)
"Barren" (vandhyā): Raurava, Avīci, and Kālasūtra are the various types of hells. The meaning is that for those who take pleasure in the body, the hells alone are their places of rest. || 21 ||
Know that people whose power is barren are a heap of fuel dried by suffering; it is because of them that those blazing fires of hell burn. (22)

Regarding the word *vandhya*: know that person whose attachment is barren—that is, one for whom attachment is fruitless—to be a heap of fuel for the fires of hell; for those fires of hell blaze because of that very fuel. || 22 ||

He who remains with his own mind—free from attachment everywhere—having attained the dawning of the vision of knowledge, while ignorance has reached its destruction within its own domain, is liberated. (23)

Regarding the word *vidyā*: he who remains thus—with a mind that has attained its full manifestation in the sphere of *brahmavidyā* (the vision of knowledge), which has reached dissolution in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) that is the sphere of ignorance (*avidyā*), and which is therefore devoid of mental synthesis and consequently free from attachment to every object of perception—of him it is said: [As it has been stated:]...
In the Gītā: "That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled one is awake; that wherein beings are awake is night for the sage who sees. (23)
Vasiṣṭha said:
At all times, with everything existing, abiding together with all,
and even while performing every action, the mind should be made aware by one who possesses discernment.

The statement is made through eight verses beginning with "sarvadā" (always). By a person who knows—that is, by a wise man—*sarvasaṃsthenā*: one who exists in all conditions, meaning one who remains amidst all states such as lying down or eating; whether staying with a wise man or a fool, and even while performing all actions, including obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*).

The mind of a virtuous person is attached to various objects such as mental activities and the like; it should not be so, but rather, having taken hold of even a slight object of consciousness, let that mind rest solely in *citi*—in pure consciousness alone—and remain indifferent toward all external things, finding its own essence in the savor of the bliss of its true nature (*svarūpānanda*). Just so:
The syntactical connection is: "In that manner, one should act while remaining [in that state]. || 24 ||
It is not attached here to activities, nor to thoughts, nor to objects;
neither in space, nor below, nor above, nor in the far-reaching directions. (25)
In this context, "not in entities" is the very elaboration of the phrase "not in space," and so forth. || 25 ||
It is not in the external vast expanse, nor indeed in the functions of the senses;
it is not within, nor in the vital breath, nor in the head, nor in the palate.
"Internal" means the interior of the body. This very point is elaborated upon in the passage beginning with "nor is it the vital breath," and so forth. || 26 ||
Neither in the space between the eyebrows, nor at the tip of the nose, nor in the mouth, nor in the pupils;
neither in darkness, nor in light, nor in this sky of the heart.

"In *tārake* means in the eye. [The word] *tāraka* is a synonym for the eye because, according to the rule *arśa-ādibhyo 'c*, the suffix *ac* is applied to form *tāraka* from *tārakā*, which means the pupil (*kanīnikā*). Otherwise, since the word *tāraka* would be feminine when referring to the pupil, the form *tārake* (neuter dual) would not be appropriate. "In *ābhāse* means in the reflection of consciousness (*cit-pratibimba*). || 27 ||
It is not in the waking state, nor in the dream, nor in deep sleep, nor in the pure;
it is not in the black, nor in the yellow, nor in the red and other colors, nor in the variegated.
In the stainless, pure reality. || 28 || 29 || 30 || 31 ||
It is neither in motion nor in stillness, neither in the beginning nor in the middle nor elsewhere;
it is neither far nor near, neither in front nor in an object, nor in the self. (29)
Neither in sounds, touches, nor forms; nor in states of delusion or intoxication;
nor in the activities of coming and going, nor in the calculations of time. || 30 ||
Having come to rest solely in pure consciousness, even while occasionally leaning upon objects of thought,
let the mind abide everywhere as if devoid of flavor, finding its true essence only in the Self.
Established therein, free from attachment, the living soul has attained the state of the non-living;
it may perform all this worldly activity, or it may not.

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): one who is established therein is one whose self is fixed in the Self (*ātmaniṣṭha*). Having attained the state of being "living-liberated" (*ajīvatva* = *jīvanmuktatā*), whether he performs all worldly activity or does not perform it, there is no distinction between performing and not performing; this is the meaning. || 32 ||
Whether performing or not performing actions, the living being who delights in its own self does not incur a connection with the fruits of action, just as the sky is unaffected by clouds. (33)

He states the absence of distinction with the words "not performing" (akurvan). "Actions" refers to those of the nature of prescribed and prohibited rites. "Fruits of action" refers to heaven, hell, and so forth. || 33 ||
Or else, having abandoned even that objective aspect, let the living being remain as a mass of peaceful consciousness, utterly tranquil within itself like a glowing gem.

Alternatively: "even that object of cognition" means even while relying slightly upon an object of cognition; the meaning is: even though the connection with an object of cognition was previously admitted.
"The tranquil mass of consciousness" means having the nature of changeless consciousness. || 34 ||
The great-souled ones, who delight in the Self, are awakened and possess supreme excellence;
they are as flickering as the tips of peacock feathers on the outside, yet as immovable as Mount Meru within.

"Delighting in the Self" (ātmārāmāḥ): they are called *ātmārāmāḥ* because they delight—that is, find rest—only in the Self; such are the great-souled ones (*mahātmānaḥ*). Outwardly, in the activity of the external senses, they appear as flickering as the tip of a peacock's feather; inwardly, however, in their inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), they are as immovable as Mount Meru, due to being established in the Self. || 35 ||

That state of those whose minds have been dissolved, wherein the mind is devoid of the condition of being an object of thought, is called the cessation of all mental construction; it is a state of deep sleep even while awake.

Regarding the term *citta*: when the mind (*citta*) is devoid of the state of being an object (*cetya-daśā*) and is emptied of the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) associated with objects, that state of those whose consciousness has waned and whose modifications have ceased—a state of peaceful calculation and tranquilized latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is called "deep sleep even while awake" (*jāgraty eva suṣuptatā*). || 36 ||
O Rāma, this very state of deep sleep, when it has become mature through the practice of yoga,
is called the "Fourth" (turya) by those who are experts in the true nature of reality.
"This" refers to the following: this very state of deep sleep (sauṣuptī sthiti), when it becomes mature through the yoga of practice, is called the fourth state (turyāvasthā).
This is because, by virtue of its distinctness from waking and the other states, it is the "fourth" in relation to the triad of those three. || 37 ||
But having attained an imperishable state in this fourth stage (turyāvasthā), because his character is solely devoted to bliss, he has reached the state beyond bliss. || 38 ||

The two verses beginning with "asyām" form a single syntactical unit. Having attained a non-perishing, unassailable state in this aforementioned fourth stage (*turyāvasthā*), one whose character is exclusively bliss— that is, one whose nature (*svabhāva*) is fixed and constant in bliss, or who habitually practices and cultivates bliss alone.

Because of his state—due to being continuously of the nature of bliss—he has reached the state of Brahman, which is the "non-bliss state" in the sense that it is devoid of the bliss of one's own limited individual form (svasvarūpa). || 38 ||
Indeed, because he has transcended even the portions of bliss and great bliss, the yogi who has reached the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is called "liberated. (39)

Immediately thereafter, he transcends the states of *anānanda* (joylessness) and *mahānanda* (great joy). *Anānanda* is devoid of the experience of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), while *mahānanda* likewise exceeds both levels [of joy and joylessness] due to its non-conceptual nature and its state of being of one flavor (*samarasībhāva*) with the bliss of Brahman. Therefore, such a yogi, having reached the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), is said to be liberated.

The meaning is that one who has transcended the fourth state (*turyātīta*) is called "liberated. Furthermore, *turya* and *turyātīta* are the names for two types of living-liberated ones (*jīvanmukta*): those who possess the meditative absorption with mental constructs (*savikalpaka-samādhi*) and those who possess the absorption without mental constructs (*nirvikalpaka-samādhi*). In this context, there are the three states beginning with waking, as well as the individual souls (*jīva*) who identify with them, namely the forms of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña.

Perceiving [all things] as distinct from himself, yet contemplating the very nature of the Self as pure consciousness within that witness, he is called the Fourth (turya). But when free from even that conceptualization, being of the nature of pure consciousness alone, he is "beyond the Fourth" (turyātīta). || 39 ||

With all the bonds of birth completely dissolved and all conceit consisting of darkness entirely melted away, the great-souled one attains an existence composed of the supreme essence, like a lump of rock salt dissolved in water. (40)
"Parigalita" means: from whom all the bonds that cause birth—such as impurities (*mala*), karma, and so forth—have completely fallen away;

in whom all things consisting of darkness (*tamas*) have dissolved; and in whom the conceits born of ignorance—the notions of "I" and "mine" regarding the body, senses, and so on—have vanished. That Great Soul [attains] that which consists of the supreme essence (*parama-rasa*).
It attains an existence whose nature is supreme bliss, like a lump of rock salt dissolved in water.

For that mass of salt, once placed within the water, attains a supreme, most excellent state of being—consisting of taste, liquid in form, and identical with its own essential nature; it is just like that. || 40 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
That supreme self-nature which exists between the inert and the conscious perceivers is indeed proclaimed in manifold ways in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and other Upaniṣads. (41)

Regarding the term *jaḍa* (insentient): between the two types of perception—the insentient and the sentient—consciousness whose object is the visible world as "this" (*idam*) is the insentient perception; consciousness whose object is the seer as "I" (*aham*) is the sentient perception. Between these two, that reality which exists as the essence persisting through both "this-ness" and "I-ness"—the entity that shines forth as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone—that indeed is the supreme self (*pāramātmika*).
It is stated many times in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and other Upaniṣads that the reality related to the Supreme Self is its very nature (svarūpa). || 41 ||
That which is the ultimate happiness in the relationship between the seen and the seeing, consisting of pure experience, is therefore called Brahman, the essence. || 42 ||

Regarding the word "dṛśya" (the visible): when there is a connection with the perception of beautiful objects—that is, with the knowledge of mental modifications (*vṛtti-jñāna*)—there exists a certain ultimate happiness (*sukha*), which is born within the supreme Self (*paramārtha-svātman*), consisting of experience (*anubhūtimaya*), having the nature of experience (*anubhavātmaka*), and being experienced by itself; that alone is the essential happiness.

It is called Brahman. Why? Because of the reason stated previously; that is to say, because it was previously designated as the very nature of the Supreme Self, which is pure consciousness consisting of bliss. || 42 ||
In the relationship between the seen and the seer, the consciousness of pleasure is unsurpassed;
when it is conjoined with the seen, it is bondage, and when freed from that, it is called liberation. (43)
In that case, if even the pleasure of sense-objects were of the nature of one's own Self, there would be no distinction between bondage and liberation; therefore, he says:

"dṛśya" (the visible). When there is a connection between the visible and the seer—that is, when there is a relation between the visible object and the act of seeing—the unsurpassed experience of pleasure (*sukhasaṃvit*) is called "bondage" if it is permeated by the visible, meaning if it is conditioned by the visible object.
Released from that, untouched by the visible world, and released from the consciousness of that pleasure—that is liberation. || 43 ||
In the relationship between the seen and the seeing, that experience which is free from affliction—taking hold of that, remain; resort to your state of deep sleep. (44)
"Regarding 'dṛśya' (the visible): in the relationship between the seen and the seeing, there is an experience that is *anāmayā*—free from affliction and consisting of bliss.
Abiding by grasping and relying upon that very experience, remain; find rest in that very experience.
Resort to that state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptī*) previously described. || 44 ||
That very state attains the condition of the Fourth (turya) when that vision is attained, O Rāghava;
for in that vision, the Self is neither gross nor subtle, neither perceptible nor otherwise.

The phrase "saiva" (that very same) constitutes two verses. That very state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptī sthiti*) indeed attains the condition of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*); in that vision consisting of the fourth state, the Self is not gross because it is formless, nor is it subtle because it is all-pervading; it is not perceptible by the senses because it is other [than the objects of the senses].
And it is not indirect, because it manifests as something immediate. || 45 ||
It is neither conscious nor inert, neither non-existent nor composed of existence;
it is not "I," nor another, neither one nor even many, O Rāghava. (46)

The conscious being (*cetana*) is not the substratum of consciousness, because it is itself of the nature of consciousness. For that which is called "conscious" is defined as the substratum of consciousness, just as "white" is defined as the substratum of whiteness. Indeed, in the view of the Vedāntins, there is no essential nature of the self distinct from consciousness. Furthermore, it is not insentient (*jaḍa*), because it is the illuminator of all things; nor is it non-existent.

Because it is of the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*), it consists of being (*sanmaya*); because it is not an object of cognition as "it does not exist," it is not denoted by the word "I" (*ahaṃśabdavācya*); because it is not delimited by the body, senses, and so forth, it is not "other"; because it is the self of all, it is "one" (*eka*); because it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and because number is of the nature of a quality, it is not the substratum of the number one; and because it is not manifold, it is not "many" (*aneka*).
That which has become visible, resting upon the six senses with the mind as the sixth—O Rāma, that state transcends all; it is here as if it were nothing at all.

Regarding the word "yat": that which has become the object of perception—that is, the support (āśraya) of the senses with the mind as the sixth—meaning the locus and objective field of those senses beginning with sight—is this very world; and that from which [the world] has transcended (atīta), having passed beyond it, being of a different nature than it, is that state (pada), the reality of the Self (ātmatattva).
Therefore, for that reason, that reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is not like anything at all in this world; the meaning is that it cannot be compared to anything whatsoever. || 47 ||
Liberation is not on the back of the sky, nor in the underworld, nor upon the surface of the earth;
when all hopes have perished, the destruction of the mind is held to be liberation. (48)

"No. For liberation is indeed the cessation of bondage; and since that [bondage] consists in the nature of the mind, its cessation must likewise consist in the very nature of that [mind]. This is the intended meaning. || 48 ||
If the thought "May there be liberation for me" arises within, the mind has been awakened;
yet when the mind is born of such thinking, there is a firm, worldly bondage.

Regarding "liberation": if the thought "May liberation be mine; may it come to pass" arises within, it would have arisen from the mind. And when the mind has arisen through mental activity and volition, worldly bondage—the cause of saṃsāra—becomes firm.
[49] Or rather, when the Self has transcended everything, or is expanded as the form of all things...
What is bondage, and what is liberation? Render the notion of them rootless.

Regarding the word "in the Self" (ātmani): when the Self is transcendent to everything, distinct from the universe, or alternatively, when it is all-formed, the essence of all, and pervasive (tate), what is bondage and what is liberation? For there is an absence of both bondage and liberation whether the Self is beyond the phenomenal world (prapañca) or identical with it. Therefore, uproot your mental reflection and volition. 50.
With his intellect turned inward, he was profoundly peaceful, full, and pure in mind;
having wiped away the stains of the mire of desire, the bonds of his own delusion were severed.
When the root of reflection has been destroyed, he introduces its subsidiary member with three verses, beginning with "adhyātma" (the internal).

One whose delight is within the Self; who is tranquil and profoundly peaceful; who is full and possesses a perfectly complete vision; and whose mind is purifying—meaning one whose mind is pure because its sins have been shaken off by self-knowledge. || 51 ||
Freed from the fear of the defects of dualities, having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra,
he has indeed attained unsurpassed rest, having reached the state that is difficult to attain.
One who has attained such unsurpassed rest within the self desires nothing at all. || 52 ||
Having attained the state of non-retrogression through deed, mind, and speech, he who has initiated all attainments and desired undertakings desires nothing at all. (53)
Take hold of hopelessness—the axe that fells the *karanja* tree of calamities, the station of ultimate bliss, and the flower-cluster of the tree of tranquility. (54)
"Āpad" means a cluster of flowers, a bouquet of blossoms. 54.

To one whose form is adorned with hopelessness, O Rāma, the earth is but the footprint of a cow, Meru is a mere post, the quarters are small caskets, and the three worlds are but a blade of grass. (55)
"Goḥ padam" means "the footprint of a cow. "Āśā" means the directions. "Samudgikāḥ" means small caskets or boxes. || 55 ||
For the discerning person who perceives the Knower as distinct from the body,
nothing at all is cut away even when the limbs are being severed.
He states that even in the absence of hope, the very contemplation of the Self is the cause: "From the body," etc.

The meaning is this: when the conscious, sentient Self—distinct from the body whose limbs have been severed—is realized as one whose essential nature is bliss, there is indeed indifference even toward the body, let alone toward external objects. || 56 ||
Even though molasses is experienced as sweet, it cannot be made otherwise by burning or cutting; likewise, the vision of the reality of the Self [cannot be altered]. (57)

Regarding the phrase "experienced": just as the sweetness of jaggery, once experienced, cannot be altered even by means of suffering such as burning, cutting, heating the body, or laceration— because that experienced jaggery is remembered precisely as sweet— so it is with the Self.

Even the perception of one's own self-nature (*svatva*), once experienced, cannot be undone, because the bliss of one’s true nature (*svarūpa-sukha*) is impossible to forget and because there exists no other bliss superior to it. As the omniscient Yogin said:
"By a succession of associations with those who possess it, even ordinary people become objects of love due to its superior utility."
"Being causeless, unsurpassed, and without limit, how can my own innate state—my own indivisible bliss—be described? || 57 ||
A woman devoted to another man, even while busy with household chores,
relishes within herself that very elixir of the flavor of a new union. (58)
Establishing this very point through an illustration, he says: "The other," etc., which constitutes two verses as a single syntactical unit.

For just as a wanton woman, devoted to another man and attached to a stranger, even while occupied and preoccupied with her own household duties, relishes and dwells upon that very same fresh elixir of union— the bliss of new sexual enjoyment— experienced previously. || 58 ||
Thus, having attained rest in the supreme, pure reality, the steadfast one experiences that very state within, even while engaging in external activity. (59)

Thus, even a steadfast person who has attained rest in the supreme reality, though engaged in external worldly activity regarding the body and so forth, and though joined with such conduct, internally relishes that very same supreme reality within the mind. The sense is that for one established in reality, external worldly activity does not constitute a disruption of meditative absorption (samādhi). || 59 ||
Through non-attachment to objects, there is inner peace and liberation;
this occurs even while the body exists for one of sinless character.

"Due to non-association. Because of the non-association of objects, there is inner peace; liberation is indeed the dissolution of the mind into the Self. And that [liberation] occurs only for one of stainless character—one who is sinless—whether the body exists or not.
He who lives free from attachment is called one liberated while living;
he who lives with attachment is bound, and the third is indeed liberated.

Regarding the word "ya" (he who): he who lives having abandoned attachment—that is, being unattached to external objects and delighting only in his own Self—is called *jīvanmukta* (liberated while living). However, one who lives with attachment—that is, one whose focus is on external objects—is called *baddha* (bound). As for the third type: he who neither lives with attachment nor is free from attachment, because he has not abandoned attachment and yet is devoid of a body (*videha*). He, however—
The meaning is that he who is liberated is denoted by the word "liberated" (mukta) alone, without any qualifying suffix. || 61 ||
Nor does he look toward the future, nor does he abide in the present;
he does not recollect the past, yet he performs everything. (62)
The six verses beginning with "Not so" (na iti) form a single syntactical unit. One who is unattached while acting among those yet to be, those currently existing, and those past;
who imitates the various behaviors of devotees, rogues, children, the elderly, and others; and who is endowed with qualities such as fortitude, is liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Even toward children and others whose natures are contrary [to his own], he does not undergo transformations such as amazement. || 62 ||
While living beings were intent on their worldly attachments, he remained always with a mind unattached;
toward the devoted he behaved like a devotee, and toward the deceitful he appeared as if he were deceitful himself. (63)
Among the foolish he is a fool; among the aged he is aged; among the steadfast he is steadfast;
among those in the prime of youth he shares their youthful conduct; and among the suffering, his mind is filled with sorrow. (64)
His joy was expressed with steady composure; he was graceful, his fame was meritorious, wise, serene, and sweet, his mind free from any sense of wretchedness. (65)
Even when the sun has become cool-rayed, even when the lunar orb is intensely heated,
and even when fire spreads downwards— the one liberated while living is not struck with wonder.
"Thus do these powers of the conscious self unfold here"—one who knows this feels no curiosity toward its wondrous webs. (67)

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: for what reason does curiosity regarding the web of wonders not arise in this one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), who contemplates the play of the power of consciousness (cicchakti)—namely, why these powers of the conscious self manifest in such manifold ways? || 67 ||
Just as a circular whirlpool appears as if distinct from the water due to the movement of the water,
so too does the world appear [distinct] due to the movement of the mind.
Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): due to the movement—that is, the circular motion—of water on all sides, a whirlpool appears as if it were distinct from the water itself. || 68 ||
Just as in the sky, due to the flickering of the eye, a circle of peacock feathers or pearls appears as if real though unreal, so too does the world appear through the vibration of the mind. (69)
Likewise, due to the vibration of the mind, the world—though unreal—is seen as if real within the space of consciousness. || 69 ||
Rāma said:
O Brahmin, tell me that by which the mind vibrates or by which it does not vibrate; for it is precisely that by which I may treat this [sickness]. (70)

"By what means... || Tell me that cause by which the mind vibrates, or that cause by which it does not vibrate—that cause of its vibration and cause of its non-vibration—so that, according to the method you have taught, I may treat that very mind and render it free from vibration. || 70 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as whiteness is in snow, O Rāma, and as a drop of oil is in sesame seeds,
even so, O Raghava, the two vibrations of the mind are seen to be conjoined.

Desiring to teach the means for the cessation of the mind's vibration (*cittaspanda*), and in order to show that the very cessation of the mind's vibration is the destruction of the mind (*cittanāśa*), he states the non-difference between the mind and its vibration with the words "just as" (*yathā*).
The meaning is that, just as in the case of snow and whiteness or sesame seeds and oil, no distinction is perceived between the mind and its vibration. (71)
O Rāghava, there are two methods for the destruction of the mind: yoga and knowledge.
Yoga is indeed the restraint of its fluctuations, while knowledge is correct discernment. (72)

"Two" refers to the two means [for attaining that state] in sequence: the obstruction of those fluctuations, which is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛttinirodha*). And as stated in the *Pātañjala-sūtra*: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. (72)
Those adorned by the scriptures say that the mind is the vibration of the vital breath;
when that [breath] is restrained, the mind will surely become stilled. (73)
The two verses beginning with "cittam" constitute a single syntactical unit. "Prāṇaparispanda" means that whose vibration is by means of the vital breath;
the sense is that its movement is dependent upon the vital breath. [This refers to] in that vital air (prāṇavāyu). 73 || 74 ||
Through the subsiding of the vibration of the mind, this saṃsāra dissolves,
just as worldly activity ceases when the movement of the sun’s light comes to rest.
Rāma said:
How can the movement of the vital breaths and the rest, which move incessantly within the house of the body and travel through its depths, be obstructed by the wind? (75)

"Without ceasing" (aniśam) means for those who move through the thicket—that is, those whose movement is difficult to comprehend. By the word "etcetera" (ādi) in the phrase "of the vital breaths, etc.," the inclusion of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth is intended. || 75 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:

Through association with the scriptures and virtuous people, and through the practice of detachment, one first develops a lack of reliance toward worldly activities and establishes a firm reliance [upon the Self]. (76)

Now, the method for arresting the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa-spanda*) is described by means of eleven verses; the two verses beginning with "The scripture" (*śāstra*) constitute a single syntactical unit. "Scripture" refers to the spiritual science (*adhyātma-śāstra*). "Association with the virtuous" is fellowship with those who know Brahman. "Dispassion" is a lack of attachment toward sense objects. "Practice" is the practice of meditative absorption (*samādhi*); these indeed [are the means].

"Yogas" means skillful means; from those causes, first and foremost, when there is a firm establishment of lack of reliance—that is, indifference—toward the functions of saṃsāra, the worldly activities. || 76 ||
From meditating for a long time with one-pointedness upon the desired object, and from the intensive practice of a single reality, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained. (77)

From meditation performed for a long time, arisen as a single state— that is, arisen in a uniform manner— meaning from meditating without transgressing one's desire; and from meditation upon whatever object the desire flows toward with enthusiasm, the cause of which is the intensive practice of a single reality.
The continuous and repeated contemplation of the very nature of a single object is the means by which the vibration of the vital breath—the restlessness of the prāṇa-wind—is restrained. || 77 ||

Through the firm practice of breath-restraint beginning with inhalation (pūraka), performed without causing fatigue, and through the yoga of solitary meditation, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is restrained. (78)

Regarding the term "pūraka": due to firm practice—that is, through repeated cultivation performed in such a way as to be steadfast—and due to being free from exhaustion, meaning not produced by strenuous effort, there arises the breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*) consisting of the types *pūraka*, *kumbhaka*, and *recaka*, which culminates in the perfection of pure *kumbhaka*. From that cause, and also from the yoga of solitary meditation (*ekāntadhyāna*), [the state of oneness is attained].

Furthermore, through the practice of meditation cultivated in solitude, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is arrested. As Yājñavalkya, having introduced the exclusive practice of *kumbhaka* (retention), stated: "This is the mastery of the vital breath;
it is the means for destroying all death. (78)
(500) Through the experience of the reality of sound at the conclusion of the utterance of the syllable *oṃ*,
when consciousness becomes as in deep sleep, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is arrested. || 79 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the syllable *oṃ*": when the *praṇava* is uttered, because of the experience—that is, the continuous contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*)—of that reality of sound which exists at its final limit, the outward-turned mental fluctuation of consciousness becomes dissolved in deep sleep, and the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) is restrained. In this case, however, it is through the contemplation of the *nāda*.

Because it is the cause for the dissolution of the mind, its status as the cause for the dissolution of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through that same gateway has been stated in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*: "There is no posture equal to the perfected one (*siddha*), no breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) equal to the absolute (*kevala*), no seal (*mudrā*) equal to *khecarī*, and no dissolution (*laya*) equal to *nāda*. Fire set ablaze in wood is extinguished along with the wood; [so it is] in *nāda*.

"The mind that has been set in motion dissolves together with the sound (nāda). Having forgotten all that is external, the mind—like milk and water—becomes one with the sound and then suddenly dissolves into the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). (79)
Having diligently pressed the uvula with the tongue so that it reaches the root of the palate, when the vital breath has entered the upper aperture, the vibration of the breath is restrained. (80)

Regarding the term *tālumūla*: the two upper parts within the mouth above the root of the tongue are the *tāluni* (palates); their *mūla* (root) is the middle portion. That which is situated there—that is, located in that place—is the *ghaṇṭikā*, the *lambikā* (uvula), a piece of flesh hanging down in the form of a subtle tongue. [One should grasp it] with effort—that is, by means of a specific exertion—using the tongue as the instrument.

Having ascended, when the vital breath (prāṇa) has gone to the upper aperture—the upper aperture being the cavity of the skull which is indeed called the upper door of the Suṣumnā—then as the Śruti says:
"Between the two palates, that which hangs down like a breast is the birthplace of Indra; there, having parted the two halves of the skull, that hair-limit turns back."

Thus, when the vital breath has entered such an upward-opening [aperture], the vibration of the *prāṇa* is obstructed. By this, the yoga of the *lambikā* (the uvula) is demonstrated; that which is called *khecarī* and the "seal of the sky" (*nabhomudrā*). As it is said in the *Vivekamārtaṇḍa*: "The tongue, having entered the hollow of the skull, goes in reverse and reaches the space between the eyebrows."

"The gaze becomes the *mudrā* known as *khecarī*. And here, by the phrase 'through effort,' a specific type of exertion consisting of moving, milking, and so forth, is prescribed for the sake of achieving lengthening of the tongue.
As it is said in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*: "One should gradually increase the [tongue] tip through cutting, moving, and milking until..."

When that [tongue] touches as far as the middle of the eyebrows, at that moment the siddhi of Khecarī occurs. "Kalā" refers to the tongue; its "severing" (chedana) means the cutting of the membrane situated below which obstructs upward movement. Furthermore, "moving" (cālana) refers to the tongue when it is wrapped in a piece of moist cloth.
Grasping firmly with both hands, one performs a whirling motion to the left and right;
"milking," however, is the gradual drawing [of the breath] by means of the two hands in alternation.
At the tip of the nose, at a distance of twelve finger-breadths, within the stainless void where the vision of consciousness has become stilled, the vibration of the vital breath is obstructed. (81)
"Twelve" means: at the tip of the nose, in the foremost part of the nose,

extending twelve finger-breadths from the tip of the nose, within the stainless sky— the pure expanse of space that has become the object of the eyes— in the vision of consciousness, that is, in the functioning cognition (*vṛttijñāna*), as it becomes tranquil and dissolves.

When [this is] present, the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained. And so says Yājñavalkya: "O Gārgī, fixing [the mind] on the tip of the nose is the cause for the conquest of the wind. (81)

Through practice, when the vital breath has reached the upper limit of twelve finger-breadths above the palate via the upper aperture and consciousness has dissolved, the vibration of the breath is restrained.

"From practice" (abhyāsāt): from the practice of restraining the vital breath (*pavana*) as described in the Yoga scriptures; when the *prāṇa*—the vital air—has reached the "end of twelve" (*dvādaśānta*) above the palate by way of the upper aperture, the path of the *suṣumṇā*. By the word "palate" (*tālu*), the sixteen-spoked wheel known as *viśuddhi* is meant.

By the word "ūrdhva" (upward), the *brahmarandhra* is meant; by "dvādaśānta," the twelve-spoked wheel (*cakra*) known as the *anāhata*. Thus, when [the consciousness] has moved upward to the palate or to the *dvādaśānta*, and when consciousness has dissolved—meaning that outward-directed consciousness has vanished—the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) is restrained. And therein, by means of the upper aperture...

The explanation is that when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has reached the *dvādaśānta* above the palate—meaning it has reached the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) located twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) upward from the position of the palate—[the state arises]. As for the phrase "situated at the root of the palate" and so forth, this is disregarded as being redundant with the previously mentioned *khecarīmudrā*. And here:

It should be understood that because the palate and other such parts are locations of the vital points (*marmans*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the dissolution of the breath situated there is appropriate. As Yājñavalkya said: "The two big toes, the two ankles, the mid-shanks, likewise the roots of the buttocks, the two knees, and the midpoints of the two thighs..."

O Gārgī, O best of sages, the vital points (marmasthāna) are as follows: the root of the anus, then the middle of the body, the penis, the navel, the heart, the pit of the throat, the root of the palate, the root of the nose, the circles of the eyes, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the crown of the head.

Regarding the phrase "these [are] the [practices]," here the word "practice" (abhyāsa) refers to one who has conquered the senses, dwells in a secluded place, and eats wholesome, moderate, and pure food; whose body has been purified by means such as the cleansing of the bladder and purifications of the head and lower parts, according to the path instructed by the guru.

For one whose channels have been purified through the practices of *āsana* and *prāṇāyāma*, the intended practice is that of *mahāmudrā* and the others, which serves as the cause for the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the *suṣumnā*. These are the ten *mudrās*, beginning with *mahāmudrā*.
As it is stated in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*: "Mahāmudrā, Mahābandha..."
Mahāvedha and Khecarī, Uḍḍiyāna, Mūlabandha, and the bandha known as Jālandhara.

"Karaṇī, the one called Viparītā, Vajrolī, and Śakticālana—this tenfold group of Mudrās must be guarded with great effort. And: "Even though the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī) is blocked, for yogins it becomes straight through firm practice by means of postures (āsanas), breath-control (prāṇasaṃyāma), and Mudrās. As for the definitions of Mahāmudrā and the others:
For fear of excessive prolixity, this has not been written here; it should be understood from other texts. || 82 ||

When the light of the star [at the heart] has reached its cessation at the midpoint between the eyebrows, and consciousness is bound to that abode, the vibration of the vital breath is obstructed. (83)

Regarding the phrase "between the eyebrows": between the two eyebrows is the triangular wheel of space (*vyomacakra*); for that is the locus for perceiving the light consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*). As it has been said:
"Situated between the pair of eyebrows, the world shines like a pure peacock, lightning, and the sun; for those of meritorious vision, the [light] consisting of consciousness unfolds."

"Light," it is said. When that definition is prescribed, it refers precisely to the cessation of the light of the stars. The "star" is the pupil of the eye; the "light of the stars" is the activity of seeing. When that has ceased—that is, when it has come to rest—the "sign" (ketana) is the convention (saṃketa), which is a human construct stating, "this is the meaning of this word."

The restriction between the signified and the signifier is bound therein; that which follows it is consciousness—meaning, conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*). When that [consciousness] has reached its end, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) is obstructed. However, if the reading is *buddha*, it refers to the consciousness awakened within the "sign" (*ketana*), namely, the relationship between word and meaning.

It should be explained that when that conceptual cognition, which does not connect the word, the object, and their relationship, reaches its end in that [state], [the yogin attains the goal]. || 83 ||
When the knowledge that has arisen instantaneously becomes firm,
the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is arrested in that portion untouched by conceptual construction. (84)

"Instantly" (*jhaṭiti*) means: here, knowledge has arisen quite suddenly, having emerged all at once even without any desire to know, either by the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) or due to the proximity of the object.
When that knowledge has been made firm—having been strengthened and cultivated in that very way within its portion untouched by conceptual construction—[the state is attained].
