When the portion consisting of conceptual construction has dissolved, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) is arrested. The sense is that when the arisen knowledge of mental modifications (*vṛttijñāna*), being firmly cultivated, becomes pure existence (*sanmātra*) with its objective aspect dissolved, even then there is the arrest of the vibration of the vital breath. || 84 ||

For the sage, through the long-term perception of the solitary space within the heart and through meditation with a mind free of latent impressions (vāsanā), the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is restrained.

"For a long time" means: for a long duration, through the heart—that is, the mind—of a sage established in the vow of silence, from the perception of the absolute void (*ekāntavyoma*), which is the perception of space (*ākāśabhāvanā*) that is constant and fixed; from that arises the meditation of the mind free from latent impressions (*avāsanamanodhyāna*), which is entirely liberated from the impressions of sense objects.

The vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is also ceased by means of that meditation which is accomplished through the mind. In this regard, *rājayoga* is not perfected without *haṭhayoga*, nor is *haṭhayoga* perfected without *rājayoga*. Therefore, according to the principle that "one should practice until the pair is accomplished," one should properly practice the method of the vital breath (*māruta*) conjoined with the mind. Elsewhere:

Furthermore, based on the statement, "The wise man should not engage in mental activity," it should be understood that the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) must be practiced simultaneously with the restraint of the mind. This has been established in various places by such passages as, "When consciousness arises in deep sleep, the vision of consciousness becomes tranquil," and so forth. || 85 ||
By these methods, as well as others devised through various intentions and residing in the mouths of diverse teachers, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained. (86)

"By these" means: by these aforementioned sequences and methods, as well as by those fashioned through various mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*), those taught from the mouths of various teachers, and other sequences, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) is restrained. In that context, by the word "others," those methods for restraining the breath which rely on different locations [are implied].
The methods for the dissolution of the mind (*cittalaya*) have been demonstrated by the ancient masters; all of them are here collected together.
This is because the methods for the dissolution of the mind are themselves methods for the dissolution of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). As it is said in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"By that which the breath is bound, by that very means the mind is bound; and by that which the mind is bound, by that the breath is bound."
It is said, "one is bound. Furthermore, because those methods for the dissolution of the mind (*cittalaya*) are infinite, they cannot all be demonstrated.
As it is stated in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*: "Those methods of yoga have been described by Ādinātha as numbering one hundred and twenty-five million;
through practice, these techniques of yoga become free from obstacles."
They become means for the fortunate one in the shattering of existence.
"By practice" refers to the fortunate yogin who is destined for success. 87.
When the movement of the vital breaths has come to an end through practice, the mind attains tranquility, and nirvāṇa alone remains. || 88 ||
"By practice" means that the reality of the Self, which is liberation in the form of absolute isolation (kaivalya), [is attained]. 88.
Rāma said:
Thus has the tranquility of the mind engaged in yoga been described.
Now, O Lord, out of your grace, tell me of right knowledge. 89.

Regarding the word "yoga": the meaning is that between yoga and knowledge—the two methods for the destruction of the mind as previously mentioned—it has been shown how the pacification, that is, the destruction, of the mind occurs for a person possessing the means characterized by yoga, in the manner described above. || 89 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
The vision of reality as it truly is within these three worlds consists in this much:
having ascertained that the Self alone is the entire universe, one attains fullness. (90)

"Yathā" (as): Having ascertained that "the entire world is indeed the Self," that which is fullness—that is, the state of being the perfectly complete form—is precisely this: the vision of things as they truly are, the vision of the ultimate reality. 90, 91, 92.

When the regulation of the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) has attained firmness through practice and is marked by dispassion (vairāgya), it is considered fruitful according to one's latent impressions (vāsanā). || 91 ||
Through the total exhaustion of conceptual construction, that state remains for the living being,
from which all words, together with their entire range of mental constructions, turn back.
"These hundreds of powers in the form of objects such as jars and cloths are the Self alone; there is nothing else"—this certainty is right vision. (93)

"‘These’ means: the hundreds of objects in the form of pots, cloths, and so forth, as well as their hundreds of potencies—the forms of pots, cloths, etc., and the potencies belonging to them—all that is indeed the Self. The certainty that there is no other entity whatsoever is right knowledge; this is the meaning. || 93 || 94 ||
"The Supreme Self exists here as the essence of manifestation, without beginning or end"—the wise know this expansive certainty to be right knowledge. (94)
Everything is indeed the Self; where, then, do existence and non-existence abide?
Where are the notions of bondage and liberation? O Rāma, what else is there to be grieved for? 95.
"All" means this: the entire visible world is indeed the Self alone; therein, what existence and non-existence could possibly be designated or defined?

Since everything has the nature of the Self, the distinction that "this is existence" and "this is non-existence" cannot be established. Furthermore, by the phrase "wherein situated," even the locus of existence and non-existence cannot be defined.
Thus he said: "O Rāma, what else is there to be grieved for? Since even bondage and liberation do not exist, there is no occasion for sorrow"—this is the meaning. (95–96)
There is no object of thought other than the mind, nor is there any mind; this is only Brahman manifesting.
All is the one Supreme Brahman; what is liberation, and what is bondage? (96)
This Brahman, whose form is projected forth, vast and established in the immense—having long since transcended duality—is indeed you yourself as the Self by means of the Self. 97.
"Brahman" means that which is vast, vast indeed—existing as the gross and the grossest in the form of the earth, the mountains, and so forth. For this reason, become the Self by yourself alone;
become the full Supreme Self. || 97 ||
When form is correctly observed, there is not even the slightest difference between wood, stone, and cloth; where then are you, intent on conceptual construction? (98)

Regarding the word "properly" (*samyak*): when the forms—that is, the essential natures—of wood, stone, and cloth are properly observed and investigated, there is not even the slightest difference between them. This is because the perceived difference depends upon the perceiver, and the perceiver is non-different from its own nature. Therefore, since no object exists apart from the Self, in what object could [difference] reside?
You are oriented toward conceptual construction. || 98 ||
That which is peaceful at the beginning and at the end, the indestructible essential nature of all things and of the self—be absorbed in that, O Rāghava. 99.

"At the beginning" means: at the beginning, prior to origination, and at the end, subsequent to destruction, that which is the perfectly tranquil and indestructible essential nature of objects—those entities perceived as "this"—and of the self, which is the locus of "I-ness," namely pure consciousness (cinmātra), become absorbed in that. 99.
Through the emergence of duality and non-duality, and by means of the delusions of old age and death,
the Self alone manifests as various selves through the minds, just as the ocean manifests through its waves.

Regarding the verse beginning with *dvaita*: Through the delusions of old age and death—that is, through the manifestations of aging, dying, and so forth—there arise various distinctions and non-distinctions (*dvaitādvaita-samudbhedāḥ*), which are the emergences of difference and non-difference.

It is by means of those very minds characterized by such [distinctions] as their own selves (*ātmaiva*), that the Self alone flashes forth in many ways through its own forms, like the ocean through its waves. 100.
Embracing the pure Self with an intellect that is eternally situated within, what worldly enjoyment is capable of binding that person who remains thus? (1)

"Pure" means: having embraced—that is, having attained identity with—the Self which is eternally and at all times pure and free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika) by means of an inward-turned intellect (dhiyā), he who remains thus; for such a person, who is the Self and delights in the Self (ātmārāma), what enjoyment indeed is capable of binding him? The meaning is: none at all. || 1 || 2 ||
For one who has cultivated expansive discernment, the enemies such as sensual enjoyments cannot pierce the mind even in the slightest, just as gentle breezes cannot shatter a mountain.
There is no diversity within the mental constructs, nor any internal difference in the object itself, just as there is no difference in the water across various lakes.
Thus, the person who consists of this single firm conviction and has perceived the true reality is said to be liberated. || 3 ||

"Multiplicity": within the mental constructions—that is, within the conceptualizing intellects—there is no multiplicity of the underlying reality, just as there is no multiplicity of water and so forth within lakes. A person who consists of this singular certainty is said to be liberated. (3) (4) (5) (6) (7)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, O Rāma, hear this other perspective that bestows the [true] state, just as it was established without hesitation by the sage Vītahavya. (4)
A sage named Vītahavya, devoted to the performance of ritual acts, dwelt for a very long time in a cave within the Vindhya forest.
In the course of time, he became weary of the sequence of his own actions, which cause wandering through the terrible cycle of saṃsāra and take the form of mental and physical afflictions.
Having completely abandoned all ritual activities for the sake of non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpasamādhi),
he entered the interior of his own leaf-hut constructed of plantain trees.
There, on that level and pure seat covered with a well-spread deer skin,
he stood in the bound lotus posture (*baddhapadmāsana*), with his fingers resting upon his heels. (8)

Regarding the word *tatra*: on the two heels (*pārṣṇyoḥ*), which are the rear portions of the feet and which rest upon the thighs due to the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), the fingers of the hands are placed; that is, the fingers of the hands are situated above with palms facing upward. || 8 ||
He gradually withdrew his mind, which had been scattered throughout the world,
from the external and internal objects of touch in succession.

"He withdraws" (saṃjahāra): the connection is that, avoiding the objects of touch—the sense-objects—he gradually withdrew his mind which was scattered in all directions. In the reading "upaharat," it is an adjective qualifying the mind. 9 || 110 || 11 || 12 ||
Then, desiring steadiness of his own mind, the sage,
with a mind free from sin, contemplated this with his intellect.
Vītahavya said:
Alas! This mind is not steady; even when withdrawn, in an instant it does not attain stability, like a leaf tossed by powerful waves. (11)
From a pot one moves to a cloth, from a cloth to a formidable cart;
the mind wanders among objects like a monkey among trees.
These five gates of the mind—beginning with the eyes—are quite sufficient [for its movement]. (12)
Therefore, the eyes and other [senses] have been thoroughly examined by that omniscient Self;
they are not connected with it even in the slightest degree, just as the netherworld (pātāla) is not connected with the celestial realm (dyuta).
"Teneti" means "known. The prefix *niḥ* functions in the sense of "external.

The eyes and other senses are known as being external to the self; therefore, they are not connected even slightly with that self, just like the netherworld (*pātāla*) and the surface of the sky (*dyutala*).
The meaning is that just as the netherworld and the surface of the sky are not mutually connected, so it is in this case. || 13 ||
O Cārvāka who wanders with the mind as your mount, you who beg for food from the bellies of the four quarters:
do not undergo this fruitless distress; do not roam about here in this world! 14.

"O mind! You who are habituated to wandering through various lands like a wandering mendicant; you who are a Cārvāka, turning your back on the next world; you who are a beggar for your belly's sake in the four directions—that is, one whose nature is to beg within the interior of the four quarters—O mind, do not wander through this world in vain, do not roam about without taking up [the burden of] weariness. (14)
(509) "I am consciousness"—such is your unreal mental impression (vāsanā).
O fool, there can be no identity between consciousness and the mind, for they are utterly distinct. (15)

"I am [the Self]. O mind, that latent impression (*vāsanā*) of yours which holds "I alone am consciousness" is false. O rogue, there is no identity between consciousness (*cit*) and the mind (*manas*), for they are utterly distinct. Furthermore, this absolute distinction of the mind should be understood through its being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*) and its being insentient (*jaḍatva*). || 15 ||
"This soul is I"—this evil-mindedness of egoism is futile. Abandon this agitation of "I am he" arising from egoism;
it has arisen in vain for the sake of suffering, being neither real nor unreal.

"Regarding 'jīva'": O mind, the wicked notion of egoism that "I am indeed the individual soul (jīva)" is futile. Abandon that agitation and flurry of yours—the state of being overwrought by egoism such as "I am this" or "this is I. 16.
O virtuous one, your very nature is this alone: that you do not engage in discursive thought.
Through inquiry, you have been stilled, just as darkness is dispelled by light.
"This much," [it means]: O mind, that which is your nature—namely, non-investigation—is only this much.
The sense is that because the mind consists of ignorance (avidyā), it is thus. But through investigation, you become stilled, just as darkness is by light. 17.
Your own mind’s state of stability is not established as something that was eternally non-existent in the past, nor does it exist in form at present, nor will it come to be in the future. (18)

"Always" means: "May it be well with you, who are non-existent even throughout the three periods of time. The meaning is: "Henceforth, do not cause me affliction. The address "svamana" is a vocative. 18.
I am attaining final liberation; I am at peace; by good fortune, I am free from the fever of worldly existence.
Established in the state of the fourth form (turya), I abide in my own Self alone. || 19 ||
I am completely extinguished; I am utterly at peace. 19 || 120 || 21 || 22 || 23 || 24 ||
The unborn Lord, whose nature is consciousness, acts as the witness to everything.
Alas, you hosts of senses, why are you so pointlessly agitated? (120)
Like a traveler afraid of snakes, or like a twice-born man afraid of outcasts,
pure consciousness— indeed, the healthy state beyond all illness— remains far removed from the senses.

This very memory of consciousness, which is oriented toward conceptual construction (saṃkalpa), is the giver of suffering. Whether in the God who is devoid of all mental fabrication, or in the body or the insentient mind,
that which is called memory is nothing other than a worthless residue, utterly devoid of both consciousness and its objects.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus resolved, that sage Vītahavya,
free from all desires, forcibly concentrated his mind and remained with his senses motionless.
Within him, the continuity of his vital breaths gradually subsided, like a fire whose mass of flames flickers out once its fuel has been consumed. (24)
Like two eyes with a faint glimmer reaching the edge of the nostrils,
they simultaneously attained the beauty of half-closed lotuses.
Regarding "ghrāṇa": because they are joined at the center of the eyebrows, those two [eyes] appear as if they have reached the tip of the nose with a very slight light. || 25 ||
With his body, head, and neck held perfectly erect, that one of great intelligence remained as if carved from stone or as if depicted in a painting. (26)
He stands with his body, head, and neck even; that is, he whose position—that is, the manner of sitting—is such that the body, head, and neck are held evenly. 26 || 27 || 28 || 29 || 130 ||
While he remained exactly thus for three hundred years within a hollow of the Vindhya forest, it passed for him like half a moment.
There, at a certain time, the body of that great sage was covered with mud on the surface of the earth, which had been washed there by the torrential rains of the monsoon. (28)
In this manner, after three hundred years, that one of great luster attained awakening;
yet his body did not move at all, even though it was pressed against the hollow of the earth.
Consciousness alone seized that body which was pressed down by the earth;
however, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇamaya*) did not occur without the restraint of the breath.
There was no movement of the breath because all the apertures were blocked. (130)
Having attained full maturity upon arising, that mental construction, taking the form of his own mind, was experienced by him as if within his very heart. (31)

Regarding the word "utpatti" (origination): for one whose mental ideation (*kalanā*), which takes the form of their own mind, attains maturity through origination— that is, the full development of various births as its object— within the interior of the heart, in the very center of the lotus of the heart (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*), [that ideation], having reached such proficiency, perceives everything right there within that same heart.
He experienced the events of his previous birth. || 31 || 32 || 33 || 34 || 35 || 36 || 37 ||
In the lovely forest of Kailāsa, at the foot of a Kadamba tree,
he attained the stainless state of a sage for a hundred years, his self liberated while living.
For a hundred years, he shall possess the state of a Vidyadhara, free from mental afflictions; for five yugas, he shall hold the sovereignty of Indra, saluted by gods and celestial musicians.
For one kalpa, he indeed held the status of an attendant to the Moon-crested Lord;
Vitahavya experienced this through the power of his mental manifestation.
Immediately thereafter, the mind named Vītahavya, whose self was infinite,
once formed the desire to behold all his previous births.
Then he beheld all his other bodies, both those that had perished and those that had not;
yet he did not see that body named Vītahavya which had not perished.
Out of a desire to behold that very [form], his mind was set upon lifting up the submerged body. || 37 ||
Then he thought thus: "This body is oppressed by the mud;
in order to extract it, I shall enter the Lord Sun. (38)
The phrase "atha" (now) introduces two and a half verses. His attendant, who stands by the side of the Sun—

referring to the sage Māṭhara, Piṅgala, and Daṇḍa, according to the statement that these are the "pāripārśvakās" (attendants) of Caṇḍāṃśu (the Sun)— having assumed the body of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), [is described] by the previously mentioned passage beginning with "endowed with the portion of egoism" (*ahaṃkārakalāyuktam*).
The syntactical connection is as follows: having taken recourse to the subtle body and assuming the form of air, he internalized the powers of all the senses within the vital breath (prāṇavāyu);
being of that same nature, he entered the sun like air entering a bellows. || 38 || 39 || 140 ||
"His attendant Piṅgala will then extract my body from there. Having said this, the sage entered the Sun, assuming the form of the wind;
becoming the subtle body consisting of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka), he was like air entering a bellows.
The Blessed One, Ravi, who knows what must be done, also saw this leader of sages within his heart; beholding Piṅgala standing before him, he immediately gave him his command.
Permitted by Bhānunātha, the mind named Vītahavya entered the form of Piṅgala, who was heading toward a cave in the Vindhya mountains.

"By Bhānu... || Now, [the soul] is permitted by Bhānu to go to the mind named Vītahavya—which is tranquil in the state of Vītahavya—because that [soul] has entered the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka) in the form of Vītahavya's city of eight, and because that city of eight has the mind as its primary constituent; thus, it goes to such a mind, being authorized by Bhānu.
He entered the tawny body that was traveling toward the caves of the Vindhya mountains. || 41 || 42 || 43 || 44 ||
Leaving the sky, which was as beautiful as a mountain cave or a valley, that Piṅgala reached the Vindhya forest, resplendent with the canopy of clouds like a garment during the rainy season.
Having gone to that cave of the Vindhya mountains, he beheld the body of the sage;
then, scraping the surface of the earth with his claws, he lifted it out from the womb of the earth.
[He took] the lovely body of the sage, as a crane [takes] a lotus stalk. || 44 ||
(513) Mauna entered his own body, the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka),
while Piṅgala went to the sky and the sage to the pure lake. 45.
"Maunam" means that which pertains to a sage (muni). 45 || 46 || 47 || 48 || 49 || 150 ||
Vītahavya quickly immersed himself in a lake filled with blooming lotuses;
having bathed there, performed his silent recitation (japa), and worshipped the Sun-god, [he departed].
With her body adorned by her mind, she shone forth once again as before. || 47 ||

Endowed with that loving-kindness, supreme equanimity, and the highest power, as well as with true wisdom, sympathetic joy, compassion, and glory, the Sage— his mind liberated from all attachments— delighted in the days spent on the riverbank in the Vindhya mountains.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Once, the Sage, who had perceived the higher and lower realms of the world, again applied his mind with his consciousness in order to establish tranquility. (49)
Long ago, the collection of my senses was clearly abandoned by me; now there is no purpose in further reflection, nor in what has already been reflected upon. (150)
Having severed the conceptualization of "is" and "is not," like a tender creeper,
remain in the Residue with your continuity firmly joined, like an immovable mountain peak.
"Existence or non-existence?"— having broken, that is, having shattered, the conceptualization that delineates existence and non-existence, which is the dualistic view like a tender creeper,
I remain with my concentration fixed upon the remaining, inexpressible pure consciousness alone, standing like the peak of a mountain. 51.
Like one who has risen as if having set, or like one who has set as if having risen;
equal, appearing with the same flavor [in all things], I remain, having attained purity. (52)

"Risen" (udita) means: although manifesting, he is as if set because of his lack of activity; although beyond the range of the senses, he is as if risen because he is the witness of all. "Equal" (sama) means:
being of one form, he is one whose appearance—his manifestation—is of a single flavor (samarasa), that is, a uniform taste, with respect to the desirable, the undesirable, and so forth. Such is he.
Having attained purity, I remain stainless. || 52 ||
Though awakened, I remain as if in deep sleep; though in deep sleep, I am fully awake. Taking hold of the Fourth State (*turya*), I abide within the body with a motionless stability. (53)

Regarding the term "awakened" (prabuddha): even though awakened, one who does not perceive objects through the senses—though situated as if in deep sleep, free from joy, sorrow, and the like—is said to be "situated in deep sleep" because, by being established in samādhi, there is an absence of external mental engagement; thus, having attained the state of deep sleep, he is awakened within his own true nature.

I am ever-awake. Taking as my support the pure consciousness that persists through the three states—the fourth (turya)—I remain with my physical presence fixed within the heart of the body, my mental fluctuations restrained. 53 || 54 || 55 ||
Having reflected thus, he remained in that state of union for six more days;
then he regained consciousness, like a traveler who has slept for a moment.
Then that blessed Vītahavya, a man of great austerity, having attained perfection,
lived for a long time in that state of liberation while living.
When the perceptions of attachment to what is to be abandoned and acquisition of what is to be taken up— along with their respective relinquishment and grasping— had ceased,
the mind of the sage Vītahavya transcended both desire and aversion.

Regarding the word "heyeti": when the attachment and conceit consisting of the notions "this is to be abandoned" and "this is to be accepted," along with the two perceptions of "I shall abandon this" and "I shall accept that," have ceased, the mind of the sage Vītahavya became free from desire and aversion—that is, devoid of both—and remained in a state of non-conceptualization (nirvikalpa). || 56 ||
At the frontier of birth and karma, in the state of disembodied liberation (videha-kevalībhāva),
he conceived an exceedingly intense desire for the total renunciation of attachment to worldly existence.

"Videha" means: at the limit of births and actions, at the ultimate boundary consisting of the complete renunciation of attachments to worldly existence, he attained—that is, reached—an exceeding desire for the disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*). || 57 || 58 ||
Once, that lord of sages entered a mountain cave;
having assumed the lotus posture and remained there, he spoke within himself to his own self. (58)
O passion, go to passionlessness; O hatred, proceed to freedom from hatred.
For a very long time, I have sported here with you both. (59)
With these eight verses beginning with "O Passion" (*rāga*), he dismisses passion and the other [afflictions] that were previously associated with him, while making a prayerful request:

"O Passion, go to a state of passionlessness. This means: "Abandon your passion toward me," which amounts to saying, "Release me who am about to be liberated. "O Hatred, go to a state of hatredlessness"—that is, to a state free from hatred.
"Go! Do not harbor hatred toward me as I depart after leaving you"—this is the meaning.
"Homage be to you, O enjoyments! For hundreds of millions of births, may I be cherished by you in this world, like a child by its caregivers."
Salutations again and again to that bliss by which even this supreme, meritorious path to the state of Nirvāṇa has been made forgotten by me. (61)

"Imām iti": Homage be to that pleasure by which I have been made to forget even this supreme state of nirvāṇa, which consists of unsurpassed bliss. The repetition of the word "namas" (homage) is intended to highlight its extreme deceptive nature. || 61 ||
"O Suffering, my self was earnestly sought by me through that which was heated by you;
therefore, this path of mine has been taught by you—salutations be to you! (62)

"O Suffering! Heated by you, I have earnestly sought the Self for the sake of quelling suffering, according to the Vedic scripture: 'The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow. For that reason, this path to liberation has been taught to me by you;
it was revealed by you alone as the cause of dispassion. Therefore, salutations be to you, who are equal to a Guru. (62)
O friend through action, you, my long-standing kinsman, are being abandoned by me today;
having attained self-knowledge, I have brought about my own destruction at your hands. (63)

"O friend, who is an effect! [means: O friend, who are an effect, because you are a means for attaining dharma and the other goals, you are being abandoned by me today after I have attained self-knowledge (*ātmavijñāna*). You yourself have brought about your own destruction; the meaning is that this fault has been committed by you alone as you exerted yourself for the sake of liberation. || 63 ||
Alone, withered, and miserable, while I am at peace;
withered and miserable, while I am at peace.
O Mother Tṛṣṇā, you must not cause me suffering; salutations be unto you! || 64 ||
"Alone," [she said], "O Mother. || 64 || 65 ||
O Blessed One, may these faults arising from perverse offenses be forgiven; I seek only the state of perfect tranquility—grant me this auspicious blessing.
Salutations to you, the well-performing deity; may it be so with you, for in the past, having rescued me from the nine hells, I was established by you in heaven.
Consoling his daughter, who was distressed by the pain of separation, he said: "Namo" (Salutation). O virtuous one, salutations be to you, the Divine Being. 66.
These companions of mine, born with me and long-standing friends, have today been gradually severed as my life-breaths; may it be well with you, for I am departing. (67)
"Thus" (ataḥ) means: today, by way of sequence or turn, they have been "elevated" (utkṛtāḥ); that is to say, they have been caused to ascend (utkrāntāḥ). || 67 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus reflected within, with his thoughts and desires stilled,
he gradually uttered the Praṇava loudly, having attained the [appropriate] stage.

"Thus"—this refers to the three verses as a single syntactical unit. One whose mental constructions (*manana*), volitions (*saṃkalpa*), and desires (*eṣaṇā*)—such as the desire for sons and so forth—are stilled; one by whom the stage of yoga has been attained, reaching a higher level of hearing (*tāram śrutim*). || 68 || 69 ||
Having abandoned all external and internal entities—whether gross or even more subtle—that arise within the three worlds and are imagined solely by conceptual construction; (69)
Together with the long-continued thread of sound culminating in the *praṇava*, he cast off the web of the senses and their subtle objects, just as the wind scatters a fragrance.

Together with the long-sounding thread that culminates in the *praṇava*, he abandoned the web of the sense organs and their subtle objects, beginning with sound; the meaning is that along with the final resonance of the *praṇava*, the entire web of the senses and their objects came to rest. || 170 ||
Then he abandoned the mere state of darkness, which was like a vision in the sky;
it rose up with a throbbing form, just as a wise man might abandon a trace of anger.

"Then" (tataḥ) means: the state of pure darkness (*tamomātra*), which is a specific modification of the quality of *tamas* even within ignorance (*avidyā*) that consists of the three qualities (*guṇatrayātmikā*). "In the sky" (*ambare*) means in the space of consciousness (*cidākāśe*). || 71 ||
Then, having reflected for half a moment, he abandoned that radiance which had appeared;
and at that time, there was neither darkness nor light.
"Pratibhātam" means that the sattvic light—a particular modification of consciousness—neither became darkness nor [mere] illumination;
the meaning is that he became transcendent to the three qualities (guṇas). || 72 ||
Then, having reached that state, his mind— treating even that [object] as a blade of grass—
fell away from it in half a moment, not even quivering for a brief instant.
"Tām" (that): that state, the state free from the three qualities (guṇas). || 73 ||
Then, the consciousness of the limbs—transparent, having attained the state of manifestation, and pure with a quality equal to the cognition of a newborn infant—[arose]. (74)

"Then" (tataḥ): this refers to the consciousness of the limbs, which is the consciousness of one's own essential nature (svarūpacaitanya). The meaning is that it is free from latent impressions (nirvāsana), similar to the cognition of a newborn infant. || 7 ||
In a time measured by half of half a moment, the Lord abandoned the state of being an object of consciousness for his own consciousness,
just as the wind abandons its power of vibration.
The state of consciousness, which is non-conceptual and pure awareness alone. || 75 ||
Then, having reached the state of *paśyantī*, which consists of pure existence alone, he took hold of the state of deep sleep and remained as immovable as a mountain. (76)
Then, having resorted to the state of deep sleep—which is beyond that which is denoted by the word "Paśyantī" and consists of pure existence alone—he remained as motionless as a mountain. || 76 ||
Having attained stability in deep sleep, he reached the state of the Fourth (turya).
Though devoid of bliss, he was possessed of bliss; there he was both being and non-being.
He was both composed of consciousness and not composed of consciousness—he who is described as "not this, not this" (neti neti). || 77 ||

Regarding the term "suṣupta" (deep sleep): having attained stability in the state of deep sleep, which is non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpasamādhi*), he reached the nature of the Fourth State (*turya*), which transcends the three states. In that condition, the sage became both "without bliss" (*nirānanda*) and "with bliss" (*sānanda*). The word "api" (also/even) is used in a conjunctive sense. Among these, his state of being "without bliss" is as follows:

Because there is no bliss apart from its own essential nature (svarūpa), it possesses bliss through the experience of bliss. Likewise, because it is of the nature of Being (sat-rūpa), it became "Being" (sat). Because all worldly transactions have ceased, it became "Non-being" (asat). || 77 ||
Then that which was beyond even the range of words came into being;
it is the Void (*śūnya*) for the proponents of the Void, and likewise Brahman for the knowers of Brahman. (78)

The phrase "tataḥ" (then) introduces a passage of three and a half verses. Immediately thereafter, that Sage [describes] that reality which is beyond the range of words— that which cannot be established through the function of direct denotation (*abhidhā*)— and yet which is designated by all disputants, according to their respective systems, by such terms as "void" (*śūnya*) and so forth.
The grammatical connection is that it became the nature of that Supreme Self. 78 || 79 || 180 || 81 ||
For those who know consciousness, it is consciousness alone, the stainless abode;
for those with the Sāṃkhya view, it is the Puruṣa; and for the proponents of Yoga, it is the Īśvara. (79)
Śiva is [the deity] for those established in the Śaiva doctrine; Kāla for those who maintain that Kāla alone is the sole reality;
the Self for those who know it as such; and selflessness (nairātmya) for those whose very selves are of that nature. 180.
And it is the middle way for the Mādhyamikas, who possess entirely equanimous minds. (81)
That which is the established conclusion of all scriptures, that which conforms to the heart of all,
that which is everything, omnipresent, and universal— that very reality he remains as.
Regarding the word "yat" (that which): that reality which is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of all scriptures, because it has been so previously propounded;
which follows the heart of all, because it is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*); which is everything, consisting of everything, and all-pervading, because of its omnipresence;
which is related to all, because it is the inner controller—that reality denoted by the word "yat" is such a thing.
Having become that, he remained. || 82 ||
That which is the unsurpassed, motionless state, the illuminator even of lights, and whose sole measure is self-experience—that very reality he remains as. (83)

"Yat" means that reality which is the unsurpassed vibration (niṣpanda), absolutely motionless; which is the illuminator even of lights such as the sun, according to the Vedic scripture, "the light of lights"; and for which one's own direct experience alone is the sole measure or means of valid cognition.
That which is both one and many, both with taint and without taint, that which is both all and not-all—whatever that is, in that he abides. (84)

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): that reality is one because it is in fact non-dual; yet it is many by virtue of *māyā*. It is "with ointment" (*sāñjana*) because it is immovable, being understood through the words of the Teacher (*ācārya*), as per the Śruti; it is "without ointment" (*nirañjana*) because it is self-luminous. "Ointment" (*añjana*), "manifestor" (*vyañjaka*), and "illuminator" (*prakāśaka*) are synonyms. It is "all" (*sarva*) because its nature is the Self of all; it is "not-all" (*asarva*).
Because it transcends all conceptual proliferation. || 84 ||

Then that Lord, abiding as the unborn, immortal, beginningless, primordial, singular, stainless state—both with parts and without parts—became one whose stability was even more pure than the nature of space itself. (85)

Regarding the word "aja" (unborn): because that sage remained as the supreme, stainless reality—which is unborn, immortal, beginningless, devoid of origin, existing from the very beginning, and present in two forms, both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*)—he became the Lord whose state is more pure even than the nature of the sky; such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). || 85 ||
Having radiated light for thirty thousand years as he pleased,
the sage Vītahavya thus became tranquil, with his mind free from rebirth.
"Thirty times"—that is, for the sake of non-recurrence in the mind; that is, for the sake of the non-existence of the mental faculty, meaning for the sake of the absence of future births. || 186 ||
Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Narrative of Vītahavya," in the Section on Tranquility (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Mokṣopāya* by the venerable Vālmīki.
Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Narrative of Vitahavya," in the Section on Quiescence of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa*.
(520) The Tenth Canto.
Rāma said:
O best among the knowers of the Self, why are powers such as traveling through the sky not seen here in the bodies of those liberated while living? (1)

Previously, the abandonment of attachments, the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the practice of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) were shown for the sake of achieving the rest of the mind.

Now, by means of defining the absence of such things as traveling through the sky for one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), he concludes [the discussion] on the attainment of the mind's subsidence with the verse beginning "jīvanmukta. Regarding "traveling through the sky" and so forth: in the sky...
That power by which one goes is "going through the air" (ākāśagamana); those [powers] of which that is the first are [referred to as such]. || 1 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāga, even one who knows the Self and is liberated attains such powers as traveling through the sky by means of the potency of substances, mantras, rituals, and time.
"Anātmavit" (one who does not know the Self). "Dravya" refers to elixirs and the like; "mantra" refers to those of the Tripurā school and so forth; "kriyā" consists of forms such as firm practice;
"kāla" is the duration of long-term practice. [The phrase means] by the power of these. || 2 ||
This is not the domain of one who knows the Self; for the knower of the Self is himself a seer of the Self.
Satisfied by the Self through the Self, he does not pursue ignorance.
"No. This subject of traveling through space and so forth does not enter the scope of the intellect as something to be accomplished for one who knows the Self.

For this reason—because the knower of the Self is always a seer of the Self, constantly maintaining the realization of the Self—he, being satisfied by the bliss of his own Self, does not pursue the supernatural powers consisting of ignorance, such as traveling through space and the like. 3, 4, 5.
One who possesses the self in this world transcends everything, free from desire;
indeed, being content in the self alone, he neither acts nor strives.
Whatever worldly phenomena there may be, they know them to consist of ignorance;
how indeed could one who knows the Self and has abandoned ignorance immerse himself in them?
But he who, even though his self is cultivated, desires the networks of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), accomplishes them in due order by means of the substances that bring about those powers. (6)
The powers of substances, mantras, rituals, time, and personal capacity grant success to the virtuous;
yet none of them assist in the attainment of the state of the Supreme Self.
But for the self-knowing one who is complete, no desire whatsoever arises;
he in whom some desire exists is fully capable of achieving accomplishment.
For that attainment of the self which arises when the entire web of desires has been stilled—how could it not be obtained by one whose mind is submerged in the longing for supernatural powers? (9)
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, how do yogins live for such a long time?
Cut through this doubt of mine, O best among all knowers of Brahman. (10)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Movement arises from the vibration of the vital breaths; when these are stilled, they become like stones.
Since they remain steady in meditative concentration (dhāraṇā), the yogis do not perish.

Regarding the phrase "of the vital breaths" (*prāṇānām*): from the vibration—that is, the movement—of the vital breaths, such as the *prāṇa* and other winds, there arises the vibration of the body, which is to say its instability. Upon the cessation of that, namely the stopping of the vibration of the vital breaths, the yogis who have restrained their breaths become equal to stones, remaining for a long time like rocks, because they are established in *dhāraṇā*.
Therefore, those who remain established in the practice of breath-restraint do not perish. || 11 ||
For one in whom no vibration exists— whether external or internal, born of the mind or born of the vital breath— for such a person, both transformation and decay remain far away.

Regarding the phrase "sabāhya": for that yogin in whom there exists no vibration—whether external or internal, born of the mind or born of the vital breath—for him, whose mind and breath are restrained, the two transformations consisting of old age and death remain far removed.
When the movement of both the breath and the mind has become tranquil within and without,
the bodily constituents never abandon their stability in the body. (13)
For those of great intelligence who have known the objects of experience, who are free from passion,
and whose knots are severed— all of them remain independent while staying in the body.

"Those who... means: those whose knots [of the heart] have been severed; that is to say, when the bliss of the *suṣumnā* is pierced through the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are split. Since the practice of breath-retention (*prāṇadhāraṇā*) is the subject at hand, the meaning is that all those yogis remain independent within their own bodies (*tanau*); they abandon and assume [their forms] by their own will alone. || 14 ||
Rāma said:
O Sage, tell me: when the true nature of the mind has vanished due to the dawning of discernment, where do the qualities such as loving-kindness arise for yogins? (15)
Regarding the word "discernment" (viveka): where do friendliness and the other [immeasurables] arise, given that the self is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and the mind has dissolved? 15–16.
Vasiṣṭha said:
The dissolution of the mind is of two kinds: with form and indeed without form.
In the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), it is with form; that which arises upon liberation from the body is without form.
The existence of the mind here leads to suffering, whereas the destruction of the mind leads to happiness;
having brought the existence of the mind to its end, one should bring about the destruction of the mind.
That mind which, ignorant of reality, highly esteems the accumulation of natural qualities as "mine," is called the suffering *jīva*. (18)

Regarding the term *prākṛta*: that mind which, due to ignorance of reality, highly esteems as "mine" the *prākṛta*—the collection of qualities (*guṇa-sambhāra*), the aggregate of the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth—is called the *jīva*; it is afflicted, being a vessel for the sufferings of *saṃsāra*. || 18 ||
Know that the mind which exists as something utterly motionless, thinking "I am gripped by pleasure, pain, and so forth," is the very longing of the tree of saṃsāra. (19)

Regarding "sukha" (happiness): know that the mind—which is seized and supported by pleasure, pain, and so forth; which is fixed and firm in its egoistic conceit, thinking "I am," "I am happy," or "I am miserable"; and which is the longing of the tree of worldly existence, producing its sprouts, flowers, and fruits—exists even now. 19–20.
O descendant of Raghu, best among those who know how to inquire, I have now described to you the existence of the mind; listen now to its destruction. (20)
They know that mind to be dead which the states of pleasure and pain do not dislodge from its equanimity, just as gusts of wind cannot move the lord of mountains. 21.

Regarding "happiness": they know the mind of that steadfast man to be dead, whose states of pleasure and pain do not lift him up nor shake him from equanimity—just as the winds of exhalation cannot move the king of mountains. (21)
They know his mind to be lost when adversity, wretchedness, enthusiasm, intoxication, languor, or a great festival do not lead him to deformity. (22)

The explanation of this [is as follows]: "misfortune" (āpad) refers to calamities such as those involving sons and other relatives; "miserliness" (kārpaṇya) is poverty; "enthusiasm" (utsāha) is the joy born from the birth of a son and so forth; "intoxication" (mada) is well known; "sluggishness" (māndya) is lack of proficiency; "great festival" (mahotsava) is marriage and the like; and "deformity" (vairūpya) is a state of physical distortion. || 22 ||
Know that state of mind to be delusion, O Raghava; for when it perishes, the quality of pure being (sattva), which is designated as the destruction of the mind, fully arises.

"Manastā" means the existence of the mind (*manas-sattā*); know that very thing to be delusion (*mūḍhatā*). When that existence of the mind perishes, then the reality (*sattva*) consisting of the destruction of the mind arises as knowledge (*jñāna*). When delusion, composed of *rajas* and *tamas*, perishes within the mind—which is itself composed of the three *guṇas*—then the mind of the knower (*jñānin*) becomes composed of pure *sattva*.
The meaning is that it is accomplished. || 23 ||
The mind of one liberated while living becomes endowed with supreme latent impressions characterized by qualities such as loving-kindness, and is further liberated from future births. (24)
Regarding "friendliness": that very mind, when endowed with friendliness and other virtues and possessing purified latent impressions, becomes the mind of one who is liberated while living.
p.
524) For that dissolution of the mind belonging to one liberated while living is of the same nature [as the mind];
indeed, qualities such as friendliness toward delusion exist therein like flower-clusters on a tree in spring. (25)
"Sarūpa" means having an identical form. The meaning is that the nature of the Self manifests as distinct from the mind. || 25 ||
But that formless dissolution of the mind which I have described, O scion of Raghu—
he is indeed the one liberated while alive (videhamukta), existing as the partless Self.
"Formless" means consisting of no parts, having a nature without divisions, because even the constituent element of *sattva* has perished. || 26 ||
Even a being endowed with all the foremost virtues dissolves into the stainless,
supremely purifying state of disembodied liberation.

The four verses beginning with "samagrāgryā" constitute a single syntactical unit. For this reason, even the *sattva* (the quality of purity), which serves as the substratum for all the foremost qualities—namely, the preeminent virtues such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth—is dissolved within that supremely purifying state which is the nature of liberation from the body (*videhamukti*). || 27 ||
In that state of disembodied liberation (videhamukti), which consists of the dissolution of the mind,
nothing whatsoever exists once the mind has perished in what is called Virūpa.

Therefore, regarding that formless dissolution of the mind—which consists of the exhaustion of the *sattva* and pertains to liberation while in the disembodied state (*videhamukti*)—not even the slightest quality or defect exists. || 28 ||
Therein there are neither virtues nor vices, neither prosperity nor adversity, nor restlessness;
there is neither rising nor setting, nor any cognitions of joy or resentment.
Virtues are friendliness and the like; non-virtues are defects of the mind. Prosperity is the abundance of virtues; misfortune is the accumulation of defects. (29)
There is neither light nor darkness, neither the time of twilight and so forth nor the nights;
there is neither being nor non-being, for that state is indeed neither the one nor the other.

It is neither existence nor non-existence, because of the absence of the conventional usages of "is" and "is not"; that state, which is the form of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), is also not the "middle," for it is neither of the nature of being or non-being, nor is it of the nature of experience, due to the contradiction between existence and non-existence.
For those who have reached the further shore of both cognition and the ostentation of saṃsāra,
that vast abode is like the sky for the winds. (31)
Regarding the words "ye hi": that is the disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya), which is expansive, vibrating, and the place of rest. || 31 ||

In that state where suffering is completely stilled, which is non-inert by nature, uniquely asleep, slow with bliss, and free from *rajas* and *tamas*, the great ones— bodiless yet having the space of the ether as their body— dwell, with every fragment of the mind dissolved.

"Completely tranquil" (*saṃśānta*): that in which there is a single sleep—that is, a single state of deep sleep—because the mind is always dissolved therein; "slow with bliss" (*ānandamanthara*), meaning entirely filled with the bliss of Brahman. In such a supreme state, which is the nature of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), [the yogis] are subtle, like the interior of space, because of the absence of the three bodies consisting of the gross, subtle, and causal.
Bodiless, with the fragments of their minds dissolved, and with the portions of their mind consisting of the quality of goodness (sattva) having vanished, the great ones dwell and find rest. || 32 ||
Rāma said:
O Brahmin, what is the seed of this vast vine of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti-mṛdvīkā-latā*), and what is said to be the seed of that seed? (33)
The two verses beginning with "O Brahmin" constitute a single syntactical unit. *Mṛdvīkā* refers to the grapevine. || 33 || 34 ||
Now, what is the seed for that as well, and what might be the seed for that too?
O best among speakers, tell me all this in brief once more, for the increase of awakening and for the attainment of the essence of knowledge.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, know that the body is the seed of the creeper of worldly existence, containing within it the great sprouts of auspicious and inauspicious actions yet to unfold.

"Within" (antar): The very body is the seed of the creeper of saṃsāra, because the existence of saṃsāra follows the positive and negative concomitance with the body. It contains within it the great sprout of good and evil undertakings, that is, the great sprout in the form of merit and demerit consisting of internal exertion. || 35 ||
The mind, which follows the dictates of desire, is the seed of this body— a treasury for the states of existence and non-existence, and a casket for the jewels of suffering. (36)

He cultivates it—the sheath of the states of existence and non-existence, which serves as the foundation for the states of existence and non-existence, such as birth, death, and so forth, like a sheath. || 36 ||
From the mind alone this entire network of limbs, both existent and non-existent, arises intensely;
just as this is experienced by oneself within the delusions of a dream. (37)

He establishes that the mind is the seed of the body with the words "from the mind" (*cittāt*). This body, which consists of a collection of limbs—a network of parts composed of both the existent and the non-existent, or the manifest and the unmanifest—arises solely from the mind.
And this nature of objects appears in whatever manner it does within the delusions of dreams along with their various modes.
It is experienced by oneself; the meaning is that the mind’s status as the cause for the conceptualization of a body is established by one's own experience in dreams. || 37 ||
There are two seeds for the tree of the mind, which bears the creepers of its fluctuations:
one is the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa), and the second is firm latent impression (vāsanā).

"Two" refers to those who bear the creepers of the *vṛttis*. The *vṛttis* are of the nature of the transformations of the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and so forth; these very *vṛttis* are the creepers, that is, the branches, and they bear them. (38)
When the vital breath (prāṇa), intent upon touching the channels (nāḍīs), vibrates, then the mind consisting of pure consciousness (saṃvedana) is swiftly produced. || 39 ||

It has been stated that the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and mental impressions (*vāsanā*) are the seeds of the mind (*citta*). Regarding this, he explains the seed-nature of the vibration of the vital breath with the words "When... When the vital breath is intent upon contacting the channels (*nāḍī*), as the scripture states, "There are one hundred and one channels of the heart," and being ready to circulate through those channels which carry the mind, it vibrates; at that time, the mind [becomes active] immediately.
It arises as consisting of pure consciousness, yet abundant with the knowledge of mental modifications. || 39 ||
The existent, all-pervading consciousness is awakened by the vibration of the vital breath;
know, O Raghava, that the restraint of consciousness is the supreme good. (40)

Regarding the word "satī": although consciousness (saṃvit) is all-pervading, it is awakened—that is, stirred—by the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa). Therefore, know that the supreme good consists precisely in the restraint of that consciousness which is directed outward. 40.
(527) Consciousness itself, having quickly arisen, eagerly moves toward the object of perception;
from that perception, endless sufferings arise for the mind. (41)

Regarding the term *saṃvit*: consciousness (*saṃvit*), when aroused, awakened, or agitated, immediately becomes the object of perception (*saṃvedya*). From that perception—specifically from the continuous mental engagement with the perceived object—infinite sufferings arise for the mind. || 41 ||
When consciousness, having fallen asleep, abides in a state of non-awakening,
then that stainless state which was to be attained has been attained.

Regarding the word "asleep": when consciousness, for the sake of non-awakening—that is, for the sake of not rising again—remains asleep, resting in its own essential nature, then that stainless state which is to be attained has been attained. 42.
Therefore, if you do not cause consciousness to swell through the vibrations of the vital breaths and the impulses of latent impressions, then you are unborn.

"Therefore" means: for the reason stated previously, if you do not cause consciousness—which is swollen by the vibrations of the vital breaths (prāṇaspanda) and the impulses of latent impressions (vāsanā)—to become gross through its containing the objects of perception, then you shall remain unborn, free from birth and other such states. || 43 ||
Know that the swelling of consciousness is the mind;
by it this world is spread out—a web of misfortunes that cuts asunder and shatters the lives of living beings.

Regarding the term *saṃvit*: the swelling (*ucchūnatā*) of consciousness, which is its very state of agitation, is the mind (*citta*). By that very mind, this web of misfortune (*anarthajāla*)—in which the lives (*jīva*) of people, meaning their vital breaths (*prāṇa*), have been "torn asunder" (*ālūna*), meaning completely cut through, and "shattered" (*viśīrṇa*), meaning brought to destruction—is produced. This is how it is.
The form of saṃsāra is thus extended and elaborated. || 44 ||

Yogins perform the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa) for the sake of pacifying the mind, through breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma), meditations, and applications devised by skillful means. || 45 ||
"Of the yogins" means by means of the applications such as Mahāmudrā and others, which are constructed through reasoning and described in the Yoga scriptures. || 45 ||

The wise know that the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇasaṃrodhana) bestows the fruit of the tranquility of the mind, is the supreme cause of equanimity, and is the auspicious health of consciousness. (46)

Regarding "the mind": they know that the restraint of the vital breath alone yields the fruit of the mind's tranquility, is the cause of the state of equilibrium, and brings about the well-being of consciousness. (46)
O Raghava, hear now about another origin of the mind, revealed and experienced by the wise, which is produced by latent impressions (vāsanā). || 47 ||

Regarding the word "jñāna" (knowledge): previously, the arising of the mind was described as being fashioned by the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); now, hear about another arising of the mind, fashioned by latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 47 ||
The firm cultivation that involves the grasping of an object while abandoning prior and subsequent deliberation is proclaimed as *vāsanā*. (48)

"Dṛḍha" (firm) means: that in which the investigation of the prior and the posterior has been abandoned—where "prior" refers to the cause that invariably precedes, and "posterior" refers to the effect that invariably follows. "Upādāna" (appropriation) is the taking up of an object without any such investigation as to whether it is a cause or an effect.

Because it arises solely from firm cultivation—that is, from continuous practice over a long period—it is for that reason designated as "vāsanā" (latent impression). The meaning is that *vāsanā* is the cause for the sudden manifestation [of a state] in one who is either newly born or just awakened from sleep. Alternatively, it is that which, through long-term practice in the past, [manifests] now...

That latent impression (*saṃskāra*) from which arises the grasping of an object belonging to its own class—having abandoned prior and subsequent deliberation—is proclaimed as *vāsanā*. The meaning is that *saṃskāra* is *vāsanā*. || 48 ||
O mighty-armed one, that very state which he has cultivated within himself through intense spiritual urgency quickly becomes his, as all other memories fade away. (49)

"Developed" (bhāvita) means as follows: whatever object has been developed—that is, perfumed—by the self, which is the mind, through intense spiritual urgency and firm practice, that person who has developed [the mind] becomes that very object quickly, free from the memory of other things and no longer thinking of any other object. || 49 ||
For a person of such a nature, rendered helpless by latent impressions (vāsanā),
perceives this very world as a real entity and thus becomes utterly deluded. (50)

"Of such a kind" means: a person who has been rendered helpless by latent impressions (vāsanā), being of such a nature, becomes utterly deluded, thinking that whatever object he perceives or contemplates is the only real entity and the only valid reality. || 50 ||
Due to the helplessness caused by the force of latent impressions (vāsanā), that [mind] abandons its true nature;
one with faulty vision perceives everything as deluded, as if under the influence of intoxication.

Regarding the term *vāsanā*: A person of "bad vision"—that is, one whose sight is corrupted by evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*)—abandons the true nature of things well-known to the world due to being helplessly overwhelmed by the force of those impressions; the meaning is that he does not perceive it. Just as under the influence of intoxication, due to the power of that delirium, he sees every object as distorted and otherwise than it actually is. || 51 ||
O Rāghava, know that mind to be that which, in the absence of right vision, conceives of a self in what is not-self, and perceives substantiality in what is not a substance. (52)

Regarding the word "asamyak": the three indeclinable words beginning with *yat* are used in the sense of cause. The meaning is that the very cause which exists in the case of incorrect vision (*asamyag-darśana*), in the conception of a self in what is not-self (*anātmani ātmabhāvanā*), and in the conceptualization of reality in what is unreal (*avastuni vastutva-saṃkalpana*)—that alone is the mind (*citta*) which is the cause of erroneous knowledge (*anyathājñāna*).
Through firm habituation to the contemplation of the oneness of all things, the mind—which is otherwise exceedingly fickle—becomes the cause of birth, old age, and death. (53)

Regarding the word "firm" (*dṛḍha*): through the cultivation of the singular nature of the object of meditation, the mind—which is by nature extremely fickle—becomes firm through constant practice; this [firmness] arises as the cause for the cessation of birth and so forth. || 53 ||
When nothing whatsoever— whether of the nature of what is to be abandoned or what is to be accepted— is cultivated,
and one remains having relinquished everything, then the mind is not born.

"Yadā" (when): when no object whatsoever—whether of the nature of that which is to be abandoned or that which is to be accepted—is cultivated; rather, having relinquished everything, one remains in silence, then the mind is not born. || 54 ||
When the mind, being perpetually free from latent impressions (vāsanā), does not cognate anything, then the state of no-mind (amanastā) arises,
which bestows supreme tranquility.
"Because it is devoid of latent impressions (avāsanatva)": when the mind, as the agent, does not think and does not form volitions. || 55 ||
When no entity is cultivated anywhere in the world as a real thing,
then how can the mind arise in the empty sky of the heart? (56)

When existence—that is, being—is not perceived anywhere in the world or in any object, then, due to the absence of latent impressions (vāsanā), how can the mind arise in the empty expanse of the heart? || 56 ||
O Raghava, I consider this alone to be the nature of the mind: that which is the internal contemplation of an object as a real entity and with aesthetic relish. (57)

"Only this much," [he says]. I consider that the very nature of the mind consists merely in this: the contemplation (*bhāvana*) of an object—that is, of a thing—within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), by way of its being a real entity, by its actual form, with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and with reverence. || 57 ||
For one who naturally contemplates that nothing in the visible world is fit for conceptualization, how could the arising of the mind occur within that which is as pure as the expanse of space? (58)

"Nothing at all": for one who does not conceive of even the slightest perceivable object—such as the sphere of volition and so forth—which is unfit for mental construction (*kalanā*), how could the arising of the mind occur from that which is as pure as space? (58)

That which consists in relying on the non-contemplation of anything, the contemplation of the non-existence of anything, and the seeing of things as they truly are—that is called "non-mind" (acittatva). || 59 ||
Regarding the word "yat": having resorted to—that is, having adopted—the non-contemplation of the visible world (dṛśya), which means viewing it with disregard;

or the contemplation of its non-existence (abhāva)—that is, the non-being of the visible world—or the seeing of things as they truly are, namely the realization that "all this is indeed Brahman," which is the seeing of reality according to its true state—all of that is called "mindlessness" (acittatva). In all three ways, [this pertains to] the mind.
Because it is free from latent impressions. || 59 ||
That mind which, having completely renounced everything within, abides in a cool disposition— even while engaged in worldly activity— is declared to be of the nature of unreality.

"All this" means: this entire universe, which exists within the heart-mind (*āśaya*), is Brahman itself as coolness—the state of being cool—because it abides in a cool intention through the cessation of passion and hatred; thus, although it exists in the form of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) and possesses those modifications, it remains [Brahman]. 60.
He whose dense latent impression (*vāsanā*) no longer brings about rebirth is liberated while living; established in reality, he remains like the whirling of a potter’s wheel. (61)

Regarding the word "ghana" (thick/dense): it is like the whirling of a wheel. Just as the spinning of a potter's wheel continues for as long as the momentum lasts even after the potter's activity has ceased, so too the body of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) persists until the exhaustion of the experience of *prārabdha* karma, due to the remainder of its momentum, even though ignorance (*avidyā*) has been removed; this is the meaning. || 61 ||

Those whose latent impressions (vāsanā) are like withered seeds—devoid of further rebirth and lacking even a trace of relish—are indeed remembered as those liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 62 ||
"Fallen" means devoid of *rasa*; *rasa* is an excessive attachment toward sense objects, and she is bereft of that. 62.
Having attained a mind whose nature is pure being, they have reached the further shore of knowledge;
they are said to be "mindless," for at the end of the body they take on the form of space.

Regarding the term *sattva*: those whose minds have attained the form of *sattva*—because the portions of *rajas* and *tamas* have ceased and their minds have reached the state of *sattva* alone—are called "mindless" (*acitta*) while still alive (*jīvanmukta*). Precisely because they are mindless, at the end of the body, they become of the nature of space, having the form of the consciousness-ether (*cidākāśa*). || 63 ||
O Rāma, there are two seeds of the mind: the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) and latent impressions (vāsanā).
When one of these two is exhausted, both are quickly destroyed.

"Two seeds": having established that latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) are the seeds of the mind, it is now stated in two verses that because the seed and the sprout are mutual causes, the destruction of either results in the destruction of both. "Of the seeds of the mind" means of those two—latent impressions and the vibration of the vital breath—which constitute the seeds of the mind. (64–65)
From the force of latent impressions (vāsanā) arises the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa), and from that, the latent impressions are produced;
thus occurs the sequence of seed and sprout for the seed of the mind (citta). || 65 ||
It is said that the seed of these two— the latent impression (vāsanā) and the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇapavana)— is the object of perception, because from it those two manifest.

Regarding the term *vāsanā*: the object of cognition (*saṃvedya*) is that which is visible (*dṭśya*). For this reason, those two—the latent impression (*vāsanā*) and the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*)—proceed forth, manifesting from that object of cognition. || 66 || 67 ||
p.

532) Through the complete relinquishing of the object of perception, the vibration of the vital breath and its latent impressions perish quickly along with their roots, like a tree when its root is cut. || 67 ||
O steadfast one, know consciousness to be the seed of the object of consciousness;
without it, the object of consciousness cannot exist, just as a sesame seed cannot exist without oil.
"Saṃvidam" means: "Dhīrā" is the vocative; by that consciousness. || 68 ||
Nothing whatsoever exists as a separate object of cognition, whether external or internal;
consciousness itself flashes forth and, having conceptualized it, perceives the object of cognition from its own nature.
"Not outside" means that because the object of cognition is imagined by consciousness, consciousness alone is the seed [of all things]. || 69 ||
Just as one's own death or staying in another land is experienced in a dream through the power of one's own creative wonder,
so too is the experience of consciousness [experienced] by consciousness itself.

He establishes this very point with an illustration in the verse beginning "In a dream" (svapne): just as in a dream, through the power of one's own creative wonder (*camatkāra*) and by the force of one's own mental construction (*bhāvanā*), even that which is non-existent—such as one's own death or residence in another land—is perceived;
likewise, by the power of consciousness (*saṃvit*), the object of cognition (*saṃvedya*) appears. This is the meaning. || 70 ||
Whatever appears to this consciousness, whether previously seen or unseen, that must be diligently wiped away by one who possesses discernment. (71)

"Previously," etc. Whatever object—whether previously perceived or unperceived—manifests from this consciousness, that object of cognition must be diligently wiped away and rejected by the person who discerns it. || 71 ||
For that very [reality], when merely not cleansed, has become the great cycle of worldly existence;
but when merely cleansed of that, it is experienced as liberation. (72)
Regarding the word "that": that mere non-removal—that very failure to forget the object of cognition—is the great cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
That mere removal—that very forgetting of the visible world—is liberation (mokṣa). || 72 ||
Consciousness leads to infinite suffering because it is of the nature of birth;
non-consciousness, being established in non-inertness, leads to happiness because it is of the nature of non-birth.

Regarding "consciousness" (saṃvedanam): consciousness is the continuous mental engagement with objects of cognition; it leads to suffering in the form of transmigratory existence, which consists of endless birth. That non-consciousness which is non-inert—meaning free from connection with inertia—and which is the non-engagement with objects of cognition, leads to bliss in the form of liberation, which consists of the cessation of birth. || 73 ||
Become non-inert, free from [worldly] bliss, and devoid of sensory perception;
O scion of Raghu, you are that very one whose self is awakened and beyond all perception. (74)

"O non-inert one!"—O scion of Raghu, you must become non-inert, that is, free from dullness; with the transformation of the mind into the form of [limited] bliss dissolved, with perception abandoned, and with the mental preoccupation with objects of perception ceased. He alone is the awakened self, whose nature is luminous, who does not pursue the non-perceivable or the perceivable.
The meaning is that you are indeed the Supreme Self; this is the truth, and there is no doubt about it. || 74 ||
Rāma said:
O Lord, what is the nature of non-cognition that yet abides in non-inertness?
And how is it that inertness is excluded from that non-cognition? (75)
Regarding the phrase "non-cognition": if there is non-cognition—that is, the absence of cognition—how can that inertia be removed?
For it is observed among insentient things that non-cognition is invariably concomitant with inertia. || 75 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
He who does not abide anywhere, nor rests anywhere at all—that living being finds nothing whatsoever; for he is indeed non-consciousness and yet not inert.

Regarding the word "ya" (who): that individual soul (*jīva*) who, in all respects, toward all objects of perception, remains in a state of instability and lacks steady focus; who does not find rest in any object whatsoever, and consequently perceives or reflects upon nothing at all within the mind—that soul is "non-consciousness" (*asaṃvit*) because it does not reflect upon objects of perception, yet it is "non-inert" (*ajaḍa*) because of its nature as consciousness (*cetanatva*).
He for whom no support in the form of objective consciousness exists here is declared to be non-conscious yet non-inert, even while performing hundreds of actions. (77)
Regarding "consciousness" (saṃvit): consciousness is defined as the apprehension of an object in its actual state—the synthesis of the existence of a thing, such as an element, as "this is that.
He in whom such consciousness does not exist—even while performing hundreds of actions—is declared to be "unconscious" (asaṃvit) and insentient (ajaḍa). || 77 ||
The space of the heart is not stained even slightly by that which is perceivable; he who possesses this non-inert state beyond consciousness is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). (78)
"By that which is to be experienced": the space of the heart, the space of consciousness, is not smeared because it is free from latent impressions (nirvāsana); it is not adhered to. || 78 ||
When nothing whatsoever is cultivated within oneself due to the absence of latent impressions (vāsanā), one remains steadfast, like the consciousness of an infant or a mute person. (79)

The two verses beginning with "yadā" form a single syntactical unit. When, due to the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), nothing whatsoever is conceived or mentally constructed within the self, and one remains steady in one's own nature through non-conceptuality—just like the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth—the sense is that one abides in the state of non-conceptual knowledge, like an infant or similar beings. (79)
Then, O wise one, one comes to rest in that which is free from dullness, pervasive, and beyond perception, because of which one is no longer stained.

Then, one comes to rely upon that which is free from dullness and devoid of objective perception; because of relying on this non-perception, one is no longer stained—that is, one is not bound by the latent impressions of merit and demerit. || 80 ||
Having abandoned all latent impressions through non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi),
a pervasive state of bliss unfolds, like the blueness in the sky.

Regarding the word "samasta": because the non-conceptual (nirvikalpa) samādhi has arisen through the abandonment of all latent impressions (vāsanā), from that cause, a vast state of bliss proceeds, perceived like the blueness in the sky (kha). || 81 ||
For the yogin who is absorbed therein, whose consciousness is devoid of perception,
that [consciousness] also dissolves within due to its identity with That, being without beginning or end.

Regarding the term "of the yogin": there, for such a yogin who is absorbed in that non-conceptual samādhi and is therefore devoid of perception—meaning his consciousness is free from any subsequent mental engagement with an object of cognition—that state of bliss also dissolves within his own internal nature, which is without beginning or end, due to his being composed of that [samādhi] and because of his identity (*sāmarasya*) with the object of meditation. || 82 || 83 ||
Whether walking, standing, touching, or even smelling, he is called by that [state]:
non-inert, with bliss dissolved, having abandoned all sensory perception, and happy. (83)
Grasping this view with arduous effort, one may cross to the far shore of the ocean of suffering—that sea of boundless virtues. (84)
"Etām iti" means: this vision, which is free from dullness and consists of the nature of pure consciousness. || 84 ||
Now, O Rāma, it is said that pure existence (*sanmātra*) is the seed of this consciousness;
from pure existence this [consciousness] arises, just as luminosity arises from light. (85)

Regarding the word "atha" (now): For that consciousness which is the seed of the object of cognition, its seed is said to be pure existence (*sanmātra*), the uninterrupted nature of consciousness itself. Because, from this cause, this consciousness arises from pure existence alone, like the illumination from the light-substance of a lamp or similar source. || 85 ||
Among those two forms, one consists of existence (sattā) abiding in various shapes, while the second is of a single form; hear now this distinction between the two. || 86 ||

"Two": existence (*sattā*) has two forms, namely, the existence of its own nature (*svarūpasattā*). Among those two, one form exists as manifold (*nānākṛti*), possessing various modes; the second form, however, is of a single nature and undivided. || 86 ||

The states of being a jar, a cloth, thatness, yours-ness, and mine-ness are spoken of; yet that which is the nature of existence (sattā) is traditionally held to be formless when considered apart from such distinctions.

Regarding the term *ghaṭatā*: that which is the nature of existence (*sattārūpa*)—designated through distinctions such as potness (*ghaṭatā*), clothness (*paṭatā*), thatness (*tattā*), yours-ness (*tvattā*), and not-mine-ness (*amattā*)—is known as "existence having manifold forms. As stated by Bhartṛhari: "Existence itself, being differentiated among cows and other things due to the difference of its correlates, is called a 'universal' (*jāti*); all words are established in it. (87)
Having completely abandoned all particularity, that which is pure existence alone, untainted, uniform, and the great form—this they know to be the state of Being (sattā). (88)

Regarding the term "particularity" (*viśeṣam*): having abandoned particularity—the distinctions of name, genus, and so forth—that which remains as pure existence (*sanmātra*), untainted and flawless in form, they know that to be the Great Form (*mahārūpa*) of Being, the state (*pada*) that is of a single nature. || 88 ||
p.

536) Whether it be the existence of time, the existence of parts, or this existence of objects—having abandoned the conceptualization of such divisions, become intent solely upon pure Being (sanmātra). || 89 ||

Regarding "time" (*kāla*): the existence of time (*kālasattā*) is existence differentiated by the divisions of past, present, and future as produced by time.
