The existence of parts (*kalāsattā*)—where *kalā* means a portion—is existence in the form of gross, subtle, long, short, and so forth, produced by those distinctions. The existence produced by the differentiation of the essential nature of objects (*vastu*) is existence in the form of jars, cloths, and so forth. Furthermore, there is this existence of time, this existence of parts, and this existence of objects.
Abandoning the calculation of divisions and the conception of duality, become solely intent upon Pure Being alone. || 89 ||
Although temporal existence and self-existence, being free from all mental constructs,
are of the nature of the supreme reality, they are nonetheless not ultimately real.

"Time" (kāla) refers to the existence of time. "Own-existence" (svasattā) refers to the existence of one's own nature. By the word "and" (ca), the existence of the creative aspects (kalāsattā) is included; these are those from whom all mental constructs have been released and all parts of conceptualization have been abandoned.
Thus, although this is the supreme form of reality, nevertheless, this existence of time and so forth is not ultimately real or free from conceptualization. || 90 ||
Wherein the calculation of division bestows distinct states, how could that which is seen to be the cause of manifoldness be purifying? (91)

Regarding the term *vibhāga*: when, in regard to time, existence (*sattā*), and so forth, one perceives an adventitious condition (*upādhi*) which is the cause of multiplicity—the factor of differentiation that brings about a state of division and makes known the difference in the essential nature of things—then how could that [time, existence, etc. be pure or sanctifying in its form as existence? The sense is that it is not so because it is adventitious (*aupādhikatvāt*). || 91 ||
Meditating solely upon existence as the one, all-pervading universal,
remain filled with supreme bliss, pervading the entire expanse of the quarters.

Regarding "sattā": meditating solely upon existence (sattā) as the one reality—the all-pervasive and omnipresent universal—remain filled with supreme bliss, pervading the entire expanse of the quarters. 92.
O Lord of the Wise, that very limit which belongs to the mere generality of existence (sattāsāmānya) has become its seed; from that, this [world] proceeds. (93)
Regarding the term *sattā*: that which is the limit—the pinnacle—of mere universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*), being itself unmodified in form, becomes the seed-nature of this world;

from that, this world proceeds according to the sequence previously described. This sequence is as follows: from universal existence, consciousness (*saṃvit*) proceeds; from consciousness, the object of consciousness (*saṃvedya*).
From the object of perception arises the latent impression of the vibration of the vital breath; from that, the mind; from that, the body; and from that, transmigratory existence. || 93 ||
That primordial state, which is devoid of all mental construction, exists at the limit of the universal existence (sattāsāmānya);
being without beginning or end, no seed for it is found.

Regarding the word *sattā*: at the ultimate limit, at the furthest extremity of the universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), there is that primordial state which is well-known as being free from conceptual construction (*kalanā*) and devoid of beginning, end, or middle; for that reality, no seed exists. 94.
Therein, existence enters into dissolution and remains changeless;
having attained its footing there, one does not again encounter suffering. 95.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): he abides therein, in that aforementioned state which is the seed of all things. 95 || 96 || 97 ||
It is the cause of all causes, yet no cause for it is found;
it is the essence of all essences, yet no essence beyond it exists. (96)
In that expansive mirror, all these perceptions of objects are reflected, just as trees on the bank are reflected in a lake. (97)
That is the stainless, ageless reality of the Self; upon the realization of that, the mind attains peace.
Having realized the nature of that vast oneness, you shall for a long time abide in a state liberated from the fear of worldly existence.

Become one such as that by whom that aforementioned state—situated at the pinnacle of universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*), understood, expansive, and singular—is realized as your own essential nature (*svarūpa*). You are he whose state and essential nature is liberated from fear—that is, from the fear of saṃsāra.
That very reality of the Self is indeed pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*). For a long time, for eternity. 98–99.
Rāma said:
O giver of honor, these seeds have been described by you;
by the application of which one quickly attains the state? (99)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Whatever remedy has been declared by me for each of these seeds of suffering, by the application of that very remedy, the state [of liberation] is swiftly attained. (100)
"Of these" means: by the application—that is, by the cultivation—of each respective subsequent seed. 100.
If, by means of human effort, one forcibly abandons latent impressions (vāsanās) and [rests] instantly upon that state which stands at the pinnacle of universal existence (sattāsāmānya), || 1 ||

The two verses beginning with "sattā" form a single syntactical unit. The connection [of the meaning] is as follows: if you bind even for a moment a meditative absorption (samādhi) that abides in the supreme state situated at the pinnacle of universal existence (sattāsāmānya), then in that very moment you attain that state. || 1 || 2 ||
O knower of reality, you establish a state that is imperishable even for a moment;
in this very moment, you fully attain that excellent state.
Or if, my dear friend, you establish yourself in the form of universal existence (sattāsāmānya),
then by a slight additional effort here, you will attain that state.
Regarding the word "sattā" (existence): the meaning is that when one is established in the universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), even greater effort must be exerted than that. || 3 ||
O Rāghava, if you remain with your meditation fixed upon the reality of pure consciousness, then through that superior effort, you shall attain that supreme state.

"Regarding 'consciousness' (saṃvit)": the meaning is that in the meditative absorption (samādhi) on the reality of consciousness (saṃvittattva), there must be an even more distinguished effort than that [previously mentioned]. || 4 ||
O descendant of Raghu, one should not practice meditation upon that which is merely perceived;
for the abandonment of latent impressions regarding the perceived is even more difficult than uprooting Mount Sumeru.

Regarding the term *saṃvedya* (the object of consciousness): meditation is simply not possible when there is only the object of consciousness. The meaning is that because this very consciousness is always and everywhere present, there can be no such thing as a solitary (*kaivalya*) object of consciousness. || 5 || 6 || 7 || 8 ||
As long as the mind has not dissolved, there is no destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
and as long as the latent impressions have not been destroyed, O Rāghava, meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is not possible. (6)
Because this consciousness is always present everywhere, you must either exert effort toward the complete abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā), or [accept its persistence]. (7)
All mental and physical afflictions instantly become relaxed before you. || 8 ||
Indeed, this is considered more difficult than all previous efforts;
the renunciation of latent impressions (vāsanā) is harder to accomplish even than uprooting Mount Sumeru.
The six verses beginning with "pūrvebhyaḥ" constitute a single syntactical unit. This effort pertains to the abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Since the dissolution of latent impressions, the destruction of the mind (*manonāśa*), and the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) are mutually dependent and cannot be accomplished individually, the meaning is that one should practice all three simultaneously. || 9 || 110 || 11 || 12 || 13 || 14 ||
As long as the mind has not dissolved, so long there is no destruction of latent impressions;
as long as the latent impressions have not been destroyed, so long the mind does not become tranquil. (110)
As long as there is no realization of reality, so long is there no cessation of the mind;
as long as there is no pacification of the mind, so long is there no knowledge of reality. (11)
As long as there is no destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), how can there be the realization of reality?
As long as there is no attainment of reality, there is no exhaustion of latent impressions. || 12 ||
Knowledge of reality, the dissolution of the mind, and the destruction of latent impressions—having become mutual causes for one another, these remain difficult to accomplish. (13)
Therefore, O Raghava, with effort, through manly exertion, and by means of discernment, one should cast away the desire for enjoyment from afar and take refuge in these three. (14)
p.
540) As long as these three are not practiced equally again and again, the attainment of reality will not occur even in hundreds of aeons. (15)
O Mahāmati, for the Sage, the exhaustion of latent impressions, the [transformation of] consciousness, and the destruction of the manas become fruit-bearing when practiced simultaneously. (16)
Even if these are practiced individually for a long time,
they do not grant accomplishment, just like mantras that have been merely recited.

"Each one individually" means: just as mantras that have been proclaimed—such as the mantras of Śiva and Śakti which are mutually dependent—do not yield their fruit when practiced individually (*puraścaraṇa*), so it is in this case; such is the meaning. || 17 ||
When these three are practiced for a long time, the firm knots of the heart are severed without doubt, like fibers from a lotus stalk when cut.
O Rāma, this state of worldly existence has been practiced for hundreds of previous births;
it is never extinguished except through the yoga of long-term cultivation. (19)
Those who know the reality understand that the restraint of the vital breath is equal to the complete abandonment of latent impressions; therefore, one should practice it in this very manner.

Regarding the term *vāsanā*: because *vāsanā* and the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) together constitute the seed of the mind, the wise know that the restraint of the breath must be performed simultaneously with the abandonment of *vāsanā*. For that reason, one should likewise practice—that is, cultivate—that restraint of the breath together with these three, beginning with the abandonment of *vāsanā*. || 120 ||
Through the complete abandonment of latent impressions, the mind attains the state of non-mind;
and through the cessation of the movement of the vital breath—do as you wish.

Regarding the term "vāsanā": the meaning is that the destruction of the mind is caused either by the total abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā) or by the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 21 ||
Through firm practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), by means of the method imparted by the Guru,
and through the application of postures and diet, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is restrained.
In that regard, he states the means for the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—beginning with the word "prāṇa": by means of the method previously mentioned, namely the yoga of posture and diet;

"posture" refers to the lotus position (*padmāsana*) and so forth, while "diet" refers to the body and its requirements—that very [method] is the yoga, the means, by which [the breath is restrained]. || 22 ||
Because of acting without attachment, because of abandoning the contemplation of worldly existence,
and because of seeing the destruction of the body, latent tendencies do not arise. (23)

He states the means for the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—namely, "being free from attachment" (*niḥsaṅga*). By the avoidance of the contemplation of worldly existence (*bhava-bhāvanā*); that is, by the avoidance of those impure latent impressions which are the causes of *saṃsāra*. (Verses 23–27)
When the overpowering of latent impressions (vāsanā) has been destroyed, the mind no longer functions,
just as dust in the sky ceases to move when the movement of the wind has completely subsided.
For that which is the vibration of the vital breath is indeed the vibration of the mind;
therefore, the wise person should exert themselves with great effort to conquer the vibration of the vital breath. (25)
Even by sitting again and again with a one-pointed mind, it is not possible to conquer the mind without an irreproachable method. (26)
Like a rutting, wicked elephant without a goad. || 27 ||
The attainment of inner knowledge, association with the virtuous, the complete renunciation of latent impressions, and the cessation of the movement of the vital breath. (28)
He states the means for the destruction of the mind in two verses beginning with "adhyātma": || 28 ||
These arguments, indeed, are well-established for the conquest of the mind; by means of them, the mind is swiftly conquered, just as the dust of the earth is settled by showers of rain. (29)
By these arguments, that mind [is established]. 29 || 130 || 31 ||
Those who, despite these methods being available, restrain their minds by force,
are like those who cast away a lamp and attempt to destroy the darkness with collyrium.
Those deluded ones who strive to achieve mastery over the mind by force are like those who attempt to bind a frenzied lord of serpents with lotus fibers.
Her delicate-limbed mind, with its limbs lacerated and shattered,
finds no confidence anywhere, like a doe that has entered a village. (32)
"Intellect" (mati) refers to that which pertains to Haṭhayoga. 32 || 33 || 34 || 35 || 36 || 37 ||
For a long time, those possessed by hundreds of mental agonies waste away their lives through the delusions of sacrifice, austerity, charity, pilgrimage, and the worship of gods, like deer. (33)
Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, having abandoned this false view and taking refuge in pure consciousness, remain steadfast and free from passion.
O Great-souled One, perceiving the supreme, primordial, and singular state of pure consciousness— which is devoid of all that is to be experienced and free from conceptualization—
abide within your very heart, free from mental construction. Performing action while attaining the state of the non-doer,
may you possess the glory of peace arising from tranquility.
Vasiṣṭha said:
He by whom even a slight restraint of his own mind has been achieved through even a moment of reflection has attained the fruit of birth. (36)
This subtle spark of reflection which flickers within the heart,
through the practice of yoga, attains a hundredfold branching.
The great seat, grasped like a tree of flowers of discernment, is well-established and firm; the winds of anxiety cannot shake it. (38)
"Seized" (āgṛhīta) means that by which the great seat (mahāpīṭha)—that is, the great foundation—has been completely taken hold of;

the meaning is that its roots have taken firm hold. For this very reason, it has a stable position, being well-established and immovable due to its firm foundation. The winds of anxiety do not shake the flower-tree that consists of discernment. 38 || 39 || 40 || 41 ||
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping, he whose mind is not intent upon inquiry is as good as dead. (39)
"What might this world be? What might I be?"—thus one should constantly and gradually investigate with the vision of the inner self, either by oneself or together with virtuous people. (140)
The wise know that reflection upon the sciences of the self is the limb of knowledge;
its object of knowledge exists within itself, just as sweetness exists within milk. (41)
The light of right knowledge is itself equal to the object of knowledge for a person;
it neither fears, nor grasps, nor experiences helplessness, nor dejection.
The two verses beginning with "samyak" constitute a single syntactical unit. Through right knowledge, there is perfect illumination and even vision;
he is equal to the object of knowledge, being identical with the reality that is to be known. (42–43)

Just as one who has drunk *maireya* liquor remains perpetually intoxicated, so too do they know the supreme Brahman—the stainless form of consciousness—as equal [to all]. Merely by approaching that knowledge, it becomes manifest of its own accord. (43)
Having eaten even that which is impure, unwholesome, smeared with poison, or full of filth, he digests it quickly; and what is moist or decayed, he consumes as if it were delicious.

"Regarding 'impure' (apavitram): it quickly digests even impure things such as leftovers, just like pure food; the sense is that this is due to his equanimity and lack of attachment. In this context, 'impure' refers to food such as leavings (ucchiṣṭa). 'Unwholesome' (apathyam) means contrary to the medical scriptures.
'Moist' (klinnam) means because it has been kept for a long time. In the reading 'ārdrākliṣṭam', the word 'kliṣṭam' means spoiled by cooking and having lost its original nature."
"Naṣṭam" means that which has undergone a change of form. "Mṛṣṭam" means faultless and endowed with qualities; the verbal root is *mṛj*, meaning purification and adornment. (44)
Regarding poisons, antidotes, medicinal pastes, milk, water, and food,
one who knows the reality remains unattached in mind and is equanimous toward their tasting.

Regarding the word *viṣa*: poison (*viṣa*) is well known. *Prativiṣa* is another substance that neutralizes poison, which has been described in the section on *prativiṣā*. *Akalkam* means stainless; it refers to milk (*kṣīra*). *Andhasi* means in food (*anna*). 45, 46.
He regards even the taker of his life and the giver with an identical look, one characterized by graciousness and sweetness. (46)
That virtuous person never, at any time, allows any sense-faculty to find its range when it is directed toward an object, by means of an intellect that has abandoned sovereign attachment. (47)
"He" refers to that one who possesses equal vision (*samadṛṣṭi*). "Of the sense-organ" (*akṣasya*) means of the faculty (*indriya*). "Extension" (*prasaram*) means attachment (*āsaktim*). || 47 ||
They swiftly devour the one who does not know reality, who finds no rest, who has not attained the self, and who lacks stability—
just as deer swallow a leaf.
"One who does not know reality" means they swallow or devour [him]. 48.
Attachment is the cause of worldly objects; attachment is the cause of saṃsāra;
attachment is the cause of ignorance; attachment is the cause of calamities. 49.

Because [the topic] has been introduced at the beginning with the words "due to acting without attachment" and so forth; in order to define attachment, he introduces that very attachment as something necessarily to be abandoned, starting with the verse beginning "attachment. (49–150)
They know that liberation is the renunciation of attachment; from the renunciation of attachment comes freedom from rebirth.
O sinless one, abandon your attachment to worldly objects and become liberated while living.
Rāma said:
O Sage, you who are like an autumn wind that dispels the mist of all doubts!
O Lord, tell me briefly: what is attachment said to be? 51.
Following Rāma’s question, Vasiṣṭha will explain that impure latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone constitute attachment, and he will define its true nature.
Vasiṣṭha said:
That impure latent impression which causes the fluctuations of joy and resentment toward objects that exist or do not exist is called attachment (saṅga). || 52 ||
For those whose bodies are liberated while living, their latent impression (vāsanā) becomes pure, free from joy and sorrow, and brings about the state of no further rebirth.
For those who are not liberated while living, who are wretched and of deluded mind, that which produces worldly existence—namely, latent impression—is designated by the word "attachment. (54)
If you fall under the sway of joy, resentment, and despondency, then through that joy and despondency, the latent impression of bondage will arise. (55)
If you go without falling into either joy or sorrow,
being free from passion, fear, and anger, then, O Raghava, you are unattached.
If you do not succumb to weariness because of sufferings, nor rejoice in pleasures, having cast off the helplessness of hope, then you are unattached, O Raghava. (57)
If your self is observed to be the same in prosperity and adversity,
and you follow whatever comes to pass, then you are unattached, O one called "Passion."
O Rāma, always maintain an even disposition toward the entire range of things, with an inner spirit that is not dejected; performing whatever is at hand, remain unattached and dwell in happiness.
Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Exposition on the Absence of Movement through the Air and Other Matters," in the Chapter on Quiescence within the *Mokṣopāya* of the venerable Vālmīki.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Absence of Movement through the Sky and Other Matters," in the Section on Quiescence (*upaśamaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa*.
This Chapter on Quiescence is completed. || 5 ||
Chapter One: The Section on Nirvāṇa; The First Canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:

I am that one Brahman alone—unconditioned by space, time, and the like; beyond the two ends of the unseen (the seen and the unseen); pure consciousness, imperishable, and tranquil; and nothing else. 1.
Now, the section on Nirvāṇa is examined. In that regard, there are fifteen sub-narratives (upākhyānas):
Bhuśuṇḍa, Devapūjā, Bilvaphala, Śilā, Arjuna, Śatarudrāḥ, Vetāla, Bhagīratha, Śikhidhvaja—which contains within it the triad of narratives known as Kirāta, Cintāmaṇi, and Gaja—Kaca, and Mithyābhṛṅgī.

[Ikṣvāku, Vyādha, and Bhuśuṇḍa. Among these, the attainment of liberation through the repose of the mind resulting from the pursuit of the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*) is established by means of the narrative of Bhuśuṇḍa. Therein, he teaches what is beneficial in two verses forming a single statement beginning with "Space and time": "I am pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), unconditioned by space and so forth, and devoid of beginning and end."

Thinking within yourself and resolving, "I am indeed Brahman; nothing else such as the body exists," become one whose body is both liberated and unliberated—liberated through the abandonment of ego-identification and unliberated by the force of *prārabdha* karma—and thus, being one who finds happiness in the Self, be one who delights in the Self (*ātmārāma*). (In the reading *asti muktvā*, the meaning is: "Brahman alone exists; nothing else exists.")

"Having realized this, abandon the internal sense of 'I' (ahantā), yet remain with a body that is neither liberated nor bound; even while living, become one whose bliss is the Self"—this is the construction of the verse.

Thus, having realized this, O Great One, though possessing a body that is both liberated and unliberated, be one who is inwardly uniform, whose self is profoundly tranquil, silent, and whose bliss is the Self.

As long as there is the fabrication of ignorance, as long as there is the contemplation of [something other than] Brahman, and as long as there is attachment to the web of the world, so long does the conceptualization of the mind and its derivatives persist. (3)

He says "as long as" (yāvat) because, otherwise, saṃsāra would not cease. As long as the absence of the contemplation of Brahman—the contemplation that "all this is indeed Brahman"—persists; for that very reason, as long as the fabrication of ignorance and the bondage consisting of ignorance persist; and for that reason, as long as there is attachment to the snare of the world, so long does the conceptualization of the mind and so forth persist—[where] the mind is the individual soul (jīva).
The conceptualization of distinctions such as "knowledge" and so forth proceeds. || 3 ||
There is no mind, nor ignorance, no mental faculty, and no individual soul;
O Rāma, these conceptual constructions are created solely by Brahman.
Brahman alone, which is without beginning or end, expands like the ocean.

In reality, however, there is no conceptualization of any difference; thus he says: "It does not exist. *Citta* is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in which pure *sattva* predominates. *Manas*, on the other hand, is the internal organ consisting of resolve and doubt, in which the quality of *rajas* abounds. (4)
As long as there is the sense of "I" in the body, as long as there is the notion of "self" in this visible world,
and as long as there is the attachment that "this is mine," so long does the delusion of the mind and its like persist.

Regarding the term *deha* (body): this is an elaboration of what was previously stated. It refers to the notion of sentience (*cetanatva-buddhi*) attributed by the self (*ātman*) to an object of perception, such as another person's body.

Alternatively, it refers to the state of being the Self (*ātmatā*), that is, the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātma-bhāva*), directed toward an object of perception such as an image; the meaning is the cognition of a deity (*devatā-buddhi*). || 5 ||
For the sage who, through inward-turned awareness, offers the entire three worlds as grass into the fire of consciousness, the delusions of the mind and other such distractions cease within.

He states the means for the cessation of the conceptualization of mind and so forth with the word "antar" (within): By being inward-turned, through the contemplation of the perfect Self as "I am the Self of all," one should regard the three worlds as a blade of grass— meaning the visible world is to be disregarded like a blade of grass— by offering it into the fire of consciousness, which is one's own self-consciousness and the substratum of the entire phenomenal expansion, while remaining distinct from the [limited] faculty of sight.
Because of the non-existence of the object of perception, the delusions of the mind and so forth cease for the sage who dissolves them. || 6 ||
I am the conscious self, partless and devoid of near and far shores;
remember your own expansive form, and do not remain limited by forgetfulness.
In response to the inquiry, "What is this inwardness?", he states the nature of consciousness: "The conscious self" (cidātman).

Remember—that is, contemplate—the vast and all-pervading nature of your own self, thinking: "I am the conscious Self (cidātman), devoid of near and far, lacking the limits of before and after, and partless. This very state is what is meant by "inwardness" (antarmukhatā). Do not become limited or circumscribed through non-remembrance—that is, through forgetting your own true nature. If the reading is *asi* ("you are"), then it means: since you are the conscious Self, therefore...
The construction [of the sentence] is: "One should remember one's own expansive form. || 7 ||
He who perceives even that most extreme enemy, intent upon one's swift death, as a natural friend— he truly sees. (8)

Regarding the word "yaḥ": he who perceives even that very enemy—who is exceedingly hostile and intent on killing him immediately—as an uncontrived friend due to being free from attachment and aversion; such a person, who views enemy and friend with equanimity, sees—that is, knows—the reality of the Self (ātmatattva). This is the meaning. || 8 ||
He who eradicates both friendship and envy, like a river uprooting a tree on its bank, is the destroyer of the defects of joy and resentment.

Regarding the phrase "he eradicates": that person who scrapes away friendship and envy, as well as passion and hatred, by the roots—that is, who abandons them along with their latent tendencies (vāsanā)—destroys defects such as elation and resentment. || 9 ||
Through the internal recitation of the scripture of the self, the cholera-like poison of craving is destroyed within,
just as mist is dispelled by autumn.

Regarding the word *adhyātma*: by means of the mantra of the inner science (*adhyātma-śāstra*), which has been cultivated—that is, long perfumed—within the internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*), the cholera of the poison of craving (*tṛṣṇā-viṣa-viṣūcikā*)—that is, the cholera produced by the poison in the form of craving—is destroyed, just as mist is [dissolved] by autumn, or as frost is [melted] by the autumn season. 10.
Wherever one’s own mind has cultivated the quality of accepting words as authoritative, those words enter deeply within, just as water enters a heated field.
He says, "Where... because the inner science (adhyātma-śāstra) takes root in the mind only when heard from the mouth of one who knows the inner science, and not otherwise.

In whatever person the quality of having acceptable speech has been cultivated and ascertained by one's own mind through [recognizing him as] an authority (*āpta*), that very person’s words— the speech of that authority— enter deeply, with great intensity, into the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Like water poured onto a heated field. || 11 ||
(549) Those of dull intellect, who have not reflected upon their own true self-interest and have not touched consciousness, move about like blades of grass, devoid of sentience. || 12 ||

He says—“aparyālocita... (without having reflected)—to show that in the absence of inquiry through the teacher’s mouth and through one’s own experience, doubt alone will persist: “Those who have not reflected upon the meaning of the Self. That which has the Self as its object is the *ātmārtha*, namely the spiritual scripture (*adhyātma-śāstra*); those by whom that has not been reflected upon—that is, not inquired into—are meant.

Those of deluded intellect, whose consciousness is untouched and whose nature of consciousness is unexamined, all quiver like blades of grass, moving here and there; that is to say, they are filled with doubt. || 12 ||
And for all of these, this immutable consciousness remains ever-present;
yet, by virtue of ignorance regarding it, they have fallen into a state of supreme wretchedness. (13)
Now, one might ask: since all living beings (*jīva*) are of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), how can there be doubt for some? To this he says:

"Of all... It is true that for all these living beings, this imperishable consciousness (*cit*) remains as their very essence, existing precisely as their own nature. However, regarding this consciousness which exists as their essential nature—

Due to the power of non-awakening, through the influence of beginningless ignorance, and because of a lack of spiritual inquiry, they have fallen into a supreme, boundless state of wretchedness and pettiness. || 13 ||
Threatening and roaring from the fool, like the sound of a bow, staff, and string,
is heard as leading only to death, being utterly devoid of conscious awareness.

Censuring that very same wretchedness, he says: "Threatening" (*tarjanam*). Just as from a bow-staff and string, so too from a fool—an ignorant person—there arises threatening, scolding, roaring, and a clamor in the throat, which is devoid of consciousness (*cidbodha*), meaning it lacks the awakening to one's own true nature (*svarūpacit*). And the clamor in the throat (*kaṇṭhakolāhala*) is like the sound produced by the string (*maurvī*) when it is fixed upon the bow.

It is heard that [such talk] leads only to death and only to injury toward living beings; for a fool who possesses a bow and string, his own noise serves only to bring about the destruction of others. Therefore, the sense is that nothing at all should be heard from him. || 14 ||
Whatever was given to that lowest of men was cast away like [seed] in thick mud;
therefore, any conversation with him is like calling out to a dog in the sky. (15)
He states that such a fool does not deserve even the slightest gift, honor, or the like, with the words "In him" (tasmin).
Wealth given to that base person who is devoid of self-realization is like seed sown in salty mud; even conversation with him is like being in an open space under a cloudless sky. 15.
Ignorance is the ultimate root of calamities; for what misfortune does not befall the ignorant?
This path of saṃsāra flows forth by the power of the ignorant. (16)

He shows that the affliction caused by dogs is unavoidable. Therefore, he says—“ignorance”—that ignorance alone is the root of all calamities and of wandering in saṃsāra. “Ignorance” means nescience (*ajñāna*);
it is the *niṣṭhā*, the cause of the completion or production, of calamities such as old age, death, and so forth. Why? Because (*hi*), for this reason, [calamities arise] for one who does not know.

What kind of calamity could befall a person? Indeed, every possible calamity may indeed occur. And this path of saṃsāra flows and proceeds solely from ignorance, because the engagement in saṃsāra is rooted in the engagement of the ignorant. || 16 ||
That very world which appears as fragile as a cow’s footprint to the intellect of the ignorant, is for the Great-Souled One boundless, limitless, and unfathomable.

Regarding the word "yat": that very world which appears as slight and small—like the footprint of a cow—to the intellect of the knower (*jñānin*), that same world is perceived by the non-great-souled ignorant person as bottomless and shoreless;
the meaning is that it becomes insurmountable. || 17 ||
That which is untouched by any object of perception, tranquil, and the soul of all— this exists here as consisting of being, consciousness, and bliss, free from all mental construction.
Having stated that one must hear [the truth] from a Guru who possesses self-knowledge, he speaks the following in order to make the reality known: "By the object of perception...

(verse 18). That very reality which is untouched—that is, unconnected—with an object of perception (*saṃvedya*), which is peaceful, which is the soul of all, which consists of existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*), and which is devoid of parts (*niṣkala*) because it is free from mental construction (*kalana*), alone exists in reality.
From that, the *kalā* (power), whose nature is creative ideation (*kalana*), arises from itself;
it is conceived as threefold: subtle, intermediate, and gross. (19)

"It arises" means that from the Supreme Brahman, *kalā*—which consists of mental construction (*kalanā*), has the nature of bondage, and is ignorance (*avidyā*)—arises by itself and not through the will of another. And that mental construction is conceived as threefold, according to the distinctions of the subtle (*sūkṣma*) and so forth.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—this alone is known as primordial nature (prakṛti).
This indeed is the cycle of worldly existence for a living being; its further shore is the supreme state.
Regarding the word *sattva*: this very *kalā*, divided into subtle and other distinctions, consisting of the three qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and the rest, is known as *prakṛti*.

This same *kalā*, in the form of *prakṛti* composed of the three qualities, is the cause of bondage and the cycle of existence (*saṃsṛti*) for living beings. The "beyond" (*pāra*) of this very [kalā] is cessation (*nivṛtti*), the supreme state, which is liberation (*kaivalya*). || 20 ||
In this regard, those three qualities (guṇas) that have been mentioned are also remembered as being threefold;
thus, this ignorance, which takes the form of the qualities, is divided into nine types.

Regarding this: in this primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the qualities (*guṇas*) are each remembered as being threefold, because *sattva* and the others are intermingled with the other qualities. To explain: *sattva* is threefold—pure, mixed with *rajas*, and mixed with *tamas*.
The same applies to *rajas* and *tamas*. Thus, this ignorance (*avidyā*), which consists of the three qualities and is denoted by the term "limited agency" (*kalā*), is ninefold.
It is divided. || 21 ||
O Raghava, know that the seers, sages, perfected ones, nagas, vidyadharas, and gods— these constitute the sattvic portion of ignorance.

Regarding the term "ṛṣis": here, the seers (ṛṣis) are Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and others who were the original perceivers of the mantras; the sages (munis) are those devoted to silence. The meaning is that the ṛṣis and the rest, taken together, constitute the sāttvika portion of ignorance (avidyā). || 22 ||
The Nāgas and Vidyādharas are the portion of this [universe] characterized by *tamas*;
the Munis and Siddhas are *rajas*; and the gods, such as Hara and others, are *sattva*. (23)
Regarding that, he states the intermediate division: "Of the *sāttvika* [portion]" and so forth. Within this *sāttvika* portion are the lords of serpents (*phaṇīndra*) such as Vāsuki and Takṣaka;
the *vidyādharas*, who possess sciences (*vidyā*) such as the sword, the ring, and collyrium, beginning with Jīmūtaketu; and [the quality of] *tamas*.

Those whose portion of *sattva* is mixed with *tamas* are so because of the predominance of delusion (*moha*). The sages (*munayaḥ*) and perfected ones (*siddhāḥ*) have a portion of *sattva* mixed with *rajas*, because they are predominantly engaged in activity due to their devotion to austerity. The gods, such as Hara and others, possess *sattva*—that is, a *sāttvika* portion—because they are predominantly characterized by the knowledge arising from the *sattva* element. (23)
p. 552) This portion belongs to ignorance alone, yet it has thus attained the state of knowledge.
For pure *sattva* is called "ignorance" when it is a portion of ignorance. (24)

Regarding the term "portion" (bhāga): among the nine divisions of ignorance, this portion—which is the *sāttvika* part, the element of *sattva*—has attained the status of being denoted by the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*). For this reason, the pure *sattva*, which is the very essence of pure *sattva*, namely the portion of knowledge itself, is called "knowledge. || 24 ||
Thus, creation is threefold and each [of those] is threefold—namely, the rajasic and the tamasic.
The mass of ignorance, beginning with the immobile beings, has reached the limit of the tamasic state.

He extends the aforementioned principle to other cases with the words "rājasī" (the rajasic). In this manner, the threefold creation—both rajasic and tamasic—has been described. To explain: even among all human beings, those who are rajasic consist of three parts: the Brahmins, who are primarily characterized by knowledge, constitute the *sattva* portion; the Kṣatriyas and others, who are primarily engaged in activities such as warfare, constitute the *rajas* portion.

Good Śūdras and others who abound in delusion (*moha*) constitute the portion of *tamas*. In this way, among the tamasic animals as well—such as cows and so forth—the threefold division should be understood based on the predominance of illumination (*prakāśa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and delusion (*moha*). The "lump of ignorance" (*maurkhyapiṇḍa*) refers to a specific class of creation consisting of immobile beings (*sthāvara*) and the like, which is the nature of ignorance condensed into a mass. This represents the limit of the tamasic creation.
He has attained the state of the ultimate limit. || 25 ||
Rāma said:
O Lord, when ignorance has reached an extreme state of density and manifests, having entered the bodies of immobile beings and so forth, what does it become? (26)

Regarding the term "maurkhyam" (ignorance): having reached an extreme density and extreme compactness, ignorance—that is, nescience—having attained the body of a stationary being and so forth, what kind of state does it assume, and in what manner does it exist? || 26 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having neither attained the state of non-mind nor fallen away from the state of mind,
this consciousness remains among immobile beings by resorting to a neutral form.

"Being without mind" (*amanastvam*): It has not attained "mindlessness"—a state like that of a stone or similar objects—because of the impossibility of activity aimed at attaining the beneficial or avoiding the harmful. Furthermore, it is "fallen away even from mindness," meaning fallen away even from mental operations, due to the absence of recollection and so forth. Thus, it stands as a neutral witness, situated between mindness and mindlessness.
This consciousness, having resorted to such a form of ignorance, remains within stationary beings. || 27 || 28 ||
Rāma said:
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, wherever that consciousness, having fallen away from the state of mind, is established even in immobile things, there I consider liberation to be not far off.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Wherein the City-of-Eight (puryaṣṭaka) remains asleep, consciousness (cit) abides there bestowing bliss;
it stays there like one who is mute, blind, or dull-witted, by its mere existence alone.

Regarding the word "supta" (asleep): where, among stationary beings, the consciousness (*cit-caitanya*) known as the "sleeping puryaṣṭaka"—endowed with a portion of ego (*ahaṃkāra-kalā*) and accompanied by the seed of the intellect (*buddhi-bīja*)—is said to be that *puryaṣṭaka*. However, according to the Śaiva Āgama, the *puryaṣṭaka* is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), because it performs the functions of cognition and action; therefore, it is described as being of such a nature.

That [nature] in which the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka)—the aggregate of the senses—is dormant and dissolved remains as a bestower of bliss, acting as the cause for the manifestation of happiness as in deep sleep. Therein, among immobile beings such as the mute, the blind, and the dull-witted, consciousness (cit) exists merely as pure being (sattāmātra), but it does not shine forth through manifest clarity. || 29 ||
Rāma said:
O best among the knowers of the Veda, where consciousness abides in immobile beings through the non-duality of existence, there I consider liberation to be not far off.

Regarding the word *sattā*: where, among immobile beings (*sthāvara*), existence (*sattā*) abides as non-different from the existence of consciousness (*cit-sattā-advaitatayā*)—that is to say, as being of the nature of pure existence alone due to the absence of conceptualization, doubt, and so forth—I consider liberation to be situated not far away, but very near, in those immobile beings. The sense is that this is because they resemble the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). || 30 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having deliberated this with prior intelligence through the observation of things as they truly are, that awakening to the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) shall be infinite liberation. || 31 ||
Regarding the term *buddhi*: having investigated this world through scripture, reasoning, and the experience of the wise, and having reflected upon it, one perceives it as it truly is;

from this ascertainment of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), that conscious awareness which is preceded by wisdom—awareness that culminates in pure existence (*sattāmātra*) alone—is itself the infinite liberation (*mokṣa*) free from rebirth. Otherwise, [one is bound] by great sins alone.
The sense is that since liberation would be easily attained through the perfection of immobility achieved by means of physical [postures], the treatises on liberation would become useless. || 31 ||
The supreme relinquishment of latent impressions (vāsanās), following their full comprehension,
is known by the wise as the state of liberation (kaivalya), because it consists of the nature of pure existence-in-general (sattāsāmānya). || 32 ||

He says this very thing with the word "pari" (completely): Having fully understood—that is, having investigated—the necessity of abandoning the latent impressions (*vāsanās*), which are the causes of *saṃsāra*, that which is the supreme abandonment is an abandonment free from the attainment of further *saṃsāra*. Why? Because consciousness (*caitanya*), being of the nature of pure existence (*sattāsāmānya*), is entirely devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); therefore, they know that very state to be the form of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). || 32 ||

Having reflected and investigated the scriptures together with the noble ones through spiritual meditation, they know that which abides in the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) to be that very Supreme Brahman. || 33 ||

"Having reflected" is an elaboration of what was previously stated. Having examined the scriptures—that is, the scriptures concerning the supreme self (adhyātma-śāstra)—and having mastered them from the mouth of a guru, and having reflected with reasoning in consultation with noble seekers of Brahman (brahmavādibhiḥ), one should contemplate through internal meditation within one's own mind; that which is the state of abiding in the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) is alone the Supreme.
They know Brahman. || 33 ||
Know that state to be deep sleep (suṣuptatva) wherein the latent impression (vāsanā), slow and dormant within like a sprout in a seed, remains; it bestows birth once again.

"Antaḥ" (within): Know that state to be deep sleep (*suṣuptatva*) because it resembles a profound slumber, wherein, during that stationary phase, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) remains dormant and hidden within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), like a sprout within a seed. Furthermore, know that it bestows rebirth, because the latent impression persists there in a concealed manner, like wealth buried underground. || 34 ||

With the mind dissolved within and latent impressions (vāsanās) dormant on all sides, deep sleep (suṣupta) is characterized by inertia; because it is a state of dullness, it bestows hundreds of sorrows of rebirth. (35)

"Antar" means within; it refers to that state resembling deep sleep (*suṣupta*) in which mental activity is dissolved within, the functions of the mind are latent, and all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are as if asleep. Because it possesses the nature of insentience and exists only among insentient things, it bestows hundreds of sorrows of birth, being the cause of births and hundreds of miseries. || 35 ||
For all these beings, beginning with the immobile, possess the nature of insentience;
having ascended to the state of deep sleep, they are fit for birth again and again. (36)

Regarding the phrase "the immobile beings and so forth": because all these immobile beings and others, characterized by insentience, have entered the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*) due to their internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), they are fit for birth again and again; for those who are in deep sleep transmigrate repeatedly. (36)
Just as flowers exist within seeds and jars within a heap of clay,
so too, O virtuous one, do their own latent impressions reside within immobile beings.

Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): just as flowers exist within mango seeds and other such seeds in a subtle form— the mention of "flowers" being illustrative of fruits and so forth— and just as jars exist within a heap of clay, that is, within a mass of earth— the mention of "jars" being illustrative of bowls, water-jars, and the like— in the same way...
In stationary beings, their own latent impressions—consisting of the habitual tendencies of merit and demerit from previous lives and serving as the causes for future births—reside within. (37)
That state where the seed of latent impressions (vāsanā) still exists is not the true deep sleep (suṣupta) for the sake of spiritual perfection;
that state where latent impressions are seedless is known as the Fourth State (turya), which bestows perfection.

Regarding the phrase "yatreti": where, in the state of being stationary (sthāvara-daśā), there exists both the latent impression (*vāsanā*)—which is its seed—and ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), that is indeed the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptatva*) and not the fourth state (*turya*). And that [state] does not lead to success, that is, to liberation (*kaivalya*). Where—in the station of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta-pada*)—there is pure latent impression (*śuddha-vāsanā*), in which the seed, namely the form of ignorance, has departed (*nirbījā*).
That fourth state proceeds; it is known as the perfected state. || 38 ||
Likewise, even a tiny remnant of latent impressions, fire, debt, disease, enemies, oil, or poison causes affliction. (39)
Regarding the phrase "of the latent impression" (vāsanāyā): the meaning is that, like fire and so forth, even a small remnant of the latent impression persists and causes affliction. || 39 ||
One whose seeds of latent impressions have been burnt away, possessing the nature of pure existence, shall no longer be a partaker of suffering— whether still embodied or disembodied. (40)

Regarding the term *nirdagdha* (consumed): one whose seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been consumed—that is, one by whom both the latent impressions and their seed, which is ignorance (*ajñāna*), have been burnt—such a person, because he abides in the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*) and thus possesses that very nature, shall not again be a partaker of suffering, whether the body exists or does not exist. || 40 ||
The power of consciousness (cicchakti) of all embodied beings exists in the form of the seeds of latent impressions (vāsanā);
the non-perception of this [power] is what is called ignorance (avidyā) by the wise. (41)

Regarding the phrase "the power of consciousness" (*cic-chakti*): that which is indeed the power of consciousness—the power of *cit*, whose nature is the consciousness of Brahman—exists in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), in the form of their seeds, and in the form of ignorance (*ajñāna*) which is the seed of those impressions; it possesses the quality of sleep and is the cause of sleep.
That non-perception, that lack of manifestation, of the true nature of this consciousness—which is due to this power of consciousness—is what is well-known.

The power of obscuration is called avidyā (ignorance). Regarding the reading "yattadavidyā," it is in the neuter gender because the neuter gender of the predicate is adopted [from the subject] in the statement "that which is the cause of that vision is avidyā. || 41 ||
One should burn away the other [ignorance] by means of the primary portion of ignorance itself, until the two, through mutual friction, are extinguished and Śiva alone remains. (42)

Regarding the phrase "of ignorance" (*avidyāyā*): since ignorance, as previously defined, consists of the three *guṇas*, and since each *guṇa* is itself threefold, it is divided into nine parts. That part which is predominant, consisting of pure *sattva*—denoted by the term "knowledge" (*vidyā*)—should first consume the other part of ignorance, until both parts [are exhausted].

Through mutual friction—that is, through their mutual overcoming—the form of knowledge and ignorance would be thoroughly and completely pacified; for ignorance, being dispelled by knowledge, brings about the cessation of knowledge as well, just as the final sound [in a word] causes the penultimate sound to cease. This is the intended meaning. || 42 ||
The nature of ignorance is precisely this: the certainty that "this is not Brahman. Its destruction occurs when there is the certainty that "this is Brahman. (43)

"Only this much" means: the conviction that "this world is not Brahman, nor is it of the nature of Brahman, but rather consists solely of ether and so forth"—this alone is the state of ignorance (avidyātva), the operation of ignorance. Conversely, the conviction that "this is Brahman"—this indeed is the destruction of that ignorance; such is the summary. || 43 ||
O Rāghava, may that stainless certainty which dwells in the hearts of Hara and others, and of the sages such as Nārada and the rest, be yours. (44)

He follows the subject at hand with the words: "The certainty. Let that stainless certainty which exists in the hearts of the deities such as Hara and the sages such as Nārada be yours. The meaning is: you too should take recourse to that very path of liberation while living (jīvanmukta). || 44 ||
Rāma said:
O Blessed One, O Brahmin, tell me in truth how these wise and high-minded ones, free from sorrow, remain established in certainty.
"By what... || Tell me truly that certainty by which these [sages], Hara and the others, remain free from sorrow as liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 45 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Whatever web of the world appears as an object of experience, all that is the stainless Brahman; this vast reality is thus established. (46)
The meaning of "yad" (that which) is as follows: the conclusion of Hara and the other gods is that everything perceived and visible is indeed Brahman alone. || 46 ||
Brahman is consciousness, Brahman is the world, and Brahman is the succession of all beings.
I am Brahman; my enemy is Brahman; my friends and kinsmen are Brahman.

He elaborates on this very point with the words "Brahman" and so forth. The meaning is that Brahman is both the illuminator, which is consciousness (*cit*), and the illuminated, which consists of the sentient and the insentient. The "succession of beings" (*bhūtaparamparā*) refers to the collection of the great elements, beginning with space. The expressions "I am" and "this is my body" represent the firm conviction and the manifestation of the essential nature of Śiva and the other deities. (47)
To the ignorant, the world consists of a flood of suffering; to the wise, it consists of bliss.
To the blind, the world is darkness; but to one with clear vision, it is light. 48.
An objection is raised: "But since this world is indeed one and the same, how can it result in suffering for some and happiness for others?
Anticipating this, he provides an explanation by means of an illustration, saying: "Of the ignorant... The meaning is that this distinction is produced by knowledge and ignorance. (48)
For when everything is meditated upon as Brahman, the person indeed becomes Brahman;
when nectar has been drunk, who indeed would not become composed of nectar? (49)
He states the very mode of knowledge along with an illustration: "All... [verse 49]. When it has been cultivated and ascertained that "it is indeed Brahman."
It is experienced as the stainless mere appearance that awakens one to all beings, which is omnipresent and tranquil—the Brahman of consciousness. (50)

"Merely appearance" (ābhāsamātram) means that the reality which is mere appearance, consisting of knowledge untouched by objects, is experienced as the Consciousness-Brahman—that is, as the Supreme Brahman whose nature is consciousness. The inclusion of the term "consciousness" (cit) is for the purpose of excluding the Brahman of sound (śabdabrahman). || 50 ||

When one encounters a traveler with whom one has no prior acquaintance, and while the mind is fixed elsewhere, that faultless perception which arises—that I am the all-pervading Brahman, consciousness itself. 51.
Clarifying this very point by means of an illustration, he says: "asaṃstuta... etc.

When there is the sight (āloka) of an unfamiliar traveler—one previously unacquainted—and while the mind is fixed upon another object of its own choosing, that cognition which exists, free from all taints and liberated from all conceptual constructions, is "I am the all-pervading Brahman, Consciousness."

By the term "unacquainted" (*asaṃstuta*), it is stated that there is no arising of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) due to the power of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior experience.
By the term "traveler" (*adhvaga*), it is shown that because there is no delay in time, there is no opportunity for the arising of conceptual constructions.
And by the mention of the mind being situated elsewhere, even the postulation of conceptual constructions at that very moment is impossible.

It should be understood that this has been indicated. Nor can it be said that the cognition does not arise at all, because consciousness, when directed outward through the channel of the external senses, invariably possesses the capacity to manifest [its object]. Otherwise, in the absence of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), there would follow the impossibility of the arising of determinate perception (*savikalpaka*), which is rooted in the former; for instance, one might later wonder, "Has someone come here? regarding a previous moment.

Furthermore, because recollection of that object is possible for one who has been questioned [about it], it must be admitted that there exists a pure cognition which, being non-conceptual, is free from the defects of its objects. || 51 ||
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which bestows the fruit of all intentions, illuminates all splendors, and is the ultimate limit of everything worthy of being attained.
"Of all"—we worship that conscious Self (cidātman) who, by virtue of being the Lord of the universe, bestows the fruit of all intentions. 52–53.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, in whom all volitions are stilled, from whom every curiosity has departed, and in whom all agitation has completely vanished. (53)
Thus possessing such certainty, those great ones, free from sin, established in truth upon the true, peaceful, and even state, abide in happiness. (54)

Thus: those who possess such certainty—meaning they are endowed with the aforementioned kind of conviction—and for that very reason are free from sin (*vigatainas*), being virtuous (*satyāḥ*) toward *Sat*, the Brahman which is the Reality; those great ones, Nārada and others, remain at ease, as is fitting, in the Supreme Brahman, which is equal (uniform), peaceful, changeless, real, and of an unassailable nature. [The distinction between] the real and the unreal...
In this reading, it should be explained that [the Self] is real because its nature is the Seer (dṛk), and unreal because its nature is the seen (dṛśya). || 54 ||
Thus, the wise ones of perfected intellect, whose minds are free from passion, neither rejoice in life nor do they revile death. (55)

Thus: in this manner, those of perfected intellect—meaning those whose understanding is complete because of their steadfastness in Brahman—and therefore those wise ones whose minds are equanimous and free from passion, do not rejoice in life nor do they deplore death, because they delight in the Self. || 55 ||
Rāma said:
O Brahmin, through the play of right knowledge, upon the arising of the dissolution of latent impressions, I have indeed come to rest in the state of one liberated while living.

"Correctly" (samyak) means: by the play or the majesty of correct knowledge, or by the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), when the dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanā) occurs, how—in what manner—is one rested in liberation while living (jīvanmukti)? || 56 || 57 ||
O Brahmin, when the dissolution of latent impressions arises through the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath, tell me: how does one rest in the state of liberation while living?
Vasiṣṭha said:
The method for crossing over saṃsāra is expressed by the word yoga;
it consists of the means of self-knowledge as well as the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇas). || 58 ||
Regarding "in saṃsāra": the method or means for crossing over saṃsāra is itself yoga, and that is twofold: self-knowledge and the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 58 ||
Although both types are indeed expressed by the word "yoga," nevertheless, it has acquired a firm conventional usage specifically for the practice involving breath (*prāṇa*). (59)

"Regarding the two types": the meaning is that although the word *yoga* is common to both types, it is most firmly established (conventional) in the sense of the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇanirodha*). || 59 || 60 ||
"For some, yoga is impossible; for others, the certainty of knowledge.
Therefore, the supreme god Śiva declared two methods. (60)
That has been declared as knowledge; now listen to the sequence of yoga.
Here I shall relate to you a most wonderful account.
The word "tat" (that) constitutes a half-verse. That knowledge which is the means for crossing over saṃsāra has already been declared to you.
Hereafter, hear about the sequence of yoga, which serves as the means for the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa). 61, 62, 63.
Once, while I was staying in the assembly hall of Śatakratu in heaven,
I heard from Nārada and others those stories of the long-lived ones.
Then, during a certain course of conversation regarding long-lived beings, a sage named Śātātapa spoke there on that occasion.
On the peak that is entirely delightful, situated in the northeast corner of Meru, there is a glorious wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru) growing from a sprout made of ruby.

Regarding the phrase "of Meru": the connection is that on a peak of Meru—wherein the *udbhid* (plants) such as trees and shrubs are composed of rubies (*padmarāga*)—there exists a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*). In the reading "in the ruby-made heaven" (*padmarāgamaye divi*), the construction is that on the ruby-made peak of Meru, there is a heaven (*dyauḥ*, i.e., *svarga*), and therein exists the wish-fulfilling tree. [This is] the twenty-first [verse].
"These are the heavens situated on the summit of Mount Meru," because of the scriptural accounts of the multiplicity of heavens. || 64 || 65 ||
At the top of that wish-fulfilling tree, within a hollow in the southern branch entwined with silver creepers, there dwells one of pure intent. (65)
In that place dwelt a glorious crow named Bhuśuṇḍa,
free from passion and possessing a vast treasury, like Brahmā within his own eggshell.
"In that [place]" means: in that abode of birds, there was one known as Bhuśuṇḍa, so called because he flies and sports with ease throughout all the worlds. (Verses 66–71)
Just as he lives here for a long time within the treasury of the worlds,
so shall there never have been, nor will there ever be, another long-lived one in heaven like him.
He is long-lived, he is free from disease, he is glorious, he is of great intelligence;
he is one whose mind is at rest, he is peaceful, he is beloved, and he is skilled in the knowledge of time.
Thus was that Bhuśuṇḍa described by him when questioned further,
and how he had spoken the truth in the assembly of the gods of gods.
When the assembly of gods had departed and the occasion for conversation had subsided,
I went out of curiosity to see the bird Bhuśuṇḍa.
Where Bhuśuṇḍa was stationed on the most excellent peak of Meru,
I beheld him standing like a circle of branches upon a wish-fulfilling tree.
In its marshy banks, in its groves, in the leaves of its creepers, at its joints,
and among its flowers, I beheld birds nestled within their dwellings.
Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): *kacchāḥ* are marshy regions consisting mostly of water; *kuñjāḥ* are areas covered by creepers and the like;
*latāḥ* are branches; *patrāṇi* are leaves; and *parvāṇi* are joints. Having constructed nests upon these, he saw birds hidden therein—meaning, for the purpose of searching for Bhuśuṇḍa. || 72 ||
Then Viriñci [created] the young cygnets who chant the Sāman hymns, nourished by fragments of lotus stalks as delicate as a digit of the moon, the lord of the night. (73)

The speech consists of four verses beginning with "niśānātha. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Then Viriñci, as soon as I saw the young swans and other birds, [I saw] that in one place, within a hollow of a trunk, in an assembly, the crows were standing with undisturbed appearances. Their state of being undisturbed is due to the impropriety of restlessness in the presence of a guru, or because they were inwardly focused.

It should be understood that the swans and other such beings possess the knowledge of Sāman-chanting, the recitation of mantras, and the Śaiva Āgamas because they lived together with the great sages (maharṣis) in the world of Brahmā and other realms during their Sāman-singing and similar activities; thus it should be viewed. || 73 || 74 || 75 || 76 ||
Parrots, crows, cuckoos, and many other birds on the ground were vomiting forth a multitude of mantras with sounds resembling the utterance of *svāhā*.
The excellent peacocks of Kumāra, with masses of white crests like Gaurī’s locks of hair, were experts in all the Śaiva sciences imparted by Skanda. (75)
There, as far as I could see, I beheld the crows standing in the hollow of a branch at one side, their forms undisturbed, as if they were in an assembly.
Standing in their midst was the illustrious Bhuśuṇḍa, of lofty form, with a perfectly contented mind, observing silence, equanimous, and beautiful in every limb. (77)
By attentively observing the movement of the vital breath, he is eternally inward-turned and happy;
his mind is serene and profound, he is gentle, his speech is affectionate, and he is wise.
Then, with my body blazing, I alighted before him;
for an instant, the crow’s abode was as agitated as a pond of blue lotuses.
Immediately thereafter, Bhuśuṇḍa saw me arrive unexpectedly,
yet he perceived that this was Vasiṣṭha who had arrived.
He rose up from the heap of leaves like a young cloud from a mountain;
"O Sage, welcome," he said in sweet syllables.
That one of great splendor spoke to me with sweet words out of friendship.
With his two hands, produced by mere volition, he immediately offered me a handful of flowers, just as a cloud pours down a shower of golden dust. (82)

"He resolved" (saṃkalpeti) means that by virtue of his power of true resolve (satyasaṃkalpatayā), his two hands appeared by mere volition alone—like a golden lotus-hand, like a cluster of golden flowers. || 82 || 83 || 84 || 85 || 86 || 87 || 88 ||
Having said, "This is the seat," the highly intelligent lord of birds himself brought forward a fresh garment from the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
While flocks of birds on all sides had their gaze fixed upward in anticipation of a sight,
I sat upon that throne which was like a cluster of wish-fulfilling creepers.
Having prepared the water for honor, the water for the feet, and other offerings, Bhuśuṇḍa, with a delighted mind and great luster, spoke to me in words sweet with affection: (85)
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"Oh! After a long time, the Blessed One has shown us his grace, for we—these noble trees—have been sprinkled by the cloud of the nectar of his sight. (86)
For what purpose have you come today? Why have you distressed yourself with such hardship?
You ought to grant us an audience, for we are eager to hear your words.
O Sage, by the mere sight of your feet, everything has been known by me;
through our discussions on long life, we have come back to your memory.
Since this is already known, O Sage, why do I ask you?
Yet, a longing for the taste of the nectar of your words expands within me. (89)

"Known" means because it is known; "arrival" also refers to the arrival [of knowledge] based on its having been understood. Thus, for this reason, since I ask you in this manner, it is this very desire to taste the nectar of your words—which serves as the cause—that expands within me.
The meaning is: "Even though I already know the cause of your arrival, I ask you out of a mere desire to hear your words. (Verses 89–96)
Having spoken thus, that long-lived bird Bhuśuṇḍa,
who perceives the stainless reality of the three times, said this to me there. (90)
"O great king of birds, what you have said is true;
I have come today specifically to see you, who are long-lived. (91)
Therefore, O Blessed One, cut through this doubt of mine according to the truth:
in what family were you born, and how did you become one who has known that which is to be known?
O holy one, how long is your lifespan, and what conduct do you remember? By whom—some far-sighted being—was this dwelling place assigned to you?
Then, O Rāma, that Bhuśuṇḍa was neither delighted nor crooked-minded;
O sage, listen as I tell you everything that you ask.
"Who is capable of transgressing this command of one such as you?
Having said this, the lord of birds related everything that had occurred.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
In this world, there is a supreme one among all the inhabitants of heaven,
the God of gods named Hara, who is saluted by the God of gods.
Whose playful attendants have the faces of bears, camels, goats, and elephants, and who possess heads, hooves, trunks, tusks, mouths, and bellies. (97)

Regarding the term *śiraḥkhurāḥ*: those whose hooves (*khura*) are on their heads (*śiras*); those who have hands (*kara*) upon their hooves, or rather, those whose hands are shaped like hooves; those who have teeth located in their hands; and those who have mouths on their bellies (*udara*). Furthermore, there are those with the faces of bears (*ṛkṣa*), camels (*uṣṭra*), goats (*aja*), and elephants (*ibha*). "Bear" (*ṛkṣa*) refers to the brown bear (*bhallūka*). "Camel" (*uṣṭra*)... [text fragment ends].
Those who have faces like those of camels, goats, rams, and elephants—such are the various forms of the Pramathas, who are the playthings and instruments of sport for that God. (97, 98, 99) [p.
Just like the Gaṇas, so too are the other retinues, the Mothers;
the Mothers dance before him, while the hosts of spirits bow down.
They dwell upon mountain peaks, in the sky, and in other worlds; they reside in chasms, in cremation grounds, and within the bodies of embodied beings.
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā, Siddhā, Raktā, Alambuṣā, and Utpalā are the presiding deities. || 100 ||
Of all the Mothers, these eight are indeed the principal leaders; others follow them, and yet others follow those. (1)
O Leader of Sages,
O Giver of Honor, among those highly venerable mothers there exists one renowned as Alambuṣā.
And the one named Caṇḍa has a beak as hard as adamant and resembles a mountain of sapphire;
his vehicle is a crow, just as Garuḍa is that of Vaiṣṇavī. (3)
"Vajra" means one whose beak is made of bone. "Vajra" refers to something as hard as a diamond; he is one whose beak is bone-like, that is, whose mouth consists of bone.
He is a crow known by the name Caṇḍa; such a crow is the vehicle of that Alambuṣā. (3–21)
Thus, those Mothers, endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers and characterized by fierce deeds,
once gathered together in the sky for some reason.
They celebrated a supreme festival that revealed the ultimate truth; they laughed, danced, drank, and sang loudly.
p.
566) While this festival was underway, their excellent mounts likewise became intoxicated; they laughed, danced, and drank the *āsava* liquor. (6)
There, in one place, the female swans of Brahmā’s chariot, intoxicated by the wine [of the nectar], danced somewhere in the sky; meanwhile, the crow remained in the chariot of Alambuṣā.
Then, having conceived passion there and being agitated by intoxication, all those female swans took their pleasure with the crow Caṇḍaka.
Then those queens became pregnant and were exceedingly gratified; having performed their dances, they attained a state of tranquility and the absence of pride.
Then the goddesses and Hara himself, accompanied by their retinues,
all with contented minds, departed for their respective directions.
O Lord of Sages, those Brāhmī swans became pregnant and related to Brāhmī the Goddess the news exactly as it had occurred.
"O Vatsyas, at present you are like calves to me in the work of chariot-making; for you are no longer capable, so wander about as you please now. (12)
Having spoken thus, the goddess Brāhmī, compassionate and weary with pregnancy, remained at her ease in a state of unwavering meditative absorption.
The female swans, their embryos fully developed, gave birth in due order to twenty-one sons in the vast lake of Vairañca.
Thus, O sage, we twenty-one crows, the sons of Caṇḍa, were born from those two female swans as brothers.
Then the blessed Brāhmī, together with her mothers who were like female swans,
having been propitiated by us for a long time, emerged from her meditative absorption.
Then,
at that time, the Blessed Lady herself, intent on grace,
favored us in such a way that we remain liberated. (17)
With minds fully satisfied and tranquil, having resolved, "We shall remain established in meditation in solitude," we went to our father's side. (18)
Having there paid homage to our father and bowed to Queen Alambuṣā,
we were looked upon by her with favor, and she then spoke to us.
"Father, enough has been known; through the grace of the Goddess Brāhmī, that which is to be known has been fully understood.
However, we desire an excellent place for our solitary dwelling. (120)
Therefore, this wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa) is inaccessible to all oppressors;
this is the place described for us by the All-Knowing One who perceives everything. (21)
Then, having offered our salutations and departed from that place,
we have reached this wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru) and remain here, freed from all distress.
Today my merits, accumulated over a long time,
have borne fruit, since I behold you, the Lord of Sages, without any obstacle.
Who indeed would not be gladdened by the moonlight of association with the virtuous, which consists of elixir, is peaceful, and bestows supreme bliss? (24)

"Rasāyanā" means consisting of elixir, because it removes defects such as passion (*rāga*). "Śāntā" means peaceful, because it dispels the three types of suffering (*tāpa*). "Paramānandadāyinī" means bestowing supreme bliss, because it is the cause for the instruction of knowledge (*jñāna*). How, indeed, does this moonlight in the form of association with the virtuous (*sādhu*) not bring joy? 24–33. 130. 31. 32. 33.
I consider nothing to be more beneficial for myself than this:
that I am followed by the virtuous who have renounced all desires. (25)

O holy man, I believe that even though I have realized the Supreme Self, my birth here today has become fruitful because my evil deeds have been pacified by the sight of you; for the company of the virtuous removes all fear.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the bird Bhuśuṇḍa had spoken thus and had himself offered water for the hands and feet once more, I, Rāma, said this to him: ||| 27 ||
O Lord of Birds, why are those brothers of yours—not being of such a nature, yet possessing great intelligence—not seen here? For you alone are seen. (28)
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"O Sage, let much time pass while we remain here; O Great-minded One, the successions of ages and the cycles of kalpas have been exhausted. (29)
And in this much time, all my younger brothers,
having cast off their bodies like blades of grass, have been transformed into the auspicious state.
Whether they be long-lived, great, virtuous, or powerful,
all are swallowed up by Time, whose nature is beyond calculation.
I said:
O Great Buddha, at the ends of the eons when fire, water, and wind are surging forth,
and when the suns are likewise scorching, how do you remain free from all feverish distress?
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
When worldly activity throughout the universe subsides at the end of the aeon,
like an ungrateful person toward a friend, then I shall abandon my nest.
I abide in space itself, free from all conceptual construction,
with every limb of my nature rendered motionless, like a mind devoid of latent impressions.
"Like space": with all his limbs in a state of rigidity— that is, one whose body and all its members are rigid and motionless— he remains like a mind free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*),
like the consciousness of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), in which all conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) have vanished during that action.

I remain exactly as I am, free from all conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*). Regarding the reading "dagdhaprakṛtisavāṅgam," it should be understood as an adjective qualifying the mind (*manas*), meaning that whose nature (*prakṛti*)—which is ignorance (*avidyā*)—and all its parts, such as desire, volition, and doubt, have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge. || 34 ||
When the suns scorch [the world] while I am situated in the courtyard of the sky,
I then remain with a steady mind, having bound the *vāruṇī* concentration. (35)

Regarding the phrase "they blaze": when, at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), even all twelve suns rise simultaneously and blaze, then I, having gone to the courtyard of the sky and having fixed the *dhāraṇā*—the meditative concentration—pertaining to Varuṇa (*vāruṇī*), remain there with a steady intellect, my mind motionless. Just as Varuṇa sits in the midst of the waters, so do I abide.

Just as [the former] does not perceive the external heat of the sun, so too I, Bhuśuṇḍa, having attained identity with that through the contemplation of Varuṇa, do not experience external heat in the same way; this is the meaning. || 35 ||
When the winds of dissolution blow, shattering the great lords of mountains,
I remain motionless in the sky, having assumed the mountain-like meditative concentration (dhāraṇā).

Regarding the word *yadā*: when the winds of dissolution blow, shattering the great mountains, then—having performed the mountain-holding meditation (*pārvatī-dhāraṇā*)—I remain immovable in the sky. Since it is only the mountains situated upon the earth that are subject to destruction, the fury of the dissolution-winds occurs precisely there; therefore, I abide outside the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) in the sky, which is not an object of that fury.
The meaning is: "I remain at ease by resorting to the mountain-like concentration (dhāraṇā) so that there may be no agitation from the common winds. || 36 ||
When the world, including Mount Meru and all else, dissolves and reaches the state of a single ocean,
one should then fix the mind immovably upon the meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) on air during that deluge.
"Regarding the world": even at the time of the single ocean, during the universal deluge, I float right upon it by means of the concentration on air. || 37 ||
Having reached the far limit of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), at the end of the principles (tattva) in that stainless state,
I remain for that long in the state of deep sleep, with an unshakable form. (38)

The two verses beginning with "brahmāṇḍe" constitute a single syntactical unit. When the dissolution occurs, having reached the limit— the outer portion— of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), at the end of the principles (tattva-ante), that is, at the conclusion of the seven principles that serve as the coverings of the cosmic egg, namely earth, water, fire, air, ether, ego (ahaṃkāra), the Great Principle (mahat), and primordial nature (prakṛti).
I shall remain in that stainless state through the condition of deep sleep for as long as the Lotus-born remains engaged in the work of creation;
then, upon that new creation, having entered the cosmic egg, I shall abide in the abode of the birds (the sky). 38 || 39 || 140 ||
Furthermore, as long as the lotus-born Brahmā remains engaged in the work of creation,
I shall enter that cosmic egg and remain there in the abode of birds.
"By the power of my own resolve alone, in kalpa after kalpa, again and again, this very tree shall come into being upon this mountain peak. (140)
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Lord of Birds, why is it that other yogins do not remain unbroken by their meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās) at the end of the kalpas, as you do? (41)
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"O Brahmin, this destiny of the Supreme Lord is indeed difficult to overcome;
I must become such as I am, and others likewise must become as they are. (42)
