"O Brahmin," [he said]. Niyati is the power of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvarī-śakti) whose nature is that of constraint. || 42 ||
That which is destined to be cannot be moved;
for whatever is as it is, such is the certainty of its own nature. 43.

"Not so. To "shake off" means to transgress. "Destiny" (bhavitavyatā) refers to the course of fate; it is called "necessity" (niyati) in theistic doctrines, while it is called "destiny" in atheistic doctrines. It should be understood that according to the distinction between philosophical views, this is accepted as the determination of "inherent nature" (svabhāva) in the doctrine of inherent nature (svabhāvavāda). || 43 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
O hero, endowed with both knowledge and discernment, whose mental movement is fit for yoga—what wonders do you remember, O auspicious one, within these three worlds? (44)

Regarding the word "jñāna" (knowledge): therein, *jñāna* is the cause of liberation, which is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), as well as the specific knowledge of all worldly arts, sciences, and so forth. It is diverse and wonderful. || 44 ||
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
I remember this earth below, devoid of massive rocks and trees, and lacking grasses and creepers, as well as its multitude of mountains, forests, and trees.
"Vṛhattarā" means: below, in the past, at the end of the kalpa. || 45 ||
For ten thousand years and ten hundred years,
I remember the earth below, completely filled with a heavy burden of ashes.
"Ten years" means that after the drying up and burning, during the long-delayed final emission, the earth remained filled with a mass of ashes for eleven thousand years. || 46 ||
[He saw] another [region] at the end of the four yugas, dense with forest trees,
and another at the end of the four yugas, surrounded by impenetrable mountains.

The two verses beginning with "caturyugāntam" form a single syntactical unit. I remember the earth—the foundation of the world—existing within another kalpa as a hut for the universe; in one set of four ages (caturyuga), I remember it as being densely covered by forest trees, and in another set of four ages, I remember it as being filled with dense mountains.

I remember that in another cycle of four ages, the great seer Agastya recalled the earth to have become a single Vindhya mountain— empty because of that very reason and due to the absence of any ruler— and to have been pervaded by the Vindhya alone.
I remember this other hut of the world, which has become a single Vindhya mountain without Agastya, and which shall endure until the end of the four ages.
"O dear one, I remember a certain creation in which Brāhmaṇas drank liquor, Śūdras were forbidden from drinking liquor, and virtuous women lived according to their own will. (49)

I remember a certain creation (sarga) such as this: one in which there are Brāhmaṇas who drink liquor; one in which there are Śūdras who drink all kinds of liquor except for that which is prohibited; and one in which noble women are self-willed, acting according to their own desires. 49.
The establishment of Indra and Upendra by Janman, Indu, Bhāskara, and the others;
the abduction of Hiraṇyākṣa; and the lifting of the earth by the Boar.
The phrase "janma" refers to three verses. [It describes] the birth or origin of the Moon, the Sun, and others; the establishment of Indra and Upendra;
the boundary or domain of Indra and Upendra; the seizing of the earth by Hiraṇyākṣa and its recovery by the Boar (Varāha).

The imagining of kings and the bringing of the Vedas, the uprooting of Mount Mandara and its use for churning the ocean for the sake of the nectar of immortality—[all these were accomplished by him]. (51)

The third Smṛti exists as the originator [of the following]: the enumeration of the kings who were lords during the Manvantaras; the recovery of the Vedas, which had been stolen by Soma, the enemy of the gods, through the Fish Incarnation; and the churning of the ocean for the sake of nectar, involving its uprooting by the gods and demons for the purpose of using Mount Mandara as the churning stick.
Such are the Smṛtis, in which the sequences of the world are recorded in brief; they are the objects to be remembered. || 51 || 52 ||
"The Garuḍa with unformed wings is the source of the oceans"—such are the traditional recollections (smṛtis) which describe the sequence of the world as having occurred only a short time ago. (52)
For even children, O dear one, remember them; what attachment can there be for those [women]? || 53 ||
"Even by the ignorant" means: since these matters are remembered even by the ignorant, for that reason, what concern or what regard should there be for those traditional accounts?
The sense is: "Regarding me, you should not ask about such a history. || 53 ||
Then, O Blessed One, among those born in the world beginning with yourself—
namely Bharadvāja, Pulastya, Atri, Nārada, Indra, and Marīci— [54]

The phrase "tataḥ" (therefore) introduces a statement consisting of two and a half verses. Regarding that remembrance [of the Lord] among you and others such as Bharadvāja, Sanatkumāra, and so forth, as well as among those in the present creation—what account can there be of that remembrance? What respect or regard can it possibly command? || 54 || 55 ||
In Sanatkumāra, Bhṛgu, Īśa, Skanda, Ibhavada, and others,
and in the many [goddesses] such as Gaurī, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, and Gāyatrī;
Likewise, what need is there for calculation regarding the recollection of the creations of today?
O Sage, this is indeed your eighth birth as a son of Brahmā;
I remember that in that eighth creation, you were united with me.

"O Sage! [He says: "This birth of yours, O son of Brahmā—the mental son of Brahmā—is indeed the eighth. The meaning is that you were born as the son of Brahmā in your eighth birth. In that eighth creation, in that birth, I remember even now our union, though it occurred in the past. (56)
Sometimes you are born from the sky, sometimes you are born from water;
sometimes you are born from a mountain, and sometimes you are born from fire.
Regarding the question of from where he was born in other births, he says: "Sometimes" (kadācit). "Sometimes" means in a certain *manvantara*. || 57 ||
O Sage, the nurse vanished; she was withdrawn by Kūrma himself from the ocean of milk during five creations over a period of five days.

"Antar" means disappearance; it refers to his concealment within the waters of the single universal ocean (*ekārṇava*) specifically as a tortoise (*kūrma*), and not in the form of a boar (*varāha*) or other such incarnations. 58–59.
I remember this twelfth [manifestation]: the churning of the ocean of nectar;
on three occasions, Hiraṇyākṣa carried the earth down below.
This Hari has attained birth from Reṇukā for the sixth time;
and there are a hundred Kali Yugas, and a hundred times ten states of Buddha for Hari. (160)
I remember thirty instances of the agitation of the three cities, two destructions of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, ten defeats of Śakra,
eight battles for the sake of Bāṇa, and three crushings of sacrifices by the Moon-crested Lord.
"Thirty," he said. "I now remember ten destructions of Indras that I previously experienced from the Moon-crested Lord, who was provoked by some act of indiscipline. (61)
O Sage, I remember the Vedas as being endowed with a variety of ritual procedures and recitations, due to the deficiency or excellence of the intellects of men in each successive age. (52)

Regarding the phrase "yugam": with respect to each *yuga*, due to the deficiency or excess of the intellects of men—that is, the cognitions of individuals—the various modes of recitation are joined with differences in the performance of rituals (*kriyā*) and their auxiliary branches (*aṅga*). Ritual (*kriyā*) refers to the performance of actions prescribed by the Vedas; the auxiliary branches (*aṅgāni*) refer to grammar and so forth; and "recitation" (*pāṭha*) refers to the method of study. [This occurs] through the diversity of ritual performance and the diversity of recitation.

I remember the Vedas as they were properly established. However, in the Dvāpara and Kali ages, due to the decline of dharma and the resulting diminution of human intellect, there occurs a corresponding reduction in the recitation of the ritual components of the Vedas. Conversely, in the Tretā and Kṛta ages, through the increase of dharma and the consequent expansion of human intellect, there is an increase in the performance of rituals and other such elements.
The meaning is "variety. || 62 ||
O sinless one, the Purāṇas— which possess a single essential meaning, are complete, and exist in many recensions— circulate in each Yuga and then cease.

Regarding the phrase "having the same meaning": having ceased due to the absence of tradition at the end of an age (yugānte), and having ceased again with each successive age—considering the differences in human intellect from the perspective of ages such as the Bhārata—the Purāṇas, which possess many recensions yet have identical meanings, come forth once more. || 63 ||
I remember another most wonderful history called the Rāmāyaṇa,
a work of one hundred thousand verses, which is a scripture of knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "itihāsam iti": because it is a treatise on knowledge (*jñāna-śāstra*)— one in which there are great wonders (*mahāścarya*), meaning great marvels— and which is devoted to describing the means to liberation (*mokṣopāya*), for that very reason,
it is a work titled *Rāmāyaṇa* distinct from the well-known *Rāmāyaṇa* whose purpose is the slaying of Rāvaṇa.
I remember it as being one hundred thousand [verses] in extent. The neuter designation "another" (*anyat*) is used in reference to the *Jñānaśāstra*.
It was composed by that very same living being named Vālmīki, or by another.
And this twelfth time is being performed because it had been forgotten. (65)

Regarding the term *vālmīki*: it is by that very person who is the renowned author of the *Rāmāyaṇa*, and not by another living being with the name Vālmīki different from him. Considering that this *Rāmāyaṇa* in the form of a treatise on knowledge (*jñāna-śāstra*) had fallen into oblivion at the end of the age, it is now being composed for the twelfth time. He who previously—
That very Vālmīki, the author of the Rāmāyaṇas— which consist of both the means for the slaying of Rāvaṇa and the nature of the science of knowledge—

manifests again and again by the command of the Supreme Lord for the sake of establishing the tradition. Or, some other soul, having attained the state of Vālmīki through the power of austerity, [establishes] the tradition of the Rāmāyaṇa.
The meaning is that it causes [them] to proceed. || 65 ||
I remember its second [version], equal to it, known by the name Bhārata; composed by Vyāsa in the past, it has been forgotten in the world. (66)

"The second" means: I remember the second epic history (itihāsa) called the Bhārata, which is equal in extent to this Rāmāyaṇa—measuring one hundred thousand [verses]—composed by Vyāsa, belonging to a former age (prāktana) that transcends the current kalpa, and which, though it has fallen into oblivion in the world, I still recall. The meaning is: "I remember even those Bhāratas that have already passed away. || 66 ||
This was composed by that very soul named Vyāsa, or by another;
it is now being performed for the seventh time, having been forgotten. (67)
Regarding "Vyāsa": it is to be explained as before. || 67 ||
For the destruction of the Rākṣasas, Viṣṇu will now undergo his eleventh birth, taking on the name Rāma. (68)

Regarding the word "rākṣasa": the designation is made by way of its being conceived as something that will exist in the future, even prior to the incarnation of Rāma and before the commencement of the Rāmāyaṇa, because it is yet to come into being. (68–69)
O Lord of Sages, for the sake of relieving the earth's burden, this will now be the sixteenth birth of Viṣṇu in the house of Vasudeva.
This delusion consisting of the world never exists;
yet at times it does exist, abiding like a bubble on water. (170)

Regarding the phrase "the world": this delusion in the form of the world does not exist at all at certain times, such as at the end of a kalpa; however, it does exist at other times, during the period of stability. Therefore, it exists like a bubble on water. (170)
This undesirable delusion of the visible world, residing within the conscious self, arises and dissolves instantly, as flickering as a wave upon the water. (71)
"Visible," it is said: this [delusion] is undesirable and constant because of its extreme variety. In the reading "anaṣṭā," it means not destroyed, because it manifests again.
The delusion of the visible is nothing other than consciousness itself, residing within the Self. Therefore, like a wave in water, it is born and dissolved in a state of flux. || 71 ||
Previously, this northern quarter did not exist here, nor did this mountain;
elsewhere, that other direction was the north, and this was the eastern mountain. (72)

"Not so," [he said]. "In a previous eon that has passed, this region here was the northern quarter; this Meru did not exist [here]. The northern direction existed elsewhere, and this mountain existed elsewhere. (72)

Due to the movement of the sun and other stars from their positions on Mount Meru and other locations, the configuration of the directions is otherwise; when that [sun] is situated there, the directions follow accordingly.

Regarding the word *arketi*: from the movement of the constellations beginning with Aries (*arka*), from the movement of the planets beginning with the Sun, and from the locations beginning with Meru—that is, from the arrangement of the boundary mountains such as Meru—the configuration and disposition of the directions change; when that configuration of Meru and the others is otherwise situated, the directions proceed in a different manner.

The sense is that, since the movement of the planets such as the Sun and the configuration of Mount Meru and so forth—which are dependent [upon the directions]—are merely conceptual constructs, when those [constructs] undergo change, the directions themselves also undergo change. || 73 || 74 || 75 || 76 || 77 ||

I remember that in the Kali age people follow the practices of the Kṛta age, while in the Kṛta age they follow the conditions of the Kali age; likewise, in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, there is a total inversion of norms.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, O mighty-armed one, that best of crows was questioned by me once more for the sake of inquiry regarding the tip of the creeper on the wish-fulfilling tree. (75)
O King of Birds, how is it that death does not afflict the body of those who move about within the treasury of the world, even though they are engaged in worldly affairs? (76)
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"O Omniscient One, although You already know, You ask me specifically out of a desire to know Brahman; for masters always urge their servants to speak. (77)
Nevertheless, I shall reveal to you that which you ask of me:
they say that for the virtuous, the primary form of worship is the very carrying out of their commands.

"Even so" (tathāpi): even though I know [the answer], since you ask me, for that reason I shall explain it to you. For the virtuous, the learned say that service consists solely in carrying out their commands—that is, the performance of the tasks they have enjoined. || 78 ||
Death does not seek to slay him in whose heart the continuous thread of latent impressions (vāsanā), strung with the pearls of freedom from defects, is not knotted. (79)

Regarding the word *doṣaiḥ*: Death does not desire to strike—that is, it does not wish to kill—that person in whose heart the continuous thread of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), strung together with the very "pearls" of defects such as passion and hatred, is not woven. || 79 ||
Mental anguish does not pierce him whom it does not shatter—the tree of trust, the saw, and the woodworms that consume all the creepers of the body; Death does not seek to slay such a one.
"Trust-betraying," etc.: "trust-saws" refers to the saws—that is, the tools for splitting—the very trees of trust, which consist of confidence toward sons, friends, and others;
and "woodworms" refers to the insects skilled at gnawing through the very creepers of all bodies, by whose gnawing [the body is destroyed].
This is known as the "woodworm's letter" maxim. Mental afflictions are sufferings of the mind. || 180 ||
Hope does not burn within him whom a multitude of serpents—the trees of the body with their hoods raised in the form of anxieties—do not consume; nor does death seek to slay him.
Regarding the verse beginning with *śarīra*: For trees themselves, the "swarms of serpents" (*sarpaugha*)—meaning collections of snakes—are the causes of torment.

These are the specific forms of hope and craving (*āśā-tṛṣṇā*), which have "hoods placed upon their heads through anxiety" (*cintārpitaśiraḥphaṭāḥ*). That is to say, those [cravings] which have hoods (*phaṭā*) placed upon their heads by anxieties;
the meaning is that for these snakes in the form of hope, anxieties themselves are the hoods situated on the head-region. || 81 ||
He whom the serpent of greed does not devour— that serpent reeling from the poison of passion and hatred, dwelling in the cave-dwelling of one’s own mind— death does not seek to slay him. (82)
"Passion" (rāga) means the serpent of greed, a snake in the form of avarice. || 82 || 83 ||
Death does not seek to slay him whom anger—like the submarine fire (vāḍava) in the ocean of the body, which has drunk up all the water of discernment—does not utterly consume. (83)
Death does not seek to slay him whom the bodiless god of love cannot crush—that firm mass of sesame seeds as turbulent as a fierce heap. (84)

Regarding the word "yantram": it is hard because it is made of wood and other materials; it is a firm oil-press for sesame seeds, a machine used for extracting oil from sesame, acting as the agent; it is fierce and terrifying due to its height. || 84 ||
Death does not seek to destroy him by whom the rest of the mind has been taken refuge in that one, stainless, and supremely purifying state. (85)
"In one [place]" means: Death does not seek to kill him who has taken refuge in or attained that [state]. || 85 ||
O Brahmin, these great defects, which are the causes of the disease of saṃsāra,
do not disturb even in the slightest degree a mind that is one-pointedly concentrated.

When asked, "Whom does death not afflict? it was said that it does not afflict one who possesses no defects of disposition (*āśaya-doṣa*). Now, in response to the inquiry as to how those defects of disposition are removed, he states the means for their removal:
"These... These aforementioned great defects, which are the causes of the disease of *saṃsāra*, [are removed] when one is concentrated on the One—the Reality.
They do not disturb even slightly the mind that is joined with meditative concentration. || 86 ||
Sufferings arising from mental and physical ailments, stirred up by great delusions, do not overwhelm a mind that is single-pointedly concentrated. (87)
"Ādhīti": "Disturbed" means set in motion by great delusions, namely the confusions regarding objects such as sons, wives, and so forth. 87–88.
Thoughts born of the transformations of desire and anger do not afflict a mind that is one-pointedly concentrated, even for those whose inner space of the heart has been blinded. (579) 88.
Those things that are of evil meaning, of evil undertaking, of evil quality, of evil expression, and of evil sequence—these do not cut through a mind that is single-pointedly concentrated. (89)
"Ya" refers to: objects (*arthāḥ*) which are the causes for the failure of worldly undertakings; prosperities (*saṃpadaḥ*); enterprises (*ārambhāḥ*), meaning efforts made for those objects;

virtues (*guṇāḥ*) such as valor and the like, which are said to be conducive to them; and those "bad methods" (*duṣkramāḥ*)—the sequences for pleasing the minds of others taught in the treatises on ethics (*nītiśāstra*)—which have been uttered and proclaimed by vulgar people satisfied with renunciation, enjoyment, and the like. Of these...

The nature of suffering, its abundance of pain, and its ultimate lack of relish due to impermanence and other factors were already established previously in the section on detachment (*vairāgya*). Those [objects such as] "bad wealth" and so forth do not harm a mind that is unified in concentration;
rather, it is only the distracted mind of a transmigrating being that they afflict. || 89 ||
One should direct the mind toward that supreme truth which is beneficial in its ultimate result, free from conditions, devoid of delusion, and liberated from the state of evil intent. 190.

It has been stated that [the mind] is "concentrated on one thing" (*ekasamāhitam*); in response to the inquiry as to *where* it is concentrated, he says "that which... (*yad*) in order to show the object of mental concentration (*cittasamādhi*). That reality (*vastu*) is beneficial in its ultimate result (*udarkahita*), meaning it is the cause of liberation from bondage in the future;

it is free from delusion (*gatabhrama*) and devoid of ignorance (*nivṛttāvidya*); and because of this, it is free from limiting adjuncts (*anupādhi*, i.e., devoid of *upādhi*). For this very reason, it is distinct from the state of evil conduct (*durīhitadaśā*).

Being liberated from the state of *saṃsāra*, it therefore remains true and uncontradicted. One should cause the mind to be intent upon that [state] and established in the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*). This being so, there is no defect of the mind; and when there is no turbidity of defect, [the result follows]. Thus, both [conditions] are met, which establishes what was stated previously. || 190 ||
One should cause the mind to direct itself toward that which has not been touched by the impure, which brings about long-term alienation, and which is the demon of manifoldness. (91)

Regarding the word "yat": that reality which has long been untouched—unaffected—by the ghost of manifoldness (*anekatva-piśāca*), which for a long time has caused distress and is the cause of opposition, being impure and lacking authoritative basis; [that reality] which, according to the Śruti, "Brahman is indeed one, without a second"; one should cause the mind to be directed toward such Brahman. The reason why difference (*bheda*) is a cause of opposition is as follows: [The rest of the passage continues: ...the state of being a cause of opposition belongs to difference... [and so on].

Precisely in order to clarify this, the Śruti establishes that fear arises from the contemplation of duality: "For when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Brahman], then fear comes upon him" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7). || 91 ||
Reflection on the self brings an end to all sufferings;
it is easily attained by those such as you, yet difficult to attain for those such as we. (92)
"Self" refers to those such as ourselves; "among us" is an indication for those of dull intellect. 92.
How can those of ordinary intellect attain this state, which transcends all time and rests upon the supreme pinnacle?
He speaks of the difficulty of attainment for the dull-witted: "Samasta... etc. Those of ordinary intellect are the dull-witted.
[O] Lord of Munis, among those various ones who are equal to me in self-contemplation—my companions in self-contemplation—I have become one of them. (93–94)

He states in two verses that, precisely because reflection on the self is so difficult to attain, he has resorted to reflection on the vital breath (*prāṇacintā*), which is equal to it: "Reflection on the vital breath, which brings about the destruction of all suffering, increases all prosperity, and is the cause of life in this world, has been resorted to by me. (95)
To the bird who had spoken thus, Bhuśuṇḍa, the sage, though already knowing this, again questioned him calmly as if in sport. (96)
Śātātapa said:
O you who cut through all doubts, O one of exceedingly long life!
Tell me truly, O holy one: what is meant by "contemplation of the vital breath" (prāṇacintā)? 97.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
Listen, O Blessed One, to this "Concentration on the Vital Breath" (prāṇasamādhi) which I shall now describe; for him, this entire body is a beautiful house. (98)

"Listen"—this constitutes two and a half verses. It means the stabilization of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that is to say, the continuous contemplation of the movement of the vital breath. || 98 || 99 || 200 ||
(581) Therein, O Sage, the two winds known by the two conventions [prāṇa and apāna] extend upwards and downwards;
they are both situated within the heart-lotus in the center of the body. 99.
O Sage, those two excellent winds, known as prāṇa and apāna, are manifest; I remain standing, constantly following their movement.
To those whose bodies are respectively cold and hot, who are eternal travelers of the sky, and who operate the great machine of the physical frame without ever tiring; (1)
The three verses beginning with "śīta" constitute a single statement. Of the two whose bodies are cold and hot, *apāna* is the cold-bodied one; *prāṇa* is the hot-bodied one.
Regarding the sun and moon of the space of the heart: *prāṇa* is the sun; *apāna* is the moon. (1) (2) (3)
Of those two, known as prāṇa and apāna, which follow me and consist of the nature of fire and moon— the sun and moon within the space of the heart— (2).
The movement of the body and the vital breaths, as well as that of the embodied soul and the vital breaths, remains always identical throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
yet, like one established in deep sleep, the latent impressions (vāsanās) long for Brahman. || 3 ||
Even though it exists, its movement is more subtle than these two, being as difficult to perceive as a lotus fiber cut into a thousand pieces.
Regarding the word *sahasra*: "from one whose limbs have been cut a thousand times" means from one whose thousands of limbs have been severed;
that is, from one cut into a thousand pieces. Even more subtle and difficult to perceive than a lotus fiber is the movement of those two, the prāṇa and apāna. || 4 ||
O Brahman, this vital breath (prāṇa) is the power of vibration and is ever-moving;
it exists within and without the body, and this prāṇa is situated as that which moves upward.
Regarding "prāṇa": this *prāṇa* is one whose power is constant vibration (*spanda-śakti*), meaning its nature is vibration, consisting of movement;

it remains as such, always in motion. And this *prāṇa*, moving upward, extends for twelve finger-breadths (*dvādaśāṅgula*) both outside and inside [the body], because of its outward emission—from the external emission, it exists within the body together with the external.
That which is internal therein is situated as the upward-moving [breath].
Because of the distinction between the first and second halves [of the verse], there is no tautology in the word *prāṇa*.
O Brahmin, the *apāna* wind is also a power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*) that is constantly in motion;
it resides within this body, both externally and internally, and is situated downwards. (6)

Regarding "Apāna": this apāna, however, exists with the inherent nature of moving downwards; this alone is its distinction. The rest, moreover, is exactly like that of prāṇa—this is the meaning. || 6 ||
Whether one is awake or even asleep, this supreme prāṇāyāma proceeds for the one who possesses direct knowledge; listen now to that which leads to the highest good.

"Regarding 'while awake': listen now to that prāṇāyāma which proceeds for one who possesses higher knowledge—that is, one who knows the movement of the prāṇa and apāna—whether he be awake or even asleep; [listen] to that prāṇāyāma for the sake of the highest good. (7–8)
Just as the outward movement of the vital breaths from the interior of the lotus occurs by its own natural force without effort,
they know that to be internal *recaka*.
Then, as the breaths extend outward to a distance of twelve finger-breadths,
that contact of the vital airs with the limbs is called *pūraka* (inhalation).

"Twelve" means: the contact of the limbs— that is, the mutual conjunction of the parts of the vital breaths— which occurs as the vital functions (prāṇavṛtti) extend outward to a distance of twelve finger-breadths, is called the "filling" (pūraka), which is external in form, being outside with respect to the body.
Because it fills a space measuring twelve finger-breadths; if the reading is *svataḥ*, the construction is: "let it [the breath] itself indeed advance outward. || 9 ||
When, without effort, the external [air] enters within for the purpose of drinking [it],
that touch which fills the limbs, they know that too as *pūraka*.

Regarding the phrase "from the outside": when the apāna wind moves from the external region into the interior—that is, when it enters within the body—there occurs a filling of the limbs, a filling of the body, which is effortless and accomplished without exertion. They know that [touch] also to be pūraka; the meaning is that they know it as internal pūraka, because of the filling of the interior of the body. || 210 ||
When the apāna has subsided and the prāṇa has not yet arisen in the heart,
that state of kumbhaka is experienced by yogins. (11)

Regarding the term *apāna*: when the *apāna* wind has subsided and the *prāṇa* has not yet arisen in the heart, that steady state of the wind is called the *kumbhaka* (retention) stage, which is experienced by yogis. This specific state is called *antaḥ-kumbhaka* (internal retention), because the wind is held within the interior of the body. || 11 ||
Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka) exist in three ways;
it is that state which, like a pot formed within clay, remains established externally.
The wise know that to be *kumbhaka* when the apāna wind is held eternally in the space twelve finger-breadths away, level with and facing the tip of the nose.
The movement of the outward-moving breath as far as the tip of the nose—those who know yoga recognize that as the first external inhalation (bāhyapūraka). || 14 ||

Regarding the word "external" (*bāhya*): they know that specific movement of the outward-turned vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) which extends as far as the tip of the nose to be the first external inhalation (*bāhyapūraka*). It is designated as "first" because another external inhalation will also be described later. [This refers to] the external location characterized by the tip of the nose.
Because it fulfills [all things], it is the fulfillment of the external. || 14 ||
The wise know that movement of the breath which, having issued even from the tip of the nose, extends as far as the *dvādaśānta*, is the secondary external inhalation (*bāhyapūraka*). 15.

They know that other external inhalation (bāhyapūraka) to be the specific movement of the breath which, having also emerged from the tip of the nose, proceeds as far as the limit of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta). || 15 ||
When the prāṇa has gone outside and the apāna has not yet arisen, they know that state, which is external and equalized, as the external kumbhaka. || 16 ||

Regarding the term *bahiḥ* (externally): when the *prāṇa* has gone outside and as long as the *apāna* wind—which by nature draws [the breath] inward—has not yet arisen, they know that particular state to be the external *kumbhaka*, which is a state of complete equilibrium comparable to a full jar, because the air is held (*kumbhita*) precisely outside the body. || 16 ||
The inward-turning nature of the breath, which consists in the arising of the apāna, should be known as the external exhalation (recaka); when contemplated, it bestows liberation. (17)

Regarding the word *antar* (within): one should know that the inward-facing state of the wind, which consists of the arising of the apāna, is the external exhalation (*bāhyarecaka*), because of the exhaling of the wind held externally by means of its inward-facing nature. 17, 18, 19.
Rising from the *dvādaśānta*, it possesses a supreme fullness of form;
they know that which is external to the *apāna* as the other type of *pūraka*.
By constantly restraining those [winds] whose nature is prāṇa and apāna— both external and internal, such as the kumbhaka and others— one is not born again.
O one of great intelligence, these eight natures of the bodily winds, which grant liberation, have been described by me as those to be recollected day and night. (220)

"Eightfold" means: there are three external [breaths] beginning with *pūraka*, three internal ones, and those two additional ones which are external *pūraka*s; thus, there is an eightfold nature. Among these, by means of the first two verses, two varieties are stated based on the gross movement of *prāṇa* and *apāna*. By the subsequent six verses, the subtle [movement] is [described].
The distinction is that the six varieties have been described by relying upon the [six] destinies. || 220 || 21 ||
Abandoning the external mind in this practice without distraction,
one attains the state of absolute liberation in just a few days.
For a person practicing this, the mind no longer forms an attachment to external sensory objects, just as a Brahmin has no interest in a dog's sacrifice.
"Etat" refers to [the following]: "In a dog-skin bellows" means in a small leather bag made from a dog's hide. 22 || 23 || 24 ||
Those of steady intellect who remain firm, holding fast to this view—
they alone have truly attained everything that is to be attained, for they are indeed free from weariness.
Whether standing, walking, always awake, or even sleeping—
if this vision is maintained, then bondage is not attained.
O Brahman, the rising of the vital breath (prāṇa) occurs from the lotus-machine situated in the heart;
this prāṇa sets outside at a distance of twelve finger-breadths. (25)

"Of the vital breath (prāṇa)" means: from the lotus-mechanism situated in the heart, there is the rising or emergence of the vital breath; this vital breath goes to its setting at a distance of twelve finger-breadths outside. || 25 ||
O great sage, the rising of the apāna occurs from the external dvādaśānta; its setting, moreover, takes place within the lotus situated in the heart. (26)

Regarding the phrase "of the apāna": where there is the dissolution (laya) of the prāṇa, from that dvādaśānta [the distance of twelve finger-breadths] arises the apāna; and from where the prāṇa arises, there—in the heart-lotus—is the dissolution of the apāna. This is the meaning. || 26 ||
The apāna is the moon that nourishes the body from the outside;
the prāṇa is the sun or the fire that digests this internal body.
Regarding "apāna": because apāna has the nature of the moon, it comes from the exterior—from the form of the *dvādaśānta*—and enters the body, causing it to rise;
it nourishes and sustains it. Prāṇa, however, because it has the nature of the sun and fire, makes this body subject to digestion. || 27 ||
When the digit situated within the moon of the apāna is swallowed by the sun of the prāṇa upon reaching that [state],
a person does not undergo birth again.

Having thus described the method of contemplation in the form of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) through the movement of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, he now states the method of contemplating the Self by means of contemplating the movement of the *prāṇa*: "The *apāna*... and so forth.

The *kalā*— the internal portion or part— of the moon in the form of the *apāna*, which resides within the body, is swallowed by the sun known as *prāṇa* within that reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). Having reached and realized that state— that reality of the Self— in which it has become united through the effort of that Self, one is no longer subject to grief hereafter.
Likewise, when the breath of life (prāṇa), situated within like the sun, is swallowed by the moon-like downward breath (apāna),
the person who attains that state is no longer subject to rebirth;
for the prāṇa, performing its coming and going, assumes the nature of both the sun and the moon.

"Prāṇa... [and so on]. This is to be explained as before. The meaning is that one is liberated by contemplating the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) which consists precisely in that mutual restraint of the prāṇa and apāna breaths which occurs through the power of effort. The connection is: "the *kalā* situated within the sun of the prāṇa. || 29 ||
When the apāna is intent on consuming the prāṇa, or when the prāṇa consumes the apāna,
the man who stands in the interval between the two is not born again.

Regarding the verse beginning with *prāṇa*: when the apāna is thus intent on consuming the prāṇa, and the prāṇa has become the consumer of the apāna, that reality which exists in the interval between both prāṇa and apāna—that which functions as the witness—is the state (*pada*).
Having attained that reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), a person is not born again; this is the connection [of the verse] through the continuation [of the previous thought]. || 230 ||
Situated near the cessation of the prāṇa and reaching the peak of the rising apāna, we worship the conscious self (cidātman) which lies between the prāṇa and the apāna. || 31 ||

Regarding the term *prāṇa*: indeed, the Self, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), stands near when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is about to perish; when the breath reaches its end at the "twelve-finger limit" (*dvādaśāntara*), the Self remains nearby, being present as a witness (*sākṣitayā*), but does not itself perish. And upon the arising of the downward breath (*apāna*), it goes to the "peak" (*koṭiga*), meaning it is nearby as a witness, but does not itself arise. In this way, [one should contemplate] the witness between the downward and upward breaths.
We worship the conscious self; we concentrate upon it. || 31 ||
We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), free from all parts and blemishes, wherein the apāna has set and the prāṇa has not yet arisen for even a moment. 32.
He explains this very point with the words "apāna" [etc.]: "devoid of parts and blemish" means devoid of connection with ignorance (avidyā). || 32 ||
We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), where the apāna breath has not arisen and the prāṇa breath has set, which is the vortex in the space at the tip of the nose.

"Not exhalation" (nāpāna) means: in that state of consciousness (*cittattva*) where the *prāṇa* has set and the *apāna* has not yet arisen, there is a whirling in the space at the tip of the nose—that is, in the space at the extremity of the nose which takes the form of the "twelve-finger limit" (*dvādaśānta*).
There, acting as the initiator of the movement of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, it performs the coming and going [of the breath].
We worship that very suchness of consciousness. || 33 ||

I take refuge in that supreme state, which is free from the stain of all mental constructions (*kalpanā*), yet is eternally endowed with a multitude of divine qualities (*kalā*); it is the sovereign power of direct experience, the foremost station, and is prostrated to by all the gods. (34)

Regarding the word "yat": that supreme state (*pada*) is devoid of the stain of all mental constructs (*kalana*) because it is the very nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); yet it is encompassed and pervaded by the multitude of parts (*kalāgaṇa*), namely the expansion of ignorance (*avidyā*), because it exists in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*). I take refuge in that foremost, supreme state, whose glory is experience and which has self-experience alone as its means of valid knowledge. || 34 ||
For this rest in consciousness has been attained by me, through the samādhi of the vital breath, gradually in this manner, spontaneously within my own stainless self. (35)
"‘This’ [means]: the connection is that by this aforementioned sequence, ‘this rest in the Self, whose nature is consciousness (citi), has been attained by me. || 35 ||
I never think of what has been nor what will be;
relying solely on direct perception, I abide here by means of my own self in the present. (36)
"No," he said. "I do not contemplate the past nor the future; relying solely on the present vision, I abide by means of the self in its very own nature. (36)
"I have gained this today; I shall obtain that which is beautiful"—such thoughts I do not have, and therefore I live for a long time, free from affliction. (37)
With nine verses beginning with "idam," he explains the very mode of mental activity that is the cause of his own long life:
"This... [referring to] a beautiful, fresh object. (Verses 37, 38, 39)
O virtuous one, I neither praise nor blame anything, anyone, or at any time, whether it concerns myself or another; by that means, I live free from affliction. (38)
I am not elated upon attaining the auspicious, nor do I feel distress even regarding the inauspicious; my mind is eternally equanimous, and by that I live free from affliction. (39)
Relying upon supreme renunciation, I have indeed always abandoned everything, including my very life; by that, I live free from affliction.

"Supreme" (paramam): "Supreme renunciation" (paramaṃ tyāgam); the meaning of "renunciation" (tyāga) is that by which something is abandoned, namely, dispassion (vairāgya). Thus, it means supreme dispassion. || 240 ||
(588) O Sage, my mind is stilled, free from sorrow, and its desires have ceased; it is at peace, and by that I live free from affliction. (41)
Regarding the term *praśāntā* (calm): therein, "agitation" (*cālana*) refers to the curiosity of seeing a desired object that is currently present. As it has been said:

"Agitation is proclaimed to be the curiosity felt upon seeing something beautiful. Sorrow (*śoka*) has as its object a lost or destroyed desired thing. "The sought-after" (*samīhitam*) is the longing for a desired thing yet to come. (41–42)
"O Brahmin, I do not know, 'This one is my kinsman and this one is a stranger; this one is mine and that one is otherwise. Because of that, I am long-lived. (42)
Being composed, I do not allow the contact of my inner mental state with that which is driven by the snares of hope; therefore, I live free from affliction.
I live because, being composed in meditation, I do not grant internal contact to the mental fluctuations that are enslaved by the noose of hope. 43–44.
I am happy when people are happy, and I am sorrowful when they are in sorrow;
I am a dear friend to everyone, and for that reason I live free from affliction. (44)
In adversity I am immovably steadfast, and in prosperity I am a friend to the world; I am not affected by the presence or absence of these states, and therefore I live free from affliction.

"In times of adversity" (āpadi): in times of adversity, at the moment of encountering calamity, I am as firm as a mountain. And upon the attainment of prosperity, I am always a friend to the entire world because of my constant service to all the world. "In states of existence and non-existence, I am not [affected]"—the meaning is that I do not attend to the distinction residing in objects, thinking, "These are of the nature of existence and non-existence. || 45 || 46 || 47 || 48 ||
O Brahman, O you who have reached the further shore of knowledge, I have told you how I became long-lived through sheer audacity, solely for the sake of accomplishing your command.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Oh, how wonderful is this ornament for the ear told by you!
Your own life-story has been narrated, which is a cause for supreme amazement. (47)
May that be for your welfare; enter your auspicious inner cave.
This is my midday hour; I am departing for the abode of the gods. (48)
Saying, "Enough, O Lord of Birds, with the hardship of following me," I rose from my seat and leaped into the sky like a bird.
"Enough" (anviti) means: enough with the hardship of following, that is, the distress of pursuing; the sense is, "do not follow me. || 49 ||
At a distance of only one yojana in the sky, due to my following him, he was stopped by me with great difficulty; for association with the virtuous is hard to abandon.
By that same [merit], I have now been reunited with you at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga;
having met Bhuśuṇḍa, I came to dwell upon a tree on the peak of Mount Meru.
Now that the Kṛta age has waned for the sake of Rāma, the Tretā age is currently prevailing;
it is in the midst of this Tretā Yuga, O destroyer of enemies, that you have been born.
Furthermore, in my eighth year, Bhuśuṇḍa likewise met me right there on top of the mountain, possessing his ageless form.
Having heard this wonderful and excellent account of Bhuśuṇḍa’s experience as it was related, and having reflected upon it within yourself, perform whatever is appropriate.

"Thus" (iti): "Practice that which has been stated. This means that one should practice whatever is understood to be appropriate within the previously mentioned narratives and in the account of Bhuśuṇḍa. || 254 ||
Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Narrative of Bhuśuṇḍa," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Mokṣopāya* of the venerable Vālmīki.
Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Narrative of Bhuśuṇḍa," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa. || 1 ||
The Second Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
This appears now merely as a reflection;
this little body, which is internally thought "I am named so-and-so," exists only as a mental construct. (1)

Previously, nirvāṇa was described as the resting of the mind through the continuous application of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*). Now, it is stated that in the same manner, nirvāṇa—characterized by the resting of the mind—also occurs through the worship of the deity. In this regard, since the conceit of a body (*dehābhimāna*) acts as an obstacle to all means of attaining nirvāṇa, that which is beneficial for its cessation [is now explained].

He teaches something: "It is a mere appearance. This body is, in reality, a mere appearance, established only by cognition; yet, at present, in the state of non-investigation, it shines within the internal organ (antah-karaṇa) as an object of the conceit (*abhimāna*)—both as distinct from and non-distinct from the Self, appearing as "this" and "I. When investigated...
Furthermore, it is indeed non-existent and merely false, because it is a mental construction. || 1 ||
Abandon the delusion that "I am a body constructed of flesh and bone";
there are thousands of bodies constructed by the power of mental conception.

Regarding the word "māṃsa" (flesh): abandon that delusion which consists in thinking, "I am such a body composed of flesh and bone. This is because there exist thousands of such bodies imagined through mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*). [As it is said:
"By which dream-body, while lying on a comfortable bed, one traverses the horizons..."
O Rāma, you wander about; where is that body of yours situated?

He states the very unreality of the body: "sukha... etc. The meaning is that you yourself have already admitted the unreality of those dream-bodies which, for you while lying on a comfortable bed, were the causes of the wandering through the quarters of the world. || 3 ||
While awake, you wander through the city of heaven or Mount Meru within the realm of your imagination; where, then, does that body of yours reside?

Regarding the phrase "in the state of waking" (jāgarāyām): even during the waking state, that helplessness of the mind—which flows along the path of mental desire and culminates in the forgetting of the body—is called "mental kingdom" (manorājyam). The meaning is that even therein, one wanders through other lands by means of a false body alone. || 4 ||
Know this saṃsāra, O descendant of Raghu, to be a long dream, or a prolonged delusion of the mind, or even a far-reaching kingdom of the imagination. (5)
Regarding "long": either a long-lasting delusion of the mind, such as the error that persists for a long time, like [the perception] "the sky is blue. (5)
"This triple world is merely an appearance; it is neither existent nor non-existent"—the wise know that the complete relinquishing of such conceptualizations is right vision.
"It is mere practice" means: the three worlds are not real because they are subject to sublation; they are not unreal because they are perceived.

Therefore, the wise know that right vision consists solely in the abandonment of all other conceptualizations, [realizing] that it is merely an appearance, merely a manifestation, and not real. || 6 ||
"It is certain that I must indeed die"—this is the settled conclusion.
Since death is thus inevitable for oneself, why suffer in vain? (7)
"Unavoidably" means that since death is certain to follow birth, any distress regarding its arrival is futile;
this is the meaning. || 7 ||
Since a person who has been born must inevitably obtain some degree of wealth and prosperity,
what cause for pride is there in such gains?

"Unavoidably," [it is said]. The meaning is that since a living person who has been born must inevitably attain some degree of excellence, such as great wealth and so forth, pride regarding the acquisition of objects is likewise not appropriate. || 8 ||
O sinless one, having abandoned the distinction among the multitude of categories of objects, perceive this as a mere appearance, a universal unity.

Regarding the phrase "the distinction": having abandoned the notion of differentiation—the perception of duality—within the "multitude of clusters of categories," which consists of a collection of groups of objects in the phenomenal world (prapañca), behold and contemplate this alone as the universal:
that which merely appears, which persists through all things, and which is pure Being-Consciousness (saccinmātra). 9.
Everything is mere appearance, stained by the grasping of the intellect;
therefore, having abandoned even that, become stainless, O best of beings. (10)

"Regarding 'ābhāsa' (appearance): because even a mere appearance is stained by the reflection of the mind—that is, corrupted by its connection with the mind—therefore, having abandoned even that mere appearance, become free from appearance;
become free from conceptual construction. || 10 ||
(592) For one in whose mind the two serpents of passion and hatred have not dissolved, what indeed, my dear, cannot be obtained from that wish-fulfilling tree? 11.
Regarding "passion" (*rāga*): the two serpents known as passion and hatred have not merely dissolved or remained within the mind; rather, they have departed.

That very tree of paradise (*kalpataru*) [remains], because it accomplishes all human goals. Therefore, what excellence (*śreyaḥ*) indeed cannot be obtained in this world from a person free from passion and the like? The meaning is that every form of excellence is obtained. || 11 ||

Fie upon those who, having attained pride in their wisdom, consider themselves clever and learned in the scriptures, yet are filled with passion and hatred; they are merely donkeys in the guise of the venerable. 12.
As for those who are learned in the scriptures, clever, and proficient in both worldly and Vedic affairs,
yet having fallen into the pride of wisdom— the conceit that "we alone are wise"— and being full of passion and hatred, they are "donkeys among the venerable."
"Fie upon those who are like donkeys—those of great value capable of bearing heavy loads at a distance; the meaning is that they are not even to be touched. || 12 ||
O descendant of Raghu, this wheel of saṃsāra has mere volition as its hub; when that [volition] is obstructed, it is stopped because its movement is blocked.
Regarding the phrase "this": *saṃsāra* is the stream of birth, death, and so forth; it is itself a wheel (*cakra*) because of its nature of constant rotation.

The mind (*citta*), consisting of volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*), is its hub (*nābhi*) because it is the initiator [of the cycle]. Therefore, when the mind is restrained, *saṃsāra* is brought to an end.
When the navel-center of the mind is agitated, this wheel of saṃsāra continues to flow with force, even if one strives to block it. (14)
Regarding the phrase "when it is agitated": when the mind is agitated, saṃsāra indeed flows on; it cannot be obstructed by any other means. 14–15.
Relying upon supreme human effort, and through the proper application of strength and wisdom, one should restrain the mind alone at the hub of the wheel of saṃsāra. (15)
That which cannot be attained through human effort endowed with wisdom and nobility, and augmented by scriptural learning, is not to be found anywhere. (16)
Regarding "wisdom" (*prajñā*): wisdom is inspired eloquence; gentleness is the perfection of tranquility and so forth; scripture is the science of the inner self (*adhyātmavidyā*);
and manliness is the action of a man. 16.
Having cast off the demon of the mind— which brings fear, is unwholesome, and steals away the very essence of fortitude— be firm as you truly are.
"Bhaya" (fear) means that when the mental modification is abandoned, only the true nature remains. || 17 ||
When a person is firmly seized by the yakṣa of the mind, neither treatises, nor kinsmen, nor even teachers are able to protect that human being. (18)
Regarding the word *citta*: the meaning is that one who is under the sway of the demon of the mind cannot be protected by anyone at all. || 18 || 19 ||
The teacher, the meaning of the scriptures, and kinsmen are able to rescue one whose mind-demon has been thoroughly pacified,
just as they can lift a deer from a small puddle.
One should cast away the enjoyment and non-enjoyment of external objects and follow the path of the Noble One;
having investigated the great purpose, one should take refuge in one's own solitary self. (20)

"Bhogeti" [means]: "Bhoga-abhogāḥ" refers to the expansion of sense-objects. A noble one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) should take refuge in the single Self, which is the great goal and established as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Regarding the reading "ahāryatvam," the meaning is that having reflected upon the very unassailability of one's own Self, he should take refuge in that very Self. || 20 ||
In this regard, listen to this other vision which destroys great delusion,
which was previously told to me in a cave on Kailāsa by the Lord who bears the crescent moon upon his crest, for the sake of pacifying the suffering of saṃsāra. (21)
Regarding this: "another view" means another means for the knowledge of the Self. || 21 ||
There exists on high the supreme lord of mountains named Kailāsa, radiant with a mass of moonbeams, the abode of Gaurī’s beloved.
"He exists. Even higher than heaven, that is, more excellent than the celestial realm. 22–23.
There dwells the Blessed Lord Hara, who bears the crescent moon;
in ancient times, he was worshipping that Great God on that very mountain. (23)
Once, having established a hermitage on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
I dwelt there for a long time, firmly settled in the conduct of an ascetic for the sake of performing austerities.
The two verses beginning with "kadācit" constitute a single syntactical unit. || 24 ||
Surrounded by a host of Siddhas, he had mastered the essential meaning of the scriptures;
for the sake of flowers, he carried a woven basket and was a collector of vast collections of books.
He was one who carried a sewn pouch—a pouch suitable for depositing flowers for worship that had been sewn and stitched by him.
He was a collector of book-arrays, meaning he was habitually inclined toward gathering the collections of books concerning the subjects of the sciences of knowledge (jñānaśāstra). || 25 || 26 ||
O Rāma, while he, distinguished by such qualities, was performing austerities in a forest grove on Mount Kailāsa, his time came to an end.
Then, on one occasion, on the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada, when the first part of the night had passed and its end was approaching, he remained alone.

The word "atha" (now) introduces a set of four verses. Once, when the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa had passed and the first part of the night was coming to an end, I alone, having brought my meditative absorption (*samādhi*) to its full expansion, remained with my gaze fixed upon the external [space]. (27–29)
The quarters of the sky had become utterly tranquil, as if established in the silence of a wooden statue;
and there were thickets and dense groves where the darkness could be cut with a sword.
At that time, when the first watch had passed by half,
I remained with my gaze fixed on the external world, having brought my concentration to a state of refinement.
I beheld in the forest a splendor that suddenly arose,
resembling a hundred white clouds and like a multitude of shimmering moons.

The grammatical connection is as follows: "In the forest, I saw a splendor that had suddenly arisen, resembling a hundred white clouds and like a multitude of shimmering moons. Regarding the word *jhagiti*, Śākaṭāyana has read it in the sense of "instantly" (*jhaṭiti*). (30, 31, 32)

Having observed that [vision] which had revealed the very bowers of the directions, I then gazed upon it with a vision of the intellect (*buddhidṛṣṭi*) shining with internal light, out of wonder. (31)
I beheld him having reached that mountain peak, bearing the crescent moon,
his hand placed in Gaurī’s hand, and preceded by Nandin who cleared the way before him.
Having awakened the disciples staying there and taken the water of honor (arghya),
I, well-restrained and cheerful, went before him, purified by his gaze.
"Regarding the disciples": having awakened the disciples and raised them from their meditative absorption (samādhi), I proceeded before that Supreme Lord, my path purified by his gaze. 33–36.
There, having offered a handful of flowers from afar, the three-eyed Lord was honored and saluted by me after I had presented the arghya offering and prostrated before him.
Thereafter, I have for a long time been made the abode of her who is named Candraprabhā, by means of that cool supernatural power and her gaze which removes all suffering. (35)
Approaching him who was seated upon the flowery plateau— the witness of the three worlds—
I offered him water for his feet, flowers, and the respectful oblation (arghya).
Furthermore, many handfuls of mandāra flowers were scattered, and Śiva was worshipped with various kinds of salutations and hymns of praise. (37)

Regarding "mandāra": there is a variety [of offerings] because the prostrations therein differ according to the distinctions of eight-limbed (*aṣṭāṅga*), five-limbed (*pañcāṅga*), and so forth, and the hymns differ according to the distinctions of worldly (*laukika*) and Vedic (*vaidika*). || 37 ||
Then the Blessed Gaurī, together with her friends and the circle of Gaṇas, was likewise worshipped with such an offering.
"Tataḥ" (then): the circle of Gaṇas—that is, the assembly of Pramathas—is exactly as it was ordained for Śiva. || 38 || 39 ||
At the conclusion of the worship, the one who bears a digit of the crescent moon addressed me with words as cool as the rays of the full moon as I sat there: (39)
O Brahmin, are your cognitions—endowed with tranquility, having attained rest in the Supreme, and bringing about auspiciousness—firmly established in that state? (40)
"O Brahmin," [he asks]. "Have those cognitions attained stability, finding rest in the Supreme State? Does it mean that there are no obstacles to yoga? || 40 || 41 || 42 || 43 ||
I hope your mind proceeds toward what is auspicious without obstacle; I hope you have attained that which is to be attained, and I hope your fears are stilled. (41)
O descendant of Raghu, when the Lord of Gods, the sole cause of all the worlds, had spoken thus, I addressed him with words full of conciliation.
O Maheśvara, for those who possess the auspiciousness resulting from the recollection of you in this world, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain, nor are there any fears. (43)
For those whose minds are filled with the bliss of recollecting you,
there are none in the treasury of the world who do not bow down before them.

Regarding the word "tvad" (from you): those who do not bow down before your devotees—whose minds are completely filled with the bliss born of recollecting you—do not exist within the treasury of the universe. 44.
Those countries, those provinces, those directions,
and those mountains where people dwell with minds solely intent on remembering you.

"Those regions" (te deśāḥ): "regions" refers to Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, and so forth; "provinces" refers to villages. The meaning is that only those regions and the like inhabited by Your devotees are truly praiseworthy. || 45 ||
O Lord, the remembrance of you bears fruit for past merit, provides nourishment for present merit, and extends the seed for future merit. (46)

Regarding the phrase "the fruit": the remembrance of You is the fruit of merit performed in the past—that is, of a well-done deed already accomplished—since demerit is impossible [in this context]. It extends the watering of present merit; the meaning is that it causes merit to increase. Because merit becomes perfect through the remembrance of the Lord, it [extends] that which is yet to come, i.e., the future.
The seed of merit belongs to one whose mind is purified by the remembrance of the Lord, and who is engaged in the desire to perform meritorious deeds. (46–48)
O Lord, the remembrance of you is the unique vessel for the nectar of knowledge, the moon that brings forth the light of fortitude, and the gateway to the city of liberation. (47)
O Lord of Beings, by me, who possess the noble wish-fulfilling gem of mindfulness of you, my foot has been placed upon the summit of all calamities. 48.
Having spoken thus to the well-pleased Lord Maheśvara, I bowed down and said this; O Rāma, listen to that. (49)
"O Blessed One, by your grace all directions are filled for me.
O Lord of Gods, what doubt shall I ask about, and what is the resolution therein? (50)
Speak with a serene intellect, free from agitation and affliction, that which causes the destruction of all sins and increases all auspiciousness. (51)
"O Lord, what is the procedure for the worship of the gods like?
Maheśvara said:"
Listen, O best among the knowers of Brahman, to this unsurpassed worship of the deity.
The lotus-eyed one is not the God, nor is the three-eyed one the God;
for the God is neither of the form of the body nor of the form of the mind.
That which is uncreated, without beginning or end, and divine—that is called the God.

"No," this consists of three and a half sentences. Since an object possessing form is limited and perishable, the meaning of the word "Deva" (the Divine) is only the uncreated, beginningless and endless, divine play of pure consciousness alone. || 53 ||
How can that which is uncreated, without beginning or end, the divine Consciousness-Śiva, be known within an object that is measured and delimited by forms and the like? (54)

[They] conceptualize [it]. When an object delimited by forms and so forth is accepted as being a deity, how could the characteristic of a deity—such as its being uncreated and so on—be possible? Therefore, they know that divinity itself, characterized by being uncreated and so forth, is the auspicious consciousness (cicchiva), the auspiciousness whose nature is consciousness (cidrūpa). || 54 || 55 ||
First of all, it is said: "Who might this 'Deva' be? That very [reality] is designated by the word "Deva"; one should worship that. || 55 ||
For those who do not know the true principle of Śiva, worship through forms and other such means is performed;
for one incapable of traveling the path of *yojana*s, the path of *krośa*s is prescribed. (56)
"By those who do not know"—that is, by those who do not know such Consciousness-Śiva (cicchiva) because they are ignorant of the reality of Śiva (śivatattva). || 56 ||
Indeed, only the sky of consciousness exists here, devoid of near and far; it remains even at the end of kalpas, while all conceivable objects of thought are impossible everywhere.

Regarding the word "cit": that reality which is devoid of near and far, lacking any northern or eastern limit, in which no object of thought can possibly exist, and which remains untouched by the visible world—whatever remains even at the end of kalpas, that alone is the sky of consciousness (cidvyoma), and it exists everywhere. || 57 ||
Awakening, equanimity, and tranquility—these are its foremost flowers; those who know worship perceive that the pure, stainless Śiva, who is consciousness alone, is to be worshipped with them. (58)
Regarding "awakening" (bodha): awakening is the knowledge of reality; equanimity is the vision of its fullness; tranquility is the state of the mind free from modification.
They know Śiva—the worshipful one—to be worshipped with the foremost, most excellent flowers of that Consciousness-Śiva. 58–59.
Know that when the divine Self is worshipped with the flowers of tranquility, awakening, and so forth, that indeed is the worship of the Divine; the worship of forms is not true worship.
Therefore, that bliss which is unartificial, without beginning or end, non-dual, undivided, and not to be accomplished by external means, is attained. (60)

"Uncreated" means that the bliss of liberation (kaivalya), which cannot be accomplished by external means—that is, it cannot be achieved through external instruments or outward efforts—is obtained from the aforementioned worship of the Deity. || 60 ||
Consciousness transcends all parts (kalās), abiding within the interior of all beings;
eternally situated between existence and non-existence, it has the nature of universal being (sattāsāmānya).
Having attained the nature of the Great Being, it is designated by the word "Deva. || 61 ||

Since it will be stated later that the worship of the deity (*devapūjā*) is twofold, consisting of the external and the internal, he describes the deity appropriate for the external worship with the word "Consciousness" (*saṃvit*): [She is] transcendent to all *kalās*, meaning she has passed beyond the five *kalās* known as Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Śāntyatītā; that is to say, she is transcendent to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) whose nature consists of the five elements.

As it is said in the *Ambāstava*: "Withdrawal is said to be in the earth, foundation in water, knowledge in fire, tranquility in air, and the peace beyond peace in space; yet those who indeed reckon these as constituent parts (*kalā*) of reality—O Mother, Your state is far more remote than they. Between existence and non-existence, cause and effect, or being and non-being— [The commentary continues: ...in the midst of these, [is Your state]. Just as the center of a circle is neither the circumference nor the interior, so too, O Mother, Your state is neither existence nor non-existence. It is not the cause, nor is it the effect; it is not the manifest, nor is it the unmanifest. It is not the knower, nor is it the known; it is not the means of knowledge, nor is it the object of knowledge. It is not the agent, nor is it the action; it is not the instrument, nor is it the result. It is not the locus, nor is it the supported; it is not the substratum, nor is it the superstratum. It is not the enjoyer, nor is it the enjoyed; it is not the means of enjoyment, nor is it the act of enjoying. It is not the seer, nor is it the seen; it is not the sight, nor is it the visual organ. It is not the hearer, nor is it the heard; it is not the hearing, nor is it the auditory organ. It is not the smeller, nor is it the smelled; it is not the smelling, nor is it the olfactory organ. It is not the taster, nor is it the tasted; it is not the tasting, nor is it the gustatory organ. It is not the toucher, nor is it the touched; it is not the touching, nor is it the tactile organ. It is not the thinker, nor is it the thought; it is not the thinking, nor is it the mind. It is not the speaker, nor is it the spoken; it is not the speaking, nor is it speech. It is not the doer, nor is it the deed; it is not the doing, nor is it the hands. It is not the evacuator, nor is it the evacuated; it is not the evacuation, nor is it the anus. It is not the procreator, nor is it the procreated; it is not the procreation, nor is it the generative organ. It is not the supporter, nor is it the supported; it is not the supporting, nor is it the feet. It is not the enjoyer, nor is it the enjoyed; it is not the enjoyment, nor is it the tongue. It is not the ruler, nor is it the ruled; it is not the ruling, nor is it the intellect. It is not the witness, nor is it the witnessed; it is not the witnessing, nor is it the ego-sense. It is not the knower, nor is it the known; it is not the knowing, nor is it the mind. It is not the perceiver, nor is it the perceived; it is not the perceiving, nor is it the consciousness. It is not the experiencer, nor is it the experienced; it is not the experiencing, nor is it the bliss. It is not the creator, nor is it the created; it is not the creating, nor is it the primordial matter (*prakṛti*). It is not the sustainer, nor is it the sustained; it is not the sustaining, nor is it time. It is not the destroyer, nor is it the destroyed; it is not the destroying, nor is it destruction. It is not the beginning, nor is it the end; it is not the middle, nor is it the duration. It is not the past, nor is it the future; it is not the present, nor is it the succession. It is not the internal, nor is it the external; it is not the intermediate, nor is it the direction. It is not the light, nor is it the dark; it is not the dawn, nor is it the twilight. It is not the day, nor is it the night; it is not the month, nor is it the year. It is not the season, nor is it the solstice; it is not the year-cycle, nor is it the eon. It is not the birth, nor is it the death; it is not the life, nor is it the transmigration. It is not the liberation, nor is it the bound; it is not the bondage, nor is it the fetter. It is not the goal, nor is it the traveler; it is not the path, nor is it the vehicle. It is not the shore, nor is it the ocean; it is not the flood, nor is it the current. It is not the island, nor is it the sea; it is not the crossing, nor is it the boat. It is not the mountain, nor is it the valley; it is not the peak, nor is it the base. It is not the forest, nor is it the grove; it is not the thicket, nor is it the clearing. It is not the city, nor is it the village; it is not the town, nor is it the hamlet. It is not the kingdom, nor is it the subject; it is not the sovereignty, nor is it the territory. It is not the heaven, nor is it the earth; it is not the netherworld, nor is it the intermediate space. It is not the gods, nor is it the humans; it is not the demons, nor is it the animals. It is not the spirits, nor is it the ghosts; it is not the goblins, nor is it the imps. It is not the ancestors, nor is it the progeny; it is not the lineage, nor is it the descent. It is not the teacher, nor is it the disciple; it is not the instruction, nor is it the learning. It is not the father, nor is it the mother; it is not the son, nor is it the daughter. It is not the husband, nor is it the wife; it is not the friend, nor is it the enemy. It is not the beloved, nor is it the hateful; it is not the neutral, nor is it the indifferent. It is not the high, nor is it the low; it is not the even, nor is it the uneven. It is not the pleasant, nor is it the unpleasant; it is not the beautiful, nor is it the ugly. It is not the pure, nor is it the impure; it is not the auspicious, nor is it the inauspicious. It is not the holy, nor is it the profane; it is not the sacred, nor is it the secular. It is not the virtuous, nor is it the wicked; it is not the good, nor is it the evil. It is not the true, nor is it the false; it is not the right, nor is it the wrong. It is not the wise, nor is it the foolish; it is not the intelligent, nor is it the dull-witted. It is not the learned, nor is it the ignorant; it is not the skillful, nor is it the clumsy. It is not the strong, nor is it the weak; it is not the healthy, nor is it the sick. It is not the young, nor is it the old; it is not the infant, nor is it the decrepit. It is not the rich, nor is it the poor; it is not the wealthy, nor is it the destitute. It is not the noble, nor is it the base; it is not the high-born, nor is it the low-born. It is not the famous, nor is it the obscure; it is not the celebrated, nor is it the unknown. It is not the praised, nor is it the censured; it is not the honored, nor is it the despised. It is not the respected, nor is it the disrespected; it is not the revered, nor is it the reviled. It is not the beloved, nor is it the hated; it is not the desired, nor is it the undesired. It is not the sought, nor is it the rejected; it is not the accepted, nor is it the abandoned. It is not the gained, nor is it the lost; it is not the obtained, nor is it the missed. It is not the won, nor is it the defeated; it is not the victory, nor is it the defeat. It is not the success, nor is it the failure; it is not the gain, nor is it the loss. It is not the profit, nor is it the harm; it is not the benefit, nor is it the injury. It is not the pleasure, nor is it the pain; it is not the joy, nor is it the sorrow. It is not the happiness, nor is it the misery; it is not the delight, nor is it the distress. It is not the contentment, nor is it the discontent; it is not the satisfaction, nor is it the dissatisfaction. It is not the peace, nor is it the agitation; it is not the calm, nor is it the turmoil. It is not the rest, nor is it the movement; it is not the stillness, nor is it the activity. It is not the silence, nor is it the noise; it is not the quiet, nor is it the clamor. It is not the solitude, nor is it the crowd; it is not the privacy, nor is it the public. It is not the

Consciousness, whose nature is the universal form of existence, having attained the state of Great Existence (mahāsattā), is called by the word "Deva" because it exists as that which is denoted by the term "Great Existence," being perfectly full both internally and externally, everywhere. || 61 ||
That very [consciousness], when fashioned by conceptualization and fallen away from its true nature as pure awareness,
gradually brings about insentience and reaches the state of being an object of mental construction.

It conceptualizes: that very consciousness, when seized by conceptualization, brings about insentience; gradually falling away from its true nature as pure awareness, it reaches the state of differentiation—the condition of being an object. || 62 ||
Enveloped by the successive manifestations of the powers of space, time, and so forth,
it first becomes the individual soul (jīva), then quickly becomes the intellect (buddhi), and thereafter the ego (ahaṃ) and the mind (manas).

He explains this very point with the verse beginning "deśa" (place): Enveloped by the manifestations—the powers—of place, time, and so forth, and being thus agitated, it sequentially becomes the individual soul (*jīva*), then quickly becomes the intellect (*buddhi*), then the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and finally the mind (*manas*). || 63 ||
Having attained the state of mind, one clings to saṃsāra;
just as a twice-born man attains the status of a caṇḍāla by thinking, "I am a caṇḍāla. (64)

"Mind-ness" (manastva) [is the cause]. For the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) rests upon the mind, since that [existence] has the mind as its root. Just as, for example, a certain twice-born man (dvija), though taken to another country while still a child, lived for a long time among outcasts due to delusion; and having had his Brahminhood defiled by their food and drink, he later somehow regained his awareness and said: "I am an outcast, because of my constant association with them."
The meaning is that, thinking thus, one assumes the state of a caṇḍāla, just like that. || 64 ||
(600) Thinking "I am this," she who resides in the body and is subject to fall,
being submerged in the great mire of delusion, goes from suffering to further suffering through such cognition. || 65 ||

"This" refers to the following: this consciousness, existing within the body through the sense of limitation—"I am this"—is subject to falling away due to identification with the body; thus, with the loss of that [body], it goes from sorrow to sorrow. || 65 ||
This suffering that has arrived was nourished by mere volition; that same suffering is destroyed by mere non-volition—what cause for distress is there in this? (66)

"Strengthened" (puṣṭam): This suffering of saṃsāra has arrived by the mere power of volition (saṃkalpa), and for that very reason it is strengthened and increased. Therefore, by the mere absence of volition—that is, simply through non-volition—it is exhausted and perishes. Hence, what cause for distress is there in this saṃsāra? The meaning is: none at all. || 66 || 67 || 68 || 69 ||
Whatever one may conceptualize, a person sinks into suffering;
by not conceptualizing anything at all, one enjoys imperishable happiness.
Having exhausted the clouds of conceptualization with the winds of self-discrimination, attain supreme purity, like the expanse of the sky in autumn. (68)
Having warded off the turbidity of your own mental constructs by means of the Self, and having attained supreme clarity, become possessed of the highest bliss. (69)

For the Self, consisting of all powers, attains through the dances of the circle of its powers both saṃsāra and its cessation; it fully achieves everything, even though it is of the nature of pure consciousness alone and entirely formless. (70)

"Everything": because the Self consists of all powers, it attains everything—both transmigratory existence and its cessation—through the *tāṇḍavas*, which are the manifestations of the circle of powers. || 70 ||

O observer of noble vows, there is the existence of will, the existence of space, and likewise the existence of time; and similarly, the existence of necessity and the great existence (mahāsattā). (71)
Anticipating the question "What are these powers?", he says: the two verses beginning with "icchā" (will) constitute a single syntactical unit.
Because will and the other powers are the cause of existence (*sattā*), they are referred to in grammatical apposition by means of a metaphorical identification, such that "will itself is existence.
For instance, the existence of certain things is accomplished by will alone, as in the case of pleasure and the like; while for others, it is through space (*vyoman*).

Just as in the case of sound and so forth; for some, by time, as in the case of sprouts, flowers, and the like; for some, by necessity, as in the case of certain things existing only in another continent; furthermore, for certain entities, there exists everywhere a cause of conditions which is their own essential existence, namely, their great being (*mahāsattā*). // 71 //
The power of knowledge, the power of action, agency, and even non-agency—there is no end to such powers belonging to the Supreme Self. (72)

The power of knowledge is the cause of cognition; likewise, the power of action is agency, which is the cause of the inherence of action; and the power of existence is non-agency, which is the opposite of that. There is no end to such powers belonging to the Supreme Self. || 72 ||
Through the power of manifestation (ullāsa-śakti), the cycle of worldly existence proceeds in every direction;
