through the power of restraint (nirodha-śakti), this entire world comes to total destruction.

It causes to blossom. The meaning is that the power of expansion (*ullāsa-śakti*) is the cause of the unfolding of saṃsāra, while the power of restraint (*nirodha-śakti*) is the cause of its cessation.
In all sequences of worship, during the cremation of the body, the *pavitraka* (sacred thread) is to be abandoned;
however, the *pavitraka* which consists of the realization of the self as distinct from the body must be grasped with effort. (74)
This is the God, the supreme one to be worshipped, who is always the object of worship for the virtuous;
meditation alone is his internal worship—there is no other worship of him.

Therefore, one should constantly worship with meditation that support of the three worlds, whose nature is consciousness, which possesses the luster of a hundred thousand suns, and which illuminates all manifestations. (76)
"Therefore" refers to the sentence consisting of five verses. Since meditation alone is the worship of this God, the syntactical connection is:
"Therefore, one should thus constantly worship with meditation the God who is the support of the three worlds.
He is the illumination of all appearances—that is, the illuminator even of all luminaries such as the sun and others.

The inner light of consciousness—that form of the throbbing light of consciousness within the body, which is one's own and constitutes the essential nature of all—is the essence within the "I-ness" (ahantā), that is, the sense of ego (*ahaṃbhāva*) in the heart-center (*āśaya*).

This is because, within the *ahaṃkāra* which consists of both conscious and unconscious elements, it is the conscious element alone that constitutes the essence. As it has been said in the *Prekṣāṇaka*:

"In the primary consciousness consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, that which exists as the conscious form—Brahman, which is immediate, non-mediated, subtle, and perceivable by subtle vision—[is this]. That which is the vast expanse, the wide extension, of the boundless supreme space (*paramākāśa*) constitutes its neck, the region of the throat;
and that which is the inner cavity, the internal expansion, of the infinite lower space (*adhastanākāśa*) [constitutes its chest]."
He whose lotus-like foot it is. 76 || 77 || 78 ||
I contemplate within my heart the inner light of consciousness, the very essence of the great ones,
whose neck is the vast expanse of the shoreless supreme ether. (77)
Whose lotus feet rest upon the infinite expanse of space below, and whose circle of arms adorned the vast extent of the infinite quarters of the horizon. 78.
He holds supreme weapons of various kinds within his great world-abodes,
and within the corner of the chamber of his heart rests a continuous succession of multitudes of cosmic eggs.

He is one whose supreme weapons—those very great and various worlds beginning with the earth (bhūḥ)—have been grasped and taken into his own hands. It should be understood that the phrase "the succession of worlds resting within the corner of the cavity of his heart" refers to the intention of the future cosmic eggs he desires to create. || 79 ||
He whose form is beyond the shoreless [ocean] of the supreme space of light, who is without interval below, above, in the four cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions; 80.
He whose very form is one that has reached the further shore of light—the supreme ether—and is itself boundless. || 80 ||
One should contemplate the row of hair on his [the Lord's] body as this splendor of all beings, adorned by a circle of immortals headed by Brahmā, Indra, Hari, Rudra, and Īśa. (81)
"Brahman" means that the succession of beings is the hair on the body of that God. || 81 ||
The powers beginning with Will (icchā), which initiate various undertakings and serve as the ropes for the machine of the three worlds, should be contemplated as residing within His body. (82)

"Vividha" (various): The three worlds themselves are the machine-constructed configuration, a substance whose actions are dependent on another; its "ropes" are the causes of its activity. These aforementioned powers, beginning with Will (*icchā*), which have become thus, should be contemplated as residing within its body. 82–83.
This God is the supreme one, always worthy of worship by the virtuous;
for he is pure consciousness, the experienced Self, all-pervading, and the refuge of all. 83.
He is infinite, the supreme support, whose singular form is pure existence alone;
he has manifested the web of the universe, and Time is his gatekeeper.
"Ananta" means infinite, limitless, and the supreme support; because he is of the nature of the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), he has that as his substratum.

His form consists solely of pure existence (*sattāmātra*), for he is of that very nature. He is the one by whom the web of the world (*jagajjāla*)—the manifold network of the universe—is projected (*vivartita*);
that is, by whom some worlds are brought forth externally, some are made to enter within, and some are maintained exactly as they are.
Having performed this, he has become renowned as the Time (Kāla) who is the doorkeeper of this Lord; for, like a gatekeeper, he sets the worlds in motion according to the will of the Lord. || 84 ||
Rich with the power of sight everywhere, possessing the power of smell in every direction, consisting of touch everywhere, and endowed with the sense of taste on all sides. (85)

The phrase "in all places" constitutes two and a half verses. According to the Vedic scripture beginning with "He who has eyes on all sides," one should meditate upon the Lord of Gods—who is endowed with the power of all the senses everywhere, who transcends the mind because he is beyond mentalization (*manas*), and who is the form of Supreme Śiva everywhere—and worship him according to the prescribed rule. (85–86)
Everywhere it is filled with hearing; everywhere it is accompanied by reflection;
everywhere it transcends reflection; everywhere it is the supreme Śiva.
Having reflected thus, one should then worship the Lord of Gods according to the prescribed rules.
This deity, whose nature is one's own self-awareness, is not worshipped with external offerings;
rather, he is worshipped by his own single nectar of awakening—eternal, obtainable without effort, cooling, and imperishable. (87)
In order to show the specific detail regarding the ritual of worship, he says: "One's own consciousness," which constitutes a sentence consisting of three and a half verses.

This deity, whose nature is self-awareness, is not worshipped with external offerings; rather, he is worshipped solely with the nectar of awakening—which is effortless to obtain, cool, free from the fever of anxiety, imperishable, and unique. || 87 ||
This alone is the supreme meditation; this alone is remembered as the highest worship: that which is the uninterrupted realization of pure consciousness alone abiding within. 88.
He states that it is not only the offering of the nectar of awakening, but that worship itself is also that very thing, with the words "this" (etad).
That which exists as the uninterrupted and ceaseless awareness—the continuous connection with the pure consciousness residing within—is itself meditation;
this alone is the supreme worship. 88.
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, breathing, speaking, releasing, and grasping—one should remain composed of pure consciousness alone. (89)

He describes the manner of this uninterrupted contemplation with the words "paśyan" (seeing). The meaning is that one should always contemplate: "I am of the nature of pure consciousness alone, the witness of all, who—like the sun—sets in motion the operations of all the senses by his mere presence. This has been stated in the *Hastāmalaka*:

The Self is that which, having cast off all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and being like the ether, is the cause for the functioning of the mind, eyes, and other senses; just as the sun is the cause for the activity of the world, so am I, the Self, whose nature is eternal perception. (89–92)
The self is indeed the offering of meditation; meditation is its great worship.
Without that [meditation], this self is certainly not attained by any other means. (90)
O wise one, by performing this meditation for thirteen moments,
even a fool, having worshipped the Lord, shall obtain the fruit of giving a cow.
Having worshipped the Lord for the duration of one hundred eye-winks, a human being obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha). || 92 ||
Having worshipped his own self as the Lord for half a ghaṭikā, a human being obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. || 93 ||
He who, by means of the offering of the power of meditation, worships himself through his own self for even a single ghaṭikā, shall obtain the merit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
By thus performing the midday worship and other rites, one partakes in the merit of a hundred thousand Rājasūya sacrifices;
having worshipped in this manner for a day, a person shall dwell in the supreme abode.
This is that supreme yoga; this is that supreme rite.
This external worship has been declared as the highest [form] for the self. Now I shall fully explain the internal worship of the self.

Having demonstrated the excellence of the fruit through the excellence of the time spent in meditation, and concluding the external worship, he begins the internal worship with the three-and-a-half-verse statement beginning with "This": "It is the supreme action;
it is the supreme austerity. (96)
One should constantly meditate upon this supreme Śiva, who resides within the body—whether he is lying down, rising, walking, or standing still. (97)

The two verses beginning with "nityam" constitute a single syntactical unit. The connection [of the meaning] is as follows: one should meditate upon this very *jīva*—who resides in the body, who identifies with the body, and who is engaged in manifold activities throughout the states of waking and so forth—as the supreme Śiva. (97–98)
Touching what is to be touched on all sides, or else abandoning it on all sides;
enjoying and completely renouncing enjoyments that are abundant through non-enjoyment. (98)

One who possesses the purity resulting from bathing in the self-awareness situated within the meaning that has entered the stream [of consciousness] should worship the *bodhaliṅga* with the offering of constant awakening. (99)
The two verses beginning with "pravāha" form a single syntactical unit. "Possessing the purity of the bath of one's own consciousness situated upon the object fallen into the stream":

here, "stream" (*pravāha*) refers to the outward-turned flow of mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*). "Fallen into that" (*tatpatita*) means the object, such as a jar, which is its domain. "Situated therein" (*tatstha*) refers to the self-nature consciousness (*svarūpacaitanya*) reflected within that [modification]. That is to say, within the mental modification taking the form of a jar and so forth—

The meaning is that it is the self-consciousness reflected [in the mind]. The "awakening" (*bodha*) to that is its continuous contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*); that indeed is the "bath," for it is the awakening to one's own true nature as it remains within the flow [of consciousness]. By means of that, being pure—that is, purified—one becomes established in the "power of reflection" (*manana-śakti*) of the mind; that which is established in the mind’s power of reflection is that which impels it. [This occurs] in the interval between the *prāṇa* and *apāna*.

It is said to have arisen because it sets those two in motion. As it was stated by Sāmba: "I take refuge in that primordial Supreme Sun residing within the body, which carries the prāṇa and apāna equally when they are mutually engaged in devouring one another.
It is situated in the center of the heart, the throat, and the palate—that is, located in the middle of the heart, the middle of the throat, and the middle of the palate.

Because the heart and other organs are vital points (*marmasthāna*), the [Self] is manifested there in a special manner; thus, one should worship with constant offerings—consisting of uninterrupted contemplation—that sign (*liṅga*) whose nature is consciousness, which resides in the space between the eyebrows, in the nostrils, on the pedestal, and at the tip of the nose, and which is to be meditated upon as such. For the *liṅga* is...
The meaning is that this [reality] is likewise endowed with power (*śakti*), arisen within the *piṇḍikā*, situated in the center, and established upon the seat (*pīṭha*). || 99 || 100 ||
The mind is established in the power of mentation; it arises between the prāṇa and apāna breaths;
it resides in the heart, throat, and palate; it rests upon the seats of the eyebrows and the nostrils;
it is situated within the thirty-six million divisions [of the body]; and it transcends the state of unmanī.
One should contemplate that this deity is the manifestation of consciousness within one's own body, possessing a thousand limbs, as well as hair, nails, and teeth. (1)

The statement "sahasra" refers to five verses. That reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) which exists within one's own body, possessing consciousness in all its limbs such as hands and feet, and which is the individual soul (jīva) in the form of consciousness reflected in the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), is perceived as "I";
this alone is the deity, because of the non-difference between the original image and its reflection. || 1 ||
(607) My numerous and diverse powers, whose modes of conduct are manifold and who are perceived by the mind, worship me incessantly, like wives attending upon an excellent husband. (2)

Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for whom the mind alone is the seer (*dṛk*)," because the external senses are instruments for the mind's apprehension of external objects. Since the external senses lack the capacity to grasp their respective objects without the mind, these "mind-seers" possess various modes of conduct (*nānācārāḥ*).

Therefore, many diverse powers with distinct functions— whose nature is the capacity to perceive form and other objects— constantly worship you, the Lord in the form of the individual soul (jīvātman), who bestows life upon all the sensory powers, just as wives serve their own beloved husband. || 2 ||
This mind of mine is the gatekeeper who announces the three worlds;
this thought of mine is the female usher, pure in form, standing at the door.

For me, a god who has become thus, my mind alone is the gatekeeper who has reported the three worlds and informed me of all worldly affairs. In this way, thought itself—having pure form and being trustworthy—is my female door-keeper stationed at the entrance regarding external objects, now residing within my inner apartments. (3)
And my various cognitions are the ornaments upon my limbs; the organs of action, together with the group of the organs of perception, are my gateways. (4)

My various cognitions, which have diverse objects as their domain, are my limbs, for they constitute the ornaments residing in the members of my body by virtue of being the cause of its natural beauty. Or, the organs of action, such as speech and the rest, together with the groups of the organs of perception, are my gates, for they are the means for outward movement. And here, it is specifically the organs of perception that constitute the "groups."
Because of his manifold forms and because he is a worshiper of Śiva who is consciousness. || 4 ||
I am this very one, the infinite Self, whose form is free from all limitation;
I abide as the single, suffused Self, full, filling all things.

This very Self, perceived as immediate presence, am I—Śiva in form, whose nature is devoid of limitation. Because my essential nature is free from all circumscription, I am the infinite Self, the boundless Self, the Full One, filled by all, for all things arise within me. I am the Filler of All, because as the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), I fill all things. Thus...
The syntactical connection is as follows: one should contemplate, "I abide as the single, full Self, whose nature is indivisible and non-dual. || 5 ||
Equal in conduct, equal in the flavor of equanimity, equal in appearance, and equal in form,
one attains stainless gentleness by thus worshipping the Imperishable.
"Equal" (sama) means: equal because of fullness, his conduct is of a single flavor (samarasa); because he is free from attachment and aversion, his behavior is of one kind.
He has an "equal appearance" (samābhāsa), appearing in a uniform manner in the minds of all living beings as "this one is dear to me alone.
He has an "equal form" (samākṛti), being thus at all times due to his changelessness; being such, [he perceives] the imperishable Self in this way, by means of what was previously described.
Having worshipped in this manner thoroughly and correctly, one attains gentleness and the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 6 ||
With an equanimous and all-encompassing intellect, one should worship the supreme Lord Viṭpa as pure consciousness alone,
using all available objects according to the sequence as they arise.

Regarding the word *samayā*: one who knows the true nature of the previously mentioned deity—the Supreme Deity which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—should worship Him with *samayā*, that is, with a cognition free from passion and other afflictions, arising from all the senses; and with every object as it is obtained through the proper sequence, accomplished by appropriate activity. || 7 ||
Not even the slightest effort should be made here toward any unprecedented object;
rather, one should worship the conscious Śiva through the experience of desire.

"Even slightly" (*manāk*): in this ritual of worship, one should not make an effort even slightly (*manāg api*), that is, in the slightest degree, for the sake of obtaining a new object or a rare object. Rather, one should worship Śiva, whose nature is consciousness, by means of the experience of desire—that is, by the offering of desired objects. (8–9)
One should honor [the guest] with various kinds of food and drink, abounding in diverse luxuries, as well as with beds, seats, and vehicles, according to what is available.
Having awakened the Self through every form of happiness—the play of beloved food, drink, enjoyments, provisions, and so forth—one should worship it. 110.
He explains this very point: "By one who sports with beloved food, drink, enjoyments, provisions, and so forth"— that is,

by one who sports in every possible way with beloved and charming foods, drinks, collections of enjoyments such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and other means of pleasure implied by the word "and so forth" (ādi).
Having awakened oneself through every kind of happiness and having correctly realized one's own nature as Śiva, one should worship. || 110 ||
One who is overcome by mental and physical ailments, possessed by delusion and agitation,
and beset by all manner of calamities and suffering, should worship the Self. (11)

Regarding the term *ādhī*: here, because suffering removes the impurity in the form of sin, its status as a means of worship should be understood, since it is beneficial to the self—just like substances such as unguents used for anointing. || 11 ||
Whether in poverty or in sovereignty, with a self surrendered to the natural flow of existence and with the flowers of diverse activities, one should worship the pure Self.

Regarding the phrase "by poverty": one should worship the pure Self—the Self distinct from the body and so forth—either by means of poverty or by means of sovereignty. This poverty has entered the stream [of existence] through the flow of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), consists of various activities as its flowers, and is beneficial as the cause for the intellect to engage in diverse actions. Sovereignty is likewise characterized by such qualities. Thus, one should honor the Self. || 12 ||
One should worship one's own awakened self by either renouncing or, alternatively, through attachment to enjoyments—both those that are prohibited and those that are not—at all times. 13.
Regarding the phrase "of enjoyments": the construction is that [this occurs] through passion for those things not forbidden and through the renunciation of those things that are forbidden. || 13 ||
One should remain indifferent toward what is lost and gather what is obtained;
for this state of changelessness is indeed the supreme worship of the Self. 14.

"Lost" (naṣṭam) means this disregard for what is lost and the taking up of what is obtained. It is so called because it is changeless and because it is the cause for the cessation of fluctuations such as joy and sorrow. || 1 ||
A man who is devoted to the constant worship of the Self should make everything consist of the Self— both that which is pleasant at first sight and that which is likewise very painful at first sight.
"Āpāteti" means that which is pleasant at first sight, appearing as something desirable upon initial perception— namely, pleasure or its means—

and likewise that which is extremely difficult to endure at first, appearing as something adverse— namely, pain or its means; both of these, a man devoted to the worship of the eternal Self [regards] as consisting of the Self through the offering of himself.
One should fashion it in that form. || 15 ||
Having resolved that "everything is Brahman"— that which is beneficial, abiding everywhere, at all times, and in every form— one should practice the vow of the worship of the eternal Self. (16)

"Always" (sarvadā) means at all times; "in every form" (sarvarūpeṇa) means in various forms; "everywhere" (sarvatra) means internally, externally, and in all directions. Having ascertained that whatever object exists is entirely Brahman alone, one should perform the vow of the worship of the Self (ātmārcāvrata). The meaning is that the vow of worshipping the Self consists precisely in the determination of the state of Brahman through the offering of everything perceived to the Self. || 16 ||
Neither by desiring nor by rejecting, the wise man should enjoy the fortunes of worldly experience as they come of their own accord, just as rivers are received by the ocean. 17.

"No. By the wise one—the man of knowledge—who does not desire what has not been attained and does not abandon what has been attained, the enjoyments and prosperities that come to him by their own nature are to be experienced like rivers entering the ocean. As it is said in the Gītā:
"Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in immovability, even so do desires enter him..."
All enter [into that]; he attains peace, but not the one who desires objects of desire. || 17 ||
One should not experience agitation regarding views that are trivial or non-trivial, just as the sky remains unmoved by objects of various colors, whether they fall or do not fall.

Regarding "distress" (*udvega*): one should not undergo mental agitation (*cittavikāra*) due to distress arising from views—whether trivial or significant—and from the apprehension of objects as being either empty or non-empty. Just as when various forms such as birds, deer, and other entities fall or do not fall through the sky, no agitation or transformation is experienced by the sky; so it is here. || 18 ||
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious result arises from the conjunction of place, time, and action,
one should worship the Self with that very same [result], while remaining free from modification.

He teaches: whatever object, whether auspicious or inauspicious, comes to one by the power of place, time, and action—one should worship the Self with that very object, in its form as auspicious or inauspicious, by means of that which is grasped without modification and accepted without modification. || 19 ||
In this ritual procedure for the worship of the Self, whatever substances and riches have been prescribed, these are all to be infused with a single equal amount of mercury. (120)
Praising tranquility, which is the nature of an unchanging mind, he says in two verses: "The self... [and so forth]. This constitutes a single syntactical unit.

In this ritual of self-worship, whatever material riches and abundance of objects— whether auspicious or inauspicious in form— are said to exist, they are smeared with various flavors; yet, even when fully developed, once permeated and infused by the single flavor of tranquility (*śama*),
they abandon all other flavors such as sour, pungent, bitter, and astringent, and indeed become nothing but sweet.
Sweetness here is loveliness. || 120 || 21 ||
They were neither sour, nor pungent, nor bitter, nor astringent;
though smeared with various flavors, they were indeed said to be sweet.
Equanimity is sweet and delectable; the power of its flavor transcends the senses.
That which is permeated by it thus becomes nectar in an instant. (22)
"Equalizing them": because it is of the nature of equanimity, it is sweet; that which is the power of taste (*rasa-śakti*), the power in the form of taste, is "to be savored" (*rasyā*).
By that power of taste, whatever object of thought (*cetya*) or visible thing (*dṛśya*) is permeated, all of that would instantly become nectar—nothing but sweet. || 22 ||
Whatever indeed is contemplated in the form of the nectar of equanimity, that attains a supreme sweetness, like the nectar flowing from the moon. (23)
Regarding "equanimity" (samatā): the grammatical connection is that it attains a supreme sweetness, like the nectar (amṛta) dropped by Indra. || 23 ||
One should become like the full moon—perfect, with perfectly even radiance, transparent, a single mass of consciousness, wise, yet possessing the form of a stone. (24)

"Full" (pūrṇa): By the knower, by the wise one, who is equanimous, whose splendor is equal, and whose mental fluctuations are of a single form; and therefore, like the full moon, being full, clear, and consisting of a single mass of consciousness, he should become one with Brahman—become like a stone, having the nature of a rock, and possessing a changeless form. || 24 ||

With a mind in which all desires have been stilled, remain as the leader whose body is eternally honored by all things— the delusions of pleasure and pain arising through the sequence of place, time, and action. (25)

He teaches: "Place" and "time" are well known; "instrument" is the activity of the person. By means of these, through their sequential order, one who has eternally worshipped the Lord of the Body—the Self—by means of the delusions and diversions consisting of pleasure and pain belonging to all things, should remain characterized by an intellect in which every desire has been stilled. 25.
The Lord said:
The most excellent one remains while washing away ignorance with excellence, just as a washerman skilled in method removes dirt by means of dirt. (26)
Since knowledge is required here for self-worship, he states the means for washing away the impurity of ignorance in order to achieve that [knowledge]:

"Ignorance... The excellent, wise person, by means of the most excellent ignorance—which is of the nature of pure latent impressions (*vāsanā*) because it is born of pure *sattva*—remains while indeed washing away ignorance, which is of the nature of impure latent impressions.
Just as a washerman who knows the proper method and is skilled in means removes the dirt from clothes by using a substance such as saline earth—which is itself a type of dirt—in the same manner.

Even those factors which are not direct causes, such as the portions of ignorance, become excellent causal conditions through the gradual instruction of a guru and so forth, for the sake of attaining self-knowledge. (27)
Regarding the phrase "they are not causes": although in reality they are not causes, the portions of ignorance—such as the instructions of a guru and so forth—are nevertheless excellent;
through some means, they gradually become the causes for the attainment of self-knowledge. || 27 ||
When the sequence of the guru’s instructions proceeds toward the awakening of the disciple,
the Self— though indefinable and invisible— becomes gracious of its own accord.

To clarify this very point, he says: "In the sequence. When the teacher’s instruction proceeds toward awakening the disciple in due order, the Self—though indescribable (being impossible for the teacher to convey through words), though specifically invisible (to the mental fluctuations), and though impossible to directly perceive—becomes serene and manifests of its own accord.

As it is stated in the Sūtasamhitā: "Having attained a clear state of functioning, and abiding as the witness of that functioning, [the Self] devours by its own splendor the ignorance that is to be removed by that functioning. (28)
The Self is not understood through the meanings of the scriptures, nor is it understood from the words of a teacher;
it is understood by itself alone, through the power of its own awakening. (29)

The Self is not perceived as "this" through scriptures or the words of gurus; rather, by the power of one's own awakening and through the majesty of contemplating its true nature, it is realized by itself alone. || 29 ||
Without the meaning of the scriptures and the instructions of the guru, the Self is not realized;
it is only through the existence of this conjunction that the knowledge of one's own Self is illumined. 130.

If the Self is realized by itself alone, then what is the use of teachers, scriptures, and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he states the manner in which they are useful: "gurūpadeśa... (Through the teacher’s instruction...). This very conjunction—the mere presence of these [factors], namely the teacher, the scripture, its meaning, and the disciple—is that which illumines the knowledge of one's own Self. 130.
Through the long-standing union and presence of the teacher, the meaning of the scriptures, and the disciple,
self-knowledge proceeds just as the conduct of people proceeds through the day.
"Guru" means: like the conduct of people, that is, worldly social interaction, during the day in the presence of the sun. || 31 ||
O leader of sages, the wise man who thus performs the daily worship of the deity goes to that supreme state where we and our like serve as attendants. (32)

"Thus" means that even those such as ourselves, as well as Hari, Hara, and others, exist in that state of the Supreme Brahman as servants—that is, they abide there in a condition inferior like that of servants. || 32 ||
O Lord of Sages, these three worlds are merely a manifestation; though non-existent, they appear as if existent, and nothing else exists.
Having determined that "all self-worship is Brahman," it was stated that one should observe the vow of the eternal worship of the Self.

In that context, in order to establish the state of the world as Brahman by virtue of its being composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), he introduces the process of the manifestation of consciousness (*cidvivarta-prakriyā*) with the verse beginning "That which does not exist" (*avidyamānam*). It is a mere appearance, nothing but pure consciousness alone. (33)

Know that which is the referent of words such as "Brahmā" and so forth to be pure consciousness alone. When that [consciousness] appears as if it were an object of knowledge, it attains the fitness for the name "cognition. (34)

"Yaḥ" (who): Know that which is well-known—that reality signified by words such as Brahmā, the Supreme Self (paramātman), and the Supreme Light (paraṃ jyotiḥ)—is indeed that absolute, pure consciousness (citi). That very consciousness, though appearing as if it were going toward objects of knowledge, does not undergo any unsuitability for its own nature. || 34 ||
Because its state of being experienced is brought about in an instant, the person follows after the sense of "I" through contemplation,
just as one [assumes] the form of a forest elephant in a dream.

"In an instant" means: because she (the consciousness) has brought the object of knowledge (*vedya*) into being—that is, her state of having brought the visible object into being—for that reason, due to the contemplation of identity with the object of knowledge, she follows after the nature of "I-ness," which is the form of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
It is like a person in a dream who, through the contemplation of an elephant, attains the state of an elephant. || 35 ||
Having attained the state of space and time within this form that is non-dual, those very companions themselves become empty in nature. (36)

Regarding the phrase "of this": of this consciousness (cit), which has taken the form of egoity (ahaṃkāra) from its nature as non-egoity (ahantā), those very powers (śakti) that possess manifold forms, having attained the state of space and time—that is, the nature of space, time, and so forth—become her own companions (sakhyaḥ).
The meaning is that they assume the role of assistants. || 36 ||
That very existence, when combined with those [qualities], becomes designated as the "living being" (jīva);
though eternally situated in a state of ignorance, it attains the nature of the intellect (buddhi).

Regarding the phrase "by those": that very same consciousness-nature (*cinmayī sattā*), being conjoined with or enveloped by those powers such as space, time, and so forth, becomes designated as the individual soul (*jīva*). Abiding in the state of ignorance, it attains the nature of the intellect (*buddhitva*), that is, the form of the intellect.

The individual soul-power (jīva-śakti), being of such a nature and delighting solely in certainty, is followed by the power of sound (śabda-śakti), the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). || 38 ||

"Jīva" means the power of life (*jīva-śakti*), which is the consciousness-power (*cic-chakti*) in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*). Having attained the state of intellect (*buddhi*), it shines forth solely through the act of ascertainment (*niścaya*), because the intellect is by nature ascertainment; thus, it is followed by the powers of sound and so forth. Among these, the power of sound (*śabda-śakti*) is the cause for linguistic usage. In this way...
The powers of cognition and action are the causes of the operation of knowledge and the operation of action.
When this aggregate [of the senses] quickly brings about recollection by coming together,
it becomes the mind (*manas*), which is the pure self and the seed of the tree of volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*). (39)

Regarding the word *militvā*: this aforementioned group—the aggregate beginning with the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)—followed by the powers of sound and so forth, and fashioning the capacity for memory (*smṛti*), becomes the pure mind (*manas*), which is the clear and translucent self (*śuddhātman*) that serves as the seed for the tree of volition (*saṃkalpa*). In the reading *śūnyātman*, the meaning is "having a form imagined by *māyā*. (39)
The wise know that to be the vessel for the description of the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body;
for its infinite powers, whose sole nature is self-reflection, assume the form of space and so forth, and thus that [body] shines as the manifold world. (140)

With the following half-verse, they know that very mind to be the locus for the expression "the subtle body" (*ātivāhika-deha*); that is to say, the mind itself is the subtle body. That same mind, having assumed the form of ether and so forth according to the manner described in the section on creation, shines as the manifold world in various forms.
For this mental impression known as the "world" has arisen in this way like a hollow vampire; when it is stilled, peace remains unimpaired. (41)

"Empty" means: just as a *vetāla* (a ghost) is indeed empty because it is a mental construction and not an ultimate reality, so too, in this very same manner, it is only the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the mind that has arisen under the name of the "world" and in the form of the world. Therefore, when that mental impression is stilled, there is the unimpaired peace of the world; the meaning is that this is liberation (*kaivalya*). || 41 ||
He who places his trust in egoism, in the world, and in the water of a mirage—
that long-lived man is not to be instructed here.

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of egoism" (ahantāyām): that man who is established in the absence of egoism and the like, being endowed with the realization of the ultimate truth—he is the "slain man. 33.

Know that which is the referent of words such as "Brahmā" and so forth to be consciousness alone; when it appears as if it were an object of knowledge, it attains the fitness for the name "cognition. (34)

"Who" (yaḥ) || That which is well-known, perceived through indirect cognition, and denoted by words such as "Brahmā" and so forth—the referent of terms like "Brahman," "Supreme Self," and "Supreme Light"—is the reality to be established;
know that to be the absolute, pure consciousness (citi). That very consciousness, as it were, entering into the objects of knowledge, undergoes the appearance of being subject to names. || 34 ||

In an instant, because its state of being perceived has been brought about, the person follows after the sense of "I," just as one [assumes] the nature of a forest elephant through mental cultivation in a dream. (35)

"In an instant" means: because she (the consciousness) has brought about the state of being an object of knowledge—that is, the state of that [consciousness] by which the object of knowledge, the visible world, is brought forth—for that reason, due to the contemplation of identity with the object of knowledge, she follows after the nature of "I-ness," which is the form of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Just as a person in a dream attains the state of an elephant through the contemplation of being an elephant. || 35 ||
Those very companions, who have attained the state of space and time within this form that is non-dual, themselves become empty in nature. 36.

Regarding the phrase "of this": of this Consciousness (cit), which has assumed the form of the ego (ahaṃkāra) from its nature as non-ego (ahantā), those very powers that possess manifold forms, having attained the state of space and time—that is, the nature of space, time, and so forth—become her companions (sakhyaḥ) of their own accord.
The meaning is that they assume the role of assistants. || 36 ||
That very existence, when conjoined with those [qualities], becomes designated as the individual soul (jīva);
though eternally situated in a state of ignorance, it attains the nature of the intellect (buddhi).

Regarding the phrase "by those": that very same consciousness-nature (*cinmayī sattā*), being conjoined with or enveloped by those powers such as space, time, and so forth, becomes designated as the individual soul (*jīva*). Abiding in the state of ignorance, it attains the nature of the intellect (*buddhitva*), that is, the form of the intellect.
The power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), being of such a nature, delights solely in certainty;
it is followed by the power of speech (śabda-śakti), the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). || 38 ||

"Jīva" means the power of life (*jīva-śakti*), which is the consciousness-power (*cic-chakti*) in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*). Having attained the state of intellect (*buddhi*), it shines forth solely through the function of determination (*niścaya*), because the intellect is essentially of the nature of determination.
It is followed by the powers of sound (*śabda-śakti*) and so forth. Among these, the power of sound is the cause for linguistic usage (*śabda-vyavahāra*). Thus...
The powers of knowledge and action are the causes of the functioning of cognition and the functioning of activity. 38.
When this group of [senses] has come together and quickly brings about recollection,
it becomes the mind— the pure self that is the seed of the tree of volition. (39)

"Militvā" (having combined): this aforementioned group—the aggregate beginning with the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra)—following after the powers of sound and so forth, while fashioning memory (smṛti), that is, the power of recollection, becomes the pure mind (manaḥ), which is transparent and the seed of the tree of volition (saṃkalpa). In the reading "śūnyātma," the meaning is "having a form fashioned by Māyā. || 39 ||
The wise know that to be the vessel for the expression of the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body;
for its infinite powers, whose sole nature is self-reflection, assume the form of space and so forth, and thus that [Self] shines as the manifold world. (140)

With the following half-verse, [the author] explains that very mind as the subject of the expression "subtle body" (*ātivāhika-deha*). They know that even the statement "subtle body" has the mind alone as its referent; the meaning is that the mind itself is the subtle body.
That same mind, having assumed the form of ether and the other elements according to the manner described in the section on creation, manifests as the manifold world in various forms.
For this mental impression called "the world" has arisen in this way like a hollow vampire; when it is stilled, peace remains unimpaired. (41)

"Empty" means: just as a *vetāla* (a conjured spirit) is indeed empty because it is a mental construction and not ultimately real, so too, in this very same manner, it is only the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the mind that has arisen under the name of the "world" and in the form of the world. Therefore, when that latent impression of the mind is stilled, there is the unimpaired peace of the world; the meaning is that this is liberation (*kaivalya*). || 41 ||
Fie on that wretched man who places his trust in egoism, in the world, and in the water of a mirage; he is not fit to be instructed here.
Regarding the phrase "in [the state of] egoism": that man who is established in egoism and the like, being possessed of the notion of ultimate reality [regarding them], fie on him, that slain man!
He is not worthy of instruction here in this Brahma-vidyā. || 42 ||
(616) Those who know reality teach that the discerning soul here is noble and free from delusion, whereas the ignorant one is a wandering phantom composed of unreality.
Indeed, he who offers peace to the ignorant is like one who gives his daughter to a man seen in a dream, even though she is as radiant as gold.
Regarding the word *jīvam*: here, those who know that—namely the knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*)—instruct and awaken the discerning qualified seeker in this manner.

They do not instruct the deluded one, whose contrary knowledge has arisen; nor do they instruct the fool (*bāla*), who is abandoned and discarded by the noble, the refined, and others, being composed of unreality (*asanmaya*) and virtually non-existent.
The meaning is that because such an unworthy person instructs [him], that teacher is as futile as giving a daughter in marriage to a man seen only in a dream. || 3 || 44 || 45 || 46 ||
Īśvara said:
"O Sage, you have spoken exactly as asked. May it be well with you!
We shall go to our desired destination; arise, O Pārvatī! (44)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, that blue-throated one, while I was still holding the handful of flowers,
crossed into the expanse of the sky together with his retinue.
From that time forward, I have remained here, free from distraction, performing my own worship according to that very same sequence until this day.
O Rāma, by means of this method of worship, these latent impressions (vāsanās) are carried away by me without weariness, even while I am engaged in worldly affairs.
"By this": these latencies of saṃsāra are being carried across and led away by me, as if I were untiring and as if free from distraction.
Just as my own worship with flowers consisting of performed actions and conduct has never been interrupted by me, day or night, at any time—whether it be severed or unsevered—[so be it]. (48)

"Yathā" (as): Just as for those who have attained [realization], the performance of rituals according to traditional conduct—even if their self-worship with those very flowers has been interrupted, and even if it appears from a worldly perspective to be interrupted—never becomes severed at any time, day or night, for one such as I who possesses uninterrupted contemplation. || 48 ||
The relationship between the grasped and the grasper is common to all living beings;
that which consists in the yogi’s state of attentiveness is the worship of the Self. (49)

Anticipating the objection that such worship of the Self is indeed easily accessible to all, he states the distinction of the yogin: "The object of perception... and so forth. Although the relationship between the perceived and the perceiver is common to all embodied beings, nevertheless, the ignorant (pāmaras), being outward-turned and afflicted by hunger, thirst, and the like, think, "We shall eat various kinds of food and drink."

[Ordinary people] become agitated, thinking, "We shall drink [this]. The yogi, however, remains attentive, understanding that according to the method previously described, the Self alone is the deity and this manifold abundance of enjoyments is his very worship; this is the distinction. Therefore, the meaning is that the aforementioned continuous contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) itself is the worship of the Self. || 49 || 150 || 51 ||
O Lord of the Raghus, with this vision and a mind liberated from attachment, wander in this sparse forest of saṃsāra; you shall not suffer.
Rāma said:
Now, O Brahmin, my doubt has been completely dispelled;
everything that was to be known has been known, and a natural satisfaction has arisen.
The mind has attained perfect fortitude in the battle of worldly existence— a state that is supreme, impenetrable by others, and which crushes the elephant of desire.
"Parā" means that which has crushed the elephants of hope, shattered the elephants of the quarters, and turned back the elephants in the form of mental desires.

My mind is supremely joyful within, having attained a state where conceptual constructions have dissolved, where longing has been stilled, and whose essential nature is undaunted; it possesses an exceedingly serene form throughout the three worlds. 153.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "My mind—free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), with longing dissolved, undepressed, devoid of wretchedness, exceedingly essential, and possessing supreme knowledge; being of a serene form and joyful—is existing as the eternally unsurpassed, the best of all. (153)
Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Narrative of the Worship of the Deity," in the section on Nirvāṇa within the *Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭhasāra*, the means to liberation.
Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Narrative of the Worship of the Devas," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa*, known as the *Saṃsārataraṇi*.
p. 618) The Third Chapter. Rāma said:
No satiety arises from the sprinkling of the nectar of your words;
O Brahmin, tell me once more some story consisting of the ultimate reality.

Previously, it was stated that Nirvana results from the inward-turning of the mind through a previously unmentioned method of deity worship. Now, demonstrating the example of a *bilva* fruit to show that non-dual Brahman alone exists pervading all things by having internalized all objects within itself, he begins another narrative. In this regard, there is another way for the concentration of the mind:
He begins the effort to awaken [the disciple]. || 1 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as an object at the moment of attainment brings initial satisfaction, who has not experienced that it does not do so even for a single moment thereafter? (2)

Regarding the word "yathā": who has not experienced that just as a desired object brings satisfaction at the very moment it is first obtained, it does not bring satisfaction after even a single moment subsequent to that moment of attainment? The meaning is that this fact is experienced by everyone. || 2 ||
Just as an object brings satisfaction at the time of desire but not at any other time,
so the fool, and no one else, fixes his attachment upon momentary pleasure.
Therefore, only the fool, and not the discerning person, binds himself with attachment to this momentary pleasure. || 3 ||
At the moment of desire, that satisfaction which arises has desire itself as its cause;
yet satisfaction ends in dissatisfaction—therefore, abandon desire. (4)

He says that even that momentary pleasure is merely imagined and not real—starting with the word "vāñchā" (desire). For the satisfaction that arises at the very moment of desire, that desire itself is the cause;
since satisfaction follows the positive and negative concomitance of desire, even that imagined satisfaction ends in dissatisfaction, for it exists only within the state of dissatisfaction.
It culminates in disaster; therefore, abandon the desire for that which results in misfortune and serves as the cause for momentary pleasure. || 4 ||
May hope turn into hopelessness, and may mental ideation turn into non-existence; may the mind turn into mindlessness for you who live in non-attachment.

"May hope cease. Therefore, for you who live without attachment and without reliance on sense-objects while engaged in worldly activity, may "hope"—the longing for desired things—go to its end in hopelessness, which is the absence of effort. May "mental cultivation"—the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of objects—go to non-existence. And may the mind, being free from impressions, go to "mindlessness," which is the state of being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatā*). || 5 ||
Performing action with internal organs free from latent impressions (vāsanā),
you do not undergo transformation even amidst hundreds of disturbances, remaining like the sky.

Regarding the term *vāsanā*: therefore, even while performing actions with the sense organs—such as the eyes and so forth—which are free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), you do not undergo any modification within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Just as the sky (*kha*) does not undergo modification despite hundreds of disturbances such as wind, rain, and the like, so it is with you. || 6 ||
The creation and dissolution of saṃsāra occur through the opening and closing of the eyes of the mind;
by restraining the latent impressions and the vital breath, make the mind unblinking.
Regarding "the mind": through the opening and closing of the mind—its manifestation and disappearance alone—the dissolution and emergence of saṃsāra occur.
Therefore, by means of the previously mentioned restraint of mental impressions or the restraint of the vital breath, make that very mind ceaselessly dissolved. 7.

Through the expansion and contraction of the vital breath (prāṇa), there arise the dissolution and emergence of transmigratory existence. Render that [breath] free from expansion through the practice of repeated application. (8)

Regarding the word *prāṇa*: since even the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is a cause for the manifestation of the mind, it is a cause of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*). Therefore, by means of practice and application—either through the practice of restraining the breath (*pavana-nirodha*), through intense exertion, or through the restraint of the mind—make that breath motionless and without blinking. For by that which the mind is bound, the breath is also bound.
Because the cessation of the vital breaths is also a cause for the cessation of the mind. || 8 ||
The dissolution and emergence of karmas occur through the opening and closing of the eyes of ignorance;
dissolve that [ignorance] by force through the restraint of the meaning of the Guru's teachings and the scriptures. (9)
Regarding the term "ignorance" (*maurkhya*): ignorance is lack of knowledge, and that too is a cause of *saṃsāra* by way of karma.
To explain: from ignorance comes false knowledge; from that, attachment and aversion arise; from those two, activity in the form of merit and demerit occurs;
and from that follows *saṃsāra*, consisting of the sufferings of birth and so forth. That ignorance [is removed] by restraint regarding the meaning of the Guru and the scriptures.
By the instruction of the guru, by the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures, and by self-restraint, forcibly dissolve—that is, destroy—[the afflictions] through human effort. || 9 ||
By the mere cessation of the vibration of non-awareness, the mind attains the state of no-mind;
or by the restraint of the vital breaths, that very same supreme state is reached. || 10 ||

"Non-consciousness" (asaṃvit): The mind is the agent. "Vibration of non-consciousness" (asaṃvitspanda) refers to the absence of the vibration of consciousness—that is, the manifestation [of consciousness] through extroversion. By means of that alone, or by the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), it attains the state of non-mind (acittatā), which is freedom from conceptual construction (nirvikalpatva). That very state is the appropriate condition, the supreme station, and liberation. || 10 ||

In the relationship between the seen and the seeing, that which is the ultimate happiness—through the realization of its final limit and through the vision of Brahman, there is the dissolution of the mind. (11)

Regarding the word *dṛśya*: when there is a connection between the object of sight and the act of seeing—that is, when there is a connection of the desired objects with the sense organs—whatever ultimate (*pāramārthika*), supreme (*paramārtha*) bliss arises within one's own self, that [bliss] manifests through an internal, exclusive realization (*antaikāntasaṃvitti*). The word *anta* denotes one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Its [meaning is as follows]:
The inner nature of ultimate bliss is the uninterrupted contemplation through its exclusive realization;

that is to say, the very realization of the bliss of one's own nature through the realization of Brahman is what is meant by the "vision of Brahman" (*brahmadṛṣṭi*), according to the Vedic scripture: "This Self is Brahman. Likewise, through such a vision of Brahman, the destruction—that is, the dissolution—of the mind occurs. || 11 ||
Where the mind has not arisen, that indeed is the unsurpassed bliss;
free from decay and excellence, it neither arises nor ceases. (12)
When the mind has dissolved (*cittalaya*), that very state of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) becomes the bliss of absolute liberation (*kaivalya-sukha*); thus he says: "Wherein...

In that bliss wherein the mind has not arisen—that is, wherein the mental fluctuations (*citta-vṛtti*) such as volition and conceptualization do not arise—that alone is the uncreated bliss, one's own innate joy (*nijānanda*). This is what is meant by the "bliss of absolute liberation" (*kaivalya-sukha*). And that—
Being free from decay and excellence, and being eternal and unsurpassed, it neither arises nor ceases. || 12 ||
The mind of the Knower is not called "mind"; the mind of the Knower is said to be Truth.
The mind, which partakes in various objects and states of difference, becomes like gold when purified by awakening, just as copper [is transformed]. (13)
Now, one might ask: since there is no dissolution of the mind for the knower (*jñānin*), how can there be liberation while living? To this, he says: "Of the knower" (*jñasya*).

The mind of the knower is not called "mind"; rather, being the mind of a knower, it is said to be the Truth—that is, Brahman itself. For this reason, it does not partake in the diversity of various objects, nor in various forms.

The mind—the referent of the word "citta"—partakes in otherness from Brahman and indeed exists as something distinct when characterized by objects such as desires and volitions. However, for the knower, the mind becomes non-different from that [Brahman] through awakening—that is, through the realization of the perfectly full Brahman—just as copper attains the state of gold through the application of a proper method. || 13 ||
The mind attains the state of pure consciousness for a short time during the maintenance of the world;
having dwelt in the fourth state (turya), it indeed becomes that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta).

The mind alone. The mind is the agent in the maintenance of the world; having remained for some time, when the state of *samādhi* is accomplished through the sequence of hearing, reflection, and so forth, within the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*), the essence of the mind (*cittattva*) attains the nature of pure consciousness (*citsvarūpa*). Beyond this, it becomes that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*). When the triad beginning with waking exists, in comparison to them, in the state of *samādhi*— [Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on a verse beginning with "cittamitti. The translation reflects the philosophical content of the extant portion.]
The meaning is that because of the absence of the states such as waking and so forth during constant samādhi, even the state of the Fourth (turyatva) does not exist. || 14 ||
Brahman alone, having become the manifold delusion of the many worlds, thus remains as the one, equal,
and all-pervading essence; it is nothing else, my dear, nor is there anything such as the mind, for its arrangement is not like that of a physical object within the heart.
"Brahman" means this: Brahman, the Self of all, is one alone;

yet, through the successions of the playful manifestations of the manifold delusions of the world, it exists simultaneously and together with multiplicity in the form of space and the other elements. Apart from this, there is nothing else here, such as the mind or anything else.

The arrangement and configuration of space and so forth, though perceived, do not exist. To the question, "Where has the falsity of what is perceived been seen? he says: "As in the heart," and so on. Just as in the state of dreaming, the object and its configuration perceived within the heart—that is, in the mind—do not exist, so it is here. (15–16)
Vasiṣṭha said:
In this regard, O Rāma, listen briefly to this unprecedented and beautiful story, which is full of the splendor of wonder and intended for your enlightenment. (16)
There exists a great bilva fruit, thousands of yojanas in extent, vast, stainless, and radiant, whose form remains undecaying even through the ages.

The three verses beginning with "yojanānām" form a single syntactical unit. Brahman alone—which is a mass of consciousness and contains all objects within it—is described as being like a marvelous bilva fruit; it is of an undecaying nature because Brahman is devoid of transformations such as old age.
Though ancient, it is as beautiful as the softness of a crescent moon's edge;
it remains unshaken even by the forceful gusts of the winds at the end of a great kalpa.
Though ancient, it is beautiful with the softness of a crescent moon; it is unshakable because it is devoid of impurities and consists of pure bliss. || 18 ||
Even by hundreds of lakhs of millions of ten-thousand yojanas, the root and foundation of the world's existence is immeasurable in its vastness. (19)
It is immeasurable in its vastness due to its infinity; it is the primordial root of the world's existence because it is the material cause. Such is the great bilva fruit that exists. (19)
The vast cosmic eggs are situated near that bilva fruit;
they bear the semblance of mere playthings to the rows of atoms upon the mountain peaks. (20)

"Of that" (tasya): near that bilva fruit, even the lofty cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) bear the semblance of grains of black mustard seeds for those situated at the base of the mountain; what can be said of its greatness? This is the meaning. "Rājikā" refers to the black mustard seed. || 20 ||
That [body] never attains equality with the end of its ripening;
for even though it is always "ripe," my dear, it is not afflicted by old age. (21)
"No," [he replied]. "That fruit is never joined with, nor does it coincide with, a ripening that culminates in falling away, because of its eternity. (21)
Within this great fruit of the essence of the *masastaphala*,
the wondrous manifestation of the power of consciousness attains the state of being its inner marrow.

"Entirety," etc. Because the essence of all fruits consists in the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), the wondrous manifestation (*camatkṛti*) of the power of consciousness (*saṃvicchakti*)—that is, the very flash of the power of consciousness (*cicchaktisphūrti*)—of this subject at hand, attains the state of being submerged within, that is, the state of being the internal essence, since Brahman has consciousness as its essence. || 22 ||
By that power of consciousness, which there assumes various shifting forms, the vision is thus extended toward its own very nature, which is equanimity.

"Consciousness (saṃvit)"—therefore, in its own very form, which is identical with the power of consciousness that is infinite like a bilva fruit, shimmering in its fluid nature, and manifesting through manifold transformations; in this manner, by the method to be described, the vision preceded by the desire to emit was fully extended and set in motion. || 23 ||
This is the infinitely vast ether; this is the digit composed of time;
this is destiny exerted in action; this is activity whose form is vibration.

He explains that very manner by means of two verses beginning with "idam": "This is destiny (niyati), intent upon governing the worlds, prepared [for its task], consisting of vibration, having motion as its nature, and being the power in the form of action. It is the wonder of the marrow of one's own [being]—the manifestation of the power of consciousness (saṃvit-śakti)—because the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) is of the nature of the play of consciousness. (24–25)
"This universe is a pavilion; these are the quarters; such indeed is the sequence"—this is the wondrous essence of that very wood-apple fruit. (25)
Rāma said:
O Blessed One, Knower of the Essence of All, it is my conviction that you have described this being in the form of a bilva fruit as the mass of great consciousness (mahācidghana). 26.
"O Blessed One! [This refers to: "The great mass of consciousness-existence" means the great existence of Brahman, which is the mass of consciousness. || 26 ||
This entire vast expanse, beginning with Mahant, has the form of pure consciousness;
there is not even the slightest difference consisting of the conceptualization of duality or unity.

"Consciousness (cit)"—this entire universe, which is expanded and pervaded by egoism, the primordial nature (prakṛti), the Great Principle (mahat), and so forth, has consciousness as its very marrow. Therefore, there exists not even the slightest distinction consisting of the conceptualization of duality or unity—that is, a distinction in the form of an inquiry into difference and non-difference, or the perception of difference. || 27 || 28 ||

Just as the arrangement of Mount Meru and other features exists within the marrow of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), so too does this entire world, beginning with the cosmic egg, exist within the marrow of the bilva fruit of consciousness (cidbilva). || 28 ||
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Narrative of Bilva," in the illustrious Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa.
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Narrative of Bilva," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa.
The Fourth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, O moon-faced one, listen to this other beautiful and wonderful tale, full of marvels, which I am about to relate.

Previously, consciousness (*caitanya*), which contains all objects within itself and is indeed non-dual, was described as being like a *bilva* fruit. Now, however, that very same [consciousness]—which is a single undivided essence, free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpā*), and solidified—is described as a great rock of consciousness (*cinmahāśilā*) by means of the passage beginning with "atha": "Variegated, never heard before, and therefore causing wonder... (1)
There exists somewhere a great stone, glossy, clear, soft to the touch, possessing vast extent, dense, and eternally without interstices. (2)
"Smooth" (*snigdhā*) because it is the object of the mind's affection; "clear" (*spaṣṭā*) because it manifests by itself;
"soft to the touch" (*mṛdusparśā*) because it is the cause of happiness; "possessing great extension" (*mahāvistāraśālinī*) because it is limitless; "dense" (*nibiḍā*) because it is continuous;
"eternally without interstices" (*nityanīrandhrā*) because it is unmixed with heterogeneous substances. Such a great stone exists somewhere.

Because it is impossible to define a substratum distinct from Himself, He is said to be "somewhere. To the question, "In what is that Blessed One established? the answer is: "In His own glory," according to the Śruti. (2)
Within it, O Raghava, there are many beautiful lotuses in full bloom, as numerous as those in a lake.

Regarding the phrase "in that," there is a statement consisting of two and a half verses. Here, by the word "lotuses" (*padmāni*), the worlds and so forth are intended, because they possess the capacity for contraction and expansion, and because they serve as the abode for the bees that are living beings. (3)
With petals interwoven with one another, yet mutually separated;
growing upon one another, both hidden and manifest;
with roots above, roots below, and others entirely rootless. || 4 ||

Some of these have their petals interwoven with one another, being mutually connected; others, however, are separated from each other, lacking such connection. Among them, some have their roots directed upwards, because they rest upon the polar sphere (dhruvamaṇḍala) situated above the worlds of the immortals and so forth; others have their roots directed downwards.

[Some worlds] rest upon the tortoise situated outside the netherworlds (*pātāla*) and the earthly realm (*bhūloka*). Some are rootless, because the worlds of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others are eternal. By the phrase "and others," those with horizontal roots (*tiryaṅmūla*) are indicated;
for some worlds are supported by the wind itself, which has the inherent nature of moving horizontally. Such are these [worlds].
The grammatical connection is that there are lotuses within that stone slab. || 4 ||
And near them there are conchs by the hundreds of thousands,
and masses of wheels of great size, arranged like lotuses. (5)

Regarding the phrase "of them": near those lotuses there are hundreds of thousands of conch shells (*śaṅkha*). By the word "conch," the luminous spheres (*jyotirmaṇḍala*) consisting of constellations, planets, and stars are meant, because they appear like a multitude of conchs in the ocean-blue sky. By the word "wheel" (*cakra*), the continents (*dvīpa*) in the form of circles are meant.
Because they are characterized by oceans that appear like the rims of wheels. || 5 || 6 ||
Rāma said:
This is true; such a great stone was seen by me.
Such a stone exists upon the head of Hari at Śālagrāma.
Vasiṣṭha said:

This "cicchilā" (consciousness-rock) has been described by me to you, within which the existence of the world resides; by virtue of its density and its nature as a single essence, this consciousness itself is indeed a rock.

Regarding the word *cit*: due to the factors of density (*ghanatva*), oneness of essence (*ekātmakatva*), and so forth—where "density" means compactness and "oneness of essence" means having a single form—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes multiplicity and other such qualities—it is by virtue of these, through their power and because it resembles them, that this very stone of consciousness (*citta-śilā*) [is so called]. || 7 ||
Even within one whose body is extremely dense and whose form is without any gaps, there exists the multitude of worlds, just as the vast wind exists within the sky. (8)
"Even" (api): Within that very stone, though it be solid and without interstices, the multitude of worlds exists;
for since the multitude of worlds is non-different from it, there is no contradiction between its solidity and its lack of interstices. || 8 ||
The sky, the earth, the wind, the ether, the mountains, the rivers, and the directions—
all these exist within that stone, yet it is not even slightly porous.
"Like the sky": and that [sky] is not even slightly hollow or porous, because the world and its elements, such as the sky, are non-different from it.
Just as the world of conch shells, lotuses, and so forth is inscribed upon a stone, so too [is this].
The past, the present, and the future are but a statue carved from the rock of consciousness.

Regarding the term *śaṅkhā* (conch): just as a stone is not affected at all even when carved into the forms of a conch, a lotus, and so forth, so too is this statue made of the rock of consciousness (*cicchilā*), which consists of the past, present, and future. The meaning is that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) itself, though variegated by manifold diverse patterns, is not divided. || 10 ||

Just as a clod of earth, though composed of many elements within its internal structure, maintains the state of a single mass, so too does Consciousness, though containing the universe within its womb, never relinquish its unity as a single mass.

Regarding the term *upala*: just as an internal configuration—the arrangement of conch shells, lotuses, and so forth situated within—is perceived as having various forms even while being a single mass in reality, so too does Consciousness, though containing the universe within it and containing the world within its womb, never relinquishes its state as a single mass. 11.
Just as a lotus is non-different from the stone matrix that constitutes its body,
so indeed the creation is always non-different from the form of consciousness.

As for the word "yathā" (as): just as a lotus imagined upon a stone is non-different from the stone-receptacle because it consists of the very form of that stone due to its being made of stone, so too the creation imagined within consciousness is non-different from the nature of consciousness. 12.
Just as a line of lotuses within a stone or a wondrous flash within a ray of light neither rises nor sets, so too is creation within Consciousness.

Regarding the word *śilā* (stone): Just as a row of lotus-designs imagined upon a stone, or the internal wonder within a flash of light—the cause of amazement and the manifestation of a pungent taste—neither arises because it is not inherent, nor does it set because the substance remains until its destruction; so too is the creation and maintenance of the world within Consciousness (*cit*). 13.
Just as a mortal is within a pregnant woman, or as marrow is within a wood-apple fruit,
so too the circle of the cosmic eggs resides within Consciousness, which is enriched by infinite transformations.

"Just as" (yathā): Just as a mortal in the form of an embryo dwells within a pregnant woman, and just as the marrow, which is the essential core, dwells within a wood-apple fruit (*bilva*), even so the entire sphere of the universe (*brahmāṇḍa-maṇḍalī*), rich with infinite transformations, dwells within Consciousness (*cit*). || 14 ||
Just as the carvings of wheels and lotuses remain within a stone during the state of deep sleep, so does this series of worlds abide within Consciousness. 15.
"Suṣuptā" means: the lines in the form of wheels and lotuses remain within the interior of the stone in a state of *suṣupti*, that is, in a motionless state like that of deep sleep. || 15 ||
Just as it is in whatever form and wherever it may be, so indeed is that very same Brahman; being the self of all, it exists as everything, remaining like one in deep sleep.

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): in whatever place, whatever form, whatever nature, and in whatever manner Brahman—which is the self of all—manifests, there that very reality is perceived in that same way and by that very mode. Therefore, everything remains as Brahman alone, changeless, like one situated in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), as if having entered the state of deep sleep; for Brahman consists of the essence of space (*kha*).
The sense is that, because his volition is true, it is logical for him to abide in various forms according to his own will.
Know that this great delusion of the world, so rich with manifold transformations of being,
is indeed like deep sleep, comparable to a lotus and such within a stone.

"Bhūri" means: know that this vast delusion in the form of the world, which is enriched by numerous transformations of existence such as birth and so forth, is indeed Brahman itself in a state of deep sleep, like a lotus and other things within a stone. || 17 ||

The manifestation of the world is eternally nothing but the state of deep sleep within the Self, which is perfectly tranquil, uniform, and a mass of consciousness; like a lotus carved out of stone, these insubstantial states of creation, once seen as such, never again enter the body.
(18) "Eternally," etc. Within the Self—which is perfectly tranquil, uniform, and a mass of consciousness—this manifestation of the world is perceived in this manner.
It is like a lotus within a stone, or like the state of deep sleep belonging to Brahman; it is indeed abiding in the state of profound slumber.

As for the states of creation—the conditions of the beginning of manifestation—they are seen to be essence-less and without foundation. Therefore, they never at any time attain the status of being the body’s true nature. || 18 ||
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Narrative of Śila," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Yogavāsiṣṭha-sāra*.
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Narrative of Śila," in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa*.
Fifth canto.
Rāma said:
Everything that is to be known has been known, and everything that is to be seen has been seen without flaw;
nevertheless, I ask this again as a matter of sport for the further increase of my understanding. (1)

Previously, consciousness—though diverse—was described as being like a solid stone of undivided single flavor. Now, however, in order to demonstrate that for the man of discrimination who realizes "all is Brahman," even battle and the like do not obstruct the repose of the mind, the narrative of Arjuna is related. || 1 ||
O Blessed One, tell me what the form of the *puryaṣṭaka* is, which serves as a mirror for the majesty of the creation of thousands of worlds.
Regarding the word "jagat": Tell me, what is the nature of that city of eight (puryaṣṭaka), which possesses the majesty of creating a thousand worlds and is as stainless as a mirror? || 2 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:

That Brahman which is without beginning or end, the seed of the universe, and free from all affliction— it is that very same reality, when joined with conceptualization, that is known here as the *jīva*.

The three verses beginning with "anādyantam" form a single syntactical unit. Brahman alone, which is the seed of the universe, when joined with *kalana* (differentiation) and joined with *avidyā* (ignorance), is known as the *jīva*. || 3 ||
The human form is pure consciousness alone, devoid of all parts and their manifestations; when it becomes oriented toward manifestation, it is known here as the *jīva*.

Māyā is, in reality, a power (*kalā*) of the individual soul (*nūrjīva*); its "calculation" (*kalana*) is its grasping. When [the soul] has become devoid of that, it has itself gone toward the state of being oriented toward ignorance (*avidyā*). Here, when the forgetting of the true nature of the self as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is recognized, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is said to arise from the conceit of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*), namely the notion "I am. From the act of thinking (*manana*) in the form of volition and so forth, it is called the mind (*manas*).
It is said: || 4 || 5 ||
That living soul (jīva), indeed, clearly accumulates [karma] and vibrates within this body.
Due to the sense of "I," it is called the ego (ahaṃkāra); due to the act of thinking, it is called the mind (manas). (5)
Through the conviction of being an awakener, one becomes the intellect; likewise, through the vision of Indra, one becomes the sense organ.
Through the conception of a body, one becomes a body; through the conception of a jar, one becomes a jar.
This very self-nature is remembered by people as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka).
The intellect (*buddhi*) is so called because of its function, which consists of the determination of consciousness. Likewise, regarding "seen by Indra" (*indra-dṛṣṭa*): Indra is the Self (*ātman*);

because they are seen by Him and acquired through His various actions, they are called sense organs (*indriya*). This is because the word *indriya* is derived in the sense of "seen by Indra" by the rule beginning with "the sense organ is the mark of Indra, seen by Indra," and so forth. [This occurs] through the contemplation of the body as having that form.

It becomes a body; through the cultivation of the form of a jar, it becomes a jar. This very Self, whose nature is such and whose essential character is of this kind, is remembered by those who know reality as the *puryaṣṭaka*. Its definition is as follows: "Endowed with the element of egoity (*ahaṃkāra-kalā*), and joined with the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*)."
"That is called the city of eight" (tat-puryaṣṭaka), as was previously stated: "the bee at the heart-lotus of the elements" (bhūta-hṛt-padma-ṣaṭpadaḥ). || 6 ||
That consciousness which is directed toward the states of being a knower, an agent, an enjoyer, and a witness is called the *jīva*; indeed, they know that to be the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city).
Now he states the definition by way of another method, beginning with the words "having known."

That consciousness which falls into [the roles of] knowerhood, agency, enjoyership, witnesshood, and so forth—possessing the egoistic conceits such as "I am the knower," "I am the agent," "I am the enjoyer," and "I am the witness"—is called the *jīva*.

The wise know that very nature of consciousness to be the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body). It is this [consciousness] reflected in the jewel of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that possesses the egoistic conceits of agency, enjoyership, and the like.
The meaning is that consciousness itself is the individual soul (jīva) and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka). || 7 ||
Just as people, by the power of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), perceive one dream after another as something unreal, so too do they perceive this world.
Regarding the term "puryaṣṭaka": just as people, by the power of the puryaṣṭaka alone, perceive one unreal dream after another, so too do they perceive this world. || 8 ||
O lotus-eyed one, you have pointed out that auspicious state of non-attachment;
embracing which, O mighty-armed one, the sage becomes one whose mind is liberated while living. (9)
Having thus ascertained the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—like a dream—one should engage in worldly affairs with detachment, as Arjuna did;
to introduce that discourse, he begins with the words "O lotus-eyed one" and so forth. || 9 || 10 || 11 ||
Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, will spend his own life happily and free from suffering; likewise, you too should spend your life in such a manner.
Rāma said:
