O Brahmin, when will that Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, appear? And what kind of unattached nature will Hari describe to him?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Sometimes, at the end of every four yugas, the blessed Yama performs penance out of fear of sin arising from the destruction of living beings.

The two verses beginning with "Yama" constitute a single syntactical unit. It is said that the Lord Yama, at some point after the four yugas had passed, fearing sin arising from cruelty toward living beings, performed austerities for the sake of its cessation. (12)
Sometimes for eight years, or even ten or twelve;
sometimes for five or seven, and sometimes even for sixteen.

At times he indeed performs penance for eight years; at times ten, at times twelve, at times five, at times seven, and at times sixteen years—in this manner, he performs penance in many ways. || 13 || 14 ||
While he remained seated like one indifferent, established in his self-restraint, death did not harm any living beings within the web of the world. (14)
By that [wind], the surface of the earth becomes a dense mass of beings with no passage for movement during the rainy season,
like a sweating elephant covered by gadflies.

"By that"—that is, by that cause of not engaging in the violence of death—during the rainy season, the earth becomes impassable due to the dense mass of living beings, like a sweating elephant in rut being swarmed by mosquitoes; it becomes impossible to traverse. (15–18)
Then, O Rāma, those gods, by means of many stratagems, brought about the destruction of those various beings in order to remove the burden of the earth. (16)
In this way, thousands of ages, hundreds of worldly transactions, infinite beings, and worlds have all passed away. (17)
O virtuous one, this Yama named Vaivasvata, who is the leader of the ancestors,
has now [arrived] when some [of their merits] have been exhausted.
In order to prevent obstacles during the ages, one should here perform the practice of vows for twelve years within oneself, staying far away from people and cultivation.

The two verses beginning with "vaivasvata" form a single statement. Even by Yama, the son of Vivasvat (the Sun), for the very same purpose of destroying sin, such a practice of vows—austerity consisting of drawing away those who cause death from afar and keeping people far removed from slaughter—must be performed. || 19 ||
Therefore, this earth will become densely packed with mortal beings who are as if immortal; oppressed by those who have become a burden, it will be like a forest thick with undergrowth.
"Teneti" means: "praghanagulmā" refers to that [city] in which there are *praghanas*—that is, *gulmas*, meaning thickets or clusters—that are *nirantara*, or continuous, without gaps. 20, 21, 22.
With her body overwhelmed by the burden of the earth, she will seek refuge in Hari;
then Hari shall descend in two bodies as the Great One (Mahā).
The son of Vasudeva alone shall be known as Vāsudeva;
he will be one body of Hari, while the second shall be the son of Pāṇḍu.
In this exceedingly terrible battle with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
all these kinsmen of his will come to fight with Arjuna.
Seeing all those kinsmen of his standing on the verge of death, Arjuna will fall into despondency and will not exert himself for battle.
(633) Hari will awaken that body named Arjuna by means of logical arguments, using the body of Buddha, for the sole purpose of accomplishing the task at hand. || 25 ||
"Tam iti" means: by the Buddha-body, which possesses awakening and takes the form of the incarnation as Kṛṣṇa. || 25 ||

O lion among kings, contemplate the Self as infinite, unmanifest, and without beginning or middle; you are the expansive embodiment of consciousness, free from defect—you are unborn, eternal, and beyond all affliction.
"Endless," it is said. "O lion among kings"—this is an address intended to dispel the distress of grief.

Behold, that is, investigate, the Self alone, which is distinct from the body and so forth, and characterized by infinity and other such qualities. Since you have awakened [to this], you are therefore eternal and free from affliction. In this regard, *saṃvidvapuḥsphāram* is a single compound word; [it means] by means of a body whose nature is consciousness (*saṃvidrūpeṇa vapuṣā*).
"Sphāram" means extensively increased; that is to say, pervaded. || 26 ||
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it will not cease to be again.
Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain. (27)
"No. This Self, which is distinct from the body and so forth, is never born nor does it ever die;

for birth and death are attributes of the body. This Self, having come into being—that is, having experienced the act of becoming—does not "not become" again, meaning it is not devoid of the act of becoming. This Self is not such that, having not come into being, it is devoid of becoming.

Furthermore, the phrase "having come into being, he will not come into being again" should be applied in both ways. Since, having come into being, he will not come into being again like a jar or similar objects, therefore he does not die. And since, having not previously come into being, he will either come into being again at another time or not, he is unborn; this establishes the meaning of the statement "he is not born. Thus, he is unborn and eternal.
By the word "eternal" (nitya), even that modification consisting of occasional existence is excluded. "Everlasting" (śāśvata) means devoid of decay;

"ancient" (purāṇa) means devoid of growth. For a new object indeed grows. Thus, it is stated that this Self, even when the body is being slain, is not itself slain nor is it transformed—meaning it is free from the six modifications of being. || 27 ||
Established in yoga, O Dhanañjaya, perform your actions while abandoning attachment;
with your conduct dedicated to Brahman, you shall become Brahman itself in an instant. (28)

"Established in yoga": Yoga is equanimity toward success and failure; being established in that, having abandoned attachment—even the desire for results such as "May the Lord be pleased with me"—perform actions for the sake of propitiating the Lord. Thus, one whose conduct is offered to Brahman and whose good deeds are offered to Brahman becomes Brahman itself. 28.
One who has dedicated all purposes to the Lord, whose very self is the Lord, who is free from affliction,
who is the Lord— the Self of all beings— become one who adorns the surface of the earth.

With all objects surrendered to the Lord—meaning one by whom all objects, whether auspicious or inauspicious, have been offered to the Lord—and with the self surrendered to the Lord—meaning one whose very self has been dedicated to the Lord—become the Lord himself: free from affliction, the self of all beings, and the ornament of the earth. 29.
Having renounced all volitional thoughts, equanimous, with a peaceful mind, a sage whose self is united with the yoga of renunciation—act while remaining liberated in intellect. (30)
"Renounced" (saṃnyasta): "One whose self is disciplined by the yoga of renunciation"—the yoga of renunciation is the relinquishing of the fruits of action. 30, 31, 32.
Arjuna said:
O Blessed One, [please explain] the renunciation of attachment, as well as the offering to Brahman, and the renunciation (saṃnyāsa) consisting of the offering to the Lord in every respect. || 31 ||
Likewise, O Lord, what is the distinction between knowledge and yoga?
Tell me this in due order for the sake of dispelling my great delusion. (32)
The Blessed One said:

When all mental constructions have completely subsided, that state in which dense latent impressions are stilled and which possesses no form of conceptualization—those wise ones know it as the supreme Brahman. (33)

"Of all"—when there is the complete subsiding of all volitional thoughts (*saṃkalpa*), the mind is one whose dense latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been stilled and which is free from impressions; therefore, there exists no form whatsoever that is an object of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
That which remains is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) devoid of even the slightest form suitable for cultivation; the wise know that alone to be the Supreme Brahman. || 33 ||
Those of perfected intellect know that exertion to be knowledge and yoga;
they know the offering to Brahman to be the realization: "Brahman is everything—the world and I. (34)
"Tad" means that; "tad-udyogaḥ" means exertion for that purpose. || 3 || 35 ||
The wise know that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is the relinquishing of the fruits of actions;
the abandonment of the web of mental constructs is called non-attachment (asaṅga). || 35 ||
The contemplation of the oneness of the Lord within the entire web of time,
in which the appearance of duality has dissolved— this alone is the offering to the Lord.

"Entirely," etc. The contemplation of the oneness of the Lord (*īśvaraikatvabhāvanā*)—in such a way that the entire web of all mental constructs (*saṃkalpa-vikalpa-jāla*), including the whole network of temporal divisions, is free from the appearance of duality (*galitadvaitanirbhāsa*), devoid of the manifestation of difference—consists precisely in this: the contemplation of being identical with Him, realizing that the Lord alone is the inner controller of all (*sarvāntaryāmī*) and acts accordingly, and that this entire worldly transaction is His own manifestation (*tadvilāsa*). This alone [is the goal].
The offering of every worldly activity to Him alone is the dedication to the Lord. || 36 ||
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
Thus, with your self disciplined and making Me your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone. 37.
"Fixing your mind on Me": having thus, in this manner, disciplined the self—that is, the mind—and having yoked it to Me, being one whose supreme goal is Me, you shall come to Me alone. (37)
"O sinless one, know that my two forms are the Universal (sāmānya) and the Supreme (parama).
The Universal form is endowed with hands and other limbs, and bears the conch, the discus, and the mace. (38)
The four verses beginning with "sāmānyam" form a single syntactical unit. I have two forms: with form (*sākāra*) and without form (*nirākāra*).
In that regard, during the state of non-awakening, the form bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus is to be worshipped;
and through that worship, by means of the gradual transformation of the mental fluctuations, the second form—the supreme Brahman—is realized.
The meaning is that it culminates in isolation (kaivalya) and thus becomes perfected. || 38 || 39 || 40 || 41 ||
The supreme form of mine, which is without beginning or end, unique and free from affliction,
is expressed by such terms as Brahman, Ātman, and Paramātman. (39)
As long as you remain unawakened, abiding in the state of not knowing the self,
so long remain devoted to the worship of the deity in the form of the four-armed one.
Through that sequence you shall become fully awakened, and from that you will know my supreme form, which is without beginning or end, by means of which you shall not be born again. 41.
Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever established in the inner self, with desires turned away;
liberated from the dualities known as pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable state.
"Free from pride and delusion": pride means arrogance or egoism;

delusion is the ignorance caused by it—they have emerged beyond these two. Those by whom the faults of attachment have been conquered, who are constantly devoted to the inner self—that is, intent on the contemplation of the Self—and for that reason, whose desires have ceased.
Freed from the dualities of the notions of pleasure and pain, undeluded, wise, and devoid of attachment to dualities, they go to that state. || 42 || 43 ||
The wise call him a learned man whose every undertaking is free from desire and volition, and whose actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge. 43.

Free from dualities, eternally established in purity, indifferent to acquisition and preservation, self-possessed, and following whatever comes to you— thus become one who adorns the surface of the earth.

Constantly established in your own qualities, free from the concern for acquisition and preservation (niryogakṣema), indifferent to the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired, self-possessed, and with a vigilant mind, you should remain following whatever comes to pass; thus may you become one who adorns the surface of the earth, one who beautifies the world. 44.

Even if the earth should split apart, or the mountains should burst, or the wind of universal dissolution should blow, the path that follows the teacher and the scriptures must not be abandoned by the wise. (45)
"Even so": even in the face of great calamity, the path of the scriptures taught by the guru must not be abandoned by the wise. 45–46.
O virtuous one, through ignorance of the Self, latent impression (vāsanā) comes into being;
through the great awakening of self-knowledge, latent impression goes to dissolution. (46)
When the Lord of the Three Worlds had spoken thus and remained silent before him for a moment,
then the son of Pāṇḍu addressed these words there, like a bee approaching a cluster of blue lotuses.
The word "iti" indicates that he will utter these words; the meaning is that he will speak. || 47 ||
Arjuna said:
The entire burden of my grief having been dissolved, this mind of mine has become exceedingly joyful, O Blessed One;
it has been awakened by your word, just as a lotus-pond is awakened by the sun, the lord of the world.

Thus: O Lord of the Three Worlds, my intellect, awakened by your word like a lotus-plant by the sun, has reached the highest state of flourishing and clarity, its entire burden of grief having completely dissolved away. (48)
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Narrative of Arjuna," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-sāra.
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Narrative of Arjuna," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa.
p. 638) The Sixth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, O Raghava, I shall relate this ancient history; listen to it, which concerns a certain mendicant who was possessed of profound reflection. (1)

Previously, the story of Arjuna was recounted to show that even war and the like do not obstruct the mental repose of one who possesses discernment (*vivekin*). Now, in order to demonstrate that this succession of births is established as nothing more than a succession of delusions consisting of one's own volitions (*svasaṃkalpa*), the story known as the Śatarudra is presented by way of illustration. || 1 ||
There was a certain great monk who was devoted to the practice of meditative absorption; he spent his entire day constantly engaged in his own religious observances. (2)

"He was," it is said. A "great mendicant" (mahābhikṣu) is a great wandering ascetic (parivrāj), according to worldly convention, by virtue of his practice of meditative concentration and so forth. (2)
That mind of his, purified by the practice of meditative concentration, reaches whatever state it contemplates in an instant, just as water quickly becomes waves.

Regarding "concentration" (samādhi): through the practice of concentration, the mind of that monk becomes pure and stainless; whatever he thinks of or meditates upon, it quickly attains the state and essential nature of that object, becoming of that very form, just as water [takes on the form] of waves. || 3 ||
And once, having ceased from his meditative concentration, he remained with a one-pointed mind;
seated upon his own throne, he reflected for a moment on the sequence of ritual actions.
"At some time" means: having ceased from meditative absorption, that is, having emerged from samādhi; [he perceives] the sequence of actions, which is the manner of worldly transaction. || 4 ||
As he was reflecting, this intuition arose within him spontaneously:
"I shall quickly manifest the conduct of an ordinary person for the sake of my divine play."

Regarding the word "tasya" (of him): as he was reflecting, for the sake of play—that is, for the sake of diversion—a specific intuition or resolve arose spontaneously within him, thinking, "I shall manifest the state of being an ordinary person; that is, I shall embody the conduct of a common, ordinary individual. (p.
Having reflected thus, his mind remained for a while as something distinct from the body;
then, by the mere abandonment of vibration and form, it revolved like water.

"Thus" (*iti*) means: having reflected in the manner previously described, his mind then became another person, a different individual, in accordance with that reflection. For instance, by the mere abandonment of vibration (*spanda*) through the power of thought, the mind undergoes a transformation. "Vibration" (*spanda*) means movement;
"abandonment of configuration" (*saṃsthāna-saṃtyāga*) means the abandonment of the previous arrangement—that is to say, the abandonment of former latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

By that alone it revolves and attains another human state, just like water. For just as water, when moved by the force of the wind, abandons its previous configuration and assumes the form of waves and so forth, so it is in this case. (6)
Then, by that man of thought, a name was assumed according to his own desire; "I am Jīvaṭa," he suddenly wished, as if by the chance occurrence of the crow and the palm fruit.

"By him" means: by that other person, a man imagined through thought, the name "Jīvaṭa" was given—meaning it was a name produced by himself, a designation fashioned by his own mind—which was desired by chance like the "crow-and-fig" coincidence (*kākatālīya*), and not obtained through lineage, learning, conduct, or the like. The meaning is that some name arose spontaneously within himself. || 7 ||
Then Jīvaṭa, that man of the dream,
wandered for a long time through the streets of a certain city created within a dream.
"Jīvaṭa," and so forth: here, this is the succession of dreams of the mendicant, beginning with Jīvaṭa and ending with Rudra. (8)
There he drank the beverage, became intoxicated, and fell into a deep sleep;
in a dream, he beheld himself as a Brahmin, satisfied by his study and religious observances.

In his dream, Jīvaṭa saw [the Lord] satisfied by the recitation of the Vedas and the performance of what is taught therein—satisfied, that is, with the study of the Vedic scriptures and the practice of the conduct prescribed by them—and thus fulfilled in purpose. || 9 ||
Endowed with mere eloquence, like one who has reached another land in his mind,
that best of brahmins at times remained intent on his daily duties.

He perceived that his state of being a Brahmin was established by mere appearance, like the mind’s attainment of another location. For just as the mind moves from one place to another, so it was in this case. And that best of the twice-born, due to the exhaustion caused by the burden of his daily activities and the intensity of his daytime labors, became like a tree reduced to the state of a seed. (10–11)
Then, while his internal activities were suspended as he slept, the twice-born man saw himself in a dream in the state of a feudal lord, just as a tree exists in the state of a seed.
Having finished his meal,
that vassal once beheld in a dream, through a deep sleep, the sovereignty that protects the circle of the quarters.

Having fallen into a deep sleep, he saw in a dream that he had attained the status of a *sāmanta*— the lordship of a regional circle— surrounded by a multitude of clouds like an army of elephants, horses, and banners belonging to himself. And that *sāmanta*, in his dream,
beheld the sovereignty of a universal emperor (*cakravartin*), capable of protecting the entire circle of the quarters and guarding the expanse of all directions.
Once, that king, being at ease and having ceased all worldly pursuits, fell asleep;
in a dream, he beheld within himself the irreproachable form of a celestial woman.
And that king [attained] the state of a celestial woman. || 13 ||
Exhausted from lovemaking, that celestial woman fell into a deep sleep;
in a dream, she beheld within herself the state of a fawn, which is exceedingly restless.
And that celestial woman [attained] the state of a deer. || 14 ||
Once, while that doe with tremulous eyes was overcome by sleep,
she saw in a dream that she had become a creeper grown upon herself through her own habitual practice.
That female deer became a creeper. || 15 ||
Even animals perceive dreams naturally within their minds;
and for those things seen or heard, the mind's recollection remains unimpaired. (16)

Then follows the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroborative illustration): "Even animals [possess this]. Because the memory—the recollection—of things seen and heard remains unimpaired and unhurt in their minds, for that reason, by the power of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), even animals see dreams. || 16 ||
She became a creeper, resplendent with flowers, fruits, and tender shoots,
sporting like a forest goddess in a bower-creeper used for woodland play.
And that creeper, like a vine-house for the forest goddesses during their woodland sports, became a playful and graceful presence. || 17 ||
By means of an internal consciousness that had ascended to a state comparable to the form of a sprout within a seed,
she clearly perceived her own descent. (18)

And that creeper was seen by him hanging upon certain trees and such, assuming the state of a creeper, through an internal consciousness that had taken hold of a hidden object of knowledge— an object similar in form to the sprout existing within the seed— by means of this consciousness which had ascended and resorted to his own creeper-like body.
Such was the condition of the creeper that was shown. || 18 ||
Having experienced a state of dense insensibility for some time through a portion of deep sleep,
he then beheld himself situated as a bee.

Then that very creeper, by means of a power (kalā) residing in deep sleep—just as the power of consciousness is for one situated in deep sleep—experienced a dense insensibility, a stupor in the form of sleep; and within that dream, she saw herself existing as a bee. || 19 ||
He became addicted to the lotus stalks within the lotus pond;
for even the mind of one with dull intellect finds delight in something or other. (20)

And that bee, being addicted to and attached to the lotus-pond, became stuck upon its stalk. For indeed, even the mind of one who is dull-witted, ignorant of aesthetic flavor, or even of a mere worm or insect, finds delight in some particular female form. (20–21)
An elephant came to that lotus pond to agitate it;
for the step of the foolish expands only for the destruction of beautiful things. (21)
Together with that Nalinī, he there attained the state of being ground to powder,
due to his perception of her as an elephant and his constant contemplation of her as an elephant.
And that bee, being crushed by the elephant together with that lotus, [died] through the contemplation of the sight of its form.
He saw himself arisen in the form of a scent-intoxicated elephant;
indeed, like an elephant, he fell into a pit as deep as the dried-up ocean.
He saw himself manifested in the form of an elephant intoxicated by *āmoda*—that is, by a particular kind of fragrance—and that elephant was cast into a pit dug by a certain king. || 23 ||
He became a favorite of the king and was quickly trained by him;
however, having been struck down in the thick of battle at one point, he met his end. (24)
Bound and trained, having become a favorite of the king, he was slain somewhere in battle. || 24 ||
Through the practice of [mistaking] bees situated on its temples, the elephant again became a bee;
then, by being trampled by the elephant's hooves, it was reduced to powder by the lotus plant.
Through the mental cultivation of being a bee situated on the elephant's temple, he again became a bee; and that bee was crushed by the trampling of the elephant's foot. || 25 ||
Through the consciousness of being a swan dwelling at his side, Kalahaṃsaka came to be;
for a very long time, Kalahaṃsa had been wallowing in other wombs.

Through the consciousness of being a swan by the side [of his former self], he became a *kalahaṃsa*. And that *kalahaṃsa*, rolling through various wombs, was once born by chance as a *sārasa* crane from the lotus-born Brahmā; having attained the state of a Brahman-crane, he sported as that *sārasa*.
By the will of the lotus-born Brahmā, he was born as a swan-like crane. || 27 ||
Then, at one time, that bird saw Rudra in the city of Rudra;
there, the conviction arose within him, "I am Rudra," with absolute certainty.

And once, while that bird, the swan, was traveling to the city of Rudra during Brahmā’s journey, he beheld Rudra; through the contemplation of him and by the force of latent impressions, his intellect became certain of the thought, "I am Rudra. || 28 ||
There, assuming the form of a Rudra-bhūta, he sported according to his will,
engaging in various practices of the city of Śiva and delighting in the assemblies of the Gaṇas.

Regarding the word "Rudra": there, in Rudrapura, this Haṃsa—possessing a body in the form of Rudra—wandered at will according to his desire, through the celebrated customs of Śiva’s city, the social practices of the world of Rudra, such as the descriptions of Śiva’s majesty and so forth, by those well-known attendants of the assembly of Pramathas who delight in the company of the Gaṇas. 29.
Then, by means of that [wisdom] which sports with unsurpassed knowledge, Rudra perceived through his intellect his entire previous history. (30)

Regarding Rudra: that Rudra, by means of an intellect that sports with unsurpassed knowledge and expands the highest knowledge, beheld that entire account of events arising from his previous birth in its entirety. || 30 ||
That Blessed Lord Hara, whose body is consciousness free from all veils,
spoke of his own accord in private, amazed by the hundreds of his own dreams.

Regarding the term *nirāvaraṇa*: the Blessed Lord Hara, whose very body is consciousness (*vijñāna*) free from obscuration—meaning devoid of veils even across other births—was struck with wonder by his own hundred dreams; being thus amazed by those hundred of his own dreams, he spoke thus to himself in a solitary place. || 31 ||
Oh, how wondrous is this illusion that utterly deludes the universe!
Though it is unreal, it appears real and is perceived with great firmness, like water in a mirage.
"Aha! This illusion, though indeed unreal and false—like the water of a mirage—is so very firm that it appears to have real existence and utterly deludes the universe. "Vata" expresses grief. 32.
Thus, in these many and exceedingly variegated forest-lands of saṃsāra, which appear as if they were not empty, I have wandered repeatedly with the delusion that "I am. (33)

"Thus," refers to the three verses as a single syntactical unit. Wandering through many extremely diverse terrains of the forest of saṃsāra, I have traversed hundreds of wombs in the form of Jīvaṭa and others, moving along numerous paths conceived merely by my own imagination, until I reached the state of Rudra for these bodies. (33, 34, 35)
In one creation I was named Jīvaṭa;
in another, I was an eminent Brāhmaṇa; and in another, a lord of the earth.
Having been a swan in a lotus grove and an elephant in the thickets of the Vindhya mountains,
thus passing through hundreds of wombs, I have attained the state of Rudra.
p.
644) Here, infinite thousands of years and hundreds of four-yuga cycles have passed, as well as days and nights that have been traversed. || 36 ||
In this regard, there is a pair of verses forming a single syntactical unit: "This Rudra—here, throughout various births, a vast period of time such as thousands of years has passed. (36)
Having arisen, I behold all those various individual transmigrations;
by granting them perfect vision, I act for their very sake.

Therefore, having arisen and gone to those various forms of their own cyclic existences, I behold them; and by bestowing perfect light and bestowing perfect knowledge upon them, I unite them with myself. || 37 ||
Having reflected thus, Rudra went to that place of creation where the mendicant was staying in his monastery, lying asleep like a corpse. (38)

Having reflected thus, he went to that creation where the mendicant was staying in a monastery (*vihāra*) or situated in a hermitage (*maṭha*). A *vihāra* is so called because mendicants dwell within it; [therein] he remained like one in deep sleep, like a corpse. (38)
Then, having awakened that monk through his own mind and volition, he illuminated [the truth] for him; the monk also remembered his own delusion. (39)
"Having awakened him": then, having awakened that monk, he joined him with an awakened mind, with volition, and with knowledge. The monk also remembered his own delusion. (39)
Beholding Rudra as his own self, as well as [the self] consisting of Jīvaṭa and others,
that mendicant, though not subject to astonishment through his awakening, nevertheless experienced wonder.

Regarding the word "Rudra": that mendicant, having perceived himself as Rudra and likewise having perceived himself as consisting of Jīvaṭa and others, attained wonder through the power of Māyā, even though he was not worthy of astonishment due to his realization of the supreme truth through awakening. || 40 ||
Then Rudra and the mendicant both rose up and went together to some unknown place—
the worldly existence of Jīvaṭa, situated in a single corner of the space of consciousness.

Now, with the words beginning with "atha" [the text continues]: Then, when Rudra awakened Jīvaṭa and the others just as he had awakened the mendicant, they all shone forth like Rudras, being portions of Rudra due to their divine knowledge. Thereafter, having taken account of the remainder of the *prārabdha* karma—which was to be experienced by the mendicant for a hundred births—the [powers] sent by the Supreme Reality-Rudra were transferred to Jīvaṭa and the others.

The portions of Rudra each reached their own respective abodes. Because there are many Rudras and many locations for them, the term "their own" (*svaṃ svam*) is used with distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). They too—Jīvaṭa, the Brahmin, and the others—having reached their own respective stations and remaining there together with their wives and so forth, shall attain Rudra at the end of the body; such is the meaning of these six and a half verses. || 41 ||
Having quickly awakened him and directed him with both mind and consciousness,
the three of them remained both astonished and yet unastonished as they brought him back to awareness. (42)
Those Rudras, Bhikṣukas, and Jīvaṭas were either uniform or possessed three forms; they entered the worldly cycles of Brahmins and others, and likewise became united with them.
Possessing divine knowledge, those one hundred supreme Rudras, who were portions of Rudra, shone brightly;
sent by Rudra, they all departed for their respective abodes.
Having observed that illusion thus manifested by Rudra,
his own partial manifestations were sent forth once again into that very state of worldly existence.
Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the others also returned to their own abodes;
then, having cast off their bodies along with their wives over the course of time,
they all attained Rudra at the end of their lives together with Rudra himself.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Everything exists within the treasury of consciousness; in whatever manner it perceives, it undoubtedly attains that very thing, because it is the self of all. 47.
"All" means: in the sheath of consciousness—which, like a treasure-chest, is the repository of all things—everything exists as its very own nature. || 47 ||
Whatever is seen in a dream and whatever is beheld through mental constructs exists in that very way there, being of that nature at all times. (48)

Therefore, because it is the self of all, this Consciousness exists at all times as that which consists of whatever [form], in whatever manner, and in whatever way, since everything is a transformation of consciousness. || 48 ||
The object that is reached through the state of mental construction or dream is not attained without the practice of supreme meditation and yoga. (49)

If it exists, then it must be attainable; to this he says: "By resolve" (saṃkalpa). That very state of perfection (*siddhadaśā*) by which an object situated in resolve—that is, existing within the imagination—is attained, cannot be obtained without the practice of yoga, repeated cultivation, and the restraint of the vital breath (*vāyu*). || 49 ||
But those for whom the insights born of yoga and wisdom have borne fruit and remain steadfast—they, such as Śaṅkara and others, perceive everything everywhere. (50)

Regarding the phrase "of those who": for those perfected ones (*siddhas*) whose insights arise from the knowledge of yoga— where "yoga" is meditative absorption (*samādhi*), "knowledge" is the understanding of the inner science (*adhyātma-śāstra*), and their resulting "insights" or visions are "fruitful," meaning they have become effective—
these individuals, such as Śaṅkara and others, [can manifest] every object everywhere according to their own volition.
They perceive [them] in place and in time. || 50 ||
For every desired task is accomplished by one who is single-mindedly devoted;
for who, looking toward the southern quarter, can reach the northern direction? (51)
Even every desired task is accomplished only for one who is single-mindedly devoted to that [one goal]; for who, looking toward the southern quarter, can ever reach the northern direction? (51)
The object of intention is understood only by those intent upon the object of intention;
the object situated at the tip is understood only by those intent upon the object situated at the tip. || 52 ||

It is understood through the very intent of one's resolve. Even an object situated at the forefront is understood only by those intent upon that foremost object—by those whose minds are fixed on the thing standing right before them. || 52 ||
He who desires to attain a resolve established in the intellect situated at the highest point will,
due to the absence of one-pointed concentration, destroy that very duality.

Regarding the phrase "situated in front": when an object situated in front is present before the intellect—that is, when it stands established in the mind—a fool desires to obtain the intended object through his volition. At that time, the undiscriminating person, due to a lack of single-mindedness and an absence of focused intent, would not rely upon either of those two: neither the object situated in front nor the mentally constructed one. That which is present in the intellect, he does not desire to attain.
Since that [object] does not reside in the cognition, the destruction [of the object] is unestablished for both parties as well. || 53 ||
"May I be a Vidyādhara here; may I be a knower of the Vedas"—the fulfillment of this single cognition serves as an illustration for the attainment of one's goal. (54)

"Here" means: "In this place and at this time, may I become a Vidyādhara for the sake of my resolve," or "May I become a knower of the Vedas here"—whatever constitutes the success of single-minded meditation, that is, the connection with the fruit of meditation directed toward a single object, is itself the illustrative example for the accomplishment of the task. || 54 ||
Therefore, because it was fixed upon a single purpose, the life-force of the mendicant attained the state of Rudra;
and through that identity with Rudra, the reality of his intended object was achieved.

"Therefore" means: for the reason previously stated—namely, because of being established in a single object, that is, being established solely in the object of volition (saṃkalpa)—the soul, having attained the state of Rudra in the form of a mendicant, achieved the reality of the object of volition by means of that very nature as Rudra.
Those who live with the intention of being monks each perceive that world as distinct; because they possess the nature of Rudra, they have all attained reality.

Regarding the word "bhikṣu": those living beings who have achieved their intentions through the resolve of being monks—because their resolves possess truth and efficacy due to their nature as Rudras—therefore perceive that world individually as distinct and unique, owing to their autonomy and the reality of their volitions; such is the meaning. || 56 ||
Thus, by the power of Rudra’s consciousness, those such as the Brahmin Jīvaṭa went to cities created by their own volitions through the mental resolve of the monks.

"Thus. Those previously mentioned—the Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the others, who were fashioned by the mental constructs of the monks—went to, that is, reached, their own cities of mental construction, the abodes fashioned by their own volitions, through the majesty of Rudra. (Verses 57–61)
Then, having united with Rudra, they entered that supreme state.
Rāma said:
In this way, how did those [beings] such as the Brahmin Jīvaṭa come to possess reality through the mental construction of the monks? Wherein lies the reality of an object of mental construction? (59)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as this Janārdana becomes one and then a thousand,
he maintains the stability of the world through his playful incarnations and partial manifestations.
Thus, through the mental construction of those monks, Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the others—though they were merely portions of pure consciousness—stood there as if they were real. (61)
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Hundred Rudras," in the chapter on Nirvāṇa within the *Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭhasāra*, the means to liberation.
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Hundred Rudras," in the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhavivaraṇa.
p. 648) Seventh Chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having become one who maintains the silence of deep sleep and having abandoned the playfulness of the mind,
remain established in the firmly grasped state, liberated from the impurity of conceptualization.

To demonstrate that this succession of births was previously established through the delusion consisting of one's own volition (*saṃkalpa*), the narrative of Śatarudra was told. Now, a series of Vetāla riddles—difficult to resolve like a cluster of questions regarding a cucumber that induces the silence of deep sleep—is being set forth, beginning with the verse "suṣupta... and so on.

Having abandoned the playfulness of the mind—the mental sport consisting of volitions and the like—and being free from the impurity of conceptualization, that is, devoid of the stain of latent impressions (vāsanā), become possessed of the silence of deep sleep characterized as will be described hereafter; thus, having firmly grasped that state, remain established in the nature of Brahman. || 1 ||
Rāma said:
O Lord of Mauna, O Brahman, I know the silence of speech, the silence of the senses, and the silence of wood;
tell me, what is called the silence of deep sleep? || 2 ||

Regarding the word "vāk" (speech): the definitions of speech, silence (*mauna*), and so forth will be stated. O Mauneśa—*mauna* is the assembly of sages (*muni*), and you are its Lord; thus, it means "O best of sages. || 2 || 3 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, the sage is here declared by the best of sages to be of two kinds:
one is the ascetic of wood, and the other is the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 3 ||
When spiritual practice remains uncultivated and withered,
one who is firmly resolved yet forcibly subdues the collection of his senses becomes a "wooden ascetic" (kāṣṭhatāpasa), a mere sage in name.

If one remains firmly resolved upon ritual action— which is uncultivated, devoid of the meditation on Brahman, and consequently dry and sapless— consisting of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and the like, such a sage, though having conquered the collection of his senses through Haṭha-yoga, would be a mere ascetic of wood. || 4 ||

Having understood this as it truly is, those whose selves are cultivated and who abide in the Self—even if they appear like ordinary people—are inwardly satisfied; such a person is remembered as a liberated sage.

"Yathā" (as): That sage who, having understood this world as it truly is, has resolved that "all this is indeed Brahman," and whose self is cultivated—meaning one who has determined the reality of the Self as "I am indeed Brahman"—who abides in the Self, contemplating his own true nature even while appearing like an ordinary person through mere worldly transaction; |||
Satisfied by the experience of the bliss of his own inner nature, that sage remains; he is known as one liberated while living. || 5 ||
That state which existed between these two lords of sages when they were tranquil—
a state whose essence consists of mental certainty— is expressed by the word "mauna" (silence).

He states the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) that follows from both [the preceding verses] with the words "of these two" (*etayoḥ*). Of these two aforementioned lords of sages, whose minds are tranquil and free from modification, as they proceed, there is a state of mind characterized by certainty; such a state—whose essence (*ātman*) or nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the mind’s certainty, its single-pointedness through yoga or the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)—is the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*).
It is described by the word "mauna" (silence). || 6 ||
Vāṅmauna is the restraint of speech; indriyamauna is the forcible suppression of the senses;
akṣamauna is the renunciation of all physical activities, which is designated as kāṣṭhamauna.

In order to define the silence of deep sleep (*suṣupta-mauna*), he first describes the other types of silence, beginning with the verse starting "vāk" (speech): The silence of speech (*vāṅ-mauna*) arises from the restraint of words; the restraint of the senses such as the eyes through force—that is, by means of *haṭhayoga*—is the silence of the senses (*akṣa-mauna*).
By that very [restraint], the abandonment of all activities—the movements of the body and its limbs—is the wooden silence (*kāṣṭha-mauna*). || 7 ||
This triad of silences, which consists of the flickering movement of the mind, remains established;
the domain of these silences of forceful restraint is the wooden ascetic.

"Prasphurat" (throbbing): this aforementioned triad of silences (*mauna*) exists as a throbbing mental fabrication (*cittakalana*), that is, as a manifesting mental latent impression (*vāsanā*). Therefore, the object and support of these "silences by force" (*haṭhamauna*) is merely the state of a wooden log (*kāṣṭhatāpa*), and not one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*);
such is the meaning. || 8 ||
That which is without division, without effort, and established as being without beginning or end—
whether one is meditating or not meditating— that is called the silence of deep sleep.

Now, with four verses, he describes the silence of deep sleep (*suṣupta-mauna*): "The undivided" (*avibhāgam*), etc. For a sage—whether meditating or not meditating, whether inward-turned or outward-turned—there is the undivided, meaning the absence of the distinctions of waking and so forth; it is effortless, meaning the absence of the exertion required to restrain the organs of action; and it is without beginning or end.
That state established in Brahman which is devoid of beginning and end is called the silence born of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-mauna*);
the meaning is that great yoga itself is the silence of deep sleep. As the omniscient Yogi said: "Whether the phenomenal world appears or does not appear, that which remains the same—"

"With the limbs embraced by both knowledge and ignorance—that very nature of the Self, dense with bliss, they call the state of the Supreme Brahman, the Great Yoga. And as it is said in the Śaiva tradition: "When Śiva alone is contemplated as the one innate nature, free from all adjuncts, that very mental modification is here called the Great Yoga. (9)
Having understood this delusion of the world's diversity as it truly is,
when one remains established therein without doubt, that is called the silence of deep sleep.

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): having understood the manner in which this world—which is deluded by multiplicity and wandering in diversity—has come into being as it truly is; and having ascertained that it is of the nature of Brahman because it is superimposed upon Brahman; and having reached a state free from doubt, which is non-conceptual and established in the state of Brahman—that indeed is the silence of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-mauna*). However, in some places...
The reading is *sauṣuptaṃ maunasaṃgatam*. In this context, *maunasaṃgatam* means "associated with silence," that is, the state of silence or the manner of silence. || 10 ||
"This entire expanse is indeed Śiva, whose nature consists of manifold consciousness"—
this infinite state thus established is called the silence of deep sleep (sauṣupta-mauna). (11)
"Aneka" (manifold): this world has as its nature many forms of consciousness—that is, it is such that its selves or inherent natures consist of manifold consciousness.
That which is thus extended and pervasive is Śiva-Brahman alone. That infinite, boundless state of abiding in Brahman is called the silence of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-mauna*). || 11 ||
Space is neither space nor is it anything at all; it exists and yet does not exist.
That which is thus established—equally poised and tranquil—is that silence which is like deep sleep.

"Space": the entire world is space because it is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*); it is not [space] in the sense of possessing material form. It both exists and does not exist: it exists because the reality of its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is perceived as being of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*), and it does not exist because it is a mental construction (*kalpita*).
Having thus ascertained that the world has no existence apart from Brahman, one realizes that which remains—equal, of a single form, peaceful, and changeless. That which...
The culmination is silence like that of deep sleep; the meaning is that silence is equal to deep sleep. || 12 ||
Indeed, the silence of deep sleep is attained by two kinds of masters of yoga:
some are Sāṃkhya-yogins, while others are Yoga-yogins. (13)
Regarding the term "suṣupta" (deep sleep): those who practice Sāṃkhya and Yoga, as well as those who practice the yoga of union, will be described [in the following verses]. || 13 ||

Those who, through the awakening of right knowledge, have attained the perfectly accomplished singular samādhi, are known as Sāṃkhyas; they are understood by their very number [of principles] and are remembered as Yogins.

Regarding the word "samyak" (perfectly): those yogins who, through the awakening of perfect knowledge—that is, through the dawning of the knowledge of reality—have attained the well-perfected single-pointed concentration (*ekasamādhi*), which is the resting of the mind in the one, non-dual Brahman, are remembered as *sāṃkhyayogins* because they are understood by means of that very number, namely, perfect knowledge itself. || 14 ||

Those who, through skillful means, have attained the state where the vital breaths such as prāṇa and the rest are completely stilled—being free from affliction and without beginning or end—they are remembered as the yogins of yoga. || 15 ||

Regarding the phrase "prāṇādi": those who, through reasoning and the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga), have attained the state that is free from disease and without beginning or end when the vital breaths such as prāṇa and the others have been completely stilled—they are remembered as yogayogins. || 15 ||
But what is to be accepted by all is the peaceful, unconditioned state;
for that very same supreme station which is attained by the Sāṃkhyas is indeed attained by the Yogins as well. (16)

"Upādeyam" means: the peaceful, unconditioned state alone is to be accepted by all yogins; for this reason, that supreme state which is attained by the Sāṃkhya yogins is also attained through yoga. || 16 ||
Know that to be the supreme state where the activity of breath and mind is not perceived at all, and which is free from the snare of latent impressions (vāsanā). 17.

To the question "What is that state?", he says: "Wherein... In that state, wherein the activity—the functional operation—of the vital breath and the mind, being pervaded and encompassed by the snare of latent impressions (vāsanā)—for vāsanā itself is a snare due to its binding nature—is not perceived at all, know that very nature of the Self to be the supreme state, the essence of the Supreme Brahman.
Know this. || 17 ||
The mind has arisen in vain and is indeed non-existent, because it does not perceive [its own reality];
like one observing the form of one's own death in a dream, it is not found to exist.

Regarding the word "mind" (*mana*): the mind, in reality, is indeed non-existent; because it is not observed and cannot withstand inquiry, it has arisen in vain, like the cognition of death in a dream. Therefore, when examined and investigated, it is not found to exist. The sense is that the cessation of that which is established only through a lack of inquiry is entirely logical upon investigation. || 18 ||
The intensive practice of a single reality, the dissolution of the vital breaths,
and the restraint of the mind— this is the summary of the meaning of the word "liberation."
"Ekam" (one) means: the intense practice of a single reality (*ekatattvaghanābhyāsa*), which is the uninterrupted contemplation of one's own chosen principle;
as well as the dissolution of the vital breaths (*prāṇavilaya*) and the restraint of the mind (*manonigraha*). This triad alone constitutes the summary of the term "liberation.
Therefore, the meaning is that this much alone is the means to liberation. || 19 ||
The practice of a single object, the restraint of the vital breath, and the dissolution of the mind—
when even one of these is fully perfected, the others are spontaneously accomplished.
"Of one" (eketi): the meaning is that among the three—beginning with the practice of a single principle—if even one is accomplished, the others are also accomplished. || 20 ||
The vital breath and the mind are eternally inseparable in living beings; they exist as a mixture, like the fragrance of a flower or like sesame oil and sesame seeds. (21)
The two verses beginning with "avinābhāvini" form a single syntactical unit. The vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*cetas*) are the agents for living beings;
because they are inseparable, like sesame seeds and oil, or like a flower and its fragrance, they remain mixed and mutually connected, like the container and the contained. || 21 ||
Like the container and the contained, they perish in the absence of either one;
and through their own destruction, they bring about the supreme effect known as liberation. || 22 ||
For this reason, in the absence of one, both perish; and by their own destruction as the cause, they produce the supreme effect known as liberation. || 22 ||

One should contemplate the state of being within a single, firmly established reality; through one's own repeated practice, that state of being attains its full manifestation until it is completely pure.

Regarding the word "ekasmin" (in one): One should cultivate the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) toward a single reality that is firmly established and authoritative, until—by means of one's own practice—that expanded state of being reaches the nature of what is being cultivated. || 23 ||
When the mind becomes one-pointed, it instantly becomes—by virtue of its nature resulting from long-term cultivation—a state in which the entire flood of particularities has been stilled. (24)

Regarding the word "yat": the mind (*cetas*), that is, the consciousness (*citta*), when it becomes one-pointed—that is, focused on a single object—due to its nature of long-term cultivation and by virtue of sustained contemplation over a long period of time, then, having stilled the entire flood of particularities and ceased all distinctions, it becomes that very object in an instant. || 24 || 25 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen to these auspicious questions uttered by the Vetāla during the delusion of the dream of saṃsāra, which have come to my memory through this occasion. (25)
In the great Vindhya forest there was a Vetāla of massive form;
out of pride, he came to a certain sacred circle with the intent to kill.
"It exists" means the mandala is the location. "With the intent to kill" means with the desire to devour. || 26 ||
Formerly, that Vetāla dwelt in a certain abode of virtuous people; being constantly satisfied by the offering of many oblations, he lived in happiness. (27)
By means of the offering of much strength, that is, by the presentation of various kinds of oblations prepared from meat and other substances. || 27 ||
Even though he was hungry, he did not kill the man who had arrived before him without cause or offense; for the virtuous are indeed observers of justice. (28)

"Without cause" (nirnimittam): That Vetāla, even though hungry, does not kill a man who has arrived before him without fault and for no reason. For (hi) because of this reason, the virtuous are the perceivers of justice and the promoters of justice. The meaning is that the Vetāla, by virtue of his knowledge of Brahman, does not kill unjustly. || 28 || 29 ||
In due time, that dweller of the forest went to another city, impelled by hunger to devour a man according to his custom. (29)
There he encountered the king who had gone out on his nocturnal round;
that fierce night-stalker addressed him with a deep and terrible voice.

Regarding the word *tatra* (therein): it means "having emerged from his night-wanderings. For kings, in order to deliberate upon the stability of their kingdom, wander about at night alone in disguised attire. It is [the chariot] that has emerged from such a night-wandering. 30, 31, 32, 33.
The Vetāla said:
"O King, you have now been captured by me, Bhīma the Vetāla!
Where will you go? You are destroyed; become my food this very day! (31)
The king said:
O night-stalker, if you devour me here by force against all justice, your head shall split into a thousand pieces; of this there is no doubt.
The Vetāla said:
"I shall not devour you, for that would be unjust; indeed, this is called justice by the wise.
You are a king, and all the hopes of those who seek must be fulfilled by you. (33)
O King, fulfilling this request of mine which seeks the truth of existence,
you ought to correctly explain these questions posed by me. (34)
"Mine" (mameti). It means "possibility" (saṃbhava) or "that which has the sense of possibility" (saṃbhavad-arthām). 34.
To which sun do the universes belong as mere atoms?
In what wind do the great particles of the vast sky manifest? (35)
Now, the questions of the Vetāla by means of five verses—beginning with "Of whom" (kasya)—these six also become clear at the time of the answers. 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40.
Moving from one dream to another by the hundreds and thousands, who abandons their own pure and luminous essential nature when they do not actually abandon it? (36)
Just as a plantain trunk consists of nothing but layers upon layers of leaves,
one within another and further within, so too is that very same subtle atom.
And since the suns, the solar orbs, and Mount Merus have assumed the form of the cosmic egg, for what atom would these be "atoms" if it does not abandon its atomicity? (38)
Within the solid, single interior of a stone from a great mountain—an atom that is indeed without parts—the marrow of the three worlds is contained. (39)
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the Vetāla had spoken thus, the king smiled and, making the space white with the luster of his teeth, spoke these words to answer the questions.
The king said:
This sun of consciousness has risen; it illumines all this.
This supreme sun of pure awareness is the one whose inner disposition has been purified. 41.

Regarding that, he provides the answer to the question—"Whose are these cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*), and what are the minute particles or subtle fragments of whose sun’s rays?"—in two verses beginning with "This" (*eṣa*). When asked, "Of which sun?", you have stated by way of a different turn of phrase that it is indeed the Sun of Consciousness (*citsūrya*). For it is this very Sun of Consciousness that previously heated—that is, illuminated—this world.

"By its light all this shines," according to the Śruti. In some versions, there is the reading "this sun of consciousness has risen" (*eṣa citsūrya uditaḥ*). In that case, the meaning of "risen" (*uditaḥ*) is simply "declared by you. He states the distinction of this [sun] from the well-known physical sun: "This is the supreme sun, the self of consciousness whose disposition is purified, who, in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), impels all internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*)."
For even the light of the sun and other luminaries is but a mere fraction of that [divine] splendor. As it is said in the Gītā:
"Know that splendor which, residing in the sun, illuminates the entire world, and that which is in the moon and in fire—that splendor is mine. (41)
These expanses of worlds are but motes of dust belonging to that very sun of supreme consciousness; they shine and exist by its radiance alone. (42)
These expanses of worlds are but particles, like motes of dust, belonging to that very supreme sun of consciousness; they exist, arise, and dissolve by its light alone.
The existence of time, the existence of space, the existence of motion, as well as that consisting of consciousness and the existence of pure intellect—all these and so forth are purifying. (43)

He explains the second question—“In what wind do the great voids and other particles flicker?”—with two verses beginning with *kāla*: The existence of time (*kālasattā*) is the manifestation of the power whose form is time.

Likewise, the manifestation of the sky (*nabhaḥsphūrti*) is the existence of the sky (*nabhaḥsattā*). The existence of vibration (*spandasattā*) is the existence of the wind, whose nature is vibration. Now, [the existence] consisting of consciousness...

The existence of pure consciousness, the creation of mere consciousness, and so forth—this is the purifying form, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, reflected within consciousness. || 43 ||
In the wind consisting of the Supreme Self, the restless dust vibrates; like fragrance in a flower-bodied object, it is by its very nature both identical to and different from that form.

The five elements are restless; just as fragrance exists within the parts of a flower—the constituent members of the flower—it likewise exists in the wind, which consists of the supreme self (paramātman). Therein, that which is both of that form and not of that form manifests by its own nature. Its being "of that form" is due to its being the essential nature (svarūpa), because it is manifest, and because it serves as the cause for cognition through some particular aspect. It is "not of that form" [because it is not limited to that specific form].
It should be understood [that this is] due to its being changeless, insentient, consisting of suffering, and so forth. || 44 ||
In the great dream called the world, as one passes from one dream to another,
the tranquil Brahman— augmented by its own tranquility— does not abandon its peaceful form. (45)

He explains the third question with a verse— beginning with "jagat"— showing that even while passing from one dream to another hundreds of thousands of times and abandoning previous dreams, it does not abandon its own nature, which is pure and brilliantly luminous.
The entire world is a great dream because it consists of illusion; within it, individual births are like minor dreams.

Even while experiencing such dreams, the Self does not abandon its peaceful form, which is imagined within the changeless nature of Brahman and augmented by tranquility. Although transmigrating as a *jīva*, it does not abandon its state of being Brahman, for the world of transmigration [is illusory].
The meaning is: "because it is imagined. || 45 ||
Just as a plantain trunk consists of nothing but layers one within the other,
so too this entire universe, though it is Brahman itself, unfolds as a mere succession of inner and inner layers.

He states the answer to the fourth [objection] with the verse beginning "rambhāstambha": Just as a plantain trunk (*rambhāstambha*)—that is, a banana stalk—is seen to consist of nothing but layers of leaves when repeatedly peeled apart, so too this entire universe, though appearing in manifold variety, is upon internal investigation found to be Brahman alone. 46.
Because of its subtlety and its unattainability, the Supreme Self is the supreme atom;
yet because of its infinity, it alone has attained the state of being the foundation for Mount Meru and all else.

Even great entities such as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) do not abandon their atomic nature; thus, with the half-verse beginning with "sūkṣmatvāt," he explains the fifth question—namely, "Of which atom are these atoms?"—as follows: Because of His subtlety, the Supreme Self is the supreme atom (*paro'ṇuka*), being impossible to grasp as a specific "this," unobtainable, and impossible to reach.

It is equal to an atom. This very Supreme Self, because of its infinity—being undivided by space, time, and so forth—attains the state of being the root of Meru and other such things; that is, it becomes the material cause (upādānatva) of Meru and the like, which are themselves limited. || 47 ||
Before him, Mount Meru and other such things appear like a mere atom.

And that object, such as Mount Meru and the like, appears before that Supreme Self like a minute atom; for, in comparison with the greatness of the Supreme Self, things such as Mount Meru are exceedingly subtle. || 48 ||
This Supreme Person is an atom because he is unattainable, yet he is a great mountain because he fills [all space];
though he consists of all limbs, he is devoid of limbs. (49)

With two and a half verses beginning with "para," he explains the sixth question— that this triple world, which is partless in the form of atoms, is like the marrow, the essential core, and the single hard-natured substance within the stone of a great mountain— stating: "This person, because it is unobtainable and unattainable, is also denoted by the word 'atom' (paramāṇu)."
Because it fills all sound and because it is all-pervading, even the Great Mountain—though appearing as a gross manifestation composed of all constituent parts—is in reality devoid of parts. || 49 ||

Because it has representation-only as its essence and consists of the forms of all bases, know, O virtuous one, that this triple world is merely the marrow of this representation-only; indeed, know that the triple world is the very core of consciousness-only. (50)

Since this [person], whose nature is the substratum of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), has consciousness-only as its essence, it is understood that consciousness alone is his essential constituent;

thus, for this person who is consciousness-only, the three worlds are merely his marrow—their essence being nothing but a solidified portion of him. For this reason, the three worlds abide within the midst of consciousness-only.
Therefore, the sense is that because it occupies a middle position, its nature as a cat is appropriate. || 50 || 51 || 52 ||
Having heard this from the mouth of the king, the Vetāla attained peace through that contemplation which had arisen there by virtue of his purified mind. (51)
Having become tranquil in body and having gone to a secluded and blameless place,
he became absorbed in uninterrupted meditation, forgetting his slight hunger.
Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Narrative of the Vetāla," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Yogavāsiṣṭha-sāra*, concerning the means to liberation.
Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Narrative of the Vetāla," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa. || 7 ||
p. 359) The Eighth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Withdrawing the mind from all directions with a tranquil inner self,
making it fall into a continuous flow, remain without desire, your intellect at peace.

Previously, the questions of the Vetāla were presented to demonstrate the discernment that brings about the silence of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-mauna*). Now, however, the story of Bhagīratha is told to show that even this rest of the mind, though difficult to attain, is obtained through one's own effort alone—beginning with the words "having withdrawn" (*saṃhṛtya*). Having withdrawn—that is, having drawn back—the mind from all external objects.

Remain with a tranquil mind, characterized by an inner self (antaḥkaraṇa) that is steady and established in its own true nature, performing actions that have entered the stream and come down through the succession of traditional conduct, yet free from desire. || 1 ||
Having made the mind itself as clear as space, the sage should remain with a single-pointed, tranquil self, seeing with equanimity everywhere.
"Regarding 'ākāśa' (space): by the mind alone—that is, by one's own mind intent upon inquiry. || 2 || 3 ||
For a king of steady intellect, free from delusion, who follows what has been attained, even that which is difficult to accomplish succeeds— just as it did for King Bhagīratha.
Rāma said:
O Lord, please tell me how King Bhagīratha’s descent of the Gaṅgā was accomplished through the wondrous power of his mind.
The "marvel of the mind" (cittacamatkṛti) is a mental state that produces wonder; [it is] by means of that. || 4 || 5 || 6 || 7 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
There was a king named Bhagīratha, supremely righteous, who was like an ornament upon the circle of the earth bounded by the oceans. (5)
Immediately upon their resolve, supplicants obtained whatever they desired from him,
whose face was as bright as the moon, just as if from a wish-fulfilling gem.
By him, the friend of the world, his kinsmen dwelling in the netherworld were led by a series of steps along the Ganges to the realm of Brahmā. (7)
Even for that lord of the earth, while he was in the prime of youth and reflecting upon this worldly course which is so full of turmoil, [the following occurred].

"Youth" refers to a pair of verses. "Possessing the wonder of excellent dispassion" means that in which there is a beautiful wonder of dispassion, a firm resolve toward detachment. "A particle of inquiry" means subtle investigation. (8) (9)
A spark of reflection on the wonder of dispassion arose;
yet, by fate, even in my youth, [this] creeper withered like [a plant] in a desert.
Then, in a secluded place, this lord of the earth reflected upon this course of worldly existence, which is eternally crowded with inconsistencies.
"In solitude" means crowded with what is improper; that is, crowded—that is, agitated—by what is improper and unjust. 10.
Again the day, again the night, and again hundreds of acts of giving and taking;
yet by one performing such actions, only that which is dry and tasteless is obtained. 11.

"Again" (punar): "Śyāmā" means night. "Karma" refers to worldly activity. "Dry" (śuṣka) means tasteless, sapless, or possessing a contrary flavor. "A hundred acts of giving and taking" (dānādānaśata) means that a hundred instances of renunciation and enjoyment are obtained. || 11 ||
I consider that deed alone to be well-done by which, once attained in this world, nothing remains unattained; all other action is but a mere colic.

"By which"—meaning: I consider that very thing to be well-done (*sukṛta*) by which, once attained, not even the slightest desired object remains unattained. Any other remaining action is like cholera (*viṣūcikā*), because it is the cause for repeated engagement [in rebirth]. The meaning is that only an action which is the cause for the cessation of bondage is a "good deed. As Prahlāda said: "That is not an action..."
"That knowledge which leads to bondage is for liberation; other action leads to exhaustion, while another knowledge is skill in the arts.
(12, p. 661) Again and again, he feels no shame while performing stale actions.
But one who is not deluded in intellect—what indeed would he do like a child? (13)
Then once, his mind agitated and fearing worldly existence, Bhagīratha questioned his guru Tritula in private.
O Blessed One, how does the end of all sufferings—consisting of forms such as old age, death, and delusion, which cause fear—come about? (15)
Tritula said:

O King, by means of the full awakening to the object of knowledge—which has arisen from the self through long-standing equanimity, which delights in non-differentiation, and which fills the very soul—[the world is pervaded]. || 16 ||

The two verses form a single sentence. By that which has arisen—that which has emerged—as the self of eternal equanimity, in the form of eternal equanimity, as the aspect perceived by all; by that which sports in non-differentiation, which flashes forth without distinction, which is full, undivided, and of a nature filled with pervasion;
[this occurs] through the awakening to the object of knowledge, that is, through the direct realization of the supreme reality (*paratattva*).
All sufferings are exhausted. The knots—the causes of bondage such as egoism and the rest—are shattered and severed.

Doubts—such as whether liberation exists or not, or whether the Self is of the nature of supreme bliss or not—come to rest. All actions, both meritorious and non-meritorious in nature, all actions whatsoever, come to rest.
For there is the scriptural text beginning with, "The knot of the heart is severed," and so forth. || 16 || 17 ||
All sufferings are exhausted, the knots are severed on all sides, doubts go to dissolution, and all karmas, O sinless one, [come to an end]. 17.
But they know the Knowable to be the Self, whose nature is perfectly pure consciousness;
it is omnipresent and eternal, neither setting nor rising. (18)

To the question "What is that which is to be known?", he says: "The knowable. The meaning is that the Self alone—whose nature is consciousness, eternal, all-pervading, and pure—is the knowable. || 18 ||
Bhagīratha said:
O Lord of Sages, I know that there exists only pure consciousness—omnipresent, tranquil, stainless, and immutable; nothing other than this, such as the body and so forth, exists. (19)

The two verses beginning with "cinmātram" constitute a single statement: "I know that there exists only the attributeless Brahman, whose nature is pure consciousness and which is characterized by peace and other such qualities; nothing else whatsoever—such as the body and so forth—exists in reality apart from the Self. (19) However, O Lord, my realization of this does not yet become clear.
How might I always possess consciousness consisting of this much alone? (20)
However, in this matter, realization—that is, knowledge—does not attain firm establishment. Therefore, the meaning is:
"In what manner, by what means, might I come to possess such a mere awareness, consisting of the continuous contemplation of pure consciousness? Please explain that method. || 20 ||
Tritula said:
Through knowledge, the mind attains absorption in the object of knowledge within the sky of the heart;
thereafter, having become the universal body, the individual soul is not born again.

Regarding the phrase "by means of knowledge" (*jñānena*): when the mind, through knowledge—characterized as will be described hereafter and serving as the means to knowledge—attains a state of being fixed upon the object of knowledge, that is, a state of being fixed upon its own true nature (*svarūpa*) within the "sky of the heart" (*hṛdambare*), or the space of the heart; then, at that time, the individual soul (*jīva*), having become the body of all and having become the self of all, is not born again. This occurs spontaneously when, through inward-turnedness, there is a state of being fixed upon one's own true nature.
The meaning is that, having become Brahman whose self is everything, one does not return again to the state of an individual soul. || 21 ||
Non-attachment and absence of clinging toward children, wife, home, and so forth;
and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant. 22.

To the question "What is that knowledge?", he says: non-attachment is lack of attachment to sense objects; it is the absence of infatuation and freedom from the sense of "mine" regarding children, wife, home, and so forth; and it is constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the desirable and undesirable—that is, being free from joy and dejection in the face of the pleasant and the unpleasant. (22)
The constant contemplation of that [Self] through the yoga of non-difference from one's own self;
resorting to solitary places; and a lack of delight in the assembly of people. (23)

"By means of non-dual yoga"—that is, through the meditation on non-difference—the continuous and uninterrupted contemplation of one's own true nature is the "contemplation of Brahman," which is the constant realization that "I am indeed Brahman. "Resorting to secluded places" means having the habit of dwelling in a place that is solitary, pure, and devoid of people. "In the assembly of people" refers to a gathering of common folk.
Discontent and instability. || 23 ||
p.
663) Being established in inner knowledge and seeing the purpose of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge; that which is otherwise is ignorance. (24)

Devotion to the knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātmajñānaniṣṭhatva*) means being intent upon the knowledge whose object is the Self. The vision of the purpose of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānārthadarśana*) is the contemplation of the ultimate cessation of suffering, which is the goal of the knowledge of reality. These aforementioned factors are called "knowledge" because they serve as the means to knowledge. Anything other than this—that is, contrary to the stated means—[is not knowledge].
Ignorance consists of attachment to sense objects and so forth; the meaning is that it is the cause of saṃsāra. || 24 ||
O King, that knowledge which brings about the destruction of passion and hatred and serves as the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra is attained upon the subsiding of the ego-sense.

Regarding "rāge" (in passion): the meaning is that because the state of identifying with the body and so forth is an obstacle to the knowledge of the Self, it is only when that [identification] has subsided that the true nature of the Self is realized. || 25 ||
Bhagīratha said:
O illustrious one, tell me how this sense of "I," which has long been firmly rooted in this body like a tree on its own mountain, is to be abandoned.

Regarding the word "body": the sense is that because saṃsāra is beginningless, the ego (ahaṃkāra), which is its root, has taken deep root; therefore, its abandonment is difficult to accomplish. || 26 ||
Tritula said:
Having abandoned the inclination toward the flood of enjoyments through manly effort,
and having attained the blossomed state of being, one should proceed to the dissolution of the ego.

Regarding the phrase "by human effort" (*pauruṣeṇa*): human effort refers to the exertion consisting of the practice of right knowledge, meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and so forth, which is the cause for the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). By means of that human effort, having abandoned the flow of enjoyment—that is, the latent impression of sense objects—and having attained, or resorted to, an expanded and perfect state of being, [one achieves] the dissolution of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
"He should go" means "he should accomplish. || 27 ||
As long as the entire cage of the bodily mechanisms— consisting of shame and the like— is not shattered,
so long does the ego-sense remain manifest, even when one is reduced to utter poverty. (28)

Regarding the term *yantraṇā*: shame (*lajjā*) is the contraction of the mind toward an improper action; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), pride in one's caste, family, and other such factors are included. As it has been said: "Compassion, apprehension, longing, shame, and disgust as the fifth—along with family, character, and birth—these eight are proclaimed as the fetters (*pāśas*). Such [is the nature of]...

The cage of the machines [of the senses] consists of shame and the like; "one who possesses nothing" (*akiñcana*) is one for whom there remains nothing whatsoever beyond his true nature due to the state of having nothing at all.
The meaning is that as long as everything has not been shattered and abandoned through the mere residue of that state of possessing nothing, egoism (*ahaṃkṛti*) does not clearly cease. || 28 ||
If you remain motionless, having abandoned all this through the intellect, then, upon the dissolution of the ego, you yourself are the supreme state. (29)
"Everything" means all this—shame, pride, and so forth; that is the meaning. || 29 ||
With all distinctions stilled, free from fear, and having utterly renounced all desires, he surely attained a state of total possessionlessness; having abandoned his entire fortune among his enemies,
with his egoism pacified and his sense of bodily identity vanished, if he were now wandering for alms even among them, he has indeed forsaken me as well.
Because you are high above existence, you are exceedingly high.

"Peaceful" (*śānta*) means one for whom all particularities—such as "I am a Brahmin" or "I am a householder"—have subsided; one from whom fear and its causes have departed; and one by whom all desires, such as longing for children, wife, and so forth, have been completely renounced. Being such a person, having abandoned all prosperity among enemies and having attained and taken recourse to a state of absolute possessionlessness (*akiñcanatva*), [he remains].

If you have completely abandoned even that Guru who must not be forsaken—wandering for alms among those very enemies with your egoism stilled and all notions of "body" destroyed—then indeed you are high, you are most high; you are higher than the highest.
The meaning is: you are none other than the Supreme Brahman, the most excellent of all. || 30 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having heard this from the mouth of his preceptor, Bhagīratha,
having resolved upon what was to be done in his mind, became intent on his own task.

"Then" (atha): "Having placed the duty in his mind" means having fixed in his heart the task instructed by his guru. "Devoted to his own duties": his own duty was the administration of the kingdom; he became as if intent solely upon that. || 31 ||
Then, after only a few days had passed,
he performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice for the sole purpose of attaining complete renunciation.

"Then" (tataḥ) means for the sake of accomplishing the singular goal of total renunciation, that is, for the purpose of bringing about the occasion for the relinquishment of all wealth. 32 || 33 || 34 ||
Discerning between the virtuous and the non-virtuous, he gave away his entire wealth— cows, land, horses, gold, and so forth— to the twice-born, the gods, the afflicted, and his kinsmen.
