Within just three days, King Bhagīratha renounced everything entirely, remaining with nothing left but his own clothes.
Then, his kingdom being empty of all wealth and its subjects and citizens exhausted, he gave his own realm to his enemy like a blade of grass to a border-dweller.

Now, regarding the word *atha*: Then Bhagīratha gave away his own kingdom—which was empty of all resources (*sarvārtharikta*), meaning devoid of all wealth, and in which the subjects (*prakṛti*), such as ministers, and the citizens (*paura*), the people of the city, were distressed (*khinna*, i.e., miserable)—to his enemy dwelling on the border (*sīmāntin*), like a blade of grass. (In the variant reading *sāmantinaḥ*, it would mean "to a neighboring vassal").
The *sāmantas* are those born everywhere; they are like that. The meaning is: lords of neighboring regions. || 35 ||
When his kingdom, his hermitage, and his entire circle were seized by the enemy,
he departed from his own realm, leaving nothing but his lower garment.

"Overrun" (ākrānta): When his kingdom—meaning the royal palace, his own home, his domain, and his sovereign territory—had been overrun by an enemy, this Bhagīratha, remaining with nothing but his lower garment (adhovāsa) and devoted to silence (muni), departed from his own realm. 36, 37, 38.
Where he was not known by name, and where he was not known from his appearance,
there— in villages, forests, or cities— the steadfast one dwelt. (37)
Thus, in a very short time, having stilled all desires through supreme tranquility, he attained rest within his own self.
Wandering over the islands on the face of the earth, he once, by the turn of fate and against his will,
reached that very city of his which had been seized by an enemy.

"Roaming about," etc.: being helpless because there was no other place for him to go, he followed the traveler and eventually reached that city which had been seized by his enemy; such is the meaning. || 39 ||
There he slowly begged for alms from various houses, including those of the citizens and the ministers who had fallen into misfortune.
"Nānā" means those obtained in accordance with the flow of the mind as it falls into the stream [of worldly existence]. 40 || 41 || 42 || 43 || 44 ||
Then the citizens and ministers honored King Bhagīratha, who was deeply dejected, with respectful service. (41)

Although entreated by his enemy with the words, "O Lord, accept the kingdom," the sage did not take it; for he would not accept anything that was not entirely free from the covering of worldly ties, nor anything other than mere food.
Having spent a few days there, he departed for another place;
this Bhagīratha was lamented by the people, crying out, "Alas! What a tragedy! (43)
Then, elsewhere, with his self pacified, his intellect fully at rest, and happy, delighting in the Self,
he once encountered his teacher Tritula.
Having offered his own hospitality, Bhagīratha dwelt for some time with him on the mountain,
in the forest, in the village, in the city, and among the people.
"His own" (svam) means: having performed his own welcome; that is to say, having performed the hospitality appropriate for himself, such as the greeting of welcome and so forth. || 45 ||
Having attained equanimity, the teacher and the disciple remained equal;
established in themselves, they both felt despondency regarding the maintenance of the body. (46)
"Equanimity" means the maintenance of the body [without attachment], which is the cause of despondency and suffering. 46.
"Why is this body maintained, or what is gained by abandoning it?
Let it remain as it is, according to its natural state, following its course and its conduct. (47)
"What is it?"—this constitutes two verses as a single sentence. They did not rejoice—that is, they did not take pleasure—in *ānanda*, which is the cause of happiness;
nor in *duḥkha*, which is the cause of suffering; nor in the "middle," which is the cause of experience. 47. 8.
Having thus resolved and remaining there, those two who were traveling from forest to forest felt neither joy, nor sorrow, nor anything in between.
Wealth, the eightfold sovereignty beginning with horses and riches—even when offered by the Siddhas out of satisfaction—they regarded as mere withered grass. (49)

Regarding the phrase *dhanādi*: "wealth" refers to well-known riches; "the power of horses" refers to the excellence of cavalry and so forth—whatever sovereignty belongs to kings—and that too, as well as the eightfold [powers] beginning with *aṇiman* mentioned above, even though they were bestowed by the Siddhas who possess the eight great perfections (*mahāsiddhis*) and by the various classes of divine beings who were pleased and satisfied, they considered them all to be worn out and decayed, on account of their being subject to obstacles.
Then once, in a certain district within that preeminent city,
death carried off a childless king as if he were its own prey.
There, the subjects, weary and having lost the traditional order of their land, sought a king endowed with vast excellence and fortune. (51)
Having approached that sage Bhagīratha, who was staying there as a mendicant,
they recognized him and, bringing him near, installed him as the lord of their army.
In an instant, Bhagīratha, mounting his elephant, was surrounded by his heavy army like a lake filled with water during the rainy season.
(668) "Bhagīratha, the Lord of the World, is victorious!"— with such clamor from the people,
the great caves of the lords of mountains became completely filled. 54.
While he was protecting that kingdom there, the subjects, who had previously been devoted to their deceased king, approached the new monarch and spoke thus: (55)
O King, that lord of ours whom you formerly appointed has been swallowed up by death, like soft meat by a fish. (56)
It behoves you to protect the kingdom and uphold the truth;
it is not proper to reject wealth that has come unasked. (57)
Vaiṣṭha said:
Thus entreated, the king accepted those words and became the lord of the earth marked by the seven oceans. (58)
"Thus" (iti) means: that such speech—that speech of those constituent elements (prakṛtis). 58 || 59 ||
Equanimous, with a tranquil mind, silent, free from passion and devoid of envy, he delights solely in performing his duty at the proper time and has cast away all pride. || 59 ||
Then, having performed most severe austerities for thousands of years,
he established Gaṅgā upon the earth for the sake of delivering his grandfather.
"Now" (atha): [It refers to] the Grandfathers, the sons of Sagara; for the sake of their deliverance—that is, for the sake of rescuing them from hell. || 60 ||
From that time on, while King Bhagīratha reigned, that river became a pathway for the spread of his fame as it flowed along its course across the surface of the earth.

Regarding "Bhagīratha": the phrase *yaśaḥpracāravīthikā* means the path for the movement of Bhagīratha’s fame; *tadādi* means that action in which he, Bhagīratha, is the starting point, occurring in such a manner. *Mahītalam* (the surface of the earth) is an adverbial modifier of the act of descending. 61.
Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Narrative of Bhagīratha," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Laghu-yogavāsiṣṭha, which is a means to liberation.
Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Narrative of Bhagīratha," in the Śrīvāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa.
Ninth Sarga. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having first abandoned this [world] and having brought the bird of the mind under control,
remain peaceful within the Self, as immovable as Śikhidhvaja.

Previously, the story of Bhagīratha was told to show that even the rest of the mind, though difficult to attain, is obtained through one's own effort alone. Now, however, [the following is told] containing several anecdotes to show that even self-knowledge— which is difficult to attain in the absence of the destruction of the accumulated sins that act as obstacles— is obtained through the excellence of the teacher’s inquiry.
The narrative of Śikhidhvaja begins with the words "This": Having first abandoned this universe,

having cast off the perception of the phenomenal world and its latent impressions, and having brought under control the bird-like mind— which by nature wanders like a winged creature— making it one-pointed and remaining peaceful, stay immovable within the Self like Śikhidhvaja.
Rāma said:
Who was this one named Śikhidhvaja, and how did he attain that state?
O Brahmin, tell me this again for the further increase of my understanding.
Vasiṣṭha said:
In the past, during the seventh Manu who has passed away,
there was a glorious lord named Śikhidhvaja in the city of the Mālavas in the Dvāpara age.

Endowed with fortitude, magnanimity, compassion, truthfulness, forbearance, self-restraint, and tranquility; he was a hero of auspicious conduct, honorable, and a mine of a multitude of virtues. || 4 ||
Śikhidhvaja married Cūḍālā by name, the virtuous daughter of the lord of Surāṣṭra, who was his own equal. (5)
The affection between those two, whose hearts were surrendered to one another, increased because they were constantly engaged together and because their activities were mutually pleasing.

"Her love increased" (avardhata): the syntactical connection is that their mutual affection grew because of the pleasantness and desirability of their activities, such as looking at one another and conversing. || 6 ||
Those two became experts in the entire range of arts with one another;
having attained friendship, they maintained their very nature in this very way.
"Secretly" (mithas) means [in secret] from the entire collection of arts (kalākalāpa), consisting of song, instrumental music, dance, and so forth. || 7 || 8 ||
Thus, for many years, the couple, filled with intense longing,
took delight day after day in the endless playful diversions of youth.
Then, after many years had passed and were filled with obstacles,
youth gradually ebbed away like water from a broken jar.

The word "atha" (now) introduces a group of six verses. Now, after many years had passed, the couple consisting of Cūḍālā and Śikhidhvaja— having determined the worthlessness of worldly existence through such means as "while youth was slowly fading away, old age arrived with its face upturned"— long studied the science of spiritual self-knowledge (*adhyātma-śāstra*), which is the medicine for the disease of worldly existence.
The syntactical connection is "he reflected. In that context, *tumbī-latā* refers to the bottle-gourd (*alābu*). || 9 || 10 || 11 || 12 || 13 || 14 || 15 || 16 ||
Death is as unavoidable as the falling of a ripe fruit;
old age falls upon one like a frost-bolt upon a lotus. 10.
Life flows away incessantly like water from the palm of the hand;
while life is like a gourd-vine in the rainy season, craving alone has grown long.
Youth passes away like the current of a mountain river;
pleasures flee away like arrows shot from a bow. 12.
(671) Worldly activity is as essence-less as the interior of a plantain tree; it brings about detachment.
Therefore, there is nothing so exceedingly beautiful here in this saṃsāra. (13)
When, having attained it, the mind is no longer distressed by the various states of existence. || 14 ||
Having thus determined that couple to be the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra,
he reflected for a long time upon the scripture in accord with the inner self (adhyātma).
Having resolved that the cholera-like disease called saṃsāra is pacified solely by the mantra of self-knowledge, they remained devoted to that alone.
With their minds fixed on Him, their life-breaths directed toward Him, established in Him, and taking refuge in His nature,
they shone at that time, intent upon His worship and engaged in His service.

"Those whose minds are fixed on That": the word "That" refers to the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). Their vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are absorbed in That because the mind is absorbed in That, and because there is an inseparable connection between the mind and the vital breath. "Fixed in That": those two for whom there is a firm commitment (*niṣṭhā*) or discipline (*niyama*) in that very knowledge of the Self. "Taking refuge in those of such a kind": those of such a kind are those who are steadfast in the knowledge of the Self; they are the "refuges," meaning those who are to be relied upon.

"Of whom they were [the two]" refers to those two who were intent on worshipping Him, devoted to honoring the Knower of the Self; "engaged in His service" means endowed with activities appropriate for that purpose. || 17 || 18 ||
Right there, intensely practiced and awakening one another, they became mutually delighted by that and engaged in its commencement after a long effort. (18)

Then, O Rāma, she incessantly heard from the mouths of those who know the supreme self the meanings of the scriptures, which are capable of delivering one across [the ocean of existence], through their beautiful progression of words. (19)

The word "atha" (now) introduces the two verses as a single syntactical unit. Whether unoccupied and sitting silently, or occupied and performing her appropriate duties, she reflected upon her own self with her intellect in the manner about to be described;
in this way she reflected upon her own self day and night.
Whether unoccupied or occupied, one should purify [the mind] with an intellect that is as white as a horse.
Cūḍālā said:
"Let me first examine my own self: 'What might I be?
Of what has this delusion come, how has it arisen, and where does it reside? (21)
The body, for its part, is inert and deluded; the certainty is simply "I am not this.
And the group of organs of action is non-different from that [body], and is therefore likewise inert. (22)
Regarding the body: the body is indeed insentient. The reason for this is that it is "deluded," meaning devoid of consciousness; the certainty is simply "I am not [this].
Furthermore, the group of organs of action is also insentient, as it is non-different from this body. || 22 ||
In this same way, the group of sense organs is seen to be entirely insentient, for it is impelled by the mind, just as a clod of earth on the ground is driven by a staff. (23)

Regarding the word "buddhi": since even the group of sense organs is impelled by the mind—just as a clod of earth is [impelled] in the light of day—it is seen and determined to be indeed insentient (jaḍa). || 23 ||
I consider the mind to be thus inert, possessing the power of volition; it is impelled by the determinations of the intellect, just as a stone is propelled by slingshots.

Regarding the word *manaḥ*: because it is subject to the nature of volition (*saṃkalpa*), I consider the mind to be insentient, as it is impelled by the determinations (*niścaya*) produced by the intellect (*buddhi*), just like slings (*kṣepaṇa*) are made of stone. "Slings" (*kṣepaṇa*) are specific types of mechanical devices made of rope, wood, and so forth, by means of which things are thrown.
The intellect, though inherently insentient, possesses the nature of determination; yet it is only when the intellect exists that determination occurs.
It is moved by the ego-sense, just as the bank of a river is eroded by its own current.

Regarding the term "intellect" (buddhi): the intellect, which is of the nature of ascertainment, is moved and impelled by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), just as a river is diverted by a hollow dug out by digging; thus, it is certain that the intellect is indeed insentient (jaḍa). || 25 ||
Even the ego is devoid of substance, inert, and of the nature of a corpse;
it is produced by the living soul like a delusive yakṣa created by a child. (26)

Regarding the term *ahaṃkāra*: it is "insubstantial" (*niḥsāra*) because its nature is false cognition; it is "without essence" (*niḥsattva*) because it is devoid of activity and is of the nature of a corpse. Thus, even this *ahaṃkāra* is produced and imagined by the living being (*jīva*), like a phantom (*yakṣa*) created through the delusion of a child.
In the reading *jaḍa eva avaśātmakaḥ*, the meaning is that its very nature is dependent on another (*paravaśasvabhāva*). || 26 ||
And the individual soul (jīva), whose form is ideation and whose nature is wind, resides in the heart; delicate, it is sustained by some other internal principle. (27)
Regarding the term *jīva*: it is situated in the heart, existing within the heart because it is the nature of consciousness reflected in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

For this very reason, its form is one of conceptualization (*kalana*), its nature is imagined (*kalpita-svabhāva*), and its essence is wind (*vātātman*) because it consists of vital breath (*prāṇa*); thus it is delicate and unstable, for it dissolves daily into the Self during deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Such a *jīva*, moreover, [is perceived] by that which resides within.

One continues to live because one is sustained by a certain indefinable Person who has entered within oneself and bestows life-force; therefore, the meaning is that even the *jīva* (individual soul) is not the ultimate nature of the Self. This is what is being said: just as...

Just as there exists both space delimited by adjuncts such as a jar and space that is undelimited, so too do the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) exist within the hearts of all living beings. Accordingly, the Sūtra of Vyāsa states: "The two selves have entered the cave, for that is seen. In this regard, the distinction is that the individual soul is subject to *māyā*, while the Lord is one whose *māyā* is subject to his own will. As it was said by the teacher Gauḍapāda:

"This individual soul (jīva) has the effect as its limiting adjunct; the Lord (īśvara) has the cause as his limiting adjunct. Having abandoned the state of being cause and effect, pure, perfect consciousness remains. || 27 ||

Ah! It has been realized by him who is stained by the conceptualization of "I think": that the living being lives by means of the ancient form of consciousness, which is the very nature of the Self. (28)

"Ā aho!"—*ā* is an indeclinable particle indicating recollection, and *aho* expresses wonder. "Aha! This has been realized by me. To the question "What is that?", he says: this manifestation as the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a connection with the visible world; by that [soul], which is stained—possessing the stain of being a reflected image—and which is ancient, beginningless, of the nature of the Self, and the very self of all.
By means of the nature of consciousness, that is, by the very essence of consciousness itself, it lives, meaning it sustains the vital breaths. || 28 ||

The individual soul (jīva), possessing the delusion of being a cognizer, lives by means of its very nature as consciousness, just as fragrance [lives] by means of the wind, or the current of a river by means of the sky. (29)
He states this very point with an illustration: "cetya... etc.

[Verse 29: For one who possesses the delusion of the objectified (cetya) and who, through its reflection in those objects, identifies with them, the body of consciousness (cid-vapuḥ) becomes inert due to the accumulation of the unreal and insentient portions of the objectified.
For it casts off its form, like a fire that has entered into a great body of water. || 30 ||

"Asatya" (unreal): The *cidvapuḥ* (the body of consciousness), which is the very nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*), because of the accumulation (*cayanāt*)—that is, the gathering or increase (*upacayāt*)—of unreal and inert portions of the cognizable (*asatyājaḍacetyāṃśa*), abandons—that is, casts off—its own nature as consciousness (*svarūpaṃ citsvabhāvam*), becoming inert like a fire submerged in a great body of water. || 30 ||
In this way, although this very nature of consciousness is itself directed toward the object of cognition, it is awakened by consciousness as if it were inert, void, and unreal. (31)

This very form of consciousness, having thus—by way of being directed toward objects of thought and through the ideation of the visible world—become itself inert, possessed of dullness, like a void, and almost non-existent, is nevertheless awakened again by consciousness, by that consciousness which has entered into it; for the Śruti says: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing. (31)
Now I behold: by whom is this consciousness perceived?
Ah! After a long time, that which is to be known—the stainless—has finally been realized.

"Now" (*idānīm*) constitutes one sentence, consisting of half a verse. "By what cause is this consciousness perceived—that is, set in motion in the form of the mind, intellect, and so forth?—this I shall now observe and investigate. "Oh! (*aho*) constitutes another sentence, consisting of half a verse.

"The knowable has been known" (*jñeyaṃ jñātam*): the meaning is that that which was desired to be known—the cause of the manifestation of consciousness (*cid-vivarta*), which is to be understood—has been known. || 32 ||
For all these—the mind, the intellect, the senses, and so forth, ending with the play of consciousness—are indeed non-existent; alas, they arise only in the absence of attentive awareness. (33)

Regarding the phrase "ete hi": "ending in the play of consciousness" (*cidvilāsāntāḥ*) means that the play of consciousness (*cidvilāsaḥ*) is the attribution of sentience to insentient objects; these—the mind, intellect, senses, and so forth—all end in or culminate in that [play]. Although all these are in fact non-existent, they have arisen or manifested from the Self without *avadhāna*, which is one-pointedness of attention (*aikāgryam*); that is, they appear by way of its absence.

The meaning is that through negligence (pramāda), which consists in the absence of abiding in one's own true nature, there arises non-attention (anavadhāna) alone; this is the cause of the manifestation (vivarta) of the consciousness as having manifold forms. || 33 ||
p.
675) There exists here only one Great Consciousness, which is called the "Great Being" (mahāsattā);
it is stainless, equal, pure, and characterized by the absence of egoism. || 34 ||

The two verses beginning with "mahācid" constitute a single syntactical unit. The meaning is that that which exists as the stainless Great Consciousness (*mahācit*), which is synonymous with Great Being (*mahāsattā*), is indeed celebrated by such names as Brahman, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and so forth. The word "sama" is used twice;

of these two, one instance of the word *sama* is a synonym for "all" (*sarva*). Thus, the meaning is "equal" in the sense of being the self of all. The other, however, expresses the absence of inequality (*avaiṣamya*).
"Of identical form" does not constitute tautology. || 34 || 35 ||
She shines forth once for all, stainless, eternally risen, and equal;
she is celebrated by such names as Brahman and Supreme Self.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Day by day, through such delight in her own self and through constant inward-turnedness, she remained established in her true nature.

"Day after day" (dinānudinaṃ): "day" (dina) refers to what occurs previously, and "after-day" (anudina) refers to what occurs subsequently; thus "day and after-day" (dinānudina) means on all days. This refers to Cūḍālā. || 36 ||
Free from passion, free from attachment, free from dualities, and free from desire,
she neither abandons nor grasps, moving according to her natural conduct.
"Free from passion" (nīrāga): Passion (*rāga*) is desire, attachment, clinging, the dualistic perception of the desirable and undesirable, and the exertion toward what is sought.
He does not abandon [anything] because of the absence of aversion (*dveṣa*), nor does he grasp [anything] because of the absence of passion (*rāga*). || 37 || 38 || 39 || 40 || 41 || 42 || 43 ||
Filled at intervals with the great attainment of the Supreme Self,
he reached a state beyond description due to his transcendence of all that is most excellent.
By the power of her own practice in the wealth of discernment, she shone with the dawning of the Self, like a beautiful flowering creeper newly emerged. (39)
Then, on one occasion, having beheld that woman of faultless limbs and unprecedented beauty, Śikhidhvaja spoke with a smile: (40)
O slender one, adorned again and again as if endowed with renewed youth, you shine all the more with the stainless luster of your body. 41.
O beloved, you shine intensely as if filled with the essence of nectar, as if you have both attained and not attained your station, and as if you are overflowing with the nectar of bliss. 42.
"O beloved, I perceive your mind to be free from worldly attachment yet compassionate, tranquil yet powerful, attained to equanimity, profound, and serene. (43)
Cūḍālā said:
Having abandoned this form of "nothing at all," I have come;
because I am nothing at all, I remain as the Illustrious One (Śrīmatī).

Then, with eight verses, Cūḍālā reports her own experience to her husband, beginning with "na kiṃcit" (not anything): First of all, no world whatsoever comes into being; for it is sublated by the realization that "there is no diversity here. Nor is it non-existent, because it is perceived.
And what is non-existent is unfit to be treated as existing. Therefore, [the world] possesses some form [only] through its nature as the Great Existence (mahāsattā).

By whatever cause [I] have come—that is, attained—the Supreme Brahman characterized by some form; that is to say, [I] have reached the state of Brahman which possesses no form whatsoever. By that, I remain here as the illustrious one, the radiant one. The word *asmi* is an indeclinable used in the sense of "I. Here, *śrī* refers to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Its power (*prabhāva*) is truly real, transcending the world, and divine.
Splendor. || 44 ||
Having renounced all this and having taken refuge in everything else—
that which is both true and untrue— by that I remain established as Śrīmatī.

He says this very thing: "This" (idam). Having abandoned all this world, because I have taken refuge in that other [reality] which is distinct from the universe, which is everything, the self of all, the truth, the uncontradicted, and yet—within the unreal, imagined world—it is the non-real Brahman; therefore, I remain glorious. 45.
Whatever exists and whatever does not exist, I know that as it truly is—how it arises and how it perishes; by this, I abide as the Illustrious One (Śrīmatī). (46)

"Whatever it may be": whatever object exists, because it is of the nature of Great Being (mahāsattā), yet is "nothing at all," because it is distinct from the universe; that object I know as it truly is, in its arising, and in its destruction. The meaning is: I know everything exactly as it functions within creation and the other cosmic processes. || 46 ||
I am satisfied by enjoyments as if they were not enjoyed at all, or like food that has been eaten and is far away;
I neither rejoice nor am I provoked to anger, and for that reason I remain possessed of prosperity.

"By enjoyments," etc. The sense is: I am satisfied by enjoyments even when they have not been experienced—that is, when they are far removed and distant—as if they had already been enjoyed or previously consumed; for since there is no distinction in their being far removed, there is no reason for partiality. I neither rejoice nor am I provoked, because of the absence of passion and hatred. || 47 ||
I delight in the solitary heart, which is like the infinite sky;
I do not delight in royal pastimes, and for that reason I remain Śrīmatī.
"Alone" (ekā): In the heart that is like the sky—meaning as all-pervasive as space—and which is solitary and pure;
in my own Self, which is within all like the heart—I delight alone. I do not delight in the pastimes of kings, such as singing, instrumental music, dancing, and the like. || 48 ||
"I am indeed the sovereign of the worlds, not one whose form consists of even a mere atom;
thus I find contentment in the Self alone, and by that I abide as the Illustrious One (Śrīmatī). (49)

"Of the worlds," etc. Since Brahman is not of the nature of "nothingness"—for it is not nothing at all, because it is distinct from everything—it is of the nature of that [everything]. I am indeed the Lord of the worlds; because I am the controller of all, as it is said, "He who, from within, governs all beings," I find satisfaction in the Self alone in this manner. || 49 ||
With my intellects, which possess only slight aversion and attachment toward the views of the scriptures, I delight together with my companions; therefore, I remain possessed of glory. (50)

"Tanviti": With those female companions (vayasyābhiḥ) whose hatred and passion were attenuated—that is, with those whose intellects (prajñābhiḥ) possessed a vision of the scriptures, meaning through discourses on the state of one free from passion—I take delight; that is, I find diversion. || 50 ||

Whatever I see here, O Lord, by means of the rays of my eyes, the sense faculties, or even the mind, that is nothing at all; yet, being devoid of those, I see nothing within. Thus, seeing correctly, I find relief. (51)
"I see"— whatever object I see with the rays of the eyes because it is at a distance,
whatever I see with the sense organs such as the skin because it is nearby, and whatever past or future thing I see with the mind—
all that, even in the slightest degree, I do not see, nor do I connect with it. That which is devoid of those [objects], distinct from the visible, is not that.
I console myself with this thought: "I clearly perceive within me a supreme reality that is in some way distinct from the universe."
Vasiṣṭha said:
To that excellent woman who was speaking thus, resting her mind upon the Self, the king, failing to understand the meaning of her words, laughed and said: || 52 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"You are a chatterer of incoherent words; you are a fool, O woman of excellent complexion! You take delight in royal diversions, while I am thus [left behind], O princess. (53)

Regarding the word *asaṃbaddhā*: "O princess, you take delight in royal pastimes; just as I do, so too do you take delight. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that by saying "I do not take delight," she is one whose speech is incoherent (*asaṃbaddhapralāpā*). In the reading *rājalīlābhir ramasvāvanipālātmaje*, the meaning is: "O daughter of a king, enjoy yourself in royal pastimes just as you do now; continue to enjoy yourself in the future as well"—[not] "I do not take delight."
The meaning is: "Do not be one who speaks falsely. || 53 ||
Having abandoned something, he has gone to nothingness that is established in direct perception;
having abandoned the reality of direct perception, how indeed can he be said to shine? (54)
He mocks that which was said—"having abandoned this [world], which is nothing at all"—with the words "something."

Having abandoned whatever object exists as perceptible, such as the earth and so forth, and having reached—having attained—nothing that is indefinable, he who has abandoned the nature of what is perceptibly real, how can he be dignified? The sense is: because of the abandonment of that which is authoritative and the acceptance of that which is unauthoritative. || 54 ||
How indeed can he who abandons enjoyments while thinking "I am content even without enjoying them" shine, being as unfortunate as a pauper? (55)

He ridicules what was said regarding "not being satisfied with enjoyments" with the verse beginning "bhogaiḥ": That fool who, thinking himself content with enjoyments even while they remain unenjoyed, abandons the enjoyments he has actually obtained—he, by abandoning the enjoyments he has attained, becomes as unfortunate and luckless as a pauper; how then can he shine?

Regarding the reading *ruṣevāsanaśayyāyām*: the meaning is that just as someone who is angry, even when food has been served and his own beloved is present, might remain on his seat as if it were a bed due to the force of his rage and thus turn away from enjoyment; so too [is the case here]. || 55 ||
What I see, I do not see; yet I see something else entirely.
This is but the prattle of the unreal—how indeed could it be beautiful?

Regarding the phrase "that which I see": whatever object I see—that is, whatever I make an object of through the eyes and other senses—I do not see such an object; I do not perceive it. Yet, there is this idle chatter: "I see something entirely different, a reality distinct from the visible. How can one be dignified without abandoning this meaningless speech? This is mere prattle.
Regarding the reading *ityasatyasya*, the meaning is: how can one who possesses such false and unseemly prattle (*pralāpa*) appear beautiful? || 56 || 57 || 58 || 59 ||
Therefore, you are a child, you are deluded, and you are fickle, O playful one!
You sport with various conversations and charms; play on, O beautiful one! (57)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Laughing loudly with a boisterous laugh at his beloved, Śikhidhvaja rose at midday to bathe and departed from the women's quarters.
"Alas! He did not find rest in himself and did not understand my words;
he is but a king," Cūḍālā thought, distressed by the failure of her own efforts. (59)
Then, O dear one, as those two possessed such dispositions,
a great deal of time passed there amidst those royal pastimes.

"Then" (tadā) means at that time; "there" (tatra) means in that place; "in that place" (tasmin deśe); "thus" (tathā) means in that manner. While the two were situated in such a way, much time passed with those royal pastimes. "Aṅga" is a term of address. 60.
Once, although she was eternally satisfied and free from desire,
Cūḍālā herself felt a longing for the playful coming and going through the sky.
"Ekadā" means at one time. "Khagamāgamaiḥ" means by means of going to and coming from the sky. 61 || 62 || 63 ||
Then, for the sake of attaining the power to travel through the sky, that princess disregarded all enjoyments and went to a secluded place.
Devoted solely to solitude, her body established in its own posture,
she practiced for a long time the upward movement of the vital breath.
Rāma said:
O Brahmin, tell me, what playful movement of mine, resulting from long practice and endowed with singular effort, has this flight through the sky as its fruit? (64)
"Of what? [It refers to] the play of vibration, which is a specific movement of the vital breath (prāṇa). "Of long practice" means that which has been practiced for a long time. 64.
Vasiṣṭha said:

Having abandoned all latent impressions (vāsanās) other than those pertaining to its own goal, [the breath] remains within, due to the contraction of the locations such as the anus and through the sequential processes of the places of articulation (sthāna) and so forth. || 65 ||

The four verses beginning with "antasthā" constitute a single syntactical unit. Having abandoned all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) residing in the mind—namely, those impressions directed toward objects other than one's own goal—even all of them, by means of practices such as the contraction of the senses being repeatedly cultivated, [are abandoned] because of that person's sovereignty and power of restraint. All of them...

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: the vital airs, such as *prāṇa* and the rest, come under control—like servants—in the acts of exhaling, inhaling, and retention (*recaka*, *pūraka*, and *kumbhaka*), which consist of the relinquishing, taking up, and stopping [of the breath]. Regarding that, he states the cause for the contraction of the openings such as the anus: "by means of the sequence of actions such as postures" (*sthānakādikriyākramaiḥ*).
"Postures" (*sthānaka*) refers to specific positions such as *mahāmudrā*; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), practices such as *yama* (restraints) are included.

The *sthānaka*s and so forth are sequences of action (*kriyākrama*) which are varieties of means (*upāyabheda*); the distinction is that by these, through the *mūlabandha*, there is the contraction of the anus, and by the *khecarī*, the closing of the upper aperture. Regarding the definition of *mūlabandha*:
"Having pressed the perineum with the heel, one should contract the anus and draw the *apāna* upward."
"This is intended as the *mūlabandha*. As for the definition of *khecarī*, it has been stated many times previously. || 65 || 66 ||
In connection with the narrative of the illustrious Śikhidhvaja,
hear now this practice of the cultivation of the vital breaths and other winds, which yields the fruit of supernatural powers.

Through purity of food and seat, through contemplation on the meaning of the scriptures of the virtuous, through one's own proper conduct, through association with good people, and through the blissful seat of total renunciation; || 67 ||

Through the purification of food and the seat, there is the purity of the food—that is, the state of being wholesome, moderate, and pure—and the purification of the seat, which is its freedom from defects. This arises from reflecting on the meaning of the authentic scriptures and from the correct investigation of the Yoga scriptures. One's own conduct consists of the practice of the limbs of yoga; "virtuous people" refers to those who know yoga.
The renunciation of everything [arises] from that, preceded by a comfortable posture. 67 || 68 || 69 ||
O Rāma, O observer of noble vows, through the intense practice of breath control over some period of time,
and by the abandonment of anger, greed, and the like, as well as the renunciation of enjoyments— || 68 ||
In the matters of relinquishing, acquiring, and restraining,
all the vital breaths come completely under the control of the person who knows that [reality], just as servants are subject to their master’s authority. (69)
O Rāghava, all prosperities, from sovereignty up to liberation, are achievable for everyone only through mastery over the body and the vital breaths.

"Kingdom and so forth" means that even powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, which are accomplished by bringing the body and breath under control, are achieved through the conquest of the vital breath (prāṇajaya). || 70 ||
Circular in shape and resting upon the vital points (marmasthāna),
the channel named Āntraveṣṭanikā is accompanied by hundreds of channels.

"Parimaṇḍalitā" refers to a group of three verses. She whose form is "parimaṇḍalita"—meaning made circular all around—is one who has taken recourse to the vital point (*marmasthāna*). Above that is the location of Kuṇḍalinī; it is situated transversely, below, and above the navel. She, whose nature consists of the eight *prakṛtis*, is indeed coiled eightfold. Thus [it is said].

Because Yājñavalkya has defined the location of Kuṇḍalinī as being above the *kanda*, across and upward from the navel, and because the navel is a vital point (*marman*), she becomes one who rests upon the navel—that is, she rests upon a vital point. Furthermore, Yājñavalkya [has stated] among the vital points: "The navel, the heart, the throat, and likewise the hollow of the neck."
Because of enumeration. || 71 ||
Resembling the whorl at the tip of a lute and similar to a whirlpool in water,
it is said to exist in all living beings, from insects to those born from lotuses.
"Resembling the whorl at the head of a lute" means it is like the whorl consisting of the winding of string for the wires on the upper part of the lute's neck;
thus, it is similar to a whirlpool in water. (72)
Forming a circle like the coils of the lord of serpents sleeping from the cold,
she remains there, constantly vibrating with the wind.

The grammatical connection is as follows: because the serpent-king was asleep from the affliction of cold, a certain channel known as *āntraveṣṭanikā*— which is coiled like the body of a serpent, pervades all vital breaths, and is surrounded by hundreds of channels— remains constantly vibrating due to the wind called *pavamāna*.
Within that [lotus], which is as tender as the sheath of a plantain tree,
resides the supreme purifying power (pāvanī), the bestower of the vital energy of all powers. (74)

The two verses beginning with "tasyāḥ" form a single syntactical unit. Within that aforementioned channel (*nāḍī*), which is as tender as the interior of a plantain trunk, there dwells one who—like an enraged female serpent—is constantly hissing; she has become the cause of its pulsation, her face turned upward, the bestower of speed to all powers (*śakti*), the cause of their exaltation, and the purifier associated with the wind (*pavana*).
The supreme power is firmly established. || 74 || 75 ||
Constantly sighing like an angry female serpent,
she remained with her face turned upward, having become motionless.
Within this [body], all the channels connected to the cavity of the heart are present;
therein lies Kuṇḍalinī, whose stainless nature consists of the powers of vibration, touch, and consciousness.

The three verses beginning with "asyām" form a single syntactical unit. Within this very power of *prāṇa*, all the channels (*nāḍīs*) residing in the cavity of the heart are connected and established; she is the cause of the subtle movements, sensations, consciousness, and creative activity, as well as the cause of the experience of touch. That stainless and purifying power alone is therefore called *kuṇḍalinī*. (76)
By being reckoned, she is quickly called "Kālā"; by consciousness, she is called "Citi";
by living, she has attained the state of "Jīvatā"; and by thinking, she resides as the "Manas. (77)

Regarding the phrase "called *kalā*": she alone is called *kalā* because of her nature as *kalana*, which means the cause of bondage. She is called *cit* because of consciousness, that is, the production of knowledge. She has attained the status of being denoted by the word *jīva* due to *jīvana*, which is the setting in motion of inhalation and exhalation.
She is established as *manas* because of *manana*, which is the cause of recollection. (77)
Through volition she is volition, and through awakening she is established as the intellect;
having attained the nature of the ego, she is this very one known as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka).

From various volitions—that is, from the mental construction of desires—she is indeed called "volition" (*saṃkalpa*), being designated by that term; yet, because she brings about awakening and the production of certainty, she is also known as "intellect" (*buddhi*). That same [power], having attained the nature of ego through the conceit "I am," becomes what is designated by the term "the city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*)—such is the syntactical connection. || 78 ||
The Kuṇḍalinī, the unsurpassed power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), resides in the body;
because it consists of the nature of prāṇa and apāna, it moves downward and upward. (79)

Regarding the word "sthitā" (situated): that unsurpassed power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), which exists within the body and is denoted by the term Kuṇḍalinī, moves both downward and upward because it consists of the nature of prāṇa and apāna. || 79 ||
When it moves upward as a whole, it ascends; then, when it moves downward as a whole, it descends.
When that [vital force] reaches its end, the person meets death; it is known as being composed of breath (prāṇamayī).

"Samastā" (entirety): That vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*), being entirely concentrated, sometimes moves upward; immediately thereafter, it likewise descends downward. Therefore, because the movement of the *prāṇa* is unstable, the person—the living soul—undergoes death.
For this reason, [the body] is traditionally said to consist of *prāṇa*. || 80 ||
If one should abide entirely within the self, having abandoned the upward and downward movements of breath,
then the disease of that person is destroyed through the internal obstruction of the vital air.

"In every way" means: if that vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*), by the power of the practice of restraint (*nirodha-abhyāsa*), abandons its upward and downward movement and remains entirely—in every manner—within the self, that is, within the body, then, due to the internal obstruction of the wind (*māruta*)—that is, because the wind is restrained within—the disease of the person is abandoned; it is cast off. The term "disease" is used as an illustration [for all afflictions].
The meaning is that even old age, death, and so forth are abandoned. || 81 ||
Rāma said:

O Lord of Sages, what is the cause of their destruction and what is the cause of their arising in this body—both mental afflictions and physical diseases? Please explain this to me quickly and accurately. (82)

"What is it? [The answer is: By the words "destruction" (vināśa) and "arising" (utpatti), their causes are indicated. It is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning: "those for whom what is destruction? and "those for whom what is arising? 82.
Vasiṣṭha said:

They know bodily suffering to be disease, which is called mental distress and consists of latent impressions; for they should understand that both have their root in ignorance when the knowledge of reality has perished. (83)

Regarding the term *deha*: the wise know bodily suffering (*dehaduḥkha*) to be disease, which is the cause of physical pain; they know that which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanāmaya*), the cause of mental suffering, to be called *ādhi*. One should understand that both these types of suffering have their root in ignorance (*maurkhya*), existing when the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) has perished—that is, in the absence of the knowledge of reality. (83)
But by the power of ignorance regarding reality, without even the gradual mastery over the senses,
one incessantly abandons restraint within the heart toward passion and hatred. (84)

The two verses beginning with "atattva" form a single syntactical unit. Due to the power of ignorance of reality—that is, from the absence of knowledge of reality—there is an assault upon one's own senses; when there is a lack of mastery over the senses, having abandoned that attenuation or meagerness, then by the force of dullness, because of the arising of passion and aversion in the heart, [one perceives] this object...
"Has this not been attained?"— such thoughts arise as dense, deluding anxieties, like mist or frost during the rainy season.
"This has been obtained, this has not"—from such dullness arise mental agonies that bestow dense delusion, just as mist arises during the rainy season. (85)
When desires throbbed violently and folly reached its height, through the consumption of what was difficult to digest and by the invasion of an evil land, [the people perished]. (86)

The four verses beginning with "bhṛśam" constitute a single syntactical unit. When the aforementioned desires have become fully manifest and delusion has reached its peak, [this occurs] through the consumption of tainted food—which is the cause for the intensification of faults that are difficult to end—and through the entering upon a wicked place such as a cremation ground. || 86 ||
Through the conduct of an evil time, through the manifestation of painful actions, through the fault of association with wicked people, and through the arousal of evil intentions; || 87 ||

In times of distress, such as during the twilight hours (saṃdhyā) and so forth, by the performance of activities like eating, by the manifestation and undertaking of painful actions in the form of carrying corpses and the like, and by the provocation of evil states such as anger through the fault of contact with people afflicted by leprosy and other diseases. || 87 ||
Due to the depletion or excessive fullness of the channels and their network of openings, when the vital breath has fallen into disorder and the body has been rendered impaired; || 88 ||

When the channels—the pathways for the movement of the vital breath—have become either depleted or full, and when, due to that continuity of their openings, the vital breath has fallen into a state of distress or imbalance, and the body has consequently been rendered impaired; || 88 ||
Due to the fault of instability, disease arises from the body,
just as the alteration of the river's form occurs due to the rainy season and the summer heat. (89)
Due to the cause of instability, from the fault that is the cause of suffering—namely, [the imbalance] consisting of wind (vāta) and so forth—disease arises in the body.

The syntactical connection is as follows: through the rainy season and the summer, which are the causes of increase and decrease respectively, there occurs a transformation of the river's form, as if consisting of increase and decrease. || 89 ||

Whether it be a destiny from a previous life or one pertaining to this world, whether auspicious or inauspicious, whichever is predominant, that very one impels [the person] accordingly in that sequence.

Whichever tendency— whether auspicious or inauspicious— is more predominant and powerful, whether originating from a previous birth (*prāktanī*) or arising in this present life (*aihikī*), that very tendency impels and directs one toward a corresponding course of action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, in that very manner.
The sense is that, under the influence of evil latent impressions (durvāsanā), one engages in improper conduct which becomes the cause of disease. || 90 ||
Thus, mental afflictions and physical diseases arise within the five elements;
hear now, O upholder of the Raghu lineage, how they are destroyed. 91.
"Ādhayaḥ" (anxieties) means: in this manner, by the method previously described. 91.
For there are two kinds of pledge here: the common and the essential.
The common is that which pertains to legal transactions, while the essential is said to be that which exists at the time of birth. || 92 ||

"Of two kinds" means that the mental affliction (*ādhi*) is twofold: the common (*sāmānya*) and the essential (*sārabhūta*). Among these, that affliction which is the cause for mere worldly transaction is known as "essential. The intended meaning is that the affliction consisting of pure latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is the common one, whereas that consisting of impure latent impressions is the essential one. || 92 ||
Upon the attainment of that which is desired, worldly concerns perish;
and with the exhaustion of the substrate (ādhikṣaya), the afflictions of existence (ādhibhava) and even diseases are thoroughly destroyed.

"By having obtained" means: worldly anxieties (*ādhi*), which have as their sole purpose mere worldly transaction, perish by the very object desired once it has been obtained, for it is logical that the attainment of the desired object brings about the cessation of desire. Furthermore, the diseases born of anxiety (*ādhibhava*) also perish when the anxiety itself is exhausted. || 93 ||
O Rāghava, without the knowledge of the Self, the essence of the higher state does not perish;
just as, without the realization that it is a rope, the [illusory] snake does not vanish. (94)
Regarding the term "self": the essence, however, is the underlying substrate; it does not perish without the knowledge of the self, because it consists of ignorance. || 94 ||
Diseases not born of mental afflictions, however, are cured by substances, mantras, and auspicious rituals as prescribed in medical treatises and other sciences; and you yourself know this. (95)
[The term] *anādhī* [refers to]: substances in the form of pastes, decoctions, and so forth; mantras that are causes of health, such as those dedicated to the Sun (*saura*) and others;
and auspicious rites, such as the satiation of gods and Brahmins. (95–96)
Rāma said:
"How does mental anguish become physical disease, and how is it destroyed?
O Blessed One, tell me this with words of gracious tone. (96)
Vasiṣṭha said:
For when the mind is disturbed, the body indeed falls into agitation;
thus, a person who is enraged does not even see what is right before him. 97.
The six verses beginning with "citta" form a single syntactical unit. When the mind (*citta*) is disturbed—that is, distracted—the body undergoes agitation.

Demonstrating that the body is dependent on the mind and bound to the elements (*dhātu*), he says: "For instance" (*tathāhi*). An enraged or angry person does not even see what is directly in front of them (*agram*); let alone anything else—this is the implied meaning. || 97 ||
Without looking at the path ahead, he runs off-course, like a deer afflicted by an arrow that has abandoned its natural track. 98.

Likewise, disregarding the forward path, he rushes toward the wrong way and what ought not to be done, like a deer pierced by an arrow. (98) Due to this agitation, the vital breaths abandon their equilibrium and flow unevenly;
when the vital breath flows unevenly, the channels fall into disorder. (99)

Consequently, due to the agitation of the body composed of the seven constituent elements (*dhātu*), the vital breaths (*prāṇavāyu*) abandon their equilibrium and flow in an uneven manner. When the vital breath flows unevenly, the channels (*nāḍī*) fall into a state of disorder—that is, an irregular condition. || 99 ||
Just as when a king is improperly established, the order of the castes and stages of life [falls into] indigestion, non-digestion, or even over-digestion; (100)

Thus, due to the reversal and imbalance of the channels, food that has been consumed leads only to disorder—that is, it results in an aggravation of the humors—either through improper digestion or complete indigestion. || 100 ||
Food leads only to disease when there is a disorder of the channels and the vital breaths;
those foods which remain in opposition within the body [cause harm]. (1)

In this way, those very foods that remain in the body in a state of contradiction, such as through indigestion (kujīrṇa) and so forth, undergo the nature of disease by virtue of their transformation and the power of their maturation. || 1 ||
Those very [disturbances] turn into diseases by the nature of their transformation.
Thus, from mental affliction (ādhi) disease arises, and with the destruction of the affliction, it perishes.
Listen to that sequence by which diseases are destroyed through mantras. || 2 ||

In the manner thus described, disease arises from the lower [element], and it perishes through its destruction. Just as diseases are destroyed by mantras or by the causes of health, I shall explain that sequence; listen—this is the connection [of the verse]. || 2 ||
Just as myrobalan fruits cause purgation by their very nature,
so too do the letters ya, ra, la, va, and others perform their function through the power of mental cultivation (bhāvanā).

Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): just as *harītakyaḥ*—that is, the fruits of the *harītakī* tree—by their very nature effect purgation, which is the elimination of impurities; in exactly the same way, the mantra-syllables such as *ya-ra-la-va* perform the action consisting of the cessation of disease through the power of contemplation (*bhāvanā*), that is, by virtue of meditation appropriate for health. || 3 ||
O virtuous one, through pure and meritorious action and service to the holy,
the mind attains clarity, just as gold does upon the touchstone.

According to the principle that "that very thing which produces a particular result is itself the cultivation [of it]," [the disease] is indeed cultivation. To address the inquiry as to how it is said that "the disease produced by that [cultivation] perishes through the destruction of its substrate," he states the method in three verses beginning with the word *śuddhyā*. These three verses constitute a single syntactical unit (*vākya*).

When sins are destroyed through pure, faultless, and meritorious actions such as the worship of Śiva, through service to the virtuous, and through attendance upon great souls, the mind attains purity, just as gold does through rubbing on a touchstone. || 4 ||
O Rāghava, when the mind is purified, bliss increases within the body,
just as clarity prevails throughout the world when the full moon has properly risen. (5)
Then, when the mind has become pure, bliss and happiness increase within the body, just as clarity and light appear in the world when the full moon has risen. || 5 ||
When the sattva is purified, these vital breaths flow in their proper sequence;
they thus digest the foods, and by that means, disease is destroyed.

Likewise, when there is purity of the constituent elements (sattva) and clarity of the mind, the vital breaths flow in their proper sequence. Flowing thus in equilibrium, they digest the foods; by that digestion of food, disease is destroyed. || 6 ||
The sequences of the destruction and arising of mental and physical afflictions have been declared to you;
now listen to the present subject, the discourse on Kuṇḍalinī.

Regarding "ādhīti": The sequences of the destruction and arising of mental anguish (ādhi) and physical disease (vyādhi)—namely, the sequence of destruction and the sequence of arising—have been explained according to the previously mentioned method.
Now, listen to the discourse on the practice of yoga concerning Kuṇḍalinī, which is being described in relation to Kuṇḍalinī. 7.

Know that Kuṇḍalinī, known internally as Prāṇa, belongs to the individual soul (jīva) whose other name is the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka); she is like a flower-cluster belonging to the fragrance within.

Regarding the word *purī*: the *Kuṇḍalinī* mentioned previously is the city. Know that she is the life-force (*prāṇanāmikā*), the very breath of the individual soul (*jīva*) who has the other name of *puryaṣṭaka*. It is like a cluster of fragrance; for just as fragrance exists only when the flower-cluster is present, so too does the individual soul exist only when the *Kuṇḍalinī* is present—this is the intended meaning. (8)
When one remains in equilibrium after filling that [body] through the practice of inhalation (pūraka),
then the stability of Meru is attained, as well as the fullness of the body. (9)

Regarding the word "tām" (her): when, by means of the practice of *pūraka* (inhalation), through the power of that practice, one fills her—Kuṇḍalinī—and remains steady (*sama*) and unwavering (*nirvikāra*), then one attains *mairava*—that is, stability related to Meru—and the body's firmness (*sthiratva*) as well as its plumpness (*pīnatā*) or stoutness (*sthaulya*). Through such practice of *pūraka*, the body becomes stable and stout like Mount Meru.
The meaning is that it comes to be. || 9 ||

When the vital breath (prāṇa), restrained within by the fullness of inhalation (pūraka), is led upward as pure consciousness itself to endure the heat, fatigue, and exhaustion [of the practice], [then one attains success]. (110)

The three verses beginning with "When" (*yadā*) form a single syntactical unit. When that Kuṇḍalinī is led upward— by means of consciousness through the contemplation of an upward movement— to the upper region of space, in such a way that the vital breath (*prāṇamāruta*) is filled by inhalations (*pūraka*) and is drawn inward (*antarāyata*) and extended (*dīrgha*) within that action.

As if to endure the exhaustion and fatigue of the heat; for instance, just as when someone weary from the heat, seeking to dispel his fatigue in some shade, practices the "pot" (kumbhaka) breath-control known as "cold," whereby he leads the Kuṇḍalinī upward by means of the vital breath (prāṇa) drawn inward and expanded through inhalation—such is the meaning. || 110 ||
Like a serpent, it moves swiftly upward, having assumed the likeness of a staff;
taking hold of all the channels that bind the body like a creeper, it ascends. (11)
Then that Kuṇḍalinī, like a female serpent or a snake, having assumed the form of a staff, takes up all the channels bound within the body like creepers and ascends rapidly upward. || 11 ||
Then it causes this entire body to float,
just as a leather bag filled with dense air floats upon the water for a man.

Then this entire body is made to float, that is, it is caused to rise up. The meaning is: just as a leather bellows (*bhastrā*), when completely filled with air—meaning filled with air in such a way that there are no gaps—and being situated in water, causes a person to float, so it is in this case. || 12 ||
(691) By means of yoga, through the playful mastery of practice,
yogins attain the lofty state of moving through the sky, just as the wretched [attain] the status of Indra. 13.

Thus: by means of yoga characterized by such a specific practice through the play of repeated cultivation (*abhyāsa*), yogis attain the power of moving through the sky; the syntactical connection is that those who are wretched and impoverished [attain] the state of Indra, as if reaching the station of Indra himself. || 13 ||
When the Kuṇḍalinī energy, by means of the flow through the Brahma-nerve,
moves outward and upward to the top of the skull, twelve finger-breadths above [the crown], || 14 ||
The two verses beginning with "brahmanāḍī" form a single syntactical unit. When that vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*), in the form of *kuṇḍalinī*,

flows upward through the channel of Brahman— that is, through the flow within the *suṣumnā*— to the exterior of the cranial aperture (*brahmarandhra*) at a height of twelve finger-breadths above the head;

When, by means of a superior yoga consisting of the practice of exhalation (*recaka*), which obstructs all the channels through the suppression of hundreds of channels, one attains a state of stability for even a mere *muhūrta* in the upper portion of a space measuring twelve finger-breadths, then at that time there is the vision of Vyoma.
There occurs the vision of the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and other sky-dwellers. || 14 || 15 ||
By means of the practice of exhalation (recaka), which restrains the other channels, one attains stability for a moment; then, there is the vision of the sky-dweller.
O Rāghava, by means of the eye of the intellect situated not far from consciousness,
the Siddhas moving through the sky are seen, like dreams, even as they bestow their own specific fruits.

He states the very manner of perception: "By means of consciousness," etc. By means of the eye of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is situated not far from consciousness—that is, from the consciousness that is one's own essential nature (*svarūpacaitanya*)—and which is therefore proximate and thus an illuminator through the transfer of that consciousness, the perfected beings moving in the sky are seen, just as in the state of dreaming.
The meaning is that they do not merely grant vision; they also bestow the supernatural powers (siddhis), such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, which are required for one's own purpose. || 16 ||
By means of the practice of exhalation (recaka), when the vital breath is brought to remain for a long time outside the mouth at the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta), it enters the supreme city.
He describes the method for entering another's body with the words "from the mouth" (*mukhāt*). From the mouth— that is, from the face— outward, as far as the *dvādaśānta*,

which is the limit of the space measuring twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been brought to remain for a long time through the practice of exhalation (*recaka*)— that is, by means of a specific yoga consisting of the practice of exhalation— one [attains] another [body].
He enters another city, which means that the siddhi of entering another's body is attained. || 17 ||
Rāma said:
How can this body be made to enter through subtle apertures and the like, or to fill the entirety of space, or even be reduced to atomic size or increased to a massive bulk? (18)

Regarding the word "subtle" (*sūkṣma*): the sense is that for the purpose of passing through subtle apertures and so forth, for the sake of accomplishing movement, and for the purpose of filling or pervading space (*kha*), how can this body be led to either minuteness or grossness?
For since the body is a single entity, if there were a difference in its transformation, it would follow that the body itself must be divided. This is the underlying thought. || 18 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
There exists here only one pure consciousness, pure, serene, and untainted;
subtler than the subtlest, peaceful, neither the world nor those who dwell within the world.
"One" means: there exists only the one pure consciousness; even the abundant objects found within the world do not exist. || 19 ||
When that [consciousness], having turned toward volitional construction (saṃkalpa), gathers itself by itself and falls into a state of turbidity,
it is then called the "living being" (jīva).

Regarding the word "tat" (that): when that very reality of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), having become oriented toward volition (*saṃkalpa*), fashions or accumulates itself by means of itself—meaning, it becomes delimited—it then attains turbidity and impurity and is called the *jīva* (the individual soul).
This body is indeed unreal, yet through the delusion of mental construction,
the foolish-minded living being perceives it as real, just as a child sees a ghost that has arisen.

"Asatya" means this: the deluded soul, the individual living being (jīva), through the error of its own volitions, perceives this body—which is indeed unreal—as if it were a real yakṣa, just as a child might perceive such a thing. || 21 ||
For those who have thus realized the self cultivate [their understanding] in whatever manner; by means of that firm cultivation, they perceive it exactly as it is. (22)

Thus it is said: This being so, those persons who have known the Self and are certain of the Self perceive that very object exactly as they contemplate it, and by means of firm contemplation, they see that object in that very way immediately. 22.
O Raghava, through the persistent contemplation of firm conviction,
even the deluded turn poison into nectar, and nectar even into poison.

Regarding the word "dṛḍha" (firm): even the deluded, who are devoid of self-knowledge, by means of the continuous pursuit of firm contemplation—where "bhāva" means contemplation—lead forbidden action (*niṣiddha-karma*), which results in suffering, to the state of immortality (*amṛtatā*) through the persistence of that firm contemplation;
and they lead prescribed action (*vihita-karma*), which is like nectar, to the state of poison, which is the cause of suffering. || 23 ||
Thus, when that very thing is cultivated here exactly as it is through firm cultivation, one indeed becomes that very thing quickly; for this has been observed repeatedly. (24)

"Thus" means: in this way, whatever object is meditated upon in a certain manner, it becomes exactly so; that is to say, it is experienced. This very nature of the object has been repeatedly observed; that is to say, it has been investigated. || 24 || 25 ||
When this body is perceived with truthfulness, it truly becomes bodiless; however, when perceived with untruthfulness, the physical body attains the state of space.

O one of great intelligence, such is the method of cultivation for attaining the states of *aṇimā* and the rest; this is easily accessible to those who possess the realization of the perfect accomplishment of yoga. (26)

Regarding the phrase *aṇimādi*: for those who possess the realization of the perfection of yoga—that is, those whose consciousness has attained firm mastery through the conquest of the vital breath (*pavana*)—even upon reaching the state of *aṇimā* and the other powers, this method of contemplation (*bhāvanā-yukti*) remains as follows: it is easily accessible that through the contemplation of minuteness one attains *aṇimā*, and through the contemplation of magnitude one attains *mahimā*; thus, it serves as the means for accomplishing *aṇimā* and the rest.
The meaning is that the reasoning is easily obtained. || 26 ||
Endowed with the sovereign powers of the *aṇimā* and other qualities, that royal lady Cūḍālā thus became a perfected being (*satī*) through intense practice.

Regarding the word *aṇimā*: the connection is that Cūḍālā, having thus become possessed of intense practice, became endowed with the sovereignty of the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest. || 27 ||
She traveled by way of the path of the sky, entered the hollow of the ocean,
and moved across the surface of the earth, cool as nectar like the Gaṅgā. (28)
"She went" (jagāma) means that she wandered at will even throughout the three worlds like the Gaṅgā; therein, her descent into Pātāla by entering the cavity of the ocean is described. || 28 ||
Whenever she came near her husband’s chest even for a moment,
she would look for a means to awaken him, thinking, "I shall wake my husband."

"Kṣaṇam" (for a moment): When that Cūḍālā went even for a moment to her husband’s chest for the sake of an embrace, she then considered—meaning she reflected upon—the very means of awakening him, with the thought, "I shall awaken my husband"; she did not, however, look toward the embrace itself. The sense is that this was because of her lack of regard for the pleasures of the senses. || 29 || 130 ||
And with great effort, he repeatedly instructed his husband regarding the nectar of self-knowledge, just as a father instructs his young son.
And that king, the protector who had fallen [into misfortune], found no rest within himself,
like a pure pearl that has been severely marred.

"Nor [did he find rest]" (na ca). Just as a pearl, even if it is perfectly polished, does not find rest within another spotless pearl, so too that king did not find rest within himself. In the reading "asaṃkliṣṭam" (unblemished), the sense is: just as a pearl, being unblemished, does not find rest [within itself], so it was with him. || 31 || 32 || 33 || 34 ||
Even after such a length of time, that king did not recognize Cūḍālā, who was endowed with such virtues, just as a child does not recognize a branch of knowledge.
She too, because she had not yet attained repose within her own self,
did not reveal to the king her own perfection or her splendor, just as a sacrifice is not revealed to a Śūdra.
Rāma said:
O Lord, even Śikhidhvaja did not attain union with that great Siddhayoginī despite his efforts; how then could another understand it?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, the sequence of instruction is merely the maintenance of formal order;
the sole cause for the realization of knowledge is the pure intelligence of the disciple alone. (35)
Regarding "instruction" (upadeśa): the method consisting of the guru’s instruction is the means for merely maintaining the established order.
"Established order" refers to the boundaries prescribed by the scriptures of knowledge; it is simply the maintenance of those alone.
However, as for the direct realization of the Self through pure consciousness, the cause is solely the disciple's own purified intelligence. || 35 ||
In the ninth [chapter], the story of the Kirāta; Rāma said:
This being the case, O Sage, tell me how this sequence known as the instruction of the Guru can be the cause of self-knowledge for the maintenance of the world? (36)

"Thus. This being the case, regarding the stability of the world and worldly transactions, the meaning is: "In what manner, by what means, is this sequence known as the instruction of the Guru the cause of self-knowledge? Tell me that manner. || 36 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
A certain merchant, extremely miserly yet possessed of wealth and grain, lived with his family on the banks of the Vindhya forest like a Brāhmaṇa or similar caste member. (37)

Regarding the word *atyantā*: a *kirāṭa* is a Vaiśya, based on the etymological derivation that he "scatters" (*kirati*) for the sake of gaining wealth, "wanders" (*aṭati*), and "obtains again" (*punar āpnoti*) in the form of double, triple, or more. This is supported by the statement in the *Vaiśyaviḍambana*: "In the mockery of Vaiśyas, the *kirāṭa* is like a straw mat. However, the reading *kirāta* is not correct, because [the context implies] the possession of wealth and grain, as well as being a householder with a family, just like Brāhmaṇas and others.
And because searching for a single cowrie shell in the forest for three days was improper toward the Kirāta. || 37 ||
Once, O Rāma, as he was walking through the Vindhya jungle covered with a thicket of grass, a single cowrie shell fell from him. (38)

Regarding the word "tasya" (of him): *vindhya-jāṅgale* refers to a region consisting mostly of forest (*jaṅgala*) in the Vindhya mountains; if the reading is *jāṅgala*, it means a place with little water and very few trees. *Varāṭikā* means a cowrie shell. || 38 ||
Out of stinginess, he diligently shook everything— grass, chaff, and so forth—
for three days in every direction for the sake of a single cowrie shell.
"Out of meanness" (kārpaṇyāt): the state of being a miser is meanness; the meaning is an excess of greed.
"Chaff and straw" (tṛṇabusādikaṃ busaṃ) refers to agricultural waste. "For the sake of a cowrie" (kapardikārtham) means to search for a fallen small shell.
Then, at the end of three days, by him [from] that piece of bad land...
He has obtained a great wish-fulfilling gem, resembling the orb of the full moon.
"From there" means from the wretched forest region of Kujāṅgala. || 140 ||
Just as in that case, by the Kirāta’s persistent search for the cowrie shells, that jewel of world-inestimable value was obtained without weariness day or night. (41)

The phrase "yathā" (as) introduces a pair of verses as a single syntactical unit. For just as a merchant, in his search for cowrie shells, obtains a jewel that is the very price of the world, so too is self-knowledge attained by a disciple through the oral instruction of the Guru. Indeed, for this reason—namely, because of the lineage of Gurus and by means of the method taught by the Guru—one searches for another, superimposed reality.
Something else, an unconditioned reality, is sought after and is obtained—that is, it is directly realized. || 41 || 42 ||
In this way, through the instruction of the scriptures, knowledge of one's own self is attained; for by following the lineage of the Guru, one seeks one thing and indeed obtains another.
The teaching of this most precious reality has come from the mouth of the Guru;
[otherwise] it would be as causeless as a mere cowrie shell [attempting to produce] the causal power of a gem. (43)

Regarding the phrase "of this reality": for this reality—that is, for the knowledge of reality—which is of great value and high price, the instruction of the Guru is the cause; even though it is not the direct cause, like a small coin [kapardika] for a gem, it has become a cause through a traditional succession. || 43 ||
Thus ends the story of the Kirāta in the ninth canto of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-sāra.
Thus ends the ninth canto, the Narrative of the Hunter, in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa.
Then King Śikhidhvaja, lacking the state of knowledge of reality, fell into supreme delusion, just as living beings fall into the blinding darkness of ignorance. (44)

"Then" (tataḥ) means that without the state of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), there can be no state of repose (*viśrāntipada*) which consists of that very knowledge of reality. "Darkness" (*tamaḥ*) refers to blindness. "Subjects" (*prajāḥ*) refers to people. || 44 || 45 || 46 || 47 || 48 || 49 ||
With his mind set ablaze by the fire of suffering, he did not take even the slightest delight in those prosperities brought about by his desires, as if they were tongues of flame.
He gave away gifts most abundantly, undertook pilgrimages to sacred fords,
performed austerities such as the Kṛcchra penance, and wandered in all directions.
In every way, he did not obtain even the slightest freedom from sorrow;
overcome by anxiety and dejected, he regarded his kingdom as if it were poison.
Then once, having gone to a secluded place, Śikhidhvaja spoke these words in a sweet voice to Cūḍālā, who was seated upon his lap.
Śikhidhvaja said:
I have enjoyed the kingdom for a long time and beheld the grounds of worldly prosperity;
now, joined with dispassion, I am going to the forest. (49)
Neither pleasures nor pains, neither calamities nor prosperities embrace the forest-dwelling sage, O slender-limbed one. (150)
"Not so. They "embrace," meaning they bring under their own control. || 150 ||
p.
698) There is no delusion regarding the ruin of one's country, nor is there the destruction of people in battle;
I consider the happiness of those dwelling in the forest to be greater even than sovereignty over a kingdom. (51)

"No, [it is not so]. For those who dwell in the forest, there is no confusion caused by the collapse of their country, nor is there destruction of people in battle; there is no slaughter of living beings for the sake of war. Therefore, I consider the happiness of forest-dwellers to be even greater than the happiness of sovereignty. (Verses 51–62)
As the mind becomes pure when secluded in solitude,
it does not become so even amidst the orbs of the moon, nor in the abodes of Brahmā and Indra.
O slender one, you ought not to create an obstacle to this counsel of mine;
for noble women do not thwart the desire of their husband even in a dream.
Cūḍālā said:
O Lord, this task is resplendent when its time has arrived, and not otherwise;
a flower shines in spring, and fruit shines in autumn. (54)
Resorting to the forest is appropriate for those whose bodies are worn out by old age, but not for the young; therefore, this does not please me, especially one such as you.
Śikhidhvaja said:
Enough of this obstacle to my desired goal, O lotus-petal-eyed one!
Know that I am going from here to a remote forest in solitude.
"You are but a child, O lady of faultless limbs; you must not come to the forest.
For even for men, O soft-limbed one, this forest refuge is difficult to penetrate. (57)
"You must remain here protecting this supreme kingdom;
for when the husband has departed, it is the vow of women to bear the burden of the family. (58)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to his beloved, whose face was like the moon, the self-controlled king rose to bathe and performed all his daily duties.
Then, having abandoned his course through the world, the sun went to the mountain of setting;
the night attained its youth, with the lotus buds for her breasts. (160)
Having performed his evening rituals together with Cūḍālā,
he slept again upon his bed like Mount Maināka in the ocean.
Then, at the hour of midnight, when the region had fallen into silence and all people were hidden within the stone-receptacle of deep sleep,
the king left his sleeping beloved on his lap and departed.
Thinking, "I am going for the sake of the Vīrakrama," that one of perfected intellect went forth from the city, having first dispatched his own attendant to that very place.
"Vīra" means for the sake of the heroic progression (*vīrakrama*) and for the sake of the heroic conduct (*vīracaryā*). 63, 64, 65.
Having said, "O dull-witted Lakṣmī, salutations to you," he departed from the circle and entered the formidable forest alone, like a river entering the ocean.
Again at dawn, and again after spending ten nights,
he traversed with speed circles of territory, mountains, and rivers.
Then he reached a forest situated on the slope of Mount Mandara, inaccessible to people and far removed from any human settlement.

The phrase "tataḥ" introduces a sentence consisting of two verses. [It describes a place] where from afar the crowds of people and the cities can be heard—that is, they resound—because of those ponds and oblong lakes whose water flows through channels and irrigation ditches;
