and where the trees are surrounded by these pools; and where the sacrificial altars and other structures are decayed and loosened.

The grammatical connection is as follows: they reached that forest situated on the slope of Mount Mandara, where the former hermitages of the twice-born were known from the presence of altars, leaf-huts, rice-fields, and the like.
(66–68) [It was a forest] where the trees were surrounded by ponds with flowing water from gurgling channels.
The former hermitage of the twice-born, where the altars and other structures had crumbled away, was now merely a memory within consciousness.
700) Free from small creatures and containing vine-bowers frequented by perfected beings (siddhas),
he constructed a hut there on a level piece of ground.
In that same way, everything suitable for the duties of an ascetic has been accomplished.
A smooth bamboo staff, a vessel for eating fruit,
a water-offering bowl, a flower-basket, a rosary, and a water-pot (69).

The two verses beginning with "masṛṇam" form a single syntactical unit. "Masṛṇam" means smooth or glossy. "Bṛsīm" refers to a deer-skin used as a seat for those observing religious vows. || 69 || 170 ||
Then the king, having brought a patched cloak to ward off the cold, as well as a grass mat and a deer-skin, arranged them there in the small cottage.
He performed his recitation in the first watch of the morning, preceded by the twilight prayers;
in the second watch, however, he gathered flowers, and thereafter performed his bath and the worship of the deity.
He states his daily regimen in two verses beginning with "sandhyām": [at] *prahare*, meaning in a watch (of three hours). 71 || 72 ||
Later, having eaten some wild fruit as well as forest roots and lotus stalks,
the self-controlled one spent a single night devoted to the recitation of prayers.
Thus Śikhidhvaja remained in the forest in a hut of leaves;
now hear what Cūḍālā did while at home.
"Thus. What was her conduct like? Of what kind of character was she endowed? || 73 || 74 || 75 || 76 ||
There, at the time of midnight, when Śikhidhvaja had gone far away,
Cūḍālā woke up in fear like a doe sleeping in a village.
Deprived of her husband, she beheld the bed fallen into emptiness;
with her face somewhat withered and filled with sorrow, she rose up. (75)
Like a great creeper with its shoots and limbs devoid of vigor due to a bad friend, she, seated upon her bed for a moment, reflected with a distressed mind:
"Alas! Having abandoned his sovereignty, the Lord has gone from his home to the forest. (76)
"What should I do now that I am filled with this [emotion]? I shall go into his presence;
for the husband alone is ordained by fate as the refuge of a woman. (77)

The phrase "that" refers to the two verses as a single syntactical unit. According to the rule—that is, by the scripture—it has been declared that for a woman, her husband alone is the proper course of action, just as [the wind] enters through a lattice-window. 77–78.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā rose up to follow her husband;
emerging through a wind-opening, she ascended into the sky. (78)
She created the illusion of another moon by means of the face of the caravan leader who had attained his goal; then she beheld her husband at night as he went along, bearing a sword.

"He made" means: with his own mouth, he created the delusion of another moon—the error that "this is another moon"—in the minds of the company of perfected ones (siddhasārtha), that is, the assembly of perfected beings. || 79 ||
Beholding such a husband and remaining within the hollow of the sky,
she reflected upon the entirety of her future with her husband unbroken.
"Such as that" means she contemplated everything—both auspicious and inauspicious—that was destined to happen to her future husband, leaving nothing out and without exception. 180–195.
Seeing that which was destined to happen standing before her husband,
she turned back from the sky in order to bring that very thing about.
Let my departure today be postponed for a very long time;
I must go to his side—this is the decree of destiny.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā entered the inner apartments once more and lay down upon her bed like the lunar digit in the sky.
"For some reason, that lord of the earth has departed at this moment";
having thus consoled all the citizens, the woman remained there. (84)
Observing with equanimity, she protected her husband's kingdom in due order;
then days passed, as did fortnights, months, and likewise years. (85)
(702) What is the use of saying more here? For eighteen years, while Śikhidhvaja had gone to the forest, the woman Cūḍālā dwelt in his palace.
Then, reflecting that this was the time for her to go to her husband,
she resolved to depart with slow steps.
He departed from the inner city at night, traversed the path of the sky,
traveled by means of the wind-vehicle, and reached a cave in Mount Mandara.
Remaining invisible and stationed in the sky, she entered the interior of the forest;
through her yogic power, she perceived the king as if he were situated in another body. (89)
Deprived of necklaces, armlets, bracelets, earrings, and the like,
her husband had become emaciated in body, dark in complexion, and worn out by age.
Beholding him, the faultless-limbed Cūḍālā, with full breasts, feeling a slight sense of dejection, spoke thus within her own mind: (91)
"Alas! How terrible is the folly of one who perceives the meaning of all the scriptures, that such a person should fall into such a miserable state through negligence. (92)
Therefore, I shall certainly lead this Lord, who has known all that is to be known, to the glory of both worldly enjoyment and liberation this very day; of this there is no doubt.
Abandoning this form, I shall go to him in some other form to grant him supreme awakening. (94)
"She will not do as I say, thinking 'Bāleya is my beloved';
therefore, in the guise of an ascetic, I shall awaken my husband in an instant. (95)
The Master, whose intellect has been fully ripened through the maturation of the astringent dyes, now abides;
within his stainless mind, his own true nature reflects.

Regarding the word *bhartṛ*: "Kaṣāya" refers to passions such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth; their "maturation" (*pāka*) consists in engaging in what is prescribed by avoiding what is forbidden.
By that [maturation], [one becomes a husband]. 96.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā became the son of a twice-born;
through a slight meditation, having undergone a change of state, she fell indeed before her husband. (97)
Thus: "the son of a twice-born" means the child of a brahmin; "from slight meditation" means from even a small amount of meditative concentration; "otherness" means a different form.
Śikhidhvaja beheld that son of a brahmin walking before him,
his limbs fair as molten gold and adorned with a necklace of pearls.
"He saw"—this constitutes two verses. "Situated only a cubit above" means existing at a height of one *hasta* (cubit) above the ground. [Verses 98, 99, 200, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.]
His body was adorned with a white sacred thread (yajñopavīta) and covered by a pair of white garments;
his feet did not touch the ground, as he stood upon a space of only one cubit (kiṣku). || 99 ||
Upon seeing that son of a brahmin, Śikhidhvaja rose up,
having cast aside his sandals, thinking him to be the arrival of a son of the gods.
"O Devaputra, salutations! Here is a seat; please be seated.
Thus he pointed out a seat of leaves with his hand.
Having said, "O royal sage, salutations to you," he sat down;
and accepting the shower of flowers offered by him, he indeed sat there.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O illustrious son of a god, from where have you come?
I consider this day fruitful, since I have seen you today. (3)
Having spoken thus, O sinless one, Śikhidhvaja offered water for the feet, the arghya offering, and garlands of flowers,
in due order, to his chosen deity.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
O sinless one, by this charming, fitting, and humble demeanor, I truly believe that you will certainly live for a very long time.
O holy one, have you perhaps accumulated for the sake of nirvāṇa that noble austerity performed with a tranquil mind, free from conceptual construction?
"By means of a peaceful mind"—that is, having cast away all conceptual constructions from afar, have you perhaps accumulated noble and great austerity for the sake of Nirvana? || 6 ||
O gentle one, this vow of yours is like the edge of a sword; it is peaceful yet difficult, for you have renounced a flourishing kingdom to dwell in the great forest.

"Like the edge of a sword" (*asidhārasama*) means equal to the vow of the sword's edge (*asidhārāvrata*). Its definition is as follows: "When a young man behaves like a naive husband in the company of a young woman, yet remains inwardly free from attachment—that, they know, is the vow of the sword's edge.
And its similarity [to that vow] consists in his renunciation of enjoyment, despite the presence of royal fortune and the capacity for pleasure. (7)
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Blessed One, you know everything; you are a god—what wonder is there in this? You are recognized by your very splendor, which is the most supreme and serves as your distinguishing mark.
Who are you, whose son are you, and by what grace have you come here?
O you whose face is like the stainless moon, sever this doubt of mine.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O King, listen as I speak to you without omission regarding what you have asked;
for what man would deceive one who is humble and inquiring? (210)
Within this treasury of the world, there exists the sage Nārada, whose pure self is like a camphor tilaka upon the lovely face of auspicious Fortune. 11.
Once, that divine sage was established in meditation within a cave;
there, on the golden bank, the Ganges flows with its vast waves. (12)
Once, at the conclusion of his meditation on the riverbank, the sage Nārada heard the tinkling sound of jingling bracelets, a playful and melodious clamor.
"What is this? he thought, feeling a slight sense of curiosity;
looking down casually, he beheld a multitude of women upon the ground.
In a place devoid of men, he was sporting intensely in water-sports with women such as Rambhā and Tilottamā, having cast off their garments.
Everywhere its entire body was visible, standing like the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa),
with all its limbs reflected so as to appear as if they were mirrors for one another.
Beholding that lovely woman, the mind of the sage—suddenly devoid of discernment—became thrilled with joy and began to quiver. (17)
When his mind was filled with bliss, agitated, and his vital breath (prāṇānila) was established therein, an emission of semen occurred for him as he experienced that satisfaction. || 18 ||
Tell me, how did this sage—though such a man, though possessed of vast knowledge, and though liberated while living—fall under the sway of passion in such a manner? (19)
The Brahmin said:
When one's own nature—pure and true—is forgotten for even a moment, the visible world bursts forth into manifestation, like a rain cloud in the monsoon season. (220)

Again, Cūḍālā’s words: "In one's own nature" (svarūpe). When the stainless and true nature of the Self is forgotten for even a moment, the visible world attains manifestation, that is, it comes into appearance. || 220 ||
Even due to incessant mental construction, this demon of the visible world does not manifest within consciousness, whose own nature remains unforgetting and undiminished. (21)

Regarding the term *anārata*: because of the cause of uninterrupted contemplation within one's own nature, which is consciousness (*citi*) consisting of pure awareness (*cinmātra-svabhāva*), as long as even the slightest flash [of that nature] is not forgotten, this demon in the form of the visible world does not arise and does not manifest. || 21 ||
The vibration of even a fraction of pleasure and pain is bondage for the individual soul (jīva), and nothing else;
indeed, the absence of that is liberation—thus is the twofold established doctrine. (22)

"Sukheti" (Regarding happiness): The vibration of even a fraction of pleasure and pain within the individual soul (*jīva*)—that is, the mere manifestation of a trace of pleasure and pain—is itself bondage.

The absence of that—the absence of the vibration of even a fraction of pleasure and pain—is liberation (*mokṣa*). Thus, this is the twofold determination or conclusion regarding the two modes of bondage and liberation. "Dedhā" is the feminine dual form of the locative case. || 22 ||
Through pure awakening to awakening, by means of the self whose nature is the knowledge of one's own self,
once it is known that pleasure, pain, and so forth do not exist, the knower attains tranquility.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the pure": when it is known that there is no pleasure, pain, or the like—by means of the pure awareness of the object of knowledge (*bodhya-bodha*), which is non-different from the knowledge of one's own nature (*svasvarūpa-jñāna*) because its essence consists in the knowledge of one's own self—the knower (*jña*) is the wise one (*jñānin*). This occurs through the experience of the Supreme Brahman, which is non-different from one's own nature, by means of the realization of the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), the object of knowledge.
He attains gentleness and liberation while living. || 23 ||
When the firm conviction arises that everything is indeed the space of consciousness, Brahman,
the individual soul attains equanimity, like a lamp devoid of oil.

"All" means: when one has attained a firm conviction that the entire world is indeed Brahman, whose nature is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), the state of being an individual soul (jīvabhāva) comes to rest. || 24 ||
This great world is born from the power of the self-nature;
having attained its stability through latent impressions, it remains subject to merit and demerit.

Regarding the term "Self": this world has arisen as the very nature of the Self; having attained its persistence through latent impressions (vāsanā), it remains under the sway of merit and demerit, subject to the dependence of karma. || 25 ||
Having removed the portion consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one is not grasped by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*);
therefore, O Sage, it is our view that a living being is not born again. (26)

"Vāsanām" (the latent impression). Having removed the portion consisting of latent impressions from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), one is neither grasped nor bound by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).
Therefore, due to the absence of the bondage of karma, the living being is not born; such is our view, our established doctrine (*siddhānta*). 26 || 27 || 28 || 29 || 230 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O best among speakers, you describe that which is exceedingly noble and a great marvel; it has ascended to the level of direct experience and is firmly established like the ultimate reality. (27)
O handsome one, by hearing this splendor of your speech today, I have attained an inner coolness as if I had drunk nectar. (28)
Therefore, first tell me briefly and quickly about that origin of yourself;
thereafter, I shall listen with effort to your speech which contains the essence of knowledge.
Tell me today exactly how that heroic deed was performed by that noble sage Nārada, the son of Padmaja.
The Brahmin said:
Then, by him who was binding the intoxicated elephant of the mind to the vast tethering post of discernment with the excellent rope of pure intelligence; (31)

The phrase "tataḥ" (then) introduces two verses as a single syntactic unit. In the expression "viveka-vipulālāne," *ālāna* refers to the post for tying an elephant. In "śuddha-buddhi-varatrāyā," *varatrā* is a leather thong. 31 || 32 || 33 || 34 || 35 ||
The Sage placed his semen into a crystal jar standing at his side;
that jar was then filled by him with milk produced through his resolve.
Then, after a month, he grew like the moon emerging from the interior of a mountain;
with all his limbs fully developed, the embryo emerged from the jar.
When all the ritual preparations were complete, the sage Nārada applied his entire wealth of knowledge to that [sacrifice], just as one pours the contents from one vessel into another.
Then, taking his son with him, he went into the presence of Brahmā;
the Lord Creator made that grandson a master who had reached the further shore of knowledge.
"O virtuous one, I am indeed he who is named Kumbha, born from a jar;
the four Vedas are my friends, dwelling with me as if in play. (36)

The two verses beginning with "Sādho" constitute a single statement. By saying "the four Vedas are my friends," he indicates his knowledge of the true essence of the Vedic meaning. "Gāyatrī is my mother’s sister"—since Sarasvatī is his mother as the nourisher, Gāyatrī is her sister; by this, [he shows] that which was obtained through the grace of Sarasvatī.
The words of Kumbha indicate his omniscience. || 36 || 37 || 38 || 39 || 240 || 41 || 42 || 43 ||
Gāyatrī is my maternal aunt, and Sarasvatī is my mother;
thus, I traverse the worlds entirely according to my will.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O virtuous one, by virtue of having encountered you today with speech that flows like nectar, I stand at the forefront of the blessed. (38)
No other things whatsoever cool my mind in such a way as the company of the virtuous does—even the acquisition of a kingdom and the like. (39)
Kumbha said:
Let this story rest for now; I have told you everything.
O virtuous one, tell me: who are you on this mountain, and what are you doing? (240)
Śikhidhvaja said:
"You are a son of the gods; you know this. If you have asked me, I shall speak—listen!
Out of fear of the terror of saṃsāra, I dwell within the forest. (41)
"I am King Śikhidhvaja; having renounced my kingdom, I remain here.
O Knower of Reality, I am deeply afraid of birth again within this cycle of existence. (42)
Even while performing this unimpaired practice correctly, I go from suffering to a flood of suffering; for me, nectar has become poison. (43)
Kumbha said:
For knowledge is the supreme good; by means of it, one fully realizes absolute liberation (kaivalya).
Ritual action has been taught merely for the purpose of passing the time and as a diversion.

Regarding the word "jñāna" (knowledge): knowledge is the means to knowledge. Ritual actions, such as austerity and the study of sacred texts, are prescribed merely for diversion—that is, for the purpose of passing the time, for the sake of killing time. || 44 ||
For those who have not attained the vision of knowledge, ritual action is their supreme goal;
for the ignorant person, whose essence consists of nothing but latent impressions (*vāsanā*), all ritual actions are fruitful.
For the one who knows, however, all such actions are fruitless because of the total exhaustion of latent impressions alone.

Regarding the word *alabdha*: for those who have not attained the vision of knowledge—that is, for those who do not know the Self—ritual action alone is the supreme resort, the highest goal. This is because, since the essence consists merely of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and due to the presence of powerful impressions, actions bear fruit only for the ignorant person, but not for the wise one who is free from impressions; such is the meaning. || 45 ||
Just as the seasonal fruit of a previous year perishes at the change of seasons, even so the fruit of action comes to an end when the latent impressions (vāsanās) are destroyed. 46.

Regarding the phrase "in another season": just as a previous seasonal object—such as a flower or fruit produced during a particular season (*ṛtu*)—comes to dissolution in another season through the departure of the former season and the arrival of another, even so, when the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) are destroyed, the fruit of action also meets its destruction, because the fruit of action has the latent impressions as its cause. || 46 ||
Just as the fruit of the *śarala* reed does not ripen by its own inherent nature, so too,
an action devoid of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) does not bear fruit in the hereafter.

Establishing this very point, he says: "No. Just as a *śaralatā*—the stalk of the grass called *śara*—does not bear fruit by its very nature, that is, by the very nature of the thing itself, because it terminates merely in a flower; likewise, even actions devoid of latent impressions (*nirvāsanā*) do not bear fruit in the next world, in another birth, because they too possess such a nature.
For one whose ignorance comes to an end through the contemplation that "all is Brahman," no latent impression arises, just as the ocean does not exist in a desert for a wise man. (48)
By the complete abandonment of mere latent impressions (vāsanā), the individual soul attains within itself that state which is free from old age and death, and further devoid of rebirth. (49)
The mind accompanied by latent impressions is ignorance; the mind free from latent impressions is the object of knowledge.
Having attained the state of being known through knowledge, the living soul is not born again.
"Knowledge alone is the supreme good"—even Brahmā and the others [have said this].
Knowledge is the means of crossing over saṃsāra; why then do you remain ignorant? (51)
"Who am I? How was this born? And how is it extinguished?
O King, why do you not investigate this; why do you remain like one who is ignorant? (52)
"O King, why do you not serve the feet of those who know the further and near shores, while raising such questions as 'What is bondage? and 'What is liberation? (53)

How so? For those who know the near and the far shore—namely, for those who know that Brahman alone is both the further shore (pāra) and the hither shore (avāra) of the ocean of saṃsāra—the words "near" (avāra) and "far" (pāra) indicate the end and the beginning [respectively]. 53–59.
That yoga, by which one is liberated, is obtained through inquiry, service, and association with the virtuous who possess equal vision. (54)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus enlightened by his beloved, who possessed a divine form,
Śikhidhvaja, his face filled with tears, spoke these words.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O son of a god, today at long last I have been awakened by you!
Out of folly, I abandoned the company of noble beings and dwelt in the forest. (56)
"Aha! I believe my evil has now completely gone to its destruction, since you have come to the forest and awakened me here. (57)
"You are my guru, you are my father, and you are my friend, O fair-faced one;
today as a disciple I bow at your feet—please show me your grace. (58)
Teach me quickly that Brahman which you know to be the most sublime, by knowing which one does not grieve, and through which I may become liberated.
Kumbha said:
O royal sage, if you are one who accepts my words, then I shall speak to you;
otherwise, even if spoken in many ways, my speech would be fruitless. (260)
Again, the words of Kumbha: || 260 ||
When questioned in jest by one whose words are not to be accepted, the speaker's utterances go to fruitlessness, just as visual perceptions do in the presence of darkness. (261)

"Unworthy of acceptance" means as follows: the words of an unreliable speaker whose speech is not to be accepted—when questioned with indifference or even in jest—go to fruitlessness, just as the functions of the visual faculty (the eyes) become useless for one whose consciousness is immersed in darkness. 61.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Whatever you say must be carried out by me, like a scriptural injunction;
this which I have spoken is true and should be done immediately without hesitation. (62)

Regarding the word "yat": whatever you say—that is, what you speak—I must perform it without hesitation, just as one performs a Vedic injunction or a scriptural duty; this which has been spoken by me is indeed the truth. 62.
p. 712) The ninth [chapter] contains the narrative of the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
Kumbha said:
Just as a child accepts his father’s words that establish the means for liberation, so too should you accept my speech. 63.

Again, Kumbha says: "As such... Just as a child accepts and takes to heart his father's words—accepting only the presentation of the means to liberation while discarding the logical arguments supporting it—in that very same way, you too should grasp my speech. 63–64.
First, O King, listen to a certain wonderful account;
afterwards, I shall describe the established state of the matter at hand. (64)
There is a certain illustrious man who knows the true meaning of all the scriptures and is the abode of all virtues and splendors, yet he does not know the unborn state.
He set out to accomplish that which is achieved only through infinite effort—the attainment of the wish-fulfilling gem—just as the submarine fire strives to dry up the ocean. (66)
Through great effort over a long period of time,
that sage remained resolute and persistent, yielding only to the power of time.
What accomplishment is not achieved by those who exert themselves, for whom the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) is their success?
He beheld the gem standing almost before him, within reach of his hand. (68)
Standing upon the rising peak of Mount Meru, the sage appeared like the risen moon;
yet, O lord of the best of jewels, he was not one who possessed certainty.
When the queen had arrived so suddenly, like a commoner who has become utterly dejected, he reflected thus in his mind, which was filled with wonder: || 270 ||
"This is a jewel; if it were not a jewel, it would not be so.
I see it, yet I do not touch it; perhaps it has slipped away through contact. (71)

This is the statement consisting of seven verses beginning with "ayam" (this). "This"—referring either to the jewel standing before one or to this very gem being seen—is not necessarily a jewel. If it were a jewel, then it would not be a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem).
Therefore, while in a state of doubt, I see it indeed, but I do not touch it; for why? Because by touching it, one might perhaps depart [from this world]. || 71 ||
The supreme jewel is not indeed accomplished by this much time alone;
according to the sequence of the scriptures, it is accomplished through effort that lasts until the end of one's life. (72)

It is said that the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), the sovereign of gems, is not accomplished in such a short time; rather, it is accomplished only through great effort exerted at the cost of one's life and vital breath—such is the sequence for the ritual practice of attaining the jewel according to the scriptures.
Miserable, with my eye squinting, I behold the light of the jewels like the flickering movement of a fly’s wing, as if seeing two moons through delusion. (73)

But I, being wretched, with my eye that is squinted and contracted, see that gem-light—which resembles a flickering flame or a brand of fire and is like its branch—as if it were two moons, due solely to delusion. || 73 ||
Whence has such an abundant abundance of fortune come together, that even now I obtain this sovereign jewel which grants all perfections? (74)

"From where has such vast, abundant, and supreme fortune come to me? It is for the sake of this attainment of fortune that I have now obtained the sovereign jewel (maṇīndra) which grants all perfections. || 74 ||
Indeed, only some great souls become truly fortunate, for whom the goddesses of prosperity become manifest in a short time. (75)
Only a few great and highly fortunate individuals are such that prosperity comes face-to-face with them in a very short time. || 75 ||
"I am indeed a mere human, a wretched man of little austerity;
how can the supernatural powers come to me, who am the sole vessel for misfortune? (76)
I, moreover, am one of little austerity, a wretched man, and an object of pity for the virtuous; being thus solely a vessel for misfortune, how can the supernatural powers come to me? (76)
Thus, for a long time, the ignorant man, reflecting through conceptual constructions and mental fabrications,
was deluded by his own folly and made no effort to grasp the jewel. (77)
Thus, for a long time, reflecting with conceptualizations and volitions— deluded by ignorance, enslaved by nescience— he made no effort to grasp the jewel.
While he remained thus, the jewel flew up and departed, along with the supernatural powers (siddhis).
For those who treat others with contempt are abandoned by them, just as arrows are cast off once their string has been released.
The man again exerted effort toward the acquisition of the supreme jewel;
for resolute people do not falter in their own undertakings. (79)
Then he saw a piece of glass, unbroken yet possessing a shimmering appearance,
placed before him by invisible, laughing, and deceptive Siddhas.
"He saw," it is said. Then he beheld a piece of unbroken glass, its form shimmering and radiant, placed before him by invisible, laughing, deceptive Siddhas. || 280 ||
Thinking, "This is a wish-fulfilling gem," the fool perceives reality in that [clod of earth];
for the ignorant man, deluded, regards clay as gold. (81)

"This is it": that fool perceived that piece of glass as being "this," [thinking] "This is the wish-fulfilling gem" (*cintāmaṇi*), [imagining] its reality—that is, its status as an ultimate wish-fulfilling gem. For an ignorant person, being deluded, perceives a mere clod of earth—a specific kind of soil—as if it were gold. (81–84)
Then, having taken that jewel, he abandoned his former prosperity, thinking, "Everything is obtained from this wish-fulfilling gem; what is the use of other riches? (82)
"This land is unpleasant and harsh, filled with sinful people;
having gone far away, I shall dwell happily according to my desire in prosperity. (83)
Having thus taken the jewel, the fool went to the empty forest;
there, by means of that glass trinket, he fell into great calamity. (84)
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Narrative of the Wish-Fulfilling Gem" in the *Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭhasāra*.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Narrative of Cintāmaṇi" in the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa.
In the ninth [chapter], the narrative of Gajendra; Kumbha said:
Now, O protector of the earth, listen to this other delightful account, which is a supreme awakening for the intellect and worthy of yourself, O virtuous one. (85)

"It exists. [He is] the leader of the leaders of great herds, the most excellent leader even among the leaders of great herds. "Vajrāsthiviṣamau" means harder than even a diamond (vajra) or bone; in the reading "vajrāstraviṣamau," the meaning is that they are as formidable as the tip of a diamond weapon. || 85 || 86 ||
In the Vindhya forest there was an elephant, the leader of a great herd;
his two white tusks were long, as hard as adamant, and formidable. (86)
Bound with an iron net by the elephant-keeper and struck with a goad, he was fastened down, suffering the restraint and tormented by cruel chains. (87)
"He" refers to that elephant. He was bound on all sides by the elephant-driver (the agent) using an iron net as the means—that is, with chains.
And being thus bound and tormented by the cruel chains, he fell into restraint, which is to say, into dependence;
because this constitutes a different sentence from "bound," there is no tautology. || 87 || 88 ||
Out of exhaustion, that elephant broke his fetters with great effort using those two tusks within a period of two muhūrtas.
Seeing that severing of his shackles, the enemy, who was determined to bind him, fell upon the head of the lordly elephant like a palmyra fruit. (89)

"Of him" (tasya): he whose certainty regarding the capture of that [elephant] was fixed upon the binding of that beast—the enemy elephant-driver—fell from the palm tree onto the head of the lordly elephant. 89 || 290 || 91 || 92 || 93 ||
That evil-minded man fell to the ground before reaching the elephant's head;
seeing him fallen before him, the great elephant was moved by compassion.
p.
716) There are some virtuous beings of expansive qualities even among the animal realm;
what kind of manliness is it on my part to think, "I shall crush those who have fallen"? (91)
Thinking, "He too is an elephant," he did not strike that enemy;
instead, the elephant merely abandoned him and went to his own country.
When the elephant had departed, the mahout rose up, his body and mind restored to health.
He searched diligently for the elephant within the forest, obscured by the glare of the firebrands;
after a long time, he found the lordly elephant situated in a certain grove.
That rogue elephant trainer had a circular pit dug all around him in the forest;
then, that deceitful man covered it over with a mass of withered creepers.
"Sa" refers to him. "Khātavalaya" means a circular pit or chasm. "Asthagayat" means he covered or concealed it. || 94 || 95 || 96 || 97 ||
Within just a few days, while roaming in that forest, the elephant fell into a pit like a mountain falling into a dried-up ocean. || 95 ||
Thus, having been bound even more firmly by that elephant-driver,
he remains even today in his own house in misery, like Bali.
If that elephant had struck the enemy who fell before him with his trunk, he would not have experienced the pain caused by the digging up of his own tethering post.
Out of folly, a man who does not purify his future time by means of the sequence of present actions goes to suffering, just like the elephant of the Vindhya mountains. 98.

"Due to folly," etc. The syntactical connection is as follows: because of folly—that is, due to the cause of ignorance—a man, failing to purify the future time through present sequences of action and various means, and thus acting without a remedy, undergoes suffering just like a wild elephant of the Vindhya mountains. (98)
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Narrative of Gajendra" in the *Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭhasāra*.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Narrative of Gajendra" in the *Śrī-Yogavāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa*.
p. 717) Ninth: An exposition of the narrative of the *Cintāmaṇi*.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Son of the Immortals, reveal once more to me that web of stories which was indicated by you through the binding of the Vindhya elephant by the practitioner of the jewel-mantra.
Now Śikhidhvaja asks for the purport of the two stories, beginning with the word "maṇi."
The meaning is: from the binding of the Vindhya elephant by the jewel-attainer, that is, from the binding of the Vindhya elephant by the one who has mastered the power of jewels. || 99 ||
Kumbha said:
O Lord of the Earth, you alone are he who is described as one skilled in the meaning of the scriptures yet unlearned in the knowledge of reality—a seeker of jewels. (300)

The phrase "He who is such... constitutes two and a half verses. That person who is skilled in the scriptures—proficient in the knowledge of the treatises—but unlearned and lacking confidence in the knowledge of reality (*tattva*), is called a "seeker of jewels.
This is because, although he obtains a jewel through the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, he lacks certainty regarding its true nature. And he...
You alone are the man who accomplishes the jewels. || 300 ||
You are knowledgeable in the treatises, yet you are untrained in the knowledge of reality. || 1 ||
Since you are one who knows the reality within the scriptures, yet there is no repose in your heart nor any firm abiding in that reality. (1)
O virtuous one, know that this unartificial renunciation of everything is the wish-fulfilling gem;
you are now striving to accomplish that doctrine which brings an end to all sufferings.

To the question, "What then is the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi)?", he says: "Know..."—this constitutes two verses as a single syntactical unit. Since you have renounced your kingdom and since you have come to this very remote hermitage, the logical connection (*anvaya*) is that you are intent upon accomplishing the wish-fulfilling gem called "renunciation of everything," which destroys all suffering. (2–3)
You have renounced your kingdom, along with your wife, wealth, and kinsmen;
having come from a place very far from your own country, you have arrived at my hermitage. (3)
718) When all has been renounced, only the notion of "I" remains within you;
therefore, the total renunciation of everything does not reach its fulfillment until that [notion] is also gone.
At that moment, the conceptualization of renunciation enveloped you, just as a cloud covers the sky.
How then is it that the wish-fulfilling gem was not obtained by me? To this he says: "Only," etc.; this constitutes three half-verses as a single sentence.
The meaning is that although you have renounced everything, the notion of "I" alone has been left behind; thus, pride has not been abandoned.
Therefore, for that reason, because this total renunciation is incomplete, conceptualization regarding it has enveloped you, just as a cloud covers the sky. || 4 ||
This is not that supreme bliss, the great success of total renunciation;
it is something else entirely, exceedingly lofty, difficult to achieve over a long time, and vast. || 5 ||

The two verses beginning with "nāyam" form a single syntactic unit. This [renunciation] which has now been established is not merely that renunciation of everything which consists of supreme bliss—that is, wherein there is supreme joy—and wherein there is a great arising or awakening;
for that renunciation of everything, being the cause of supreme bliss, is something else entirely, a certain great thing that must be accomplished over a long period of time. || 5 ||
When thought has increased as a conceptual construction in your mind,
like the movement of trees in a whirlwind, renunciation has flown away from you.
When the mind has thus grown in its proliferation of thoughts, your renunciation flew away— just as a bird flies off when the trembling of a tree increases due to a whirlwind, a mass of wind.
O lotus-eyed one, when that great jewel of universal renunciation had departed,
you beheld with the eye of your resolve the glass-gem of asceticism.
He who abandons immeasurable bliss that is easily attained and instead exerts himself toward a limited object that is difficult to achieve is considered a rogue and a destroyer of his own self.
"Immeasurable" means infinite bliss and total renunciation, which are easy to accomplish; whereas "measured" means limited bliss, which is in fact difficult to accomplish. (8)
(719) "I have obtained a wish-fulfilling gem"—thus you have thought;
yet, O virtuous one, you have not even obtained a fragment of crystal. 9.
He reflects: "I have obtained the jewel of asceticism, yet I have not obtained even the slightest bit of spiritual excellence"—this is the meaning. || 9 ||
Thus ends the section titled "The Explanation of the Story of the Wish-Fulfilling Gem" from the *Yogavāsiṣṭhasāra*.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Exposition of the Story of Cintāmaṇi" in the *Śrī-Yogavāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa*.
In the ninth [chapter], there is an exposition of the narrative of Gajendra;
Kumbha said:
That elephant which was in the Vindhya forest is you here upon this earth;
that detachment and discernment of yours are its two white tusks.
Now he explains the story of Vindhya-hastin with the passage beginning with "yo'sau" and ending with "nṛpa baddho yathā balir."
You are the Vindhya elephant because of your foolishness; and detachment and discernment are your two tusks, because they break the bonds of fetters and the like. || 310 ||
And that elephant-driver who is intent upon treading down the elephant is well known;
your ignorance, which is intent upon treading you down, is exceedingly painful to experience.
But your ignorance is like the elephant-driver, because it is a cause of bondage and a cause of suffering. || 11 || 12 ||
O King, though you are exceedingly powerful, you are led by your own folly from sorrow to sorrow and from fear to fear, like an elephant by a powerless mahout.
Just as an elephant is encircled by a net of iron ropes,
so too are you completely enveloped by the net of the snares of desire.

The net of iron chains is the net of the bonds of desire. The breaking of the shackles, however, is the renunciation of royal enjoyments. (13–15) For desire is more treacherous, more expansive, and more firm than iron ropes. Iron may decay with time, but craving only increases. (14)
Just as the elephant broke the binding of the enemy's chain-net,
so did you abandon enjoyments, the earth, and a thornless kingdom. (15)
Just as the elephant-driver who fell from the palmyra tree onto the ground, so too did ignorance fall when you abandoned that kingdom. (16)
The falling of the elephant-driver from the palm tree is, in fact, the falling away of your ignorance now that you are abandoning the kingdom.

To neglect the fallen elephant-driver and allow the elephant to flee into the forest is, for you, the taking of refuge in the wilderness through the complete eradication of ignorance by the great sword of total renunciation. 16–23. 320. 21. 22. 23.
When a dispassionate person desires to abandon the hope for enjoyment, then ignorance trembles like a demon in a tree that is about to be cut down. || 17 ||
When the flood of enjoyments has indeed been cast off, the state of ignorance falls away;
for when a person of discrimination remains having completely renounced enjoyments. (18)
Then ignorance flees like a demon from a felled tree;
when you went to the forest, then knowledge was wounded by you—
fallen and weakened, yet not slain— by the great sword of total renunciation.
Having risen once more and remembering the insult he had suffered,
he then cast you into this dense pit of conceptual proliferation.
If you had known that [the situation] was thus gone, you would have had me killed at that very moment;
for if you had known the truth regarding the relinquishment of the kingdom, you would not have allowed me to perish.
Because that enemy elephant was made to circle the moat, he has,
through his ignorance, inflicted incomparable suffering upon you.
O best of kings, that splendor of the elephant-enemy’s retinue which spread abroad was merely the mental manifestation of your own ignorance, O King. (23)
The circular moat, enveloped by young creepers,
was like the hardship of asceticism, slightly obscured by the conduct of virtuous people. (24)
The elephant-driver’s repeated preparation of pits in the forest for the purpose of binding elephants, his employment of ascetic observances through ignorance,

and his covering of the circular pits with young grass and creepers— the essential meaning is that these are merely slight disguises for the suffering of penance by means of the conduct of virtuous people. (24–25)
Thus, even now, O King, you remain in this most terrible pit of suffering created by your own asceticism, bound in the depths of Pātāla like Bali.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Narrative of Gajendra" in the *Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭhasāra*.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Exposition of the Legend of Gajendra" in the *Vasiṣṭha-vivaraṇa*.
Kumbha said:
Why was that knowledge not accepted then by you, Cūḍālā, who were eloquent and had realized what is to be known? (26)
As it has been said: "By means of the praiseworthy Śālinī [meter]. || 26 || 27 ||
For she is the foremost among those who know reality; whatever she speaks and whatever she does, all that is indeed true, my dear, and should be practiced with reverence. (27)
If, O King, you did not carry out her word, why was this total renunciation not skillfully performed? (28)

"Now," [it is said]. If her words, Cūḍālā’s, had not been carried out, then for what reason was this total renunciation being performed by you not made "nipuṇa"—that is, not brought to completion? || 28 || 29 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
The kingdom has been abandoned, the home abandoned, and likewise the country;
wives have been abandoned, sons abandoned—why has total renunciation not been performed? (29)
Kumbha said:
Wealth, wife, home, kingdom, land, the royal parasol, and kinsmen—all these are not yours, O King; for what indeed is yours that you could renounce? (330)

"Regarding 'wealth' (dhanam): the royal umbrella is an indicative mark for all other royal insignia. Thus, all of this—all that—does not belong to you; therefore, what indeed is 'renunciation of everything'? How [is it renunciation]? The meaning is that the renunciation of what is not one's own does not constitute renunciation. || 330 ||
You still possess a supreme attachment that has not yet been abandoned;
by relinquishing it entirely, you shall attain the highest state of sorrowlessness.

To the question "In that case, who is mine?", he says: "Thine. There exists within you a supreme passion—an unrenounced, unabated desire for some object; having completely abandoned that passion, you shall attain the state of supreme sorrowlessness.
Śikhidhvaja said:
If my entire kingdom were not mine, then all this forest would be mine;
even these mountains, trees, shrubs, and so forth—I renounce them all.

Regarding the phrase "the kingdom": the syntactical connection is as follows: "If the entire kingdom is not mine—that is, my own—then let the whole forest, including its mountains, trees, shrubs, and so forth, be mine; whatever exists, even that I renounce. || 32 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus speaking, O Rāma, the self-controlled and steadfast Śikhidhvaja, urged by the words of Kumbha, [vanished] in the mere twinkling of an eye.
The phrase "iti" refers to the two verses as a single syntactical unit. The construction is: he wiped away that dwelling in the forest—that is, his attachment to the forest—of the self. (33, 34, 35)
With firm resolve, he wiped away that desire for the forest from his heart,
just as the flood of the rainy season washes away a streak of dust upon its own bank.
Śikhidhvaja said:
Indeed, even from the forest filled with trees, mountains, groves, and chasms, my latent desire has been utterly abandoned; total renunciation now abides within me.
Kumbha said:

The unseen, the forest, the chasm, water, trees, dry land—none of these belong to you; how then can there be "renunciation of all" for you? For you still possess that which has not been relinquished: attachment, the most excellent of all things. (36)
"A mountain"—this is a sentence consisting of three and a half verses. It is to be explained as before. 36 || 37 || 38 || 39 || 40 || 41 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
If all this does not belong to me, then let all that—the vessels and so forth, along with the pond, the ground, and the hut—belong to me; I shall quickly abandon that very [self] alone. (37)
Kumbha said:
Even the hermitage is not yours when it has been abandoned; renunciation is not all-pervading.
For you, the supreme attachment to everything remains unabandoned. (38)
Śikhidhvaja said:
If all this does not belong to me, then all those things of mine—the vessels and so forth, the skins, walls, granaries, and so on—I shall abandon them for now. (39)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, he rose and, gathering all those items— the rosary, the deerskin, and so forth— in one place, he burned them with the resolve of renunciation.
The king said: "In the fire, a collection of goods is consumed along with dry fuel; yet one who is devoid of oil and possesses only his own form is content. (41)
Having completely abandoned all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) therein, I remain as one who has renounced everything. Oh! By the auspicious time, I have been awakened by the son of a god.
I am perfected, absolute, pure, and awakened through bliss.
What indeed is this thing called "substance" that is conceived as having a sequential order, which serves as the support for vessels, utensils, places, houses, and so forth? (43)

"What is its name? [It is] that which relies upon vessels, utensils, places, dwellings, and so forth—wherein the sequence is mentally constructed and the utility is imagined by the intellect; "vessel" (*bhāṇḍa*) means a container, "utensil" (*upaskara*) means household equipment, "place" (*sthāna*) means a site of residence, and "dwelling" (*sadana*) means a house—it is the reliance upon these and similar things.
What kind of entity is this so-called "possession"? It is no entity at all, because it is the sole cause of suffering. // 43 //
To the extent that various causes of bondage are abandoned,
to that same extent the mind attains supreme peace.
As it is said in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa: "To whatever extent a living being forms relationships dear to the mind, to that same extent are stakes of sorrow driven into his heart. (Verses 44–53)
I am at peace, I am completely extinguished, I am happy, and I am victorious;
all obstructions have come to an end, and I have performed the renunciation of everything.
I am indeed naked, standing here equal to the directions; O son of a god, having given away everything through great renunciation, tell me what else remains. (46)
Kumbha said:
O King Śikhidhvaja, you have not relinquished anything at all;
do not vainly pretend to the supreme bliss of universal renunciation.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed one, O lotus-eyed Rāma, while speaking thus, that king reflected for a moment and said this: 48.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O son of a deity, when I have renounced everything, only this body remains—a form composed of blood and flesh, a collection of serpents that are the sense faculties. (49)

Having risen from that [state], I shall again bring this body to its state of destruction by means of leaping from a cliff or other such methods without obstacle, and thus become one who has renounced everything. (350)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having said this, as he was making a sudden effort to rise in order to cast his body into the pit situated before him,
Kumbha spoke to him.
Kumbha said:
"O King, why do you cast this innocent body into a great pit? For even a bull, when enraged, kills a calf without knowing its own nature. (52)
O lotus-eyed one, even though you have abandoned your body,
it is said that the renunciation of all things has not yet reached completion for you, for that is indeed difficult to achieve.
If you renounce that by which this body is agitated and that which is the seed of births and karmas— since it is that which must be renounced— you are truly one who possesses great renunciation.
Śikhidhvaja said:
By what is this body moved? What is the seed of births and karmas? O handsome one, when what is abandoned does everything become relinquished? (55)
Kumbha said:
O virtuous one, the mind—named by such terms as "the living soul" (jīva) and so forth—is omnipresent in its form;
it is neither inert nor non-inert, yet it is deluded and abides as everything.

"O virtuous one," thus begins the statement consisting of two verses. [The Self] has a form that pervades all, having transformed itself into the form of the entire world; yet it is not insentient (*jaḍa*), because it is luminous due to the transference of consciousness (*caitanya*) unto it. Nor is it non-insentient (*ajaḍa*), because, being imagined (*kalpita*), it is distinct from the Self. (56–57)
Know that the mind is the web of the world; the mind is declared to be bondage. O virtuous one, when that [mind] is relinquished, there occurs the renunciation of everything. (57)
The mind is declared to be the seed of both births and actions;
the body is moved by the mind, just as a tree is shaken by the wind. (58)
Those people who know true renunciation understand that the renunciation of the mind is the renunciation of everything;
when the mind is renounced, duality and even unity everywhere dissolve into absorption.
What remains is the supreme, peaceful, one, pure, and healthy state;
the renunciation of everything is the highest bliss, while anything else is most terrible suffering.
Saying "So be it" (Oṃ), accept this and do whatever you desire.
Having renounced everything, being peaceful, self-abiding, and like the sky, O King, become that which you wish to be—gentle and of such a form. 61.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Blessed One, tell me first the true nature of the mind as it is;
thereafter, O best among speakers, tell me how to relinquish the mind.
Kumbha said:
O King, know that latent impression alone is the true nature of the mind;
indeed, the word "citta" is declared to be a synonym for "vāsanā. (63)
O Great-minded One, know that this sense of "I," which is the sole vessel for all misfortunes, is the seed of this tree of the mind. (64)

"I" — know that this arising of the sense of "I," this emergence of egoism, which is the sole vessel for all misfortune and the root cause of this entire cycle of existence (saṃsāra) consisting of nothing but misfortune, is itself the seed and the primary cause of this tree of the mind.
From this first sprout that has emerged, which has the form of experience and consists of ascertainment yet is formless, it is precisely called "intellect" (buddhi). (65)

"From this" means: from this very ego (ahaṃkāra) which has first emerged—that is, which has first arisen—the sprout that is born in the form of experience, consisting of experience, having the nature of ascertainment, being of the essence of certainty, and being formless—unaffected by the forms of external objects—is declared to be the intellect (buddhi). || 65 ||

The swelling of this sprout called "intellect" (buddhi), which consists of volitional construction (saṃkalpa), is designated by the terms "mind-stuff" (citta), "consciousness" (cetas), and "mind" (manas). (66)

Regarding this: the "fattening," which is the grossness consisting of volition belonging to that sprout in the form of intellect—the sprout being what is designated as "intellect"—it is precisely to that grossness consisting of volition that the designations or names "citta," "cetas," or "manas" apply. || 66 ||

For such a mind, which is like a wicked tree, while pruning its branches at every moment, apply yourself to the scraping away of its roots. Those who know renunciation understand that true renunciation is the swift uprooting [of the mind] from its very foundation.

"Of such a kind" means: performing the lopping of the branches—namely, the severance of the branches consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the form of desire, volition, doubt, and so forth—of this tree of the mind of the aforementioned type;
apply yourself with great intensity to the scraping away of the root, that is, to the cutting off of the root which is the nature of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*). || 67 ||
The various latent impressions (vāsanās) are like branches that bear diverse fruits;
when not cultivated, they are indeed severed within by the power of pure consciousness.

He describes the manner of cutting those branches with the words "vāsanā" (impressions). Various branches in the form of impressions—which bear and bestow diverse fruits consisting of pleasure, pain, and so forth—become cut and severed when they are not nurtured within and are instead disregarded through the power of consciousness, that is, through the power of self-reflection. || 68 ||
One whose mind is unattached, who observes silence, whose speech and reflection are stilled,
and who acts only when the time is right— he is one whose mental creeper has been cut down within. (69)
"Unattached" means: that person whose mind is unattached, who is not clinging to sense objects; who is silent, established in silence;

and whose investigation into the debates and discourses of others—consisting of such thoughts as "what," "by what," or "how"—has been stilled and ceased; being such, he is one who performs his necessary duties.
A person becomes one whose creeper of the mind has been cut within, and whose branches of the mind have been severed. || 69 ||
The pruning of the branches of the tree of the mind is secondary; its primary task is the cutting away of the roots. Therefore, be intent upon scraping away the very roots of that tree.
"Secondary" (gauṇa) means subordinate; "primary" (mukhya) means principal. || 370 ||
O one of great intelligence, by means of this primary method, effect the complete burning away of the root;
in this way, the thorn of the mind becomes indeed "no-mind."

Regarding the phrase "as the primary [task]": the "thicket of mental thorns" refers to the mind itself as a mass of thorns; thoroughly and completely perform the burning away of that very root. When this is done, the state of true mind arises. 71.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Sage, what fire known as "burning" could be effective in this task for the seed of the tree of the mind, which consists of the sense of "I"? (72)

Regarding "I": what fire whatsoever could be effective—that is, capable of performing a purposeful action—in burning the seed of the tree of the mind, which consists of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and has the nature of the "I-feeling" (ahambhāva)? || 72 ||
Kumbha said:
O King, this inquiry into one's own self, in the form of "Who am I?", is considered the fire for burning the seed of the wicked tree of the mind. (73)

"O King," [it is said]. For the burning of the ego—the seed of the tree of the mind's corruption—it is the very inquiry into the Self, in the form of "Who am I?", that is traditionally known as the fire. (73)
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Sage, I have investigated this many times with my own intellect:
at that time, I was not the world, nor was I the body consisting of flesh, bone, blood, and so forth.

The two verses beginning with "O Sage" form a single syntactical unit. The construction is as follows: "The category [of phenomena] beginning with the universe and ending with the ego-sense, because of its insentience, has been repeatedly investigated by my own intellect as 'not I'. (74, 75, 76)
It is neither the organs of action nor the organs of perception;
it is not the mind, nor the intellect, nor even the ego, because of its insentience.
Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, so does the state of "I-ness" exist in the conscious Self.
Kumbha said:
O sinless lord of the earth, if you do not know even this much of that great intellect, then tell me who he is, for you are dull-witted. (76)
Śikhidhvaja said:
O best of the learned, pure consciousness alone is the unborn, stainless self-awareness, wherein these phenomena take delight or by which they are determined. (77)

"Cit" (consciousness). These perceived entities—objects of experience—which find their relish (*svadante*) in that reality, which are supported by it, and which shine forth (*rocante*) yet are not determined or ascertained by it—that pure, stainless, unborn, and absolute consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is pure awareness itself, is "I";
this is the primary meaning of the word "I. || 77 ||
"Surely such a stain has clung to me without cause—this seed of the tree of the mind, consisting of the sense of 'I', which resides within my heart. (78)
Thus: That which is the seed of the tree of the mind is the impurity consisting of the sense of "I-ness.
Such a thing has become attached to my heart—which is of the nature of pure consciousness alone—without any cause whatsoever. 78.
And yet I am unable to renounce it; though renounced again and again, it returns to me.
O Sage, because I am unable to renounce it, I suffer most grievously. (79)

"And that" refers to this: although that impurity consisting of the sense of "I" has been abandoned again and again, it returns to me; therefore, I am unable to abandon it. And because I am unable [to do so], for that reason I suffer most grievously—I become tormented. (79)
Kumbha said:
O Sage, that which consists of the sense of "I" arises from a cause;
having investigated that cause, tell it to me now. (380)

Regarding the term "cause": an effect-entity arises solely from a cause; therefore, having searched for the cause of this effect which consists of the sense of "I," tell me [the answer] by means of the Self itself. 380.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Sage, I recognize that the perception of "I" is the cause of this defect;
tell me, O Lord of Sages, how it may be brought to cessation. (81)

"O Sage! I know that the very cause of the perception of the defect of 'I'—that is, of egoism—is the mind's orientation toward objects of cognition. Tell me how that perception may come to rest. || 81 ||
"O Sage, tell me how to bring about the cessation of the objects of thought, so that this 'I,' which exists as suffering due to its orientation toward those objects, may find peace. (82)

He explains this very point with the words "of consciousness" (citaḥ): The tendency of consciousness (caitanya) toward the object of cognition (cetyonmukhatva)—that is, the mental engagement with the visible world (dṛśyānusaṃdhāna)—is the cause by which this ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) exists for the sake of suffering. Therefore, for the cessation of suffering, tell me how to bring about the cessation of the object of cognition, that is, the non-manifestation of the visible world. || 82 ||
Kumbha said:
"You are a knower of causes; tell me quickly the cause of this sensation.
Therefore, I shall instruct you in the sequence of causes and non-causes. (83)

"Regarding the cause": you are a knower of causes; therefore, tell me the cause of sensation. Consequently, immediately after the investigation into the objective conditions (*nimitta*) of sensation, I shall instruct you in the sequence of cause and non-cause—that is, the method regarding both cause and the absence of cause—such that you may understand: "this is the cause of this," and "this [is the cause] of this."
The meaning is that this is not the cause for my intending to awaken [him]. || 83 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
Perception arises through the objective existence of forms such as the body and so forth, just as movement occurs through the appearance of a non-existent streak in the wind. (84)

"Deha" (the body) etc.: The subject arises through the reality of the object—which is a false appearance in the form of the body and so forth, a manifestation that is unreal—just as vibration or trembling arises from a streak of wind. 84.
I do not perceive the non-existence of the reality of things by means of that [non-perception] through which the seed of the mind—the non-cognition of "I-ness"—is thoroughly pacified. (85)

Regarding "non-existence" (asattām): I do not perceive that non-existence—which is the unreality of the existence of things—as being false, by means of which non-existence the seed of the mind, the feeling of "I-ness," the ego-sense, its cause, and the resulting feeling are completely stilled. 85.
Kumbha said:

If the existence of entities such as the body and so forth were real, then that [consciousness] would belong to you; but since there is no existence of the body and so forth, upon what is your cognition based? (86)
"It exists": if the existence of entities such as the body were to exist, then for you there would be cognition—that is to say, it would be possible or logical.
However, since the existence of the body and so forth is absent, upon what could your cognition be based? The meaning is that it would be without an objective support (*nirālambana*). || 86 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:

O Sage, how can it be that this body—which possesses the playful manifestation of the fruits of actions involving the hands, feet, and so forth, and which is constantly being experienced—does not exist? (87)
"Hasta" means: how can the body—which possesses parts, performs purposeful action, and is constantly experienced—be denied?
This is the meaning. || 87 ||
Kumbha said:
O protector of the earth, that effect for which no cause exists does not exist at all;
any perception of it is merely an illusion.
Regarding the term "cause": an effect perceived in the absence of a cause does not exist at all; its cognition, however, is a delusion, meaning it is an error. || 88 ||
Know that everything arisen from delusion is indeed non-existent;
for whatever thing is without a cause is false, like a snake [seen] in a rope. (89)
"Non-existent" means: know that everything arisen from delusion, imagined through error, is indeed non-existent.
For this reason—because whatever object is perceived without a cause, that is to say, without a cause for its production, is false, like a snake in a rope. 89.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Sage, tell me: how could he who is the primordial Grandfather, by whom this world was created, not be its very cause? (390)
Regarding the word "primordial": since this world was created by the Grandfather (Brahmā), how could that very Grandfather not be its cause? || 390 ||
Kumbha said:
O Lord of the Earth, at the beginning of creation, there exists only the tranquil Brahman;
because of the absence of any second thing, there is no cause for the Creator.
"At the beginning of creation": at the beginning of creation, there exists only the non-dual Brahman; however, that is not a cause, because it is changeless (*nirvikāratva*).

Nor is there any other entity existing as a cause, because of the absence of any conception of a second. This is because there is no perception of a second reality distinct from Brahman, according to the Vedic scripture: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, one only; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking."
Therefore, the logical conclusion is that there is no cause for the Creator (Vedhas). || 91 || 92 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Sage, what is the supreme Brahman, the cause of the Creator?
O virtuous one, I do not believe that the Creator is without a cause."
Kumbha said:
That which is infinite, unborn, unmanifest, the primordial object of perception,
beyond ratiocination, unknowable, imperishable,
tranquil, infallible, non-dual, without beginning or end— that is Śiva, the peaceful and immutable. || 93 ||

The three and a half verses beginning with "anantam" constitute a single sentence. Since that primordial perception—which is characterized by infinity and so forth—is an existent reality whose nature is knowledge, and because that reality is auspicious (śiva), peaceful (śānta), and immutable (avyaya), [it is so described]. || 93 ||
p. 733) Therefore, how, by whom, and when could there be an agent or an enjoyer?
Consequently, nothing here has been created; this world does not exist. 94.

How, then, and in what manner could there be an agent? In no way whatsoever can there be agency for anyone, because of the non-existence of any distinct effect. Or by what instrument? By none at all, because that too is non-existent. Thus, due to the absence of agency, there is also no state of being an enjoyer; this is the meaning. Therefore, due to the absence of an agent, this world is not anything at all.
Therefore, this world is a mere construction; it does not exist in reality, nor does it truly exist. || 94 ||
The Creator is determined to be consciousness alone, imagined by consciousness itself;
the creation produced from that alone is of that same nature—this is the established conclusion. (95)

And for this reason, because the Creator is fashioned from pure consciousness alone, He is indeed consciousness itself. Furthermore, since creation is produced by the Creator—who is himself of the nature of pure consciousness—and is generated solely from pure consciousness, it is established and certain that it consists of that [consciousness] and has pure consciousness as its very essence. (95)
"I am neither an agent nor an enjoyer; everything is peaceful, unborn, and auspicious"—with such a firm conviction, bring about the thinning of internal ignorance. 96.
"No. Everything perceived as "this-ness" (idantā) and "I-ness" (ahantā)—every object whatsoever—is peaceful, unborn, and auspicious.
Therefore, being one who possesses the firm conviction that "I am neither doer nor enjoyer," lead the ignorance residing within you to thinness, to attenuation. 96.
The wise know that ignorance has thus perished once it has become slackened;
for there is no emergence [of knowledge] without the destruction of the fall from one's former state. (97)
Regarding the term "ignorance" (*ajñāna*): in this way, according to the method previously stated, they understand that ignorance which has become loosened is destroyed.

For without destruction, the displacement from the previous state does not arise; because it is logical that the destruction of an effect-substance occurs upon the destruction of its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), and because the displacement from the previous state consists in the destruction of that non-inherent cause.
The state of being. || 97 ||
When attenuation is observed in that [body] of its own accord through a gradual process,
its cessation also becomes possible due to the disappearance of its former configuration. (98)
"Diminution" (tānava) means that very same pacification of the object; it is either the destruction of the substance or its state of being changeless. || 98 ||
Therefore, O King, because he is of the nature of consciousness, this God of gods eternally shines by himself within the self through the mind;
for that very reason, the Self has declared itself as "the Lotus-born" (Brahmā), and thus this entire universe is the peaceful form of the Self.

"Therefore" means: for this reason, the God of gods, the Supreme Self (paramātman), being himself thus constituted as the nature of consciousness (cidātmaka) within his own self, shines forth and manifests through the mind by the power of his own volition (*svasaṃkalpa*) in the form of this perceived phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
By that very God of gods, the Self himself—his own essential nature—was declared by the Self alone to be "the Lotus-born" (*padmaja*). Therefore...
For this reason, all of this is the peaceful nature of the God of gods. || 99 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"I am enlightened, O Blessed One; you have spoken what is most logical and appropriate.
Because there is no state of an agent, the world does not exist; therefore, there is no perceiver of objects. (400)

"Buddha" means: I am awakened. Because there is no agent, the effect—the world—does not exist. And because of that non-existence of the world, the perception of objects does not exist; thus you have spoken what is consistent with reason. || 400 ||
This being so, I am awakened, I am fully enlightened, and I am Śiva;
salutations to myself, for there is no object of cognition whatsoever—thus have I realized.

"Thus": because I have been awakened to the realization that there is nothing whatsoever beyond this "I" or "this," I am one who possesses the knowledge: "I alone, whose nature is pure consciousness (cinmātra), shine as the Self of all. For this very reason, abiding thus in pure consciousness alone, I am pure, stainless, and possessed of the awakening to my own pure essential nature. And by that, I am Śiva, the Supreme Self itself. And therefore—
Salutation to me alone, because there is no other deity to be saluted. || 1 ||
The perception of objects and so forth appears in this way as something non-existent;
today I am enough with this, and I remain peaceful like the expanse of space. (2)

Regarding the phrase "padārtha": because of the recollection of objects through their distinction from the knowledge of the [underlying] reality, this world appears in this manner as something truly non-existent. Therefore, enough with this knowledge of objects;
now I remain peaceful, like the interior of space, like the womb of the sky. || 2 ||

Alas! The vision that distinguished the objects of the world—including existence, space, direction, time, divisions, and the flood of activities—has finally been stilled after a long duration; now only the peaceful Brahman remains, the immutable Self.

Regarding the word *jagat* (the world): the perception of the differentiation of the objects of the world—consisting of the multitude of existence, space, direction, time, parts, and actions, together with the consciousness of place and so forth—is the consciousness whose object is the world and whose object is the distinction between things. When that [consciousness] has gradually subsided and ceased, the imperishable Self remains established as the tranquil Brahman alone. || 3 || 4 || 5 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus awakened by Kumbha, he attained full realization;
having emerged from the casket of great delusion, he then shone resplendent.
Thus, King Kumbhava, cultivating that unartificial state,
in that very moment became transformed into his own true state of self.
With his mind and eyes closed, the sage became silent;
with the form of his limbs motionless, he appeared as if carved out of the surface of a stone.

"He became [thus]" means: with his mind and eyes closed. "Closing the mind" refers to the cessation of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti-nirodha*). He was as if carved out from a stone slab by chisels and other tools, as if he were fashioned by being engraved upon a stone surface. (6–7)
Then, after only a moment, Cūḍālā, who had assumed the form of Kumbha, spoke to him as his eyes opened and sparkled: "O mighty-armed one! (7)
Kumbha said:
I hope that you have found rest in happiness upon this vast, pure, soft, and stainless couch, which is the state of those free from conceptual construction.

"Kaccit" (I hope) [is used here]. For those who possess meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and are free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), there is rest in a "good bed," which is the place of repose. || 8 || 9 ||
Are you awakened within? Have you abandoned delusion?
Has that which is to be known been fully understood, or has that which is to be seen been truly seen? (9)
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, I have beheld a great station, adorned with immense splendor, situated above all. (410)

"O Blessed One! [He replied: "The 'great manifestations' (mahāvibhava) are the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, adorned with which one is 'adorned with great manifestations. The 'great state' (*mahatīpadavī*) is the path of liberation while living (*jīvanmukta-mārga*). || 410 || 11 || 12 || 13 ||
Oh, how wonderful! The association of the great-souled ones—who have realized that which is to be known—is composed of a unique and unprecedented nectar, bestowing the fruit of the essence. 11.
That great nectar which I had not obtained even through my birth has today been attained by me precisely through association with you.
O lotus-eyed one, why was this beginningless, endless, and immortal state of the Self not attained by me previously? (13)
Kumbha said:
When the mind has attained tranquility, when it remains with the desire for enjoyments abandoned, and when the ripening of the passions of the entire collection of sense organs has ceased; (14)

The three verses beginning with "manasi" form a single syntactical unit. [This occurs] when the desire for enjoyments has been abandoned, when the longing for sense-objects has been relinquished, when there is ripening of the *kaṣāya*—that is, the ripening of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—and when there is the ripening of the entire group of sense-faculties. (14)
The stainless words of the Teacher find rest in the mind,
just as drops of flower-water settle upon a pure white cloth. (15)
When the favorable conditions have ceased and [the result] has been accomplished; of the "flower-water," that is, the juice of safflower and other such flowers. || 15 ||
O lotus-eyed one, O virtuous one, all impurities fall away from the body over time due to ripening,
just as fruits fall down from a tree.
Through that ripening which occurs in due time, all impurities fall away from the body, just as fruits fall from a tree. || 16 ||
The mind that perceives duality and unity is called ignorance;
the dissolution of these two perceptions is knowledge, which is the supreme goal.

Regarding the word "dvitva" (duality): the two views—that is, the perspectives regarding duality and unity—are themselves the mind and themselves ignorance. The dissolution of these two views is itself knowledge; that alone is the supreme goal, which is liberation (kaivalya). 17, 18, 19.
You are awakened, you are liberated; the mind has been relinquished by you, O King.
You are a sage of great exaltation, silent, remaining stainless in your true nature. 18.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Lord, for one who is awakened and knows that [reality], there is indeed no such thing as "mind";
tell me, how do these people who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta) move about? 19.
Kumbha said:
The latent impression (vāsanā) that is capable of producing rebirth is called "dense impression" (ghanavāsanā);
it is designated by the term *citta*, and it does not exist for one who knows reality.
"Again" means: the mind is indeed the previously mentioned impure latent impression (*vāsanā*); however, for one who knows that [reality], it does not exist—this is the meaning. || 420 ||
Know that latent impression which those who know it employ here in their activities—termed "sattva"—to be free from rebirth. (21)

Regarding the phrase "yayā" (by which): for one who knows that [Reality], it is the pure latent impression (*śuddhavāsanā*)—the cause of worldly activity—that is designated as *sattva*, not the mind (*citta*). || 21 ||
The mind that is deluded is called *citta*; the awakened is said to be *sattva*.
For those who are unawakened abide in *citta*, while those of truly great intelligence abide in *sattva*. (22)
He says that very thing: "The deluded is permeated by impure latent impressions (*vāsanā*); the awakened has pure latent impressions.
(22) "Whatever grants fruits such as heaven or liberation—all that indeed must be abandoned. That which is its [the mind's] mere appearance (*ābhāsa*), that alone you truly are. (23)
Abide grasping the flood of objects while remaining on the ground of the unmoving mind;
for one whose mind is without vibration, saṃsāra does not run here.
O Lord of the Earth, whatever sufferings manifest here in the three worlds, each and every one of them arises solely from the fickleness of the mind. (25)
Therefore, O knower of reality, having brought both movement and stillness into a state of oneness within the mind, remain as you wish, having attained eternal unity. (26)

Regarding the word "atha": *spanda* is the outward diffusion of the mind, while *aspanda* is meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Having brought these two to a state of unity by means of constant contemplation of one's true nature, and having brought about the non-differentiation of distraction and non-distraction, reach the eternal, perpetual oneness—the non-duality of Brahman—and remain there as you desire. 26.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O All-pervading Lord, how have these two—motion and non-motion—attained oneness?
Tell me that quickly, for it is the cause of severing all my doubts. (27)
"How so? [The answer is: "They have gone" (*yātaḥ*) is the dual form in the present tense (*laṭ*). O All-pervading One, O Kumbha! 27.
Kumbha said:
The entire world is a single reality, pure consciousness alone, like water in the ocean; that very reality vibrates through the functions of the intellect, just as pure water moves in waves.

"One" means: the entire world is a single reality consisting of pure consciousness (cinmātra), just as the entire ocean consists of nothing but water; that very reality of pure consciousness vibrates through the fluctuations of the intellect (dhī-buddhivṛtti), like waves upon pure water. || 28 ||
(739) That which is sung as Brahman— pure consciousness, stainless, and named Truth— is this very thing that fools perceive, my dear, as the world. (29)
"Brahman" means that they perceive Brahman itself as the deluded world. || 29 ||
That which consists of the mere vibration of the consciousness of creation dissolves through right vision;
yet it arises through wrong vision, just like the delusion of a snake in a rope. (430)

Regarding the term *sarga* (creation): this creation is merely the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*).
