It dissolves when there is right vision—that is, the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). However, through wrong vision, it arises like the delusion of a snake in a rope. || 430 ||

Through the practice of continuous association with the scriptures and virtuous people, when the mind has attained purity over time—like the moon risen in the sky—[it becomes fit for the realization of truth]. (31)
"Śāstra" refers to the two verses as a single statement; it consists of one's own experience and is self-luminous. 31 || 32 ||
O one of great intelligence, this entire expansion, consisting of one's own experience and appearing as mere manifestation, arises spontaneously within the great-souled ones. (32)
Thus, O King Śikhidhvaja, everything has been told to you:
how all this arose and how it dissolves away.

The phrase "iti" refers to the two verses as a single syntactical unit. Having performed this—having held it in the mind, having reflected upon it, having investigated it through reasonings, having understood it, and having realized it according to its true nature—one may remain in whatever way one desires in that state which is the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), a state whose form is clearly perceived and whose ground is manifest; such is the grammatical connection. || 33 || 34 ||
"O Leader of Sages, having performed this, and having reflected upon it, and having understood it, remain as you wish, with every step clearly seen.
I, the sage Nārada, shall go to heaven at this time of the festival. (34)
Having returned from the world of Brahmā, he goes to the assembly of the immortals.
"‘To heaven’—this constitutes a sentence of three verses. ‘Amarasaṃsad’ means the assembly of the gods. || 35 ||
If he does not see me there, he may become angry;
for a worthy disciple should never cause his teachers any agitation. (36)
In that assembly of the gods, they are not to be agitated, nor are they to be led into distraction. || 36 ||
With all mental constructs abandoned and desiring nothing at all,
you must always dwell [thus], for this very vision is purifying.

You must always remain without desiring anything at all, having abandoned every trace of conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa-lekha*). A "trace" (*lekha*) means a line, a streak, or a collection. 37 || 38 || 39 || 440 || 41 || 42 || 43 || 44 || 45 || 46 || 47 || 48 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed Kumbha vanished in an instant;
when Kumbha had gone, the protector of the earth was filled with supreme wonder.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Oh, how cool, pure, and peaceful is this path of my own!
Its form, as if born from an elixir, seems to bring tranquility to my very being. (39)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Reflecting thus, the king, clearly intent on banishment,
remained in silence as if carved out of stone.
Then, having attained an unwavering firm foundation in that very state of silence— free from volition and without support— he stood like a mountain peak.
Through non-conceptual meditative absorption, his state became like that of wood or a wall;
now hear how King Śikhidhvaja [beheld] Cūḍālā. 42.
Having awakened her husband Śikhidhvaja by means of that disguise as Kumbha,
she vanished and swiftly ascended into the sky from that place.
He assumed a beautiful feminine form, clever yet innocent in appearance;
then, having gone to his own city, he entered the inner apartments in an instant. (44)
She became visible to the world and performed the duties of a king;
then, after three years, she returned once more to the sky.
Kumbha became [invisible] through yoga and went to the forest of Śikhidhvaja;
then, right there in that forest region, he saw the king who had gone to the woods.
Seeing the lord of the earth there established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, [he thought]:
"I shall first awaken this king from this supreme state. (47)
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā let out a lion’s roar repeatedly before her lord, striking terror into the forest-dwellers.
When he did not move, even though that roar was repeated again and again like a boulder upon a mountain, she then caused him to waver.
And she was Cūḍālā. || 49 || 450 ||

When the king was shaken and even cast down, yet did not wake up, Cūḍālā, who had assumed the form of Kumbha, then reflected: cālitaḥ pātito'pyeṣa yadā na bubudhe nṛpaḥ | sā tadā cintayāmāsa cūḍālā kumbharūpiṇī || 450 ||
"Aha! This holy lord has indeed ceased [from worldly activity] in his own state.
Let me first behold this body of the king. (51)

"Aho!"—this refers to a group of four verses. The meaning is: "I observe my body; I investigate whether or not there remains any portion of life. *Sattvaśeṣaḥ* means a remainder of life-force. || 51 || 52 || 53 ||
If there remains within his heart even a vestige of being, a seed of awakening,
then I too shall live for the sake of the Lord’s fulfillment of his conjugal union.
Otherwise, having abandoned this body of a woman, I shall go to the supreme state from which there is no rebirth; for what use have I here? (53)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, the beautiful Cūḍālā, perceiving her husband through touch and sight, spoke with apprehension.

The syntactical connection is as follows: by touch, which indicates the movement of the vital breath through contact with all the vital points (*marmasthāna*) within the body; and by sight, which indicates life through the non-falling of the eyeballs and the presence of blood-red lines in both eyes, he perceived that some living being remained. 54, 55, 56.
There indeed remains a residue of goodness within his heart, which serves as the cause for awakening;
when the conditions for awakening arise, that residue of goodness awakens.
Rāma said:

O Brahmin, how is one who possesses meditative absorption known—his mind being utterly tranquil and remaining as motionless as a piece of wood or a clod of earth, with only his vital essence remaining? (56)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Within the heart of the knower, there exists a remnant of *sattva*— the cause of awakening— which has the subtle form of a barely perceptible atom, just as flowers and fruit reside within a seed.

The three verses beginning with "prabodheti" form a single syntactical unit: Within the heart of the knower established in samādhi—whose body is composed of atoms difficult to perceive, and whose form is subtle and hard to behold—there exists a remnant of internal being (sattva) within the seed, like a flower or fruit [within a seed]. || 57 ||

For one who is liberated from the vibration of the mind and remains in a state of total immovability, the body experiences an even distribution of energy; it neither suffers exhaustion nor feels elation.

For one who is liberated from the vibration of the mind and established in unwavering equanimity, the body neither suffers nor exults, because it is characterized by perfectly balanced engagement. || 58 ||
It neither sets nor rises; it remains perfectly equanimous.
O Rāma, that which you asked has been told; now hear what is relevant to the present subject.
It neither sets nor rises; rather, it remains in a state of equilibrium, as has already been asked and explained. Now, listen to the subject at hand—this is the syntactical connection. || 59 ||
Having thus resolved, Cūḍālā abandoned her body as it remained there and attained stability in the principle of consciousness (cittattva), which is devoid of beginning and end. (460)

The phrase "iti" refers to the two verses as a single syntactical unit. Thus, having determined the existence of the residual essence (*sattva-śeṣa*), Cūḍālā—being skilled in entering the bodies of others—abandoned her own body and attained stability within the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*).
Remaining there in that consciousness which is common to both herself and another, she caused a vibration in the mind of her lord, Śikhidhvaja.
Like a bird entering its own nest, she entered her body once again.
There, having stirred the mind of that powerful lord who possessed great courage,
she entered her own body once more from the sky, like a bird returning to its nest.
Then, rising in the form of a water-jar, she entered her own seat and began to sing the Sāman hymns with a sound like the humming of a swarm of bees.
Hearing that sound of the Sāman chant, she who was endowed with the quality of pure consciousness awoke within the king's body, like a lotus-pond awakening at the arrival of spring.
"Tam iti" || The consciousness of the lord of the earth awakened.
(63-74) At that time, like the sun causing the lotus to bloom, he opened his eyes;
with a composed mind, Śikhidhvaja beheld the pitcher standing before him. (64)
"Aha! How blessed we are that the Lord of Sages has come again!"—saying this, the king gave a flower to Kumbha.
"By good fortune you have been seen, O Blessed One; you have come once again to the forest.
The purpose of your arrival is to purify us. (66)
Kumbha said:
From the moment I departed from your presence, O blameless one,
my mind has remained fixed here solely upon you.
I take no pleasure in the delights of heaven; I shall dwell together with you.
One such as you is a kinsman, a trusted one, a well-wisher, a friend, and likewise a companion.
I believe there is no disciple in this world who is as trustworthy as I am.
Śikhidhvaja said:
Oh, how the trees of merit accumulated over a long time have indeed borne fruit!
For even you, though free from attachment, desire our company. (69)
"O virtuous one, through the yoga bestowed by the Blessed One, I have found rest;
I consider that such rest as this could never be found even in heaven. (470)
Relying upon this very pure and luminous state of my own, may I wander at will both in heaven and upon the surface of the earth. (71)
Kumbha said:
Have you perhaps found rest in that supreme state of great bliss? Have you perhaps completely abandoned this suffering consisting of duality? (72)
O King, has your delight in those mental constructions that are pleasant only at first sight been utterly uprooted, now that you perceive the true nature of reality? (73)

Is your mind established in that which transcends the states of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, which is peaceful, equanimous, and steady—remaining undisturbed by whatever arises as it may? (74)
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Blessed One, by your grace, the state that transcends all objects of perception has been seen;
the very limit of saṃsāra has been reached, and the certainty regarding all that is to be attained has been gained.
Nothing whatsoever should be taught to us;
we are entirely satisfied in every respect, and we abide free from all feverish distress.

Free from wandering, devoid of delusion and fear, dispassionate, eternally risen, with a mind of tranquility and entirely gentle; being the self of all, liberated from all mental constructions, as pure as the expanse of space—I have arrived at equanimity. (77)

"Free from worldly involvement" (niḥsaṃsṛti) means: being entirely gentle through a disposition of tranquility—that is, through a tranquil state of mind and intention—he is gentle in all respects, free from joy and dejection, and liberated from all mental constructions (*saṃkalana*).
"Mental constructions" refers to the bonds of possessiveness toward wife, children, and so forth. "I have attained the Equal" means I have reached the Brahman that is equal and omnipresent.
The meaning is: "I have attained that. || 77 || 78 || 79 || 480 || 81 || 82 || 83 || 84 || 85 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, those two, the knower and the known, sat together with each other, conversing on various spiritual topics as they wandered through the forest. (78)
Forests of many forms, jungles, riverbanks, lakes, thickets of shrubs, and dense haunts of deer and other wild animals. (79)
Equal in every way, equal in affection, and united, those two remained together;
with equal courage and equal zeal, they moved about and stayed together.

O Raghava, they worshipped the ancestors and the gods and partook of the offerings; meanwhile, their minds were free from the conceptualization of doubt as to "this should be accepted" or "this should not. (81)
O Rāma, they did not leave those three behind, just as the mountain [does not leave] its waters;
those two friends wandered here and there, grey with dust.
In some places their limbs were smeared with sandalwood paste, and in others they were stained with ashes;
in just a few days, through that state of equanimity, [they became so].
And by virtue of his noble nature, the king shone like a jar;
then Cūḍālā beheld that Śikhidhvaja, who resembled the offspring of a god.
Seeing that he had attained such splendor, the beautiful woman reflected: (85)
A noble-souled husband, freedom from anxiety, fresh youth, and houses filled with clusters of flowers—she is not a woman who is not struck down by these. (86)
The phrase "nijaḥ" constitutes a set of four verses. Her own husband is noble-souled and noble-minded, free from anxiety and care;

both are in the bloom of youth. Although there exists such a collection of means for happiness—namely, clusters of flowers which are the very houses formed by flowering creepers—the woman who does not possess a desire for enjoyment is truly lost.
Because of the abandonment of pleasure that is not prohibited. || 86 ||
Even when abandoning what has been attained, the knower of the Vedas should always act in a way that is irreproachable and of noble purpose; indeed, such is what should be done by the wise man.

"By one who abandons" (samujjhatā): by what wise person—having attained the knowable Brahman, knowing the knowable, and having abandoned their own blameless, noble purpose, which is great happiness exactly as it was obtained—what indeed could have been done, or what purpose could have been accomplished? The meaning is: nothing at all. One who abandons rightful happiness would be utterly futile.
Thus, the meaning is exactly as stated previously. || 87 ||
Therefore, I shall quickly compose some new literary elaboration with my wisdom, by which this lord of the earth, my husband who bestows honor, may take delight in me. (88)

"Thus": for that reason, by means of my own wisdom (*prajñā*), I shall specially compose—that is, fashion—some new conceptual elaboration (*prapañca*). By means of this fabricated conceptual elaboration as a cause, this husband shall desire me. || 88 ||
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā, assuming the guise of Kumba and standing in the midst of the forest, spoke to her husband like a female cuckoo to a male cuckoo. (89)
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā spoke to her husband; such is the grammatical connection. || 89 ||
Kumbha said:
This is the great first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra;
today, indeed, a grand assembly of Hari takes place in heaven.
"Caitra"—this is a statement consisting of five verses. 490 || 91 ||
I must manifest my presence there before my father;
for destiny, as it has been ordained, must never be disregarded. (91)
While wandering here upon this earth, you must maintain yourself by sporting with the two flowers of meditative concentration, without falling into agitation.

Playing with the two flowers of *dhyāna*—with *dhyāna* when there is concentration (*samādhi*), and with the flower when there is no concentration—the word "flower" (*puṣpa*) here denotes a genus; therefore, it is used in the dual number. || 92 || 93 || 94 ||
Today, at the end of the day, I have come from the realm of the sky, free from conceptual thought;
indeed, association with you brings me even greater joy than from heaven itself.
Having spoken thus, Kumbha gave a flower-cluster to Mitra—
just as Śiva gave his beloved Pārvatī born from the Nandana tree— for the sake of his pleasure.
When the king spoke thus, "You must come back very quickly," he sprang swiftly into the sky like an autumnal cloud at its onset.
"Like an autumnal cloud": the meaning is that just as at the beginning of autumn a cloud (payoda) swiftly glides through the sky due to its lightness, so too [does he]. || 95 ||
At the end of Śikhidhvaja’s vision, she who had the form of a jar vanished into the sky;
like the beauty of water when its whirlpools have subsided, the charming maiden returned to her own true form.

Regarding "Śikhidhvaja": the glances, which are the rays of the eyes, are like the beauty of water when the whirlpool has subsided; just as the splendor of water assumes its own true nature when the vortex ceases, so it is here. 96.
Having reached the city, which resembled the Kalpa tree and was filled with blossoming clusters,
he entered the inner apartments, crowded with women, as if unseen.

Regarding the word *prāpya*: "having the form of a cluster of blossoms" (*mañjaritākāram*) means that its structures, such as palaces and the like, have been made into clusters (*mañjaritāḥ*), and thus it is like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣopamam*) for that very reason. 97 || 98 ||
Having swiftly completed all the royal duties there,
she fell before Śikhidhvaja, assuming the form of Kumbha. (98)
There, with an undaunted mind, she made her face lose its luster, like a dark night clouding the moon with mist, or like a withered lotus.

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): there, in the presence of Śikhidhvaja, Cūḍālā—with a mind that felt no weariness—quickly caused his face to lose its luster through her artifice, just as the dark night causes the moon to appear veiled in mist, or just as it causes the lotus to wither and close its buds. || 99 || 500 || 1 ||
Seeing him in such a state, Śikhidhvaja rose up;
his heart became distressed, and he spoke these words with reverence: || 500 ||
"O son of a god, homage be to you! You appear as if distracted.
O Kumbha, casting aside your agitation, please accept this seat."

Those who are virtuous and have known what is to be known do not resort to a state born of joy or sorrow; established in their own nature, they remain unaffected, like lotuses by the moisture of water.
Regarding the word "santaḥ" (the peaceful ones): just as lotuses (*padmāḥ*), though dwelling in water, do not take on the moisture produced by that water, so it is with them. || 2 || 3 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the lord of the earth had spoken thus, Kumbha, sitting down upon his seat,
spoke with a dejected voice that resembled the sound of a broken bamboo pole.
Kumbha said:
Those who, throughout the various states of the body, do not remain with equanimity through their organs of action, are not knowers of reality; they are deceivers.

Regarding the word "yāvat": those who, throughout all states—that is, during conditions of pleasure and pain—do not remain with an even mind, that is, with a mind free from modification, by means of their organs of action as long as the body lasts, they are not knowers of reality; rather, they are merely rogues and deceivers. || 4 ||
O King, those fools who do not know reality, on account of their very childishness,
flee from the states that have naturally been grasped by them. (5)

Furthermore, those fools who do not know reality, by reason of their very childishness, flee from the states of pleasure and pain which are grasped as inherent by nature; the meaning is that they are led into transformation by these states. || 5 ||
As oil exists as long as there is sesame seed, so does the state [of suffering] exist as long as there is the body;
he who does not fall into the state of the body cuts through the sky with a sword.

"Up to this point": just as oil exists within all sesame seeds, so too do the states of pleasure and pain exist within all bodies. Therefore, he who does not transcend the state of the body—such a person cuts his own garment with a sword;
the meaning is that even one devoid of the state of the body does not exist, like one who cuts his own garment. || 6 ||

This renunciation of the suffering inherent in the state of the body is indeed unsurpassed; it consists in the equanimity of the mind through yoga, and not in the cessation of the activity of the organs of action.

"This" refers to the following: that equanimity of the mind—its state of changelessness—which arises from yoga, that is, from samādhi, is itself the unsurpassed relinquishment of the suffering inherent in the bodily state. However, the relinquishment of the suffering of the bodily state is not said to occur merely through the equanimity of the organs of action, because even among those possessed of knowledge, such [relinquishment] is impossible [by that means alone]. || 7 ||
As long as the body lasts, one who understands the ten limbs should abide according to proper conduct through the organs of action,
but never through the organs of perception.

"As long as... means: therefore, until the end of his life, a person should remain with the organs of action alone—according to his conduct throughout the various stages of the body, following the practices appropriate to his own caste and stage of life—and not with the organs of cognition, because the activity of the organs of cognition is preceded by conscious deliberation (*buddhi-pūrvaka*), whereas the withdrawal [of the senses] occurs through the withdrawal of the organs of action.
Because activity occurs even without prior cognition, it is impossible for activity to cease simply upon the cessation of cognition. || 8 ||
Parameṣṭhin and all the others, though their intentions have already been fulfilled, remain within the states of embodied existence; such is the certainty of destiny.
Regarding the term "Parameṣṭhin": Parameṣṭhin and the others refer to Brahmā and the rest. (9)

Indeed, whatever collection of visible things exists— whether belonging to those who do not know reality or to those who know it— all of that runs toward necessity (niyati), just as water flows toward the ocean. (510)

Regarding the word *ajña*: "the ignorant and those who know reality" refers to living beings who are either ignorant or knowers of reality. Then, raising the doubt as to what the distinction between the ignorant and the knowers of reality might be, [the author] speaks two verses to demonstrate that distinction. || 510 ||
Those who know this [soul] perceive it through the similarity of the intellect and other faculties, as well as through the movement of the hands and other limbs,
as long as the body remains unbroken and this destiny continues its course.

For those who know that: first, by means of the similarity of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, the similarity of the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) and so forth, the movement of the hands and other [limbs], and the exertion of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), they carry out their unbroken destiny as long as the body lasts—that is, until the very end of the body. || 11 ||
But the ignorant, O dear one, being struck by states of pleasure and pain through the agitation of all [the senses],
pass their time under the sway of destiny, which is fragmented across hundreds of thousands of bodies.

But the ignorant, being struck by the states of pleasure and pain through the agitation of all their senses, pass through—meaning they cause to be spent—countless millions of bodies by which destiny (niyati) has been variously shattered and fragmented. || 12 || 13 || 14 || 15 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
This being the case, O illustrious one, best among those who know what is to be known, tell me how even you, a god, have come to experience such agitation. (13)
The potter said:
"I shall tell you everything that happened to me today in heaven;
when suffering is disclosed to a friend, it reaches its greatest attenuation. (14)
Having first gone from here and given a cluster of flowers to your honor,
I have crossed the sky and reached heaven.
Then, having stood in due order with his father in the assembly hall of Indra,
he was dismissed by his father at the time of rising.
Having abandoned heaven, I have come here to the sky;
together with the horses of the sun, I travel along the path of the wind. (17)
Then, while the sun had gone one way,
I came through the sky by another path, appearing as if fallen from the ocean.
Then, ahead of me along the path between the clouds filled with water, I saw the sage Durvāsas approaching with great speed.
Having paid him homage, I, traveling through the sky, said:
"O Sage, you are like a woman going to meet her lover, with playful clouds for your garment. (520)
Having heard this, O giver of honor, he uttered a curse upon me:
"She shall become a lovely woman, possessed of breasts and long hair, and subject to the transformations of amorous gestures and emotions. (21)
"Go; because of this ill-spoken word, you shall become a woman at night.
Having heard these auspicious words uttered by the decrepit Brahmin, [she departed].
"O virtuous one, as soon as I reflected for a moment, the sage vanished;
thus, with a troubled mind, I have arrived here from the surface of the sky. (23)
"How can my womanhood alone be passed over at the ends of these days by me, whose soul is overcome with shame before gurus, gods, and the twice-born? (24)
How should I, as a woman of the night, properly conduct myself from now on? (25)
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Devaputra, there is no purpose in lamentation;
let that which comes come, for the self of the body is not defiled.
If you, being learned in this matter, feel weary even though you are unworthy of weariness, then what other means could there be for others, O ornament of the scriptures? (27)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus consoled one another with such words,
the two remained in the forest like affectionate friends who were themselves weary.
Then the sun, the lamp of the world, also set, as if producing femininity in this jar, like a lamp going out due to the exhaustion of its oil.
Then those two friends rose, paid homage to the twilight and the rising moon, performed their silent prayers, and remained within the thicket.
Then Kumbha gradually assumed a feminine form there and, standing before Śikhidhvaja, spoke to him with faltering words: 31.
O King, I feel as if I am falling, trembling, and melting away with my slender limbs;
out of sheer shame, I am entering the forest in the midst of women.

"I am as if falling"—this is the sense: "O slender-limbed one, by shame alone, with my limbs so attenuated, I am as if falling to the ground. I am as if quivering, as if melting away. In the forest, devoid of kinsmen, friends, and the like—note that this does not refer to the beginning of life—I attain womanhood;
behold, O King, these hairs of my head are growing.
"Behold, these two breasts of mine are growing, turned upward toward my chest. (33)
My garments have become so long that they hang down to my ankles;
yet I am conscious of these very same garments reaching only to my hips and loins. (34)
"Up to the ankles," it is said. The word "clothes" (*ambarāṇi*) is in the plural because there are many, both external and internal.

These two—the hips (*nitamba*) and the loins (*jaghana*): the hips are the region behind a woman's waist, and the loins are the front part; I experience both of these through consciousness (*saṃvidā*) as an inner perception. Here, because the hips and the loins are fashioned by *māyā*, [they are perceived as such].

It should be understood that because they do not initiate a body, they lack the status of being limbs of a living being, and thus the grammatical rule for forming a singular compound (*ekavadbhāva*) was not applied.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having said, "Kumbha in the forest," Khinka became silent;
and the king, beholding him, spoke with a distressed heart.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O virtuous one, you have known all that is to be known and you understand the course of destiny;
do not let your heart be distressed over this matter which was inevitable.
Kumbha said:
"So be it; I shall carry out your command, O King. I feel no distress regarding my own womanhood—for who can transgress destiny? (37)
Having thus resolved, as if diminishing that grief,
the two of them spent the night in silence on a single bed for a long time.
Then at dawn, having cast off that female form and youth,
Kumbha became once more like a jar, his body now divested of breasts.
Thus that queen Cūḍālā, of excellent complexion,
having first assumed the state of a water-jar, subsequently attained womanhood once more for the sake of her husband.
She dwelt in the forest regions at night, observing the conduct of a maiden,
while by day she lived with her husband and friend, assuming the form of a water-jar.
Then, after some days had passed in this manner, that virtuous woman, assuming the form of Kumbha, spoke thus to her husband: || 42 ||
O King, lotus-eyed one, listen to these words of mine:
every night, I indeed become a woman. (43)
Therefore, I desire to perfect this feminine duty:
I shall give myself in marriage to some husband. (44)
(754) "In all the three worlds, only you as my husband are pleasing to me.
Accept me through marriage; I shall always be your wife by night. (45)
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O friend, O one of great intelligence, by performing this deed I perceive neither good nor evil; therefore, do as you wish. (46)
Kumbha said:
If this is so, O protector of the earth, then today’s conjunction is auspicious;
for yesterday was the full moon of this month of Śrāvaṇa, as I have calculated everything.
"If it is thus," [this] constitutes a statement consisting of four verses. || 47 ||
O mighty-armed one, when the night is illuminated by the full-orbed, stainless moon, the wedding ceremony for both of us shall take place.

*Rākā* refers to the day preceding the full moon by virtue of its association with the full moon. *Janyatra*—the bridegroom's affectionate kinsmen and relatives who protect (*trāyate*) or sustain them by accomplishing their desired aims—is by the word *janyatra* used to denote the wedding ceremony.
[The phrase] "nau" means "between us two alone," [indicating] that our marriage shall take place. 48, 49, 550.
Arise, O lotus-eyed one, for the sake of your own marriage;
O King, prepare an abundance of sandalwood, flowers, and other materials, together with jewels.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, Kumbha rose up along with that king and gathered flowers as well as a collection of jewels and other treasures.
Likewise, having prepared their equipment for the journey, those two great friends went to the river Mandākinī in the golden cave to bathe.

"So be it. [The phrase] "janyatrasambhāram" refers to the collection of materials required for the wedding, such as jewels, flowers, and other substances. "Mahāmītre" means two very dear friends. (51)
Having bathed, they both worshipped there the gods, the ancestors, and the sages;
just as they were indifferent to the fruits of their actions, so too were they toward the abandonment of action. (52)

"They both worshipped" means as follows: just as they were without desire for the fruit of action—that is, devoid of longing for the result of their virtuous deeds—so too were they without desire even for the renunciation of action; because of their dispassion (*vairāgya*), they had no longing for the fruits of action, yet they did not abandon action for the sake of maintaining the world order (*lokasaṃgraha*). || 52 || 53 || 54 || 55 ||
Having put on white silken garments from the wish-fulfilling tree and having eaten its fruits, the two of them proceeded in due order to the place where the bridegroom was staying.
After this much time had passed, the sun went to the mountain of setting;
when the evening rites were completed, Kumbha attained the state of a bridegroom.
And she said this: "O Lord, adorn me with ornaments;
having gradually kindled the fire, perform my marriage ceremony."
"I am your wife, named Madanikā, O lotus-eyed one.
When addressed thus, the protector of the earth reflected upon all of that.
They [are the arrows] of Madana, who is equal to Madana himself. 56 || 57 || 58 || 59 || 60 || 61 || 62 || 63 ||
Thus, on Mount Mahendra, both Kumbha and Śikhidhvaja were married by their own accord; they took pleasure in one another and became an affectionate couple.
Day after day they sported in the various forest groves, which were laden with the weight of fully ripened fruits and abounded in flowers and tender shoots.
When Śikhidhvaja had fallen asleep after traveling for three days at a time,
Cūḍālā, having performed her royal duties, returned once more to her own [abode].
Then, after several months had gradually passed, Cūḍālā, who possessed the form of a son of the gods, reflected: || 560 ||
Kumbha said:
Now, I shall test Śikhidhvaja with the burden of enjoyments,
so that his mind may never again find delight in sensual pleasures.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā went to the forest region and showed him Hari, who had arrived accompanied by the gods and apsarases.
Having seen Indra arrived with his retinue,
Śikhidhvaja, while dwelling in the forest, honored him in due manner.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O King of the Gods, you ought to explain to me properly, through your grace, what has caused this distress from traveling such a great distance.

Śikhidhvaja said: "Of yourself... [etc. "The distress of your coming from afar" means the exertion of having traveled from a great distance. 64 || 65 || 66 || 67 || 68 || 69 || 570 || 71 || 72 || 73 || 74 || 75 || 76 || 77 ||
Indra said:
We have been brought here by the excellence of your virtues, which cling to our hearts like birds held by a string. (65)
Arise and come to heaven; there all the hosts of celestial nymphs stand, looking up at you with wonder as they listen to accounts of your virtues. (66)
"Until the end of the kalpa, various enjoyments are to be experienced by you, who are liberated while living, in the abode of the gods; for that reason, I have come to you. (67)
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Lord of the Gods, I know all the conduct pertaining to heaven;
however, for me, heaven is not fixed in any single place. (68)
O Lord, I am satisfied everywhere and I rejoice everywhere;
because my mind has no desires, I am full of bliss in all things. (69)
O Śakra, I do not know how to go to anyone else established in such a creative act; I shall not carry out your command. (570)
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the Lord of the Earth had spoken thus, the entire host of gods,
saying "May it be well with you, O Kumbha," vanished from sight.
Having brought that illusion to an end, Cūḍālā reflected:
"By good fortune, this lord of the earth is not being carried away by his desire for enjoyment. (72)
Tranquil and with an even distribution of attention, he thus conducted his worldly affairs in the assembly of Śakra, without agitation or negligence. (73)
Once again, I shall reflect with reverence upon this matter in detail, through some captivating [discourse] dominated by passion and aversion. (74)
Having reflected thus, at night when the moon had risen in the forest, while Śikhidhvaja was staying on the bank of the river intent upon his twilight prayers and recitations, she [acted].
Filled with longing and possessed by passion, she entered the inner apartments of the forest goddesses— a dwelling dense with clusters of flowers.
There, upon that bed of flowers prepared by him who was garlanded with wreaths, she remained seated,
holding her beloved to her own breast as he stood with his arm placed around her neck.
Having arrived and searched within the bower at the end of twilight, Śikhidhvaja then beheld that couple with faces smiling at one another;
seeing them, he was greatly pleased with an unchanging heart.
"O, how happy the *khiṅgas* are in their state! said Śikhidhvaja. "O dear ones, as you remain according to your desire, so are the *khiṅgas* happy in their ease. (79)
Having said, "Do not cause an obstacle; we are afraid," he went out.
Then, in just a moment, she approached that manifestation.
She went forth, displaying her own body agitated by the battle of passion;
she beheld that king seated upon a golden stone slab.
Approaching that spot where he sat in solitary concentration with his eyes slightly opened,
she lowered her face in modesty.
Madanikā’s wife remained silent for a moment, distressed and withered;
then, after a moment, Śikhidhvaja ceased his meditation and spoke to her.
With a serene mind, he spoke these sweet words:
"O slender one, why have you come so quickly, with your joy thus obstructed? (84)
Go once more to please your beloved with acts of affection;
for mutual love desired by both is indeed rare throughout the three worlds. (85)
Madanikā said:
Thus, O illustrious one, this feminine nature is indeed fickle;
for women possess eightfold passion, so you ought not to be angry. (86)
"I am a weak woman, as well as young and foolish; I have committed an offense.
O Lord, you ought to forgive me, for the virtuous are indeed forgiving. (87)
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O young girl, anger does not exist within me, for it is like a tree in the sky;
solely because you are censured by the virtuous, I do not desire you as my daughter-in-law. (88)
Vasiṣṭha said:
While Śikhidhvaja remained there in such a state of equanimity, Cūḍālā, her own disposition awakened by his composure, reflected as follows: (89)
Oh, how wonderful! This Blessed One has attained supreme equanimity;
neither desires for enjoyments nor even great riches can distract him.
I shall remind him of this entire account of my own life;
having abandoned the form of Madanikā, I shall become Cūḍālā once again.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā assumed the form of Cūḍālā;
he beheld her before him, with faultless limbs and charming in her affection.
Then, seeing his beloved, Śikhidhvaja, his eyes wide with wonder, spoke these words in a voice agitated by amazement: || 93 ||
Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one? From where have you come, O beautiful lady?
Why are you here, for how long, and for what purpose do you stay? (94)
By your gestures, your conduct, your smile, and your conciliatory manner, you are recognized by me as Cūḍālā through the playful charm of my wife.
Cūḍālā said:
"In this very way, O Lord, know that I am Cūḍālā; of this there is no doubt.
Today I have been obtained by you in person, with my natural body. (96)
It was solely to awaken you that I assumed the creation of bodies such as Kumbha;
thus have you come here into the midst of this forest, possessing the hundred branches of phenomenal expansion.

O Knower of Reality, you who have known all that is to be known through the intellect and other faculties, you see this entire undivided universe through meditation; therefore, behold it now by means of meditation. 98.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having been addressed as "Cūḍāla," the king girded his loins and beheld the entirety of his own life-story through meditation.
From the renunciation of his own kingdom until the sight of Cūḍālā,
the king observed everything and then desisted from his meditative absorption.
Quickly extending his arms, which were radiant with horripilation,
the king, having emerged from his meditative absorption, embraced his beloved for a long time.
Having remained silent for a moment in dense bliss, Śikhidhvaja then placed her, who was tender with affection, upon his lap and spoke to her.
By what indeed can she be compared, by whose skillful means I have been rescued from this cave of saṃsāra so difficult to cross? (3)
Even from the beginningless, dense, and infinitely treacherous darkness of delusion,
noble women rescue those who have fallen and are intent on making an effort to rise.
For you who have departed without desire, having reached the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra—
how shall I ever perform a return service for such a kindness as this?
Cūḍālā said:
O Lord, while you were intent upon a web of fruitless actions and your own mind was distracted,
I became increasingly and intensely distressed on your account again and again.
"By that very [act], through your awakening, my own purpose has been accomplished;
how then, O Lord, can you show me honor in this matter? (7)
O Lord, those trivial stirrings of thirst and those wicked fabrications of conceptual thought are no longer seen in you today, just as mountains are not seen in the sky.
Śikhidhvaja said:
I am effortless, I am partless, I am as pure as the sky, and I am free from desire;
I am the nature of peace, I am the ultimate reality, and I have existed for all eternity.

"Free from effort": I am of the nature of a peaceful *aham-artha* (the sense of "I"); that is, I am one whose form is such that the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) has become tranquil within it. I am established in nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Self-abiding and settled, I am neither pleased nor distressed; I am not this, nor am I anything else. (610)
"Akiṃcit" means: I am established in that which is merely nothingness, the mere consciousness (cinmātra) which is entirely full. || 610 ||
I am equal to that light which has departed from the orb of fire, which has not fallen upon a wall,
and which is free from both decay and excess.

I am equal to that light which has issued forth from the orb of fire or the disc of the moon, which has not fallen upon another support such as a wall or a partition, and which is eternal and unsurpassed, being free from decrease or increase. || 11 ||
I am unable to say that which is what it is;
O you whose eyes have corners as tremulous as waves, you are my guru—salutations to you! 12.

Regarding the word "yat": the indeclinable *asmi* has the sense of "I. That which is well-known as the existing reality—I am that very thing; yet I am unable to describe that reality because it is devoid of name, genus, and so forth. 12 || 13 || 14 || 15 || 16 || 17 || 18 || 19 ||
Through the grace of the large-eyed one, I have crossed over the ocean of worldly existence;
transcending all and omnipresent, I remain like this very sky.
Cūḍālā said:
This being the case, O Great Being, O Lord of Life, O Beloved of the Heart: tell me now, O Master, O High-minded One, what pleases you? (14)
Śikhidhvaja said:
I do not know your prohibition, nor do I know your desire;
O slender one, whatever you do, I understand it exactly as it is.
Whatever you know, do that very thing, O beautiful one;
I shall hold that alone, just as a gem reflects an image.
I neither praise nor blame; do as you wish. 16.
Cūḍālā said:
If it is so, O mighty-armed one, then listen to my thought;
having heard it, O self-liberated one, you ought to put that very thing into practice. (17)
Through the realization of oneness everywhere, we remain free from the fear of the destruction of ignorance;
devoid of desire, we abide as clear as the sky. 18.
Therefore, O Supreme Person, we who exist at the beginning, the end, and the middle,
having abandoned this singular ignorance, shall once again attain that very nature.
"O Lord, having spent this time in our current state as kings, we shall indeed gradually attain the state of being bodiless by some means of time."
"O King, remain established upon your own throne in your very own city;
I, however, shall become your queen, the most excellent among those who desire you. (21)
When this duality of "this is pleasure" and "this is not" has come to an end,
remain in that very same state of peace, free from all longing.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O large-eyed one, you have spoken rightly with this measured wisdom:
what indeed is the purpose of a kingdom, whether in its acquisition or its relinquishment? (23)
Having abandoned concern for the states of pleasure and pain and being free from envy, let us both remain exactly as we are, having returned to our natural clarity. (24)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then Cūḍālā, having risen, mentally envisioned her beloved standing before her with a jeweled pitcher full of the waters of the seven oceans.
With that auspicious jar, she, his wife, consecrated her husband— who stood facing the east— in private within his own kingdom.
Having thus seated the Great Goddess upon her throne and likewise consecrated Cūḍālā, the king spoke to his beloved wife.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O beloved lotus-petal-eyed one, you ought to bring forth in an instant a vast and formidable army produced by mere thought."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these words of her beloved, Cūḍālā, the woman of excellent complexion,
conjured up an army that made the forest appear dense and impenetrable.
There, the king and queen ascended the excellent scent-elephant, which was adorned with royal ornaments and guarded by joyful vassal lords.
Then King Śikhidhvaja, together with his beloved queen,
though on foot, drew along his exceedingly powerful army without obstruction.
Departing from that great lord of mountains, Mahendra,
he reached his own city, which was as beautiful as heaven, in a very short time.
The neighboring kings residing in their cities, honoring his arrival, recognized him by the sound of victory and went forth with uplifted hearts.
He was met by that neighboring king, who had come forward with high-pitched trumpets and other instruments, having joined together in a single harmony.
Accompanied by those two forces, that king entered the city;
having ruled the kingdom upon the earth for ten thousand years, [he passed away]. (35)
Together with Cūḍālā, O Rāma, he desisted from maintaining the body;
casting off the body, he attained nirvāṇa like a lamp without oil. || 36 ||
The high-minded king went [to that place] for the sake of not being born again. || 37 ||
Having enjoyed infinite pleasures on earth and having remained for a long time as the crest-jewel of all sovereign kings,

he attained the supreme, immortal, and infinite state, leaving nothing but emptiness behind. Thus, following that which had come to Rāma, one should attend to the multitude of duties with a mind free from sorrow.
Having remained there, he himself continued to abide, forcibly pursuing the fortune of worldly enjoyments, liberation, and so forth.

Thereafter, with each other’s consent, intent upon their own royal births, they were consecrated by one another with the waters of all sacred fords, which grant the fulfillment of one's resolve; having entered their own city with great royal splendor and experienced the bliss of imperial sovereignty for ten thousand years, they both attained the disembodied liberation (videhamukti) that is free from further rebirth.
A summary of the remainder of the narrative. || 638 ||

Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Narrative of Śikhidhvaja," containing within it the three narratives of the Kirāta, Cintāmaṇi, and Gajendra, from the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Rāmāyaṇa*.
Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Narrative of Śikhidhvaja," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-sāra.
Tenth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus has this entire narrative of Śikhidhvaja been related to you;
proceed by this path, and you shall never suffer weariness.

Previously, it was shown through the narrative of Śikhidhvaja— which contains numerous sub-stories— that even self-knowledge, though difficult to attain, can be obtained through the extraordinary efforts of a teacher when there has been no prior destruction of obstructing sins. Now, [it is taught that] the abandonment of the mind alone is what is called the "renunciation of all."
This is explained by means of the narrative of Kaca. || 1 || 2 || 3 ||
O Rāghava, understand how Śikhidhvaja gradually attained awakening, just as Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, did. (2)
Rāma said:
O Blessed One, please describe in brief how that blessed Kaca, the son of the blessed Bṛhaspati, became awakened.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having transcended childhood and being intent on crossing over saṃsāra,
Kaca, who understood both words and their meanings, spoke to Bṛhaspati.

"Because he is a fool" means: due to his state of being a fool, that is, because of his stupidity, he is one who knows the words and word-meanings; "word-meaning" (padārtha) refers to the meaning of those two—the word and the [underlying] reality-word (tattvapada)—at every step, and he is one who knows that. || 4 ||
Kaca said:
O Blessed One, Knower of all Dharmas, tell me how a living being, bound by the thread of life, may emerge from this cage of saṃsāra. (5)

"O Blessed One! [Thus he addressed him. By means of the "life-thread"—the life-force (*jīva*) is the sustaining of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and that itself is the "thread," the string which is the cause of movement; by that [he was bound]. (Verses 5–23)
Bṛhaspati said:
O son, by renouncing everything, one crosses over this ocean of saṃsāra, which is a house for sea-monsters of misfortune, once the stream of rebirth has been stilled.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these most purifying words of his father,
Kaca abandoned everything and went to a solitary forest.
Bṛhaspati’s departure did not cause him any distress;
for those of great magnanimity are not agitated by either union or separation. (8)
Then, O sinless one, when eight years had passed,
Kaca once again encountered his father in a certain great forest.
Having worshipped and saluted him, and having embraced his son,
Kaca again questioned the Lord of Speech with a pleasing voice.
Today is the eighth year since I have practiced total renunciation;
yet even so, O father, I do not attain blameless peace.
Vasiṣṭha said:
While Kaca was speaking such piteous words in the forest,
the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), having said "Abandon everything," departed for heaven.
When he had departed, Kaca likewise cast off even his bark garments and other belongings from his body;
thereafter, he became like the autumnal sky, free from clouds, the sun, and stars.
Then, after another three years, with a grieving mind, he reached that very same father and teacher in a certain part of the forest.
To him, who had performed worship and salutation and was embracing his son, he spoke again with a voice faltering from distress: || 15 ||
Kaca said:
"O father, everything has been renounced, even my patched garment and the forest creepers;
yet still there is no rest in my own true state—what shall I do? (16)
Bṛhaspati said:
They say that the mind is everything; having abandoned it, my son, you shall shine.
Those who know all things understand the abandonment of the mind to be the abandonment of everything. (17)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) swiftly leaped into the sky;
Kaca, his mind unwearied, sought to abandon his own consciousness.
When he could not perceive his own mind even while reflecting upon it in the forest, he then reflected with an undaunted intellect as follows: (19)
Kaca said:
The collection of objects, such as the body and so forth, is said to be not the mind;
why, where, or for what purpose should I abandon this which is useless and innocent? (20)
I shall go into the presence of my father to understand the mind of my great enemy;
having understood it, I will then quickly abandon him and remain free from the fever of anxiety.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, Kaca went to his father, his guru;
becoming composed, he asked him: "Father, what is meant by 'citta'? (22)
Bṛhaspati said:
Those who know the mind understand that one's own egoism is the mind;
that internal sense of "I" which exists within a living being is called the mind. (23)
Kaca said:
I think that its renunciation is difficult and does not lead to perfection;
how indeed can this be abandoned, O best of yogis? (24)
Bṛhaspati said:
Even from the crushing of a flower or the closing of one's eyes, the abandonment of egoism is easily accomplished; there is not even the slightest difficulty in this. (25)
There exists that single, beginningless and endless, pure consciousness alone, stainless and all-pervading; clearer even than space, it is the knower of all. (26)
"One" means: the connection [of the words] is that there exists only the reality which is pure consciousness, the witness of all. || 26 ||
Cultivating that very state, remain as a virtuous person, peaceful and free from distress;
for the false nature of the ego-sense dissolves through the contemplation of reality.
Regarding the word "tat": it means from the contemplation of reality, that is, from the contemplation of the nature of consciousness. || 27 ||
O Consciousness, what is this sense of "I," and how indeed has it arisen?
What is this internal sense of "I," from where does it come, and how has it arisen? (28)
"Consciousness," thus [it is said]. || 28 ||
Where is the mass of dust born from water, and where is the water arisen from fire?
O son, abandon this futile conviction that "this is I."
The meaning is that the sense of "I" (ahambhāva) is not appropriate even in the nature of consciousness (citsvarūpa), just as a mass of dust is not appropriate in water, or water in fire.
This refers to the notions: "This is I" and "That is I. || 29 ||
It is empty, of limited form, and rendered subject to space and time. || 30 ||
Abandon this insignificant cognition, which is limited in form and rendered helpless by space and time.
Unconditioned by space, time, and the like, pure, eternally manifest, all-pervading,
consisting of all objects yet having a single object, you are stainless pure consciousness alone.

"Digiti"—the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: that which, although consisting of all objects, is a single object and of a single form—that stainless pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is You.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus attained this supreme yoga, the unsurpassed instruction,
that son of the preceptor of the gods became liberated while yet living.
Free from possessiveness and free from ego, with the knots of bondage severed and the intellect thoroughly pacified,
remain without modification, O Rāma, just as Kaca remained.

Know that the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is unreal; do not rely upon it, nor abandon it. For how indeed can there be the relinquishing or grasping of that which is non-existent, such as a rabbit’s horn? (34)
"I" — the meaning is: do not rely upon the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which is as non-existent as a hare's horn, nor abandon it. || 34 ||
Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Narrative of Kaca," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-sāra;
thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Narrative of Kaca," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa.
p. 769) The Eleventh Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Abandoning the notions of duality and unity, remain established in what remains and be happy;
do not be miserable in vain like a deluded person.

Previously, it was stated that the renunciation of the mind alone constitutes the renunciation of everything. Now, the story of the "false man" is presented as an illustration for the point that this ego, which is delightful only so long as it is not scrutinized, grieves in vain within saṃsāra—beginning with the words "dvitve... (in the state of duality).

Since the cognition of duality has difference as its object, and the cognition of unity implies difference by virtue of having difference as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), abandon both of these. Abiding in that which remains—the reality whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and which cannot be designated as either different or non-different—be happy. Do not, like a deluded person, be pointlessly and without cause miserable. 1, 2, 3, 4.
Rāma said:
I have attained supreme internal satisfaction through the nectar of your knowledge;
yet, O Lord, though already satisfied, I ask you this further question.
O best of sages, why is that which is called "the false person" said to be a reality made of unreality? Tell me quickly how the entire collection of things in the world is thus constituted.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, listen to this beautiful narrative uttered by me, which produces laughter, for the sake of awakening you from your false conception of a person. 4.
O mighty-armed one, there is a certain man made of illusory machinery;
he is foolish, conceited, and possesses a mind as tender as a child's, being solely defined by his own ignorance.
"It exists. This person, composed of the machinery of illusion, is of the nature of ego; his intellect is as tender as a child's, possessing a wisdom as meager as that of a child.
Born somewhere in solitude, he remains right there in that void, like a tuft of hair seen in the sky or a mirage in the desert.

"He" refers to the person who has arisen within that certain indefinable reality which is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*)—solitary, devoid of conceptual proliferation (*niḥprapañca*), empty, and without distinction.
He remains in that very reality, like a mass of hair seen by one with cataracts in the sky, or like a mirage in a desert; he exists as something established solely through delusion. (6)
Therefore, there is nothing else there; that which exists is only that itself.
And as for that which appears as something else, the dull-witted person does not perceive it as such.

"Therefore" means: in that space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), there is nothing other than that *māyā-puruṣa* (the illusory person) who is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). And whatever does exist, that is he alone, because everything is composed of the ego-sense; it appears as this or that form, such as ether and so forth, manifesting as various appearances.
He does not see, nor does he perceive, any other reality apart from this phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
Because of being of evil intellect and because of being of dull intellect. || 7 ||
As that [desire] grew within him, the thought arose:
"I shall zealously protect my own cherished object by establishing it in a place where it may be guarded. (8)

The two verses beginning with "saṃkalpa" form a single syntactical unit. Therein, having established the void—meaning the ether—of that illusory person (māyā-puṃsa) who has attained growth within the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), and having fixed it upon some support, I protect it.
For from this arises the volition (saṃkalpa): "This desired object must be protected, it is to be guarded, out of respect. || 8 ||
Reflecting thus, he built a house for the protection of the sky;
and within its interior, he placed the sky, thinking, "The sky has been protected by me. (771) || 9 ||

Reflecting in this manner, that man built a house for the purpose of protecting the sky; and within the interior of that house's chamber, he placed his trust and devotion, thinking, "The sky is protected by me here. || 9 ||
Then, in the course of time, that house of his went to ruin,
like a cloud at the end of the season or a wave by the wind.
The word "atha" (now) [is used]. Just as a year consisting of the rainy season comes to an end through another season called autumn, so too [does this]. 10.
"Alas, O space within the house, you are lost! Alas, where have you gone in an instant?
Thus he lamented for it when the house was broken, thinking, "This is the space within the house. (11)
"Alas, the house! and so forth. First the house; upon its destruction, the well. (Verses 11–15)
Having thus lamented a hundred times, the evil-minded one again dug a well right there for the sake of protecting his donkey, becoming intent upon the space within that well.
Then, in the course of time, even that well of his met its destruction;
when the sorrow regarding the space of the well had passed away, he subsequently became immersed in [another] grief.
At the conclusion of his discourse on the space within the well, he quickly fashioned a jar;
having become the space within the jar, he himself attained final liberation.
O descendant of Raghu, even Kumbha was brought to destruction in time;
for whatever direction an unfortunate person takes, that very direction perishes.
At the conclusion of his prattle regarding the space within the jar, he dug a pit there for the sake of a donkey;
because of that, he became devoted to the space within the pit (Kuṇḍākāśa). || 16 ||
Then [he should place] a water-pot, then a pit (kuṇḍa)—meaning a specific kind of excavation—or a cooking vessel (sthālī). || 16 || 17 ||
After some time, even his sacrificial pit met with destruction; thus, like darkness before light, he grieved for the space that had once been the pit. (17)
Before the destruction of the space within the sacrificial pit was complete, he built a great four-winged mansion for the sake of his own protection; thus, he became intent upon that space.
Then, [he saw] a great mansion (mahāśāla) endowed with spacious rooms, a four-winged house (catuḥśāla), which is a collection of four halls.
Time, which devours all creatures, swiftly swept that away as well, like the wind blowing off a withered leaf; thereafter, he became consumed by grief. (19)
At the edge of the four-hall structure, he built a granary shaped like a water-cloud for the sake of protecting his donkeys; he remained there, intent upon the sky.
Then, having made a granary and a place for sowing grain, he grieved at their respective destruction; such is the summary. || 20 ||
Time quickly snatched that away from him as the wind carries off a cloud;
because of that grief over the space within his granary, he was consumed by torment.
In this manner, through houses, four-sided halls, jars, basins, and granaries, his time, consisting of nothing but suffering, passed away without end. (22)
Remaining thus in the cave of his own mind, that fool seizes the sky with his house, imagining it to be the self;
deluded by the attachment of coming and going, he comes and goes from one mass of suffering to another even denser mass of suffering.

Thus it is said: Being composed of suffering, that person of poor intellect, perceiving the sky situated within the cave as being contained by some house—that is, by a dwelling place—and grasping at it, develops a notion of self (*ātmabuddhi*) regarding that sky; through that notion of self directed toward the sky, he comes to experience a mass of dense suffering arising from an even denser state of suffering.
Deluded by the association with coming and going—that is, being deluded by the connection with the coming and going of limiting adjuncts—he himself goes [along with them]. 23–24.
Rāma said:
O Lord, why have you spoken of this illusory person through an association with a false man? And what is meant by the "protection of the sky"? || 24 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
O descendant of Raghu, that which is called a person is said to consist of the machinery of illusion;
know this very thing to be the ego (ahaṅkāra), arisen from the empty sky.

Regarding the word "māyā": know that this person who has been described as consisting of the machine of *māyā* is actually the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) arisen from the void of space, that is, arisen from the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). || 25 ||
O virtuous one, within this sheath of space wherein this world is situated,
there exists at the beginning of creation that infinite, unreal void by itself;
from that arises the ego, like the first vibration from the wind.

Regarding the phrase "in which": that which is infinite (ananta), undivided, void (śūnya), and devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and therefore non-existent (asat) in the sense of being beyond the scope of empirical discourse—according to the Śruti, "In the beginning this was indeed non-existent;
from that, the existent was born"—such a reality exists at the commencement of creation; from that reality, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) arises first of all.
"From the wind" means from that which is still air; "motion" refers to movement, as it were. || 26 ||

Having fallen into a state of agitation, this non-self [ego] repeatedly creates various kinds of bodies from the self for the sake of its own protection, even though they are subject to destruction again and again. (27)

"Non-self" (anātman): Non-self is, in reality, other than the Self; this very ego (ahaṃkāra), for the sole purpose of protecting the Self—which is of the nature of the space of consciousness—creates various kinds of bodies again and again, even though they undergo destruction. || 27 ||
Having fashioned the body as a well, a pond, a quadrangle, a jar, or the like, and thinking "the self has been protected," he directs his contemplation toward that space.

Regarding the word "kūpa" (well): this egoism, having made bodies comparable to wells and the like, thinks, "The Self, which is like space, has been protected"; thus it directs its contemplation toward that void, that sky of consciousness. || 28 || 29 ||
Just as a deluded man, protecting [the space] out of fear for his own self, becomes distressed regarding the space within jars and so forth— so too, do not be one who suffers from afflictions. (29)
Vaster even than space, pure, subtle, auspicious, and beautiful—how and by whom can that Self be grasped, or likewise protected? (30)

"From space," etc. The meaning is: how can that Self which is even more expansive than space be grasped, or by whom is it grasped and protected? For there is no entity whatsoever distinct from it. || 30 ||
When the body, which is merely the space within the heart, perishes through decay, living beings grieve in vain, suspecting that the Self has been destroyed. (31)

Regarding the verse beginning with *hṛdaya*: when there is the destruction—that is, the dissolution—of the abode characterized by the body, which is merely the space within the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*) as delimited by the lotus of the heart (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*), living beings grieve in vain out of the suspicion that "the Self has perished. || 31 ||
Just as space remains undivided when jars and other objects have perished,
so too the embodied soul remains eternally untainted when bodies have perished.
Regarding the phrase "in jars and so forth": by the word "and so forth" in the expression "space and so forth," there is an inclusion of direction and other formless substances. (32)
This Self is pure consciousness alone; subtler than even space, it does not perish like the sky, O Rāma, because it consists solely of the portion of its own self-experience.

"Pure," etc. That Self which is pure consciousness alone, subtler than even the subtle ether (ākāśa) because it is partless, does not perish like the sky, because the Self consists solely of the portion of its own experience and has the nature of mere self-experience. 33.
Nothing whatsoever is ever born, nor does anything ever die;
it is only Brahman that expands in the form of the world's manifestation. (34)
"No. There is no object whatsoever that is ever born or ever dies in any place; rather, Brahman alone expands and manifests in the form of the world as a phenomenal transformation (*vivarta*). 34.
"All this is one, peaceful, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and liberated from existence and non-existence; having realized this, be happy. (35)

"All this" means: realizing that this entire world is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; and therefore, being liberated from existence and non-existence—that is, birth and destruction—it is the peaceful, one, and non-dual Brahman; remain happy in this conviction. 35.

Having completely abandoned the state of egoism— which is the abode of all calamities, unstable, lacking self-mastery, prone to downfall, devoid of discernment, conceited, and ignorant— attain through awakening the state of the perfectly enlightened one and proceed to the highest excellence.
"All" refers to that entire object which is the abode of all calamities, unstable, lacking independence, prone to imminent fall, perishable, devoid of discrimination, without self-respect,
lacking authority, ignorant, inert, the locus of egoism, and consisting of the form of egoism.
Having liberated oneself from all this through awakening— that is, through the realization of the true nature of the Self— one remains in the remainder, which is free from egoism.
Abiding in the state of perfect awakening, the state of gnosis, one attains supreme liberation while living. || 36 ||
Thus ends the eleventh canto, titled "The Narrative of the False Man," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-sāra. || 11 ||
Thus ends the eleventh canto in the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa. || 11 ||
p. 775) The Twelfth Canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, this world has come into existence solely through the forgetting of that invisible reality of the Self; it has not come from anything else, like a snake imagined upon a rope.

It was previously stated that egoism alone is the false cause of sorrow. Now, in response to the inquiry as to how, then, the mind may find rest, it is demonstrated through the narrative of Bhṛṅgīśa that the rest of the mind is accomplished even without the great sense of agency and so forth—beginning with the words "tasya" (of him). This world belongs to him.

The persistence of the reality of the Self, which is the substratum of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), has attained the status of a valid cognition solely through its being forgotten—that is, through its non-recognition—and not from any other cause, just like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope.
For just as a snake superimposed on a rope is established solely due to the ignorance of the rope's true nature and not from any other cause, so it is here. (1)
O Rāghava, for one who contemplates this network of rays as distinct from the sun, it appears as if it were something other than that shining orb. (2)

Regarding the word "āditya": that person who conceives this web of rays as distinct from the sun—that is, conceives it as separate from the sun—for him, this web of rays appears as if it were something other than the luminous one. || 2 ||
For one by whom the armlet is conceived as being distinct from gold, that is indeed an armlet for him; it is not gold for him. (3)
"Kanaka," etc.: the meaning is exactly as previously stated. || 3 ||
He by whom the rays are realized as non-different from the sun—he is indeed the sun itself; he is called "free from conceptual construction" (nirvikalpa). || 4 ||
Now he speaks of the meditation on non-duality: "The sun... and so forth.

For that person by whom the rays have been meditated upon as non-different from the sun, even those rays are indeed the sun itself; that person, seeing non-duality, is called one who is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). || 4 ||
He by whom the armlet is perceived as not distinct from gold,
possessing the great wisdom that gold alone exists, is called one who is free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa).

Regarding the term *kanaka*: A man who possesses a single, great cognition (*mahābuddhi*) such that he perceives "gold" alone even in objects like armlets and the like is called one who is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). (5)
Having abandoned all diversity within the hollow of pure consciousness alone,
remain steadfast in the reality of awareness, which is entirely free from any object of perception.

"Regarding 'diversity' (nānātām): having abandoned all diversity, remain steady and composed in that very essence of consciousness (saṃvittattva) which resides within the cavity—the womb—of pure consciousness alone, being entirely free from anything to be perceived. || 6 ||
When the Self itself, by its own power, quickly brings about the shimmering mental construct called "mother-of-pearl," just as the wind brings forth the vibration of movement, || 7 ||

The two verses beginning with "svayam" constitute a single sentence. When the Self, by itself and not through any other cause, causes its own power called *saṃkalpa* (volition) to vibrate—just as the wind causes the power of motion—it makes that power, which is oriented toward its effects, manifest.
Then the Universal Self (*viśvātmā*), consisting of the fabrication of volitions, appears as if separate, appearing as if other than the Self.
By itself contemplating its own form and its own appearance, which are the cause of all conceptual proliferation, the mind comes into being. || 7 || 8 ||
Then the mind, which consists of the fabrication of conceptual constructions, becomes the soul of the universe, appearing as if separate while itself imagining its own form.
Behold this expansive world as nothing but mere conceptualization;
it is neither real nor unreal, having arisen like a web of dreams.

He reflects: For this reason, let it be seen that this expansive, manifold world is composed solely of mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) and is not real, because it is sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Nor is it merely false, because it functions within empirical discourse (*vyavahāra*). What then? It has arisen as something indefinable (*anirvacanīya*), like a web of dreams. 9, 10, 11.
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, speaking, acting, and sleeping—perceiving that nothing new exists and that everything is indeed real, one should contemplate thus. (10)
Whatever one does, know that to be the stainless, pervasive Pure Consciousness;
it is Brahman appearing in various forms, and nothing other than that exists. 11.
Since the entire multitude of objects exists with consciousness as its essence, this whole world is nothing but consciousness; there is no other conceptualization.

Regarding the phrase "padārtha" and so forth: since consciousness alone exists as the authority within the entire collection of categories—that is, within the totality of things—by virtue of having consciousness as their essence and being nothing but consciousness, it follows from the maxim that "consciousness alone remains the refuge when the existence of objects subsides. || 12 ||
Since everything arises from a single consciousness alone in all its various forms, even the object of cognition does not exist at all; how, then, can there be bondage and liberation? (13)

Let it be ascertained that this entire world is consciousness alone. In this regard, there is no other conceptualization, nor any conceptualization of duality, because it is possible for a single consciousness to exist in every form.
Having forcibly cast away all such thoughts as "this is liberation" or "this is indeed bondage," one whose conceit regarding the whole has been destroyed [attains peace].
Silent, self-controlled, free from pride and intoxication, a great soul, perform your own duty and remain indeed without egoism.
O sinless one, you are a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer;
casting aside all doubts and relying upon eternal fortitude. (15)
Rāma said:
Why is he called the great doer? Why is he called the great renouncer? Why is he called the great enjoyer? O Lord, tell me correctly. (16)
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, these three vows were formerly proclaimed by the moon-crested Lord to Bhṛṅgīśa, by whom he was rendered free from his fever.
Formerly, on the northern peak of Sumeru, which resembled fire, Śaśikalādhara stood together with his entire retinue.
O Rāma, desiring to know the truth, the highly resplendent Bhṛṅgīśa, bowing with palms joined in reverence, respectfully questioned Umāpati.
Bhṛṅgīśa said:
O Lord, beholding this construction of saṃsāra, as flickering as a wave, I am bewildered, being devoid of rest in the ultimate reality. (20)
Having firmly adopted this beloved internal certainty,
I remain in this dilapidated house of the world, free from all feverish distress. (21)
The Lord said:
Abandoning all doubts and relying upon eternal fortitude,
O sinless one, become a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer.
Bhṛṅgīśa said:
What is meant by "the great doer," and what is meant by "the great enjoyer"? What is meant by "the great renouncer"? O Lord, explain this correctly to me. (23)
The Lord said:
He who acts without regard for passion and hatred, pleasure and pain, merit and demerit, or fruit and its absence— he is called a great doer.
He who acts with silence, free from egoism, devoid of pride, and liberated from envy,
performing his duties without agitation— he is called a great doer.
He who is free from attachment everywhere and remains like a witness,
acting in his duty without desire— he is called a great doer.
Free from both agitation and joy, with an equanimous and pure intellect, he neither grieves nor exults; he is called a great doer.
He whose mind remains entirely equanimous during birth, existence, and destruction, as well as during rising and setting, is called a great doer.
He hates nothing, nor does he desire anything;
he consumes everything as it comes to him—he is called a great enjoyer. (29)

He who is not agitated by pleasures or pains, by ritual actions or their application, nor by existence and non-existence which cause delusion— he, having experienced all these, is called the Great Enjoyer.
He who enjoys even old age, death, calamities, sovereignty, and poverty as if they were delightful— he is called a great enjoyer.
Whether it be bitter, sour, salty, pungent, unrefined, or refined,
he who approaches all with equanimity and is a great enjoyer is called such.
He who perceives with equanimity the flavorful and the flavorless, as well as sexual union and its cessation, is called a gentle and great enjoyer.
He whose equanimity remains steadfast toward milk and various kinds of sugar, as well as toward the auspicious and the inauspicious— he is called a great enjoyer.
Having abandoned the conceptual distinction that "this is edible" and "this is inedible," he who eats with all desire gone is called a great eater. (35)
He who experiences adversity and prosperity, delusion and bliss, one after another,
with an equanimous intellect, is called a great enjoyer.
He by whom merit and demerit, pleasure and pain, as well as death and birth, have been renounced through wisdom—he is called a great renouncer. (37)
He by whom all desires, all doubts, all endeavors, and all certainties have been abandoned through wisdom— he is called a great renouncer.
He by whom dharma and adharma, the mind and mental activity, and all that is sought after have been completely renounced within, is called a great renouncer.
Whatever extent of this entire perceived world is observed, he by whom it is thoroughly renounced is called a great renunciant. (40)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus was it spoken by the God of gods to Bhṛṅgīśa in the past, O sinless one:
"O Rāma, maintaining this vision, remain free from all feverish distress. (41)
Brahman alone exists—eternally risen, pure in form, infinite, and primordial—not even a fraction of anything else can be conceived.
Meditate thus; having attained the state of stainlessness, reach Nirvana with all your mental fluctuations purified and stilled. 42.
The Brahman is free from ailment, the sole seed of all the effects of every kalpa, and the very form of the Supreme Self;
it is vast, having expanded all states of being, and like the ether, it exists as if shining as something, O dear one. (43)
"O virtuous one, remain with a firm internal conviction that nothing whatsoever else exists anywhere at any time—neither as being nor as non-being—and dwell thus, free from the play of doubt. (44)
Being inward-turned while constantly performing the entire multitude of external duties, you never experience weariness and attain the state of one whose egoism has been cast aside. 45.
Inward-turned and intent on contemplation, you do not fall into weariness while performing the multitude of external bodily activities;
moreover, you attain the state of having discarded egoism. 45.
Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Narrative of Bhṛṅgīśa," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-sāra. 12.
Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Narrative of Bhṛṅgīśa," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa. || 12 ||
The Thirteenth Chapter. Rāma said:

O Blessed One, Knower of all Reality, when the mind—known by the name of egoism—is dissolved, or in the state of being dissolved, what becomes of the subtle body (liṅga) of the sentient being? || 1 ||
