Previously, it was stated that the resting of the intellect (*dhī-viśrānti*) is accomplished even without meditative absorption (*samādhi*), solely through the state of being the Great Agent (*mahākartṛtva*). Now, by means of the narrative of Ikṣvāku, it is explained that even a reality (*tattva*) which cannot be understood through one's own inquiry can indeed be understood through the instruction of a Guru—beginning with the words "O Blessed One. When the mind named ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) has dissolved and its form has vanished...
Or, if such a thing existed, what mark or sign would there be for a sentient being, a living creature? || 1 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
For even when produced by force, defects such as greed and delusion do not stain the pure disposition, just as water does not cling to a lotus.

The six verses beginning with "balāt" form a single syntactical unit. When the mind consisting of egoism dissolves—that is, when it becomes slackened—and when evil deeds dissolve, then even those defects such as greed and delusion, though produced by the extraordinary efforts of others, do not stain or touch the pure and stainless disposition, just as water does not stain a lotus. || 2 ||
The glories beginning with sympathetic joy (muditā) never abandon the face [of the practitioner], provided that the painting consisting of egoism dissolves and evil karma dissolves. (3)
Joy and the other [immeasurables], as well as loving-kindness and the others, which are the causes of beauty, never for a moment abandon the face of Fortune. || 3 ||
The knots of latent impressions (vāsanā) are completely severed and gradually snap asunder; anger comes to attenuation, and delusion indeed reaches a state of feebleness.
The knots in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā) are severed as it were and gradually snap; even anger and the like fall away and perish.
Desire goes to exhaustion, and greed flees somewhere far away.
The senses flash forth intensely, yet exhaustion does not manifest with great force. || 5 ||
The senses do not exult loudly, nor do they manifest; likewise, weariness and dejection no longer appear as they did before. (5)
Sufferings do not increase for him, nor do pleasures cause him to exult;
equanimity arises everywhere in his heart, bestowing a cooling serenity.

Sufferings do not increase nor do they grow; pleasures do not surge forth, nor do they become causes for dependence. Within the heart, equanimity toward all objects arises, bestowing a sense of coolness.
Furthermore, these things such as pleasure and pain may indeed be seen on the face;
however, because they are trivial, they do not stain the mind.

Although pleasure, pain, and so forth appear on the surface and are inferred through their respective transformations, they do not smear the mind because of their insignificance and their being merely imagined. || 7 ||
As the mind dissolves, it attains the state of being envied by the hosts of gods; for the practitioner, equanimity arises like the cool moonlight.

The two verses beginning with "citta" form a single syntactical unit. When even a slight trace of the mind has dissolved, that practitioner becomes an object of longing and desire even for the hosts of gods. || 8 ||
Tranquil, lovely, serviceable, and unobstructed;
restrained, powerful, and clear—thus does the stainless body become.

And his physical form— tranquil, lovely, radiant, unobstructed, not a hindrance to meditative absorption, composed, changeless, vigorous, free from dejection, clear, and stainless— is to be served in this manner, by this method. || 9 ||
Though it is afflicted by existence and non-existence, though it is diverse, and though it is vast,
the delusion of worldly existence causes neither joy nor sorrow to the wise.

Regarding the phrase "existence and non-existence": the delusion of saṃsāra, though afflicted by existence and non-existence—that is, though struck by birth and death, diverse, and vast—does not lead to joy nor to distress for the virtuous, those who possess the knowledge of reality. The meaning is that it does not become a cause for either elation or despondency. || 10 ||

Fie upon that lowest of men who, out of delusion, does not proceed toward this reality— which is to be accomplished through the illumination of the intellect and in which all calamities have subsided! (11)

"Buddhyā" means: that which is the illumination through the intellect—that is, inquiry—is accomplished by that alone; fie upon him who, out of delusion, does not apply himself to this matter characterized as liberation, wherein all calamities have subsided! || 11 ||

For one who desires to cross the ocean of birth—a mine of jewels that are the sorrows of long-standing attachment—in order to attain the rest that is appropriate, the supreme means is this thought: "Who am I? How is this world? Who might there be beyond it? And what is the use of enjoyments? (12)

Regarding the word *viśrāntim*: For a person desiring to cross the ocean of birth—which is a mine of jewels of suffering caused by long-standing attachment—in order to attain the appropriate rest that consists in abiding in reality (*tattva*), what is the use of enjoyments?
Thus, preceded by dispassion (*vairāgya*), [he reflects]: "How and by what manner was this world produced, and who is the Supreme (*paraḥ*), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)?"
The intellect whose nature is inquiry as to "who" and "of what kind" [the self] might be, is the supreme means to liberation. || 12 || 13 || 14 || 15 || 16 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen to how your first ancestor, the king named Ikṣvāku,
who was born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, attained liberation.
A king named Ikṣvāku, while protecting his own kingdom, once went into solitude and reflected in his mind: (14)

"What could be the cause of this phenomenal world of appearances, which exists in a state of agitation through old age and death, and fluctuation through pleasure and pain?"—thus [he reflected] within himself. (15)
Although he reflected upon it, he did not discover the cause of the world.
Then, on one occasion, he questioned Manu, who had arrived from the realm of Brahmā.
He saw the Blessed Lord Prajāpati, seated in his own assembly hall, being honored.
Ikṣvāku said:
O Blessed One, O Treasure of Compassion, it is through your very grace that you impel me with such boldness to inquire directly of you. (17)
From where has this creation come, and what is its true nature?
How large is this world, to whom does it belong, when did it arise, and by whom was it created? Please tell me this. (18)

Why is this? It must be told: what is this world like, and what is its magnitude? To whom does it belong—to the Lord (Īśvara) or to the individual souls (jīvas)? At what time did it manifest, and by what cause was it born? || 18 ||
And how might I be liberated from this treacherous delusion of saṃsāra, like a bird from a thickly spread net? (19)
"I" (aham). "Densely spread" (ghanāstīrṇāt) means as if spread out without any gaps, that is, extended. || 19 || 20 || 21 ||
Manu said:
Aha! After a long time, in this state of solitude so full of clarity, you have posed an essential question that discerns the vast meaning. (20)
Whatever is seen here, O King, that does not exist at all;
it is like a city of the Gandharvas, or like water in a desert. (21)
That which transcends the six senses including the mind, which is never seen anywhere, and which is indestructible—that exists here; it is called the True Self (Sadātman). || 22 ||

Regarding the word "manas": that entity which is not perceived anywhere as "this," which is not cognized through its specific identity, and which transcends the six senses—namely, the mind (manas) being the sixth among the senses such as sight and the rest—is imperishable. That very entity exists as the nature of reality; that entity is called the Self (Ātman). || 22 ||
But this entire succession of creations, O King, beginning with all that is visible, has attained the state of a reflection in that very same great mirror. (23)
"In this" means: in that very Self; "in the great mirror" means in a large looking-glass. || 23 ||
The radiant powers of Brahmā, arising from their own inherent nature, are capable of manifesting;
some attain the state of the cosmic egg, while others become living beings. (24)
The lights (*bhās*) are self-originated, having arisen from the very nature of fire (*tejas*), because fire has the nature of radiance (*sphuraṇa*).
The divine powers (*brāhmyaḥ*)—the powers of Brahman related to Brahman—are powers of manifestation (*sphuraṇa-śaktayaḥ*) and powers of projection (*vikṣepa-śaktayaḥ*).
Some of these powers of manifestation attain the state of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍatā*); they evolve as the cosmic egg. Other powers of manifestation...
They attain the state of being real entities, that is, the form of living beings. || 24 || 25 ||
There is no bondage, there is no liberation; there is only Brahman, free from all affliction.
There is neither unity nor duality; it is the essence of consciousness that unfolds.
Just as a single body of water manifests through the breaking of waves, so too does consciousness manifest; this [world] is nothing at all.
Casting far away the conceptualization of bondage and liberation, remain established in yourself—you are indeed the essence of fearlessness, free from the fear of becoming and non-becoming.

"Single": Just as a single body of water manifests through various breaking waves, so too does consciousness alone manifest everywhere; this visible world does not exist at all. For this reason, casting far away the conceptualization of bondage and liberation, being free from the fear of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), and becoming one whose very essence is fearlessness—Brahman being fearlessness itself—remain thus.
Be at ease. 26.
O King, when the consciousnesses of pure awareness, which are truly real, turn toward conceptualization, they become the state of living beings, just as water turns into the form of waves. 27.

"Regarding the phrase 'the state of being oriented toward volition' (saṃkalponmukhatām): having become oriented toward volition, these very waters—which are consciousness itself whose nature is pure spirit—attain the state of living beings, just as [water] attains the state of waves. (27)
(787) Those living beings transmigrate here in this world that has arisen before;
the delusion regarding the states of pleasure and pain exists only in the mind, not in the Self. (28)

Regarding the word "they": those living beings (jīvas) wander within the previously arisen cycle of existence (saṃsāra). Pleasure, pain, states of being, and delusion exist only in the mind; they do not exist in the Self (ātman). 28.
Just as the invisible Rāhu is perceived by means of the eclipsed moon,
so too is the self, whose nature is pure experience, beheld through the object of perception.

Regarding the term "invisible": just as Rāhu, though invisible and impossible to see, becomes visible by means of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the eclipsed moon, so too the Self, although consisting of pure experience alone, is perceived through the visible limiting adjuncts such as the body. 29.
The Supreme Lord is not seen even through scripture or by a teacher;
the Self is seen only by the self, through one's own intellect established in purity.
"No. By one's own self, by one's own human effort alone, and by one's own intellect established in the quality of *sattva*, the Self—the Supreme Lord—is perceived. (30–31)
Just as travelers are seen on the road by one who is free from passion and hatred, in that same manner these enemies of the senses are to be viewed. (31)
One should not show disrespect toward these things, nor should a virtuous person treat them with contempt;
let them remain as they are, existing merely as objects.

"In these" means: A wise person who exists [in the Self] should not show regard for these things, such as the body and the senses; nor should he practice disregard, that is, contempt. These things, the body and so forth, being merely objects of the intellect—having entered the state of being mere objects—should remain exactly as they are. 32, 33, 34.
Having cast far away the entire collection of objects through the notion that they are the body and so forth,
with an inner organ perpetually cooled, become forever absorbed in the Self.
The notion that "I am the body" is what binds one to saṃsāra;
indeed, this notion must never be accepted by those seeking liberation.
"I am of the nature of pure consciousness alone, not even a mere atom compared to the sky"— this eternal realization is not a binder to saṃsāra. (35)

"No, not so. He is not merely of the nature of pure consciousness (cinmātra), nor is he merely that which is "nothing" (na kiṃcinmātra) and distinct from the universe; rather, his form is that very pure consciousness which is such. || 35 ||
Just as the solar light exists everywhere, both outside and inside clear waters, so too does the Self abide in all things. (36)

Regarding the word "atha": Just as the solar light belonging to the sun exists everywhere—both outside and inside—within pure waters, even so the Self exists everywhere—both outside and inside—within all things. 36.

Just as the diversity of the parts of a configuration belongs to gold through its forms such as armlets and the like, so too does the world and other such forms belong to the Self through those very forms and non-those forms. (37)

Regarding the term *sanniveśa*: just as there is a variety of parts in the arrangement of gold—where "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*) means configuration (*saṃsthāna*), and "parts" (*aṃśāḥ*) mean portions (*ekadeśāḥ*), and their "variety" (*vaicitryam*) is simply their manifold forms through the state of being ornaments such as armlets (*aṅgada*) and bracelets (*keyūra*), yet this is not a different entity [from the gold]—in exactly the same way, there is a variety of parts in the arrangement of the Self when it has Māyā as its companion. Thus...
That which consists of both conscious and unconscious nature, having the form of both that and not-that, exists as the worldly and non-worldly manifoldness beginning with the world itself. || 37 ||
The waves of living beings, which are the ripples upon the net of the world, go toward the great ocean of the end of the eon, overtaken by the submarine fire of destruction. (38)

"Vināśeti" means: those rivers which are the nets of the world—those whose waves are the elements, that is, living beings themselves—go toward the great ocean of the time of universal dissolution, which is the very deluge-time and is pervaded by the submarine fire of destruction; just as rivers go into the sea.
The meaning is that the world-webs dissolve at the time of universal dissolution. || 38 ||
O King, always contemplate yourself as that great Agastya who is the one that dries up even this ocean of time, which remains yet unfilled even today.

Regarding the word "tasya" (of him): even now, even after millions of kalpas have passed, even at this very moment, meditate always upon yourself as being of greater power than Agastya—upon that Mahāgastya who is the drinker, the destroyer, of that very ocean of Time (Kālārṇava), which is the destroyer of all and remains unfilled even now. 39.
Having abandoned the notion of selfhood in this non-self— the web of visible objects such as the body and so forth—
ascend to pure being and remain hidden, dwelling in ease as you please. (40)

"Regarding 'anātmani' (in the non-self): having abandoned the notion of self—the egoistic identification with the body and so forth, which are but a web of objects—remain as you please, established in being (*sattva*), which is knowledge, hidden and with your outward form concealed. (40)
Just as a mother weeps for her son, having forgotten him while he was sleeping in the hollow of her breast,
so does this person weep for his own sake.

Regarding the verse beginning with *kuce*: Just as a certain mother, a woman who has given birth, having forgotten her son sleeping within the hollow of her breasts— unaware of his presence there and not seeing him on either side of her bed for the sake of her child—
alas, cries out for his sake, "Where has my son gone?", so too does this [person] forget the Self, though it is extremely close at hand.
For that purpose, people weep and suffer in their search for the self. || 41 ||
Not realizing that the self is ageless and immortal, one weeps at the dissolution of the body, crying out:
"Alas, I am slain! I am helpless! I am destroyed! (42)
"O Ageless One!"—this person, failing to realize that the Self is ageless and immortal, wails aloud when the body perishes: "Alas! I am destroyed! I am helpless! I am ruined! || 42 ||
Just as water appears in various forms through its own movement,
so too is the consciousness of Brahman expanded by the power of volition.

"Yathā" means: just as water (*vāri*), by virtue of its movement, is seen in various forms such as waves, foam, and bubbles, so too Brahman, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), when expanded by the power of volition (*saṃkalpa*) and increased on all sides in the form of space and the other elements, is seen in various forms. || 43 ||
Having established your mind—freed from the stain of volitional construction—within the Self, with all doubts stilled;
like the Lord-Self, remaining unmoved even amidst movement, self-abiding and happy, rule this kingdom.

"Having established," etc.: having established the mind—freed from the stain of volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*)—within the Self; being one whose volitions have subsided, even amidst movement and distraction, remain as if unmoving, as if devoid of movement, self-abiding, changeless, and blissful as the very Self of the Lord (*īśvara*);
rule and protect this kingdom. 44.
Manu said:

The All-pervasive One himself sports like a child through emanations consisting of creative pulsations; then, by means of his power of withdrawal, he withdraws [all things] and abides within himself. (45)

Regarding the word "sarge" (in creation): the all-pervading (*vibhu*) Self plays like a child with vibrations whose nature is creation. Then, by its own power of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), which is by nature the act of reabsorbing, it withdraws everything and remains within itself alone. || 45 ||
In such a way that he is bound by it, his own power arises within him;
in such a way that he is released from it, his own power arises within him. 46.

"By itself" (svayam) means: for this Self, such a power arises by itself—by which power it is bound and by which it is liberated by itself; even such a power arises for it by itself. The meaning is that both powers, which are the causes of bondage and liberation, are established by the very nature of the Self. 46.
Just as there are rays from the moon, the sun, fire, heated iron, and gems;
just as there are leaves and so forth from trees; and just as there are droplets from waterfalls. (47)

The two verses beginning with "candre" constitute a single syntactical unit. Just as the rays or flames of substances possessing luster—such as the moon, the sun, fire, heated iron, gems, and so forth—which are essentially non-different, are conceived as being different; and just as [the difference between] the leaves of trees [is conceived]; and just as [the difference between] waterfalls...
The droplets of the streams are *śīkara*s. || 47 ||

Likewise, within this expansive Brahman, the world, the intellect, and so forth are imagined; they bring suffering to those who do not know that [Brahman], and thus they remain exactly as described. 48.

In the same way, this world—consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, including the intellect of the world, the intellect of the elements, and the intellect of elemental objects—is all imagined within the expansive Brahman; being of the very nature of that Brahman, it exists through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), and for those who do not know it as such, it proceeds as a source of suffering. (48)
"O dear one, how wondrous is this illusion that deludes the entire world,
since the self does not perceive itself even though it is threaded through every limb! (49)

"Aha! This is a wondrous illusion that deludes the entire world; for this reason—because the Self, the Person, does not see, does not perceive, His own nature, even though it is woven through all limbs, pervading every part. (49)
He who remains inwardly tranquil, contemplating that the entire universe consists of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), is happy, being armored with Brahman.

Regarding the phrase "the sky of consciousness" (cidākāśa): one whose armor is Brahman—that is, for whom the contemplation of the all-pervading Brahman itself serves as the protective armor—is indeed happy, being liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 50 ||
One should meditate that everything is empty, without support, and of the nature of consciousness, through a state of being free from the sense of "I" and devoid of objective form. (51)

"I" [refers as follows]: "I-ness" (ahamartha) is the ego (ahaṃkāra). One should contemplate the entire world—devoid of that [ego], consisting of non-existence, designated as being without attributes, yet existing as a pure intention—as being without support, without foundation, of the nature of consciousness, empty, and the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 51 ||
"This is pleasant, this is not"—this is the seed of that continuous stream of suffering.
When that seed is consumed by the fire of equanimity, whence can there be any occasion for suffering? (52)
"This," namely, the conceptualization of duality—thinking "this is pleasant" and "this is unpleasant"—is the seed of that succession of suffering.
When that seed is consumed by the fire of equanimity, what opportunity is there for suffering? || 52 ||
O King, let this [doubt] be swiftly severed within yourself by your own extraordinary human effort—the weapon of non-conceptualization which distinguishes between the beautiful and the ugly. (53)

"O King! [It is said: "Let it be severed—that is, cut—internally itself by means of the weapon consisting of non-contemplation (*abhāvanā*), which distinguishes between the pleasant and the unpleasant, and by one's own excellence of human effort. || 53 ||
Having cut down the forest of karma through the cultivation of non-cultivation,
and having attained supreme attenuation, remain indeed free from sorrow, O noble one! (54)
"By non-cultivation": cultivation is the cultivation of duality and the forest of karma rooted therein;

having shaken these off with the weapon of non-cultivation, and having attained supreme attenuation—that is, the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā)—remain indeed free from sorrow. "Bho" is a term of address. 54.
Having filled the entire expanse of the world, yet transcending all divisions; with the manifestation of the appearance of mental constructs dissolved, he possesses the play of discernment.
Having attained the vibration of supreme bliss, he is for long free from affliction, his pure experience equalized through tranquility.
The embodiment of consciousness, free from the fear of worldly existence. || 55 ||

"Filled": having become one whose expansion of the world is filled— that is, whose vastness of the universe is saturated by the contemplation of the perfect Self— one who is excluded from division, devoid of the cognition of duality, in whom the manifestation of the appearance of mental constructions has dissolved, who is the play of knowledge free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), possessed of the splendor of discernment, vibrating with the attainment of supreme bliss, free from affliction, equal through tranquility, white, radiant, and pure.

Being one whose expansive manifestation is stainless and perfectly complete, become for all time one whose body is fearless consciousness—that is, one whose form is fearless and whose very nature is consciousness. 55.
Manu said:
One should first increase one's wisdom through contact with the scriptures and virtuous people;
this is said to be the first stage of yoga for a novice practitioner. (56)
Now, showing the seven stages of knowledge (*jñānabhūmikā*) in brief, he says: "The Teacher," and so forth.

The meaning is that the increase of wisdom through the study of scriptures, the company of the virtuous, and so forth, constitutes the first stage of yoga; previously, however, this was called "the desire for the auspicious" (śubhecchā). || 56 ||

The second stage is investigation (vicāraṇā), the third is the cultivation of non-attachment (asaṅgabhāvanā), and the fourth is the state of dissolution (vilāpinī), which consists in the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 57 ||

Regarding "vicāraṇā": vicāraṇā is the second [stage]. Non-attachment through contemplation (*asaṅgabhāvanā*) is the third; this very stage was previously called *tanumānasī* because it brings about the attenuation (*tanutva*) of the mind. The fourth, however, is called *vilāpinī* because its nature consists in the dissolution (*vilaya*) of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Previously, it was called *sattvāpatti* because the mind, through the dissolution of latent impressions, attains the state of pure being (*sattva*). || 57 ||
The fifth state consists of the bliss of pure consciousness;
here, one who is liberated while living remains with the appearance of being half-asleep and half-awake. (58)

"Pure" (śuddhā): Pure means free from latent impressions (nirvāsana) and consisting of pure consciousness; such is the fifth [stage]. Here, in this stage, the one who is like one half-asleep and half-awake—that is, the one who remains in that state of worldly activity—is a liberated-while-living (jīvanmukta). || 58 ||
And the sixth stage is of the nature of non-perception;
it is a state resembling deep sleep, consisting of a single mass of bliss. (59)

The phrase "asaṃvedanā" (non-perception) constitutes three quarters of a verse. The sixth [state], however, is of the nature of non-perception, a state resembling deep sleep, consisting of a single dense mass of bliss. || 59 ||
The fourth state, which is tranquilized, is indeed liberation alone;
it is equanimity, clarity, and gentleness—this is the seventh stage. (60)
And that state is completely tranquil; because it transcends the triad beginning with the waking state, it is the fourth state (turyāvasthā), which is liberation alone. || 60 ||
But the state that transcends the fourth (turyātītā), which is supreme and of the nature of Nirvāṇa—that seventh state is fully matured; it is not an object for those who still live.
This very state, which is of the nature of non-perception and wherein no objective entities exist, was previously described. "Equanimity" (*samatā*) constitutes three lines of verse.
That equanimity which is omnipresent perfection, or that gentle clarity, is the seventh stage;
it is of the nature of *nirvāṇa*, transcending the fourth state (*turyātīta*), the supreme condition, fully matured. That seventh stage is not an object for those who are still living.

The meaning is that it has the disembodied-liberated (videhamukta) as its sole object. This transparency, however, which consists in abiding in one's own true nature, was previously described as the "Fourth" (turya). || 61 ||
In this context, the first three states are established as the waking state alone;
the fourth is called dream, wherein the world indeed appears like a dream.
The first three verses constitute a single sentence. Among the seven states mentioned, the first three are established as the waking state (*jāgrat*).
The fourth is called the dreaming state (*svapna*), because therein the world exists like a dream. (62)
The fifth stage, called deep sleep (suṣupta), consists of the complete condensation of bliss alone;
the sixth stage, however, is of the nature of non-perception. (63)

The fifth, however, O Ānanda, is the state called deep sleep (suṣupta), consisting of a single mass of bliss and characterized by non-perception; the sixth is designated as the plane of the Fourth (turya);
the seventh is the supreme stage, the state beyond the Fourth (turyātīta), which cannot be grasped by mind or speech and whose nature is the self-luminous state. (64)
The seventh stage, which is beyond the mind and speech, whose nature is the state of self-luminosity, is the supreme state of the plane beyond the fourth (turyātīta). || 64 ||
If, through the power of internal withdrawal, the object of thought is no longer manifested, then he is undoubtedly liberated by that great equanimity. 65.

"Antar" means: if, by virtue of the inward withdrawal of the mind (*citta*) and for the reason of its internal cessation, the object of thought (*cetya*) has not been manifested, then by that cause—the Great Equanimity (*mahāsamatā*)—you are undoubtedly liberated indeed. || 65 ||
When a man remains with his intellect fully realized and untouched by any portion of the pleasure or pain derived from enjoyments,
delighting only in the Self— that is declared to be liberation.

Regarding the word "yat" (that): that which has been declared as liberation is this state where a person, possessing a full intellect untouched by the portions of pleasure and pain found within enjoyments—that is, within sense-objects—remains delighting in the Self;
whether he be engaged in worldly affairs or tranquil, a householder or even an ascetic.
Whether embodied or disembodied, the person whose mind is thus disposed becomes [liberated]. || 67 ||

"Regarding the term 'vyavahārī' (one engaged in worldly activity): the meaning is that a person who possesses such a mind—one endowed with the aforementioned state of mind—whether he be engaged in worldly affairs or tranquil, whether a householder or an ascetic, whether embodied or disembodied, is in every respect indeed liberated. || 67 ||
"I do not die, nor do I live; I am neither existent nor non-existent.
I am nothing but consciousness"—having realized this, one who lives does not grieve. (68)

"No, I do not die, nor do I live. The meaning is that the relinquishing and the sustaining of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are attributes of the body and so forth alone, and not attributes of the Self. "This 'I' exists, yet I am also non-existent," because I am not an object of the conventional usages of "existence" or "non-existence. Thinking, "I am nothing at all; I am consciousness distinct from the universe, whose very nature is consciousness," one does not grieve even while living. 68.
"I am untainted, ageless, free from passion, with tranquil latent impressions;
I am the partless space of consciousness"—having realized this, one does not grieve. (69)

Regarding the term "alepaka" (untainted): the untainted soul, free from passion, with its latent impressions stilled and partless, does not grieve, having realized, "I am the space of consciousness. 69–71.
Regarding the term "alepaka": it means one who is unstained.
Free from the notion of "I," pure, awakened, ageless and immortal, peaceful, and appearing as the equal of all—realizing this, one does not grieve. (70)
Realizing that whatever exists on the tips of blades of grass, in the sky, in the sun, or among men, serpents,
and gods is precisely that [same essence], one no longer grieves.
"My greatness as consciousness pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards; knowing this of that which possesses infinite manifestations, who indeed would be subject to decay? (72)
"Horizontally," etc.: Having realized that my majesty—the infinite play of whose nature is consciousness—pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards, who indeed could be diminished? (72)
An object that is pursued because it accords with one's ingrained tendencies brings happiness;
yet that very same thing which leads to happiness quickly turns into suffering through its destruction. (73)
Regarding the word "baddha": that object which is pursued and enjoyed with fixed latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and intense attachment brings happiness;
it produces pleasure. Yet, that very thing which arises for the sake of happiness quickly becomes a cause of suffering due to its destruction and ruin. || 73 ||
The inseparable connection between pleasure and pain is well known.

Whatever object is pursued, whether it be one that leaves behind subtle latent impressions (*vāsanā*) or one that is devoid of them, it does not lead to true happiness; therefore, at the time of its destruction, it does not cause suffering.

"Avinābhāva" (inseparable connection). Thus, the fact that pleasure and pain are established as being inseparably linked is well known; therefore, they both proceed and cease together. However, that object which is enjoyed with attenuated latent impressions (*vāsana*) or without latent impressions does not lead to pleasure or to intoxication; nor does it become a source of suffering, because it perishes in due course. || 74 ||
O sinless one, whatever action is performed with an intellect whose latent impressions have been exhausted does not produce a sprout again, just like a burnt seed. (75)

Regarding the word "exhausted" (kṣīṇa): that action which is performed by an intellect whose latent impressions (vāsanā) have been exhausted does not, like a burnt seed, again produce a sprout in the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth. || 75 ||
Action is performed by the multitude of instruments such as the body and the senses;
for what single agent or enjoyer could possibly exist here, my dear? (76)

Action is performed by means of the body, the sense organs, and so forth—the entire collection of instruments. In this assembly of instruments, who can be established as the agent or the enjoyer? (76)
Having completely cast off all states of being and arisen [from them],
he shines like the sun with its light, full and cool as the moon.

Regarding the phrase "bhāvanām": having completely cast off and withdrawn from all existences—that is, from all objective entities—the mental cultivation directed toward them, the person who has arisen, being fully intent upon absolute liberation (kaivalya), shines like the moon, cool and full, and like the sun, with its radiance and splendor. || 77 ||
The splendor of the cotton-wool of karma, produced upon the silk-cotton tree of the body,
once it is set in motion, is blown away by the wind of knowledge and flies off somewhere unknown.

Regarding the phrase "being performed" (*kriyamāṇā*): the body itself is the *śālmali*, a specific type of tree; the "cotton-wealth" (*tūlaśrī*) belonging to it—consisting of meritorious and non-meritorious actions (*puṇyāpuṇyakarma*) in the form of a mass of cotton—is, when produced by the wind of knowledge (*jñānānila*), that is, scattered by the great wind of the realization of reality (*tattvajñāna*), cast upward and blown away.
He goes somewhere. || 78 ||
For every other art of a living being perishes through lack of practice;
but this art of knowledge, once born within, [grows] day by day. (79)

Every single art or branch of knowledge belonging to a person perishes through lack of practice—that is, through the absence of repeated cultivation. The word "hi" indicates what is well-known; this meaning is a matter of common experience. || 79 ||
It increases by its very power, like seed sown in a fertile field. (80)
But knowledge, like rice sown in a fertile field, increases from within. || 80 ||
The one Self, whose form is the universe, vibrates within all things, like pure water in lakes and oceans;
O dear one, know that this entire world is but a single portion of existence, wherein the manifold collection of mental constructs has been stilled.
"Single. Just as water appears as one in lakes and oceans, so too does the Self, whose form is the universe, manifest as one alone within all things.

For this reason, know that the entire world—its manifold collection of diverse parts having been stilled, its abundance of mental constructs having become tranquil—is but a single reality consisting solely of the element of existence. 81.
Manu said:
As long as there is the hope for the enjoyment of sense-objects, so long does the designation "living being" belong to the self;
that hope arises from a lack of discrimination, and not from its own nature.

The phrase "as long as" constitutes two verses. As long as—that is, for as long as a time—the desire for the enjoyment of objects persists for the self, the person (*puruṣa*), for that very duration does the state of being a living being, called "living-ness" (*jīvabhāva*), exist. That desire, moreover, is produced by a lack of discrimination (*aviveka*) and not by its own nature. (82)
When hope has reached its end through the power of discernment,
then the self, having cast off the state of being a living soul (jīvatva), attains the state of Brahman, free from all affliction.

But when that hope has come to an end through the power of discernment, then the Self, being free from affliction, casts off the state of being a living soul and attains the nature of Brahman. || 83 ||
Moving for a long time from above to below and again from below to above, do not become a water-jar on the rope of anxiety for the water-wheel of saṃsāra. (84)

"From above," etc. Moving from the upper worlds below toward the lower worlds, and again from below upward, by the power of karma, do not become like a water-pot on the wheel of the *araghaṭṭa*—the water-wheel that is the nature of *saṃsāra*—upon the rope of anxiety, which is the binding cord consisting of mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*). Do not become an object of rotation like a pot on a water-wheel.
Do not be! || 84 ||
Those fools who, out of delusion, cling to this dense confusion of worldly convention— thinking "this is mine" and "I am this"— go downward, from the lower realms to even further below. (5.85)

"Regarding this [verse]: those who, out of delusion, pursue the worldly practice of dense error—thinking 'this wife, children, and so forth is mine,' 'it belongs to me,' or 'I am related to this father and so forth'—those rogues go downward, to the depths;
they repeatedly attain only a downward state. (85)
"‘This belongs to her,’ ‘this is mine,’ ‘that is his,’ ‘I am this’—those by whom such delusion has indeed been abandoned through wisdom go higher and ever higher. (86)
"Of this" means: "I am related to this father and so forth; this son and so forth is mine; this is I; I am such-and-such.
Those discerning ones by whom such delusion has been abandoned through their intellect proceed higher and higher; they go to ever-increasingly superior states. || 86 ||
Relying without delay upon your own self-luminous Self, remain filling the entire space; O King, behold the worlds! 87.

"Self-luminous" means: having relied upon your own self, which is self-luminous, and having ascertained it in its true nature without delay, remain at ease; and behold all worlds as being nothing but the Self, which fills the entire space. 87.
As soon as the nature of consciousness is thus realized as all-pervading, awakened, and undivided,
at that very moment one has crossed over saṃsāra and attained the state of the Supreme Lord.

Regarding the word *yadā*: as soon as the nature of consciousness (*cit*), which is thus extended and pervasive, is realized in its undivided state—exactly as it is—at that very moment, having crossed over saṃsāra, one attains the state of the Supreme Lord through awakening. || 88 ||
One should cultivate the conviction: "Whatever Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Varuṇa are prepared to do, I, whose body is consciousness, perform all that. (89)

"Brahmā" means: whatever Brahmā and the others are intent upon performing, such as creation and so forth, one should contemplate that "I, whose body is consciousness (cidvapuḥ), perform all of that," because of the oneness of the Self whose nature is consciousness. || 89 ||
Whatever is proclaimed in whichever philosophical systems at whatever time, my dear, all of that is indeed true; for the play of consciousness is unrestrained. (90)

"In which [systems]" means: in whichever philosophical systems, whether Vedic or non-Vedic, whatever doctrine is proclaimed at whatever time, all that is indeed true; for this reason, the play of consciousness (*cidvilāsa*) is unrestrained and unimpeded. (90)
By what can that supreme bliss be compared, which belongs to one who has become pure consciousness alone, who has crossed over death, and who is free from the mind? (91)

"Consciousness (cit)"—for one who has attained the state of pure consciousness, and for that very reason has crossed over death and transcended saṃsāra, there arises a bliss of the mindless one (acetasaḥ), that is, of one whose [ordinary] mind has vanished. With what other bliss could this bliss be compared?
For there exists no bliss equal to the bliss of Brahman. || 91 ||

Meditate upon the world as neither non-empty nor empty, neither of the nature of the insentient nor consisting of consciousness, neither of the nature of the Self nor of another nature; having attained this true nature, primordial matter (prakṛti) comes to rest. || 92 ||

The phrase "nor even" constitutes three quarters of a verse. The world (*bhuvana*)—the universe—is not the creator; nor is it empty, nor is it non-empty, because there is no other entity apart from the Self (*ātman*). Thus, O Bhava, contemplate the world as being thus indefinable. Having attained such an indefinable form, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is ignorance (*avidyā*) manifesting in the form of the world and so forth, comes to rest.
There is no place called liberation, nor time, nor any other state;
this [bondage] dissolves through the destruction of the delusion of egoism. Nature, which is known by the name "mental cultivation" (bhāvanā), is itself liberation; this indeed is it.

"No" constitutes three half-verses as a single sentence. There is no place called liberation—that is, no place denoted by the word "liberation"—nor is there any time called liberation, nor is there any other state or condition called liberation. Rather, this very nature, consisting of latent impressions known as mental cultivation (bhāvanā) and characterized by ignorance, dissolves through the destruction of delusion in the form of egoism; this indeed [is liberation].
That liberation would indeed be the dissolution into primordial nature (prakṛti). || 93 ||
With the restlessness of investigating the meaning of the scriptures stilled, with the curiosity for poetry and its various aesthetic sentiments ceased,
and with the turbulence of all conceptual constructions entirely dispelled, he remains at ease, equanimous, and established in his eternal nature. (94)

"Tranquil" (praśānta): he whose restlessness, consisting of the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures, has been stilled; he whose curiosity regarding the subject matter of poetry, which possesses manifold aesthetic flavors (rasas), has ceased; he from whom all delusive errors of conceptual construction (vikalpa-vibhrama) have been entirely dispelled—such a person, equanimous and established in sameness, remains in eternal bliss. || 94 ||
Manu said:
Clothed in whatever [is available], fed by whatever [is available], and sleeping wherever [he may be], he shines like a sovereign emperor. 95.
"By what": covered—that is, provided with clothing—by whatever不定 (aniyata) means such as rags, bark garments, woolen blankets, or patched cloths;
fed—that is, nourished—by whatever不定 (aniyata) edible substance; and sleeping anywhere on the bare ground or on a couch:
he who is thus indifferent to external objects shines like a knower of Brahman, like a sovereign emperor (samrāṭ), the lord of universal sovereignty.
Abandoned by the constraints of the scriptures concerning caste, duty, and the conduct of the stages of life,
he emerges from the snare of the world like a lion from its cage.

Regarding the term *varṇeti*: by the constraint of the scriptures concerning the duties of the castes (*varṇa*) and the conduct of the stages of life (*āśrama*), the "castes" are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth;

the "stages of life" are studenthood (*brahmacarya*) and so forth. A person who is "abandoned"—meaning devoid of the conceit of being the body and so on—by that constraint, which consists of the regulations and boundaries of the scriptures that teach the duties of the castes and the conduct of the stages of life.
Like a lion emerging from its den, he emerges from the snare of the world. || 96 ||
Transcending the range of speech and abandoned by any likeness to worldly objects, he attained an indescribable splendor, like the expanse of the sky in autumn.

The two verses beginning with "vācām" form a single syntactical unit. A man who has abandoned the desire for sense-objects—that is, one who is utterly dispassionate—transcends the domain of speech; having transcended the sphere of words, he attains an indescribable, unconditioned splendor, like the expanse of the sky in autumn. || 97 ||
Profound and serene like a great lake in the mountains,
undisturbed by the essence of supreme bliss, he rejoices in himself by means of his own self. (98)

Standing on the mountain like a great mountain, he is both deep and serene; undisturbed by the flavor of supreme bliss and immovable in his tasting of that supreme bliss, he delights within his own self, by means of his own self, in his own true nature. || 98 ||
Renouncing the fruits of all actions, eternally contented, and without dependence, he is stained neither by merit nor by sin, nor by anything else. (99)
"By nothing else": he is not smeared by anything other than merit and demerit; nor is he smeared by their maturation in the form of birth, lifespan, and experience. || 99 ||
Just as a crystal is not stained by a reflection, so the knower of reality is not stained within by the fruit of action. (100)

Regarding the term "crystal": just as a crystal gem does not undergo coloring—that is, the transfer of its color—by a reflected substance such as blue or yellow, so too the knower of that [reality], the knower of Brahman, does not undergo coloring by the fruit of action through the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). || 100 ||
Dwelling amidst the multitude of people, he experiences neither weariness nor joy through the wounding or honoring of his body, as if these were occurring in a reflected image.

"Living" (viharann iti): among the multitude of people— where "people" refers to crowds consisting of various classes of beings— one who knows [the truth] dwells within that assembly free from the conceit of duality, as if the cutting and piercing of the body and its worship with offerings such as perfumes and flowers were merely the cutting and worship occurring within a reflection, namely, within the reflection of one's own body.
One knows neither weariness nor refreshment. || 1 ||
He is beyond praise and free from transformation, devoid of both the worshiper and the object of worship;
yet he is both united with and separated from all methods of conduct and discipline.

"Beyond praise" (niḥstotra): The man who knows that is beyond praise, having emerged from praise concerning both his own domain and the domain of others, and being changeless, he is devoid of the worshiper and the object of worship, because there is no object of worship distinct from himself.
He exists sometimes joined with and sometimes separated from all modes of conduct and methods. || 2 ||
Therefore, the world does not tremble before him, nor does he tremble before the world; he is neither abandoned by nor joined to passion, hatred, fear, and joy. (3)

"Therefore" means: because he bestows fearlessness upon all beings, the world does not tremble before him who knows that [Self]. And he does not tremble before the world, because there is no entity distinct from himself that could be a cause of fear. He is sometimes abandoned by passion and the like, and sometimes joined with them. || 3 ||
A person of great magnanimity does not ascend to the status of an object of cognition for anyone;
yet one of pure intention is made an object of cognition even by a child. (4)

"Regarding the term *prameya* (the object of knowledge): one who knows that [reality], because of his noble disposition (*mahāśayatva*), does not ascend to the status of being an object of knowledge—that is, an object of valid cognition—for any lord whatsoever.

The meaning is that he is sometimes difficult to attain even for the great. On the other hand, this knower of reality, because of his lack of arrogance (*adurāśayatva*), is sometimes made an object of knowledge even by a child. The meaning is that he is sometimes easily accessible even to a child. || 4 || 5 || 6 || 7 || 8 ||
O King, whether he casts off his body at a sacred ford or in the house of a dog-cooker, or at any time whatsoever, or even at this very moment— || 5 ||
At the time of the perfection of knowledge, he is liberated and free from latent desires;
for the delusion of "I" leads to bondage, while liberation is the destruction of that [delusion] through knowledge.
He who is endowed with this [perfection] is always worthy of worship by men;
he is to be honored, he is to be praised, and he is to be saluted with diligent effort.
He is to be beheld and saluted by one who desires the manifestation of spiritual power.
That supreme state of purity is not attained through sacrifices, sacred fords, austerities, or gifts;
rather, it is attained through devotion by the virtuous who know the Self and whose worldly afflictions have been exhausted.
"No, it is not so. For those who know the Self and whose afflictions of worldly existence have been exhausted, the supreme state is attained through devotion and service;
yet that pure, supreme state is not attained even by sacrifices, pilgrimages, austerities, or gifts.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Manu went to his brahminical home;
Ikṣvāku, too, remained firm, holding fast to that vision.
Having spoken thus, that Blessed One [departed] for the abode of Brahmā, the world of Brahmā. 110.
Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Narrative of Ikṣvāku," in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīyogavāsiṣṭhasāra*.
Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Narrative of Ikṣvāku," in the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa.
The Fourteenth Canto. Rāma said:
This being so, O Blessed One, best among the knowers of the Self, what unprecedented excellence does one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) possess according to the true doctrine? (1)

Previously, it was shown that even a reality difficult to understand through one's own inquiry becomes easily understood through the instruction of a guru. Now, in order to demonstrate that for one who has rested in the reality of Buddhahood there is generally no worldly activity, the story of the sage and the hunter is related—beginning with "In this way. Such being the case for the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*):

It has been stated previously that extraordinary powers such as traveling through the sky do not exist. This being the case, what unprecedented excellence belongs to this one of right-mindedness who is liberated while living? || 1 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
In some particular limb of the knower, there arises an excellence of intellect;
ever-satisfied and tranquil in soul, he abides in the Self alone.
"Of the knower" (jñasya): the intellect of the knower arises with excellence toward some specific reality that is entirely distinct from the universe;
and being satisfied by that alone, with a tranquil self, he abides in the Self itself and desires nothing else. || 2 ||

By those perfected in mantra, perfected through austerity, and perfected in tantra, feats such as traveling through the sky have been performed in great numbers; what novelty could there be in that? (3)

He objects: "What novelty could there be therein, since traveling through the sky and so forth is common to birds and the like; or what extraordinary excellence could there be in the cessation of the state of being a living being (jīva)? This is the meaning. || 3 ||

Even powers such as *aṇimā* have been attained in great abundance by those very same [yogis], because they were accomplished through effort; they are not attained by one who perceives the Self through other means.

Even the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā* has been attained in abundance only by those who have achieved perfection through mantras and the like; it has not been attained by another who perceives the Self. Why? Because it is accomplished with great effort by those very ones perfected through mantras and so forth, whereas the perceiver of the Self has no need for *aṇimā* and the rest.
Because it has not been established through effort. || 4 ||
This alone is his distinction; he is not equal to those of deluded intellect, for his mind is stainless and free from passion due to the relinquishment of attachment to everything.

"This very [is his distinction]" means that because this wise one has abandoned attachment toward all external objects, his mind is everywhere free from passion and pure; this indeed is his specific distinction, which is not common to those of deluded intellect. || 5 ||
This indeed is the very mark of one who has realized that which is beyond marks, who is stilled from the long wandering of worldly existence and has attained peace:
that for such a knower, lust, anger, despair, delusion, greed, and misfortune daily and skillfully diminish.
He states that very distinction: "to this extent. Of the one who is without marks (*aliṅga*), meaning devoid of the marks of caste, stage of life, and so forth;

who is tranquilized from the long-lasting delusion of transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*), meaning he for whom the long-lasting delusion in the form of *saṃsṛti* has been stilled; and therefore, being tranquilized, free from anxiety—that knower [is beyond] the afflictions of passion, anger, despair, delusion, greed, and calamity.

The meaning is that the sign, or rather the distinguishing characteristic, is simply this: the daily, skillful, and unwavering attenuation—that is, the destruction—of calamities caused by desire, anger, and so forth. || 6 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as a Brahmin, through evil desire, gradually abandons his own being and accepts the state of a Śūdra, so too does the Lord assume the state of a living soul.

Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): For instance, a certain Brahmin, disregarding and failing to consider the excellence of his own being (*sattva*) by virtue of his birth and other qualities, accepts the status of a Śūdra through wicked conduct— such as illicit union with a Śūdra woman extending even to the procreation of a son— due to evil intent (*durīhayā*).

And so Manu says: "By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a downward state; by procreating a son upon her, he falls away from Brāhmaṇahood. Likewise, even the Lord, through false desire (*durīhā*), His own volition (*svasaṃkalpa*), or His own ignorance (*svāvidyā*), accepts the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*). [As it is said: "Entering with this living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me manifest names and forms."
Because of the scriptural statement. || 7 ||
Indeed, at the time of re-absorption, beings of two kinds alone manifest; born from the vibration of primordial consciousness, they are truly without cause.

The two and a half verses beginning with "bhūtāni" constitute a single syntactical unit. There are indeed two kinds of beings (*bhūtāni*): living creatures in the form of the mobile and the immobile, which manifest and appear at every creation. Among them, those beings that are born from the primordial vibration of consciousness—where "vibration" (*spanda*) means throbbing or the desire to create—are without cause, being produced solely from the primordial vibration of consciousness.
Because there is an absence of karma and other causes of birth, and because the self, being changeless, is not a cause [of birth]. || 8 ||
Having emerged from the Lord,
O dear one, beings undergo further successive births solely through their own performed actions;
such is this relationship of cause and effect arising from births and deeds.

Having emerged from the Lord, living beings experience successive births again and again solely through their own performed actions. This relationship of cause and effect between birth and action is of such a nature as described:
first, birth is the effect caused by action in the form of good or evil deeds; subsequently, action is the effect of birth.
The meaning is that it is the cause of name-and-form. || 9 ||
p.
806) All living beings initially approach their supreme state without cause;
subsequently, their own past actions become the cause of their pleasure and pain. (10)
He clarifies this very point with the three-and-a-half-line statement beginning with "without cause."

The mention of "pleasure and pain" is illustrative; for birth and lifespan as well, which take various forms, one's own actions alone are the cause. However, the cause of actions is volition (saṃkalpa), which arises from ignorance of the self—that is, from ignorance of the true nature of the self. || 10 ||
Volition, which arises from ignorance of the Self, is the cause of action.
For the state of conceptualization is the cause of bondage; abandon that. Liberation, however, is the absence of conceptualization; practice that with your intellect.
Be vigilant in the encounter between the grasped and the grasper,
gradually abandoning the states of conceptual construction at all times.

Regarding the phrase "be attentive": the word *ca* (and) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). For this reason, gradually abandoning the states of your own mental constructs through the process of practice, remain constantly attentive—that is, uninterrupted—in the encounter between the grasped and the grasper, which is the relationship between the seen and the seeing. || 13 ||
Do not become the nature of the grasped object, and do not become the nature of the grasper. Having abandoned all mental constructions, become absorbed in that which remains. 14.

He explains the manner of focused attention itself with the words "mā bhava" (do not become). Do not become one whose nature is the object of perception—that is, one who identifies with the state of being the visible world. Do not become one whose nature is the perceiver—that is, one who identifies with the state of being the seer. What then? Having abandoned all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding objects such as the action and the agent, that which remains is the Reality.
Become absorbed in that which is distinct from karma and the like.
O sinless one, whatever object the group of senses constantly falls upon,
there it is bound by attachment and liberated by detachment.

Regarding the word *ajasram*: this collection of sense-faculties (*akṣagaṇa*), this aggregate of the senses, whatever object it constantly (*ajasram*) falls upon—that is, moves toward—if it falls there with attachment (*rāga*), then it is bound; if it falls there with detachment (*virāga*), then it is liberated. || 15 ||
Whatever is pleasing to the mind, by that you are bound to worldly existence; when nothing is pleasing to the mind, then you are liberated from worldly existence. (16)
He says this very thing with the words "that which" (yad). || 16 ||
Therefore, O Rāma, let nothing from this collection of objects—whether stationary or moving, from a blade of grass up to the gods—be pleasing to you. (17)
"Therefore" means "for you. 17 || 18 || 19 || 20 ||
When you feel aversion toward what you eat, what you do, or what you abandon, you are neither the doer nor the enjoyer; therein your mind is liberated and you are at peace.
The virtuous do not grieve for the past, nor do they worry about the future;
O sinless one, they always accept the present as it arrives in its proper sequence.
The snares of craving, delusion, pride, and the like are knotted within the mind;
the mind itself must be severed by the mind alone by one who possesses discernment. (20)
With the extremely sharp sword of discernment, as if with iron against iron, cut the mind with the mind itself for the sake of pacifying the delusions of saṃsāra. (21)
"By means of discernment" (vivekena): the meaning is that one should cut through the defiled mind with that mind which has become exceedingly sharp through discernment.
Those skilled in cleansing wash away impurity by means of impurity itself;
they ward off blood with blood, and poison with an antidote.
The individual soul has three forms: the gross, the subtle, and the supreme.
Among these, worship that which is its supreme form and abandon the other two.
This body, composed of hands and feet, which moves about for the sake of enjoyment—this gross form of the individual soul (jīva) exists here for the purpose of experience. (24)

O Rāma, know that the mind— which exists as long as saṃsāra lasts and which takes on forms consisting of one's own volitions— is the subtle, transportive body (*ativāhika*) of the individual soul (*jīva*). (25)

"His own" means that the mind itself is the *ātivāhika* (conveying) body of this living being; the meaning is that it is a subtle form capable of traveling to and returning from other worlds. || 25 || 26 ||
Know that which is without beginning or end, the truth, pure consciousness, and free from conceptual construction— that is the supreme form of the individual soul, the first of the third [set].
This is the pure state of the Fourth; take your firm stand here.
Having completely abandoned the first two states, do not let your mind dwell upon them as the Self.
"Etat" (this) refers to the fourth state, which is the fourth in relation to the gross, subtle, and causal bodies. || 27 ||
Rāma said:

O leader of sages, having distinguished it, please explain specifically the fourth state (turya), which remains present throughout the three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, yet is unperceived in all of them.

"Regarding the word 'jāgrat' (waking): the meaning is, 'Please explain the fourth state (turya), which, though situated and present within the three states beginning with waking, remains unperceived by waking and the others, is the sole remainder, and is free from vibration. || 28 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having abandoned both the sense of "I" and the sense of "not-I," as well as existence and non-existence,
that which remains unattached, translucent, and established— that is called the Fourth (turya).

Regarding "I": that consciousness which, having abandoned the states of "I-ness" and "not-I-ness"—that is, the conceit of "I am" and "I am not"—as well as the conceit of existence and non-existence—remains unattached and pure, such consciousness is called the Fourth (turya). || 29 ||
That state which is transparent, equanimous, and peaceful— the established condition of one liberated while living—
is called the reckoning of the fourth (turya) state in worldly discourse.

Furthermore, that state which is transparent, stainless, and characterized by equanimity and tranquility—the state of being a witness during the worldly activity of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), which is a state of indifference—that is the fourth mode of consciousness; it is called the state of the Fourth (turya). || 30 ||
This is neither waking nor dreaming, because of the impossibility of conceptual constructions;
nor is it the state of deep sleep, because of the absence [of consciousness] and the persistence of insentience. (31)
"It is not this": this fourth state (turyapada) is neither waking nor dreaming, because of the absence of mental constructs (saṃkalpa);
it is also not the state of deep sleep (suṣupta), because of the absence of remaining in a state of insentience (jaḍatā). || 31 ||
For those who are peaceful and perfectly awakened, this world exists as it truly is;
they say that for the unawakened, what is dissolved is the fourth state (turya), while for them it remains fixed and stable.

Regarding the term "peaceful" (śānta): for those who are perfectly awakened, this world, as it truly exists, is dissolved in Brahman; they call that the Fourth State (turya). For the unawakened, however, it remains fixed [as the world]. 32.
When the subtle trace of egoism is abandoned and equanimity arises,
and when the mind is rendered dissolved, the fourth state (turya) manifests.
"I" [is used] in reference to that which is perishable, having the nature of disintegration. 33–34.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, O wise one, listen to this illustration being told by me, so that even though you are already awakened, you may attain further enlightenment. (34)
Seeing a certain sage established in great silence within a certain expanse of the forest, the hunter asked him about this wonder.
"In what? [The answer is: "Established in great silence. Great silence (mahāmauna) means the non-contemplation of the phenomenal world of duality. 35–36.
Having arrived later, he saw a deer wounded by an arrow and fleeing;
the sage replied to him, "O King, this deer has come here pierced by my arrow. Where has the deer gone? (36)
O virtuous one, we are forest-dwelling sages of equal character;
we possess no egoism regarding those worldly activities for which one might be fit. (37)

They are equal-minded (*samaśīlāḥ*). They are called "equal-minded" because they practice and maintain the same *brahman* with equal discipline; the verbal root for *śīla* is *śīl*, meaning "to concentrate" or "to practice. || 37 || 38 ||
"O friend, the mind performs all the functions of the senses here;
that [mind] of mine, consisting of egoism, has surely long since dissolved away. (38)
I do not perceive any states whatsoever known as waking, dreaming, or deep sleep;
I abide solely in the fourth state (turya), wherein no object of perception exists.
"Jāgrat" (waking) refers to the previously mentioned fourth state (*turya*), the state of *turya*. 39–40.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these words of the chief of sages, O Raghava,
the hunter, not understanding their meaning, departed in his desired direction.

Therefore I say, O mighty-armed one: there is no state other than the fourth (turya). For the mind free from conceptual construction is indeed the fourth; that alone exists here, and nothing else. 41.

"Thus" means: there is no state other than the Fourth (*turya*)—that is, distinct from the Fourth—in reality, because it is merely imagined. For, as a matter of fact, the Fourth is nothing but non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpa-cit*). 41.
The three states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are indeed the forms of the mind; here, the mind exists with a threefold nature—tranquil, turbulent, and deluded. (42)

Regarding the word "jāgrat" (waking): for this reason—because the triad known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep is merely a form or state of the mind and not of the Self—the mind remains in the states of waking and so forth as having a threefold nature; that is, its essence consists of these three aspects: the terrible, the peaceful, and the deluded. || 42 ||
The mind that consists of wakefulness is terrible; when it remains in the state of dreaming, it is peaceful;
when situated in the state of deep sleep, it is deluded; and when devoid of these three, it becomes dead. (43)

He explains this very point: the mind consisting of the waking state (*jāgranmaya*) is terrible (*ghora*) due to the abundance of the agitation of pleasure and pain; the mind consisting of the dream state (*svapnamaya*) is peaceful (*śānta*) because of the absence of such agitation; and the mind situated in the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptabhāvastha*) is deluded (*mūḍha*) because it is preponderant in inertia (*jāḍya*). [These are] the three.
But the mind devoid of the forms of tranquility and so forth would be dead, because of its lack of transformation. || 43 ||
That mind which is dead and that single sentient being who remains the same—
indeed, all yogins strive with effort to bring about that very state. (44)

"And that which... || And that mind which has been described as "dead," that very same mind remains as a single, equalized *sattva*, in the form of the quality of *sattva*. Therefore, all yogis strive with effort to bring about that very state of mind. || 44 ||
Abide as the stainless Self in the fourth state (turya), which is free from the play of all mental constructs;
therein always remain those great sages who are liberated, perfectly peaceful, and forever freed from duality.
"Samasta" means: in which, that is, in the fourth state (turya-pada). || 45 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Sage and the Hunter," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-sāra.
Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Sage and the Hunter," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa.
Fifteenth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
The final conclusion of the spiritual scriptures is indeed the negation of everything:
here there is no ignorance, nor is there illusion; this is the supreme Brahman, which is quiescent. (1)

It has been shown previously that for one who has attained rest, there is no burden of external worldly activity. Now, since this entire science of knowledge (*jñāna-śāstra*) has its essence in the stages of knowledge (*jñāna-bhūmikā*), this final narrative is commenced in order to describe its nature in detail—beginning with the words "The Siddhānta. This subsequent [state] is peaceful; it is indeed Brahman itself.
Ignorance, illusion, and their effects do not exist; this negation of the entire phenomenal world is indeed the established doctrine of the spiritual sciences. || 1 ||
In the tranquil space of consciousness alone, which is self-abiding, equanimous in nature, and inlaid with all powers—that which is designated by the name "Brahman"—[all things reside]. (2)

The two verses beginning with "śānta" constitute a single statement. Regarding Brahman, which is characterized by tranquility and other such qualities, some disputants—having designated it with various names—determine it to be the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) itself; some resolve it to be emptiness (*śūnyatva*); some to be mere consciousness (*vijñānamātratā*); and others again to be the nature of the Lord (*īśvararūpatva*). Having thus determined it, they dispute with one another. (2–3)
Having reached a definitive conclusion, some [assert] emptiness, some the state of mere consciousness, and some the nature of God; thus they dispute with one another. (3)
Having renounced everything, O sinless one, you have become a great silent sage—
possessing liberation, free from mental fabrication, with the mind exhausted and the intellect profoundly stilled.

"All this": You, having abandoned every dispute, being free from the mind (nirmanana), free from conceptualization and mental construction (niḥsaṃkalpavikalpa), with the mind exhausted (kṣīṇacitta), with the mind devoid of latent impressions (nirvāsanacitta), and with the intellect perfectly tranquil (praśāntadhī), become a great silent sage (mahāmaunī); not pursuing external objects, you shall be possessed of Nirvāṇa and liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 4 ||
With your mind stilled within yourself alone, like one who is mute, blind, and deaf,
remain forever inward-turned, with your intellect fulfilled within.

Regarding "in the self": having become eternally inward-turned, remain within the self alone with a tranquil soul and a contented mind, like one who is mute, blind, and deaf; because the mind is turned inward, its external sensory activities are rendered fruitless, and you should abide with an intellect filled within. || 5 ||
O Rāghava, while remaining awake, abide in the state of deep sleep and perform your actions;
internally renouncing everything, act externally according to circumstances as they arise.

"While awake" means: while indeed awake, while the external senses are active, remain as one established in deep sleep with an unmodified mind and perform your actions. He clarifies this very point: "internally renouncing everything"—having abandoned all things such as attachment and aversion—perform action externally just as it comes, just as it is obtained. 6.
The existence of the mind is supreme suffering; the non-existence of the mind is supreme happiness.
The mind within is of the nature of pure consciousness alone; bring it to dissolution through the absence of sensation. (7)

Regarding "citta": since the existence and non-existence of the mind alone constitute the ultimate suffering and happiness, therefore, being of the singular nature of consciousness and having the singular essence of consciousness, bring the mind to its dissolution by means of non-perception—that is, by not connecting with external objects. 7.
Having seen what is pleasant or unpleasant, one should remain as equanimous as a stone;
by this much effort of the self, cyclic existence is conquered. (8)
"Having seen" means: having seen what is pleasant or unpleasant, one should remain like a stone—equanimous and free from modification.
By this much effort alone, the cycle of worldly existence is conquered. || 8 ||
There is no sensation that is pleasant, unpleasant, or even neutral;
by this much effort of the self, the infinite end of suffering is attained.

"Regarding 'to be experienced'": this triad—namely, "this is pleasure," "this is pain," and "this is the neutral state consisting of experience"—is neither to be experienced nor to be mentally constructed. By means of this much self-effort, the infinite end of suffering—that is, the absolute cessation of suffering—is attained. || 9 ||
Like the full orb of the moon within [the sky], the knower of that reality attains bliss consisting of the glorious elixir;
having realized the essence of all things in the three worlds, he does not merely act, but acts as one who has attained the supreme state. 10.

Regarding the word *āpīna*: like the full moon within its orb, the knower of That (the Self), being internally filled with the glorious elixir (*rasāyana*)—that is, consisting of nectar—attains happiness, which is the bliss of one's own true nature. Having realized the essence of all things in the three worlds, that knower, having attained the Supreme, the Supreme Self, does not truly perform actions even while performing them; he does not act at all.
Because of the absence of conceit. || 10 || 11 ||
Rāma said:
How is the practice of the seven stages of yoga performed? And what are the signs for the yogi regarding each stage? (11)
Vasiṣṭha said:
The person is of two kinds: one who is engaged in worldly activity and one who has withdrawn from it.
Listen now to the characteristics of these two, who are oriented toward heaven and liberation respectively. (12)

Regarding the term "pravṛtta" (engaged in worldly activity): one who is oriented toward heaven through the performance of dharma with desire is *pravṛtta*; one who is oriented toward liberation (*apavarga*) through the performance of dharma without desire is *nivṛtta*. || 12 ||
"What is that so-called nirvāṇa? Better for me is cyclic existence itself"—having thus resolved, he who acts is described as one who has entered into worldly activity (*pravṛtta*). (13)

"How much? [means: that which is called *nirvāṇa* is indeed very little, because there is no other object to be enjoyed. "Saṃsāra alone is better for me" [is said] because the objects of enjoyment, the pleasures of the senses, are infinite. Having thus resolved, the person who performs actions that serve as the cause for worldly engagement is described as one who has entered into activity (*pravṛtta*). || 13 ||
Like the entry of a tortoise's neck into the hole of a yoke amidst the four oceans, at the end of many births, a man of discernment is born. 14.

It wavers. Just as when a tortoise’s neck enters the opening situated between the two shores of a pair of swaying oceans—acting as the means for entry—it retreats backward after emerging forward, and likewise finds no rest whatsoever while remaining in that opening; so too [is this].
For the individual soul (*jīva*) who has abandoned the previous ocean of existence and is about to enter another state of being, there is no rest anywhere.
To explain: in the previous birth, there was a succession of sufferings such as old age and death; in the future [birth], a continuity of sufferings such as childhood and so forth;
and in the intervening state, there is great suffering in the body of torment and in the dwelling within the womb. Thus, these [states] consist of nothing but suffering.
At the end of many births, a person becomes discerning due to the ripening of some merit. || 14 ||
Alas, the condition of cyclic existence is indeed essence-less; enough for me with it! What is the use of stale actions, when the day is spent on those very things? (15)
He reflects: "Alas, the conditions of saṃsāra are essence-less and devoid of substance! Enough for me of these conditions of saṃsāra.
What fruit is there, what result, in these stale and exhausted karmas? Why is the entire day spent with those very same stale karmas? (15)
"What could supreme rest be, if it were devoid of the excellence of activity?"— one who possesses such certainty within is known as "the one who has desisted" (nivṛtta). || 16 ||

Regarding the phrase "excess of action": that seeker of liberation who possesses the internal conviction, "What could be the supreme, most excellent rest, free from the excess of action and devoid of the gradations of the fruits of karma?"—he is known as "nivṛtta" (one who has turned away).
"How can I, having become free from passion, cross the ocean of saṃsāra?
When the one of noble intellect is thus intent on such reflection, (17)
"How so?"—this is a statement consisting of six verses. *Virāga* means dispassion (*vairāgya*). || 17 ||
Day by day he attains detachment within his latent impressions;
he proceeds toward noble actions and rejoices daily.

Day by day, or every single day, he attains detachment from latent impressions (*vāsanā*). He proceeds toward—that is, he exerts himself to perform—those [impressions] that are noble in form and praiseworthy.
The *ātmanepada* ending is used here according to the rule: "The root *kram* takes the *ātmanepada* when meaning 'to proceed,' 'to create,' or 'to extend'. (Pāṇini 1.3.41) || 18 ||
He constantly feels hesitation regarding vulgar and dull activities;
he does not utter words that strike at the vital points [of others] and cultivates meritorious deeds. (19)

Regarding the phrase "in village [matters]": the meaning is that he hesitates—that is, he is possessed by doubt—regarding village-born activities of the dull-witted, such as agriculture and the like. He does not expose or reveal the vital secrets (*marmāṇi*) of others, because of the prohibition: "One should not touch anyone on their vital spot. || 19 ||
He practices gentle deeds that cause no agitation to others;
he constantly fears evil and does not look toward worldly enjoyment. || 20 ||
Actions that cause no agitation to others, which grant fearlessness to others, are gentle actions; they are non-violent actions. || 20 ||
When he addresses words that are imbued with affection and intimacy, charming, appropriate, and suited to the place and time,
then he has reached the first stage. || 21 ||
"Filled with affection and intimacy": "affection" (sneha) is love, while "intimacy" (praṇaya) is trust; [the words] are filled with these. || 21 ||
In thought, deed, and speech, he serves virtuous people;
having brought them from wherever they may be, he studies the treatises on knowledge. (22)
