The syntactical connection is as follows: by serving and attending upon virtuous and wise persons with both mind and speech, one who acts in this manner becomes a person of right-mindedness (sanmati) and attains the first stage, which consists of the "desire for the auspicious" (śubhecchā). || 22 ||

He who possesses such discernment regarding the crossing over of saṃsāra is said to be "one who has attained the stages" (bhūmikāvān); the rest, however, are remembered as merely "noble ones" (ārya). || 23 ||

"Thus. Regarding the crossing over of saṃsāra, he who possesses such inquiry in the manner previously described is said to be "one who has attained the stages" (bhūmikāvān), meaning he has reached the first stage. However, the rest are remembered as "Noble Ones" (ārya) who abide on the true path. || 23 ||
Having reached another stage of yoga named *vicāra*,
he relies upon the most eminent scholars who are renowned for their primary exegesis of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, virtuous conduct, the retention of sacred formulas, meditation, and ritual action. (24)

The sentence reflects upon these five verses: he takes refuge in those eminent scholars who are renowned for their primary and praiseworthy exposition— that is, through their commentary on the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātma-śāstra*)— and who are devoted to the performance and contemplation of the duties prescribed by the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the conduct of the virtuous, as well as to the Vedas and other authorities themselves.

In the reading "dhyānakarmaṇām," the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (nirdhāraṇa). The meaning is that he takes refuge in those who are the most excellent among those devoted to the Vedas and so forth—namely, the learned scholars. || 24 ||

One who knows the classification of categories and has mastered what is to be heard understands the determination of what ought and ought not to be done, just as a master of the house knows his own home.

One who knows the classification of categories, who knows the distinction between eternal and non-eternal entities, who has mastered what is to be heard, and who has studied the spiritual scriptures— a householder— truly understands the determination of what ought and ought not to be done, just as one knows the interior of a house.
He casts off his excessive intoxication, pride, envy, hypocrisy, and delusion,
as well as even a slight outward desire for gain, just as a snake sheds its skin.

He casts off, like the slough of a snake, even a slight outward longing for objects that has manifested itself, as well as the excessive abundance of pride, conceit, envy, hypocrisy, and delusion—those very qualities beginning with pride—that have come to exceed all others. || 26 ||
One whose mind is thus disposed, through service to the teacher and to virtuous persons regarding the scripture,
attains the secret in its entirety and exactly as it is. (27)

One whose mind is thus disposed—whose intellect has been permeated by the aforementioned virtuous impressions (sadvāsanā)—having reached the second stage through service to the guru and the virtuous and through spiritual practice, correctly and thoroughly desires to understand the secret reality (tattva) as it is taught in the scriptures. || 27 ||
Then that beloved one falls upon the third stage of yoga, named "Non-attachment," as if onto a stainless bed of flowers. (28)

"Non-attachment" (*asaṃsaṅga*) refers to a group of five verses. That which was previously called the "third body" by the term *tanu-mānasā* (the one with a subtle mind) is precisely its "measure" (*māna*). Because of its subtlety, there is an absence of attachment toward sense objects; thus, it has acquired the designation "non-attachment. Consequently, there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
Having established a steady mind upon the meaning of the words of the scripture as they truly are,
[he did so] through a sequence of discourses on the supreme self, resting in the hermitages of ascetics.

Having established a firm and unwavering understanding, exactly as it is, regarding the meaning of the sentences in the scriptures whose subject matter is the inner self— namely, the non-duality of the Self—
he spent his time in the hermitages of ascetics, resting with those devoted to the inner self through discourses on the nature of the inner self. || 29 ||
Likewise, by censuring cyclic existence and through the sequence of discourses on dispassion,
he sits upon a bed and seat of stone and wears away his extended lifespan.
By means of censures on saṃsāra and discourses on dispassion, he passes away and exhausts his full lifespan while remaining seated upon a stone bed or wherever else he may sit. || 30 ||
By wandering through forests and groves, which are graced by the tranquility of the mind,
the wise man passes his time in the bliss of unattached happiness.
In the state of emergence (*vyutthānadaśā*), through wandering in forests and groves, and again in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which is graced by the tranquility of the mind,

there is a bliss consisting of the happiness of non-attachment that is distinct from the happiness of attachment to sound and other objects; [the term refers to] those for whom the happiness of attachment does not exist, or rather, it refers to the bliss of one's own essential nature (*svarūpasukha*) belonging to those who delight in the Self (*ātmārāma*).
And by means of that, he passes the time, the duration of his life. || 31 ||
Through the study of excellent scriptures and the performance of meritorious deeds,
this vision of reality becomes clear for a living being exactly as it is. (32)
This is the "vision of reality" (vastudṛṣṭi); the meaning is that it is the stage of knowledge within the level called "non-attachment" (asaṃsaṅga). || 32 ||
Having attained the third stage, the Buddha himself experiences a twofold non-attachment; hear now this distinction regarding it. || 33 ||

In that very context, for the purpose of defining its internal subdivisions, he says: "The third. Having attained the third stage (*bhūmikā*), the awakened one, the man of knowledge (*jñānī*), experiences two kinds of non-attachment (*asaṃsaṅga*): the common and the preeminent. (33)
This non-attachment is twofold: general and supreme.
"I am neither the enjoyer nor the doer; I am neither the afflicted nor the afflictor. (34)
No; I am not the agent because of being devoid of action; nor am I the enjoyer because of being eternally satisfied; nor am I the sublater because of being devoid of activity. || 34 ||
Thus, the non-attachment toward objects is called "universal non-attachment. (35)
Thus, that non-attachment to objects—the state of being free from worldly ties—is called general non-attachment (sāmānyāsaṅga). || 35 ||
Everything, whether pleasure or pain, is fashioned by past karma or is entirely dependent upon the Lord; what agency of mine can there be in this? (36)

He elaborates on this very point with three verses beginning with "prāk": "Whether it be pleasure or pain, everything in the doctrine of non-divinity (nirīśvara-vāda) is fashioned by prior karma; but in the doctrine of a divine lord (seśvara-vāda), it is dependent upon the Lord alone.
In both of these two positions, what agency do I possess? The meaning is: none at all. (36)
Enjoyments and non-enjoyments are great diseases; prosperities are but calamities; unions lead only to separations; and mental anxieties are but afflictions of the intellect. (37)

The expansion of enjoyments and sense-objects are great diseases because they cause torment at their conclusion; prosperity and riches are supreme calamities because they are causes of suffering through acquisition, preservation, and so forth; mental anxieties are the "diseases" of the intellect because they are causes of affliction to the cognitive faculty. (37)
The common notion that "Time stands ready to swallow, destroying all entities" is an attachment to what is not real. (38)
And the reflection that Time, intent on devouring and prepared for destruction, remains annihilating all entities—this is the "general conjunction" (sāmānyāsaṃgama). || 38 ||
By this sequential yoga, through the association with great-souled ones and the dissociation from the wicked, and by the practice of self-knowledge, [one attains the goal]. (39)
He speaks of the supreme non-attachment with the four-verse statement beginning with "by this":

by this aforementioned sequence of yoga, by the yoga of practice (*abhyāsa*), by association with great souls (*mahātman*), by dissociation—that is, avoidance—of the wicked (*asat*), and by the application of self-cognitions, that is, reflections on the Self. (39)
Through human effort and by means of continuous practice, when the reality has become firmly clear, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, [the goal is attained]. (40)

When, through the continuous practice of meditative concentration achieved by human effort, the object comes to be clearly manifest—like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand—[then the goal is attained]. || 40 ||

"I am not the Lord who acts, nor am I the agent; my action is surely from a former life"—having thus cultivated the contemplation on the meaning of these words, [one should remain far removed from attachment]. (41)

Having placed—and having utterly abandoned—the contemplation of the meaning of words and the mental association with the meaning of words, such as "I am not the doer," "God is the [agent]," or "only past karma is the doer," [he remains]. || 41 ||
That silent, peaceful state which is on the far shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, in the essence that is the supreme cause—that is called the highest non-attachment. (42)

That seat which is supreme, peaceful, silent, and established in the Supreme Brahman—the ultimate cause, the cause of all, the essence, the unassailable, beyond the ocean of saṃsāra, and transcending all conceptual proliferation—is called the "excellent non-attachment" (śreṣṭhāsaṅga). || 42 ||
That which is neither within nor without, neither below nor above, neither in the directions nor in the sky;
neither in an object nor in a non-object, neither in the insentient nor in the sentient. (43)
He specifies that very [state] with the two-verse sentence beginning with "yad" (that which).

That which has the nature of manifestation is not delimited by internal [states] and so forth, nor by specific locations consisting of existence and non-existence, nor by entities that are insentient or sentient. || 43 ||
The supported manifestation is peaceful non-manifestation, which is non-contemplation; beginningless, endless, unborn, and beautiful—that is called the supreme non-attachment. (44)
That which has no manifestation— that is, no manifesting agent distinct from itself—
and no becoming— that is, no cause distinct from itself— is such [a reality]: the illuminator of all, the cause of all, without beginning or end, unborn, peaceful, and beautiful.
That which relies upon the form of manifestation is called the supreme non-attachment. || 44 ||
Sweet with the fragrance of contentment, possessing pure sprouts of virtuous deeds, it is nestled at the tip of the stalk of the mind, though beset by the thorns of obstacles. (45)
He states the cause for this third stage with two verses beginning with "Contentment" (saṃtoṣa).

Sweet with the fragrance of contentment, it possesses the sense of sufficiency; it is "sweet" (madhura) through the joy (āmoda) produced by that contentment, as if filled with nectar. Its pure and virtuous deeds are its stainless sprouts and leaves. Its stalk is the mind itself, upon which it rests; it is crowded and obstructed by obstacles, which act as its thorns. || 45 ||
Established within upon the lotus of discrimination and blossomed by the sun of discernment, one bears fruit in this third stage, which is characterized by non-attachment. (46)

Having taken root within the heart and been blossomed by the sun of discernment (*viveka*), it bears fruit as this very third stage (*bhūmikā*), which is non-attachment—the lotus of discernment. || 46 ||
Through the conjunction of pure qualities and the accumulation of meritorious deeds,
the first stage arises by a chance occurrence, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow.

Now he states the cause for the first stage: "from association" (samavāyāt). Through association with pure, stainless, and virtuous people, and from the accumulation of meritorious deeds, the first stage arises by chance—through the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit—or by the turn of fate. || 47 ||
That stage is like a sprout of nectar that has just emerged from within; it must be protected and guarded with great effort through the sprinkling of the water of discernment. (48)

Regarding the "ground": this first ground, like a sprout of immortality, although it has only just arisen, must be nurtured and protected with effort through discernment—that is, by means of discernment acting as the sprinkling of water. 48.
One should daily and with effort bring that very portion which shines forth through inquiry to its full development, just as a farmer tends to a sprout. (49)
"By which": one should, through inquiry and with effort, daily bring that very portion by which this stage shines forth to its full manifestation, just as a farmer brings a sprout to growth. (49)
For this [first stage] is the sole ground for the production of those whose inner [nature] has been polished;
therefore, one should strive to reach the second stage, and from that, the third. (50)

"This" refers to the following: This stage, having been internally refined and brought to emergence through inquiry, becomes the sole ground for the birth of the other stages. Therefore, by means of that very stage, one may attain the second and third stages. || 50 ||

For this third stage here is indeed characterized by the absence of attachment to excellence; in it, the person becomes one who has utterly abandoned all mental constructions and conceptualizations. (51)

Regarding the word "supreme": this third stage, which is supreme and characterized by non-attachment, exists; a person abiding in this stage becomes one who has utterly abandoned all mental constructions and conceptualizations. || 51 ||
Rāma said:
For one who is deluded, born of an ignoble family, engaged in base conduct, and has not attained union with Yoga—how can there be a crossing over? || 52 ||
"Of the deluded" means of the ignorant one who is engaged in the performance of actions motivated by desire. || 52 ||
(822) O Blessed One, for one who has died after having ascended either the first, the second, the third, or even the higher [vehicle], what is the destiny? 53.
"Regarding 'one' [level]: what is the destiny of one who has ascended to a single stage—whether it be the second, the third, or another—and then dies immediately thereafter? (53)
Vasiṣṭha said:
For one who is deluded and has not ascended [to higher stages], saṃsāra extends as far as the first stage (bhūmi) has not been awakened through hundreds of other births. (54)
He provides the answer to the first question with three verses, beginning with "Of the deluded one" (mūḍhasya).

For the deluded person—one whose defects have ascended, meaning one whose defects such as passion and the like have increased—so long as even the first stage has not been attained despite hundreds of other births, for that long the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsṛti) alone remains extensive. || 54 ||
Alternatively, through association with the virtuous or by chance, detachment indeed arises from reflecting upon the nature of worldly existence. (55)

Alternatively, through a chance occurrence like "the crow and the palm fruit," by association with the virtuous, and through reflection upon worldly existence and the perception of its defects, there arises dispassion. || 55 ||
When dispassion has arisen in a person, the emergence of the spiritual stages (bhūmis) necessarily follows;
consequently, transmigratory existence perishes—this is the summary of the meaning of the scriptures. (56)
Through the arising of the [spiritual] stages, saṃsāra is destroyed; such is the summary of the meaning of the scripture. || 56 ||
For an embodied being whose life has departed while on a stage of yoga,
former misdeeds are exhausted in accordance with the specific portion of that stage.
He states the answer to the second question in five verses, beginning with "By yoga":

For an embodied soul whose life has departed—that is, one who is dead—by means of any one of the stages of yoga (bhūmikās), such as the first and so forth, former misdeeds are exhausted precisely according to the portion of the stage attained, that is, according to the excellence of the stage. || 57 ||
Then, accompanied by his beloved, he sports in the celestial chariots of the gods, in the cities of the world-protectors, and in the groves of Mount Meru.
Then, by the power of his well-performed deeds, he rejoices in the regions of heaven, such as the celestial chariots of the gods, accompanied by lovely women.
Then, when the accumulation of merit and the misdeeds committed in the past have been exhausted through the depletion of their results, yogins are born upon this earth. (59)

Then, when the store of merit previously accumulated has been exhausted through experience, and when the cause of exhaustion—the portion of the earth-element—has also been completely spent on this ground, and likewise when the store of evil deeds has been exhausted; || 59 ||
Having been born in the homes of the pure, the prosperous, the virtuous, and the wise— which are well-guarded— these people, being perfumed by yoga, devote themselves solely to yoga.

Yogis are born in the secret, well-protected homes of those who are pure, virtuous, prosperous, and righteous; and having been born, because they are permeated by yoga, they devote themselves solely to yoga.
In that regard, having seen the sequence of the stages of yoga previously practiced through cultivation, the wise leap high upward to the subsequent sequence of stages. (61)
And there, having seen the sequence of the stages of yoga previously practiced through cultivation, they descend into and practice the subsequent sequence of stages. || 61 ||
O Rāma, these three stages are known as the waking state (jāgrat),
because here the perception of duality continues quite clearly, as if one were truly awake.

Regarding the term "stage" (*bhūmikā*): these three previously mentioned stages are known as the waking state (*jāgrat*). Why? Because in this stage, the perception of duality persists quite clearly, just as in the waking state. (62)
In this [state], there arises for those engaged in yoga a state of pure nobility, seeing which even those of deluded intellect develop the desire for liberation. (63)
Regarding the phrase "it arises": here, for those engaged in yoga within these three stages, a state of nobility (āryatā) first arises;
seeing that nobility, even those of deluded intellect develop the desire for liberation (mumukṣutā). || 63 ||
He who performs what ought to be done, refrains from doing what ought not to be done,
and abides by established custom— he is remembered as an *ārya*.

He describes the characteristics of the noble one (*āryalakṣaṇa*) in two verses, beginning with "that which is to be done" (*kartavyam iti*). "Practicing what is natural" (*prakṛtācāraḥ*) means practicing that which is natural, necessary, and conducive to maintaining the body; "remaining as one is" (*yathāsthitam*) refers to one's state or established limit (*maryādā*), without transgressing it. (64–65)
He who adopts conventional practice according to custom, according to his mind, according to the scriptures, and according to what is established, is known as a noble one (ārya). || 65 ||
In the first [stage], it has sprouted;
then, in the second and third stages, it blossoms and bears the supreme fruit of nobility.
Regarding the phrase "in the first": the state of being noble (āryatva) sprouts in the first stage (bhūmi). Thereafter, having blossomed in the second, it bears fruit in the third. 66–67.
Having died while in a state of nobility, the yogi, having enjoyed for a long time the pleasures produced by his pure resolve, is born again as a possessor of yoga.

Through the practice of the three stages, when ignorance has come to an end and right knowledge has arisen in the mind, which resembles the rising of the full moon, [the state of liberation is attained].

The two verses beginning with "bhūmikā" form a single syntactical unit. Through the practice of the three previously mentioned stages (*bhūmikā*), when ignorance has come to an end and perfect knowledge has arisen, the mind becomes like the rising of the full moon. (68)
Having reached the fourth stage, yogins whose minds are disciplined perceive everything as equal—undivided and without beginning or end. (69)
Yogis whose minds are disciplined regarding reality that is without beginning or end, having reached the fourth stage, perceive the entire world as undifferentiated and equal. (69)
When non-duality has attained stability and duality has come to rest, those who have reached the fourth stage perceive the world as if it were a dream. (70)
"Advaita" means "attained" (itāḥ) or "reached" (prāptāḥ). 70.
The triad of stages is called the waking state, while the fourth is said to be dream;
the mind, however, dissolves away like a fragment of an autumn cloud. (71)

Regarding the term "stage" (bhūmikā): the fourth stage is called "dream. This is because in that stage the mind dissolves like a fragment of an autumn cloud; the meaning is that it dissolves just as a fragment of an autumn cloud does. || 71 ||
Having reached the fifth stage, he remains as one for whom only existence remains;
the conceptualization of the world does not arise here, because of the dissolution of the mind. (72)
Regarding "sattā" (existence): the yogi who has reached the fifth stage remains as nothing but existence, remaining in the form of pure being (*sanmātra*).
For this reason, because the mind is dissolved in this stage, the conceptual construction of the world does not arise. || 72 ||
Having reached the fifth stage, which is named the state of deep sleep,
he remains in that which is pure non-duality, wherein all particularities have been stilled.

Regarding the phrase "the fifth": having attained the fifth stage, which is named the state of deep sleep (suṣuptapada), one remains in non-duality alone, with all parts of particularity stilled. || 73 ||
With the appearance of duality dissolved, joyful within, and possessed of awakening, he who has reached the fifth stage remains as one whose state is like deep sleep. (74)

"He has dissolved" means: the yogi who has reached the fifth stage, for whom the appearance of duality has dissolved, being joyful and possessing inner awakening, remains as if in a state of dense deep sleep; he remains having become dense, as it were, like deep sleep itself. || 74 ||
Though remaining inward-turned, even while engaged in outward activity, he always appears as if asleep due to his state of perfect tranquility. (75)

"Internally": although here he is intent on external activity, because he abides with his orientation turned inward, he is constantly perceived as if asleep due to his state of perfect tranquility. || 75 ||
Practicing in this stage until he is free from all latent impressions,
he gradually descends to the sixth stage, which is designated as the Fourth (turyā).

"Practicing" means that while practicing in this fifth stage (*bhūmikā*), one gradually becomes free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and descends into the other, sixth stage called the Fourth (*turya*). || 76 ||
I am neither one who possesses a real form nor one devoid of such form; I am not "I," nor am I free from the sense of ego.
Having utterly ceased all mental construction, I abide beyond both duality and unity.

He describes the nature of one who has attained the sixth stage with three verses beginning with "yatra": "In which [stage]," meaning while abiding in that sixth stage, the yogi is not non-existent (*asat*), because he is not a mere non-entity; nor is he existent (*sat-rūpa*), because he is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*). He is not "I" (*na aham*) due to the absence of ego-conceit (*abhimāna*); yet he is not "non-ego" (*anahaṃkṛti*) either.

Because it is not the instigator of the body, senses, and so forth, but rather because it is solely devoid of mentation and free from conceptualization, it remains as that which cannot be designated, having emerged from both duality and unity—that is, transcending both difference and non-difference. || 77 ||
Free from knots, with doubts stilled, liberated while living, and devoid of mental constructs,
he remains like a painted lamp— appearing extinguished even though not yet extinguished. (78)

Furthermore, the Nirgrantha is so called because the knot of egoism (ahaṃkāra), which is of the nature of a knot, has been severed. With doubts stilled, free from mental projections (vibhāvana), and devoid of latent impressions (vāsana), the yogi who is liberated while living remains like a lamp in a painting—even while maintaining the body, he is "extinguished" (nirvāṇa) due to his lack of egoism and lack of latent impressions. || 78 ||
Empty within and empty without, like an empty jar in the sky;
full within and full without, like a full jar in the ocean. (79)

"Antaḥ" (within). Furthermore, from the perspective of phenomenal diversity (*prapañca*), he is empty within because of being free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*). He is empty without as well, due to the continuous realization that "all this is indeed Brahman. Thus, existing in the midst of the world, he becomes like an empty jar—a vessel devoid of contents. Moreover, from the perspective of Brahman, he is full within through constant internal contemplation, and likewise without.
He is full even externally through the contemplation of Brahman; thus, even while remaining in the ocean, he becomes like a full jar.
He has attained something, or perhaps he has attained nothing at all;
having remained on the sixth stage, he shall attain the seventh stage.

"Something": this yogi, having reached the sixth stage, has become possessed of "something" indeed, because he has attained the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*). Alternatively, he is not possessed of anything at all, because he is indefinable (*avyapadeśya*). Abiding thus on the sixth stage, this yogi shall attain the seventh stage. || 80 ||
The state of liberation while bodiless (*videhamuktatā*) is said to be the seventh stage of yoga;
it is beyond the reach of words, peaceful, and the ultimate limit among the stages of existence. (81)

The four verses beginning with "videha" constitute a single statement. The seventh stage of yoga is called "liberation while disembodied" (videhamukti); it is peaceful, inaccessible to words, and is the boundary and limit among the stages of worldly existence, because there is no other stage beyond it. For this reason, it is called "Śiva" by some and designated as "Brahman" by others.
By some she is called Viṣṇu, and by others she is remembered as Śūnya.

And although she is eternally indefinable because she is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), she is nevertheless designated by various disputants through words such as "Śivā" and so forth, by means of some imagined limiting adjunct according to their respective differing doctrines. || 82 || 83 || 84 ||
By some she is called Artha, by others she is remembered as Kāla; by others she is conceived of as the distinction between Prakṛti and Puruṣa. (83)
Although it is eternal and inexpressible, it is nevertheless expressed in some way by others through various different conceptualizations of the self that they have imagined. (84)
These seven stages have been described by me to you, O scion of Raghu;
through the practice of these, no suffering is experienced.

In this context, since the names and characteristics of the seven stages of yoga (*yogabhūmikā*) have already been explained previously, they are not mentioned here; rather, the signs of those who have entered those respective stages—which were not previously stated—are the subject of inquiry here and are thus elaborated upon.
Furthermore, whatever has not been mentioned here, such as their names and so forth, should be sought in the section on their origin within the narrative of Lavaṇa. || 85 ||
Vasiṣṭha said:
There exists one who is intoxicated by boundless pride, moving with gentle slowness, intent upon the form of a female elephant, and possessing great tusks like conch shells. (86)
"It exists. The female elephant is desire (*icchā*), and its rut is the accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā-vyūha*).

The two great tusks are merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*); Vasiṣṭha himself will clarify this after Rāma’s question, stating that it is by means of these very two great tusks that the female elephant is called "the one with the conch" (*śaṅkhinī*) because she possesses a conch-like [trunk]. (86–87)
If this [ignorance], which surely brings about infinite misfortunes, is not destroyed, then even when all these stages are complete, a person remains unconquered. (87)
As long as that female elephant, intoxicated with rut, has not been conquered by one of victorious power, what warrior indeed could prevail upon the battlefields? (88)

Regarding "the battlefields of prosperity": for Rāma, the very prosperities of saṃsāra are the battlefields; this is because it will be stated later that "those [prosperities] are his battlefields. (88–89)
Rāma said:
Who is that intoxicated female elephant, and what are those battlefields?
How is she to be slain, and where does she take her long delight? (89)
Vasiṣṭha said:
The female elephant named Rāmecchā, appearing in embodied form as "May this be mine," was intoxicated within the forest of the body, producing manifold delights. (90)
The two verses beginning with "Rāma" constitute a single statement. The term *kariṇī* means "desire," and that desire takes the form of thinking, "May this be mine.
This female elephant in the form of desire, being intoxicated within the forest of the body, is by nature prone to various kinds of frolics. (90)
With senses like fierce young elephants in rut, speaking with the sweet voice of a female elephant,
she is hidden within the thicket of the mind and endowed with the two tusks of karma.

She is one whose senses are like wild young elephants; she speaks with a voice as sweet as a young elephant’s (rasanā-kalabhāṣiṇī), for her tongue itself is a "rasanā," and she is habituated to speaking sweetly with it. She is hidden within the "gahana" (thicket) which is the mind itself—a place difficult to enter.
She is endowed with the two tusks of karma, possessing the two teeth characterized by merit and demerit. || 91 ||
This intoxication is a mass of latent impressions whose body spreads in every direction;
this "elephant of desire" destroys the wretched multitudes of living beings.
Regarding "intoxication" (mada): the very mass of latent impressions (vāsanāvyūha), whose body spreads everywhere, belonging to this one who acts according to her own will, is intoxication.
And she, this serpent of desire (icchānāgī), destroys only the miserable multitudes of individual souls (jīvasaṃcaya). || 92 ||
O Rāma, the various views of cyclic existence are its battlefields,
where a person repeatedly experiences victory and defeat. (93)
Regarding "saṃsāra": those very views of worldly existence, wherein a man or person repeatedly experiences victory and defeat, are his battlefields. || 93 ||

Latent impression (vāsanā), desire (īhā), mind (manas), consciousness (citta), volition (saṃkalpa), creative ideation (bhāvanā), longing (spṛhā)—this collection of names resides within the treasury of her disposition. (94)

Regarding the term *vāsanā*: "residing in the treasury of the disposition" (*āśaya-kośa-ga*). The "disposition" (*āśaya*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); that itself is the "treasury" (*kośa*), meaning a storehouse.

Residing therein—that is, having that as its object—is the collection of names such as "latent impression" (*vāsanā*), "endeavor" (*īhā*), "mind" (*manas*), "thought" (*citta*), "volition" (*saṃkalpa*), "meditation" (*bhāvanā*), "desire" (*spṛhā*), and so forth;
this is the multitude of synonyms for this [power] which effects desire. The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*)...
Alternatively, in the neuter gender reading, the group of words beginning with "vāsanā" should be construed as: "this collection of names of hers resides within the treasury of her heart. || 94 ||
One who desires to conquer this all-encompassing female serpent, which has spread forth with indifference by means of the excellent weapon named fortitude, should do so with his whole being. (95)

Regarding the word *dhairya*: with the excellent weapon named "fortitude" (*dhairya*), one should conquer in every way and by all means that female serpent (*nāgī*) who has issued forth through the disregard—that is, the contempt—for all other weapons; who is "consisting of all" (*sarvātmikā*) because she has attained identity with her objects due to being the object of everything; and who is of the nature of desire (*icchārūpā*). Just as one would subdue a female elephant (*kariṇī*) of the form of desire with the goad of fortitude.
The meaning is that one should bring [the mind] under control; and here, "steadfastness" (dhairya) refers to the stability of the mind within the Supreme Brahman. || 95 ||
As long as this [thought] expands within in the form of "let this be," so long does the fierce cholera of the great poison of miserable saṃsāra persist. (96)

"As long as... || This desire, which takes the form "Let this be," expands within [the mind] for exactly so long that this fierce cholera of the great poison of miserable *saṃsāra* expands. Miserable *saṃsāra* itself is the great cholera produced by poison. || 96 ||
(830) Saṃsāra is precisely this much: the mind that thinks "let this be.
The pacification of this [mind] is liberation; such is the summary of knowledge. || 97 ||

"It is only this much": that mental volition which thinks "let this be" is precisely what constitutes transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), because the entire cycle of existence has its root in the mind. Furthermore, the cessation of this very mind is liberation (*mokṣa*). This is the summary, the concise statement, of knowledge—that is, the instruction on knowledge. || 97 ||
The words of instruction rest upon one who inspires confidence, who is clear, free from desire, and pure in character—just as a drop of oil rests upon a mirror. (98)

"Clarifies" means: being clear and inherently pure, it is therefore clarifying—that is, the speech of instruction which is the cause for clarifying the minds of others. This word of another’s instruction settles and transfers like a drop of oil upon a mirror—the disciple who is free from desire and conceptualization, and thus possesses a stainless form. A drop of oil likewise...
The cause of clarity is transparency; the mirror, too, is desireless and possesses a pure form. (98)
Even a desire that has arisen only slightly, which brings about misfortune, must be severed with the weapon of non-perception, just as a row of poison-sprouts [is cut]. 99.

"Even slightly" means: this desire, which brings about misfortune, must be severed by the very weapon of non-perception (*asaṃvedana*)—that is, the absence of perception or external mental engagement—as soon as it has arisen, even to a slight degree, like a row of sprouts from a poisonous tree. (99)
The soul, though permeated by desire, does not abandon its state of wretchedness;
yet, through mere non-perception [of objects], the sprout of worldly existence born of desire does not arise. (100)

"Desire" (icchā): Being permeated by desire, the individual soul (jīva) does not abandon its wretchedness—the state of dejection caused by the failure to achieve desired objects. Furthermore, the sprout of worldly existence, which is desire itself, does not arise merely through non-perception [of the Self]. 100.
The weapon of non-perception is not the mere silent state of the mind;
that should be known as pratyāhāra (withdrawal), by which desire is warded off.

To the question, "What is this non-perception? he says: "Non-perception... The mere silent abiding of the mind is itself the weapon of non-perception; that very state is the limb of yoga known as pratyāhāra (withdrawal), and by it alone desire is warded off. || 1 ||
The supreme ones say that the cognition "may this be mine" is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); the non-mentalizing of the object is called the relinquishing of conceptual construction. (2)

Regarding this [verse]: They say that the very cognition "let this be mine" is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). The non-existence of an external object is itself called the abandonment of conceptual construction. (2)
Know that recollection is volition; they know non-recollection to be Śiva.
In that state, both what was previously experienced and what was not experienced are contemplated.

Know that recollection itself is volition; and know that non-recollection is the auspicious, peaceful Brahman. And therein, within recollection, an object—whether previously experienced or not—is contemplated and made into an objective domain. || 3 ||
Having forgotten memory— whether of what was experienced or what was not— like a piece of wood,
and having quickly forgotten everything, remain as a fool, O one of great intelligence.

"Regarding 'anubhūtām' (experienced): having forgotten and abandoned memory—whether of what was experienced or not experienced, whether of an experienced object or an unexperienced object—having forgotten everything like a piece of wood and ceased all mental synthesis, remain as one who is truly great-minded yet appears deluded; remain like a fool. (4)
With arms raised high, I cry out, yet no one hears me;
lack of volition is the supreme good—why is it not cultivated within?

"With uplifted arms" means: with my arms raised for the awakening of all, I, this seer of the supreme truth (*paramārtha*), cry out—I proclaim. Here, no one at all listens; "alas, such is the power of delusion! is the implied sense. To the question "What is that which is being proclaimed?", he says: "The absence of volitional construction (*asaṃkalpa*). The absence of volitional construction alone is the highest good.
Why, then, is this not contemplated within by all those who seek liberation? || 5 ||
It is said, O Rāma, that by remaining in silence alone that supreme state is attained,
wherein even the highest sovereignty is regarded as a mere blade of grass.

Regarding the word *kila*: that supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*), wherein even the highest sovereignty appears as trivial as a blade of grass when that state is being meditated upon—that very state is indeed attained by one who remains in silence. The implied meaning is: "Oh, how easy it is to attain the supreme state! || 6 ||
Just as the movement of the feet of a traveler who is intent solely upon his destination is free from volitional thought, so too is the movement in one's own actions [free from volition]. (7)

"Going" (gamyeti): Just as the movement or motion of the feet of a traveler—who is intent upon a single destination to be reached and focused on that goal—is free from volition because there is an absence of volition at every step; so too, the movement or worldly activity of the knower who is established in Brahman is free from volition regarding his own actions. 7–8.
What is the use of saying much here? This is stated in brief: conceptualization is the supreme bondage; its absence is liberation.
Seeing this entire world as peaceful, infinite, eternal, and immutable— the true nature of consciousness— remain at peace and dwell in happiness as you please.
"All this": beholding all this world as characterized by peace and so forth, as the reality of the nature of consciousness, and as consisting of ultimate consciousness, remain at ease in peace. 9.
They know yoga to be non-perception; it is the supreme, peaceful posture.
Established in yoga, perform your actions, and do not perform improper acts.
"Non-feeling" (avedana): They know that the peaceful, changeless, and supreme seat itself is the yoga of non-feeling, which is non-conceptual absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi).
Therefore, established in yoga, perform actions while remaining equanimous toward success and failure—that is, fixed in yoga.
Perform them without passion or desire; or else, through delighting in the Self, do not perform them at all due to the absence of anything to be done. 110.
They know yoga to be the absence of sensation, the unconditioned cessation of the mind;
having become entirely absorbed in that, O sir, remain as you are.
"Non-perception," they say: they know non-perception alone to be the uncontrived yoga, accomplished without effort, and the dissolution of the mind.
Therefore, having become entirely absorbed in that, remain as you are, in whatever form you are. 11.
Perceiving "I" and "mine," you are not liberated from suffering; by not perceiving them, you are liberated. Therefore, practice that which you desire.

"Thinking 'I', and perceiving 'you', 'I', and 'mine', you are not liberated from this suffering, from saṃsāra which consists of suffering. But by being thus without such perception, you will be liberated. This is a subtle instruction: "Practice that which is desired and approved between these two means of bondage and liberation. (12)
O Rāma, that single-pointed contemplation upon the auspicious, tranquil, unborn, and pure Śiva who exists within creation is known as the renunciation of action (karmatyāga). || 113 ||
Concluding the knowledge of the non-duality of the Self, which has been established through this great composition under the guise of a summary of the subject at hand, he says: "Śivam.
That which is indeed Śiva—the Brahman that pervades creation, complete, peaceful, changeless, unborn, and free from birth and other such conditions—is auspicious.
That which turns one away from the impure cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), consists of awakening, and consists of pure knowledge; that single meditation upon it alone—

that meditation on that very Brahman as one and non-dual, the perfect meditation that "all this is indeed Brahman"— is known as the renunciation of karma, because, like a withered leaf, it is the cause for the shattering of karmas.

The masculine gender is used in reference to the abandonment of actions that are being enjoined. Since "non-perception," "non-willing," and "silence" constitute *naiṣkarmya*—the very action under discussion—this constitutes its conclusion; thus, everything is consistent. 113.
Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Seven Stages of Yoga," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-sāra. || 15 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Seven Stages," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Yogavāsiṣṭha-vivaraṇa*, entitled "The Boat for Crossing Saṃsāra. 15.
(833) The Sixteenth Canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Ah! This eloquent speaker and poet forcibly creates the fame of Rāma, which is like a collyrium of the sentiment of wonder for the creation of the Creator. 1.
Those who, having accumulated their desired objects by wandering at will, revile Hari, Hara, and Ārya— the ocean of the nectar of compassion— [are truly pitiable].
They revile the ocean, even as it tosses them up with its wave-hands upon their arrival to bathe. || 2 ||

Even though it bathes daily, the ocean does not yet purify the moon alone; yet, O Hari-Hara-Arya-Guru, even when merely touched by the ocean of your compassion—which is as captivating as Viṣṇu—it washes away the impurity of ignorance from the twice-born. We consider that very ocean of the nectar of your speech alone to be the most excellent and worthy of praise.
Of the rivers upon the earth, whose flowing honey-dew trickles from the *nandana* and *pārijāta* trees that have blossomed forth with joy.
Vālmīki said:
When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; she, having offered salutations to the assembled sages, went to bathe.
At evening, for the performance of the twilight rites, the sun set and departed; and at the end of the night, the assembly departed with the rays of the sun.
For eighteen days, Rāmacandra held a most venerable assembly with the sage Vasiṣṭha;
then, having abandoned the delusion arising from worldly existence, he remained as immovable as the ocean when it is free from wind, filled with steadfast courage.
At that moment, a rain of flower-clusters produced by the Kalpa trees fell,
released by the hosts of contented gods, like a cloud-filled sky filled with pearls.
Having descended himself as Viṣṇu, assuming a human form under the name Rāma,
he was weary within this snare of saṃsāra and awakened by the knowledge of yoga. (8)
Then, having been honored and praised repeatedly by the awakened Rāma, who was accompanied by his father and brothers, the sage was saluted and addressed as follows: ||| 9 ||
O Blessed One, by your grace, this mind of mine has undoubtedly become free from fever, cool, peaceful, and unchanging.
"You are the remover of all suffering, the omniscient one, the teacher relied upon by all the gods, and the destroyer of the darkness of delusion, just like the sun. (11)
Then, at that time, the sage summoned and made manifest the gods who were stationed in the sky, having arrived to listen to Rāma.
The Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Ṛṣis, Vidyādharas, and Mahoragas,
bowing down to Rāma with contented minds, spoke to him.
We have heard this entire, most exalted knowledge;
we bow down to you both, who remove the affliction of delusion from the three worlds.
This entire dialogue between your preceptor Vasiṣṭha and you, the high-souled one, is knowledge of great exaltation.
Then, having been praised by the Siddhas in Ayodhyā, this [text] was brought down out of compassion for those included within the region of Kaśmīra. 16.
Then, having realized the truth of all matters,
free from distress, devoid of the sense of "mine," and without desire, Rāma remained as Janaka did.
Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf because it is immersed in water,
so too his stainless mind is not stained by the enjoyment of sovereignty.

But this scripture should be given with great effort only to those whose souls are devoted to dharma— those who are dispassionate, who associate with the virtuous, and who are intent upon righteous conduct. (19)
If you possess a virtuous intention for the benefit of all beings, then this gift of knowledge, which yields great fruit, should be given by every means. (20)
One should not reveal this secret scripture to the wicked who are possessed by evil spirits, to those who are negligent, or to those who are slanderers. (21)
He by whom the Blessed Lord who has the moon as his crest (Śiva) was not previously propitiated shall not obtain this wonder, even if it were Hari, Brahmā, or Ravi.
This supreme knowledge was proclaimed by Maheśvara, as well as by the Goddess and Viṣṇu, to the sages beginning with Nārada. || 23 ||
From that [work] known as the Mahārāmāyaṇa, which has "the means to liberation" as its other name,
this nectar has been extracted, like [nectar] from the ocean of milk.
Through general inquiry, evil action comes to an end;
through its thorough inquiry, who does not attain the supreme state? (25)
By studying this scripture even once, all the sins of men are destroyed and awakening quickly arises. (26)
Even one who is not awakened, if they contemplate this while permeated by devotion, their mind will achieve purity; of this there is no doubt.
Whether by the deluded or those seeking liberation, whether by the self-controlled or the uncontrolled, this ultimate reality should be contemplated; for the vision of Brahman is difficult to attain.
For those with even a slight proficiency in Sanskrit, there is no other treatise whatsoever that, like this scripture, removes such happiness as it does when heard. (29)
This bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it is most dear to yogins.
Having attained this form of consciousness held in one's own hand, it is obtained only through prior merits.
Vasiṣṭha is considered the supreme knower of the meaning of all scriptures;
it is proclaimed everywhere that this is the essence of the means to liberation. (31)
For an embodied being who has become weary due to separation from beloved objects and the like, what else in this world besides the scripture could provide relief from internal torment? (32)
Arising indeed from the ether of consciousness, he is the full one, the scripture, the treasure-trove of human bliss, possessed of beautiful feet;
he is the thick nectar, adorned with the essence of poetry, a flashing light that has dispelled the darkness. (33)

He has bathed in the waters of all sacred fords, bestowed the entire earth as a gift, performed a thousand sacrifices, and fully worshipped all the gods; he has even delivered his own ancestors from the cycle of existence— he by whom even that which is worthy of worship throughout the three worlds is surpassed in the contemplation of Brahman.
The mind may attain steadiness even for a single moment. || 34 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Fruit of Studying the Scripture," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha-sāra.
( p. 837) The seventeenth canto. Vālmīki said:
Having heard all this essence of knowledge spoken by the excellent sage in the Purāṇa, the foremost of the Raghu dynasty,
possessed of pure intellect and himself fully replete with the bliss of tranquility, inquired about something else.
He is established in perfect enlightenment. || 1 ||
He is indeed the supreme yogi, worshipped by the universe, the lord of gods, free from birth and death, whose very nature is pure consciousness;
he is the treasury of all virtues and the ultimate refuge.
The sovereign lord of the creation, preservation, and grace of the three worlds for Ramā.
(838) By the power of the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), the dense mass of pure consciousness, manifesting through its unfolding,
became for a moment an awakened ocean of the bliss of consciousness. || 3 ||
Free from the formal sequence of questions and answers and the like, his eyes were filled with tears of the nectar of bliss and his body was covered in horripilation. || 4 ||

Abiding as the nature of the great universal generality (mahāsāmānya) by virtue of its pervasive consciousness, his desires for the eightfold supernatural powers are eternally regarded as being like blades of grass. || 5 ||
Having attained perfection and being established in the auspicious state, he said nothing at all.
Bharadvāja said:
"Oh, how truly marvelous! Rāma has attained the great state.
O leader of sages, how can such an attainment be ours? (7)

Fools are pitiable, and those like me are somewhat more so; where are we sinners, and where is that state of being established in Rāma, which is sought after even by Brahmā and others and is so difficult to attain? (8)
"O Master, Lord of Sages, how may I find rest?
Tell me quickly how this ocean of existence, so difficult to cross, may be traversed. (9)
Vālmīki said:
The entire account of Śrī Rāma, beginning from the start and following the words of Vasiṣṭha, has been set forth;
reflect upon it yourself with your intellect, for even I must speak here only that which is to be known by you.
Through ignorance this phenomenal world exists, yet not even an atom of truth is found here;
the wise discern this, while the undiscerning engage in dispute.
There is nothing whatsoever separate from consciousness; why then be obstructed by conceptual proliferation? O friend, become clear through the practice of the secret teachings. (12)
The mental state whose object is conceptual proliferation is proclaimed as "sleeping while awake";
he, however, is truly awakened within whom the stainless lamp of consciousness resides.
O friend, this conceptual proliferation has emptiness as its root and emptiness as its summit;
because it is empty of essence, the wise man finds no reliance even in the middle.

Due to the defect of beginningless latent impressions, this manifold delusion of saṃsāra—which has the form of a city of the Gandharvas—is perceived as if it were real, though it is actually non-existent. (15)
Without cultivating in your mind the auspicious sprout of the nectar of consciousness, why do you remain deluded, dwelling instead upon the poisonous creepers of latent impressions? 16.
This world, while awake, falls below due to the grasping at supports for knowledge;
yet it dwells above all those whose consciousness is without support.
The great river of knowledge, whose form surges with the aesthetic essence (rasa) it carries, remains so until it is plunged into by the skillful in its true nature as the Self. 18.
O friend, there is no prior existence and no final existence; know that this entire world does not exist even in the interim—it is merely the occurrence of a dream.
All these diverse manifestations, originating from ignorance, are like bubbles;
having arisen for a moment, they dissolve into the single ocean of knowledge. 20.
"Having recognized this river of very cool water, let it be plunged into; let those who have wandered outside, tormented by the heat of delusion and seized by grief, now emerge. (21)
The one Self of the world remains as an ocean of ignorance;
this "I" wave, which is the eldest, arises from the wind of nescience (avidyā).

The waves of the mind’s faltering and its fragmentation, as well as passion and the other afflictions, are imagined there; from that, the whirlpool of the sense of "mine" arises and flows forth at will. (23)
As soon as the two over-graspers of passion and hatred are grasped, who can then prevent one's entry into the abyss of misfortune? (24)
Why do you, O intoxicated one, plunge into the waves of the salt ocean of dualistic grasping, when there exists the ocean of absolute nectar with its tranquil, immortal surges? 25.
Who remains? Who has departed? Whose is what, and by whom was what obtained? Why do you sink into illusion? This is the truth; remain vigilant. (26)
They declare that this entire world is the one reality, which is the Self;
therefore, O dear one, who else could there be beyond you that is the object of your sorrows? (27)
To the ignorant, this entire world is a transformation of Brahman;
the wise, however, always abide in the untransformed bliss.
An undiscriminating person grieves and rejoices without cause; but the knower of reality remains smiling, for him delusion is a mere mockery.
And this subtle reality is concealed by ignorance, just as people have doubt regarding dry land, water, and the self. (30)
When this world, composed of the atoms of the great elements such as earth and the rest, remains [in its natural state], then who here has departed that one should mourn for? (31)
O friend, there is no arising of the non-existent, nor is there the destruction of the existent;
these various forms are merely manifestations and concealments within the Supreme.

However, due to the intense efforts of many cities, it falls into the hands of enemies; therefore, take refuge in the Supreme Lord, the Teacher of the World, who possesses the fullness of all virtuous conduct. 33.
All his misfortunes have certainly not yet been fully digested;
however, the nooses of this very deity have swiftly come to a state of relaxation.
Worship with form for as long as the mind is not yet serene;
thereafter, one’s abiding in the supreme, formless reality becomes unartificial. (35)
Having surely conquered this enemy of unrestrained darkness by force, follow the meditation of Yama with a confident inner self. 36.
Composing yourself for a moment, behold the inner self within yourself;
let this night of your intellect clearly shine away at once.
That which is to be attained by men is obtained not merely through human effort and action alone, but solely through the grace of Maheśa. || 38 ||
Neither noble birth, nor character, nor policy, nor prowess—O friend, only ancient deeds alone are powerful. (39)
Why does he despair thus over a remedy that cannot be reasoned out?
Even the Lord does not erase the rosary-mark situated upon his forehead.
Where is the speaker, where is his eloquence, and where is this creeper of delusion?
Inconceivable destiny emerges, bewildered by pairs of opposites.
O Bhāradvāja, clearly abandon your delusion through discernment;
now you shall undoubtedly attain a knowledge that is extraordinary. (42)
In times of great calamity, a king of great being exerts himself for what is far-reaching;
for people of little being grieve even over a slight loss.
Awakening, which is dependent upon merit, is attained over many lifetimes;
it may be inferred from its effects in the case of the steadfast who are liberated while living. (44)
"O son, by that very same action through which such bondage was incurred when it was hostile, you shall attain liberation when it has become friendly. (45)
This agitation for virtuous deeds among the righteous, dispelling antiquity,
extinguished the forest fire of living beings, just as a torrent of rain extinguishes it.
O friend, having renounced all actions, become a lover of Brahman,
if you do not wish for the delusive wandering within the whirlpools of the wheel of saṃsāra. (47)
This world arises from conceptual construction only so long as there is grasping at external objects;
when confronted by the contrary waves of the ocean, water remains entirely still.
Why do you look upon this sorrow that causes blindness?
Let that very same unbreakable staff of wisdom lead you forward.
Those who are carried away by the waves of joy and sorrow like blades of grass are never counted among the most noble. (50)
O friend, this world, mounted upon the swing of the ten states, plays day and night with its sixfold spectacles; why then do you grieve? (51)
Time alone, full of curiosity, swiftly procreates and withdraws, and again creates and destroys the worlds through many cycles. 52.
There is no distinction whatsoever, neither this nor that, nor anything at all;
for one who enjoys his time, there is complete freedom regarding living beings and things to be consumed.
What need is there to speak of mortal bodies, which endure but for the blink of an eye?
Even the hosts of gods fall within the range of that terrible time.
Why do you dance yourself in joy when there is calamity for one whose senses are impaired?
Sitting exhausted for a moment, behold the drama of saṃsāra. 55.
O Bhāradvāja, the wise man does not despond even slightly at this world, which consists of many waves and is subject to momentary destruction. 56.
Abandon this inauspicious grief; contemplate auspicious things, and meditate upon the Self, which is pure and a mass of consciousness and bliss. (57)
For those whose minds are directed toward gods, twice-born brahmins, gurus, the wise, immortals, and holy men,
and who take the authentic scriptures as their authority, there shall be the grace of Maheśa. (58)

Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "The Instruction of Bharadvāja," in the *Mokṣopāya* (The Means to Liberation), within the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīyogavāsiṣṭhasāra*, composed by the venerable Vālmīki. 17.
The eighteenth canto. Bharadvāja said:
By your grace, all this has been understood by me in its entirety:
there is nothing higher than dispassion (vairāgya), and no enemy greater than the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra). (1)
Now I wish to hear the essence of knowledge, as presented by Vasiṣṭha, which was spoken by him in its entirety through this work.
Vālmīki said:
O Bharadvāja, listen to this great knowledge that bestows liberation;
by the mere hearing of which you shall not sink into the ocean of worldly existence.
Salutations to Him whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss— who, though being one, exists in manifold ways through the distinctions of dissolution, maintenance, and creation.
Once the dissolution of phenomenal expansion has been accomplished, I shall explain, in brief according to the teaching of the Śruti, the means by which reality shines forth.
Peaceful, self-controlled, and withdrawn from forbidden evil deeds,
he is endowed with faith and detached from the pleasure of the contact between the senses and their objects.
Seated on a soft seat, having mastered the activities of the mind and the senses,
one should utter "Om" until the mind becomes serene.
Then one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the purification of the internal organ;
afterwards, one should gradually withdraw the senses from their objects.

The emergence of the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the knower of the field occurs subsequently; because they arise from that [source], one should dissolve them back into it subsequently. (9)
Having first remained in the Virāj, and after that in the Self (Ātman),
he subsequently remains in the Undifferentiated (Avyākṛta), which is the established Supreme Cause.
One should dissolve the earthly portion, such as flesh and so forth, into the earth;
the watery portion, such as blood and so forth, into water; and the fiery portion into fire.
One should cast the element of air into the great wind and that of space into the sky;
then, having deposited the sense organs within their respective sources, beginning with earth.

Endowed with the characteristics of the ear and the other senses for the sake of establishing the agent and the enjoyer, one should assign the ear of the self to the quarters and cast the skin into the lightning. (13)
One should dissolve the eye into the orb of the sun, and the tongue into the waters;
one should dissolve the vital breath into the wind, speech into fire, and the living being into Indra.
Likewise, one should place one's feet in Viṣṇu, the anus in Mitra, the generative organ in Kaśyapa, and fix the mind in the Moon.
One should restrain the intellect within Brahman; these deities of the senses are indeed designated by the term "senses," though they are truly deities.
Having recollected the words of the Vedas, one should not manifest [the self] by one's own will;
thus, having deposited the self within the body, one should contemplate, "I am Virāṭ. (17)
That Lord who resides within the cosmic egg as Ardhanārīśvara is the support of all beings; He is declared to be the cause. || 18 ||
That [Brahmā], whose form is the creation of the sacrifice, is established in the waking state;
outside the double-sized egg is the earth, and the water is double the size of the earth.
Fire is twice the extent of water; wind is twice the extent of fire;
and space is twice the extent of wind—each increasing successively by double in order from below upward.
The great world is woven together both separately and as a whole;
having dissolved the earth into water, one should cast the water into fire. (21)
Having merged fire into air, one should cast air into space;
and space into the Great Space (mahadākāśa), which is the cause of the origin of all things.
Abiding there, the great yogi, bearing only a subtle body (liṅga-deha),
[abandons] the subtle elements consisting of latent impressions, as well as karma and ignorance.
The wise know this—the ten sense organs, the mind, and the intellect—to be the subtle body (liṅga).
Then, outside the cosmic egg, in the wind, one should contemplate: "I am the Sūtrātman."
The wise one, having placed the subtle elements established in the wind at the tip of the four-faced [Brahmā],
should then place the subtle *liṅga* in the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
Some call that in which the world abides, being entirely free from name and form, "Prakṛti"; others call it "Māyā," while still others call it "atoms" (aṇu).
Others, whose minds are deluded by sophistry, declare it to be ignorance;
having gone to dissolution therein, all remain in an unmanifest form. (27)
Devoid of awakening and devoid of relish, they arise from that once more;
they remain in their own essential nature as long as creation proceeds. (28)
Creation is traditionally taught as proceeding from the direct order (ānulomya), while dissolution proceeds from the reverse order (prātilomya).
Therefore, having abandoned the three states, one reaches the fourth, immutable state.
One should meditate on that [liṅga]; having attained it, one should dissolve the liṅga and enter the Supreme.
The elements, the senses, the mind, the intellect, the latent impressions, karma, and the vital breaths—|| 30 ||
And they would have entered into ignorance, since the subtle body (liṅga) exists in the unmanifest;
but now I am entirely liberated from the fetters of the subtle body. || 31 ||
Because I am a portion of consciousness, I have entered the ocean of consciousness-bliss;
being non-different [from it], I am the Supreme Self, devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi). || 32 ||
I am the one who is partless, all-pervading, and possessed of the powers of both consciousness and unconsciousness;
just as when a jar is absent, there is no difference between the space within a jar and the space within a pitcher. (33)
The Śruti scriptures declare with reverence that Brahman is indeed thus one;
just as fire cast into fire follows after it by attaining equality.
Having become identical with that which bears its name, it is not perceived as distinct;
just as grass and other things thrown into *rumā* salt-earth become salt. || 35 ||
The insentient world, when placed within consciousness, becomes sentient, just as a lump of salt from the Sindh region dissolves in the ocean. || 36 ||
Released from name-and-form, they enter into the state of the waters, just as water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee. (37)
These remain undestroyed and are not perceived as distinct;
likewise, I have entered into all things through my entire being when consciousness is present.
In the eternal bliss, the omniscient, the supreme and ultimate cause;
which is constant, all-pervading, peaceful, faultless, and stainless. (39)
I am that Brahman, the supreme state—partless, actionless, and pure;
I am the supreme, pure Brahman, absolute and of true resolve.
I am Brahman—the supreme cause of the universe, liberated from merit and demerit, non-dual, the highest light, and non-dual bliss. 41.
One who performs good deeds should always meditate upon the all-pervading Brahman, which is endowed with such qualities as these, yet is devoid of the qualities of *sattva* and the rest.
For a person practicing in this way, the mind indeed sets therein;
when the mind has set, his very Self shines forth of its own accord. (43)
In serenity, there shall be the destruction of all sufferings and happiness within the self;
by oneself, through the self, one realizes the self as bliss. (44)
Thus, my son, everything taught by Vasiṣṭha has been described to you; by this path of knowledge and the path of yoga.
O Bharadvāja of great wisdom, you will certainly come to know everything through the thorough investigation of the scriptures and by understanding the meaning of the teacher’s words. (46)
"Through practice, all perfection shall be attained; such is the instruction of the Vedas.
Therefore, casting aside everything else, make your mind steady in practice. (47)
Bharadvāja said:
O Sage, since Rāma has attained supreme yoga within his own self by means of the Self,
how was the highest worldly interaction carried out with the divine Vasiṣṭha?
Having understood this, I too shall strive for the sake of practice in such a way that my conduct during the state of emergence will likewise be exactly so. (49)
Vālmīki said:
When the noble-minded Viśvāmitra had attained perfection in his own true nature,
he then spoke to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
Viśvāmitra said:
O illustrious Vasiṣṭha, son of Brahmā, you are truly great;
your status as a guru was revealed at that very moment through the descent of power (śaktipāta).
He who, through sight, touch, sound, or compassion, bestows the supreme command upon the body of a disciple— he indeed is the true teacher.
This Rāma as well, pure in soul and truly detached from his own self, desiring only rest, attained the supreme state through this dialogue. (53)
The disciple’s own wisdom alone is the cause of awakening through the words of the Guru;
if the three impurities are unripened, how can one awaken as if they were ripened? (54)
This knowledge is indeed direct perception, serving the purpose of both teacher and disciple;
therefore, both are knowers of that [reality], even for all those such as myself. (55)
Now, O Rāma, out of compassion you ought to emerge from [this state], for you are occupied with your duties beyond and even further beyond, since you are worthy of worship. (56)
"O Lord, remember my purpose for which I have come;
King Daśaratha himself was entreated by me with great difficulty. (57)
O Sage, do not let all of this be in vain; perform the work of the gods and whatever other purpose exists for the incarnation of Rāma with a pure mind. (58)
Rāma, the slayer of Rākṣasas, has been brought by me to Siddhāśrama; he will then effect the liberation of Ahalyā and [the marriage] of Janaka’s daughter.
Having resolved to marry her by breaking the bow,
he will bring about his own certain end at the hands of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
Free from desire, he will renounce even this ancestral kingdom right here,
as if under the pretext of dwelling in the forest, like those who reside in the Daṇḍaka wilderness.
Under the pretext of the misfortune caused by the abduction of Sītā, he will indeed rescue from their suffering on earth those living beings who are in distress at the sacred fords.
Through the slaying of Rāvaṇa and others, he will demonstrate to all those attached to women that even their association with such beings serves only the purposes of others, such as the monkeys.
Seeking to demonstrate Sītā’s purity for the sake of conforming to the world,
he— though liberated while living and free from desire— remained devoted to the performance of ritual acts.
There will be [an opportunity] to inquire about the synthesis of knowledge and action;
for those by whom it has been seen, or even remembered, or heard, or awakened to, it shall bestow liberation while living upon all those who have reached every state of existence. (65)
(849) Thus, indeed, the task of the three worlds has been completely brought to an end by this high-souled person, Rāmacandra. || 66 ||
"Salutations to him by whom all this has already been conquered! May someone like you flourish for a long time;
O Vasiṣṭha, through your grace, please conduct the supreme worldly affairs."
Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus, the great sage Viśvāmitra remained silent;
but the highly effulgent Vasiṣṭha addressed Rāmacandra.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, O Great Being consisting of consciousness!
This is indeed not the time for rest; be the embodiment of bliss for the worlds. (69)
As long as the conceptual investigation of the world has not ceased for the yogin,
so long does the state of firmly established samādhi never become stainless.
Therefore, having reflected upon the objects of sense such as kingship as being perishable,
and having cast off the burdens of ritual duties for the gods and the like, O son, be happy.
Vālmīki said:
Although addressed in this way, when Rāma said nothing and entered into dissolution,
he likewise slowly entered the heart through the Suṣumṇā.

Having stilled his powers, vital breaths, mind, and senses, and consisting of the light of the individual soul, with all his faculties as if in deep sleep within the hollows of the channels, he slowly opened his eyes—
being one whose every desire was liberated and who was delighted by the eminent and foremost sages headed by Vasiṣṭha.
Devoid of deliberation regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, he remains waiting for everyone. || 73 ||
Rāma said:
By your grace, there shall be for me neither injunction nor prohibition;
nevertheless, that word of yours must always be carried out.
O great sage, in the Vedas, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and even in the Smṛtis,
it is declared that the word of the Guru is the injunction, and its opposite is the prohibition.
Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus, that soul of all beings, a treasury of compassion, placed his head upon the feet of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha and addressed them all.
Listen all, may it be well with you; this is my firm and well-ascertained conclusion:
there is nothing superior to self-knowledge, nor even to the teacher who knows that [self]. (77)
The Siddhas said:
O Rāma, exactly this has taken root in the minds of all;
and by your grace, everything has been further confirmed through this dialogue. (78)
"Be happy, O Great King Rāmacandra; salutations be unto you!
Having been permitted by Vasiṣṭha as well, we shall now depart as we came. (79)
Having spoken thus, they all departed, intent on praising Rāma;
indeed, a rain of flowers fell upon the head of Rāmacandra.
Vālmīki said:
All this narrative of Rāmacandra has been told to you;
by means of this sequential practice, O Bharadvāja, may you be happy.

Thus has this wonderful garland of jewels, consisting of a series of words from the excellent sage, been proclaimed by me to you as the *Raghupatisiddhi*. It is a form to be served by the entire assembly of poets and yogis; through the glance of the Supreme Guru, it bestows the path to liberation.
Whoever should constantly hear this account of the ritual between Rāma and Vasiṣṭha,
even while in any state whatsoever, enters the path of liberation through hearing it.
In this [work], there are six chapters known as Upaśama and Nirvāṇa, which constitute the origin, emergence, and persistence of the worldly conduct of those seeking dispassion and liberation. (84)

Thus ends the eighteenth canto, titled "The Dialogue between Śrī Vasiṣṭha and Rāmacandra," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the narrative concerning the lineage of Bharadvāja, composed by the illustrious Abhinanda, the ornament of the Gauḍa country and a master of poetry under Tarkavāgīśvara. 18.
This work is completed.
